Welcome to Unit 2!

Hey, how you doing? :) Welcome to Unit 2 of our Blues Immersion program! I hope you're enjoying the course so far. Please join the discussion and give us feedback as you go—we're always working to improve your learning experience. :) Now, let's look at what's on the menu for this month!

What You'll Learn This Month!

Minor Pentatonic Pattern 2 Framework

Additional notes and Bend Candidates

(Extension) Melodic sequences

Standard Vibrato and (Extension) Hand-Off and Flutter

Licks in the Pattern 2 Framework (and Medley)

Recognizing 12-Bar Blues Progression by ear

Closed shuffle in all Keys, two ways!

(Extension) 8-Bar Blues and how it's used

Three ways to use your Pet Licks

Transcribing Exercise

Learn About Chicago Blues

Learn about the key players of the 1950's

Learn Blues Standards: Johnny B Good and Worried Life Blues

Playlists: Immerse yourself in the rich Blues of the 1950's

Practice Time & Expectations

Let me clarify how this will work out regarding practice time and what I expect of you! The following is the same as last time.

You should dedicate the first days of your "practice" to watching the lessons and my explanations of what to do. That's likely to take some time, so if you have itchy fingers, feel free to watch a video or two and then play around with the ideas covered before getting into the full suggested routine. However, aim to get through the practical lessons within a week.

Load Up your Spotify/Apple Music Playlists!

You should listen to the suggested playlists as much as possible in the upcoming month. There's a lesson explaining my choices and some "listening notes" for you to read, but the listening element is the most important.

We'll start with the practical stuff—the things you need to do for the playing parts of this course. Then, we'll work on the listening and the historical elements. If you're pushed for time, focus on playing and listening and revisit the history and essay work later, though Blues Immersion will work best if you can make time for it all.

In addition to the daily practice suggestions, there are transcribing exercises. These exercises are usually done in two or three sittings and will likely take a few hours. Don't do it right away—spend some time getting to know the vocabulary first. It'll make it easier!

Ensure you understand why I ask you to do things a particular way—I don't want you to do what I say mindlessly— I want you to understand why I suggest doing things a certain way. If you don't understand why, ask; I must fix that.

👉 Now, grab your guitar! It's time to play. :)

modules.title: Ear Training - Introduction
modules.intro:
This Introduction module will explain why Ear Training is such an amazing and important skill that will help your guitar playing and musicianship in many ways. This new improved version links the shapes of intervals (distances between notes) between both the ear and the hand which I think is really powerful.

We'll also learn what I think is the singularly most beneficial exercise you can do to develop your ear (Play What You Hear). It's great fun and will help your transcribing, expressing musical ideas and ear training.

It's very difficult to train your ear if you don't sing and so I also give you a very basic introduction to singing, primarily aimed at people with little or no singing experience - how to get started! You'll find that following this course will help your pitching when you sing greatly which is great for you and those that listen to you! :)

lessons.title: The 7 Amazing Benefits of Ear Training
lessons.summary: In this lesson, we look at the benefits of ear training and why you might want to spend some of your valuable time developing your ability to listen better!
lessons.text:
Everyone seems to like a "Top 7" these days, so in this lesson, I'll go through the primary benefits of Ear Training and why I think you should dedicate 10 minutes a day to this awesome skill. if you understand why it will help you then you're much more likely to stick with the journey, there are going to be times it feels a little boring but it really is worth the effort!

1. Play What You Hear

The ability to play what you hear, that is to express melody and harmony that you can hear in your musical mind is (to me) the pinnacle of 'real' musical expression. You can let your fingers run all over the fretboard at a million miles an hour, but I much prefer music that is coming from 'someone's soul' and that I think in reality is when someone is expressing an idea that was formed in their musical mind. It's personal of course, some people express range by thrashing their guitar real hard and others play simple and let their voice release the emotion, but expression is where it's at and I think learning to express music is the kind of skill that should be the goal of the whole learning guitar journey!

2. Accelerated Transcription Skills

When you get stuck into Ear Training and learn about the relationship of intervals (distances between notes) and how to play those intervals on the instrument it becomes a lot easier to transcribe (figure out and write down) things you hear. It's how all the great players you like learned and how I learned too! There were very few TAB books and no internet so we all learned by listening to records (and later tapes and Cds) and figuring out by trial and error what was going on (and I strongly recommend that you check out my Transcribing Course too!). After some time doing Ear Training your ears will recognise the intervals and your fingers will just go there and you'll find you can play what you've heard on a track fairly easily - there are other challenges involved of course, but Ear Training accelerates how quickly you'll develop your transcribing skills!

3. Stronger Ears

With training, you'll be able to squat clean your bodyweight with your ears! One of the things I hear back from students that do this training is that they hear music differently, they hear the individual elements of a song and not just the whole, they can focus on each instrument better and be able to refine their hearing which helps with transcribing - and importantly - it makes the whole listening experience deeper! :) While the ear isn't really a muscle it develops and gets stronger as you train it. You'll hear musical textures in more detail and enjoy music better!

4. Understanding What You Hear

This links in with Music Theory which is something I recommend you work on too - but the combination is SUPER POWERFUL! You'll hear chord progressions and melody and recognise them and be able to manipulate them. I have learned songs on the way to a gig by listening to them and recognising the chord progression, I don't have Perfect Pitch (the ability to name notes by hearing them) but I have solid Relative Pitch so I can recognize the relationships between chords and notes but not know the key... however it's pretty easy to work out the key once I have the instrument in my hands and as you improve you'll find you notice other clues like open strings which might give away the key!

5. Confidence In Your Musicality

Many people without Ear Training or Music Theory don't feel as confident about their own musicality and that often shows in performance, so developing your ear will help your confidence which in turn will help your performance and musical 'swagger' which makes your playing more enjoyable (believable?) for the people listening to you!

6. Singing Improvement

There's no doubt that spending time doing the exercises in this course will help your ability to pitch in tune consistently because these exercises are given by singing teachers to help students improve their pitching! I'm not a great singer but I saw great improvements in my own pitching when I started working on the exercises in this course regularly. So you get singing and ear training development combined when you do this course - awesome

7. Fretboard Freedom

This is an incredibly big deal if you can get there - and the kind of interval ear training we do in this course will really help you break out of visual patterns we use on the guitar. I interviewed and hung out with the great Larry Carlton and asked him about how he plays so effortlessly all over the neck and he said that all that scale pattern and position stuff doesn't matter when you just playing sounds that you hear and are expressing them. He's an incredible musician so for sure he could work out what he was playing at any point if he cared to, but it really struck home with me and I now often play with eyes closed and just really focus in on the melody and sound and try to forget about scale patterns or any of that stuff and I find it helps me 'channel' my musical mind better!

I hope I've convinced you - assuming I have, move on to the next lesson!

lessons.title: Play What You Hear Exercise
lessons.summary: This is THE killer exercise to develop a better relationship between your hand and your musical mind! It's incredibly fun, effective and challenging!
lessons.text:
This exercise is something I did a lot of but never really thought about it being an 'exercise' - it was just something I did while noodling around. When I started thinking how I might help others develop the relationship between the musical mind and the hand I thought about doing this and so started doing it myself for 5 minutes a day and after just a few months I'd noticed a huge improvement, and reports back from students is that this really is the KING of ear training exercises!

And it's real simple! Just try to play a melody that you are familiar with! That's all there is to it really, although as you get better at it you might want to think about it a little more and get a bit more specific.

Getting Started

To introduce the idea I always recommend trying to play the Happy Birthday song - because its REALLY important that you know the melody that you will play really well, so there is no confusion in your musical mind as to how it goes. You should be able to sing it too - so give that a try first of all, and then try to play it.

How did you get on?

Fingering & Position

The first thing to note is that you should try to stay in the one position and not just run up and down one string which is how most people start off trying to get through this exercise. It's slightly harder but much more beneficial to stay in the same part of the fretboard where you can, obviously if the melody goes higher (or lower) than the notes allow in your position you'll have to move, but try to stay in the same place.

Some melodies will be easier to play in some positions than others and a great way to explore this is the finger you start with. Most commonly it will be easiest to start with Finger 1 and stay in that position, starting with Finger 4 can be more challenging but should be practised equally as much.

Embellishments

For this exercise, you should try to not to use embellishments on the melody - keep it straight! You'll probably find that using embellishments allows you to cheat your way through the melody if you make a mistake, which would be fine on a gig or improvisation - but as an exercise, you should try to keep the melody plain and simple and expose any mistakes you make so you can try to fix them!

Practice

I recommend that you do 5 minutes a day, 5 days a week and just play songs you know. Make a list of songs that are melodically simple and that you know really well and start playing them. If you make a mistake it's ok to work it out and try to remember how you made that interval jump for future attempts but avoid learning the whole melody.

Starting on different strings and with different fingers every time will help stop you memorising the whole melody - but you want to remember how to make the interval jumps - the rest of this Ear Training course will help with that too!

If you have time then aim for 5 minutes a day on this exercise plus 5 minutes a day working on a specific interval (singing and playing it!) that you cover in the course and maybe test yourself once every 10 days (2 weeks) and see if you're ready to step up to the next grade.

Not sure why 5 minutes (with a timer) is real important? See my Effective Practice module!

Easy Song Suggestions To Try

Remember that you have to know the melody in your musical mind really well - if you don't you'll need to figure it out properly, slowly, first! Of course, these are all personal - the best ones are any songs that you know really well in your musical mind.

Mary Had A Little Lamb Frère Jacques Twinkle Twinkle Little Star Jingle Bells

Medium Song Suggestions To Try

Only when confident with easy songs should you try harder ones like these, and be sure to know the melody properly before you try!

Superman Theme Song

You know when someone asks your favourite songs... I just can't think now - leave me some suggestions below and I'll come back to this later!

Harder Song Suggestions To Try

For harder stuff it becomes REALLY important that you know how it goes in your mind or you'll be searching for the melody with your fingers rather than expressing the idea!

Jazz Standard melodies like: Autumn Leaves Blue Bossa Alice In Wonderland

Eventually, you should aim to play any song melody in any position, but that's something I still work on myself and struggle with - but that's kinda the end game! :)

Easy melodic solos like: Sweet Child O Mine - Guns n Roses (first solo) Moonlight Shadow - Mike Oldfield (first solo) So What - Miles Davis (melody and solo - much harder!)

Avoid doing songs where there are very fast passages that you would have had to learn in advance.

lessons.title: Learning To Sing (For Ear Training)
lessons.summary: Scared to even start singing? This lesson tells you how to get going and some super basic exercises!
lessons.text:
I'm not a 'real' singer, though I've done plenty of gigs as frontman. I can sing 'mostly' in tune but I just didn't evolve with a great sounding voice, and that bit is something we're born with - though the longer I'm working on my own vocal, the longer I think part of the 'trick' is finding the right way to work with what you got... but I deviating here...

This lesson is for people very new to singing to make a start, I'm not pretending to be a vocal coach, but I know that singing will help your musicianship, ear training and guitar playing BIG TIME! If you don't sing, learning to is probably the best thing you can do to help your overall musicianship.

Learning to sing songs for your family or friends is super cool and a great party trick - much cooler than just being able to play and I really can't encourage you enough to have a go and try to work on it!

Tips For Starting Out

1. Find Somewhere Private To Explore your Voice

A lot of singing is confidence, so start somewhere where you can explore singing without your partner or kids sniggering at your attempts. I still have 'wounds' from people criticising my singing (and playing for that matter!) that undermine my confidence about doing certain things so I know first hand how hurtful people can be - even if they mean well.

2. Start Trying To Just Sing A Note

Just simply play a note and then try to sing it! Watch out for harmonies, you should make sure you are singing the same note. Try to be as 'in tune' as you can so there is no 'warble' between your note and the note you're playing. At first, you might want to explore the range of the instrument to find where is comfortable for you to sing and where isn't - you soon figure out where it's comfortable - so hang around there!

3. Starting Singing From One Note To Another

Once you're confident singing one note, you should try singing from one note to another - this is what we'll mostly be working on in this Ear Training Course and why you'll find the course helps not only your ears but your singing too!

I'll be sharing more singing exercises as we work through the course - so go on and get started! :)

lessons.title: Intervals On The Guitar Neck
lessons.text:
Using this chart below you should be able to play and therefore hear every interval on the guitar.

All on the same neck The diatonic intervals are shown in black and should be memorised first - you should be able to work out the others just from them. Notice too that it is laid out around the Major Scale Position 1. I would suggest that in the longterm you learn all the intervals in all 5 of the CAGED Major Scale shapes so you understand the 'quality' of every note you play - but start with this and at least you'll be able to play and hear all the chromatic intervals!

modules.title: Ear Training Grade 1
modules.intro:
In this first Ear Training module, we explore the Perfect 4th, 5th and 8ve - how to hear, sing and play them, and how to test yourself!

Don't be in a hurry - just take it slow and be sure to internalize the sound of each interval before moving on.

For maximum benefit really work in the finger patterns of the intervals too so you develop a link between the sounds and how your fingers make those sounds! :)

lessons.title: The Perfect 5th Interval
lessons.summary: In this lesson we learn to hear, sing and play The Perfect 5th Interval.
lessons.text:
The Perfect 5th Interval is for most people the easiest to recognise and is also commonly used so a great starting point.

Play It

To play a Perfect 5th, play a note on one of the thickest 3 strings, and then play a note on the next thinnest string, up 2 frets (toward the bridge). See the diagram below for an example.

There are a few ways to play it and anytime you cross onto or over String 2 (B string) you need to jump the top note up a fret, it's one of the quirks about the guitar tuning.

Song References

There are quite a few possible song references you can use for the Perfect 5th, we're looking for the first two notes of the melody to use the interval jump of a Perfect 5th.

I usually recommend Twinkle Twinkle Little Star or the Star Wars theme, but most important is that you find a song that you relate to and that you know very clearly in our musical mind.

Twinkle Twinkle Little Star Star Wars Theme Song One (Metallica) intro riff Baa Baa Black Sheep Can't Help Falling In Love With You (Elvis)

Practice

Dr Justin prescribes 5 minutes a day of singing a Perfect 5th (on top of your 5 mins of Play What you Hear). So 10 minutes a day of Ear Training if you can afford it!

1. Start with playing the interval on the guitar and singing along to get used to the sound and feel of the interval. Imagine your Song Reference while you are doing so, and sing the words if it helps. If you're still struggling with singing you can always hum!

2. Play and sing a root note, then stop playing and sing the interval jump and then check it on the guitar so you're sure you are getting it right and in tune.

I would recommend at least a week singing the one interval and using shapes all over the neck so that you get familiar with it everywhere - if there are parts of the neck you find a lot harder - work more on them. Play and sing this until you feel that you can sing it from anywhere and play the interval from any note! Then move onto the next interval!

lessons.title: The Perfect 4th Interval
lessons.summary: In this lesson we learn to hear, sing and play The Perfect 4th Interval.
lessons.text:
The Perfect 4th Interval is a good next interval to learn because it is similar in some ways to the Perfect 5th, but different enough that you shouldn't have too much trouble telling them apart. Be sure to pick strong song references and to spend enough time practising before moving on - don't hurry - the journey is the destination!

Play It

To play a Perfect 4th, play a note on one of the thickest 3 strings, and then play a note on the next thinnest string in the same fret. See the diagram below for an example.

XX

There are a few ways to play it and anytime you cross onto or over String 2 (B string) you need to jump the top note up a fret, it's one of the quirks about the guitar tuning. For the 4th it's only really when we go from String 3 to String 2.

XX

Song References

There are quite a few possible song references you can use for the Perfect 4th, we're looking for the first two notes of the melody to use the interval jump of a Perfect 4th.

It seems that Auld Lang Syne seems an internationally recognised song but there are some further options below - use what you feel you know best - that's really important!

Auld Lang Syne Here Comes The Bride (Wedding March) Amazing Grace Love Me Tender (Elvis Presley)

Practice

Dr Justin prescribes 5 minutes a day of singing a Perfect 4th (on top of your 5 mins of Play What you Hear). So 10 minutes a day of Ear Training if you can afford it!

1. Start with playing the interval on the guitar and singing along to get used to the sound and feel of the interval. Imagine your Song Reference while you are doing so, and sing the words if it helps. If you're still struggling with singing you can always hum!

2. Play and sing a root note, then stop playing and sing the interval jump and then check it on the guitar so you're sure you are getting it right and in tune.

I would recommend at least a week singing the one interval and using shapes all over the neck so that you get familiar with it everywhere - if there are parts of the neck you find a lot harder - work more on them. Play and sing this until you feel that you can sing it from anywhere and play the interval from any note! Then move onto the next interval!

lessons.title: The Perfect Octave Interval
lessons.summary: In this lesson, we learn to hear, sing and play The Perfect 8ve (Octave) Interval.
lessons.text:
The Perfect Octave (8ve) is not a particularly common interval is songs because it's quite a jump for a voice - but you should be able to do it and learning it has many benefits.

An octave is one complete lap of The Note Circle, and the easiest way to hear one is to play an open string and then the same string at the 12th fret.

Play It

To play a Perfect 8ve, play a note on one of the thickest 2 strings, and then play a note two strings down (thinner strings) and two frets up. See the diagram below for an example.

There are a few ways to play it and anytime you cross onto or over String 2 (B string) you need to jump the top note up a fret, it's one of the quirks about the guitar tuning. There are a few ways to approach playing Octaves and some are more practically useful than others and we'll be dealing with using them all in other lessons!

Song References

There are not loads of songs that start with a Perfect Octave jump, I always like Somewhere Over The Rainbow as the one that seems easiest to me, but I have included some other options below for you too!

Some-where Over The Rainbow Blue Bossa (Jazz Standard) Singing In The Rain (Musical) My Sharona (The Knack) The main riff!

Practice

Dr Justin prescribes 5 minutes a day of singing a Perfect 8ve (on top of your 5 mins of Play What you Hear). So 10 minutes a day of Ear Training if you can afford it!

1. Start with playing the interval on the guitar and singing along to get used to the sound and feel of the interval. Imagine your Song Reference while you are doing so, and sing the words if it helps. If you're still struggling with singing you can always hum!

2. Play and sing a root note, then stop playing and sing the interval jump and then check it on the guitar so you're sure you are getting it right and in tune.

I would recommend at least a week singing the one interval and using shapes all over the neck so that you get familiar with it everywhere - if there are parts of the neck you find a lot harder - work more on them. Play and sing this until you feel that you can sing it from anywhere and play the interval from any note! Then move onto the next interval!

lessons.title: How To Test Your Ears
lessons.text:
Once you know your intervals it's a great idea to start testing yourself regularly! There are a few ways to do.

1. Jam Buddy

This is the most fun! Find yourself a jam buddy and have them play an interval for you and you have to guess it - then swap. Do it as long as you can, 5 minutes is good but longer is fine if you're having fun!

Start by playing each interval 3 times and if going well you can try doing what I call a "Quick Fire" round where I play each one just twice.

As the listener, I aim to go for gut instinct the first listen, figure the song and then check it for the 2nd play, and the 3rd play is to confirm or try something else if I wasn't right! :) As you progress you want to just know the interval without having to think about the song reference, but you'll almost certainly need it to start with.

The Jam Buddy approach is great too because you can get a bit competitive and push each other to do well - and hopefully, have some fun jamming when you're done with the ear testing!

2. The JustinGuitar Interval Ear Trainer App

I have an awesome Ear Trainer App which follows the system that I use for this course, so for a couple of pounds you'll get a lot of use from it and we're working on some cool developments to help track your stats and stuff and we're always updating and improving our apps. Here's The JustinGuitar Interval Ear Trainer on the iTunes store.

3. The JustinGuitar Ear Training Exercise Tracks

I decided to make some ear Training Exercise mp3 tracks too - they have a load of different instruments playing the intervals (guitar, piano, violin etc.) and they also have quickfire rounds. The intervals are played 3 times and then I speak the answer, so no need to write anything down and you can answer in your head so perfect for trains, boring meetings or while at work! :) They're available on iTunes and Amazon. Ear Training Exercise Tracks on iTunes

4. Make Your Own Tracks

As a teenager I used to make my own recordings using my tape recorder, I guess you could do the same thing using your phone memo recorder, or your computer. Just play a bunch of intervals (and write down your answers) and then listen back a few days or a week later so you've hopefully forgotten the answers! They have a limited shelf life because you'll get to know the answers eventually - but it's a good place to start if the above don't work for you for whatever reason!

Next lesson I'm going to test you so make sure you're ready!! :)

modules.title: Ear Training Grade 2
modules.intro:
In this module we check out the Major 2nd and Major 3rd intervals, both are fairly easy to recognize and very useful ones to know, most common melodic steps are these two intervals!

We'll also check out a super useful Singing Interval Training exercise before doing your test!

lessons.title: The Major 2nd Interval
lessons.summary: The Major 2nd Interval is the same as a Tone, a two fret step on the fretboard. It's a VERY common melodic interval and one you should easily recognize!
lessons.text:
The Major 2nd is often called a Tone or Whole Step, two fret step on the guitar neck (2 semitones). It's easily recognizable as the first 2 notes of a Major Scale (Doh, Ray) and there are many songs you can use for reference too!

PLAY IT

The easiest way to play a Major 2nd is to just go up 2 frets (so there will be one 'empty' fret between the note you start on and the one you end on) and you can also 'step back' onto the next string.

XX

There are a few ways to play it and anytime you cross onto or over String 2 (B string) you need to jump the top note up a fret, it's one of the quirks about the guitar tuning.

XX

SONG REFERENCES

There are quite a few possible song references you can use for the Major 2nd, we're looking for the first two notes of the melody to use the interval jump of a Major 2nd (Tone).

I usually recommend Happy Birthday because that seems to be an internationally recognized melody, but most important is that you find a song that you relate to and that you know very clearly in our musical mind.

Happy Birthday Rudolph the Red-Nosed Reindeer Silent Night (Xmas song) Frere Jacques The Major Scale (first 2 notes) EastEnders (BBC Soap)

PRACTICE

Dr Justin prescribes 5 minutes a day of singing a Major 2nd (on top of your 5 mins of Play What you Hear). So 10 minutes a day of Ear Training if you can afford it!

1. Start with playing the interval on the guitar and singing along to get used to the sound and feel of the interval. Imagine your Song Reference while you are doing so, and sing the words if it helps. If you're still struggling with singing you can always hum!

2. Play and sing a root note, then stop playing and sing the interval jump and then check it on the guitar so you're sure you are getting it right and in tune.

I would recommend at least a week singing the one interval and using shapes all over the neck so that you get familiar with it everywhere - if there are parts of the neck you find a lot harder - work more on them. Play and sing this until you feel that you can sing it from anywhere and play the interval from any note! Then move onto the next interval!

lessons.title: The Major 3rd Interval
lessons.summary: The Major 3rd Interval defines the Major sound in all chords, scales and arpeggios - it's a very important interval to recognize.
lessons.text:
The Major 3rd interval defines the sound of Major in anything it is in, chords, scales and arpeggios. Because it is so definitive most people find it fairly easy to recognize.

PLAY IT

The easiest way to play a Major 3rd is to just go up 4 frets (so there will be three 'empty' fret between the note you start on and the one you end on) and you can also step back one fret back and onto the next string down.

XX

Cross onto or over String 2 (B string) you need to jump the top note up a fret, so in this case it will mean the Major 3rd from String 3 to String 2 will be in the same fret - the guitar is tuned in Perfect 4th intervals except String 3 to String 2 which is a Major 3rd.

XX

SONG REFERENCES

There are quite a few possible song references you can use for the Major 3d, we're looking for the first two notes of the melody to use the interval jump of a Major 3rd (Tone).

I usually recommend Oh When The Saints because that seems to be a well-recognized melody, but most important is that you find a song that you relate to and that you know very clearly in our musical mind.

Oh When The Saints Go Marching In Major Arpeggio (common in vocal exercises) Blister in the Sun (Violent Femmes) Blue Danube Ob-la-di Ob-la-da (The Beatles) While Shepherds Watched Their Flocks by Night Kumbaya

PRACTICE

Dr Justin prescribes 5 minutes a day of singing a Major 3rd (on top of your 5 mins of Play What you Hear). So 10 minutes a day of Ear Training if you can afford it!

1. Start with playing the interval on the guitar and singing along to get used to the sound and feel of the interval. Imagine your Song Reference while you are doing so, and sing the words if it helps. If you're still struggling with singing you can always hum!

2. Play and sing a root note, then stop playing and sing the interval jump and then check it on the guitar so you're sure you are getting it right and in tune.

I would recommend at least a week singing the one interval and using shapes all over the neck so that you get familiar with it everywhere - if there are parts of the neck you find a lot harder - work more on them. Play and sing this until you feel that you can sing it from anywhere and play the interval from any note! Then move onto the next interval!

lessons.title: Super Helpful Vocal Exercise
lessons.summary: I found this exercise a real big help when learning my intervals, particularly developing the relationship with my hands.
lessons.text:
So far, we have looked at all the Major Scale notes up to the 5th, and bigger jumps in the melody are uncommon, so it makes sense to work hard on this much.

The vocal (and hand!) exercise I recommend here is super effective at building your knowledge of the intervals in your ears and translating them into simple shapes on the instrument.

On The Guitar

With a Root 6, 5, 4, or 2, there are 3 patterns that I would call, Back, Middle, and Forward of the root. They're all important, though. I probably find the Back pattern is the least used in my playing - it shouldn't be, but it is!

From Root 3 is a little easier under the fingers (starting on finger 1 always feels better!), so I often find myself in this shape when trying to find a melody in a hurry!

Singing The Intervals In Order

Start by playing each of the intervals one after another and then back down so play R 2 R 3 R 4 R 5 R 4 R 3 R 2 R as shown on Root 5:

Once comfortable, then sing along with your playing. When you're confident with that, try singing and playing the root and then jumping the vocal up the interval and then checking on the guitar, again doing all the intervals in order. This will strengthen your ear to hear the different intervals.

Random Intervals

When you're confident with the above, you should start pushing it more by playing and singing a root, then deciding on a random interval and trying to sing it. When you're ready, check on the guitar.

Start in one part of the neck and run all the intervals from the one root note, but as you get more confident, you could try moving the root note every time and singing a different interval each time - a lot more challenging and will expose any weaknesses that you should work on.

🚨 Reminder: Don't forget to have fun! :)

Practice

If you're confident with all the intervals so far, I suggest working on this one for a week or two to replace specific intervals, but continue your Play What You Hear exercise for 5 mins a day!

lessons.title: The Major 6th Interval
lessons.summary: And now... the end is near. It's time to get the Major 6th interval into your musical mind!
lessons.text:
The Major 6th interval is a really sweet sounding interval that is not so common for melody but harmonically is very pleasing (it's an inversion of a 3rd, but that's for later!).

PLAY IT

The easiest way to play a Major 6th interval is to play the root on String 5 with Finger 2 and the 6th will be found 2 strings down and back 1 fret. See below.

XX

There are a few ways to play it and anytime you cross onto or over String 2 (B string) you need to jump the top note up a fret, it's one of the quirks about the guitar tuning. Note that you can also 'reach' for it but that is less common if you're playing what's in your musical mind because jumping out of position can make it harder to continue the idea (until you're an ear ninja!).

XX

SONG REFERENCES

There are quite a few possible song references you can use for the Major 6th, we're looking for the first two notes of the melody to use the interval jump of a Major 2nd (Tone).

I usually recommend My Way because it's very well known but Hush Little Baby is equally as good.

My Way (Frank Sinatra) Hush Little Baby (lullaby) Angels (Robbie Williams, the first 2 notes I Sit and wait) My Bonnie Lies over the Ocean (traditional) Take The A-Train (Duke Ellington)

PRACTICE

Dr Justin prescribes 5 minutes a day of singing a Major 6th (on top of your 5 mins of Play What you Hear). So 10 minutes a day of Ear Training if you can afford it!

1. Start with playing the interval on the guitar and singing along to get used to the sound and feel of the interval. Imagine your Song Reference while you are doing so, and sing the words if it helps. If you're still struggling with singing you can always hum!

2. Play and sing a root note, then stop playing and sing the interval jump and then check it on the guitar so you're sure you are getting it right and in tune.

I would recommend at least a week singing the one interval and using shapes all over the neck so that you get familiar with it everywhere - if there are parts of the neck you find a lot harder - work more on them. Play and sing this until you feel that you can sing it from anywhere and play the interval from any note! Then move onto the next interval!

lessons.title: The Major 7th Interval
lessons.summary: A big jump and hardly any songs, but you're a completist too right? Norwegian 80's stars to the rescue!
lessons.text:
The Major 7th interval is a real big jump, a semitone short of an octave! Played together the notes are pretty dissonant and so you need to be confident when you're singing this one - it WILL sound odd, so make sure you're checking you sing it right by playing it on your guitar too!

PLAY IT

The easiest way to play a Major 7th interval is to play the root on String 5 with Finger 1 and the 7th will be found 2 strings down and up 1 fret. See below.

XX

There are a few ways to play it and anytime you cross onto or over String 2 (B string) you need to jump the top note up a fret, it's one of the quirks about the guitar tuning. The shape of the Major 7 with the root on strings 4 or 3 is the same as the Octave root 5 or 6. Why is that? I hope you know - I told you in the first sentence. Not sure? Give it some thought. Here are the alternate ways to play it!

XX

SONG REFERENCES

There are hardly song references you can use for the Major 7th, but luckily the 80's Norwegian pop band came to the rescue when Morten sang Take On Me. I used Somewhere Over The Rainbow for my own study (first to third note) but if I did it again I'd get familiar with Take On Me and use that instead as it jumps right to it.

Take On Me (a-ha) Somewhere Over The Rainbow (first to third notes) Don't Know Why (Nora Jones)

PRACTICE

Dr Justin prescribes 5 minutes a day of singing a Major 7th (on top of your 5 mins of Play What you Hear). So 10 minutes a day of Ear Training if you can afford it!

1. Start with playing the interval on the guitar and singing along to get used to the sound and feel of the interval. Imagine your Song Reference while you are doing so, and sing the words if it helps. If you're still struggling with singing you can always hum!

2. Play and sing a root note, then stop playing and sing the interval jump and then check it on the guitar so you're sure you are getting it right and in tune.

I would recommend at least a week singing the one interval and using shapes all over the neck so that you get familiar with it everywhere - if there are parts of the neck you find a lot harder - work more on them. Play and sing this until you feel that you can sing it from anywhere and play the interval from any note! Then move onto the next interval!

lessons.title: The Mental Fretboard Development
lessons.summary: Building a fretboard in your mind can be super helpful for playing what you hear and this exercise will help you lots!
lessons.text:
This exercise will help you develop a mental fretboard - it's not super easy - but really worth spending some time on it. Be aware that this might take a few weeks work before you notice it getting better - it's no quick fix, but as you work on it I think (hope!) you'll find your Playing What You Hear exercises getting easier and more confident.

PRACTICE

Dr Justin prescribes 5 minutes a day of this, pause on your interval work (but continue on Play What You Hear) if you are pushed for time or add it in if you can.

1. Close your eyes and imagine a fretboard in your mind, with your fingers on it.

2. Put your fingers on the guitar neck to form a R5 Major Scale, one octave. Move your fingers around but don't actually play the notes (use your strumming hand arm to mute the strings) and try to sync your mind and your hand.

3. Then start working on intervals, decide on one, imagine the sound and then move your fingers to the corresponding position. Imagine it in your musical mind, then play it and check how you going!

4. As it develops you could try playing 3 or 4 notes and checking that - eventually you want to be hearing whole melodies there and playing them.

Playing what you hear in your musical mind is the biggest deal you can have as a musician, it's not easy, it does take work, but can you imagine how fun it is to play things you can hear in your musical mind and express them?

lessons.title: Why Your Chords Always Buzz (Fix This)
lessons.summary: If your fingers hurt or your chords buzz… you’re probably using too much pressure.
lessons.text:
Why Finger Placement Matters

Most players use far more pressure than they actually need. It makes playing harder, tires your hand out quickly, and slows everything down.

When your fingers sit close to the fret, you need much less pressure to get a clean note. When they’re further away, you have to press harder—and that’s where buzzing, tension, and finger pain start creeping in.

The goal is simple: get your fingers as close to the fret as possible without being on top of it.

Finding the Minimum Pressure

A great way to feel this for yourself is with a simple exercise.

Place a finger just behind a fret and play the note. Then gradually release pressure until it starts to buzz. From there, add just enough pressure back to make the note clean again.

That’s your minimum effective pressure—and it’s usually a lot less than you think.

Now try the same thing with your finger further back from the fret. You’ll notice straight away how much harder you have to press.

Applying It to Chords

This becomes even more important when playing chords. A common issue is placing fingers too far from the fret, which forces you to squeeze harder and still get buzzing notes.

By adjusting your finger placement—bringing each finger closer to the fret—you’ll get cleaner chords with less effort. Small changes here can make a big difference, especially for chords like A, C, D, and G.

A Simple Practice Routine

Pick a few chords and move between them slowly.

Each time you land on a chord, check your finger placement:

Are your fingers close to the frets?

Are any notes buzzing?

Can you reduce the pressure and still keep things clean?

Spend a few minutes focusing on this, and you’ll start building better habits quickly.

Scales and Single Notes

The same idea applies to scales. Play slowly and observe where each finger lands. If something sounds off, take a moment to adjust your position and try again. Over time, your fingers will naturally start finding the right spot without you needing to think about it.

Build It Into Your Playing

This takes a bit of awareness at first, but it pays off quickly.

Better placement means:

cleaner tone

less tension

faster playing

and more stamina

Once it becomes automatic, everything feels easier—and you can focus on making music instead of fighting the guitar.

lessons.title: Broad vs Focused Practice (Which Works Best?)
lessons.summary: I practiced wrong for 40 years, so you don't have to!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Introduction: What I wish I knew at 15

01:00 Guitarist A: The "Broad" Approach

02:34 My personal journey: 40 years of broad practice

03:37 Guitarist B: The Power of Focus

04:37 Visual Comparison: Slow vs. Rapid Progress

06:09 Why focus is better for hobbyists

07:31 Steve Vai’s Advice

08:33 Lessons from Scott Henderson & Wes Montgomery

09:05 Why my old advice was wrong

09:57 What I would teach my own kids today

10:31 Conclusion: Find your "one thing”
lessons.text:
Broad vs Focused Practice

In this lesson, we’re looking at two different ways of practicing guitar and how they affect your progress over time.

Most players naturally take a broad approach. We work on a bit of everything, different styles, techniques, songs, and ideas. The other option is to focus on one thing and put all of our time into developing that area.

What Happens When We Practice Broadly?

When we spread our time across lots of different things, Blues, Rock, fingerstyle, and theory, we build a wide range of skills.

That can make us more versatile over time.

But because our attention is divided:

Progress in each area is slower

It’s harder to notice improvement

Motivation can drop

⏳ We’re improving, but it’s gradual and less obvious.

What Happens When We Focus on One Thing?

When we focus on one style, technique, or goal, we repeat the same skills more often.

That leads to:

Faster progress

Clear, noticeable improvement

More motivation to keep going

🐢 Because we’re building depth, the results appear much more quickly.

Which Approach Is Better?

It depends on what we want. If we’re aiming to be a session player or teacher, there’s real value in going broad and building a wide skill set. But if we want to improve quickly, enjoy practice more, or develop our own style, focusing on one thing is often more effective.

Should We Practice Strengths or Weaknesses?

We often hear that we should practice what we can’t do.

That can be useful, but it’s not always the best approach.

Focusing on what feels natural can:

Help us progress faster

Make practice more enjoyable

Lead to a more unique playing style

💡 Many great players built their sound by developing their strengths.

How to Choose Your Focus

Pick one clear direction for your practice. That could be:

A style, Blues, fingerstyle, Rock

A technique, strumming, lead playing

A goal, learning songs, and improvising

▶️ Give it your full attention for a while and see how your progress changes.

Key Takeaway

If progress feels slow, it might be because we’re trying to do too much at once.

Focusing on one thing can help us improve faster, stay motivated, and enjoy playing more.

lessons.title: Major 7 to Major 6 Chord Change [plus Latin Groove]
lessons.summary: This quick lesson explores a really cool Major 7th to Major 6th chord change—a great finger exercise and cool Latin American groove.
lessons.text:
In this Bites lesson, we'll explore a really cool Major 7th to Major 6th chord change.

It works great as a finger exercise, but you can also apply it to create a Latin American groove.

Step-by-Step: A Major 7th to Major 6th Chord Change

We'll start with an A Major 7th chord:

Place your first finger on the fifth fret of the low E string (this note is A).

Put your second finger on the fifth fret of the B string.

Your third finger goes on the sixth fret of the D string.

And your little finger (pinky) lands on the sixth fret of the G string.

Some players find it helpful to visualize this shape as a C minor chord, but with the bass note moved. Remember to mute the A and high E strings for a clean sound.

Now for the Major 6th chord variation:

Move your second finger to the root note on the low E string.

Your first finger goes to the fourth fret on the D string.

The third and little fingers stay on the same strings and frets as before (fifth fret B string and sixth fret G string, respectively).

Although the pinky can stay down through the transition, some players prefer lifting it slightly for better tone or ease of movement. Try both and see what works best for you!

This chord change is an excellent finger independence exercise, as it requires almost a full fingering shift.

Add a Latin Groove

Let's now apply the chord change to a Latin rhythm:

"1 2 3 and 4 and 1 and 2 and 3 4..."

Keep that groove steady!

Right-Hand Technique

Here's a quick look at the plucking hand to get the rhythm just right:

"1 2 3 and 4 and 1 and 2 and 3 4..."

lessons.title: Profiling me?
lessons.summary: Maybe it’s fatherhood or the chaotic state of things around the world right now, but I’ve been reading (and thinking) a lot about the future lately.
lessons.text:
Maybe it’s fatherhood or the chaotic state of things around the world right now, but I’ve been reading (and thinking) a lot about the future lately.

We can try to hide from it if we wish, but technology is coming at us fast. The leaps in advancement are arriving very quickly in many areas. Big data collect info on us from every direction and gets to know us better than we know ourselves.

These are incredible and helpful in areas like medicine and car safety but scary in marketing and the manipulation of consent.

Yes, yes. You’re here because of the guitar. Don’t bring that stuff near my hobby; it’s what I use to escape all that! I hear you – but let me explain how these things make exciting food for thought in music land!

📒 And by the way - Prof. Yuval Noah Harari has brought up some fascinating ideas about music and arts. If you haven’t read that yet, make sure you don’t miss out on his book, Homo Deus - A Brief History of Tomorrow. That should be required reading for all humans.

Now let me explain my point.

Profile Me

I love my Kemper Profiler – it’s such a fantastic tool and makes my job a lot easier in so many ways. I find that technology quite astounding. It has been developing for some time (remember the old kidney bean Pod?), but Kemper made it real.

My Kemper can listen to any one of my amps with specific settings and then replicate it. But to the point where I really can’t tell if it’s the real one or the profiler. That means that all that tone hounding came down to zeros and ones in the end. I can now download and use, in a matter of seconds, that unique blackface tone that I’d spend years searching for!

Michael Britt profiles the amps I love. I buy them, pop them in the Kemper, and then I’m set up in a matter of minutes. It’s effortless, easy, and fast. The majority of players I know love The Kemper Profiler - and I won’t lie: I love it too. But it got me thinking about what else might be in the future for musicians. I started thinking about individual players and styles.

What else can be profiled?

Then, I realized that I do a lot of profiling myself. Manually!

I’m a Profiler Too!

I’ve listened to hundreds of hours of Freddie King, studied the notes he likes to use, the way he bends, the inflections and curls that he adds, and to which notes! I know how he phases way back on the beat…

In some ways, I have a profile of him in my mind. I can even do a poor man’s imitation of his style!

Not just him. I’ve really studied and learned from most of the guitar players I really like. I’ve analyzed licks, concepts, tones, harmonic ideas.

Now, I’m wondering how long it will be before a computer can analyze all that.

Computers can analyze big data relatively quickly. Once the technology is in place, they’ll be able to pull a music composition into its individual elements. Working out the profile of an artist will unlikely be very difficult.

It would also make quite a fascinating Blues family tree of vocabulary!

In many ways, I hope that comes in my lifetime. I’m curious.

Nowadays, computers get to know what music we like and what affects us on an emotional level. If we end up with any kind of brain implant computer link, then a computer would take all that info and make something that we find emotionally stimulating. Or could it?

When we create music, be it composition or improvising – we are mostly regurgitating and exploring things we have learned, practiced, or studied at some point. So, being aware of the ingredients that make up our own style can be quite an interesting one.

More than a few times I’ve ask students to make a lick book of the licks they play the most. We’ve analyzed and explored each one, found where they come from, and worked out many ways to use and get creative with them. You should try it too - just write down all the licks you know on tab paper and do some detective work.

That feels pretty much like some AI programs might do in the future when they make a profile of Stevie Ray Vaughan and then try to do solos in his style. Or mix that profile with Stevie Vai’s for an exciting musical adventure! :)

Will any of this ever happen? Who knows – but giving it some thought can take your mind to all kinds of places!

In the current age of short attention spans and endless scrolling, taking the time to think about anything is valuable, and what better place to direct your attention than on the future of music.

Safe travels.

lessons.title: Beauty In Dissonance
lessons.summary: Adding in dissonance is a very cool trick for making your chords sounds sweet!
lessons.text:
There’s a secret ingredient that all the coolest chords have.

My ears had figured that out a long time ago, but it was only relatively recently that it mentally clicked with me. That secret ingredient is called dissonance, and it’s something that beautiful sounds often (but not always!) rely on.

Dissonance, for those not familiar with the term, means “a tension or clash resulting from the combination of two disharmonious or unsuitable elements.” Musically, that would mean adding some notes that don’t harmonize nicely.

We’ll play some dissonant note pairs shortly, and you’ll hear it for yourself! :) Rather than just tell you all about it, we’ll check out some examples and how you can explore it on your own too.

Ready? Let’s get started!

Dissonant Chords on Guitar

Notes that are a semitone or tone away from each other (or the octave) are usually notes that create the kind of dissonance that becomes pleasing in chords.

Let’s start by exploring the sound of a semitone (Minor 2nd), so you can hear the clash! A great easy starter is to play the Note C on Fret 1 of String 2 (with Finger 1) and the note B on Fret 4 of String 3 with Finger 4).

Play them together. Most people would agree that it sounds pretty ‘wrong’ or “out” and can’t imagine it would sound nice in a chord.

Now, we’ll try adding a semitone interval (the most dissonant interval) into a minor chord. But we can’t just start adding random notes to our chords – they should come from a scale related to the chord.

💡 You can add in random notes if you are a real explorer, and you might find some gems. Still, it’s a much more haphazard approach and unlikely to bring usable and cool-sounding chords as quickly!

There is only one semitone option near a chord tone in the Dorian Mode, arguably the most useful minor scale. You’ll find it between the 2 and b3 scale degrees - the notes B and C in an A Dorian Mode: A B C D E F# G. The other semitone is between the 6th and 7th degrees. That one is also fun to explore, but it’s harder to make it sound cool.

By some strange coincidence, the notes B and C that we explored earlier are the same ones we now want to get into an A Minor Chord. So how should we do it? There are a bunch of fun options here to explore! Try those:

First, we could try just adding that note to a regular Amin chord. Technically, that could have a few names! I’d likely call it Amin Add2, but more commonly, I see it called Amin9 (which the name implies the inclusion of the b7, which this chord doesn’t have!).

Then, you can also swap places of the C and B notes and play the B on the open string, which sounds fantastic.

Explore It!

If you’re a more advanced guitar player, you should now go through and play all the Amin shapes you know! Explore where you can add a B note – don’t be worried about calling it a 2 or a 9. It’s the same in this context.

The Amin Chord is fun to explore because of the open B string, which you can easily pop into many chords. But don’t forget to explore closed chords (no open strings!) as well.

Another grip to explore is adding the G note, making it a proper “Minor 9” chord. For that, you’ll want the notes A, C, E, G, and B like this super lush chord grip that, while being a tricky one to jump to, sounds amazing! Here it is:

If you’re lucky and have long and flexible fingers, I have one more grip for you! :) This one has the semitone clash between the minor 3rd and the 9th, but also a tone clash between the b7 and the root. Ouch. But sounds great!

This one has a whole lot of dissonance going on, but I love it, and I just opened another can of worms for you… the dissonance of tones… more on that in another article. :)

Hope you enjoy this adventure in dissonance land. If you want to dig more, check out these 12 Painfully Beautiful Guitar Chords. Happy trails!

lessons.title: Manipulation vs Memorization
lessons.summary: A little theory goes a long way, and it's the difference between manipulating and memorizing guitar chords.
lessons.text:
As guitarists, we have loads of things to memorize: chords, scales, arpeggios, songs, licks, solos, rather a lot!

Many players end up hitting a limit where things get forgotten, or worse, they get muddled. :( But in this article, we’ll explore a tool that can be a game-changer in your guitar journey. That tool is called manipulation, and it cuts down all the memorization you need to do.

I know how exciting that is, so let’s get stuck in!

Manipulating Guitar Chords

We can use manipulation in many areas of music (and life!). But today, we’ll be focusing on guitar chords. With some understanding of note function and chord construction, we’ll learn how to turn one chord into many and understand the relationships between chords.

Let’s start with a look at the chord construction formula of common Triads and Quadads - my term for four-note chords. These formulas describe the notes derived from a Major Scale – the flat notes are literally a note from the Major Scale flattened. Hence, a b7 is the 7th note of a Major Scale lowered by one semitone.

Triads

Major: R 3 5

Minor: R b3 5

Quadads

Major 7: R 3 5 7

Dominant 7: R 3 5 b7

Minor 7: R b3 5 b7

Min7b5: R b3 b5 b7

Applying the Formulas

Now let’s apply these to a typical chord shape - the common “A Shape” Barre Chord. As you might know, the root note is on the 5th string. Note that I’ve removed the thinnest string note because it’s commonly not played, making this exercise easier. Take a look at the diagram below:

Now, start by examining the notes’ function in that familiar shape; you’ll see they are just Roots (R), 3rds, and 5ths.

💡 The only difference between Major chords and Minor chords is a flat 3rd.

So, without looking at the diagram below, can you figure out how to manipulate a Major Chord and turn it into a Minor Chord?

It’s pretty easy conceptually, and it works with any Major chord if you know the functions of the notes.

If we look back at the Major chord shape and the Major 7 chord formula, we’ll see that to get a Major 7, we need to add a 7th degree of the scale, which is the same as moving a root note down a semitone.

We probably wouldn’t want to do it to the lowest root note, but the higher octave and you got yourself a Major 7th Chord! Take a look at the Dominant 7 formula now. You’ll notice it’s the same as Major 7 but with a b7. So move that 7 down one fret, and you have yourself a 7th Chord! Usually, these chords are just written as 7. ;)

The only difference between a Dominant 7 and a Minor 7 is the flat 3, so go ahead and move the 3rd down one semitone and you got yourself a Minor 7!

The way we have manipulated one basic shape into many is very useful. This last example is good to know, too. When you see chord alterations of any kind, you can use the same trick! In this case, Minor7b5, take that Minor 7 shape and lower the 5th by a semitone, and you got it:

This alteration trick works all the time, and it’s a great one to use if you don’t know your Major7#5.

When you don’t know a chord, you can work it out!

A Little Goes A Long Way!

Understanding the function of notes and a little theory means you can cut down on memorization! That works for scales and arpeggios in more or less the same way. Music Theory can simplify how you learn scales and modes. It’ll also help you understand the relationships between many scales - and that’s fantastic food for thought. More advanced players should use this trick on all 5 CAGED Chords, Scale Shapes, and more chord types! Now, get Machiavellian on your chords.

And if you want to learn more about the theory behind that all, the first grades of my Music Theory course for guitar players are free.

lessons.title: Making The Blues Changes
lessons.summary: It's time to learn how to make the most out of your Blues changes. And understand the theory behind it!
lessons.text:
There comes a time in most guitarists’ journey that they decide to take the plunge and play the changes.

That means they’ll improvise over individual chords rather than a key. And that’s what we’ll be learning in today’s food for thought! We’ll explore common things new beginner guitar players miss when learning the Blues and go further into the theory behind making the changes.

For this exercise, we’ll stay in the Key of A. We’ll assume we’re improvising over the Standard 12 Bar Blues chord changes - A A A A D D A A E D A E. If you have no idea what I’m talking about, this Introduction to Blues Guitar course should help you get started. Now let’s get stuck in!

First Steps to Improvising

Most players learn to improvise using the A Minor Pentatonic Scale. Most times, beginner guitar players will mess around with the scale notes up and down. They will, perhaps, add some random bends of vibrato - but not getting too far.

Once guitarists get to grips with the concept that a scale is just an alphabet, and people need words to communicate, things usually take a bit of a leap. It’s a milestone and will enable real communication and a deeper appreciation of the language.

I strongly recommend learning Blues solos by ear. Transcribing allows you to get all the subtle but super important elements that a Blues solo has. There are so many things you should absorb: dynamics, phrasing, bend inflections, bend speeds, and time feel are the things that will further expression. Learning licks (words) and using them to make up your solos (stories) is very satisfying, and as far as some people want to take it.

But there is another big step that some people seem to forget. It requires a little more thought and theory. It’s nothing too scary, and the benefits are great!

The Note Function Trick

Being aware of the notes you are playing is the important first step. If you have learned any Chuck Berry licks, you are sure to have noticed that he uses the note C# (string 3, fret 6) a lot. But, if you transcribe and write out solos, you’ll find that he only uses that note over the A and never the D chord. Let’s take a look at why that might be!

The A Minor Pentatonic Scale notes are A, C, D, E, and G. You almost always use A7, A9, or A13 rather than a regular open A chord in a Blues. So, in an A7 chord, the notes are A, C#, E, and G.

Note that all the notes in the A7 chord are already in the Minor Pentatonic, except C#. When you play C# over the A chord in a Blues, you tell the listener that you know you’re playing over the A.

🎸 Play an A7 Barre Chord (E shape, 5th fret) and note that the C# note falls under your 2nd finger. Use it for visualization over the Minor Pentatonic Pattern 1.

But why not over the D? Well, the notes in a D7 chord are D, F#, A, and C. The C# that sounded great over the A will clash badly with the C note in the D7 chord. It also introduces another non-pentatonic note (F#), and it sounds awesome if you can nail that note only on the D7 chord! Play a D7 Chord and see where this new note is. :)

💡 It’s worth noting that both the C# and the F# work on the E7, and while it's possible to and common to make the changes on the E chord, most times it's (surprisingly) ignored or just hinted at in Blues.

When I first discovered this little trick, I started revising all the solos I’d learned. I realized that almost all the great Blues players use chord tones to highlight the chords they play over. ;)

Get the Sound!

The modern Blues players like Larry Carlton and Robben Ford use this stuff all the time, but so do the likes of B.B. King, Eric Clapton, Stevie Ray Vaughan. Even some of the early Blues artists that I suspect had no theory knowledge often nail the changes – because it sounds right! Early players like T-Bone Walker, who had some Jazz influence, play off the changes all the time. Their musical influence traveled far and wide to people without an interest in the ‘how it works’ stuff.

Conceptually, ‘playing the changes’ is a Jazz thing due to the amount of harmonic movement. I certainly found learning to make changes in Jazz helped me negotiate Blues songs which are comparatively simple harmonically. That is something I would recommend if you’re that way inclined! :)

So, then… Why Theory?

The fair question is that if great players do this stuff without learning the theory or understanding it, why should you still learn it? And the answer is time and progress! Understanding these basic theory concepts accelerates how quickly you can absorb musical ideas.

The scale pattern below shows the C# (in blue) and F# (in green), most commonly played in Pattern 1 of the Minor Pentatonic. Take a look:

We can find the same notes in other places and other patterns, but these two are obvious, commonly used, and a great starting point. Remember, the red note is the root note. It’s on fret 5 for the key of A!

Now you know about this C# on the A Chord and F# on the D Chord thing, so transcribe some solos and see if it applies. You might need to change the key, so look at where these notes are in relation to the root note so you can easily recognize them.

Here are some classics that you are bound to find interesting:

Clapton’s first solo in Crossroads;

Chuck Berry’s Johnny B Goode - intro and solos;

Peter Green’s Need Your Love So Bad, which ain’t a 12 Bar, but he makes the changes so sweet!

Now have some guitar fun. :)

If you’d like to go further, check out my Harmonic Analysis lessons. But don’t forget: the best way to get started is by playing, listening, and understanding the founding elements. Happy trails!

lessons.title: Making Music History Maps
lessons.summary: Understanding the Blues History can help you become a better guitar player!
lessons.text:
I've been listening to the Blues since I first got a guitar. As you can see in the picture below, I was still a kid.

* please note that I made sure I plugged the cable to make it look authentic! lmao.

I’ve also spent hundreds of hours trying to absorb the licks and songs of Freddie King, BB King, Stevie Ray Vaughan, T-Bone, Robben Ford, and so many others.

When I needed to lift my blues game I stumbled onto the idea of making Blues History Maps. It's helped me in so many ways; increased my Blues vocabulary, understanding the depth of history and how the language developed over time.

Today’s article is all about that - and why I highly recommend that you make your own Blues History Maps as well. If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, that would be an excellent exercise to add to your Introduction to Blues Guitar lessons. :)

But before we get any deeper, let me explain how it all started.

I was touring with The Counterfeit Stones and wanted to deepen my knowledge and understanding of the Blues. My bandmates were older and really knew their stuff, they were helpful in turning me onto a lot of great music, and a lot of life stuff too!

In my local book store, I found a book called The Devil's Music: A History of The Blues by Giles Oakley. As I read the book, I’d pick an artist or two and search for some albums in whatever town I was in. Then, I’d listen to them as much as possible while reading the related chapters.

📚 Today, with Spotify or YouTube, finding the music instantly is much easier, but using a book to offer guidance on what to listen to really helps!

There are many other books about Blues’ history. While I really like Oakley's book, Deep Blues by Robert Palmer is also excellent! If you want to go even deeper, The History Of The Blues: The Roots, The Music, The People by Francis Davis is fantastic.

Why You Should Make Your Own Blues History Map

The fast answer would be to understand what you’re playing. By making your Blues History Map, your understanding of music will grow in many ways you didn’t even know it was possible!

💭 It was like that for me. I don’t think that my understanding of music would ever get to where it is if I hadn’t traced its language development.

For example, have you heard about the influence of travelling musicians? A whole music scene could change after the arrival of a new musician in a specific town! That directly influenced the development of licks, phrases, chord progressions, and even chord grips!

Once you have that kind of framework, things fall into place a lot better, and you'll find it easier to lock in new things you learn. Your whole music experience will change when you understand a bit of the history behind it!

Here’s Robert Johnson - one of the Blues pioneers that changed music forever!

💙 Learning about the hardships of many Blues pioneers and how they lived gave me a whole new level of respect for what they achieved! It’s also not surprising that they 'had the Blues' with the great prejudice and racism they faced daily.

Here’s how you make your own Blues History Maps

1️⃣ Step 1 - Choose one (or more!) books to guide you.

No matter which books you choose, I suggest you start by dipping into a few of them and finding a style of writing that engages you. You don't want to have to trudge through it; it needs to excite you!

2️⃣ Step 2 - Write your notes down!

When making your map, make sure you write your own notes. Get to know your Chicago Blues from your Memphis Blues and listen for similarities between West Coast Blues and Texas Blues.

Get the names of the pioneers in each style and city and then read a bit about where they travelled and how they lived.

3️⃣ Step 3 - Use your ears.

We’re talking about music - and there’s no way to learn it properly unless you listen to it. Reading on its own is very interesting, but connecting that with what you’re listening to is a big deal.

Check out the British Blues players of the '60s and who they were listening to and trace it back – the lineage becomes pretty obvious sometimes! ;)

Go Further!

I took it a step further and spent most days transcribing at least a bit of what I was listening to. My goal was to memorize the phrases and language tools people were using. That expanded my Blues vocabulary so much!

Being on a session and wanted to do something in the style of someone became a much easier task! It also helped me see the influences of players I liked.

I suggest you go further too! Listen to some early Albert King, and you can clearly hear where Stevie Ray Vaughan got a load of his lick ideas. Or check out T-Bone Walker and then Chuck Berry, and you'll clearly hear where Chuck stole his licks (and moves!) from.

💡 Listening and reading about the Blues will introduce you concepts you wouldn’t encounter as a casual listener.

When I was in my teens I loved Howlin' Wolf's guitar work, and I still remember telling people he was one of my favourite guitarists. When reading that history book I figured that I didn't love Howlin' Wolf's guitar work at all. He didn't even play guitar!! It was the incredible Hubert Sumlin that played on most of his big records.

The great Willie Dixon played bass on many of the most outstanding Chicago Blues records – but he also wrote many of the songs!

Things like that made me feel a bit ignorant and gave me the start point to do my research. But I know we all have a lot to learn, and this kind of study can create as many holes as it fills. The more you know, the more you know you don't know!

It was (and is) a fascinating journey, and I really can't encourage you enough to give it a go.

It helped me realize that Blues is a language that we can all speak and understand if we take the time to learn it. This kind of musical study will make you a better guitar player and musician. And it's not just for the Blues - it works just as well for whatever style tickles your ears.

That reminds me... I must find an excellent Jazz history book and get started with that too! :)

Happy trails,

Justin Sandercoe.

👉 Check out my Blues Lead Guitar course to start improvising and jamming the Blues

lessons.title: Altered Tuning Fun (Part 2)
lessons.summary: Let's explore Open G Tuning and some classic Rolling Stones moves. :)
lessons.text:
Up for exploring some more altered tunings?

In a previous Food for Thought, we had fun exploring Drop D and Double Drop D. Now - we’re only one step away now from Open G Tuning, which is a foundation Open Chord Tuning and loads of fun to explore! It will open the door to a huge amount of music, especially if you dig The Rolling Stones and slide guitar.

🚨 Missed the previous post? Please - check out Altered Tuning Fun - Part 1 here, so you make the best out of this one!

Now - let’s get stuck in and learn more about how to play Open G Tuning on the guitar!

Open G Tuning

If you’re in Double Drop D, all you need to do now is lower the A String (String 5, second thickest) down a tone to the note G - you can use String 3 as a reference. If you’re not in Double Drop D, you also need to tune both outside strings down a tone to the note D.

In Open G Tuning, you’re playing the notes DGDGBD when you play all the open strings. As any of you who have studied basic Music Theory will know, those are all notes of a G Major Triad (GBD). Notice that it’s “Open G,” but the lowest note is the note D. If you take off the thickest string, the lowest note becomes the low G which makes more sense - and one of the reasons Keith Richards plays his infamous 5-string Telecaster!

💭 Does that famous Keith Richards guitar make more sense to you now? Let me know in the Discussion section!

In Open G Tuning, chord shapes now start to get a little interesting! Regular chord shapes would need notes on the 6th, 5th, and 1st strings moved up a tone. That’s quite often impossible, but trying it will take you to some interesting places and increase your understanding of both the tuning and the function of chord tones in regular tuning, which is extremely valuable.

The Open A Chord is a great place to start if you move Strings 5 and 1 up a tone. You end up with all the notes of the chord in the one fret, which is easy to barre, and the reason this tuning works so well for slide guitar! The root note is on String 5, but up two frets from where you might usually find the note. So, I find it easier to think of the root on String 3 of the shape, but that requires knowing the notes on the neck well - which you should. :)

The Rolling Stones Trick

The famous Stones move you need to know about is the 6sus4 chord, which you get by adding your 2nd and 3rd fingers in front of the barre, as shown below. Don’t worry about the name - just explore its cool sound!

Just adding the 6th on and off (like in a Blues Shuffle) is a simple and super effective move, and the sus4 on its own is easy and sounds cool. Change the 6th into a dominant 7th by moving it up one fret.

💡 You can also try two frets higher than the barre on String 3! That gets you an add9 chord, a really tasty sound to mix with the sus4 or the 6. Try it!

Playing a Sus 4 and also a 7 chord are also fun extensions to experiment with - ones you will hear for sure on many Rolling Stones songs and any band that they influenced (like MANY!)

Explore!

Now you have lots of cool grooves to explore! Can you figure out how to play a 12 Bar Blues shuffle using that grip? Try it on your own!

🚨 Next - we’ll explore how to do that! But if you can do it, don’t read the answer. Just grab your guitar and go play!

So, G is open, C is fret 5, and D is fret 7. Remember, G is also at the 12th fret. Try the straight bar and then add the 6th in the basic shuffle groove on beats 2 and 4.

3 Tips to Start Playing Slide Guitar

If you want to get experimenting with slide guitar, now’s your chance. :) I have an Introduction to Slide Guitar lesson for beginners, but here are the main tricks to play slide guitar and sound great:

Don’t press it down very hard. The slide should only touch the strings, never the frets.

Try to mute the strings behind the slide with the fingers on the nut side of the slide.

I find playing slide with a pick near impossible. So, you might like to start doing it fingerstyle and muting (with your strumming hand) any strings you don’t want to ring out.

But have fun! Don’t worry too much about what you’re doing and why if you are new to slide guitar. The best trick is to enjoy the ride and the fresh sounds you may not have explored before.

A fun place to start is Little Red Rooster by The Rolling Stones, basically a Blues in G - so the info above plus your ears should get you most of the way there! Listen and try to emulate the slides and the vibrato.

If you are a more experienced Open G player, start trying to find other chords, pick an open chord and figure out how you might play it if String 1, 5, and 6 are up a tone and see what happens.

🎶 Some great (non-slide) examples of Open G tuning are Brown Sugar by The Rolling Stones, Romeo & Juliet by Dire Straits, and Bohemian Like You by the Dandy Warhols.

If you want to solo in Open G (and if you’re playing a blues, that might well come up!), remember that you can play on Strings 2/3/4, and nothing changes! If you want to get out onto the String 1, 4, or 5, just move the notes up a tone.

It might sound complex, but it’s just practice and experimenting! It’s not difficult when you’ve played around with it a bit – but you won’t have so many pet licks to explore! Remember that most Blues solos are played mainly on the thinnest four strings anyway, so you just need to shift notes on String 1 up a tone. Or do you? Try all your favorite licks and see how they sound – some will be awesome, so will not. Let your ears guide you more than your brain!

Re-tuning is nothing to be afraid of, and for creative guitarists, it can breathe a lot of new life into the instrument! Chords have a fresh resonance, and you’ll play new sounds that you just can’t get in regular tunings.

I hope that this taste will whet your appetite for experimentation. If you’d like to learn more, check my Altered Tuning lessons here. Safe travels!

lessons.title: Altered Tuning Fun (Part 1)
lessons.summary: Altered tuning on guitar is a real fun thing to explore, so don't miss out on this food for thought!
lessons.text:
I've loved messing with guitar tunings since I first heard someone playing Brown Sugar by The Rolling Stones with the correct tuning - a long time ago!

I was floored by how much better it sounded compared to my hack standard tuning version. That was game-changing! Since then, I've been playing around with guitar tuning constantly.

It still surprises me that so many guitarists are afraid of changing the tuning of their instrument or thinking it’s something hard to do. The truth is that altered tuning on guitar is a real fun thing to explore.

In today’s Food For Thought, I hope to inspire you to give altered tuning a (real good) try too. And we’ll start by demystifying the feeling that many guitar players have that changing the guitar’s tuning is hard. It’s not. :)

And if you dig it, I’ll have another article exploring more common Open Tunings shortly. Make sure you’re a JustinGuitar Student, so you don’t miss out on any new lessons!

But I’d like to mention a couple of things before we get going.

Common Altered Tuning Problems

If you tune a string up a lot, you might break it. If your strings are old and rubbish, the chances of breaking one or more of them are even higher.

If you tune many strings up or down and dramatically change the string tension, you might bend the neck a small amount. That has never been a significant issue in the 30 years that I've been re-tuning my guitars. Still, if you plan on leaving your guitar in a particular tuning, you might need to adjust your truss rod.

None of this is the end of the world! If your strings were old, you probably should have changed them anyway. :) Also, don't try altered tuning on a guitar with a floating tremolo. It's a massive headache.

🎸 Now grab your guitar, and let’s start this little journey. :)

Introduction to Drop D Tuning
