The best way to get started with altered tuning is with Drop D tuning. That means you’ll drop the thickest string down a tone to the note D. To do that, you can use String 4 as a reference and slowly tune down the thickest string until they sound the same note but an octave apart.

Drop D Tuning allows you to play all the strings with your open D Chord, and it sounds fat! It's quite a simple tuning, and it’s pretty easy to do because it only affects one string!

That's important for a few reasons - let’s take a look!

How to Play Chords in Drop D Tuning

The chords that don’t use the thickest string remain the same, like D, C, Am, etc. But if the chord you want to play has a note on the thickest string, you’ll need to move that note up a tone, meaning two frets.

So in Drop D, all the familiar chords that just use strings 1-5 stay the same. If you want to play a G (or F), you need to figure out how to move the thickest string note up while playing the rest.

There's no wrong answer, but lots of correct answers! Let’s explore two of them and the super simple Power Chord. :)

If you want to solo in Drop D, it's no problem. Nothing changes; just avoid the thickest string! Go have some fun, then come back here later. :)

💬 So, how did that go? Let me know in the comments below!

Double Drop D Tuning

Now, let's tune down the thinnest string a tone (down to D) as well. Now you're in Double Drop D, a very common Folk and Blues tuning.

💡 You should try to play all your familiar chords in the new tuning, and l listen! There are some super tasty chords living here, and you don't need to do a thing. There is some magic living here, so go find it.

But if you want to play any other chords, you need to move the note on the thinnest string up a tone. It's not that hard, and it's actually quite fun! Make sure you experiment and listen to it lots because it's not always about knowing what you're doing! Just make some cool sounds and enjoy it.

I'm sure you can figure out most chords on your own, but here are a few ways you'd play some common open chords in Double Drop D and a few super lovely grips to explore.

You'll find some problems (like Open C Shape) but look for magic where you can't find an easy answer, like playing Cadd9 instead! Take a look at the diagrams:

It's a lot of fun exploring chords in altered tuning. To understand the theory behind all of that, my Theory Course is your way to go.

Also - soloing still shouldn't be a problem. Either stay off the outside strings or remember that the notes you usually play on the outside strings are now located two frets higher! It might seem a little awkward at first, but it can also be quite refreshing to get some fresh sounds out of tired old patterns!

Altered Tuning Songs

Playing Blues in Double Drop D is quite fun. It will force you out of playing many of the tired old blues vocabularies that fall under your fingers quickly and maybe take you to some fun places.

If you fancy checking out how some of the greats use Double Drop D, you might like to learn Song For George by Eric Johnson and Harvest Moon by Neil Young. Some great examples of basic Drop D tuning are Killing In the Name by Rage Against The Machine or Monkey Wrench by the Foo Fighters!

Now, grab your peg, twist it and enjoy yourself. :) Want to explore more? Check out my Altered Tuning lessons!

lessons.title: Shaking Off The Nerves
lessons.summary: Stage anxiety is real - and much more common than you think!
lessons.text:
Over the 35 years that I've been performing as a guitarist, I have met many different types of anxiety.

Not only in myself, but in people I have worked with, in students, and other musicians I have met along the way. Performance anxiety is something I often get asked about, and I have a few tools that might help you. It may also come as a comfort to know that anxiety is a very common thing that most musicians deal with regularly. ;)

So here are some of my tips on dealing with anxiety, especially - but not only - when performing.

Anxiety or Excitement?

It helps to define the kinds of things that can happen and why.

When we start thinking about performing or going on the stage, our adrenaline surges in our bodies. Many people notice sweaty palms, butterflies in the stomach, shaking hands, and even nausea! Although they are collectively not great things to feel, it helped me realize that these are normal human reactions to a stressful environment.

By having these feelings, you are just proving you are human! Over the years, I've been able to change how I perceive these anxious feelings. Instead of thinking about them as something showing that I am nervous, I know they are something I feel when I'm excited by what I'm about to do. Getting to that point hasn't always been easy - so don't beat yourself up if you can't do it right away.

I remember fondly the first time I played a national live TV show, and I felt pretty peaky. There were big stars everywhere backstage! It was a live show (as in no miming to track!), and I had to take a solo. I had butterflies in my tummy, clammy hands, and had buckets of adrenaline surging around my body.

While waiting to go on, I mentioned to one of the other band members (who has worked with some of the greatest musicians of all time on the biggest stages!) that I needed a pee, and he replied: "me too, most people get that before a big show, let's go!" And since then, I've noticed that many artists take a nervous pee (or three!) before going on stage. It's nothing to worry about if it happens to you too!

Later in my career, I quite randomly had a pretty severe panic attack mid-tour. I felt pretty embarrassed and managed to keep it to myself at the time, but I was terrified of going on stage; no reason and no trigger that I could think of, but just a real feeling of dread before going on stage. Luckily for me, we had a week off between tours. I sought a Cognitive Behavioural therapist who worked incredible magic on me.

💡 Cognitive Behavioural Therapy works by re-programming your brain!

Over three sessions, we made squeezing my right-hand thumb and first finger together (how I hold a pick) a trigger for many good feelings related to performing, and it worked! I certainly recommend looking into it if you have any anxiety problems.

Do You Know The 6 Ps?

I am a big believer in the famous 6 P's: Prior Preparation Prevents Piss Poor Performance. If you don't put enough practice in, you are likely to make a mistake, so you probably should feel nervous. Making sure you are well prepared should always be top of the list to prevent anxious feelings!

That said, even the greatest artists make mistakes. I've seen Neil Young start with a wrong harmonica and have to start a song again! Mistakes happen, and it's not a big deal if one does – nobody other than your ego is going to get hurt! So don't worry about them, and whatever you do, don't raise your hand or admit the mistake. If you must do something, give the bass player a dirty look or blame your gear. ;p

💡 You'd be amazed at the power of your mind to create a stressful environment to practice dealing with your nerves.

I studied classical guitar at The Tasmanian Conservatorium of Music. The classical exams we had to perform each semester were quite a terrifying experience. We'd have to walk into a big concert hall, set up, and perform our repertoire for four examiners who would not say a word, keep blank expressions, and offer no feedback at all. And we'd have no audience, just the examiners.

In my first exam, my hands were shaking; I swear my palms were dripping with sweat! I felt (and played) awful. I knew I had to prepare myself for the exam better, and not just the music. So I started setting up my living room as the exam room. I would sit outside the room and imagine that I was about to do the exam. After some practice, I was able to get myself into quite a nervous state just thinking about going into the room to play. Once I could do that, I started trying to calm myself down by using slow breaths and another old psychology trick of imagining myself blowing all the nervous energy into a red balloon. When I'd got it all out, I would watch the balloon float away.

I never managed to kill off the nerves completely, but it helped get them to a manageable level so I could get on with letting the music out and not thinking too much.

What can go wrong? And Why?

It's also worth remembering that when we get anxious, we worry about what can go wrong. And the more you think about it, the more likely it is to happen!

In a musical performance, the goal should be to let the music flow out relaxed. If you start taking yourself out of the moment, you are much more likely to make a mistake and have something actual to freak you out. If you keep worrying about that difficult section coming up, not only are you more likely to mess it up, but you'll be much more likely to mess up the bit before it too!

💙 A related side note of advice is to remain aware of your heartbeat – especially for solo performances. Our heartbeat is the body's natural built-in metronome! So, you are likely to rely on it to judge tempo when you start a song. :) However, if you feel excited and your heart is beating faster than normal, you are likely to start a song faster than normal. If it's a technically difficult song, you're going to face some challenges.

If you're starting a song with a band, ask the drummer for a tempo. If you have to start on your own, take a few seconds to run the melody through in your mind to avoid setting off too fast.

Just Pretend :)

One last tip that I found super helpful is to pretend to be confident, even if you are not feeling it! Fake it until you make it. Your posture can affect your thinking, and by putting on a super confident mask, you are likely to find that something eventually clicks. You become the thing you were pretending to be! It can be very powerful and well worth trying if you start to feel like you're losing your cool.

I hope this might help or comfort some of you that have anxiety issues - it really can be quite debilitating if you are working professionally. For further reading, you might like to check out The Inner Game of Music by Barry Green and Tim Galloway, which has advice on not only anxiety but on practicing effectively too - a great book on many levels.

If you're finding it very difficult to deal with, I strongly recommend getting some help from a professional therapist. The difference it can make may transform your performing experience! And don't be afraid to discuss it with other musicians. Sharing these feelings and realizing that you are not alone can offer a lot of comfort in itself.

I hope you enjoy this food for thought and that sharing my experience can help you go further in your performing journey.

If you’d like to be the first one to receive my Food For Thought articles, make sure you’re following me on socials and are signed in here or have registered here ! Good luck and best wishes.

lessons.title: Play Piano In 15 Minutes
lessons.summary: I hate those misleading ads you see all over the internet: so this one is surely not one of them. :)
lessons.text:
Ok, strummers, wanna get yourself in front of a piano or keyboard?

I hate those misleading ads you see all over the internet: so this one is surely not one of them. :) If you’re a guitar player with even just a rudimentary understanding of music theory, this micro-course will get you up and running on the piano! Yep - this Food For Thought will get you playing a load of songs in just a few minutes. :)

Let’s get directly to the point!

How to Play Piano in 15 Minutes (For Guitarists)

The white notes on the piano are C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C, and the black notes are the sharps and flats. Remember that E to F and B to C are just a semitone apart, so they are the ones that don’t have a black note between them. You’ll notice that black notes are grouped in 2’s and 3’s. The note C is to the left of the groups of 2.

🤔 Got confused? Check out my free Music Theory lessons. That’s a premium product, but the first beginner grades are free and will get you started with the basics!

If we only use the white notes, we are playing in the key of C Major, which is all we’ll be working on today. :)

Music Theory Applied to the Piano

One of the cool things about theory applied to the piano is that it’s a lot more obvious than guitar. Basic triad chords, for example, are the root note, the 3rd, and the 5th. On piano, that’s an easy and visual thing to do: you’ll play a note (root), miss a note (2), play a note (3rd), miss a note (4), play a note (5th). It’s right there in front of you!

There are many fingering options to play triads on the piano, but stick to this one to start:

Use your right hand. Your thumb goes on the root, your middle finger on the 3rd, and your pinky on the 5th.

This fingering will help you to ‘miss’ the notes that would have been under your index and ring fingers.

🚨 Note that I’m avoiding finger numbers here because they’re different from the guitar!

So, start that triad shape with your thumb on the note C. Do the play a note, miss a note, play a note miss a note thing, and you have the C Major chord. Keep the same shape but move it up one note, so the thumb is on the D, and you have a D minor chord! It follows the diatonic chord sequence for the key of C, which is: C Major, D Minor, E Minor, F Major, G Major, A Minor, B diminished, and then back to C.

💡 Check out this Intermediate theory course to learn the theory behind chords in keys and diatonic sequences.

We number chords in keys using Roman numerals for convenience. And we use capital letters for Major chords and lower case for minor chords. So, C (I), Dm (ii), Em (iii), F (IV), G (V), Am (vi), and Bdim (vii). Don’t worry too much about the vii chord for now. We don’t use it often!

Got it? If you have any questions, log in to your account and drop me a message in the Discussions section!

Playing the Rhythm

I recommend you start with the following pattern:

Play a root note of the chord (just one note) in the left hand, somewhere to the left of where you plan to play the chord. Then, the triad with the right hand. Do that all twice, and you have the bass root on 1 and 3 and the chord on beats 2 and 4.

A chord pattern that works for gazillions of songs is the ol’ I V vi IV (1, 5, 6, 4). So, doing each of those for a bar and you got yourself the ability to play hundreds (really!) of songs at parties and show off your new awesome piano skills. :)

So you’ll be playing C, then G, Am, then F. Remember, the C root will be just left of the pair of black notes, the G G will be between the first and second black notes in the groups of 3 (move up to it!). Then the Am, which is simply one step up. Then down to F, which is just to the left of the group of three black notes! Simples!

4 Easy Songs to Play on Piano

Now it’s time to have some fun! You can play simplified versions of many songs! You might like to sing over the following ones:

I’m Yours by Jason Mraz)

Let It Be by The Beatles

When I Come Around by Green Day

Wherever You Will Go by The Calling

You might need to leave some bits out if you’re just getting started, but the idea here is just to give you some food for thought. :)

If you fancy trying something a bit more old-school, try using the I, vi, ii, V (1, 6, 2, 5) chord sequence. It’s the foundation of many more songs like I Got Rhythm (George Gershwin) or The Rainbow Connection (Muppets). The so-called “50’s progression” is used in lots of songs too! It’s the I, vi, IV, V (1, 6, 4, 5) sequence, and you’ll find it in songs like Stand By Me (Ben E. King) and All I Have To Do Is Dream (Everly Brothers).

Later on in your journey, explore how you can use these ideas to help your guitar playing! That should help you get a little more creative. :) For now, tinkle those ivories and have some fun. :)

Want to go further? Explore my Intermediate & Advanced Music Theory lessons for guitar players!

lessons.title: Mindful Listening
lessons.summary: Really learning to get inside the music is becoming a lost activity and one I recommend all musicians get back into for their musical health!
lessons.text:
You’ve probably heard about this Mindfulness thing before, which has been gaining popularity over the last few years.

In today’s Food For Thought, we’ll explore how to apply some mindfulness concepts to improve your musicianship. Ultimately, to improve your guitar playing!

If you’re not familiar with it, here’s a quick definition. Mindfulness is a kind of meditation that comes from Buddhist practices. The most common way to learn it is by focusing on your breathing while maintaining your focus. The aim is always to be present for every moment.

I got into Mindfulness around the start of 2016, mainly because I needed something to help clear my mind and relax. I get lousy monkey mind moments where I just won’t turn off! So, I’ve found mindfulness to be a beneficial activity in my day-to-day life. It helped me sleep better and generally feel more relaxed, which is a big positive.

Then, I discovered Mindful Running, where instead of focussing on the breath, you move your attention to the fall of your feet and let that become the sole focus of your attention. That was great because I could do both a morning run and my meditation in one go.

But what’s that got to do with guitar practice? I hear you ask. Well, let me explain.

These days everyone seems to treat music as a background thing; I don’t feel like many people get into it as deeply as we used to (sounding like an old man!)

So, I’ve been trying to make time each day to listen to music. But not normal listening - getting completely absorbed and lost in it, not just having it on in the background, or doing it because of work! I mixed this mindful practice with my listening, and I love the results, so I have to share!

I feel I’ve regained that deep kind of listening I used to do back in the days when I’d have to order a new album from the record store, wait months for it to arrive, and then spend weeks listening to that one record over and over again. I’d truly absorb it and appreciate its value to my life.

How to Get Started with Mindful Listening

Some experience in Mindfulness will probably be a big help to get yourself started. I used an app called Headspace for a few months to get going and found that helpful! The one I currently use is Sam Harris’s Waking Up app. It’s got a great beginner course and a lot more advanced and conceptual stuff (and some Stoic courses, one of my other passions!). There are also many websites devoted to the practice, which you can seek out on your own. You can also check out Mindful.org or this actionable guide.

When it comes to transferring the ideas to music, I start in the same way as regular meditation, getting comfortable and trying to get myself still. I prepare a playlist in advance (usually 30 minutes) or just pick an album I’d like to absorb. While listening, I start by letting my focus wander over the music and see where it lands. Then, I try to get really into that aspect of the music and drill deeper into it.

It might start off being the guitar tone and then precisely how it sits in the track, and then maybe into the sound of the pick hitting the strings. It might be the drum groove and then the high-hat and then the locking in of the high-hat and the acoustic guitar, or the pattern it makes – it’s not especially important where your focus ends up. Still, I think it can be helpful to try to guide yourself deeper into wherever your focus drifts.

💡 I’ve found that practice has opened up some albums that I was already very familiar with - I’ve discovered new depths to explore.

Now, sometimes I listen to something with a precise aim. For example, I wanted to explore Angus Young’s vibrato, so while AC/DC is probably not the kind of music one would associate with meditation, I found myself entirely in a mindful state with all of my attention centered on this one thing.

Another thing I got into was exploring the ‘pocket’ of funk grooves and trying to focus on the relationships between the instruments and how tight or loose they were rhythmically.

Focusing on music production, reverbs and textures, and exploring guitar layers are also fascinating journeys. You can choose to get into the zone with a goal or just let yourself get absorbed into the music. It’s all good - there are no rules, just fun things to explore.

If you’ve been following my lessons, you probably know that I recommend using a count-down timer for practice, and learning to keep your focus while practice is pretty much a mindful approach anyway!

I hope you find this idea of some benefit and that, at the very least, it inspires you to get into deep listening.

If you’d like to go deeper and develop your ears, don’t hesitate to check out my free Ear Training course too. Happy days, J.

lessons.title: 5 Minute Miracles
lessons.summary: Learn to improve your focus and make the most out of your practice sessions.
lessons.text:
When I was 18 years old, I got accepted at the local classical conservatoire.

I had a lot of stuff I had to study. On top of the classical repertoire, techniques, and harmony mandatory for the course, I was desperate to learn more about jazz and rock guitar. Luckily, I had a great teacher (thanks, Johnny Mac!) who helped me sort out a proper practice routine. For the first time, I was able to cover everything I needed.

I was doing 8 hours of practice a day. I broke my sessions into half-hour chunks, and I got into ticking boxes on a chart that I had made up. I found that to be a very self-motivating and rewarding way to practice.

💡 I developed My Practice Assistant so that you don’t have to make anything up! :) Log in to your JustinGuitar account, and you can use it for free.

I don’t expect you to practice 8 hours a day. I don’t even expect you to practice a couple of hours a day! But, in my journey, I learned a lot about practicing properly; in today’s food for thought, I want to share some of it - I hope it helps you too!

Improve Your Focus

The big personal breakthrough came when I realized how much better I could focus when I had a set amount of time to practice something. The danger of not using any timer is that you will practice much more on some things than others. For example, you’re more likely to stay longer in exercises you like more than in ones you don’t - or sometimes you might just get lost in the music and use up all your time on something you didn’t need to spend lots of time on and neglect something important.

I started exploring this idea. So, I experimented with how much time I could stay properly focused and how much time I needed between exercises.

I’ve since looked more into the concept and learned that many specialists had studied the effect of using a timer to maintain focus. Science knows that working with a set endpoint is more effective than not!

The 50/50 Split: Get the Formula!

Here’s my recommendation. Divide your total available practice time in two, and have half for completely free fun. Play whatever you like and enjoy your guitar - explore songs, sounds, techniques, whatever. Then, make a set routine for the other half of your time.

🚨 I recommend doing the set routine first, or you might jam your way out of time for the serious stuff. Eat your vegetables before dessert. ;)

The short-timed sessions are a big deal. There is a lot of science behind using a timer to help you focus. If you have ever run a long race, you will know that your body can find an extra energy reserve when it sees the finish line that would be hard to drag out earlier. It’s much like that when practicing - your brain will allow you to run at peak performance if it knows it will get a rest at the end!

Start small with your set routine. Pick four technique exercises that you would like to work on and try using this timer idea. Just 5 minutes on each exercise! And ensure you have a minute break between each exercise.

For most people, 5 minutes is about the limit for proper focussed practice. Any longer, and it’s easy to drift off into jamming and to lose concentration.

But. There are times where you should learn to distract yourself while practicing - like working on automating fingerstyle patterns - so make sure you are aware of the most effective way to spend your 5 minutes.

Now, let’s look at some tips to help you make the most out of your practice time.

Tip #1: What Countdown Timer?

I find the countdown timer on my phone easiest to use, but make sure you don’t get distracted every time you touch your phone. :) You could use a kitchen timer or whatever you have - but try to use something that has a beep at the end, so you are not clock watching.

Tip #2: Don’t Miss The Breaks!

Don’t be tempted to leave out the breaks! They help you retain new information better, moving from short-term to long-term memory. And it will also allow your muscles to have a break - just like when you’re doing physical workouts.

Tip #3: Don’t Wander

You will find that random thoughts can drift into your mind. You might want to help them pass by renewing your focus on the exercise you are on! Try not to let your mind wander at all. That’s very likely to happen when you start trying out this method, so your challenge is to keep your focus on your practice. It’s very much learning to meditate. In fact, for me, practice is a kind of meditation.

Tip #4: Always Know Why

It’s important to remember that you need to know what to focus on for everything you practice. If you’re not sure why you are practicing something, either find out or don’t practice it!

Tip #5: Be Prepared

Prepare all you need before you start. If you’re using an amp, get it on and its tone right. Make sure you have any notes you need out - scale diagrams, transcriptions, or whatever. You should be ready to start playing as soon as you hit start on your timer!

Tip #6: Turn Distractions Off

You’ll find it helpful to turn your phone off, or at least on silent mode. Don’t let yourself get distracted in the 5 minutes unless it’s an emergency.

Make tea, drink water, check emails or Facebook, whatever you need to do before starting. If you got family around, ask them not to disturb you for the next half hour or however long you are doing your focussed practice.

Get Into The Zone!

I found that I go into a practice zone as soon as I hit the start button on my timer. Random thoughts rarely interrupt me, but it took a few months of consistently working on my focus to get that.

The results of these 5-minute blocks can be quite profound. Many students said that they were making noticeably more progress once they started employing this timed practice approach.

I doubt this kind of thing is good for everyone, but I highly recommend giving it a try. See if it works for you! You might find your own five-minute miracle. :)

Want some more insights on how to practice the guitar efficiently? Check out this free Effective Practice course. Good luck and best wishes!

lessons.title: Unlock Neck With Step Up On The B
lessons.text:
I discovered this fretboard logic a few years back, and I still remember when it happened.

I was exploring tuning in 4ths - E A D G C F - and trying to figure out how chord logic worked in that tuning when I stumbled onto something that helped me unlock the guitar neck in regular tuning. So, in today’s food for thought, I’ll share a bit of it with you - and I hope that helps you go further in your guitar journey as well.

Perhaps you are aware that there are five major chord shapes on the guitar. If you draw all the notes of a major triad on a big neck diagram, you can see how they fall together into the five shapes, commonly known as The CAGED System. But it gets deeper than that, and to explore it, I invite you to try playing along with this little adventure!

Grab your guitar, and let’s find another way to identify the CAGED shapes on your instrument.

Understanding The Guitar Neck

Play a regular Open E chord. Now move all your fingers down (toward the ground) one string. Move the note on the B String (String 2) up one fret. You got yourself an A chord, right? Now move it down another string and again move the note on the B String up one fret - and you got a D chord.

Now put down a G Chord - if you can, play the 3-finger variety using fingers 2, 3, and 4. Move it down one string and move the note on the B String up a fret; you got a C Chord. Try again, move the C Chord down a string and move the note on the B string up a fret and you’ll find yourself with a small F chord (which is an E Shape barre chord).

So I hope you see the cool logic going on there, but I also hope you noticed that I skipped over the change from the D to the G. It works still, but it’s just not quite as obvious. Moving the D down and moving the B String note up gives us XX0033 which is the top part of a big 4-finger G, and you’d have to add the notes on the thickest two strings.

🎸 We find that by moving any chord down one string, we can use the same shape if we move the B String note (or notes) up a fret. Even more cool is… It works with scales and arpeggios too!

That’s useful and helpful in many ways. Most obviously, it can help with memorizing chords and scales, and arpeggio. However, it can also be great to find new chord grips on different string sets and move licks or lines to another part of the fingerboard.

One exercise that can be fun to start with is looking at how the Minor Pentatonic Shapes change as you move them down a string – all the shapes are remarkably similar when you look at them from this perspective!

Give this some thought, and you’ll find many other interesting uses for this little nugget that will help you make sense of our 6-string friend. Good luck!

Do you want to learn more? Explore my guitar lessons. :)

lessons.title: Playing What You Hear
lessons.summary: But... what does playing what you hear actually mean?
lessons.text:
What does playing what you hear mean? How does it work? And how can you develop that skill?

I’m sure you have a lot of questions like that, don’t you? In this Food for Thought, I want to delve into the mystical world of playing what you hear. And to start with, what is hearing music?

💡 Think about your favorite guitar solo. Can you hear the notes in your mind? Can you hear the rhythm? Can you imagine the tone?

Like most things, learning to hear music in your imagination is a skill you can develop by practicing a lot. A little time each day imagining riffs, licks, or lines is a great way to develop your ears and musical imagination. If you can sing what you hear in your mind, you can be sure what you hear is properly in there! So, I highly recommend trying to sing what you hear, even if you’re not a confident singer.

But how does being able to hear in your imagination help you become better at playing guitar? Well, I’ve got a great exercise for you! :)

Try It Yourself!

🎸 Put Finger 1 on the 8th fret of String 3. Then, try to play Happy Birthday while staying in that position - don’t go up or down the neck.

We all know Happy Birthday well, so we know how that song goes. If you can’t do it, then there is a disconnection between your imagination and your hand! If you found that one easy, pick another slightly more difficult song - Standard Jazz melodies might be fun!

Try to play somewhere else on the neck again. If you can play all the melodies you can think of, then you’re doing it for real – you’re playing what you imagine, and I believe that to be the purest form of expression. Congratulations!

Need Some Extra Work?

If you found it difficult or impossible like most people do (and I did), then you’ll need to work on Ear Training. Again - the solution is practice.

💭 I start almost every practice session with 10 minutes of playing my imagination. Over the last few years, I’ve seen great improvement, though still far from perfect.

I have a list of songs that I add to all the time, and I just pick one at random, put my hand somewhere on the neck and try to play it. Sometimes I find that I actually can’t hear the melody clearly in my imagination! That means that the problem is not with the hand/imagination connection but getting it right in my imagination in the first place! I’m also working on playing solos I know well in my imagination on the wrong parts of the fretboard - that might be a great exercise if you find basic melodies too easy. :)

Transcribing

You can do quite a few things to develop your ability to play what you hear, but transcribing is my favorite tool! You hear a note on the recording, find it on the neck, hear the next one, play it, etc. When you transcribe, you’re playing what you hear in slow motion – but at the same time, you are installing the music correctly into your imagination too, which is important. After a while, you’ll find you can transcribe whole phrases because you recognize them and know where to make those sounds on the guitar neck.

💬 So, will you have a try at playing what you hear in your imagination? Let me know in the Discussion section! I promise - it’s a wonderful feeling when you can do it and well worth the effort. :)

Doing Interval Ear Training is also something I highly recommend if you can’t express your musical mind on the fretboard.

Grab my Ear Trainer App here to help you out. Good luck

lessons.title: What You Can’t Do?
lessons.summary: I've given and received this "practice what you can't do, not what you can" advice over the years so much. Does that really make sense?
lessons.text:
I've given and received this "practice what you can't do, not what you can" advice over the years so much that it felt very wrong to question it.

But when I had the pleasure of meeting and interviewing Stevie Vai a few years ago, he dropped some pearls of wisdom that shook my practice beliefs to the core. So, I want to share with you here some food for thought that I wish someone had shared with me when I started to get serious about playing the guitar.

Practice... What?

The conventional wisdom of "practicing what you can't do" makes perfect sense in many circumstances. If your time is not good, you need to work on it. Don't know your scales? Learn them. Never understood harmony and theory? Study it.

But there is one area where, sometimes, it may be better to develop your strengths than battling your weaknesses. And that area is technique!

💡 Your technique can profoundly shape your playing style and character.

Mr. Vai said that rather than struggling with techniques that he found difficult, he preferred to develop those that came quickly. Whether you're his fan or not, you can't deny that he has a very unique and identifiable voice on the instrument. One that he created by developing his strengths to their extremes!

Around that same time, I had a chat with fusion virtuoso Scott Henderson about how he developed his style. He noted that much of it came from his inability to pick fast, finding it difficult and cumbersome. Still, he had greater fluency and got the notes he heard out easier by using legato techniques. So, Henderson is also a terrific example where technique preference played a big part in creating his style!

I started thinking of other examples of easily identifiable players… Jeff Beck uses fingerstyle for rock. Eddie Van Halen's characteristic tapping and tremolo picking or Malmsteen's speed picking and sweeps. It seems that one of my favorite players, Eric Johnson, also has a style with deep roots in his picking technique choices. And the list goes on.

💡 That's a fascinating thought path to explore on your own, with your idols.

But - let's have a further chat.

Where Do You Want To Go?

Most great artists focus on what they can do. They make it part of their unique voice! It's an entirely opposing view of 'working on what you can't do,' but it works – if you want to be an artist! And I think that is where the distinction lies.

🚨 To be a 'session' guy, you need a diverse range of styles and techniques to draw on. To be an artist, you need to define and refine who YOU are.

The guitarists that make it to the top of the tree are usually brilliant at what they do - being themselves! I don't think we want Mark Knopfler to be a brilliant finger tapper or David Gilmour to be a master sweep picker. We want them to be themselves.

I hope this article might inspire you to explore further who YOU are, develop that and become the best you can be at being yourself.

Safe travels, my friend. Check out my Effective Practice Course if you need extra food for thought on organizing your practice routine! :)

lessons.title: The Holistic Practice Routine
lessons.summary: The fundamental areas of guitar practice fall into six areas. Learn about them here!
lessons.text:
While there is certainly no ‘one size fits all’ practice routine, these basic principles help you develop the best one for you.

Over the years, I have come across many different approaches, but I have always favored the ‘whole body’ approach to practice. Using the analogy of our own body, you wouldn’t want to go to the gym and work on just your weakest arm or your favorite arm. You wouldn’t get it looking super buff without looking at the rest of your body at the same time, would you?

When it comes to guitar practice, you should also be aware of all the essential things you need to develop - and maintain! If you’re new to JustinGuitar and have missed my lesson on Practice Makes Permanent, make sure to check that out too!

I see the fundamental areas of guitar practice falling into six areas:

Ear Training

Knowledge

Technique

Repertoire

Improvisation

Time

Depending on your goals, the type of music you want to make, and your strengths and weaknesses, you will want to manipulate the amount of time you spend on each or potentially drop areas if they are not relevant.

In this Food for Thought, we’ll look at each area and explore adding things to boost your practice routine!

The Six Fundamental Areas of Guitar Practice

#1 Ear Training

Many guitarists often neglect Ear Training, but I think it is one of the most important and rewarding areas to study. I include all exercises that help develop the relationship between your ‘inner ear’, your musical imagination and your hand, which increases your ability to express yourself. You might start with tangible exercises like Interval Ear Training or Relative Pitch studies or move into more practical methods like Transcribing and playing a melody by ear.

#2 Knowledge

Knowledge includes theory but also the application of it. Things you should know that will help you in the real world: keys, scales, arpeggios, modes, licks, chord grips… There’s a lot of things you can put in this spot, so you need to choose wisely!

#3 Technique

Technique is the physical mechanics you use to play. It’s very common for guitar players to spend far too long here and develop incredible chops but have nothing to say, no understanding of what they’re saying, and no songs to say it in! It’s important, but it’s just part of your development, and without the other elements, you’re unlikely to feel satisfied!

#4 Repertoire

Your repertoire is really what it all boils down to - what do you want to play? The other practice areas will help you play the songs you put here! Without songs to play, you can’t really perform, express yourself or even entertain friends at a party. You have to play songs! So, pick the ones you love, work on them, and allow these songs to influence how you choose the other areas in your practice routine.

#5 Improvisation

Improvisation is important for those that want to do it! If you’re a songwriter and not interested in lead guitar, it may not be as relevant, so that you might drop it. But if you want to play Jazz or Blues solos, this needs to be a priority as this is where you will put it all together with your band or a backing track!

#6 Time

The longer I play, the more I think that time is really where the whole thing is at. All the greats have amazing time feel, solid time, and ‘in the pocket’ grooves. Solid time makes people tap their feet, nod their heads, get involved with the music.

Beginners should make their strumming patterns feel good, and Intermediate guitarists can work on their riffs, scales, licks. Advanced players should ensure that they get their septuplet subdivisions right on. When your time is good, it gets people’s attention, and I think it should get yours!

💡 Now - it’s time to take a step back and organize your guitar sessions. Are you practicing everything you need to? Let me know in the Discussion section. ;)

Need extra help to organize your practice sessions? Log in to your account and explore My Practice Assistant.

lessons.title: How to Overcome Stage Anxiety
lessons.summary: Turn anxiety into excitement and overcome stage fright. It's a simple shift that can enhance your entire performance experience.
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Stage Anxiety: Justin's Experience

01:00 The Science Behind Stage Fright

03:22 Unleash the PERFORMER in You!

03:58 Guided Meditation with Cortney McDermott
lessons.text:
Turn Anxiety Into Excitement. :)

This short lesson and guided meditation will help you fight stage fright.

Even just thinking about performing makes our heart rate increase, eh? It makes our senses so heightened that we start to feel light-headed, have butterflies in our stomachs, get sweaty hands. These are all perfectly normal reactions! But often, we label them as anxiety - and, more commonly than you think, we let it keep us from doing stuff that we love, like performing.

💭 I’ve been there too. I started suffering from pretty crippling stage fright when touring with Katie Melua back in the day. We were on a European tour, and it was scary and debilitating.

It was only when working through that period that I realized those feelings, labeled as anxiety and fear, were the same ones I have when I’m about to do the thing I love.

That realization helped a lot, but it takes practice to reinforce that idea and make it a permanent reality. And there’s a whole lot of science behind that! My goal with this short lesson is to help you make sense of it. I want to help you overcome stage anxiety, just like I did. I know that you ultimately might become a better musician!

Anxiety vs. Excitement

What if we relabel these completely natural body responses as performance excitement instead of performance anxiety? It’s the same event but a very different interpretation.

🎙 To help me help you, I’ve invited my friend Cortney McDermott to join us in this special lesson about overcoming stage anxiety. Cortney is an expert in brain-body science and a performance coach. For the past years, she’s helped me overcome many challenges. Now I hope she can help you too - and it all starts with this short lesson!

Cortney’s specialty is teaching how to use your mind and body to create more of what you want and less of what you don’t! “There’s a difference between performance anxiety and performance excitement in terms of our biochemistry and our physiology,” she explains.

“In performance anxiety, we assign the meaning anxiety to the event. Then, our bodies start to release stress hormones - cortisol, adrenaline, and norepinephrine. If prolonged, this kind of biochemistry can lead to all sorts of undesirable consequences. You know what I mean - jittery hands, clenched throat, muscle tightness.”

Cortney invites us to think about a second scenario, where you decide that the sensations in your body are a sign of excitement. We start to experience an adrenaline rush, just like in the first scenario. But now - that can also help increase our focus if it’s under control! That means we have some really powerful performance enhancers joining the chemical party in our bodies.

“In this second scenario, we have things like serotonin, dopamine, and endorphins. They’re hormones that make us feel good and contribute to that excitement we’re looking for when we’re about to perform,” Cortney explains.

💡 If you turn anxiety into excitement, you’re enhancing the entire performance experience. For both you and your audience! We all know what it feels like to watch a nervous performer: it’s just not very comfortable for anyone! When you’re excited to perform - that’ll boost your audience’s confidence in you. It’ll vibe so much more. :)

The simple act of reframing our perception of the same event can change your result entirely!

Release Your Oxytocin!

Now - what if you go even further and replace the concept of performance with a much more empowering idea of playing music? It’s all tangled up in all kinds of expectations and pressure, but we all love to play, don’t we? And when we create that environment, we connect with our audience and release oxytocin. This hormone binds us all together!

🎥 Explore these ideas a little deeper in a Guided Meditation with Cortney McDermott. You can download the audio in the Resources tab under the video!

You’re Not Alone. :)

I always get so many questions from my students asking how to handle stage fright. Well, the first thing I need you to know is that I’m not immune to it - and I think no musician is. Many of the greatest musicians have battled it. We’re not alone! It surely affects different people in different ways.

💡 Learning to relax on the stage is an essential part of your journey. We start approaching this in Grade 3 of my Guitar Courses. :)

Once again - always remember you’re not the only one. It’s not unusual to have stage fright, but now you have great tools to fight it!

Learn more about mind-body science on Cortney McDermott’s website. Happy trails!

lessons.title: How To Rekindle The Love For Guitar?
lessons.summary: If your guitar life feels pretty boring right now, don't buy new gear. Not before trying out these 6 tools to rekindle your guitar love!
lessons.text:
People usually try to reignite their passion for playing by buying a new guitar, amp, or effect box! I’ve been guilty of it too. I’m not sure if there’s a guitar player alive that hasn’t. Unfortunately, the passion is usually short-lived. We end up searching for the next guitar toy before we’ve even put the last one to good use.

I fall out of love with playing guitar. What now?

I suspect many of us fall out of love with playing because of frustration. Sometimes you feel like you’re not making any progress or don't feel like playing your favorite riff again... It can be tough to find your way out of the rut without the right strategy. The good news is that the right tools for this gig are free and easy!

Six Tools to Rekindle Your Guitar Love

Tool 1. Change things up!

A change is as good as a holiday! The first tool is also my preferred one. If I start to feel like things are getting stale, I completely change what I’ve been practicing. If I’ve been working a lot on blues, then I’ll get into something else. I’ll dig some jazz, acoustic fingerpicking, explore effects. Maybe I'll try some new theory idea or play left-handed… Whatever it takes to fire up the passion again.

Tool 2. Refine your Goals

Long-term goals should be fluid and flexible! If you find yourself in a rut, it’s worth checking in with your long-term goal. If your goal has changed, it’s time to try a different path. Having goals is an excellent way of maintaining motivation. If you’ve not seen the Effective Practice series, check it out now.

Tool 3. Expand Your Listening Palette

I’ve found myself a couple of times falling out of love with music, not just guitar. That’s pretty scary for a professional musician. I’ve heard the same from many colleagues and students over the years. Sometimes, we struggle to connect with music. If that's your case, expand your listening palette!

Does it seem a bit obvious? Well, maybe, but it’s something that very few people actually do. Thanks to services like Spotify and YouTube, it’s easier than ever to explore new music. Finding a good curator can be tricky!

Here's my suggestion: Start with an all-time favorite on YouTube. Then, check the suggested videos. It’s an excellent place to start! I like the suggested playlists on Spotify, too. Feel free to look for some of my favorite guitar music playlists! :)

Tool 4. Dig Deeper

If you don’t fancy going too far away from music styles you like, dig deeper into the music you do like. Try and dig deeper into your favorite artists! I suggest picking your all-time favorite and finding a complete discography. Listen to the stuff you are not so familiar with!

If you’ve already gone there, you might read a biography or find interviews. Discover out who they like and try that. ;) I found this route a great tool for finding incredible stuff I would never have found otherwise.

Tool 5. The Forced Five Minutes

I’ve often had students say that they haven't found time to play anymore. Work gets in the way, ‘life takes over’... To be honest, I think that is rarely the case. It’s much more likely that motivation is down. There’s always that 15 minutes you wasted watching rubbish TV when you could have been playing.

There’s a tool for this scenario too!

Finding 30 minutes a day to practice can be tricky for many people. Finding just 5 minutes to play sounds more achievable for most of us! So do it.

When I’ve used this tool myself, the 5 minutes have flown by, and I often find that I play a lot longer because I’m enjoying it! There should be nothing set. The aim is to play. And I mean to play as in play around and have fun – the real meaning of play!

Tool 6. Take Some Time Out

It’s also fine to have time off – without guilt! I’ve often found that taking even as much as a month off seems to have helped things fall into place when I came back. But I do expect to need some time to get the muscles working again!

Well, I hope these tools are useful if you fall out of love or struggle to make time for our six-string friend. It’s quite normal to have times when you’re not practicing as much. Ensure you recognize it and have some tools to help you get back in the saddle when you want to. ;)

Safe travels, my friends.

lessons.title: Is Reading Notation Worth the Effort?
lessons.summary: Story Time! I'll share how I learned to read notation in only 2 weeks - and all the reasons why you shouldn't!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Welcome! :)

00:45 How & Why I Learned Notation

08:03 Should You Read Music?

11:18 When to Learn Notation

13:45 The Best Approach
lessons.text:
How long does it take to learn music notation?

Well - I learned it in only 2 weeks. But should you?

Today’s lesson is a bit different. I’d wanted to talk about how I learned to read music notation in only 2 weeks and all the reasons why I think you probably shouldn’t do that. :)

🚨 If you're one of those who often put "less talk, more play" in the comment box, this video is definitely not for you. :)

We'll basically be talking about why I think most people should not learn to read music notation. We'll also outline the reasons you might want to do that!

Reading traditional notation is helpful on certain occasions. Still, there's a way better approach to understanding the guitar fretboard and where the notes are. So, stick with this lesson if you want to know what that is. :)

To start with, I'll share a little bit of a story about how I learned to read music. In only two weeks!

My Experience

When I started to learn guitar, I did it mostly by ear. Back in the day, we used to have chord books with some basic chord progressions, some The Beatles songs, that kind of stuff.

But most of the learning process was just listening to songs and trying to figure it out. I'd mostly get it all wrong to start off! :)

When I was playing in bands, it would be like we'd all agree on a particular song. We'd all go home and try to learn our parts before playing it together.

As a band between friends, we'd share loads of information. Even when I was getting guitar lessons, that was the idea! My teacher would say, "try to sort this out. And yes, you can draw some chord boxes down if you want."

My point is: when I first started learning, there was very little reading and writing of music.

The Turning Point

A real turning point came when I was 17. I had to decide what exactly I was going to do with my life - was I actually going to pursue music as a career? Would I go to University and study Engineering or Business or whatever?

The only Music University in my hometown, Hobart, was the Tasmanian Conservatory of Music, a Classical Music school, and I decided to try that. :)

At that point, I could only get along with the tabs my guitar teacher had previously shown me. I remember learning a classical piece he'd written out in a tab, and I tried to figure it out. Still, as soon as I could get away from the music, I would.

But if I wanted to go to that music school, I would learn how to read music.

How I Learned To Read Music

I knew that the guitar teacher at the Conservatory was John McMillan, and he used to own a local music store. So, one afternoon, I popped into the music store and asked to have a little chat with him. I wanted to know if I had the chance of actually getting in or not the school!

He was a nice guy, so we went downstairs, and I played some songs for him. He asked me how was my sight-reading. I said right away: "I can't read for guitar. I know the notes are a little bit, but I can't read."

He explained I couldn't come to a Classical Music school if I couldn't read music. In my mind, that sounded like I would have to go study Engineering or do something different. :( But then, John said he'd give me a chance.

The Book

He disappeared off the back of the store and came back with this book by Fernando Sor. He opened it in this very complicated page, popped it down in front of me, and said: "if you can learn this and come back to play it for me in two weeks, I'll let you in."

Ok, challenged accepted.

😅 But I'm looking at that picture now, and I'm like… happy I didn't give this a serious think before accepting the challenge!

All I thought was that I could play this piece in a couple of weeks, which would solve all my problems! I now knew what I was doing with the rest of my life, and that was pretty exciting.

The 2 Weeks

I remember coming home, still living at my parents' house, and opening up this book to start studying. It didn't take too long to encounter my first really big problem. I always mention in my theory lessons: the fact that we can play one note in more than one place on the guitar neck.

So, I've got this chart showing all of the notes on the stave. They had little lines pointing to where they went on the neck. I ended up just converting it to tab, working out the notes, calculating how it was even possible to play some of those chords.

But I managed to get my way through it. It took me about 10 days to figure out those notes and calculate how to play them. I learned the piece, not really how to read music.

How to Get Away Now?

I had a few days left to try and memorize this piece. I knew that if I went down and put the music up, I wasn't reading the music, and I couldn't take the tab in. That would give the game away that I hadn't learned to read music!

😅 I think John McMillan had figured it out pretty quickly that that was the case, but still. :)

So, I managed to learn it. I memorized most of the tune - not particularly well, but most of it.

Back to the Music Store

I remember it was a really miserable cold day, and I was really nervous going back in there to play the piece to John. It was just terrifying.

We sat at the back of the store, and I played through it. I knew I wasn't getting it right, and I got the order of some of the bits right. So, I kind of got the right notes in the wrong order.

😅 Sometimes, I struggled because I was looking at the page to pretend I was reading the music sheet when I should have been looking at my hands. :)

Anyway - I just remember looking up and thinking that I'd blown it. And that it was all going to be over soon! But no.

The teacher had a big smile on his face. And then he told me I'd have a place on the course as long as my grades were okay. "Go home and practice this for the official audition, but don't worry about it. You're in.", he said.

A New, Exciting Adventure

I was just so excited that John started talking about all of the stuff we could do together. And it was just like the beginning of this whole massively exciting adventure for me.

John was a fantastic teacher. He didn't just teach me a classical guitar because he was a classical guitar teacher at the school. In fact, John wasn't really a classical guitar player. He was a Jazz guy, a Rock guy.

He was really into music and guitar, and he taught me all about practicing. He was pretty ruthless! He had an eight-hour-a-day practice routine for me, but he was a great teacher. John really helped me with a lot of stuff.

The moral of this story? I'm not really sure if there's one. Still, you're probably wondering: should you learn to read traditional music notation as a guitar player?

Music Notation for Guitar Players

It's worth learning to read music if you really need to. Part of the reason for this video and doing this little talk was the feedback from guitar students who spent frustrating periods trying to read music.

Learning these little single-note melodies and reading the dots and all of that is just not a great way to start playing guitar. If you just want to play your favorite songs and stuff, chances are you don't need to learn how to read music.

Learning single notes might be cool, but learning chords and songs is a much better idea to understand how music works. Ultimately, that allows you to understand your guitar fretboard and make music yourself!

Reading music on guitar is kind of tricky because of that thing that you can find the same in more than one place. That makes it even more complicated than learning to read music for piano, for example.

If you're going to learn how to play Rock or Blues, reading music becomes a lot harder than it would be just to listen to it!

Do This Instead! :)

It's much more important to develop a good ear and a good sense of rhythm. For most people, learning to read traditional notation is a waste of time! You'll probably be much better off learning other things!

When Should You Learn Music Notation

You should definitely learn to read music if:

You want to play jazz.

If you want to play classical guitar.

If you need to read music to play in reading gigs.

If you wanted to arrange for instruments that read music.

If you're a songwriter, even if you want to write out stuff for a violin or any other instrument on a most basic level.

The Best Approach

Guitar tabs are really fantastic for guitar players because they show you the note and where to play it on the fretboard.

Learning tabs is great, but don't forget to study your fretboard and learn where the notes are. People still learn guitar and think it's okay not to know the notes, but it's not!

So, to me, the secret to fretboard freedom is that combination of understanding the tab and knowing the notes on the neck.

💡 Reading rhythms is a really good thing when you're learning to read standard notation! You can learn rhythm independently! I learned rhythm using The Lewis Belson Modern Reading. Still, I created a great book to help you read rhythm for guitar playing.

So, if you meet somebody who's learning to play guitar, please don't recommend starting with learning to read music.

Want to learn more? Understanding how music works is your way to go!

lessons.title: ToneWoodAmp 2: Acoustic Guitar Effects with Mike Dawes and Justin
lessons.summary: ToneWoodAmp creates effects that come straight out of the soundhole. You don't need an amp or pedalboard—just your guitar and this device.
lessons.text:
ToneWoodAmp 2: Acoustic Guitar Effects with Mike & Justin

The ToneWoodAmp 2 is the ultimate acoustic guitar effects device, often described as an acoustic guitarist's pedalboard. While electric players have long enjoyed reverb, delay, chorus, tremolo, flanger, and phaser pedals, acoustic players have rarely had access to such creative tools. That changes now—with Mike and Justin testing this incredible gear.

Unlike traditional pedals, the ToneWoodAmp 2 attaches magnetically to the back of your guitar (as long as it has a pickup) and uses the body's natural vibrations. The result? Studio-quality effects that literally come out of your guitar's soundhole—no amp or pedalboard required. Just your guitar, the ToneWoodAmp 2, and endless inspiration.

Mike and Justin show how different and inspiring this device is for acoustic players who want to unlock new sounds and creativity without the bulk of a traditional setup.

What's New in the ToneWoodAmp 2

The first ToneWoodAmp was already cool, but this version takes it up a notch. Here's what's different:

It's USB-C rechargeable and lasts much longer than the old AA battery setup.

A companion phone app allows you to save presets, adjust settings, and control a whole pedalboard.

You get more effects and ways to combine them — reverbs, delays, chorus, phaser, flanger, tremolo.

There are tools for feedback control, like a "Feedback Assassin" and a six-band notch filter.

You can still use the buttons on the unit itself, but the app makes everything easier and more flexible.

How It Sounds

The difference between it being on and off is night and day. With the effects running, the guitar fills the room with lush sound — Justin even thought his studio monitors had been left on. Please turn it off; suddenly, the guitar feels much more raw and bare.

It can do short room reverbs that add a bit of space, or big plate reverbs with chorus and delay that sound huge. Slapback delay, atmospheric space sounds, tremolo that feels like a Leslie speaker—all in there. And it's not just for advanced players. Even simple strumming or fingerpicking feels more inspiring when you've got effects happening from the guitar.

Installing and Using It

To get started, pop a little magnetic brace inside the guitar, and the ToneWoodAmp clips onto the back. Justin's had the same brace in his main guitar for almost 10 years with no problems. Once it's in, you can move the unit between guitars easily. The cool thing is you don't need to buy a special guitar with effects built in—you can use your favourite guitar and still get all the magic.

Playing Live

This isn't just for the sofa at home. You can run the ToneWoodAmp live like pedals by plugging the output into a PA or amp. Mike even uses it in shows, walking through the audience with effects, and people are blown away, wondering where the sound is coming from.

Who's Behind It

Ofer and Helene, a husband-and-wife team from Arizona, invented the ToneWoodAmp. The first version came out almost 10 years ago, and even though it was a rough-looking prototype, it sounded so good that it immediately caught attention. The ToneWoodAmp 2 takes everything further with more power, flexibility, and polish.

Final Thoughts

The ToneWoodAmp 2 isn't just a gimmick. Sure, it's fun to call it a "guitar toy," but it's more of an "inspiration box." Once you play with it, turning it off feels like something's missing. It makes practicing at home more fun, writing songs more creative, and live performances more engaging.

lessons.title: Review: Boss Katana Gen 3 Guitar Amplifier
lessons.summary: Guitar amplifiers have seen many innovations, but few have made as much impact as the Boss Katana series!
lessons.text:
Exploring the New Boss Katana Gen 3: An Amplifier Revolution

Guitar amplifiers have seen many innovations, but few have made as much impact as the Boss Katana series. As a long-time fan of the Katana amps, I've used them extensively in workshops and live settings. When the Katana Mark 2 was released, it quickly became a go-to for its versatility, sound quality, and ease of use.

Whether you're a beginner or an intermediate player, the Katana Mark 2 offers an exceptional experience, making it one of the best amplifiers on the market. So, when the opportunity came to check out the new Katana Gen 3, I was eager to see how Boss could improve on what was already an outstanding piece of gear.

The Katana giveaway winner is Neil (@nellicus). Congrats! 🥳

Under the Hood: The Core Platform

The first thing you'll notice about the Katana Gen 3 is its familiarity. The top panel remains largely unchanged, a nod to the "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" philosophy. However, significant changes lie beneath the surface. The core platform has been completely revamped, making this amp more powerful and versatile.

The Katana Gen 3 continues to utilize a class AB power amp, a feature that emulates valve amps at an almost component level. This is where Katana stands out, offering a tube amp's dynamic feel and response, which is often missing in digital alternatives. The Tube Logic technology embedded in the Katana Gen 3 ensures that you get the authentic tube amp experience, where the harder you play, the more the amp responds.

New Features: Vintage Tones and Modern Convenience

One of the most exciting additions to the Katana Gen 3 is the new "Pushed" amp channel. This channel is designed for players who crave a more vintage-inspired sound. With previous Katanas, you typically had to choose between a clean or crunchy sound, but the Pushed channel fills the gap, offering that sought-after vintage amp vibe.

The Katana Gen 3 also introduces Bluetooth as an optional feature, allowing music streaming and remote control via a smartphone or tablet. This addition is a significant upgrade for those who want more flexibility in interacting with their amp. The updated editor software is now more user-friendly, making it easier than ever to tweak your sound. Additionally, the headphone output is now stereo, greatly enhancing the practice experience when you need to keep the noise down.

The Sound: A Deep Dive into Tone

The Katana Gen 3 offers five main amp sounds: Clean, Pushed, Crunch, Lead, and Brown. Each sound can be further customized with variations, allowing you to dial the exact tone you want. For instance, the Clean sound now has a variation that adds a bit more top-end sparkle, perfect for those who prefer a brighter tone. On the other hand, the Pushed channel gives you that "on-the-edge" sound that's great for Blues and Classic Rock.

As you move up to the Crunch sound, you'll find yourself in AC/DC territory, with plenty of scope to adjust the gain and volume for a wide range of tones. The Lead and Brown channels take you into high-gain territory, ideal for solos and heavier music. The Brown sound, in particular, has a sustain that seems to go on forever, making it perfect for those Van Halen-inspired riffs.

Dialing In: Controls and Effects

The Katana Gen 3 is designed with simplicity in mind. Nearly all settings are intuitive, with the knobs at noon serving as your basic starting point. This "What You See Is What You Get" (WYSIWYG) approach makes it easy for beginners and experienced players to find their sound without getting lost in menus or presets.

The amp also includes a three-band EQ with an added Contour feature, allowing you to shape your tone further. The Contour settings provide different EQ curves that can enhance various aspects of your sound, whether you need a low-end boost or a mid-range cut for soloing.

When it comes to effects, the Katana Gen 3 doesn't disappoint. With five effects blocks—booster, modulation, effects, delay, and reverb—you have all the tools to craft your perfect tone. These effects can be controlled directly from the top panel, or you can dive deeper into customization using the editor software.

Gigging and Recording: The Power to Perform

The Katana Gen 3 is available in a 100-watt version, which is powerful enough for live performances. It features a power control that allows you to switch between standby (silent for recording), half a watt, half power, and full power. This flexibility ensures you can get the best sound at any volume, whether at home, in the studio, or on stage.

For those who love to experiment with sound, the amp includes a cab resonance feature that allows you to adjust the low-end response, giving you even more control over your tone. The presence control adds that final bit of sparkle to your sound, while the solo option provides a clean boost for when you need to stand out.

This Amp is an Investiment!

The Boss Katana Gen 3 is more than just an upgrade; it's a significant step forward in the world of guitar amplifiers. Whether you're a beginner looking for your first amp or an experienced player searching for versatility, the Katana Gen 3 has something to offer. Its powerful core technology, user-friendly design, and wide range of tones make it a must-have for any guitarist.

So, if you're in the market for a new amplifier or are curious about what the Katana Gen 3 can do, I highly recommend checking it out. With its ability to grow with you as a player, this amp is not just a purchase—it's an investment in your musical journey.

Unboxing the D'Addario XPND Pedalboard

Coated or Plain Acoustic Guitar Strings? Which Sounds Best? Which Is Better For You?

D'Addario has just sent me their new XT strings, so we will compare those with the regular XS Coated Strings, which I've been using for some time, and the Uncoated Phosphor Bronze strings.

GIVEAWAY! 🍀 🎁 D'Addario is celebrating Change Strings World Day, and you can get free strings and more. :) The prizes are as follows: 100 Students win a set of XS Strings. The first place wins 12 sets, a maintenance kit, an AutoLock strap, and a Nexxus 360 Rechargeable tuner. Due to competition laws, this giveaway is only open to the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, and Canada residents. 👉 Enter the Giveaway Here. Good luck!

Before we explore these different acoustic guitar strings and which one might be the best for you, let me share a bit about my journey and preferences!

My Favorite Acoustic Guitar Strings

I didn't like coated strings for the longest time. Way before trying the D'Addario ones, other popular brands would send coated strings to me occasionally, but I didn't think they sounded good. They always sounded flat and dead, and they got rid of some string noise, like that little finger scratchy thing that seems to disappear on the coated strings, but that sometimes sounds nice. They last longer, but why would I put them on when they didn't sound as good?

But with the D'Addario XT Strings, I thought they sounded as good as the out-of-the-box ones and lasted much longer. I'm constantly putting new regular strings on for the guitars I use for recording just for that bit of brightness, but today's test might change that! I might put the coated ones on straight away. But I always put coated strings on guitars I don't play as often because they last long before you have to change them. So, coated strings are something that I use now all the time, which means I'm very curious to test these out!

Testing & Changing Strings!

I've left my old strings on to start this video. They're coated strings, but I haven't changed them for months. I'll strum and pick with them, then change for the XT and the Uncoated Phosphor Strings.

My Setup

I normally record my acoustic guitar plugged into the Kemper. I use this free patch called Acoustic Jr. Shelter. It's plugged in, but a little microphone generally picks up the acoustic guitar. I have a microphone hidden in my hat here! And in addition to that, I use a nice Neumann U87. It's an old vintage microphone that belonged to Hugh Padgham and probably recorded a few Police songs in its time. That goes directly into my Logic door!

💬 Watch the test! Then, Join the Discussion and let me know which strings you prefer. :)

lessons.text:
The BOSS Waza-Air headphone amp is way cooler than I expected!

I didn't get it when BOSS first offered me a pair of their WAZA-AIR Wireless Personal Guitar Amplification System to try. I already had great amplifiers and incredible headphones, so why did I need an amplifier in my headphones? But after giving some of them as a gift to my workshop students and seeing how they were fans of it, I decided to check them out. And I'm really impressed!

🚨 Disclosure: I received these headphones for free from BOSS, but they didn't pay me to make this video.

Waza-Air: Product Review

One of the coolest things about Waza-Air is the convenience factor. They're wireless, so you only need to plug the transmitter into your guitar and put on the headphones. No more dealing with cables and amplifiers! Waza-Air is also great for travel - they're so compact. But convenience isn't the only feature that impressed me!

Waza-Air also comes with a gyro sensor and moving 3D space to deliver natural "amp-in-room," way cooler than I expected. It helps with the fatigue of using regular headphones. This effect is also cool for playing with a backing track: it feels like you're playing on stage with a band!

🦶BOSS also sent me their Wireless Footswitch, which can control the headphones hands-free. You can change patches using the little buttons on the side, but you must stop playing. The footswitch is cool if you're jamming with a backing track and want to move from a clean to a dirty sound. You can also add additional effects and stuff, toggle on an extra gain or a delay using the foot switch, so it's a really cool little addition.

The build quality of Waza-Air is definitely pro. They feel well-made and sturdy, and the removable headphone pad is a useful feature for cleaning. You can use them as regular Bluetooth headphones as well!

👎 Of course, there are some cons to consider. The built-in tuner could be more accurate. I also found the initial setup a bit fiddly and was disappointed they didn't use a USB-C connection. Also, remember you cannot substitute an amplifier for these headphones to play a gig, for example!

However, I'm impressed with the BOSS Waza-Air headphone amp. They're great for practicing at home or while traveling, and the gyro sensor is super cool. They might be slightly expensive, but the convenience and quality make them worth considering if you're in the market for a headphone amp!

lessons.title: All About Travel Guitars
lessons.summary: Let's review two great travel guitars and explore the best option for you – Wooden or Carbon Fiber?
lessons.text:
This is a bit of a different video. :)

It's rare that I review gear, but I've been looking for an excellent travel guitar to take to my workshops around the world. In my search, I ended up in contact with Journey Instruments. They have an amazing range of instruments and accessories, including carbon fiber and wooden acoustic travel guitars. If you go shopping, check out the coupon code they're offering my students at the end of this post!

Naturally, I don't feel like taking my customized Gray Guitar or my I-gave-my-kidney-for-it Froggy Bottom on my adventures. Humidity, sand, salty water, and airlines are not your guitar's best friends. If you've tried that before, you know that traveling with a full-size guitar can be pretty awkward.

So, the folks at Journey Instruments sent me two travel guitars to try out, and I thought I'd make a video comparing them! It was my first time playing these guitars, and unboxing them was a cool experience – it's so great that their necks detach from the body! I think you'll like watching that in the video. :)

Now, let's get my honest opinion on the Overhead+ Solid Sitka Travel Guitar and the Burgundy Top Matte Carbon Travel Guitar.

Carbon Fiber Travel Guitar vs. Wooden Travel Guitar

Both instruments have identical specs.

According to Journey Instruments, "the OF422 Overhead® collapsible acoustic travel guitar features a solid Sitka top with solid Pau Ferro Rosewood back with a wider 13.25″ lower bout. It collapses to the carry-on size of 22 * 14 * 9 inches! It assembles in 20 seconds with our patented detachable neck system that's guaranteed for life. A full 24.5-inch scale, a versatile 1 3/4 nut width, locking 18:1 Journey Tuners, best-in-class components, and a wedged ergonomic design make this the most enjoyable guitar you’ll ever play! Tri-piezo pickup and a full-featured TSA-compliant carry-on backpack included."

Great Cost/Benefit!

Well, in a nutshell, I can say that the OF422 Overhead® sounds incredible and way better than most 700$ acoustic guitars. That was pretty surprising – especially when the neck detaches from the body. Ah, by the way, when I unpacked the guitar, she was pretty much… in tune. Awesome!

I'd definitely recommend the OF422 Overhead® if you plan to travel around with your instrument. It is not a high-end instrument, but it's great value for money. You can fly with it, and in a matter of seconds you can put it together and start strumming it!

When I go camping or stay in a caravan with friends and family, I'll bring the OF422 Overhead® with me instead of taking a full-size guitar! It's way more practical and way more fun!

The Top Matte Carbon Travel Guitar

Let's take a look at the Burgundy Top Matte Carbon Travel Guitar.

The first thing you'll notice is that the soundhole is in a different place, and that influences the tone. It's a lot quieter than its wooden counterpart. The Burgundy Top Matte Carbon Travel Guitar (OF660R1M) is less bright and punchy, but rounder and richer.

If I were recording, I'd prefer the carbon fiber one, but I'd go with the OF422 Overhead® for social occasions like parties. The carbon fiber guitar is also almost double the price of the wooden one. It does feel pro!

Here's the official description of the Burgundy Top Matte Carbon Travel Guitar: "This travel guitar collapses to the carry-on size of 22 * 14 * 9 inches! It assembles in 20 seconds with our patented detachable neck system. Our patented soundboard technology and all-carbon construction create a durable instrument with a massive tone. A full 24.5-inch scale, a versatile 1 3/4 nut width, best-in-class components, and a wedged ergonomic design make this the most enjoyable guitar you’ll ever play! Tri-piezo pickup and a full-featured TSA-compliant carry-on backpack included."

Now, the big question is…

Which Travel Guitar do I Prefer?

So, which travel guitar do I like the best? Well, the conclusion is that they're both fantastic, but they're different! I wouldn't say one is better than the other. If I really had to choose just one, I'd go with the OF422 Overhead®.

The OF422 Overhead® is way cheaper than the Burgundy Top Matte Carbon Travel Guitar. I thought I'd prefer the carbon fiber one – it's a high-end instrument, and it has a mellow sound that I love! But the OF422 is brighter and punchier, and that's what I'm looking for when playing outside.

The Overhead® is almost twice as loud as the Burgundy Top Matte, and that makes a huge difference when you play outdoors. The wooden travel guitar gives a more defined sound to the fingerstyle guitar.

Overall, both instruments are very high-quality! I'm impressed with Journey Instruments – definitely try them out when you shop for a travel instrument.
