lessons.title: Boss Katana mk.II REVIEW
lessons.text:
Meet the Incredible Boss Katana Mk. II Amp!

In this tutorial, we'll play around with the Boss Katana Mk. II amp and see what cool sounds we can get from it. This is a special amp - big thank you to Boss for sending it over to me!

The Boss Katana Mk-II is still the same Katana but they've added on lots of features that many people were requesting.

I'm using two classic guitar microphones, both are placed on axis, and they're going into my Universal Audio Apollo. I won't edit or change the effects on Logic Audio. Little trick before we begin: make sure you explore your new amp. Find the settings that work best for your guitar and your playing style!

Changes to the Previous Katana

The Katana Mk. II now has 10 amp styles instead of five. The modulation and booster are now split, meaning you can control them separately. They still light up, and there are still three modes for each.

Amp Settings

Let's look at finding the right settings for this amp. This is the 100W version, but I've set the power to 50W because I'm sitting next to the amp! Either setting can work for gigs, but 100W gives you a little more space when you're playing with a clean sound.

I've put the master volume to maximum and will control the overall volume using the volume knob. That way, we'll get the best dynamic sound from the amplifier. This works best for me – try it for yourself!

I have Presence at half volume, and I've turned off all the effects. On Boss equipment, having bass, middle and treble at halfway is the best starting point. If I put the volume high, I turn the bass down a little. As for the volume, I've put it a little below 9 o'clock to protect my ears, and the gain is at 12 o'clock.

💡 Buy your Katana Mk-II from Reverb and support the site! I get a small comission on your purchase, which helps me grow the site. Thank you!

How Does It Sound?

I love reverb, so let's put some on. From what I hear, the reverb on this amp is a little more "sparkly" than the previous amp. In Clean mode, you can hear that the amp has a very warm sound. Press the Variation button, and you get a sound that’s a little brighter and "Fender-y"!

The amp has a fantastic sound in Crunch mode and is great for blues. And with the Variation, the sound is heavier, thicker, and better for rock music.

In Lead mode, the sound is more sustained and saturated. This amp just sounds wicked in lead mode! I think it's best to play without Variation if you're playing in a band.

Brown mode sounds a bit more like Eddie Van Halen. Turn on Variation, and the sound is full of gain. It’s so cool that there are now 10 different sounds. The Variation button makes a huge difference!

Effects on the Boss Katana Mk. II

There are three different Boost modes, and each has a unique sound. On Clean, Green mode sounds bluesy, Red is muffled and rocky, and Orange gives a distorted rock sound. As for Modulation, Green has a chorus effect, Red sounds funky, and Orange is a flazer sound.

As for FX, Green mode gives you a rotary sound. It’s great for rhythm parts and blues. Red is a touch-wah effect – fantastic for funk. I love this sound! And Orange mode is the octave sound. Great with a bit of gain!

Moving onto the Delay effects now. The old Katana had three options: Digital, Analogue, and Tape Delay. You’ll find that Digital mode (Green) doesn’t change the sound – the delays are the same as what you play. Analog mode (Red) sounds a little muffled, and Tape (Orange) is a little more bouncy and degraded. I suggest you keep the delay subtle.

Onto my favorite: Reverb! I set this to halfway so we can really hear it. The Green setting is a plate reverb – nice and bright, great for atmospheric music. Red mode is a spring reverb, and Orange is a room or hall effect. All three modes are super useful and you’ll find using them all the time. Experiment with them, especially when trying to copy your favorite guitarists.

We haven’t looked at EQ options – I haven’t changed Bass, Middle, Treble, and Presence. We also haven’t touched the foot switch, loading sounds, or Tone Studio. But we haven’t needed to – there’s so much to explore on this amp! To access all the effects, check out the Tone Studio.

So, go explore the Boss Katana Mk. II and see what cool sounds you can find. This is my recommended budget amp – it's a fantastic piece of kit. Have lots of fun with it! :)

🎁 Learn more about Boss Katana and download free presets!

lessons.title: Matt Schofield: Groove, Chords & Blues Language
lessons.summary: Justin sits down with Matt Schofield and learn how he approaches modern Blues guitar.
lessons.text:
Groove, Chords & Blues Language

In this lesson, we learn how Matt Schofield approaches modern Blues guitar through the ideas behind his track "Catch My Breath" from Many Moons Vol. 1.

Matt Schofield is one of today’s most respected modern Blues guitar players, known for his groove, touch, chord vocabulary, and deep sense of feel. Rather than only learning a lick or copying a solo, this lesson gives us a closer look at how Matt thinks about Blues music as a language.

We explore how groove, harmony, rhythm guitar, chord voicings, soloing, phrasing, and altered sounds all work together to create a more expressive Blues sound. Matt breaks down the musical choices behind the track and shows how small details can completely change the feel of a progression.

This is a great lesson for guitar players who already know some Blues basics and want to understand how to move beyond simple pentatonic scale ideas. We learn how Matt connects rhythm and lead guitar naturally, how he uses small chord shapes to add color, and how he brings tension and release into his soloing without losing the feel of the Blues.

Learning Blues Guitar Beyond Pentatonics

Many Blues guitar players start with the minor pentatonic scale, and that is a great foundation. But to sound more musical, we also need to understand groove, chord movement, phrasing, timing, and harmony.

In this lesson, Matt shows how Blues vocabulary can become much richer when we listen to the chords, respond to the groove, and choose notes with intention. We look at how altered sounds, chord tones, and small voicings can add more color while still keeping the playing rooted in Blues feel.

The goal is not to make Blues complicated. The goal is to hear more, feel more, and make stronger musical choices.

What We Learn In This Lesson

How Matt Schofield thinks about Blues guitar language

How groove shapes the sound and feel of a Blues track

Why rhythm guitar and lead guitar are deeply connected

How small chord voicings can create movement and color

How to move beyond basic pentatonic scale patterns

How altered sounds can fit naturally into Blues guitar

How phrasing, touch, timing, and space affect every line

How chord harmony can guide better Blues soloing

How Matt builds musical tension and release

How to make simple ideas sound more expressive and intentional

Who Is This Blues Guitar Lesson For?

This lesson is ideal for intermediate and advancing Blues guitar players who want to go deeper than basic licks and scale shapes.

If we already know some pentatonic patterns, 12-bar Blues ideas, or basic Blues rhythm guitar, this lesson helps us understand how those pieces can become more musical. Matt’s approach gives us a way to think about Blues guitar as a conversation between groove, chords, melody, and feel.

It is especially useful if we want to improve Blues phrasing, expand our chord vocabulary, understand modern Blues harmony, or make our soloing sound more connected to the music underneath it.

About Matt Schofield’s "Catch My Breath"

"Catch My Breath" comes from Matt Schofield’s Many Moons Vol. 1. In this breakdown, we use the track as a starting point to understand how Matt builds a modern Blues sound.

We listen to the way the groove works, how the chords support the feel, and how the lead ideas sit inside the rhythm. Instead of treating the song as a collection of separate parts, we look at how everything connects.

That is what makes this lesson so valuable: we are not just learning what Matt plays. We are learning how he listens, thinks, and makes musical decisions.

lessons.text:
In this lesson, Justin sits down with Chris Buck to explore what makes rhythm guitar feel musical, expressive, and alive.

Chris is known for his incredible touch and feel, but one of the most interesting parts of his playing is how much attention he gives to rhythm. Instead of treating rhythm guitar as “just chords,” he approaches it as a creative part of the music: something that can support the song, shape the groove, and add personality to even the simplest progression.

We talk about how rhythm guitar connects to feel, dynamics, timing, and space. Chris also shares ideas on how to make chord parts sound more intentional, how to listen like a band member, and how small changes in touch can completely change the way a part feels.

This is a great lesson for anyone who wants to move beyond simply playing the right chords and start making rhythm parts sound more musical.

What We Learn

How Chris Buck thinks about rhythm guitar

Why feel and groove matter as much as the chords themselves

How to make simple parts sound more expressive

Why space and dynamics are such important parts of rhythm playing

How rhythm guitar supports the song and the other musicians

Ways to develop a more musical touch in your playing

Who This Lesson Is For

This lesson is ideal for intermediate guitar players who want to improve their rhythm playing, groove, and musical feel.

It’s also helpful for blues, rock, and roots players who want to sound more confident when playing with others, writing parts, or supporting a singer or soloist.

About Chris Buck

Chris Buck is a Welsh guitarist best known for his expressive, vocal-like playing style and his work with Cardinal Black. His touch, tone, phrasing, and feel have made him one of the most admired modern blues-rock guitarists. In this conversation, we look beyond lead guitar and dig into the rhythm side of his playing: the choices, instincts, and details that help make his parts sound so good.

lessons.text:
Philip Sayce on Finding Your Blues Voice

In this conversation, Justin sits down with blues guitarist Philip Sayce to talk about guitar tone, phrasing, practice, improvisation, and the lifelong journey of finding your own voice on the instrument.

Philip shares stories about discovering guitar through players like Stevie Ray Vaughan, Eric Clapton, Jeff Healey, Albert Collins, Buddy Guy, and B.B. King, and explains how listening, repetition, and real emotional connection shaped his playing.

Learning Blues Like a Language

One of the central ideas in this interview is the comparison between Blues guitar and language.

Philip talks about how Blues has its own vocabulary—certain phrases, bends, rhythms, and expressions that many players share. But just like spoken language, every player eventually develops their own accent and personality through the way they use those ideas.

Rather than trying to copy another player perfectly, Philip explains how we can take inspiration from great players and slowly turn those influences into something personal.

Playing From the Heart

Throughout the conversation, Philip returns to one important idea: getting out of the head and into the heart.

While technical practice and repetition matter, the goal is not robotic perfection. The goal is expression.

Philip explains that some of the most powerful moments in Blues music are not technically perfect—they feel human. Small imperfections, dynamics, touch, vibrato, and phrasing all contribute to emotional impact.

This idea connects strongly with Blues improvisation. Instead of overthinking every phrase, Philip encourages us to react emotionally, stay present, and allow the music to flow naturally.

Practice, Repetition, and Feel

Justin and Philip also discuss the balance between focused practice and free expression. Philip describes spending years listening closely to recordings, rewinding performances, learning by ear, and constantly refining his playing. Even after decades of touring and recording, he still approaches guitar as a student.

The conversation explores:

Practicing bends, vibrato, timing, and phrasing

Building vocabulary through repetition

Learning by ear

Playing with great drummers and developing pocket

Staying relaxed while keeping strong timing

Practicing enough that the body reacts naturally during performance

Philip compares this process to athletes training movements until they become instinctive.

Finding Pocket and Groove

Another major topic is groove and timing. Philip explains how great Blues and Rock players do not always play rigidly to a metronome. Sometimes the music pushes forward slightly or lays back behind the beat, creating tension, movement, and feel.

Justin and Philip discuss how difficult it can be to explain “the pocket,” but also how obvious it feels once we experience it. The conversation highlights the importance of:

Listening deeply

Playing with strong drummers

Staying relaxed

Letting music breathe naturally

Developing feel over time

Philip’s Guitar Tone and Gear

Philip also shares details about the gear behind his sound. He talks about his beloved 1963 Stratocaster “Mother,” which has been his main guitar for decades, along with his relationship with Seymour Duncan and the recreation of his pickups.

The conversation also covers:

Fender-style tube amps with headroom

Super Reverbs and Twin Reverbs

Cesar Diaz amplifiers and pedals

Vintage Tube Screamers

Fuzz Faces

Dynamics and touch sensitivity

The importance of human feel in tone

Rather than chasing perfection, Philip focuses on touch, expression, and emotional connection.

A Lifelong Student of Guitar

One of the most inspiring parts of the interview is Philip’s mindset toward learning.

Even after years of professional touring, recording, and performing, he still approaches guitar with curiosity and humility. Whether listening to Hendrix bootlegs, studying phrasing, or refining timing, he continues searching for new ideas and new ways to express emotion through the instrument.

This interview is a powerful reminder that Blues guitar is not just about scales or licks—it is about communication, feeling, and personal expression.

If you love expressive Blues playing, great tone, improvisation, and the art of developing your own voice, there is a lot to learn from this conversation. Play on!

lessons.text:
Watch Jens Larsen Teach Me About Jazz Guitar!

I want to get back to playing Jazz guitar - it's always been fun for me, but there were a few hurdles that I couldn't get over before. But Jens Larsen knows his stuff, and I'm hoping he can give me a hand this time around. :)

💡Check out Jens Larsen's YouTube Channel! He's an awesome Jazz guitarist with excellent guitar lessons for you.

I had a 1-hour session with him the other day and decided to make that available to you. It helped me with my Jazz guitar questions and might help you too!

Justin's Jazz Guitar Background

Long story short - I played Jazz quite a bit over the years. I played in a Swing band when I was about 15 or 16, playing standards like "Night and Day," but I never did much soloing because we had an incredible saxophonist with a Paul Desmond vibe, so soloing wasn't my bag. And I never felt very comfortable in that zone anyway because, at that time, I was still primarily a Rock guitar player.

However, I've always enjoyed Jazz, and I've particularly liked Joe Pass, who was always a big hero for me with his solo guitar. I've learned a few Joe Pass things that I've transcribed over the years, and at some point, I could play roughly along with him. But mostly, I spent my time learning Fusion things like Larry Carlton and Robin Ford.

I haven't played much Jazz in the last 15 years. So, like now and again, I've picked it up, and I've tried to walk a bass, and I've done a few lessons on kind of slightly jazzy things, even maybe made a couple of arrangements of Jazz songs that I've enjoyed just as something creative to do. But there have been a couple of sticking points that I've had each time when I've tried to push through, and Jens Larsen doesn't appear to suffer from any of them, so I thought, "Let's see if Jen's can help me through." :)

Making the Changes: Connecting Scales & Arpeggios

My primary problem when playing Jazz guitar is not sounding like I'm making the changes. If I'm playing a Blues, I've got enough Blues vocabulary to play and imagine it. I always think too much when playing Jazz, which is probably a problem. That might be a separate one, but I tend to be running arpeggios because I'm thinking.

If I play Blues, I outline the chords, all arpeggio-based things. I make it melodic and find a little phrase. But I have trouble finding a motif to run through a pattern of changes when playing Jazz. :( Does that make sense? According to Jens Larsen, yes, it does - and he highlighted several things we can do to approach that. Keep reading to learn more about it.

Jens explained we must be able to play the changes, and there's nothing wrong with playing arpeggios. However, you still want to make it melodic, and it has to be more than just technical - more than just playing the right notes. One really useful thing is this idea of connecting scales and arpeggios so that you're not only playing arpeggios but also putting them in the context of where you need to make melodies. You're not only going to be playing arpeggios; you need to put them together with the scale to create the vocabulary of lines you listen to. If you listen to Joe Pass, Parker, or any of these guys, there's a mix of arpeggios, scales, and many other things. That's the thing to look at!

Watch for More!

Jens Larsen provided me with a valuable lesson in Jazz guitar. We discussed the challenge of connecting scales and arpeggios and how to overcome this challenge. He draws upon the teachings of the American pianist Barry Harris. He highlights the importance of understanding Diatonic chords in a scale and how to use them to connect different musical elements. Interesting insights!

Moreover, Jens Larsen stresses the significance of listening to and transcribing Jazz musicians like Grant Green, George Benson, Joe Pass, and Charlie Parker, who mostly use one-octave arpeggios. He explains how learning from these musicians can help in mastering the art of Jazz guitar and how this technique is often used in saxophones due to their limited range. By staying within one octave, jazz musicians can create intricate and complex musical phrases that are expressive and impressive.

We discussed practicing Diatonic arpeggios, Jazz linguistic marks and vocabulary, and other learning systems and things we should be practicing to be able to play Jazz guitar freely!

💡Jazz is not only the notes; it's also how you play them. :) Explore some of my Jazz experiments and lessons here!
