Fingerstyle Insanity!

I had a fascinating chat with Mike Dawes about his cover of Jump.

Mike Dawes' cover of Jump (Van Halen) is fingerstyle insanity - and he played it live in my studio! Mike is an incredibly talented guitar player and one of the most innovative guitarists of his generation. His ability to replicate the sounds of different instruments on the guitar is truly impressive, and his arrangement of Jump by Van Halen is a testament to his skills.

🔥 Mike Dawes' arrangement of Jump is unique and innovative. You can watch his original video here! ► Learn all Mike's acoustic guitar techniques in his 9-hour USB Mastercourse. ► Check out his Progressive Fingerstyle First Steps. ► Progressive Fingerstyle Essential Riffs (Immediate Download)

In our chat, Mike explained the techniques he used to replicate the sounds of the bass and keyboards in the song and how he used a Travis-like picking fingerstyle to give the bass notes a distinct voice and make them sound more interesting. For the keyboard part, Mike used hammer-ons and tapping to emulate the sound of the keys. He used different strings to create different inflections!

🎵 Tuning! Jump is actually in C, but Mike transposed it to D because it worked better in the D-A-D-G-A-D tuning.

Mike emphasized the importance of understanding the aesthetic of a song when transcribing it. It is essential to figure out what makes a song interesting and unique and replicate that in the arrangement. :)

The Importance of Rhythm

Mike also talked about the importance of rhythm in his arrangements. He mentioned often using a haptic pulse metronome to get into a rhythm before going on stage. Having a good sense of rhythm when playing live is crucial because adrenaline can cause you to play faster than you should. Mike's attention to rhythm is evident in his playing, and it is clear that he has a deep understanding of how rhythm works in music.

One of the fascinating aspects of Mike's arrangement of Jump is how he replicates the kick drum sound. He said that he played the bass notes in a way that emphasized the kick drum, which is typical in Rock music.

I Learned So Much From This!

Having this chat with Mike was incredibly insightful. I even wanted to give this arrangement a go and try to play it as well! :) Check out my attempt at transcribing his arrangement here - it's so difficult on many levels.

I can't wait to hang out with Mike Dawes again.

👉 Check out my interview with Mike Dawes from 2012. Oldie but goldie. :)

lessons.title: Ariel Posen & Music Philosophy
lessons.summary: In this video, Ariel Posen & Justin Sandercoe discussed Dynamics, Improvisation, & Music Philosophy.
lessons.text:
Over the last lockdown, I had the chance to spend a cool hour with Ariel Posen.

Ariel Posen is a fantastic musician from Winnipeg, Canada, who has just released the album Headway.

🔥 Rolling Stones wrote that Ariel is a modern-day guitar hero. I’ll just say that I completely agree. Watching Posen plays is a delightful experience; don't miss him out!

In this video, we discussed Music Philosophy and explored what makes sense when studying music and what doesn't. If you're up for improvisation and developing your musical mind, I wouldn't miss out on this lesson.

You'll learn about Posen's tips on how to use licks and scales, connect with your music thoughts, and express your ideas through your guitar. Which details do you have to pay attention to when telling a story with a song? :)

We also explored what makes an audience connects with your music. People respond to specific things when listening to a song, and knowing what they are can be essential when composing.

But keep this message in mind: the most magical musical things happen when you don't overthink them!

Up for more Food For Thought? Let's play!

lessons.title: Simon McBride: Rock
lessons.summary: Simon is an incredible rock guitar player - crazy technique but moderated with taste and quality songs. If you dig rock then check this out!
lessons.text:
I've always found it cool how Simon McBridge's playing sounds effortless.

He's an incredible rock guitar player and will share some of his best tricks about Rock guitar with us! We'll discuss how to balance Music Theory, technique practice, and the ability to play and create (great) music from scales.

🔥 There is so much you can do with just simple four notes. Use simple techniques and your ears, and you'll be surprised of how much you can do. :)

Watch the video interview for some incredible Rock guitar tips and food for thought on making music out of scales and basic techniques.

Have some free time?! Let's Play!

lessons.title: Tim Pierce: Layering Parts
lessons.summary: Tim Pierce explains his approach to layering guitar parts. This interview is pure gold!
lessons.text:
Tim Pierce is one of the finest session guitar players of our time.

Pierce has worked for artists such as Joe Cocker, Goo Goo Dolls, Michael Jackson, Roger Waters, and Alice Cooper and is a reference session guitarist for Alternative rock, Pop, and Metal.

Pierce explains his approach to layering guitar parts in this lesson, which is gold. We'll discuss balance, technique, and how to create guitar parts that work great for recording with other instruments.

💡 This video is part of my Lockdown Session, which contains Interviews with incredible guitarists recorded during the first Covid-19 outbreak! Don't miss out on the other chats. :)

We'll get into some real-world examples and explain common tricks found in songs by The Beatles, The Smiths, Coldplay, and much more. We'll even answer common questions I get in my popular song lessons!

And if you feel like you need to rewire your love for guitar, stick around to the end of the video and get some extra food for thought on how to keep your motivation high regarding guitar practice.

Let's Play! Explore my Playground and feed your inspiration. :)

lessons.title: Jim Campilongo: Misty Chord Melody
lessons.summary: Jim is one of my all-time favorite guitar players. In this lesson, we dig into his approach to chord melody and explore the jazz standard, Misty.
lessons.text:
A Lockdown Lesson with one of my favorite guitarists: Jim Campilongo.

Jim Campilongo is a country-jazz virtuoso from South San Francisco. His unique approach to guitar improvisation has captivated audiences and guitar enthusiasts for years.

Campilongo primarily plays Fender Telecaster guitars-he's even nicknamed the Telecaster Master! He has this incredible ability to weave sounds with his guitar.

🎸 Jim's live performance shows all that's possible with just a Telecaster and a small tube amp. There's a lot to learn from this guitar master!

Jim and I go way back! I met him on a trip to New York ten years ago while recording his Orange album. In this lesson, we have the privilege of picking his brains and learning some of his skills!

We'll discuss how Jim approaches chord melody, he has this nifty way of playing that brings out melody notes from chord progressions. We'll dig into his solo guitar techniques, harmonics, some of his signature tricks, and the jazz standard Misty.

Want more guitar fun? Explore my Playground!

lessons.title: Josh Smith: Killer Blues Chords
lessons.summary: Josh Smith is among the finest Blues guitarists ever, certainly in the top 10 living Blues guitar players!  In this lesson, he teaches Justin some killer blues chords!
lessons.text:
Josh Smith: one of the finest modern-day Blues guitarists ever.

If you love the blues, then you need to know Josh Smith. No, really - Josh Smith is a true master of the form and is undoubtedly among the top 10 living Blues guitar players. He's played at the Grammy awards and with icons like Mick Jagger, Raphael Saadiq, and others.

🎸 He's praised worldwide as a blues rock guitarist, singer-songwriter, and producer who blends his signature styles into dynamic original songs. So yeah, he's a big deal. And you'll learn more about him in this Lockdown Lesson.

For Jim, all guitar starts with Blues. His depth of knowledge is astounding, and he has an uncanny ability to memorize hundreds of songs and solos from those same musicians. This makes him an incredible player on stage or in the studio.

In this video, we'll explore some of Josh's killer blues chords and how he applies jazz grips in a Blues context. Smith also shares where he gets his inspiration and gives you solid tips you can use in your playing. If you dig his playing, check out Josh's fantastic course on Truefire (I got it!).

More interviews with guitar masters available here.

lessons.title: Chris Buck Articulations
lessons.summary: We're diving into Chris Buck's signature trademark articulation in this interview!
lessons.text:
Blues-Rock Guitar player Chris Buck shares his signature trick.

We've got an incredible guest today: Chris Buck. He's a seriously talented British musician and guitarist for Cardinal Black. If you haven't checked out their music yet, do it now!

⚡ Chris has been voted 'Best New Guitarist', 'Best Blues Guitarist' and 'Best Pop Guitarist' in successive years by the readers of Guitarist Magazine. No biggie, right? ;)

I was lucky enough to get Chris to come by the studio for this interview. In this video, he'll teach us how he does his trademark articulation - a speedy slide that he uses with significant effect to make his playing very vocal and dynamic!

Chris uses it in loads of different ways, and we picked out 4 of them and tabbed them out for this lesson. It's a LOT to explore, and the best way to absorb it is one by one. Choose one, and work it in until it starts to appear without thinking about it. TAB and Guitar Pro files are available in the 'Resources' section under the video.

Let's chat more about Chris Buck's guitar journey!

lessons.title: Chat & Play
lessons.summary: Chat & Play with Chris Buck, and learn more about this guitar maestro's influence, career, and guitar journey!
lessons.text:
Chat & Play with Chris Buck.

Super special guest today - Chris Buck. As I was trying to transcribe some of the licks, I thought, why not invite him over? In this video, we'll get to know a bit more about Chris. We chat about his influence, career, and his guitar journey.

😯 Did you know? Slash has played onstage with Buck on more than one occasion and refers to him as an ''amazing guitar player''. No bigger, right? ;)

You can check out his Instagram, where you'll see snippets of how talented he is. And if you want to learn more about him, his current projects, and tour dates, head to his official website.

Explore Chris Bucks' signature guitar embellishments!

lessons.title: Playing Behind The Slide
lessons.summary: In this interview, Ariel Posen teaches us how he plays behind the slide.
lessons.text:
Ariel Posen Interview: Playing Behind The Slide

In this lesson, the master slide man Ariel Posen walks us through how he plays 'behind the slide,' and you get to watch me fumble about trying to get it together. How fun! ;)

💡 Finding this technique tricky? Don't fret! Take it easy and start with the simplified slide lessons in the Beginner Guide to Slide Guitar.

Playing behind the slides means mixing your fingers while you're playing the slide. Ariel teaches us some of his bests practices and tips, and we'll explore what you need to apply this technique to your playing.

Join us as we chat about Ariel Posen's single How Long.

lessons.title: How Long (Fine Tuning)
lessons.summary: In this lesson, we explore the finer points, chord variations & how melodic approach to Ariel Posen's song How Long.
lessons.text:
Ariel Posen's How Long: Chords variations, melody & adding 'oral treats.'

As you might know, I did a song lesson on Ariel's song How Long. A fortunate set of circumstances brought Ariel to the studio so we can check it out up close and personal!

🎵 This song has got such a great feel, and Ariel knows how to get the most out of his guitar. He plays with such emotion and feeling that it's almost impossible not to get swept away by it.

We chat about chord variations and his unique approach to adding the melody. Posen teaches us how he plays with his slide, which he does in live performances. He'll also define what it means to add 'oral treats' to your playing. His effortless approach to playing and creating music is inspiring. I hope you dig it! :)

Next up - join us again, and let's get into slide guitar.

lessons.title: Getting Into Slide Guitar
lessons.summary: In this lesson, Ariel Posen shows us how to start playing Slide Guitar.
lessons.text:
Getting Started on Slide Guitar with Ariel Posen.

In this lesson, Ariel gives us the low down and how you can get started with Slide Guitar. We'll talk about techniques, gear, and ideas you need to apply to make this technique work with your playing.

💡 If you haven't already, learn slide guitar fundamentals with my Beginner Guide to Slide Guitar.

First things first: the slide itself is the first important factor here. What works for one might not work for others; think of your slide guitar as a comfortable glove, not a random accessory. You shouldn't necessarily buy the first one you see at your guitar store!

It needs to fit properly and feel good enough to move freely while playing. The slide type will affect how you play, as some slides work better than others on certain types of strings and frets.

Then there's the actual technique itself. It's embellishing what you're already doing. You aim to play notes on the fretboard with one hand and move up or down the neck with another, plucking strings and sliding along them at different fingerboard points. Lots to digest here!

Up for more slide tips? Explore how to Play Behind the Slide with Ariel.

lessons.title: Ant Law. Interview with a Jazz Monster
lessons.summary: I met Ant many years ago and gave him just one lesson and he's gone off and become a great jazz guitar player!
lessons.text:
Interview with Ant Law: Jazz journey, adventures, and more!

Ant Law is a fantastic British Jazz guitarist. The Guardian hailed him as a "game changer" in the industry, and he has a unique start with music. Born in Saudi Arabia, he explored early blues, rock n roll, and Arabic music from a young age.

🎸 I met Ant Law many years ago, and back then, he was new to Jazz guitar. He came for a private Jazz lesson, and off he went on an incredible adventure and became a total Jazz monster!

In this video, we chat about his guitar journey, his new record, and some general stuff about jazz. If you're a jazz enthusiast, you'll want to check out his album Life I Know.

Up for more? Explore my Playground!

lessons.title: "Violining" technique with special guest Quist!
lessons.summary: In this interview with guitar master Quist, you'll learn more about one of his signature guitar sounds: the violining technique.
lessons.text:
Interview with Quist: guitar lesson on his violining technique

Quist - aka Jacob Quistgaard - is a Danish guitar virtuoso from Copenhagen, Denmark. He studied Jazz at the Royal Academy of Music on a scholarship and is seriously talented. He's the lead guitarist for British rock legend Bryan Ferry's rock band Roxy Music and has some cool guitar tricks up his sleeve!

🎸Quist has performed worldwide, including at The Royal Albert Hall, The Hollywood Bowl, Coachella, Glastonbury - the list goes on!

In this lesson, you'll learn the 'violining' technique Quist uses in one of his original songs. This technique has a few names: bowing, violoning, and Quist will teach us his approach by wrapping his little finger around the volume knob of his Strat guitar. Really neat stuff!

You'll also learn how to set up your guitar effects correctly, the different nuances of this technique, the tempo you should aim for, and what to do with your hands!

What are you waiting for? Loads more guitar fun on the Playground!

lessons.title: The History Of Guitar Techniques Magazine
lessons.summary: In this interview, you'll learn about the history of Guitar Techniques Magazine with Neville Marten and Jason Sidwell.
lessons.text:
Let's dive into the history of the Guitar Techniques Magazine.

In this video, Neville Marten and Jason Sidwell, both editors of Guitar Techniques Magazine, came to visit me. Neville has met and interviewed dozens of legendary guitarists, like Eric Clapton, Mark Knopfler, and George Harrison. As for Jason, he's the senior tuition editor of Guitarist and has written and edited over 20,000 printed articles since 1998.

📝 You'll find my Food For Thought column on the first few pages of the magazine. I've been doing bits for over 15 years! Get your print or digital copy available here.

Back in 1994, the magazine's very first cover was supposed to be Flea against Satriani in a who's the best competitive format. Instead of pinning them against each other, they opted to digest both individual musicians separately.

We had a great time chatting about the history of GT Mag & how this techniques-only magazine came to be. And we touch on their streamlining influence on guitar tabs we're familiar with today and what it takes to be a music writer.

More Playground fun awaits you.

lessons.title: Gordon Giltrap Interview [2012]
lessons.summary: In this interview, we sit down and chat fingerstyle guitar with legendary guitarist Gordon Giltrap.
lessons.text:
Interview with a fingerstyle guitar legend: Gordon Giltrap.

Gordon Giltrap is an English fingerstyle legend and has been hailed as one of the most revered guitarists of his generation. If you're not already familiar with his work, Giltrap, a creative genius with a signature acoustic sound, has seven album releases and has been praised by artists like Jimmy Page.

🔥 Check out Scattered Chapters, Giltrap's dynamic multimedia project created during lockdown.

I was thrilled when his management contacted me to set up a visit. Gordon is an excellent fellow, and we had a great time hanging out. In this video, we jam together and chat about his signature sounds and techniques, how his guitar journey started (with a plastic ukulele!), and more about his impressive career.

Got some time to spare? Let's play!

lessons.title: Mike Dawes Interview [2012]
lessons.summary: Come along as we chat with Mike Dawes, an acoustic guitar virtuoso with impressive percussive techniques.
lessons.text:
Interview with a master of acoustic solos: Mike Dawes.

Mike Dawes is an acoustic guitar virtuoso, and he's sitting down to chat with us today. Mike shot to fame with his unbelievably awesome cover of Somebody That I Used To Know, and I got in touch with him on Facebook after seeing the video.

💙 This video was one of the first times we met. We have since become good friends, so it's super fun to watch this back all these years later! :)

In this video, Mike shares some of his best tips and approaches for acoustic guitar playing, so make sure you tune in! You'll see that Mike is a cool and funny dude but also undoubtedly a master of the acoustic solo arrangement and percussive techniques. Join us as we pick his brain!

Up for more interviews with guitar masters?

lessons.title: Michael Fix Interview [2012]
lessons.summary: In this interview, we discuss fingerstyle techniques with acoustic guitar master Michael Fix.
lessons.text:
Let's get into fingerstyle techniques with Michael Fix.

Michael Fix is widely acclaimed as one of the world's finest acoustic guitarists, and he won numerous awards, including three Golden Guitars.

In this video, I catch up with the Maton player at the Frankfurt Musikmesse show. I manage to find a few minutes to make a video where he talks about his techniques, tricks, and musical influences.

🎵 We also get the change to hear Fix play some of his music. If you’re an acoustic guitar lover, I highly recommend you go see him live if he's playing near you!

More specifically, Fix will teach his use of the thumb pick - a signature fingerstyle technique that he got into in the 80s. Fix has developed his style of playing that uses a thumb pick that allows him to simultaneously play both bass lines and chords, giving him an almost orchestral sound when he plays. Exciting stuff to learn here!

Take your first fingerstyle steps with Fingerstyle for Beginners.

lessons.title: Martin Taylor Interview [2015]
lessons.summary: Interview with Jazz fingerstyle legend and Grammy Award-winning guitarist Martin Taylor.
lessons.text:
Interview with Jazz fingerstyle legend: Martin Taylor.

In this second interview with Grammy Award-winning guitarist Martin Taylor, we talk about ear training, melodic development, and how Martin approaches learning new material.

🎸 Guitarist, composer, and guitar teacher, Martin is considered by many (and myself!) a jazz fingerstyle legend. He's praised as one of the world’s foremost exponents of solo jazz and fingerstyle guitar playing.

In this video, Martin shares his insight & tips to strengthen the connection between the ear and your hand might. And unlike myself, it doesn't start with transcribing. Martin couldn't read music for the first 15 years of playing, but he had an incredible ability to visualize phrases and sounds on his guitar neck.

Martin possesses a signature style that artfully combines his virtuosity, emotion & skill you'll want to dig into. Dig his approach? You can learn fingerstyle and jazz guitar directly on his website.

If you haven't already, watch Martin's first interview.

lessons.title: Pierre Bensusan Interview [2015]
lessons.summary: Interviewing Pierre Bensusan, a French-Algerian acoustic guitar virtuoso, vocalist, and composer.
lessons.text:
Let's sit down and chat with Pierre Bensusan: the acoustic guitar maestro.

Pierre Bensusan, a French-Algerian acoustic guitar virtuoso, vocalist, and composer, has taken his unique instrumental sound worldwide. He is known as "Mister DADGAD."

Pierre is a true master of the instrument, and I am amazed by Pierre's DADGAD tuning ability. And we get to chat all about it in this interview! We get the treat of watching him play jazz and classical music for us in this impressive tuning.

💡 Check Pierre Bensusan website! He has awesome guitar lessons and is a fantastic musician!

In this video, Pierre shares some theory and insight to get you started with DADGAG, open tunings, and how to explore chord shapes. He emphasizes the importance of studying the fretboard and how playing chords is essential to diving deeper into this tuning. A little theory goes a long way, right? Fascinating guy, and he's got a lot of gems to share!

New to this tuning? Learn about DADGAD fundamentals.

lessons.title: Jim Campilongo Interview [2010]
lessons.summary: In this interview, guitarist Jim Campilongo sits down and chats about all things guitar and his musical journey.
lessons.text:
The Telecaster master, Jim Campilongo, is here to share his guitar journey and what inspires him to play.

It's not too often I get around to listening to albums that people say I should check out, but I'm sure glad I did when a mate told me to check out Jim Campilongo. His album Orange quickly became a favorite, and it was the soundtrack (along with another great New York songstress Kelli Scarr) for my amp schematic tattoo!

Jim Campilongo is a New York roots rock guitarist with some serious credentials. I was pretty excited when I found out that he would be performing in New York City, so I reached out and asked if he'd be interested in interviewing with me. He said yes, and here we are. :)

🎸One of Jim's signature technique employs a hybrid right-hand technique using both a plectrum and fingers. It's seriously awesome!

In this video, we chat about all things guitar. Jim is a super nice guy and humble about his achievements, and he walks us through how he started playing music and what inspires him today. Some excellent advice for aspiring guitarists.

I'm seriously obsessed with the way he plays the guitar. His tone, his touch - he's got some serious talent. Campilongo has this fantastic ability to get the right note in the right place all the time, and it's something I finally get to dive into. Hope you dig it!

Learn more about the Telecaster Master! Watch my most recent Campilogno interview.

lessons.title: Martin Taylor Interview [2010]
lessons.summary: Martin Taylor is one of the finest jazz fingerstyle players and this was the first time I met him for an interview. Real nice guy and explains some interesting stuff.
lessons.text:
I was shocked to learn that Martin Taylor, a jazz-guitar virtuoso, doesn't transcribe.

While hanging out at Guitar Nation waiting to interview Steve Vai, Martin Taylor came by to say hello to him. I've been a big fan of Martin's playing for years and spent hours transcribing his arrangements of standards. He kindly agreed to do this interview and share some of his tricks!

If you don't already know, Martin Taylor is one of the world's best solo jazz fingerstyle guitarists around. He has a unique approach to practicing & ear training which we dive into in this interview.

🎸 Martin is an absolute guitar master. His arrangements of standards are some of the most impressive fingerstyle guitars I've ever heard.

In this video, he talks about his musical approach and how he practices to get his sound. I was pretty shocked when he told me that he doesn't do transcribing! Turns out he practices in a different (but very effective) way. If you're interested in learning from this master musician, learn more about his guitar teaching here.

Years later, we met up again! Check out Martin's second interview.

lessons.title: Stevie Vai Interview [2010]
lessons.summary: All-time guitar hero Steve Vai granted me a really great interview back in 2010; he's so humble and down to earth!
lessons.text:
In this interview, I meet one of my all-time guitar heroes for the very first time: Steve Vai.

Steve Vai needs no introduction for guitar fanatics - the legendary guitarist is not only a three-time Grammy Award winner and fifteen-time nominee but also a songwriter and producer.

He's an inspiration to thousands of guitarists for decades now, and his playing is absolutely awe-inspiring! In this video, we get to chat with him about his beginnings as a musician and how, from a young age learning the guitar gave him a sense of achievement

🎸 Some of his most important advice regarding guitar is to find what excites you the most and go for it.

You'll learn about his systematic approach to practicing music and breaking things down into manageable chunks so you can master them one step at a time.

We'll discuss his music studies, where he surprisingly started composing before he even started playing the guitar. And Steve talks about his famous 10-hour workout that was famously published in magazines - which was more than 10 hours!

Up for more? Let's play!

lessons.title: Pat Martino Interview [1/2]
lessons.summary: In this interview, Pete fills in as we dive into the inspirations and musical approach of legendary jazz guitarist Pat Martino.
lessons.text:
One of the greatest guitarists in jazz, Pat Martino, shares how curiosity and imagination inspired his start.

We're honored to present this interview with legendary jazz guitarist and composer Pat Martino. Pat was a great person, he sadly passed on in 2021, but his legacy is a gift to us all. His playing style is full of soul and energy; there's a lot to learn from this master!

🎸 Martino has been nomiated for Grammys and multiple awards. He's been a recording artist for Vanguard, Prestige, Warner Brothers, Muse, Columbia - the list goes on.

In Part 1 of this interview series, Pat Martino talks about learning and playing the guitar, his career, and practice tips. Pat explains how curiosity and imagination inspired him to pick up the guitar. He has an incredible outlook on learning! If you're looking for inspiration, Pat has meaningful analogies that will inspire guitar players at any level.

Big thanks to Pete Whittard (the Guitar Institute director) for taking over this interview and Charl Coetzee for filming. Thanks to Guitar Getaways and The Guitar Institute for organizing the clinic and inviting me to participate.

Part 2 of Martino's Interview.

lessons.title: Pat Martino Interview [2/2]
lessons.summary: Part 2 of the Pat Martino Interview. What a legend and real nice guy too!
lessons.text:
Part 2 of legendary guitarist Pat Martino's interview: his philosophical take on music.

Pat Martino is a legendary jazz guitarist who spent years mastering the instrument. In this video, Pat talks about his unique approach to harmony and melody and how to develop those ideas.

🎵 Martino explains how listening to many genres develops a more powerful understanding of music. What are your thoughts on this concept? Share in the discussion area.

His philosophical take on music is worth exploring! Martino shares his thoughts on the relationship between nature and music, how they tie into harmony, and how you can apply that to your guitar playing. He also discusses his studies and how the piano had a place in his learning journey.

Missed Part 1? Watch Now!

lessons.title: Larry Carlton Interview [2008]
lessons.summary: Larry Carlton is one of my all-time favorite players and has been since I was a teenager. What an honor to chat with him!
lessons.text:
Watch me interview my long-time guitar hero: Larry Carlton.

Larry Carlton is an American guitarist who built his career as a studio musician with artists such as Steely Dan and Joni Mitchell. He has been a member of the Crusaders jazz fusion group and the smooth jazz band Fourplay and is an incredible solo musician.

The first time I heard his album "Last Night," I was floored and spent months transcribing the solo! Big thanks to Guitar Getaways and The Guitar Institute for organizing & inviting me to participate in this clinic.

😅 I was a bit nervous for this interview and forgot many of the questions I had wanted to ask. Funny how meeting your hero can do that to you!

Carlton is one of those guitar players I discovered in my late teens, and it changed my life! We got to jam one of his most famous tracks, "Room 335," at the end of his clinic. Safe to say, I was smiling for weeks. :)

In this video, we discuss all things guitar and how Carlton's inspiration started with his mom playing the acoustic guitar. His fascination with the instrument began when he was only four years old!

Carlton has the perfect touch when it comes to guitar playing. He plays real simple things that are just the ideal notes and perfect phrasing. Then, he burns it up and plays some challenging, yet meaningful fast passages. Lots to learn from this legend!

Want more? Lots of guitar fun available on the Playground.

lessons.title: Tommy Emmanuel Interview
lessons.summary: Back in 2006, I got Tommy Emmanuel on the phone for a chat. He's a fascinating guitar legend!
lessons.text:
Tommy Emmanuel has been a hero of mine ever since I saw him play at a theatre in Tasmania in the early 80s.

The passion and beauty I heard that night inspired me in a way that still resonates. So, it was a great honor for me to spend a little time talking with one of the greatest guitar players of all time! In this interview, we discovered some paths that helped Tommy Emmanuel become the incredible musician he is today.

Tommy is known worldwide for his unique and passionate playing. He employs great use of harmonics and rhythmic effects, which also makes him a fantastic drummer! His solo shows are amazing, and I strongly advise witnessing him in concert - you won't forget it!

He has been nominated for a Grammy Award twice. In 1999, Chet Atkins honored Tommy with the rare title of "Certified Guitar Player" for his lifetime contribution to the art of fingerstyle guitar playing.

For more information, head to his website for information, and tour dates and purchase his fantastic CDs and instructional materials. If you have not seen or heard Tommy before - check out his YouTube and prepare to be AMAZED (and buy some albums!)

The Interview

• You began playing guitar at a very young age - what things do you remember working on when you started?

Tommy Emmanuel - I remember everything. The first things I remember learning were chords and how to count bars and how to learn chord changes - changing from one chord to another one when I first started. That was the biggest hurdle, changing chords at the right time and understanding the meter. That was the first thing my mother showed me when I was four years old. It wasn't until 20 years or so later that I understood half bars, 2:4 bars, 5:4 bars, and all that kind of stuff. So that's the basics…

I learned song structures as well. I learned a way that really helped me figure out songs by looking for the patterns in songs and so learning that this verse repeats for that's an A [section], and then A [section] and then the chorus comes around, and that's B [section] so A A B is verse chorus, and then back to A for the second time and then to B and C is the bridge, key change etc. So I learned all that basic stuff that is really important.

And in actual fact, that has really helped a person like myself that plays everything by ear. It's really helped me to learn things quickly. Just using those basic principles.

• Did you find that you transcribed a lot, not necessarily writing it down, but learning songs and solos by ear - working out fingerpicking and strumming patterns?

Tommy Emmanuel - I have done that all my life as well, but what I'm talking about is learning a new song, and when my brother [Phil Emmanuel, also an amazing guitar player] wanted to learn a song, I had to work out the chords and work out the best way to play the rhythm for him. That kind of stuff was my job, y'know.

When I was getting into Chet Atkins, Merle Travis, and Jerry Reed, I could kinda hear what was going on, although in some of Jerry Reed's pieces - they were incredibly difficult, but a lot of CChet'sstuff, I could work it out, and not necessarily the right way. When I eventually met Chet, I got him to show me some of the things I was struggling with, and I figured out that I was basically trying to do it the hard way. There was a lot easier way of doing things.

That was a great lesson for me; always look for the way that's the easiest to play the song, get the melody out strong and also find the right key to play the song in where you can get as many open notes as possible, and get the melody to feel good.

📸 Tommy with brother Phil.

• A lot of players these days use the internet and find tabs (which are invariably wrong). I find it hard to convince them that all the great players learned a lot by learning by ear.

Tommy Emmanuel - I learned everything by ear. I have never read a piece of music in my life, and I have never read a piece of tablature in my life. But I have many books [laughs]

• Were you never tempted to learn theory and notation?

Tommy Emmanuel - I can do it quicker by ear! I tried to learn to read music when I was about 18 years old, and I was just no good at it. I just kept drawing a blank. I didn't understand it at all. I could work out things quicker by ear than by anything.

• Did you ever follow a practice routine? Tommy Emmanuel - I learned songs. I practiced technique. I practiced playing the songs, then developed my own kind of ritual of working out things to play that were difficult and then playing them over and over and over. And then I also developed the strength in my hands and in things like my little finger. I developed ways of making that strong and all that kind of stuff. I worked on motor skills as well as trying to learn about how music works and all that - I still don't really understand the theory of it, but I can pretty much play over any changes that you gave me. If I was lucky… :)

• That's a pretty mean feat…

Tommy Emmanuel - You train your ear. What my brother and I used to do was turn our backs to each other and play a note. And the person who didn't play the note had to guess it. And so we trained our ears to hear pitch and then hear chords. My brother would play an E7, and I would say that's E7, and then he'd say well, what's this, and then he would play an Eb9, and I had to figure out what that was by the sound of it. So I developed my ear like that.

• My teacher told me that story and I always wondered if that was true or not.

Tommy Emmanuel - Well it is true. We didn't do it on a regular basis like every day ‘cos we were always traveling. We would do it while we were driving along in the car, just to keep ourselves occupied.

• You started touring when you were very young…

Tommy Emmanuel - Just before my 6th birthday.

📸 The early days...

• Was that a dream come true or hard work?

Tommy Emmanuel - IIt'salways been hard work, but it's always been what I believe is what I'm called to do. I'm working harder than ever now. I am learning more, I'm playing better all the time, I'm writing new songs all the time, meeting players all over the world, and when I play, something happens to people who listen to it - so there is my reason for being there.

• Do you find your technique is consistent?

Tommy Emmanuel - I have up days and down days, just like everybody else, I think. There are some days when I go out there all prepared and I just can't string it together at all, and there are other times when it just seems to flow so easily that I have a magic carpet ride.

• It's a nice feeling when that happens.

Tommy Emmanuel - That's the one we live for!

• I heard a great story once about Chet Atkins. At the end of an interview, the interviewer said to Chet, "that guitar sounds amazing" Chet put the guitar down on the chair and said, " How good does it sound?" It's funny, but there is much to learn from that. Can you share any guitar stories that you found inspiring?

Tommy Emmanuel - Well there is an awful lot of them. I remember one time when Chet and I were recording our album together, the second track on the album called "To Be Or Not To Be." I was overdubbing a solo, I had already played all the melody parts, and then we were putting our solos on. And I had about ten goes at it, and I wasn't getting anything that I was really thrilled about. So I said, "Hey Chief, where shall I start with this?" And he said, well, you can't beat the melody! So I started the solo quoting the melody, and then it just flowed naturally. So instead of starting to take the solo somewhere immediately, I just started playing the melody first and that really opened it up for me, and away it went from there.

💡 "You can't beat the melody." That's the exactly the words he said.

• You are the master of guitar harmonics - how did that develop? Experimentation? was there someone who showed you the basics?

Tommy Emmanuel - Chet Atkins again. He recorded a song back in 1947 or 48 or something called "China Town, My China Town," and he made that sound. And he drove us all crazy. And then he came out with "When You Wish Upon A Star," and that stuff was the most beautiful harmonics, and I remember in my teen years trying to figure this out, and it seemed impossible. The truth is that he got a lot of his ideas from Lenny Breau, and Lenny kinda took it to another level, approached it in a different way. Then I have begged and borrowed and stolen as much as I possibly can from Chet and Lenny and made up my own stuff as well.

📸 Tommy Emmannuel and his Maton Guitar.

• And the harp harmonics specifically…

Tommy Emmanuel - Chet was doing that; I just have different ways of doing it. But I think the original idea belongs to him.

• I feel silly not having come across Lenny Breau…

Tommy Emmanuel - If you want to hear something really beautiful, you might get it on iTunes. If you go and find an album called " the best of Chet Atkins and friends,"- Chet and Lenny play Sweet Georgia Brown. Check that out. That is a masterpiece.

• Lastly, have you any words of wisdom or inspiration for the guitar players out there?

Tommy Emmanuel - Yeah, make sure you have some good songs to learn. Good melodies, good strong melodies, good grooves, that's what it's all about. DDon'twork about all this too much noodling around and trying to impress other musicians. Just play a good song. That's what people want to hear.

• They are fine words of wisdom. Thank you very much for your time.

Tommy Emmanuel - Alright, Justin, thank you very much for asking. I appreciate it, and maybe we can do it again sometime.

💡 Tommy Emmanuel plays Maton Acoustic Guitars.

Up for more? Let's Play!

lessons.title: Justin's Main Acoustic: Froggy Bottom
lessons.text:
This Froggy Bottom was the first acoustic guitar I've bought in years!

I had no intention of buying it, but I happened to be at The North American Guitar and played a few guitars - this one just spoke to me. As soon as I mortgaged my kidney, I had her! :)

💡 The Froggy Bottom became my main acoustic guitar! I've used it to almost all of my latest acoustic songs lessons.

Electrics She's fitted with a K&K Trinity Onboard system, mic, under-bridge pickups, and an additional Dimarzio Black Angel magnetic pickup which I use for driving effects. They come from a stereo jack and are split into two cables on my pedalboard.

Nick Benjamin was responsible for the setup and did an amazing job. This guitar plays and sounds sweeter than any other acoustic I've ever owned!

👉 Watch me explore my Froggy Bottom in this Live Session from 2018!

lessons.title: Gray Guitar Custom Build
lessons.text: In this video I take you through the spec (and why) of my new custom guitar made by Tom Gray (Gray Guitars: http://www.grayguitars.london). It's got Radioshop pickups (http://www.radioshoppickups.com) a Mastery Bridge (https://masterybridge.com) and it came in a sexy Reunion Blues Case (https://www.reunionblues.com) which I'll do a video about soon. Hope you enjoy finding out about "Little Sixes" and enjoy the vids coming up! Big thanks to Tom for making me such and awesome instrument!

lessons.title: Gretsch Malcolm Young Model
lessons.summary: This is simple and classy guitar is the only way to get 'that' AC/DC rhythm sound of the finest ever rock rhythm guitarist Malcolm Young.
lessons.text:
The Malcolm Young G6131SMY is a customized 1962 Reissue Jet with a single Filtertron pickup, master volume and tone control.

Basics

Brand: Gretsch

Model: Malcolm Young Signature G6131MY

Year of Manufacture: 1997-2007 (exact year of this instrument is unknown)

Country of Manufacture: Japan

Colour: Natural

Serial Number: JT041070-0

Mods

Sperzel locking tuners (not at time of video!)

History

Purchased from: Vintage & Rare Guitars (Bath, UK)

Date purchased: March 2010

Previous owners: Unknown

Setup

Strings: D'Addario NYXL Balanced Tension 11-52.

Not done much setting up on this - it's pretty much as it came from the store!

lessons.title: Fender Strat Plus Deluxe
lessons.summary: My very first 'proper' high-quality guitar that I bought when I was in my teens, and it's my most treasured instrument.
lessons.text:
Basics

Brand: Fender

Model: Strat Plus Deluxe

Year of Manufacture: 1989

Country of Manufacture: USA

Colour: Red

Serial Number: (coming)

Mods

Roller nut replaced with Buzz Feitin Tuning System nut.

Sperzel pro locking tuners

String Tree added

Stainless steel jumbo frets

Kinmann "Woodstock" pickup set

High tension springs in the back.

Schaller locking strap buttons.

History

Purchased from: McCanns Music Centre (Hobart, Tasmania, Australia)

Date purchased: 1990

Previous owners: None

Setup

Strings: D'Addario NYXL Balanced Tension 10-46.

The guitar was looked after by Charlie Chandler who did the rewire and set up including using the Plek machine. Charlie is amazing at guitar setups and is highly recommended if you are in the UK, a setup makes a HUGE difference!

I have the tone knobs set to control the neck and bridge pickups and not tone on the middle pickup. No other wiring mods.

lessons.title: Maton Court Jester (Custom Shop)
lessons.text:
This video introduces "Jessie" my Maton Custom Shop acoustic called "The Court Jester". I ordered this guitar just before the Katie Melua tour in 2007 and it arrived about halfway through the UK leg... I really like this guitar and play it more than any other.

It's a lovely guitar, a sweet very bright sound, and I love it for fingerstyle stuff... I thought it was a one off, but someone posted a comment on the original video that I had up and they had noticed that the picture on the Maton Web Site os the twin of my guitar, exactly the opposite woods. Cool. Wonder who owns that one? (link below)

The song I play is one of my own compositions called "From Katie's Window" that I wrote for my sister (not Melua as some people assume). For those interested it is in double drop D tuning. There is a better recording on Myspace if you wanna listen. This performance was a little sloppy too, I normally play it tighter than that, but this was a bit off the cuff, I didn't actually plan to play that tune, it just happened!

Sorry about the name confusion of the song... In the first go at uploading the video I had mistakenly called the song Broken Roses which I had been playing before I started editing the vid... and then I just had it in my mind and wrote it wrong. The song Broken Roses has had it's name shortened too, now it's just called Broken, so I screwed up lots all at once ;)

Anyhow, hope you dig it.

lessons.title: Maton Messiah
lessons.text:
This video introduces "Messy" my Maton Messiah acoustic. This was the first Maton I bought back in the late 90's (i think?). Was nice feeling to be working enough to afford the dream guitar that I had stood in front of in my local music store as a kid and dreamed of owning one day. I don't think I was even allowed to play it... just look at it in the window, I can remember it like it was yesterday...

It records incredibly well. It just sits in a mix perfectly and all the other dudes in my studio complex are always coming to steal it to play on their tracks, even though they all own nice guitars too!

For those few interested... the bits of tunes I played were "Cutting Out", "Every Dad's A Hero" and "Waste This". All my own tunes... album on it's way!

lessons.title: Maton Mini
lessons.text:
This video introduces "Mini" my Mini Maton acoustic. She is a fine sounding gal with a big fat voice for such a little thing. I play a bit of a new tune I am working on in a strange tuning (for the record it's: Db Bb Gb Db Gb Eb from thin string to thick - which is kind of a Open G tuning, with the thick E string at regular pitch, and then all down a semitone).

Hope you like it!

Because so many people asked already... This guitar is in a different league to the Taylor Baby guitar and the Martin Traveller. I have owned both of those other guitars, and I can promise that I would NEVER have used them in the studio. They were fine for hacking around in the back of the car and taking camping, but the Mini Maton, sounds amazing. Crowded House have used them live... now that is a proper endorsement!!!

lessons.title: Justin's Guitars - List and info.
lessons.summary: No demos or anything - this is just the old list while I make video's about each one!
lessons.text:
Last updated 26 April 2021. Yes I know I need to do a video about them all - will do it when I get back to my main studio, promise!

I've thinned out the collection quite a bit over the last few years - rather just have a few guitars that I really connect with than lots gathering dust :)

Acoustics

Most of my acoustic guitars are made by Maton a relatively small Australian company. They were the guitars I dreamed about owning one day as a kid and now I've got a few. So lucky!

Froggy Bottom - M Deluxe This was one of those accidents. I was at The North American Guitar store in the UK, the owner Ben is a friend of mine, and we were just playing a few things and I just totally LOVED the sound and feel of this instrument. I bought it pre-loved, they're a premium instrument, but you can really feel it. It's the most well rounded and rich sounding acoustic I have and it's the only one I kept with me while I moved out for 9 months while I renovated my studio! My Messiah sounds better for strumming or playing hard, but it's hard work too, you have to earn it - the Froggy gives it to you ;)

Maton - Messiah This is my main dreadnought style guitar, awesome for strumming, playing hard and this is the one that bought Hayden Bendall (the Abbey Road studio engineer) out from the control room to say "this is one of the finest sounding acoustic guitar's we've ever had in here!". It records amazingly, hardly needs any EQ and just sits real nice. It's a little hard to play, doing a whole song with all barre chords is quite an effort, but worth it when you hear it back... just means I never want to do too many takes!

Maton - Court Jester (Custom Shop) This is a Custom Shop guitar, it does have a twin but there were only two made, both by Andy Allen who is THE man at Maton. Smaller bodied and better for fingerstyle guitar, a lot more definition for that type of playing, a lot less powerful than The Messiah. It sounds great, but not as rich as the Messiah or the Michael Fix, but looks totally awesome and I toured with it for a long time so it carries a lot of fond memories.

Maton - Michael Fix Model I got this after knocking the Court Jester and wanting a guitar to take with me on tour, take home and take to parties and stuff... something that sounded great but was "standard" and wouldn't devastate me if something happened to her. But it's becoming close family now because I play it a lot and the sound is really opening up. I think these instruments take some time to reach their full potential cos it certainly sounds better now than it did for the first 6 months!

Maton - Mini I use this small sized guitar mostly for Nashville Tuning, and sometimes for parties or travelling. Sounds awesome, a tight sounding midrange, but somehow very open too, bright and sparkly. I like it a lot. It's not a toy guitar at all like some of the other small body guitars which are generally hard to play and sound very average. This plays and sounds amazing imho!

Maton - Messiah 12 String Always wanted a 12 String guitar and so finally took the plunge. So much fun to play, kinda tricky, but it really sounds great. Still needs some breaking in I guess, the sound is quite 'tight' but I like it a lot. I leave this guitar tuned down a tone which is pretty common for 12 Strings, which makes them a lot more playable than in standard tuning.

Journey - Burgundy Top Matte Carbon Travel Guitar - OF660R1M I get to travel to some awesome places to play guitar and when I got booked to do a workshop on a tropical Island bear Barbados I started worrying about taking one of my main acoustics... I got in touch with Journey and they sent me a couple of their travel guitars, this carbon on and a similar one in wood. The neck comes off and they fit in an overhead size bag for flights - super cool. And they sound great too! :) The perfect travel acoustic!

Richard Morrison - Custom Richard made this guitar for me in 2012, and it's a wonderful instrument. Very thin top and a very full sound, kinda quirky in a lovely way. Richard contacted me via the web site and just offered to make me a guitar, I told him something that I quite fancied and a year later he emailed and said it was ready! I popped over to his workshop in France and picked it up :) Big thanks Richard! :)

Electric Guitars

I've had hundreds of electric guitars in my life, but I'm trying to settle down now to just one of each of the main types of guitars that I need for sessions and recording, without going over the top... still on the hunt for an original Steinberger, a Dobro, a pedal steel... but then I'll stop buying guitars... honest :) ha ha yeah right!

2019 Gray Guitar - VIVI Custom I discovered Gray guitars when I was doing a workshop at the London Guitar Show, thought he made incredible guitars and asked him to make me one. He did. It's awesome, and it's my main guitar, the pink one with VIVI (My daughter's name) at the 12th fret. It's got pickups by Radioshop - a splittable humbucker in the bridge (controlled by the lowest 'tone' knob), Chris Buck ID in the centre and a filtertron style in the neck!

1964 Fender Jaguar (Sunburst) I got this from a shop in the UK in 2004, it is a beautiful old girl, she got a few bruises, but has loads of interesting sounds. I am still not sure what all the knobs do, in fact I don't really want to! I just fiddle about until I find a sound I like and off I go, I use this as more an "interesting sounds" guitar for quirky stuff, it not a "great sounding" guitar. I never use it live because it goes out of tune too quickly, so this is a studio only guitar. It is pretty much all original as far as I know.

1965 Gibson SG (Cherry) I bought this from Fil SoloDallas Oliveri in 2021 and it's a killer guitar. He calls it a project, the body and plastics are original but the pick-ups and wiring, frets and all that have been tweaked and upgraded. It's a players guitar, not for collectors :)

1966 Fender Telecaster (Blonde) This was one of my dream guitars that I'd wanted for a long time. I still love it but she's not been my man ride for a while now... not really sure why. Bought from Guitar Centre in Hollywood maybe 2011-ish? All original and the perfect example of this type of guitar - and with a strange red dot behind the bridge!

1967 Gibson EB3 Bass (Cherry) I'd been on the hunt for near a year for the right bass and then this one came by... well actually it's one of the very rare times I've bought a guitar on ebay without trying it, but I've played a few and will get it set up how I like when it gets here!

1969 Gibson ES-335 (Sunburst) I was really missing that fat Gibson sound for some of the recordings I was doing, bluesy jazz things, so I invested in this, my other "dream guitar". It's absolutely superb, plays and sounds fantastic, one of the finest guitars I have ever played, really quite special. Mostly original, but it's a player, certainly not a collector!

1979 Gibson Les Paul Gold Top (Gold) This guitar I bought in about 1997 when I joined The Counterfeit Stones tribute band and was playing the part of Brian Jones and Mick Taylor. It is a great sounding guitar. I keep thinking about selling it because I don't play it much, but when I get it out and have a play I remember what a great sound it has and I decide to keep it :) It really plays lovely... It has some bruises but is in pretty good condition for it's age.

1989 Fender Stratocaster Plus (Red) This was my first ever Strat I bought in Tasmania, one of the very few new guitars I ever bought. I got it cos a great Aussie guitar player called Simon Patterson came to see me play in my covers band, and he said I played great but my tone sucked and I should go buy a Strat... so I did and then started my "tone quest" so I blame Simon for all the money I've wasted on gear :) ha ha. Not much original left in it now... I was already heavily customised but in early 2011 I pulled out all the old electrics and pickguard and replaced the lot to make it sound like a strat again! Completely new wiring, new pick guard, Kinmann Woodstock pickups, Back in the early 90's I upgraded the Roller nut (the first wide ones they had sucked big time), added Teflon saddles (great idea!!) and it's been re-fretted a couple of times.

200? Gretsch Malcolm Young (Natural) This I bought for the AC/DC competition because I couldn't get any of my other guitars to sound right for the backing track!! I bought it online, had it delivered the next day and recording with it within 15 minutes of it coming in the door. I don't play it very often but it's got a great tight punchy sound for rock rhythm guitar and so unique that I have to keep her. For playing AC/DC its THE one to have. And being that Mal is my favourite rhythm guitar layer of all time, this guitar is a keeper!

2015 Suhr Classic Antique (Tobacco Sunburst) I loved the Suhr Modern but wanted something that would stay in tune and be good for traveling and that could do classic sounds as well as modern stuff, so I got this as a birthday treat for myself! It's a roasted maple neck which doesn't seem to move at all, a HSS pickup configuration so it does big rock sounds and classic strat sounds and with big frets and a great set up it plays a dream. A wonderful instrument.

2017 Patrick Eggle Drop Top 96 (Koa Top) I LOVE how this guitar plays. The setup and feel of the neck is incredible. I'm not massively feeling the pickups though so I have a set of Radioshop pickups that Tom Gray will be fitting next week. Update to come!

Other Stringed Instruments

Maton - Ukulele I love my Maton Uke and find the uke a great party instrument, especially cos if I go to a party and play people expect me to do fancy stuff but with the uke it's just all about fun. It's a great sounding uke, best I heard and plays very easy too - it's concert size which is great for me as soprano ukes are just too small for me to get my fingers into the frets!

1908 Gibson A Mandolin This is easily my oldest instrument, it doesn't play as easily as modern ones, maybe doesn't sound as wonderful either to tell the truth buy it's got bags of character and is over 100 years old! I often get a funny vibe playing it thinking about the things it's seen in it's life. Must get around to adding some mandolin lessons at some point!

194? National New Worker Lap Steel I'm pretty hopeless at playing lap steel but I really enjoy it, and I found this on ebay while looking at resonators and just loved it. Sounds real cool and learning to make it really sing is on my to do list when I find time!

2020 Kala U-Bass A Ukulele Bass - yep - it's super cool :) and actually sounds HUGE for recording. Makes no sense, but it really does!

RE-HOMED :)

2016 Gibson L-175 (Tobacco Sunburst) I really wanted a guitar for home and the big bodied old girl filled the spot beautifully for a late night tinker when the mrs is in bed! It's not ventured into the studio yet but I really must get the jazz series cooking again and she's bound to make an appearance then at some point! SOLD in 2020 to Pete Whittard!

2009 Fender Jeff Beck (Custom Shop, White) This strat I bought cos all the other whammy bars are blocked up and I love JB's playing and wanted to learn some of his tunes. I'm not sure it's a keeper though, so she might finding a new caretaker on ebay at some point. It sounds great and all that but... I dunno, I guess we never quite hit it off... we've has some fun, but... it's not you, it's me :) SOLD in 2020 at Andertons

2006 Fender Telecaster USA (Yellow) I bought this in 2007, I had wanted a tele for a long time and had been looking second hand when I found this one on the internet. I bought from Ralph and Sandy's Custom shop on ebay, the service was really crappy and I'd never buy from them again, took quite a lot of work to get it right really, and wasn't a good overall experience. It started as a standard USA Telecaster but was then modified to include a Gibson "Original Mini Humbucker" in the neck position, a Seymour Duncan "Hot Stack" pick up in the centre and a Seymour Duncan "Vintage Stack" in the bridge. It has other fancy stuff too - a Soundcraft output socket, reversed volume plate, a push pull pot in the centre position (split and boost), Fender locking tuning pegs and Hovland capacitor on the tone control... and a bunch of other things. It is based on the guitar played by the country guitar legend Brent Mason (and I mean LEGEND, the guy is amazing). SOLD in 2020 at Andertons

1991 Ibanez FM-100 Frank Gambale (Fluro Yellow!) I really figured I should have a proper shred guitar in the collection, and when I saw this hanging on the wall in Charlie Chandlers I knew I had to have it. It's MINT condition, came with original case and all case candy (strap, booklet, cable etc) so I'm careful with this one to keep it mint. Fun to play too, super low action and at some point I'll make some rock videos with it! SOLD in 2020 at Andertons

lessons.title: Brown Eyed Girl [Legacy Lesson]
lessons.summary: Here's the original Justin's Lesson for Brown Eyed Girl by Van Morrison, released in 2012.
lessons.text:
🚨 An updated version of this song lesson was released on January 17, 2025. Check it out here!

This Van Morrison song is a classic!

He wrote Brown Eyed Girl in 1967. Since then, this song has been a regular on rock radio all over the world, and many bands have covered it during the last decades.

Brown Eyed Girl is a cracking tune, very popular at parties and stuff. The best news? It’s also a super fun song to learn on the acoustic guitar.

💡 If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you can learn this song right in the beginning. Great tune for Grade 1 practices!

You’ll only need open chords. And for those up for a little challenge, the riff in the intro is useful to learn. ;) Now, let's get stuck in.

The Strumming Pattern for Brown Eyed Girl

If you’re a beginner, start very simple and then fancy it up with time. Brown Eyed Girl is a 4x4 tune, so just playing one strum per beat on each bar will sound great!

If you’re comfortable playing things a bit faster, try out an all-down strumming pattern for the chorus. Make sure you experiment with the song's dynamics - a good way to practice it is by playing along with the original record.

🚨 TIP: An awesome way to change the dynamic from the verse to the chorus is holding your pick a bit harder when you want the song to sound fuller. Watch the tutorial to see it. If you’re comfortable with rhythm, use this handful of strumming patterns for the verses.

We’ll also take a good look at how to play the Brown Eyed Girl intro on guitar. The riff will work better if you’ve got a jam buddy playing the chords with you. But this riff is a Triad Chord Grip, so it's a super useful little trick to have in hand! Guitarists learning to play with me will get started with triads in Grade 4.

👉 Want Verified TABS for Brown-Eyed Girl? Check out JustinGuitar Tabs!

lessons.text:
Updated song tutorial here!

Learn "House of The Rising Sun" by The Animals. It's one of the most classic songs to play on guitar!

In this lesson, we'll learn how to play House of The Rising Sun on the acoustic guitar. This is one of those acoustic songs that all guitar players should know how to play! In this tutorial, we'll explore The Animal's cover - the one you're probably familiar with. :)

We'll learn the chords and two ways of playing the rhythm: an easy fingerstyle version and a way that sounds more like the original recording. This is a 6x8 song, so I hope you're familiar with its vibe—make sure you've listened to it a lot. It'll make it much easier to play!

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, this song is great practice for Grade 2+ students. We'll need an F Chord - but it's an open version. 😅 Let's get stuck in and check out what's on today's menu.

House of The Rising Sun - Guitar Chords

You can play House of The Rising Sun using open chords only. You'll need the Am, C, D, E, and F Chords - but don't worry if you cannot play barre chords yet! We'll use an open F Chord variation, and the best news is that this is how we usually play this song.

If you want chords, tabs, and lyrics to follow along with my song tutorials, check out JustinGuitarTabs. :)

House of The Rising Sun - Strumming Pattern

The easiest way of playing this 6x8 song is by only playing down strums on beats 1 and 4. That means you'll strum twice per bar. If you can keep a steady rhythm while changing the chords, you'll be able to sing along with it and have loads of fun!

Many guitar players like to strum this song with short down strums on all beats, accentuating beats 1 and 4. You should explore that as long as you keep your hands moving consistently! The big advantage here is that you'll be able to go further and add some up strums as well - it'll sound fuller and faster.

Try playing along with the original recording, too; that's a great way of getting the song's vibe right. Muting the strings and concentrating on the rhythm until it is consistent is also a good idea, especially if you struggle with strumming patterns. ;)

House of The Rising Sun - Finger Style

When I first learned how to play House of The Rising Sun, it was in fingerstyle. So I thought I'd teach you that, too. It's an easy and great pattern if you're getting into fingerstyle.

Your thumb will play the bass notes, and the other will pick the thinnest strings. To play it right, you should be aware of the bass notes of each chord. If you're not, check out their chord boxes. ;)

Are you feeling adventurous? You can go a bit further and try to do some pick picking. :) The tricky here is the angle of the pick, so you don't get stuck between the strings. It might require some extra practice, but it's worth it. That sounds fancy!

👉 Want chords, tabs, and lyrics to follow along with my song tutorials? Check out JustinGuitarTabs!

Learn to Play "Fast Car" by Tracy Chapman on Guitar

In this lesson, we'll learn how to play Fast Car on the guitar. This beautiful and iconic song is perfect for those wanting to explore fingerstyle guitar playing. Fast Car is a fantastic introduction to fingerstyle guitar playing. Instead of using a pick, we'll be using our fingers to create that signature sound that makes Fast Car so recognizable.

To match Tracy Chapman's original recording, we'll use a capo on the second fret, though you can play without one if you're not planning to play along with the record.

The Main Fingerpicking Pattern

The heart of Fast Car lies in its memorable fingerpicking pattern. We'll start with basic C and G chords, but what makes this song special is how we pick the strings with our thumb and fingers. The pattern creates a beautiful rolling effect that carries throughout most of the verse.

What's great about this pattern is that it becomes almost meditative once you get it down. Take your time with it–there's no rush! The key is to maintain a steady rhythm and keep your movements minimal and efficient.

Chord Progression

The song follows a lovely progression that creates its dreamy, introspective mood. In the verses, we move through C, G, Em, and D chords, while the chorus introduces some variations in timing that give the song its distinctive feel.

Strumming Pattern

For the chorus sections, we switch to strumming, and here's where you can really let the song breathe. You can either keep your pick handy or use your fingers–whatever feels most comfortable for you. The key is to keep that steady rhythm while allowing the song's emotion to come through in your playing.

Pay special attention to the timing of the chord changes, particularly when we transition from C to Em. There's a subtle push that gives the song its forward momentum, making it feel like you're actually in that fast car, racing toward a better future.

Final Thoughts

This song is a beautiful piece that's well worth the effort to learn. Whether you're playing it for yourself or others, it's one of those songs that never fails to touch people's hearts. Take your time with it, enjoy the learning process, and remember that every great guitarist started exactly where you are now.

The most important aspect of playing Fast Car is maintaining steady timing. I recommend practicing with a metronome until you can feel the rhythm in your bones. Start slowly and gradually build up speed as you become more comfortable with the patterns.

When you're learning the fingerpicking part, focus on getting clean, clear notes. Don't worry if it takes some time–this is a skill that develops with practice. The goal is to make each note ring out clearly while maintaining that hypnotic rhythm that makes the song so special.

Ready to start learning? Watch the video carefully to see these techniques in action. We'll see everything at various speeds and angles to help you understand exactly what your fingers should be doing. Remember, the key to success is patient, consistent practice. You've got this!

Learn How to Play "Dreams" by Fleetwood Mac on the Guitar

In this lesson, we'll learn how to play the iconic song Dreams by Fleetwood Mac on the guitar. This classic tune, written by the supremely talented Stevie Nicks in the late 70s, has stood the test of time and remains as captivating today as when it was first released. Let's dive into this fantastic journey and uncover the magic behind its melody!

Structure and Chord Progression

We'll start by exploring the song structure and the chord progression. Nicks built the song primarily around F and G chords, which form the backbone of the intro, verse, and pre-chorus. If you're familiar with the regular Barre chord F, you can move that up two frets to get the G chord. However, it's all about what sounds best to you. Feel free to use a big four-finger G chord if you prefer.

In the version we are learning today, we will use a slightly simplified version focusing more on strumming. We'll also see additional tips to make your rendition feel more like the original. One trick you can use when playing this song is substituting the regular F with an F major seven. It brings a different flavor to the song, making it sound more open and floaty.

Strumming Pattern

While the original track is primarily lead lines, we will focus on strumming for this lesson. A simple strumming pattern that works well for this song is down, down, up, up, down, up. It's often referred to as Old Faithful, and it's a reliable pattern that fits well with many songs. However, remember, it's your choice; you can experiment with other patterns you're comfortable with.

The Chorus

Regarding the chorus, we return to the F and G chords. A good way to differentiate between the verses and the chorus is to use a big Barre chord F for the chorus. This sets a distinct tonal shift, indicating we're now in the chorus. Small things like these can elevate your performance, making it sound more polished.

Wrapping It Up

Remember, playing the guitar is all about expressing yourself and having fun. Use this lesson as a foundation, and feel free to add your unique flair. Whether it's experimenting with the strumming pattern or adding some new chords, the sky's the limit! So, go ahead and grab your guitar, and let's bring "Dreams" to life! :) Don't forget, the best way to learn is by playing, so watch the video and play along.

"Wonderwall" by Oasis is lots of fun to play and great for working on your strumming!

This song is such a hit - and a good one! I know many guitar students who have picked up their guitars to learn this song. :) Wonderwall gotta be one of the most played songs on acoustic guitar!

In today's lesson, we'll learn how to play it exactly the right way. Getting the strumming pattern for this song seems the hardest job for new guitar players, so we'll go through it in small little chunks.

The chord progression uses the Stuck 3&4 grips! If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you'll learn more about them right at the beginning of Grade 2. These chords are known as The Wonderwall Chords because they're used in many 90's classics. A fun thing about these chords is that you'll keep the fingers 3 and 4 in the same position throughout the entire song!

Now let's check out a few important details on how to (really) play Wonderwall by Oasis on the acoustic guitar.

Wonderwall - Chords & Guitar Capo

You should first get used to playing the chord progression without stopping your strumming pattern. Start by using only down strums - you'll be able to fancy it up once you're confident with the chord changes. Some of the chord changes happen pretty fast and will need more practice than others!

I'd also recommend you learn this song in short sections. For example, move on to learn the verse when you're fully comfortable playing the introduction. Check out the video lesson to learn how I suggest you go through the song. We'll also sing its chords together: E minor don't believe that G chord-body...

💡 Want chords, tabs, and lyrics to follow along with my Wonderwall song tutorial? Check out JustinGuitar Tabs!

The chord progression on Wonderwall is easy to remember, which makes this song a great campfire plus one! It's ok if, at first, you're reading tabs or have the chords written in front of you, but don't miss out on your medium-term goal. You should aim to play songs from memory!

To sound like the original recording, put your guitar capo on the second fret of your instrument. If you're singing along with it, remember you can always adjust the capo position to fit your voice best.

Wonderwall - The RIGHT Strumming Pattern

Wonderwall is a 4x4 song with a 16th Note Strumming Pattern. It can take some time to get it right, and changing chords in the right way of the strumming pattern is an important detail to play this song with the right vibe.

To start, I recommend you only use down strums on each beat of the bar. When you can keep the rhythm and chord changes steady and consistent, you can fancy it up.

Check out the video lesson for the accurate strumming pattern. If you want to get it written on paper with some more incredible guitar tips, check out my Beginner Guitar Songbook.

You'll get away with that strumming pattern through the entire song! There are some minor variations, but as long as you keep your hands moving consistently.

Why Is Your Little Finger Hurting?

If you're a beginner guitar player, chances are you haven't been using your little finger a lot! To play Wonderwall, you'll use your little finger at the same position during the entire song. Expect some pain level. :)

Make sure you take enough breaks to let it heal a bit between your practice sessions, and if you haven't already - set up your practice sessions with My Practice Assistant. This free tool helps set up effective practice sessions to prevent overplaying.

💡 Don't be in a hurry - you will learn BETTER and FASTER if you give yourself time to heal.

Nitsuj found his Finger 3 was hurting a lot when learning the Stuck 3&4 Chords. Finger 3 overcompensates for the weakness of Finger 4 by pressing harder than it should - so be mindful of this. He knows what was going on and still struggled with it. It's normal if you struggle too! Stay aware, and don't hurt yourself. :)

Learn How to Play "Everybody Hurts" by R.E.M. on the Guitar

In this lesson, we'll learn how to play Everybody Hurts on the guitar. This is a fantastic song, especially if you're diving into fingerstyle guitar. It's built around some really accessible chords, with a few slightly trickier ones in the bridge section. We'll explore a simple fingerstyle approach, perfect for beginners, and then look at a more advanced version, just like the original recording. If you're new to fingerstyle, stick with the simpler pattern. If you're more advanced, have a go at the intro and the other more complex patterns, just like on the original record. It's a beautiful song with some different layers, so we'll take a look at how to add to the song if you have two guitars.

One unique aspect of Everybody Hurts is its 6/8 time signature, which gives the song its distinctive flowing feel. Think of it as having two main pulses per bar, each divided into three beats. So, it's "one-two-three, four-five-six." This creates that gentle, swaying rhythm that's so characteristic of the song.

Intro, Verse, and Chorus

The basic chord progression revolves around a few simple chords. The song starts with two bars of D, then moves to G, and repeats that sequence for the intro. In the verse, you'll play the D chord, then G, then D again, and then G. After that, move to a G with an F# bass note. Then comes the E minor chord.

For the chorus, you'll need E minor, then A, and then back to E minor. Remember to keep that 6/8 pulse in mind–it makes a big difference to how the song feels. So, even when you're just strumming, try to make sure that you're thinking "one-two-three, four-five-six."

The Bridge

The bridge is where things get interesting, with some different chords. The version that sounds closest to the original uses power chords. We'll start with an F# power chord, then go to a B power chord, and then back to the F#, and then another B. We'll follow with F# and B, then move up a fret to C. Then we'll go G, B, C, C, C, and then a G with a B bass, which goes to A or A minor, and then back to the verse.

Each chord is played once in the original recording and allowed to ring out. You can also use full barre chords, such as a regular F# chord or even F#7 if you are more advanced. You can also play F# to B minor, as it's a nice change because it's the same shape, just moved down. For the C, you can switch back to open chords. I like keeping the bridge different from the rest of the song, using those power chords.

Fingerstyle Patterns

We'll explore two main approaches to playing this song. For beginners, there's a simplified fingerpicking pattern that captures the song's essence while being easier to master. Once you're comfortable with that, we can move on to the more complex pattern that matches the original recording. The key is to start slow and build up your speed gradually.

Need some extra help? Check out these Fingerstyle lessons!

Extra Strumming Part

There's a strumming overdub part that you can add, featuring a little walk down. Start with the E minor chord, strum twice, then move to A. Then play a third fret on the thickest string, a second fret on the thickest string, and then back to the E minor. You can also play this part fingerstyle.

Wrapping Up

This is a fantastic song to learn, especially if you are new to fingerstyle guitar. I remember learning this when I was young and just enjoying the simple chords and the fingerstyle that sounds like the record. I didn't learn the bridge for ages because the chords seemed so difficult. But if you know your power chords, you can get it done! Play along with the original song as much as you can to keep in time. Watch the video, take your time, and remember to enjoy yourself as you learn. You've got this!
