lessons.text:
Hey, how are you doing? Justin here, with a video I recorded on August 1, 2023.

Twenty years ago today, I launched the very first JustinGuitar website. It seems so long ago! My life has changed so much since then. This morning, I thought about what I'd like to do on the website in the next 20 years. I was going to do something like "JustinGuitar Reacts" to one of the early videos, but as I looked through those early videos, so many memories came back. So I decided to give you a little rundown on how JustinGuitar.com started and go through a few early videos. I'll tell you some funny stories about behind-the-scenes stuff, what was happening in my life, and how it all came about.

🎂 How long have you been learning with me? You can join this Community discussion and let me know how the site impacted your life; my ops manager started the "celebration" vibes there, and I've had a great time reading all your kind comments and birthday wishes!

Let's get stuck in and chat about the story of JustinGuitar. I hope you enjoy it!

The Early Days

I can't exactly remember how I got into websites, but I do remember a friend of mine, Cyan, who taught me the basics of HTML, and I made a website for my band at the time. I was already doing a lot of teaching. I was teaching at the Guitar Institute, a posh boarding school called Wellington College, and doing a lot of private teaching. I've always been teaching ever since I was a little kid! Teaching has always been part of my game.

I was playing with the Counterfeit Stones, the most famous Rolling Stones tribute band in England, according to Mick Jagger. We were touring a lot, so much of the early website was just text and little notations. A lot was done on the back of the tour bus driving from venue to venue while we were on tour!

It was mostly a promotional thing. If I got an inquiry from a new student, I could say, "Here's an example of some of the lessons I can do," but it was mostly text and images. Later on, I incorporated some audio. I remember getting quite excited about getting emails from all around the world from people saying, "Oh, I really enjoyed that lesson," or "You explained that well," or whatever. It was exciting to be on the internet! It seemed like a very new thing. It was still all dial-up and very slow, but feeling like I was part of this thing was exciting! No one knew where it would go, but it felt like it was somewhere positive. The internet would be the way of the future, and it's turned out like that for me and my work situation!

🎸 I hesitate to call it work. I get to play guitar and muck around the studio every day. It's hardly any work. :)

Anyway, the website was mostly text for that time, and then YouTube came along. I can't exactly remember what happened, but I had quit the Counterfeit Stones and was playing with Katie Melua's band. I lived in an apartment in Chiswick High Road in West London, above the optometrist's place. I had two apartments - I lived in one and built a recording studio in the other.

I remember seeing YouTube and thinking, "Oh, well, we can do video. That will be so good for doing guitar lessons, like video guitar lessons." I had no idea about videos or video editing. I remember my friend Jed had done some video stuff, so I rang him and said, "Hey, would you come and film some videos?" He kindly came over, and we filmed five or six video lessons.

🪂 Interestingly, the first video on my YouTube Channel was a skydiving video. If I remember rightly, you had to upload a video when signing up for a YouTube channel; the only video I had on my computer was this skydiving one!

The first guitar video on my Main YouTube Channel was Silent Night, the Christmas classic. You can't even see my eyes, just these dark spots where they should be. I was so skinny! :) It was interesting to see the drum kit in the background…

There was a pub behind my flat called Sam's Bar, where we often hung out. Quite often, late at night, my friends would show up, and we'd end up piling into my studio to have a jam. I remember one of the neighbors sent a message saying, "You know, Jimi Hendrix would be turning in his grave or something. You guys should stick to your day jobs." I remember finding that funny because almost every person there was a professional musician. Whoever wrote that got it slightly wrong. :)

We used a handheld camera in my first videos. Back then, I used to have a long video introduction, and no one cared. I used to wear a funny beanie all the time, and I hadn't shaved. The sitting-on-the-floor thing started around this time, and I didn't used to wear shoes. My first videos would teach Major Scales and Finger Tapping!

YouTube was so new, and this wasn't my job. It was just something fun to do between tours and writing. I always felt privileged that I could make a living out of music. I'm lucky to have fallen into this journey where I get to do something that I have loved my entire life. There was an element of these early days of YouTubing where I was like, "If I can help people get better at guitar and enjoy the instrument and play some songs that they love, then that's already kind of giving back to music a little bit." I always felt like that was important!

Jazz Up Your Blues!

One of my first series, Jazz Up Your Blues, has an interesting backstory about the. They were some of the first videos that I edited on my own. Jedi had done nearly all the editing, and at this point, I was trying to figure out how to do the editing on my laptop when I was on tour. The night before the Jazz Up Your Blues video, I'd been sitting on the hotel roof with Jeff Beck, Tal Wilkenfeld, Jason Rubello, Vinnie Collier, and several other famous musicians. It was an incredible night!

That moment was the turning point for me for YouTube. I filmed these videos, edited some, and put them live. Then, I went away to the gig, did the gig, came back, and the videos had more views than there were people in the audience at that festival. I said, "Yeah, this YouTube thing is something I should be pursuing." It wasn't that long after that I quit that band and went full-time to doing YouTube videos.

Full-Time YouTuber

Interestingly, I did another version of Silent Night one year later. How much did I learn? :) One thing I became conscious of is that I was always smacking my lips together; people used to say, "Stop smacking your lips together!" and I'd watch it back and realize, "Oh yeah, I'm doing that." :) My new setup looked nicer; I had some lights going on and a lapel mic clipped onto my t-shirt, improving the sound quality.

Something interesting was happening when I released the Power Chord video. Aside from the atrocious haircut and the big rack of stuff that I had, it was a period where I was using a lot of rock guitar things. I was at my first big recording studio, taking a room in Hugh Padgham's recording studio. It was the Stanley House in Acton, a dodgy location between an industrial park and sewage treatment works. But it was an amazing recording studio full of amazing musicians! Some killer people were around in 10 recording studios, including the producer who did a lot of stuff with Phil Collins and the Police/Sting.

A great hub! Everyone was doing a lot of pop songwriters and library music, pulling ideas and planning on each other's records. It was an amazing, vibrant time for me. I was doing a lot of touring then, so I'd be back in the studio for a few weeks, doing sessions, filming lessons, and then I'd disappear on tour for three or four months or whatever and then come back. I had an amazing time at Stanley House, and I'll be forever thankful for the people I met there!

I became a better teacher, and hanging out with people doing sessions and proper records made a big difference!

The JustinGuitar Hat

The JustinGuitar hat first appeared on the Guitar Lesson for Complete Beginners video! Pretty atrocious-looking shirt there, playing a Maton Messiah, the same acoustic guitar I still have! That was a great time, still in Stanley House - just the opposite side of the room!

🤠 These days, I mostly wear the hat because I have a microphone in it. It's not so much that I'm fussed about losing my hair or anything like that. I'm losing my hair, but I'm not bothered about it. :)

The First Beginner Course

I'm okay at guitar but not incredible - I'm a good teacher because I can break down fairly complex ideas. I always had courses on the website and felt like my superpower wasn't playing guitar but working out a progression of things to learn, making a difficult thing easier by breaking it into many component pieces to teach people how to play.

Fourteen years ago, I became more serious about making YouTube videos and writing courses. I got into remaking a Beginner Guitar Course, and I scripted it all, planning all the learning paths and how students should practice.

I filmed the new Beginner Course videos at my friend Jed's house. We had lighting here, and we hired a Sony camera. It was a big step up in production. Jed did amazing work here! He worked hard filming and editing the stuff. We could have done it better with the gear I've got now, but this was massive at the time.

A Bigger Studio!

When the YouTube channel started doing better, I moved to the upstairs studio in the Stanley House, which had a separate live room. So I had one room full of all my guitars and amps all set up with mics and stuff all the time, and then I had a nice recording studio in the other half of it.

The beautiful brown leather sofa wasn't a great functional sofa, but I loved it! It wasn't mine - it was Hugh Padgham's sofa, the producer I mentioned that owned the building, and his wife, a clothes designer or fashion designer called Cath Kidston, decided that she wanted their sofa back, so I lost it. :( I was very sad when it left!

The Blanket!

The blanket first appeared on the Functioning & Static Chords, and it came about because I used to nap during the day. I started working early in the morning, and after lunch, I would normally nap, covering myself up with that blanket. :) Quite practical!

Volunteering in Ghana

I went to Ghana with my girlfriend, and through the website and YouTube, we raised quite a few thousand pounds and bought a load of pens, t-shirts, and medicines to donate in Ghana.

🖊️ Pens were a big thing over there, so we've got boxes and boxes of pens. The kids would just run up to you if you were some sort of volunteer there, and they'd just be asking for pens right away that they could use at school.

We volunteered in an orphanage there in Pando, Kpando, in the Volta region of Ghana. I'm so thankful I did. It was an amazing and humbling experience!

This experience made me more appreciative of my life and realized how people can be happy with not very much. A lot of the people that we met there had next to nothing. I won't dwell on that too much, but that was an amazing experience. If you want to watch the little videos, there's even a funny one where I attempt to teach music notation to a school in Ghana, and they're schooling me in rhythms. Their sense of rhythm and groove playing drums is awesome and made me feel inadequate. :)

Interviews, Original Music, & AC/DC

The day I was supposed to interview Pat Martino, someone broke into my car, parked close to the Stanley House - which used to be a tricky, dangerous neighborhood. Now it's all gentrified, and only wealthy people live there, but at that time, it was pretty gnarly, so somebody had smashed the windows of my car when I went down to drive to interview Pat Martino. A bummer! It's the only interview on my site that I didn't do - my friend Pete Whittard interviewed him for me.

Around that time, I also got an album out - "Small Town Eyes," produced by a guy called Fessa, a great producer. We got a lot of good sounds there, but I've taken it off Spotify because I hated the sound of my voice when I listened back to it. I'm doing okay singing now, but it wasn't any good at that time. That album hardly sold any records, but I mostly sold out the Bush Hall, a concert venue in London, and I played it with my band.

🎵 I have a song tutorial for my song From Katie's Window. I think that stands up an instrumental tune. 🙂

Around that time, there was also an AC/DC "Shoot to Thrill" competition. It was amazing because AC/DC got involved! Their record company emailed and said, "Hey, we'd love for you to do a lesson on this song because we're going to promote it because it's on this film. Would you do it?" It was the first time I had contact with a record label that was actively going, "This guy can reach the people that we want to be able to advertise to." Very interesting experience!

I solidified many things in my presentation: the hat, blanket, and sofa. Then, on November 14, 2010, I interviewed Steve Vai. That was a big deal for me! It was one of the first major interviews I had ever done, and Steve is such an amazing guy. He is down-to-earth, helpful, friendly, and full of pearls of wisdom. The guy seems to speak, and amazing things come out. I was very, very nervous to meet Steve Vai!

🤘 When I was a teenager, I loved Steve Vai, Joe Satriani, and Eric Johnson. I spent a lot of my tens of thousands of hours probably learning Metal tunes. I didn't pursue shreddy Rock and got more involved with Jazz, Blues, songwriting, and production. But wow, I loved meeting Steve. It was such a thrill for me!

Around that time, I also got to interview Martin Taylor. He's another absolute proper gentleman. I've interviewed him several times, and he always has fascinating things to say.

At that moment, I worked on my Ear Training Method and interviewed Jim Campilongo. He was amazing! He is such a fantastic guitar player, an absolute hero of mine. He has a unique voice and personality when he plays and is a great guitar player! We filmed the interview in his apartment in Brooklyn. It was one of the first few times I went to New York to hang out with other musicians, and hooking up with Jim was a real big deal. It was amazing to realize the reach of the internet and that I could contact people from far away, and there was a chance they'd be interested in chatting with me!

10 Years Ago…

I was releasing a lot of lessons on 12 Bar Blues and original Blues solos. I also met Mike Dawes 10 years ago. It was the first time I met him, and I remember seeing that video of him doing the "Somebody That I Used to Know" thing and going, "Oh my God, this guy's incredible." I emailed him, and almost a week later, he just came to the studio, and we hung out, jammed, and went for food.

Michael Fix was also there, and Gordon Giltrap used to get loads of people popping by the studio, then people in the building recording something else, and they'd pop in. I never did get to meet Dominic Miller, who had a room opposite mine for a little while, nor Pete Gordino, a fantastic keyboard player who plays with Depeche Mode. I should have interviewed them, but I never got around to it.

Ten years ago, the first We Came as Strangers album came out. We Came as Strangers is still technically going, but we've all paused because we've all had kids. This band was one of my proudest moments. Four of my great friends got together in a house for two weeks in a residential recording studio, and we just made a record in two weeks from nothing. We didn't even know each other. We just went there and said, "Okay, we got two weeks. Let's write some tunes." We spent the whole day jamming and trying out ideas, and then drilled it down, took the idea, and got it into a song.

Ellen, the singer, would go off and work on the lyrics while we'd be tracking up stuff. We've done three albums now, and each was done in two weeks, only from scratch, with no songs at all. We finished the whole album and usually mixed it afterward!

💙 I love We Came as Strangers. I think it's important that I still have this passion for making music and writing songs because that motivates me to do lessons. After all, 20 years is a long time to be doing that. I must start cultivating it again because it's been a little while since I've done a record, and it's the thing that keeps it all fresh for me, keeps me excited, and keeps everything fairly new.

The second album of We Came as Strangers was eight years ago. I was mindful of trying to keep content coming out on the YouTube channels all the time, so I had lick lessons and the Blues Lead Guitar series. Interestingly, we're looking at revamping that very soon.

Recent Years

The Stanley House got sold, and they turned it into a flat, which was an absolute bummer. It was a great music studio and a very sad loss for music. I had to move to another studio. Again, it was full of great, but mostly pop, songwriters in that building. Charlie Hugo, the producer, was in the room behind mine, and there was always this funny thing like if he was tracking stuff, I had to go, "Hey man, I'm filming. Can you keep the volume down for a little bit?" And he'd be quiet while I filmed, and then it'd be like he could make a racket again.

It was around this time as well that I got the Kemper, and that was a game-changer for me as far as my audio quality went because, before that, it was always like setting up a microphone into an app, putting it through a preamp, recording it into Pro Tools. It was a lot of mucking around, and I wasn't paying as much attention to it as I should have, especially as I was doing a lot of recording sessions. I should have paid more attention to the audio quality of those early lessons.

Eventually, we sold up our flat and moved out to Farnam in Surrey, and I converted a pretty decent-sized wine cellar into my recording studio. Moving out of London was a big deal, and I was scared. I thought it would be terrible, but I wish I'd done it years ago. I love living in the countryside, in the fresh air, and walking the dog in the woods instead of running around in smoggy streets.

I've been writing the guitar techniques magazine guys, Nev and Jason, for around six years. I've been writing the guitar magazine article. I've also recorded the Rut Busters series, and hooking up with Lee Anderson was great. He's become a really good friend of mine. I love his whole vibe! I also started doing dog walks and guitar talks content and working more on the audio and video quality. I learned a bit about color grading, shooting, and more.

I was in that same studio for a couple of years until lockdown. During that time, I taught Tammy, Lee, Ariel Posen, Chris Buck, and many other people also came to hang out. It was a fun time, and I did things that I never dreamed of doing as a kid. I learned to play left-handed, and you can still see the left-handed PRS up there, which reminds me of all the things I went through to learn.

Lockdown, New Studio, and Team!

There was a little period during lockdown when I had to rent a studio because we were renovating the house. It was a rough time, but I'm thankful I could still work and help people through the lockdown. The pandemic was amazing for JustinGuitar as a business because everyone was stuck at home playing guitar. What better way to spend your time stuck at home than learning something new?

Then, I moved back to my house - the studio where I am now. My friend Lee helped me set up the lights and cameras, and I've tweaked it a little since then. The first lesson I released on my Main YouTube Channel in the new studio was the 6 Guitar Areas You Should Practice.

JustinGuitar expanded during the lockdown, and I could hire full-time employees. I found an amazing operations manager, Laryne, who oversees almost everything. We also had great developers, Ben and Mike, and now Kris, our full-time developer, and Barbara, our designer. We managed to keep growing the Community and have three moderators who do incredible work there: Lieven, Richard, and David!

I can't believe how different it was when I remember those early years! All those things that happened because I love playing guitar and sharing what I learn have enabled me to live this amazing life. Not a day goes by that I don't appreciate it. Being grateful for what we have is important for staying happy and sane.

🎯 I spent the morning thinking about everything I want to achieve in the next years. I went back through the website and noticed how many things were slightly unfinished for one reason or another, so I started making a big list of things to start ticking my way. Lots of exciting things are coming!

Personal Life

The biggest change recently in my life was just before we moved to the country: my daughter Vivi was born. That was a profound thing that changed my whole life. Suddenly, there was someone much more important to me than myself.

I worked a lot less after that. Given the choice between playing guitar or hanging out with my daughter, I will generally hang out with her. I still love playing guitar, but my daughter Vivi and partner Evelina are my priority.

I've also gotten into Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu, so I spend a lot of time doing that. That's my main hobby outside of the guitar. I feel sore today because I got beat up pretty badly at sparring last night. It wasn't a good one for me, and I felt bruised and sore, but it was amazing, and I can't wait to return to it tomorrow!

Thank You!

I want to finish off with a few big thank-yous. I'm worried about forgetting people, so if you've worked with me and helped me on my journey, I massively appreciate you. A lot is happening in my head, but a couple of big standout ones are Jed Wardley, who helped me out and got me into videos in those early days. Without his help, this whole thing wouldn't have happened! Tom, from Music Sales, helped save me from getting sued by the music industry and got me into writing my books, which is amazing. The Musopia crew works on the JustinGuitar Lessons & Songs App development. Thank you!

I'm so lucky now to have the support of an amazing team: Laryne, Barbara, Kris, Lieven, Richard, David, and Jon. I know I'm going to forget people, which will make me feel terrible, but there are so many people around that help me with the site, not only the website but the design of it, constructing everything. It's amazing the support that I've had.

I save the biggest thank you to… YOU!

Thank you for being interested in what I do, learning guitar with me, leaving comments, making donations, buying t-shirts, courses, books, or whatever. All those things together have enabled me to make this thing, which I hope is an amazing resource for guitar players for many years! I have no plans on retiring anytime soon. I still love it, and I'm still passionate about it. I was so excited this morning going through and thinking about what I could do. I still have the vibe and the energy for it, so I'm hoping you'll stick with me and enjoy learning guitar with me for many years. Thanks again for the last 20 years. It's been amazing, and I appreciate it so much.

THANK YOU! 💙

lessons.title: What's the JustinGuitar Grade System All About?
lessons.summary: I developed the JustinGuitar Grade System to help you have a clear view of the learning pathway available to you at JustinGuitar.com!
lessons.text:
Understanding the Grade System

I feel like the special skill I was given in life was not playing the guitar but breaking down complicated things into easily digestible steps. Just happened that I also love guitar, and so that's where my superpower expresses itself :)

To help you understand the steps, I created a grading system of 9 grades. I color-coded them along the lines of a Karate grade system which will help you quickly identify lessons or songs at your level.

🎯 The JustinGuitar Grade System boosts your online learning experience. You always know where to head next and where to look back when you need to! :) Also, you can easily identify the best song tutorials for you. 👌

Linear path or pick n mix?

I recommend that beginners follow the course and get a decent understanding of all the essential skills you need to make music, then figure out what things you like best and then focus your further study in those areas!

If you've been playing for some time, you will likely want to dip in and out of different courses or pick a specialization that interests you. Exploring the All Courses Page and the All Lessons Map is the best way to overview all the content I have available for you.

🎂 JustinGuitar turns 20 years in 2023! I still think it's crazy I've got over 2,000 lessons for y'all. Imagine how that would be without a Grade system to organize them! :)

Fun-facts

🥋 Each Grade has a color. :) If you ever wondered why my song tutorials have different color thumbnails, it's because of the Grade's color! I'm describing the lesson stuff here - the song grade decisions are a bit personal, and while I do my best to work out the 'minimum grade needed to play a basic version of the song,' some will find some songs easy and others hard...

⚪️ Beginner Grade 1 - Easy Open Chords and Basic Strumming

🟡 Beginner Grade 2 - Open Chord Embellishments, Power Chords, Fingerpicking, and more!

🟠 Beginner Grade 3 - Further development and consolidation of beginner material and developing self-development and style focus!

🟢 Intermediate Grade 4 - Intro to barre chords and positional playing. Modules on Blues, Jazz, Transcribing, and many more.

🔵 Intermediate Grade 5 - All essential bare chords and further style development modules

🟣 Intermediate Grade 6 - Complete CAGED System for chords, scales, and improvisation.

🔴 Advanced Grade 7 - Modes of the Major Scale, Minor Scales, Chord Extensions, Playing over changes, Jazz theory, and more.

🟤 Advanced Grade 8 - Not started yet* Modes of Minor Scales, Chord Alterations and substitutions,

⚫ Advanced Grade 9 - Not started yet* All other complicated fun stuff!

* It's more important that I get the beginner grades well sorted before working on the last few - the people who reach those grades will (or should be!) aware of the things they need to learn and be able to find the info elsewhere until I get to them ;)

👉 Each Lesson is inside a Module, which belongs to a Grade. This is what the Beginner Course looks like, for example:

📽 A Lesson is one single tutorial, almost always a video. Sometimes, it will be an article. Especially when you're in the Playground, exploring things like Food for Thought.

🥄 I ensure to spoon-feed my beginners, so they build a strong foundation. Things get a bit more flexible from Grade 4+! You will have to make more decisions about how you spend your practice time, but if you've been learning with me from the Beginner stages, don't worry: you will surely know what to do!

♻️ If you haven't learned to play with me from day 0, revisiting some Beginner lessons might be a great idea. All the basics are there, and my best tips for a solid rhythm feel. :)

Always Improving!

JustinGuitar.com will always be a work in progress - I'm always thinking of new ways of making it all better and easier for you! Also, some of my older content might not be as up-to-date as it should be.

We're a small team, and keeping over 2,000 free lessons up to date is quite a big task. But we do our best to make sure everything is as slick as possible; if it's not, please know we're doing our best to get there, and donations help us work faster. :)

Got questions about my courses? Drop me a line in the Discussion section. :)

lessons.title: Understanding the Donation System
lessons.summary: At JustinGuitar, we believe that good things come to good people. That's been Justin's mantra his entire life, and that's how JustinGuitar took form!
lessons.text:
I started JustinGuitar almost 20 years ago. It's crazy how time flies.

It used to be me, a camera, a laptop, and some incredible friends helping me along the way. It looked just like this - not long ago!

Over the years, JustinGuitar accumulated more than 2,000 free guitar lessons and became an incredible Community of people from all walks of life who have one thing in common: the guitar. We're over 650,000 registered students and 2 million subscribers on my YouTube channels!

Whether you've been around for a while or just arrived, you probably know that my mission is to provide high-quality guitar education to everyone, regardless of circumstances. That's why I don't charge for most of my lessons and run the website as paywall-free as possible.

👉 The Donation System started as a way of making it possible to grow the site and still keep most of it free! If you can contribute, please consider doing so. :)

My business exists to help you meet the musician in you, inspire change, and do no harm. :) And that's how I lead my team and run my business, making sure most of the content and features available on this website are free of charge. At JustinGuitar, we believe good things will come to good people. That's always been my mantra, and that's how JustinGuitar took form.

And it's even weird to talk about this as a "we" thing or even as a business. But the thing is that it's been a few years now that I can't do it all on my own. The website has grown - you can see it, can't you? It gets better every day.

💭 And more and more great updates are coming, but that is also a topic for another day! :) From new courses to Dashboard improvements…

I've been lucky to gather an incredible Team to help me! They allow me more time to work on new lessons and courses, help me be closer to you and keep teaching guitar to as many people as possible.

But this all comes with a big responsibility and a huge bill. Maintaining a responsive website that hosts thousands of lessons and, hopefully, soon, a million students isn't a regular job! Especially when you operate all over the globe. :)

Guitar friend, don't read me wrong. I'm not complaining about the hard work that JustinGuitar requires - neither is my team working hard backstage to make JustinGuitar grow. We love what we do and love that you love it too. Over the years, JustinGuitar became a movement.

💙 The Independent once said that JustinGuitar is "one of the most influential guitar teachers in history."

I know that is keeping my pay-it-forward philosophy strong at our core. The idea is simple - it relies on the fact that we will is to give back and destinate part of our money - or time, or energy! - to help others whenever you can, without expecting back, rather than making your part in making this world a better place.

👌 Science shows that the best way to care for yourself isn't about you! ;) Learn more about the science behind paying it forward. ;)

But the most heart-warming feedback comes from my direct messages, emails, and comments. I get testimonials from all over the world from people who wouldn't have been able to learn without my lessons. The shy, people with low income, and those simply too busy to make regular lessons.

The Donation System

I count on donations to keep growing the website as paywall-free as possible, keeping a huge amount of content and resources available free of charge to anyone with an internet connection. That's my way of ensuring that my teaching can reach millions of people who can't afford paid tuition.

A 100% paywall-free website is my absolute dream - although I know this is a utopia because I work with the music industry and copyright and licenses are a reality. :)

🚨 Some things are just out of my control, like charging for verified Tabs or even pricing and availability of my guitar app. That's why these products are, at least for now, outside of JustinGuitar ASSIST - a program I want to keep growing which offers free access to paid products for students who can't afford them. But this is one more topic for another day!

For now, I just wanted you to understand why a large chunk of the site runs on donations. Without them, JustinGuitar wouldn't exist the way it does, and thousands of people would miss out on the chance to play their beloved six-string.

What Does a Donation Do?

A donation means you voluntarily contribute to the site, which doesn't include access to any of my paid products. You can set up monthly donations that you could cancel anytime or send some money here and there - whatever is better for you!

By donating, you get a truly special place in my heart and appreciation from my entire team. You help us hire more hands and brains to help us improve all the technology behind the website. 💙

But a few courses that could be free on the website, such as Music Theory, are behind a paywall. Well, here's why!

It's because, although we have over 650,000 registered students and millions of learners each year, very few percent donate - it doesn't come to 0,5% - which I get. Loads of people just genuinely can't afford to, and that's ok - that's more than ok. They are why we will always work hard to make everything as affordable as possible if I can't give it away for free!

But because of the bill that comes with the site - a few courses, like Music Theory or Strumming 1&2, can't be free - yet, at least.

🤝 Don't forget! Just contact us and we will assist you if you want to learn from an eligible paid product but can't afford it. We will give it to you!

How to Support JustinGuitar?

First, just by sticking around! :) I believe that if you choose to learn with me, it's because we vibe, and that's already making the movement stronger. Be an active member of the Community, and help beginners who arrive every day. That's paying it forward and money-free.

If you have the means, you can directly support JustinGuitar by making a monthly donation. You decide the amount and can adjust or cancel that subscription anytime from your Dashboard!

You can also send one-time contributions whenever you want. It could be every time you finish a new module or have nailed a song you love. It could be when something cool happens to you.

By donating, we're helping to keep most of JustinGuitar.com free, making it available to thousands of people who can't afford them. You help new people begin and pursue their guitar journey every day!

Do you support my free lessons? Come to say hi! :) I would love to get y'all to know each other and share a bit about your guitar journey!

What if you can't afford to donate or even buy stuff?

Absolutely nothing to worry about. And that's when the paying it forward way of life comes in. :) It's not about money; it's about doing good for other people, no matter how small that might seem.

I produce loads of free content because I know somehow you will give back to the universe! You can pay it forward without money:

Teach guitar to friends, family, and colleagues. Or someone less privileged than you?

Build a repertoire, and play a concert at a retirement home. How magical!

Make music with children! Help them discover a new activity they might love and build incredible memories with them.

Create beautiful music to express yourself. Music is a great way of showing gratitude and appreciation.

Donate old gear or instruments to charity instead of throwing them away.

Buy a coffee for the person behind you in line. Or compliment them!

Get second-hand guitars and gear instead of new ones to help the environment.

Recycle more - you can even recycle your strings!

What about one kind act to someone in your local Community for every free lesson you watch at JustinGuitar? :) The possibilities are endless. You can pay it forward every day without restructuring your life! Be alert for moments when you can make a positive difference in the world, and be brave enough to take that step.

Want to support JustinGuitar financially? Donate now!

lessons.title: Grade 3: New Lessons Available & Feedback!
lessons.summary: It's great to see a brand-new Grade 3 coming together. What a journey, eh?
lessons.text:
It's great to see a brand-new Grade 3 coming together. What a journey, eh?

💬 What are your thoughts about Grade 3 so far? Join the Discussion and share your feedback!

If you started in Grade 1, you probably feel like I do - Grade 3 brings an accomplishment feeling to your journey, and it fills your motivation cup! It makes you more confident and gives you the knowledge to go beyond the beginner stages. It reminds you why you've been practicing so hard and gets you where you want to go as a guitar player. 👌 This Orange grade opens up a whole new world! We take our basic open chords to the next level and get confident exploring further down the neck. Discovering new sounds using the same chord shapes will jaw-drop you! We'll also give some thought and space to discover your musicianship and improve practice habits. I know - there is so much you want to learn, practice, and discover! But how to make that all fit into your busy routine so you don't get discouraged... again? Well, the answer to that might also be here.

The Next Level!

If you're in Grade 3 - I know it: you've committed to your 6-string friend and are ready to understand how it all works and connect your fingers to your musical imagination. The lessons in this Orange grade are perfect for all of you who feel like you have hit a plateau as a Beginner but aren't quite an Intermediate yet. We will improve your technique greatly - we will go to the gym! Check Grade 3 out if you haven't yet - it's worth exploring all the modules and lessons. Even if you don't want to commit to the whole thing, I'm sure there is something in there for you - even more advanced players will benefit.

New Lessons Every Week

If you already follow the course or want to explore the latest lessons, here they are:

How to Sing & Play at the Same Time: a 10-Step Method to help you strum or finger pick, manage your chords, and sing. Yes, you can do it! 💪

A Shape Explorer: chances are you didn't know that your A chord could sound this cool! This lesson also explains why I teach the A chord like that.

The Spacing Effect: this technique helps me memorize a bunch of stuff, and it will help you too! A key thing to unleash your fretboard and be able to play without thinking. ;)

Transcribing Difficult Riffs: Are you ready to transcribe these faster, trickier riffs on the guitar?

But hey - that new Transcribing lesson is already the third one about transcribing riffs in our Grade 3! Before you get started with these riffs, make sure you've tried lessons 1 and 2. Up for it?

👉 Explore JustinGuitar Beginner Course - Grade 3.

lessons.title: 101 Children's Easy, Timeless Songs You Can Play - on the guitar or the ukulele! :)
lessons.summary: Learn super easy children's songs on the guitar or the ukulele and enhance your kids' interest in music!
lessons.text:
Learn to Play Fun, Easy Children's Classic Songs! They'll love it. :)

I've been playing music with my daughter Vivi since she was born. All the beautiful memories we create together are fantastic. Kids get interested in the instrument, the strings, and the sounds, especially if they like the music and can connect with it. Of course, Vivi wasn't always so into it. However, exploring the ukulele when she was still a baby, then songs she loved on the guitar, flourished her interest in music over the years.

It's awesome that she now wants a pink guitar just like mine, and she's practicing hard so I can get her one!

But anyway. This project started because, a few years back, Vivi was really into singing, and I wanted to enjoy that moment of jamming with her. :)

I knew that playing the songs she enjoyed would make a real difference in keeping her interested in our music time together. Still, I couldn't find reliable songbooks with the songs she wanted to sing or the ones I wanted her to enjoy. So I made them!

Meet JustinGuitar: Children's Songbooks

This project started with the Children's Songs for Mums & Dads Songbook - now called 101 Children's Songs on Ukulele! - that many of you already know. Now, it's more than time to release a Guitar Edition, and you can get it now. I'm excited these ebooks will help you create wonderful memories with your loved children!

If you already have the Ukulele Edition and are wondering if you need the guitar one, the answer is: YES. The books fit each instrument! But if you already have the first release of the Ukulele Edition, you don't need to buy it again unless you want to go for its new look. The song's content is the same. ;)

🔥 Get each ebook individually or in a bundle - with discounted price! Each ebook will get you: 101 Easy Children's Songs Chord Diagrams Strumming and extra tips!

The ebooks are beautiful, full of illustrations and quick tips and stories you can share with your children; creating the songbooks was a lot of fun! If you're happy and you know it vibes - know what I mean?

ℹ️ At this point, these books are only available in digital format! Would you like to get a hard copy of them? Email us and get into the waiting list.

Now, if you're wondering if this ebook is right for you, let's explore some of the reasons why I believe playing songs with and for children is a great win.

We'll also learn a few tips to get you started and discuss common questions!

Why Playing Children's Songs?

You probably already know that research shows music ignites child development. The benefit seems to apply to all different areas! Exposure to musical instruments and music during childhood encourages the development of social skills, but not only! It also enhances memory, motor abilities through dancing or playing, and mathematical skills. Not a bad combo, eh? :)

📚 This study about Music Interventions and Child Development explores all of that even further. Just in case you'd like to dig deeper!

Music classes may be a great way to expose children to guitar and other string instruments! Still, if your kid is still too young or you don't have access to music education for children, providing music time at home will already be super fun and beneficial.

Tips to Get Your Children Onboard!

Just open your Kindle or tablet, show them the songbooks, and ask them to choose a song you can try and play together. All songs use easy open chords, and any beginner will be able to play them on the guitar or the ukulele! Although I haven't written these songbooks to teach kids how to play, you can start showing them simple chords and notes and allow them to strum along with you. If you're completely new to guitar or the ukulele, some previous rehearsals won't hurt! :) Don't forget you can use my free lessons and tutorials to help you with any additional question or issue you might encounter, but overall - these songs are an "open the book and play!" difficulty level. ;)

It's also very important to keep music time with your children fun! If I start a sing-along with my daughter and she loses interest, I know I have to get more creative with it next time. Forcing children to participate might have the opposite effect and turn them off the music, so try to keep it enjoyable! These are a few things you can try:

Encourage children to dress up for some songs! You can create a story around your music time; it'll be loads of fun.

Use their favorite toys as props. It might help to keep them entertained and enjoying it!

Allow them to film the session and role-play!

Your children will love spending some music time with you. And I'm sure you'll enjoy it too! Music helps you form a magical and deep bond with children, which you will likely remember for the rest of your lives.

Are You a Teacher?

If you work with children and have a guitar or ukulele, these ebooks will also be super handy to entertain them! Use the tips above to create a unique experience you'll cherish forever. :)

lessons.summary: Scammers are working hard to get you and are multiplying daily. :(

Scammers are trying to impersonate Justin and his team. :(

We notified YouTube and are trying to alert our followers about the scam. Still, scammers are working hard to get you and are multiplying daily. :( Here's an example of what you might find:

So, following, we're sharing a few general tips to help you differentiate a message from Justin and his team from a scam message. You can also help us by tagging the message you received as Spam and notifying the social platform you're in about that user account!

How to recognize scammers

Here are a few tips to help you recognize scammers and differentiate their messages from our official ones:

My team will only contact you with an official account at @justinguitar.com.

When my team contacts you, they'll introduce themselves by name or use an email signature.

Our social media accounts are verified! Always look for our blue tick on Instagram and TikTok.

Please pay attention to our YouTube subscriber's number. I've got over 1 million subscribers on my Main Channel and my Song Channel, and if the comment doesn't come from one of these accounts, they're very likely to be fake.

When emailing us, you'll usually contact Fanny, Richard, Lieven, and Laryne. You can get to know my team members here. They're awesome! :)

JustinGuitar is NOT on Telegram!

JustinGuitar doesn't use Telegram, and it won't request that you contact Justin or anyone else on that platform. It seems that involving Telegram is a common part of the scams we've encountered. Please be aware that we won't contact you by phone or ask you to contact us. Ever!

modules.title: Quick Tips
modules.intro:
There are many little tid bits of information that I find myself explaining in lessons and workshops again and again that don't really fit into a proper module, so I've started this Quick Tips series to take on that kind of stuff.

That said, some of these things are pretty big deals and could really make your guitar journey more rewarding, fun or easy!

Depending on where you are at with your playing, you'll probably find some tips more relevant and helpful than others - I sure wish someone had told me lots of this stuff when I was starting out ;) Hope you find them helpful too.

lessons.title: Secure Your Cable
lessons.summary: This simple trick avoids accidentally pulling the cable out of your electric guitar!
lessons.text:
Getting ready to go on stage?

This quick video will cover a simple trick to help you avoid accidentally pulling the cable out of your electric guitar. This tip will be very handy, especially for new guitar players getting ready to play live. :)

💡 This tutorial is part of my Quick Tips series. Check out the other videos for my favorite guitar tricks!

Now let's get stuck and learn how to secure the cable when playing the electric guitar.

Why You Should Secure Your Cable

At a recent masterclass, I noticed that none of the students secured their cable correctly. Bad idea! Accidentally pulling the lead out is no fun. I should know – I once did it when playing in front of thousands of people. :(

Not only can nobody hear you playing, but you could also damage the guitar or cable. Don't be that person! This little trick prevents all that from happening.

How to Secure Your Cable

When plugging in, just run the cable behind the strap, then plug it into the jack. Now it won't fall out, even if you stand on it. It's important for all types of jacks and even for electro-acoustic guitars.

So next time you plug in, use this little trick, and you won't have trouble with your cable again!

lessons.title: Your Heartbeat Guides The Tempo
lessons.summary: Keeping a good tempo when you're a little nervous might be tricky. This trick will help you!
lessons.text:
Keeping In Time When You're Nervous

Have you ever noticed that we play guitar faster when we feel anxious? Keeping a good tempo when you're nervous can be tricky. I've seen this happening with other guitar players many times, and I still work on it!

💙 A heartbeat is the only natural metronome a human has! It gives a regular pulse within our bodies.

So, in this lesson, we'll learn how your heartbeat guides your tempo. And the solution to fix that!

Why You Play Guitar Faster When You're Nervous

It's all in the heart. If we're playing live or in front of new faces, we tend to feel nervous, and our heart beats faster than usual. Since our heartbeat guides the tempo, we naturally play faster too. And we don't notice because we're used to following our heartbeat.

Since we're playing fast, we make more mistakes, which makes us more nervous. It's a vicious circle. Even top musicians struggle with this!

What's The Solution?

How do we slow down? First, take a nice deep breath before you start playing the next song. It gives you a moment to compose yourself. I find this super helpful.

Next, imagine what the song should sound like before you play. It'll help you find the right tempo and stick to it. :)

Finally, play a little more slowly than usual. If you have to speed up, that's okay. It's loads easier to speed up than it is to slow down!

Put these tricks into practice, and your playing will sound relaxed and awesome!

🎵 Learn new songs to play live! Choose from over 700 free song lessons - filtered by bands or artists. :)

lessons.title: ALWAYS Use Strap Locks
lessons.text:
Strap Locks Are a Must!

Time for another Quick Tip, and this one is super important! I've seen some beautiful guitars badly damaged in real time because they didn't have strap locks. Not pretty. Let's look at how you can avoid that. :)

What Is A Strap Lock?

A strap lock is a little piece of rubber or metal you put on the strap button to stop the strap from coming loose. Simple, but they can save you hundreds of dollars in repair bills! You can find them cheap but at more risk. If you pay for the best, I can guarantee your guitar strap won't come loose.

Which Strap Locks Are The Best?

My favorites are the Dunlop plastic locks, Schaller metal locks, and… Grolsch beer bottle tops! (See links below.)

The Dunlop plastic locks are cheap, strong, and easy to use. The Schaller metal strap locks are more expensive and tricky to fit but are effective and my favorite ones! The Grolsch option is less reliable but still works great. :) I recommend you try them all out and see what works for you.

Whatever your choice, make sure you use one. It's crazy not to. Invest a little bit of money, and your guitar will be safe and sound. :)

🧐 Do you (really) know how to secure your cable?

lessons.title: How To Roll Up Your Cables
lessons.text:
Keep Your Guitar Cables Safe By Rolling Them Up

In this video, we're looking at how to roll up your guitar cables. Sounds silly, but this can save you time and money, and it'll keep your cables safe.

🚨 Are you sure you know how to secure your cable on the electric guitar? Don't miss that out, eh?

How to Properly Roll Up Your Cables

Doing this keeps the cables tidy and protected. It's best if you see the video for my little demo. I'm sure you'll master this trick in no time. :)

💡 Once you've rolled up your cables, secure them by tying a little knot in the end or using a velcro cable strap.

Easy peasy and this will keep your cables nice and safe.

lessons.title: Always Ask Why? Demand proof!
lessons.text:
Ask Your Guitar Teacher Why

Time for another Quick Tip! In this lesson, we'll explore the importance of asking "why?" when learning guitar and taking advice from teachers. Why's it so important to question what someone is teaching you?

Why Ask? Why?

In the internet age, there are a lot of "experts" out there. Anyone can join a guitar forum, create a website, launch a YouTube channel and start teaching.

There are some awesome teachers, but there are some incompetent ones too. These teachers offer silly advice and give sillier reasons for it.

Asking why means we'll avoid poor instruction. With time, we'll be able to make our own decisions. We'll arrive at our answers. And that's a super important part of the guitar journey. :)

When Can We Ask Why?

Simple! Whenever we hear advice for anything on the guitar, we can ask why. Always be curious. Always be alert to your teacher's instructions. You can question their approach whether you're learning scales, chords, songs, or rhythm.

If a piece of advice seems strange, and they can't give you a good reason for it, you shouldn't listen to them. Find another way that makes sense to you.

If you aren't sure why I teach something a certain way, come to the forum and ask me. I want you to understand WHY I teach the way I do. And if my way doesn't make sense to you, don't listen to me either! :)

So, always ask "why?" and don't stop until you have an answer that makes sense. It sounds silly, but it'll ignite your potential as a guitar player. :)

💭 Food for Thought...

lessons.title: Set Your Strap For Optimum Performance
lessons.text:
Adjust Your Guitar Strap For Tip-Top Playing

In this video, we're talking about where to set your guitar strap for optimal playing.

I had a lot of trouble with this when I started playing guitar in my teens. I wanted to look like Slash when I played. But I practiced sitting down with the guitar at the usual height. So it was impossible when I stood up and tried to play with the guitar at my knees!

What's The Solution?

The bottom line is that we should play at the same height in practice as in performance. That way, our arms, wrist, and body are used to that position. When it comes to gigs, we'll feel natural and comfortable.

So if you want to play sitting down, practice when sitting down too. If you want to look like Slash, practice standing up with the guitar at knee height! :)

Easy peasy, but this will make a massive difference in your performances. :)

lessons.title: It's ALL About Rhythm
lessons.text:
Rhythm is Everything!

Time for another Quick Tip – a SUPER important one! Many of us guitarists focus too much on notes, melody, and scales. In this video, we'll see just how crucial rhythm is. Get the rhythm right, and your playing will rock! Get it wrong, and it will stink.

Why Is Rhythm So Important?

Rhythm has been with us for way longer than melody. It's inside us. It drives the music. If you have rhythm, you have music!

💡 Make Rhythm! Check out my Strumming Techniques 1&2 Courses.

If you're not sure, listen to my playing in this video. Without the rhythm, it doesn't sound like I'm playing a song. Nobody can sing along or enjoy the music. It doesn't matter how complex our playing is if the rhythm sucks.

But even when our chords suck, our playing sounds okay if we stay in rhythm. The listener can still enjoy what we're doing. :) Some blues masters create long solos with just a few notes. They have an excellent sense of time, and they use it to push and pull our emotions. Bottom line, your "feel" and ability to stay in rhythm are super important. You have to pay as much attention to rhythm as you do to chords, scales, and all the rest. :)

🧐 Why Is Strumming So Hard?

lessons.title: Explore Your Gear
lessons.text:
Experiment With Your Guitar Gear

In this Quick Tip, we're covering the topic of guitar gear. Pedals, amps, dials, all that good stuff.

We've all been there. We hear some awesome guitar sounds, then we rush to the internet to find out how to get the same sound. I've been there! When I shot a video for Little Wing, it took me an entire day to find the right sound. And it still wasn't perfect.

Take The Opportunity To Explore

These moments are a huge opportunity to get to know your gear really well. Pedals, amps, and guitars all sound really different from each other. The possibilities are endless.

Only by spending lots and lots of time with all your equipment will you become familiar with it. When you do, you won't need anyone to tell you how to make it sound a certain way. And you'll learn a ton along the way. :)

💡 I spend a lot of time changing the settings on my equipment and finding different sounds. It's a powerful exercise!

How To Explore

This is a massive part of the guitar journey, so try this exercise. Grab a pedal, and spend one hour experimenting with it. Just see what sounds you can find. Change the amp and guitar settings too. Can you find sounds you've never heard before? I also recommend you play around with the dials on your guitar too.

You'll be amazed at the range of sounds you can discover. You'll know your equipment better than anyone else. And you'll likely get inspired along the way. :)

🔥 New around here? Welcome to JustinGuitar :) Create your free account now!

lessons.title: Practice Breaking Strings
lessons.summary: Get ready for the real world by practicing playing your guitar without certain strings.
lessons.text:
Yes, you read that right.

But okay, I don't mean you should practice actually breaking your guitar strings. That's silly and a little dangerous! I mean that you should practice playing your guitar with a string missing.

Why Play With A String Missing?

There are good reasons for this. In your guitar journey, you're likely to break a string when you least want it. You're on the stage or playing at a party, and POP, a string breaks. It's more common than we'd like it to be. I broke a string on stage… after just re-stringing my guitar! It happens to the best of us.

So being prepared is super important. Can you improvise a Blues without the 2nd string or the thinnest string? How do you play your chords without the thicker strings?

We guitarists are creatures of habit. This exercise forces you to think differently! You can create new licks and find new sounds by avoiding a string.

How To Practice Playing With A String Missing

The first option is to remove a string from the guitar, or you can avoid certain strings while playing. Either way is fine! You'll have to make changes to prepare for the real thing. That might mean using another string more, or jumping strings, or a combination.

💙 Check out my Blues Guitar Courses and learn more about Rhythm and Blues Guitar.

lessons.title: Express Your Feelings
lessons.text:
Put Emotion Into Your Playing

Let's talk about feelings.

Okay, not quite. We're talking about how to express our emotions through the guitar!

For a while, I didn't understand this. I just played my songs and didn't pay attention to the emotional part of the music. But at some point, I realized how important this was, and my playing has changed LOADS.

Why Expressing Yourself Is Crucial

As guitarists, we often think too much. "Is this the right scale?" "Which note should I play next?" "Which chord is this?". That gets in the way of expression. The more we think, the more we stink. And expression is not just for pro musicians. Beginner and Intermediate players can express themselves too!

👍 Great music touches us. 🙌 The best musicians can put their emotions into the music. 💙 The listener then feels those same emotions.

So as a guitarist, you should be paying a lot of attention to expressing your feelings through the instrument when you play. You'll see a dramatic difference.

How Do We Express Our Feelings Through Our Playing?

I recommend you find the song's emotion inside before you start playing. For example, if you're going to play a slow ballad, think of a sad moment in your life. Make yourself feel a little sad.

Also, make sure to really listen to the music while you play instead of thinking too much. Then you can change your playing so that it matches the song.

Practice playing along to songs that make you emotional, and try to express how you feel in your playing. That way, you'll develop your skills of expression. Seriously, this is a HUGE part of the journey! Start experimenting with this idea. Your playing will sound awesome. :)

💭 Food for Thought...

lessons.title: Use Volume To Clean Up The Dirt
lessons.text:
Use Your Volume Dial!

In this Quick Tip, we'll discuss how to use your volume control to change the sound of your electric guitar without changing other settings like gain.

Why Volume Makes A Difference

Turning the volume dial on the guitar doesn't change the volume much when we use distortion. Strange, right? What does change is the amount of gain. You can notice a difference in the sound, even though the volume is very similar. Try it!

Volume Tricks

We can use this to improve our playing. Instead of using pedals to change the effects, we can use our volume dial. We can have it low for the rhythm and then turn it up in solo parts for more gain.

And whenever you want a little more gain, try changing the volume before you look at your amp or pedals. It's much quicker, and you can change it as you play. And if you want less, turn the volume dial down.

So it's time for you to explore with your guitar. How does turning the volume dial affect the sound? :)

💡 Check out my Jam Tracks! Tons of Blues and Rock tracks, so you create incredible solos.

lessons.title: What The Listener Hears?
lessons.text:
Listen Up!

This Quick Tip will cover the importance of listening to your bandmates during the song. It means you are aware of what the listener is hearing. But why is this so important?

Keep Your Ears Open

As guitarists in a band, we often go into a bubble. We focus on ourselves and our instruments, forgetting about the drums, the bass, the singer, and everyone else. This leads to poor music. We're not in sync with the other instruments, and the sound suffers.

The listener hears the entire band, not just you! So you must listen to the other instruments and change your playing to suit. I've fallen into this trap! A keyboard player once gave me a row for not paying attention to what he was playing. :(

Get in The Groove

That's not all. If you listen to the other players, you'll be much more "in the groove." You and the other musicians will all be on time, and it'll sound WICKED. By listening more, you'll also hear the band's dynamics, tempo, and tone loads better. So keep your ears open while you're playing. Your bandmates and the audience will thank you for it, and you'll become a better musician! :)

💡 Learn more! Explore my free guitar courses.

lessons.title: Learn Basic Piano Skills
lessons.text:
A Little Piano Goes A Long Way...

This quick video lesson looks at learning basic piano skills and why it's crucial to develop your musicianship. Hey, you're still on JustinGuitar, and I'm not suggesting you change instruments, but learning a little piano will take you to the next level.

So Why Learn Piano?

You'll learn loads about guitar and music by knowing some basic piano. That's because some tricky things on the guitar are LOADS easier on the piano. For a start, Theory is tricky on the guitar. It's tricky to find notes and see the relationship between chords and scales. But on piano, it's easy.

It's also simple to see the relationships between chords, like C and F. When we change from C to F on piano, it's easy to see that only two of the notes change. Not so easy on the guitar. Learning these things makes you an incredible musician and can open up many doors in your guitar playing. :)

What To Learn

Again, you need to learn some basic skills. How to play chords and scales, find the notes on the piano, and improvise a little. That's a great start.

And you don't need to buy an expensive piano. Keyboards are great; you can now find awesome ones at low prices. As for teachers, I can recommend this teacher. She has a classical approach. But you should also search around for lessons you like!

I hope you have fun with the piano just like I do. I know it can unlock your potential.

lessons.title: Don't Play Over The Singer!
lessons.text:
Let the singer do their thing!

It's Quick Tip time! Recently I saw a band, and the guitarist didn't let the singer sing. That inspired me to make this quick video! What's the lesson? Never play over the singer! As a guitar player, your job is to accompany them. :)

Sharing Is Caring

We guitarists love our solos and licks. We want to be the one everyone looks at. But we can't be that person when playing in a band. We must let the other band members, particularly the singer, have their chance.

How To Play At The Right Time

A good rule is never to play when the singer is singing. Instead, play little licks and lines in between the lyrics. Try to complement the singer with your playing.

And as I often say, if it sounds good, it is good. Keep your eyes open, and try to hear what the listener hears. Does your playing sound musical?

You can also listen to the greats, like BB King, who master the combination of singing and guitar. There's a great album by Robben Ford and Jimmy Witherspoon, where Robben beautifully complements Jimmy's singing.

So choose the right time to play and ensure the singer gets to sing! Your band's music will sound loads better. :)

💡 Learn more! Explore my free guitar courses.

lessons.title: Eyebrow Finger Lube
lessons.text:
A Strange, Super-Quick Tip

This quick tip video might be bizarre, but it's useful for electric and solo guitars.

Here we'll look at how to lube your fingers using your eyebrows and hair… Say what?

Natural Lubricant For The Fingers

Yes, you heard it right. If your fingertips get a little tender from running up the strings all the time, there's a super easy way to remedy it.

Just take your fingertips (of your fretting hand) and rub them in your eyebrows or hair. Go back to playing, and you'll notice a big difference. Seriously, try it out!

It turns out we have natural oil in our hair. So there's no need for fret lube or anything of the sort. Just remember this trick! Strange, I know. But it works! Have fun with your eyebrows and hair. :)

🔥 Join my Community and the discussion!

lessons.title: Record Yourself
lessons.text:
The Power Of Recording Your Playing

In this lesson, we'll talk about recording ourselves playing the guitar. This fantastic habit will help you a lot on your guitar journey.

Record Yourself To Improve Your Musicianship

You hear all those things you don't usually hear by recording yourself! Sometimes you discover good things you can deliberately repeat, giving you confidence. Other times you find weaknesses that you can then improve. Examples include timing, string noise, bad habits, and singing.

In my teens, I recorded myself practicing classical guitar. I was shocked to hear that I was breathing loudly! I'd never have noticed without the recording.

Things To Look Out For

Let's look at these areas. First, recording yourself is a great way to analyze your rhythm guitar. Are you in time with the beat? Are your chords clean? How about your rhythm – is it groovy?

It's also great for lead guitar. You can hear whether your bends are good or if there is string noise and whether your playing is in time with the music. You'll also find out if you're leaving enough space in your solos. And beyond that, we often play differently when we record ourselves, which can help us discover new things. Spooky!

How To Record Yourself

You don't need expensive equipment to record yourself playing. You can even use your mobile phone. If you're a Mac user, Garageband is a great choice. It comes with drum tracks, meaning you can add several layers to the song, and it's easy to use. You can also use a dictaphone. There are many options, and you don't have to break the bank.

So have lots of fun recording yourself. You'll discover loads about your playing, which is a great help as you continue your guitar journey. :)

lessons.title: Use Someone Else's Ears
lessons.text:
See Your Playing From Another Perspective

It's Quick Tip time! Today, we'll look at how to get a different perspective on your playing. I call this using someone else's ears. :)

Listen With Someone Else's Ears

As musicians, we get protective over our work. Once we create a song or a solo, we don't want to criticize it. It's like our baby. We get emotionally attached quickly.

But this is risky because our work might be poor, and we're too protective of noticing it. We want it to sound good, meaning we ignore the bad bits. Even if our children are ugly, we don't want to hear it. To us, they're the most beautiful kids in the world. :)

Imagine You're Someone Else

The following trick is where this gets super helpful. Imagine you're someone else when you listen to your playing, songwriting, or mixing. This person could be a guitar player, producer, or pro musician. Then listen again and imagine what that person would say about it.

When I mix songs, I imagine what my friend Reece would say about my work. And I usually end up with a better mix!

Would they change anything? What would they like and dislike? Asking yourself these questions takes you out of your perspective. Maybe you'll discover some poor bits in your work, but you might find some gold too. It's a fantastic trick!

So dare to use this tip whenever you listen back to your playing. You'll learn a lot about yourself as a musician. All this is valuable for the guitar journey. :)
