lessons.title: How To Fix A Loose Strap Pin
lessons.text:
It's Guitar DIY Time!

This quick video will look at how to fix a loose strap pin. No need to pay for a repair – this is a DIY job.

How to Fix

Sometimes all you need to do is tighten the pin with a screwdriver. But if the hole has got bigger, you'll need this little trick.

We'll remove the strap pin by unscrewing it with a screwdriver. Then we'll take a match, put it in the hole, and break the end off (you can use wood glue if you like). And after that, we put the strap pin in the hole and tightened it with a screwdriver. Don't have it very tight – you might damage the wood. Job done!

I hope this saves you time and money on your repairs. You can thank me here. :)

lessons.title: Protect Your Hearing
lessons.text:
Take Care Of Your Ears!

We're here with another Quick Tip video, but this one isn't a tip but more of a warning: I urge you to protect your hearing! Our ears are super important, and they're fragile.

Why Protect Your Hearing

As musicians, ears are our medium. Without them, we have no access to music! Hearing loss is common, and not just deafness. We can also lose the ability to hear high-pitched sounds, or we might have poor hearing in one ear. All of this means we can't fully communicate with the music. Lots of my friends have tinnitus. They have constant ringing in their ears and have to avoid playing live. It's nasty! :(

How To Protect Your Hearing

You can protect your hearing without buying anything. Avoid high earphone volumes and amps, and use high-quality speakers and headphones. If the quality is good, you don't need a high volume.

I recommend, however, that you buy earplugs. Cheap ones are okay, but sometimes they block certain frequencies and change the sound. Invest more, and you'll get good protection while being able to hear the original sound. I use custom-made earplugs. They're more expensive, but our hearing is so important!

🚨 Take your hearing seriously – without it, you can't hear music. Now, let's play.

lessons.title: Sock Neck Mute!
lessons.text:
Sock String Mute Trick!

Yeah. Real socks.

In this Quick Tip, we're looking at the sock neck mute – how to mute the guitar strings with a sock, and when this trick is useful.

How to Mute The Strings With A Sock

Easy peasy. All you need is a sock! Take one and loosely tie it around the neck at first few frets. Strum the strings and make sure no sound is coming out. If you tie the sock tightly, it works a bit like a capo! But we don't want that here. :)

Why Mute The Strings Like This?

This trick is strange, but it's useful in certain situations. For example, if you find it tricky to mute the strings when you're playing short lead lines in the higher frets, using a sock is a great trick. This is especially true if you're playing with lots of distortion.

It's also awesome for slide guitar and two-handed tapping. When you use these techniques, two notes ring out – the one "in front" of the fret and the one "behind" the fret. The sock mutes the one "behind,” giving a much cleaner sound.

🎵 I use this trick when I play Joe Satriani songs! :)

lessons.title: Take Care Of Your Posture
lessons.text:
Perfect Guitar Posture

This Quick Tip video brings up a super important topic. I wish I'd been told about it when I was young! As guitar players, it's easy for us to neglect our posture. It might seem boring or irrelevant, but the fact is that poor posture can cause terrible neck and spine issues. Much better to stop it early.

The way you sit is crucial. The best sitting posture is a straight back, your feet flat on the ground, looking forward. Also, remember to keep your shoulders relaxed. Let's look at common issues that take us away from this posture.

Bad Guitar Posture Habit #1: Twisting To See The Music

One terrible habit (my personal favorite) is twisting around to see the music. It might seem harmless, but it can cause severe neck and spine issues. The solution is to buy a music stand and put it in front of you with the music. That way, you can sit upright and face forward.

When I played guitar as a teen, I used to keep my sheet music to my left, behind the guitar. I had to twist my neck and spine AND bend over slightly to see it. After years of doing that, I now have permanent neck damage. :(

Bad Guitar Posture Habit #2: Bending Over To See The Frets

Another habit is bending and twisting your spine and neck to see the frets. As guitarists, our right hand is hidden from us as we play. And when we're practicing something new, we want to see what we're doing.

There is a way to see the frets without bending! The solution is to place a small mirror in front of you to see your right hand. That way, you can look forward and avoid the need to strain your neck. :)

And in general, I recommend you pay attention to your posture as you play. It needs attention and care, and it's easy to forget. Every so often, check your posture. If you're not sitting correctly, make changes.

Professional Posture Help

You'll need professional help if you have persistent pain. I see Jennie Morton at The British Academy Of Performing Arts Medicine. She's excellent, and many of my music friends see her too. And The Alexander Technique is an excellent method for posture.

So, look after your posture. It could save you thousands of dollars and lots of pain! :)

🎯 Explore my Playground to learn more.

lessons.title: Why Is Strumming So Hard?
lessons.summary: In this lesson, I'll answer one of the questions I get the most: WHY IS STRUMMING SO HARD? Well, get ready! I've got 11 tips that will help you NAIL strumming the guitar!
lessons.text:
Let's Sort Your Strumming For Good!

Rhythm causes beginner guitarists many issues, but the good news is that learning strumming is easy – when you know how. :)

If you find strumming tricky, you likely have trouble with the direction of strumming. What does this mean? Well, nearly all guitarists (including the very best) strum using the same technique: down strums on beats 1, 2, 3, and 4, and up strums on the "and." It is the key to good strumming!

And you need to keep your hand moving, no matter what pattern you use. This is especially true if you're a beginner guitar player. Make sure the hand is moving consistently. Also, make sure to hit mainly the thick strings on down strums and the thin strings on up strums.

Check If Your Strumming Is Consistent!

If you haven't learned to strum this way, try to play the pattern 1 2 3 4 (not strumming on the "and" beats). Make sure you can play this rhythm, keeping your hand moving consistently. Make sure it moves on the "and" beats, even though you don't touch the strings. You can avoid chords here – mute the strings and focus on your rhythm.

This is crucial! If you can't play this pattern, it'll be impossible to play complex ones. But once your hand moves consistently, you won't have to think about it. Try to do the same with the super common pattern 1 2+ +4 (I call this Old Faithful).

📚 Each module in my Beginner's Course has a strumming lesson. If you can play all those patterns, your strumming is in good shape!

How To Make Your Strumming Sound Natural

Once this is automatic for you, it's time to make it feel and sound natural. The audience senses how you feel when you play. Feeling relaxed is a vital part of strumming. It should feel easy, not hard!

The key is to practice the same pattern until it feels easy. When you've mastered the pattern, you'll be able to relax. Mute the strings and focus on the pattern, making it sound relaxed.

And always make sure to keep the rhythm going, don't lose it. You can mess up the chords, but do not mess up the rhythm – it sounds really weird! :)

More Strumming Tricks

If you're a beginner, I recommend you use a pick. It's usually easier than strumming with fingers. Make sure to use a thin one – as thin as you can find! Hold it lightly, and you'll have more control.

There are several options if you want to use your fingers for strumming. You can use your thumb, index finger, or both simultaneously. They all sound different, so experiment. :)

I hope that helps with your strumming! Remember – the key is consistency. Keep your hand moving! :)

👉 Strumming SOS is the perfect course to help you nail rhythm!

lessons.title: Fingerstyle vs Strumming
lessons.summary: Ok, fingerstyle or strumming? Which one is the hardest, and which one should you learn first?
lessons.text:
Fingerstyle Or Strumming For Newbies?

In this video, we'll cover a super common beginner question. The question is: "Which is harder, fingerstyle or strumming?"

My short answer is fingerstyle. But for me, the real question is: which do you want to play? Don't let other people tell you what you should learn! And don't learn something if it doesn't inspire you on your guitar journey. Learn what you love to play. :)

Why It's Easier To Start With Strumming

That said, strumming is easier for beginners because you don't need to be precise with your fingers. The important part is keeping the rhythm solid and moving your hand in the right direction.

But fingerstyle is quite fiddly. To play even the most basic patterns, you must hit the right strings, use multiple fingers, and keep in time. It's physically more demanding. The bass note also changes from chord to chord, which is tricky when starting.

Making Fingerstyle Automatic

Because fingerstyle is physically difficult, you must practice a lot until it's automatic. It means that singing while playing fingerstyle takes much more practice than singing while strumming. But eventually, it goes on autopilot, meaning you can play patterns without thinking. To help with this, you can deliberately distract yourself when you play them. :)

That said, fingerstyle can get super complex, loads more complex than strumming does. It's a world of its own!

💡 Check out my free Beginner Guitar Course, where we master the essentials of fingerstyle and strumming.

lessons.title: Should You Buy a Guitar Online?
lessons.summary: Guitar Online vs In-Store. Here are my tips on how to buy YOUR perfect guitar! I've also shared my 'Wednesday Guitar' experience.
lessons.text:
Your Guide To Buying A Guitar Online.

But Should You?

I've been drooling over guitars for the last 35 years, and I have to say that buying a guitar online was never so tempting as it is nowadays. Beautiful high-resolution guitar images, irresistible descriptions, and good deals are on the Internet. But should you buy a guitar without trying it first?

Which Guitar Should You Buy?

I've always felt that the guitar is the tool to express our musical mind. I need a deep connection with my instrument. Whenever a student asks me which guitar they should have, I say the same thing: "it's personal; I don't know which guitar you should have!"

Your instrument has to inspire you to practice, and you'll want to enjoy its sound and feel. And every guitar sounds different!

Are You Looking For Your Wednesday Guitar?

I once heard a fantastic story about the Wednesday Gretsch. Let me share it with you.

📖 Story Time: Wednesday Guitars! Workers arrive at the guitar factory after a big weekend on Monday mornings. They have the classic hangover: tiredness, sore head. The guitars they make on Mondays aren't going to be on point, are they? By Tuesday, the hangovers are almost gone, but the workers are still suffering a little. And so is the quality of the guitars. :) Thursday comes, and the supervisor pays the worker a visit. Everyone is nervous about their weekly quota! They're told they need hundreds of guitars out the door by Friday afternoon, so they start rushing! Thursday guitars probably aren't the best either. By Friday, when the workers realize they've only got that day to meet the quota, they forget about quality. They have to get ALL the guitars in their boxes! They leave all the small details behind and get them out the door at all costs.

So – the best guitars? The ones made on WEDNESDAY! Particularly in vintage instruments, we want the one with the perfect binding and beautiful soldering. And that's the bad news: every guitar is different.

👋 Watch the story of my Vintage Telecaster. :)

No Choice But To Buy Your Guitar Online?

It's February 2021 – pandemic time. We can't go to the store and try all their mid-price acoustics, right?

And – also because it's 2021! – we can't think that guitar production is what it used to be. We used to imagine that a passionate luthier lovingly made each guitar. That's not true anymore.

The good news is that guitar production standards have increased over the years. Nowadays, quality is off the scale! Even cheaper guitars sound good right out of the box. Most of them will come with low action, and you'll unlikely find any serious problems.

🎸 I buy online too! I've just got a new baby from Solo Dallas. Oh goodness...

So, if you have to buy a guitar online – do it! If you have the chance to go to a store, even better. Try out all the guitars you can. Find your Wednesday guitar.

🆘 If you need help choosing your first guitar, check out this lesson. :)

lessons.title: Beginner Day 1: Guitar Quick Start
lessons.summary: From tuning your guitar to learning your first chords and playing your first song - in only 15 minutes!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Guitar Quick Start – Introduction

00:43 How to Tune a Guitar

02:44 Easy Two-chord Songs

06:37 Guitar for Beginners – The Basics

09:14 Guitar for Beginners – Your First Chords

12:47 Guitar for Beginners – Advice For Day One :)
lessons.text:
Hey, how are you doing?

I'm Justin Sandercoe, and I've got the BEST Beginner Guitar Course for you. :)

It's great to have you here, especially if you've just got your first guitar!

First, we'll get your guitar in tune. Then we'll learn two easy open chords so you can play your first songs on the guitar right away. We'll also check out some of my top beginner tips so that you make the most of your guitar time. :)

Of course, this quick tutorial is just a taster. You'll get loads more by following my Beginner Guitar Course. You'll find it free on the website and on my Lessons & Songs app. The app offers an interactive karaoke-style feature that lets you use your new guitar skills to play songs you love.

💡 What's the difference between JustinGuitar.com and JustinGuitar Songs & Lessons App? Well, they're pretty different: my website has guitar courses for all levels, while my app only contains Grades 1 & 2 of my Beginner Course.

The app is ultra cool – and playing along with real songs from the very beginning is a game-changer for beginners.

Now, let's get stuck in. I know you can't wait to start playing your guitar!

How to Tune a Guitar (for beginners!)

Check your guitar is in tune before each practice session. An out-of-tune instrument won't sound good, no matter how well you play. :) A clip-on tuner is my favorite. It's usually more accurate than apps, and you can leave it on your instrument at all times. Ultra practical!

If you don't have a clip-on tuner or prefer using an app, make sure your tuner is accurate. The tuner on my app is free, and it's super easy to use. Just hit Manual Mode, and off you go!

🚨 Get the Note Names! Whether you tune with a tuner or app (or by ear!), learning the names of the open string notes on the guitar will be a big help. You have an E note on your thickest string. Then A, D, G, B, E. Here's a great way to remember:

Eddie – thickest string.

Ate

Dynamite

Good

Bye

Eddie – thinnest string.

Most tuners and apps will show you the open note string name, so learn this as soon as possible. Later in your guitar journey, you'll use those note names to do super-cool stuff. :)

2 Easy Guitar Chords

You'll find some guitar lessons that teach beginners to play single notes. But my method is different! We first learn chords, allowing you to play real songs right away.

That way, you'll stay motivated. And you'll build some hand muscles to help you out later. It's a little trickier, but I encourage you to keep at it. It'll pay off – I promise!

💡 Chords are simply three notes played together. But don't worry about that for now. Let's play our first songs instead!

A and D are the first chords we learn in my Beginner's Course. There's a reason for that! When learning them, you pick up one of my favorite guitar tricks – anchor fingers. This allows you to change chords faster, so you don't struggle when playing real songs.

These chords are ridiculously common. And learning them means you can play real songs. Watch the video to find out how to play A and D!

😩 Struggling with finger pain? It's normal when you start out! Stick with it, and make sure to place your fingers correctly. The finger pain will go away soon enough!

Now it's time to check out your first song. :)

5 Easy Songs for Beginners

Here are some easy songs you can play right now – all you need are those A and D chords!

Song #1 – You Sound Good to Me by Luce Hale

Song #2 – Feelin' Alright by Traffic

Song #3 – Boys 'Round Here by Blake Sheldon

Song #4 – Dance the Night Away by The Mavericks

Song #5 – Born in the USA by Bruce Springsteen

💡 Learn to play with me! Join JustinGuitar for free and start learning now. See you in Grade 1! :)

lessons.title: Classic E Blues Shuffle
lessons.summary: 59 Second Guitar Lesson on The Classic E Blues Shuffle
lessons.text:
Blues Guitar Trick: Rhythm Shuffle

This Classic E Blues Shuffle groove is great if you already learned Blues rhythm basics and are looking for something new to explore! :)

💡 Dream of nailing the Blues? Don't miss out on my Blues Rhythm Guitar Course to learn even more.

Ready? Let's get stuck in today's Quick Tip.

The Keys to This E Blues Shuffle

You'll need to remember three chord shapes to play this E Blues Shuffle on the guitar! Here they are:

The first is an open E7 chord (020100) that you'll play with fingers 1 and 2.

The second is 040200, which you play with fingers with 1 and 3.

The third is 050400 – use fingers 1 and 2 again.

Throughout the shuffle, mute the thinnest two strings with finger 1. You should also mute the D string with either finger 2 or 3.

Note that only three strings should ring out: the low E string and the notes you play on the A and G strings.

👂 Can you hear this in the demo? Let me know in the Discussions!

As for the rhythm, I won't write out the beats here; you should try to listen to the feel of the shuffle and replicate it. It'll sound awesome!

An up strum on the "and" after beat 4 sounds super hip, but don't forget your goal: have loads of fun with this Blues Shuffle. :)

👌 Explore my Blues Guitar Courses and go even further!

lessons.title: D Chord Using A C Shape
lessons.summary: 59 Second Guitar Lesson on playing a D Chord Using a C Shape
lessons.text:
Beautiful D Chord Alternative on the Guitar

Are you tired of playing the same easy open chords? Learn a new guitar trick in under 59 seconds and get inspired. :) Let's look at how to play a lovely D chord using the C shape.

How to Play This D Chord

Okay, this is not a D Major chord. It also has 4th and 9th tones, but don't worry about Theory for now!

Hold a regular C Major open chord and move your three fingers up two frets. You'll end up with X54030, a lovely chord! Try it out instead of plain old D Major. :)

You can add your pinkie to the 5th fret on the thinnest string (X54035). Give it a try! Again, another beautiful "D" chord.

Try adding your pinkie to other notes – what other cool chords can you find?

Grab your guitar and try out these two chords! And remember, if it sounds good, it is good. :)

🎵 Up for more? My Grade 3 lessons open up your fretboard!

lessons.title: The I to IV Blues Climb
lessons.summary: 59 Second Guitar Lesson on The I to IV Blues Climb
lessons.text:
Try This Great Blues Climb Trick!

This little pick-up from the I to the IV chord will add some spice to your blues rhythm playing. :)

Playing The Climb Between E and A

Let's look at playing this climb in the open position, going from E (the I chord in an E blues) to A (the IV chord in an E blues).

On beat 2 of the final bar of E, we play the note at fret 2 on the thickest string (F#), on beat 3, we play the next note up on the same string (G), and on beat 4, we play the note up from that (G#). Then we go to the A chord on beat 1. :)

Playing The Climb Between G and C

Let's look at playing the climb in a blues in G, using barre chords. With the same rhythm (starting on beat 2, one note per beat), we play fret 5 on the E string (A), then fret 6 (Bb), fret 7 (B), before moving to C for the next bar. In the video, I keep finger 2 in place, meaning I play power chords on each beat instead of individual notes.

There are tons of options for this. Try moving between other chords, try playing it across other strings! See what other cool climbs you can find.

👋 Remember – if it sounds good, it is good. :)

lessons.title: Luke's Rosanna Bend
lessons.summary: 59 Second Guitar Lesson on Steve Lukather's super awesome bending trick in the song Rosanna!
lessons.text:
Try This Gorgeous Guitar Bend.

The solo that Luke (Steve Lukather) plays on the song Rosanne is just incredible! It took me ages to figure out how he was playing this lick... until I saw it on a hot licks video cassette.

📼 Yeah, I'm that old; learned a lot from video cassettes! What about you? Introduce yourself here!

Now, let's check out today's Quick Tip. :)

How to Play The Lick in Rosanna

The lick from Rosanna is also a super cool trick! We play a tone bend on fret 14 of the thinnest string using finger 3 (F# to G#). And while holding the bend, we add our little finger at fret 13 on the same string we are bending. We're fretting a bent string! You can use this lick over an E, E7, or F# min chord. See the video for the full lick.

🎧 If you are not familiar with the band Toto, check them out! hey're awesome and Luke is one of the finest guitarists to ever grace our planet - as good as guitar gets!

💡 Complete String Bending Guitar Lesson here!

lessons.title: Rapid Natural Harmonic Trick
lessons.summary: 59 Second Guitar Lesson on a cool rock technique - a Rapid Natural Harmonic Trick
lessons.text:
Rockstar Electric Guitar Harmonics

Learn a super cool trick for electric guitar in this quick lesson! Joe Satriani was who I first heard play it, but I'm sure other guitarists used it before he did. It sounds loads harder to play than it is!

How to Play These Rapid Harmonics

Rest one of your fingers lightly (very lightly!) on the A string at fret 5. Then start picking the string quickly, as seen in the video tutorial. You should hear a harmonic. Then start moving your finger towards the nut. The sound will change! You can run your finger between fret 5 and frets 1.2-1.3 (imagine there was a fret between frets 1 and 2), and you'll get this strange but awesome harmonic sound.

🧐 What happens if you switch strings? Interesting...

Have fun playing around with this cool rock trick :)

🎼 My song lessons come with chords, tabs, and lyrics with JustinGuitar Tabs!

lessons.title: Uber Fast Trill Tapping
lessons.summary: 59 Second Guitar Lesson on Uber Fast Trill Tapping - super easy and sounds really cool! :)
lessons.text:
Trill Tap Time!

I don't remember where I learned this trill tapping. But it sounds so fast and is easy. Use it to impress people who don't play! And by exploring, you can find lots of other trill tricks!

Trill to Trill Tap

We start with an ordinary trill, with finger 1 on fret 12 of the thinnest string and finger 3 hammering and pulling off on fret 15. No picking is needed! And make sure to mute all the other strings with your picking hand. :)

If you have that mastered, take finger 3 of your picking hand and tap it on fret 15 as soon as you flick off your other finger! Then add finger 3 of your right hand again. Repeat, and increase your speed as much as you can!

Awesome, huh? Enjoy, and see what else you can do with this trill tapping. ;)

💙 Legato Playing: Master your hammer-ons and flick-offs!

lessons.title: Capo The Chords To Best Suit Your Voice
lessons.summary: Learn how to use your guitar capo to make a song better fit your voice. A capo is a fantastic tool for singers and any guitarist working with singers!
lessons.text:
Ever wondered how to use a capo to make a song better fit your voice?

In this lesson, we'll check out how to use a capo to make a song better suit your singing voice!

Learning how to use a guitar capo properly is a super-common problem for beginners, and it takes time to learn how that works. Ultimately, it's all about experimenting, but let's review some pointers.

Singing in a Higher Key with the Capo

Let's say the song goes G, D, Em, C. Female singers tend to sing around a 3rd or a 4th higher than male singers, so we'll put a capo on fret 5 to move it up a 4th (or five semitones). Now use the same chord shapes as before, treating the capo as if it were the guitar's nut.

🎵 Singing Essentials – Brush up on your singing skills with my 10-step singing method for guitarists.

The movement of the song is identical, except everything is a little higher (the song is now in the key of C, and the chords become C, G, Am, F). Listen to both progressions, and you'll hear this.

Find the Best Key for You

Find the keys that work well for your voice to make the most of the capo. In my videos, I sing in the original key, which often doesn't fit my voice. But you don't need to!

If you find the original is a little too low, put the capo on fret 2, sing the entire song, and see how it feels. Still a little low? Move it up to fret 4. It takes experimentation, and your choice of fret could vary for each song.

🎸 Learn how to use your capo in creative ways! You can play the same chords using different grips, which is a great trick for beginners - but not only. ;)

There are few songs with the capo higher than fret 7. If you keep moving the capo and the melody is still too low, try removing it and playing in an open position. This is equivalent to using a capo at fret 12, except the chords will be an octave lower.

Add Emotion & Feeling

This doesn't mean you choose the easiest option either. The highest note in the song is often in the bridge or chorus, where the singer goes for their highest note. If you can't reach it, you have to change the key.

Try to make this one your highest note. You'll have to put in a lot of effort to reach it, meaning the song will come alive.

The key here is to experiment. With time, you'll learn which keys work for you. I hope these tips help you loads with your singing! Laters. :)

🎤 Up for some practice time? Choose from one of my free song tutorials and happy trails!

lessons.title: Rut Busters ep.1 The Language Of Music
lessons.summary: This first Rut Buster video with Captain Anderton was lots of fun, a bit rambling, but think we explore some cool ideas!
lessons.text:
Day 1 With Captain Lee

In this first video with Captain Lee (of the good ship Anderton’s) we explore the language of music and how understanding it makes us better guitarists!

What Is Rut Busters?

Lee is an intermediate guitar player who’s stuck in a rut and seeing little progress. Anderton’s and I decided to collaborate for some YouTube videos, and we came up with the idea of Rut Busters! That way, we can help players like Lee take their playing to the next level and unlock their guitar potential. :)

I reminded Lee that all guitarists fall into ruts, no matter our level. I have ruts in my playing. But on my guitar journey, I’ve found lots of solutions that help me get out of them! We’ll explore them in this series.

Lee’s Guitar Journey

Lee started playing when he was around 15 years old. He only had a few structured lessons right at the beginning of his journey. But he grew up around music stores, meeting lots of great players and picking up ideas along the way.

When he started doing videos for Anderton’s, it was a new start for him. He committed to taking guitar seriously for the first time in 20 years. In meeting guest guitarists who are fantastic players, Lee realized he’d been playing the same old music for years!

Exploring The Blues

Lee told me he could play blues, switch keys, and use the minor and major pentatonic scales, but doesn’t know which chords to use those scales with. He tended to guess at the start of a lick, hoping it sounded good.

This led to a valuable lesson: scales are like the alphabet. They’re the letters we use to make words. We don’t speak using the alphabet – we use words. In the same way, when we play guitar, we communicate through licks, not scales. If we use scales, we don’t communicate anything! We want our licks to be our comfort zone, not scales. On the other hand, if we randomly jump between licks, our playing lacks structure. We communicate more, but it still sounds strange.

💡Quick Playing Tip! Playing scales is like repeating the alphabet. Playing licks is like using words.

Make Cool Solos By Expanding On Licks

The key to expanding our solo playing is to find licks we love and use them. From those licks, we can form solos and lead lines. Try this exercise: put on a backing track, choose one of your favorite licks, then solo using only that lick, expanding on it by adding notes, changing the rhythm, and so on. Lee’s playing sounded wicked with this exercise! One of Paul Gilbert's tricks is to imagine that you’re playing a kick drum as you solo. This helps you create great rhythms in your solo playing.

Where Do Licks Come From?

Sounds silly, but really, where do they come from? When I was younger, I used to think licks came from books, so I bought a ton of them! Then I realized I was wrong.

In truth, licks come from other guitarists. That is, you steal licks from records. Look at all the greats, and that’s how they learned the trade. They transcribed the songs they loved, learning the licks along with it.

Choose a song from your favorite guitarist and find a few licks to figure out. Eric Clapton is a great player to steal licks from – he’s pretty traditional and uses old licks from Albert King, B.B. King, and Robert Johnson.

Playing What You Hear

Lee commented that he found it tricky to hear music in his mind and then find the right notes on the guitar. I'm not surprised! This skill requires an excellent ear and knowledge of the fretboard.

Getting good at this is a lifelong journey. I’ve met a few guitarists who can do it, but most people can’t, even great guitarists. Here’s a little trick: try to play Happy Birthday, starting on fret 5 of string 3. And make sure you stay in that area of the neck. Not so easy, is it? This gives you an idea of how tricky it is to play what you hear.

The Biggest Lesson From Today

💡Guitar Wisdom – You can play your way to a new way of thinking, but you can’t think your way to a new way of playing!

If you only know licks in your mind, do you think you’ll be able to play them in a real situation? Will they sound good when you play them? The answer is no. You need to practice these licks – and all guitar ideas – over and over again until they become second nature for you. Spend five minutes a day, five days a week, practicing a new idea. Within a few weeks, you’ll be a different guitar player. Guaranteed.

Stick around for more Rut Busters and take your playing to the next level! See you in the next one. :)

lessons.title: Rut Busters ep.2 Groovin' On The 6
lessons.summary: Episode 2 of the Rut Busters, we explore using the 6th of the Major Scale in a Blues context!
lessons.text:
Using The 6th In The Blues

Hey, it’s Justin here! In this edition of Rut Busters, Lee and I explore a cool note you can add to your blues solo playing. That note is the 6th! :)

What Is The 6th?

The 6th is a fantastic blues note you can use with the Minor Pentatonic Scale! Players like B.B. King used it a lot, giving them a unique sound. In the key of A, it’s the note f#. In position 1 of the Minor Pentatonic, you’ll find it at fret 7 on string 2, and at fret 4 on string 4.

Some of my students over the years have avoided the 6th because they think it’s the “wrong” note to play. But it actually sounds wicked over the A and D chords in an A blues.

Why Is It The 6th Note Of The A Major Scale?

Lee asked me why f# is note 6 in A Major and not in A Minor Pentatonic, which led to a little discussion on theory. First off, penta = 5: the Minor Pentatonic scale only has five notes. The note f# isn't part of the A Minor Pentatonic (a, c, d, e, g).

Also, Western harmony uses the Major Scale as a starting point for naming notes and chords. When we say the 6th, we mean the 6th of the Major Scale, not the 6th of the minor scale.

By the way, when I say 6th in a blues context, I only mean the 6th note in the original key, not the 6th of each chord. So in an A blues, the “6th” means the note f# and no other. :)

💡Remember: in an A blues, the 6th means the sixth note of the A Major scale (f#), whatever chord we happen to be playing. It doesn't change!

When Can We Use The 6th?

Over A, you’ll find the 6th sounds best when you play it then move away. It works, but you wouldn’t usually finish a solo on it. But over D, you don’t need to move away because it’s already part of the D chord (d f# a). It’s the 3rd in the key of D. In fact, it sounds great on the transition from A to D.

A little question for you – which scale degree is f# in the key of E Major? That’s right, it’s the 2nd or 9th degree. This means it can also work over the E Major chord, creating an E9 sound. I tend to play it less, though.

Another cool trick with the 6th is that no matter where you play it on the neck, you can always play a semitone bend from it to the b7th degree!

Exercise: Have a five-minute jam over a 12-bar blues in A and target f# over all the chords. See what awesome sounds you can find! Another exercise we tried in the video is to solo over A and D only, using only notes from the Minor Pentatonic over the A, then targeting f# during the D chord.

Where Else Can We Find The Note F#?

Exercise: Grab your guitar and see if you can find two f# notes further up the neck. Where are they?

You’ll find f# notes at fret 11 on string 3 and at fret 14 on string 1. These are in another pattern of the Minor Pentatonic scale, so I suggest you get really comfortable using the f# notes in the other pattern before learning these.

💡Quick Guitar Tip: it’s one to think about the 6th, but it's another thing to use it well. You can analyze, but always remember: it’s just a note! If it sounds good, it is good. :)

Practice Tips

I suggest we spend half our practice time on exercises and the other half playing whatever we want. Lee glimpsed the power of practicing one exercise for five minutes repeatedly. He’s right – it’s super powerful!

We all find it difficult to practice, and those five-minute periods are challenging. The trick to inspiring yourself is to practice things that are both beneficial AND enjoyable. There are some super-boring exercises out there!

And the ultimate motivator is to see the power of this focused practice. This transforms us as guitar players and takes us out of our habitual playing, our ruts! And it can happen quickly. :)

Stick around for more Rut Busters with Lee and I and take your playing to the next level! Laters. :)

🎵 Explore the 6th further in my Colouring The Blues Module.

Captain Lee runs Anderton's Music in Guildford (UK) which is a store near me and who I knew had a great presence on YouTube, so I got in touch about trying out some collaboration ideas and it's morphed into these lessons for Lee, which are a lot of fun! We also have some gear reviews planned where Lee will come hang at my studio!

lessons.title: Rut Busters ep.3 Chord Specific Licks
lessons.summary: In this session we figure out how and why some licks work over only some chords and we explore that general territory!
lessons.text:
Master Your Use Of Licks

This series is aimed at guitar players who're in a rut! Today, we explore chord-specific licks. Sounds kinda scary, but this really ignites your potential as a guitarist. :)

What Is A Chord-Specific Lick?

It's a lick containing notes that are likely to clash with other chords in the sequence, particularly in a blues. These licks sound great over some chords but horrible over others!

Knowing when certain licks sound good helps you use them in the proper context. It also means you can develop one lick into many others, adapting to each chord. Let's see how!

A Really Common Chord-Specific Lick

In the blues, there are loads of popular chord-specific licks. A typical example is the one we play in the video. In the key of G, it contains the notes b flat, b, d, and g.

When we play this lick over the G, it sounds great. But play it over the C chord (the IV chord in a G Blues) and it sounds terrible! Over the D chord, it's so-so. Try it for yourself. :)

This is all to do with the note b. It's part of the G Major chord (g b d) – that's why it works with the G chord. But it clashes with the others. So in general, the 3rd in the Major scale of the root note is chord-specific, meaning any licks containing it are chord-specific.

💡 More Chord-Specific Licks! Learn lots of chord-specific licks with my Blues Licks module.

How to Use Chord-Specific Licks

Definitely use the 3rd when you're playing the I chord, but avoid it on the IV chord and be careful on the V. In those cases, switch it for another note, then move back on the I. You can adapt your licks to the chords you're playing. :)

You can also move the entire lick up. In our lick in G, we use the notes g, b flat, b, and d. When the song changes to C, you can move this lick into C by moving up the neck. Start with the note e flat at fret 8 of string 3 and play the same shape. Can you figure out the names of the other notes?

Another option is to see the basic chord shape as you play and hit those notes. This is great for unusual chords, like a B Major chord in an A blues. Find a B Major chord on the fretboard, and play the notes from it. You can't go wrong!

💡 Quick Tip! I learned loads from transcribing artists like Chuck Berry and The Rolling Stones. You can clearly hear that they target chord shapes, like the B Major chord I mentioned.

Key Question: How Do I Know If A Lick Is Chord Specific?

You can't always move licks around as you please. Sometimes they'll just sound weird! Always ask yourself if a lick is chord specific, and use your ear as the final judge!

💡 Lee's Nugget of Wisdom: forget about the scales and chords, and LISTEN to what you're playing.

If it uses a lot of notes from the chord, it probably is, and you'll likely be able to use the same lick moved up and down the neck. If it doesn't, it probably isn't chord-specific, meaning you can't simply shift it as before. This is getting into advanced-level blues!

Jamming Game

This is a little jam game for two people! One plays rhythm guitar, using only major and minor chords for at least one bar on each. Do not use complex jazz chords!

The other player turns their back and tries to play solos without knowing the names of the chords that the rhythm guitarist is playing. That way, they really need to listen to the sound of the chords. Here's a tip that almost always works: you're only ever a semitone away from a good note! :)

The point? After doing this a lot, you start to develop your ear. You also realize whether you need to step up a semitone or a tone to get to a good note. And it stops you resorting to your favorite licks!

And as we talk about in the video, there is no such thing as a "wrong note." Context is king. If you play a note among other notes and with enough conviction, you can make it sound good in almost any context.

One Final Exercise!

A great exercise for blues playing is to write down all your pet licks – the ones you use ALL the time – on TAB. This shows you how many you have, which might be fewer than you think.

Figure out whether they're chord specific or not, and adapt them to other chords as you need to. Use this to expand your playing! I have blank TAB on my website – just follow the link.

Stick around for more Rut Busters and take your playing to the next level! Cheers. :)

💙 Now it's time to play like the masters! Check out my module Making The Blues Changes.

lessons.title: Rut Busters ep.4 How To Practice
lessons.summary: In this episode, Justin and Lee chat about how and what to practice and how to make a practice routine!
lessons.text:
Master Your Practice

Hey, it's Justin and Lee for another Rut Busters! Most people – Lee and I included – can't find enough time to practice the guitar. And even when we have time, knowing what to practice is tricky. Today, we'll create a solid practice routine. That way, we'll take full advantage of our limited time.

Learning Instruments At Different Ages

Lee commented that when he used to learn instruments at school, he'd do his music practice every day from five to six o'clock. He had a book and knew exactly what he had to practice.

But now, his schedule is so full that he only plays when he finds half an hour. And he has no structure or routine. So he finds it tough to be disciplined and know which exercises to do.

When To Practice

If we can find a block of time early in the morning or late at night, that's super helpful. Setting aside time on certain days is a great way to create consistency when you're busy. There are often gaps in our day – periods when we aren't busy. Use them!

How To Practice

I asked Lee what he practices. His usual practice is to repeat chords using a loop pedal and play solo guitar over them. By doing so, he's repeating the same exercise, which is a great start. He also sits down with his colleague Pete. They listen to tracks together, analyzing and playing the guitar parts. But he doesn't have a strict practice routine.

💡 Perfect Practice – Use the My Practice Assistant feature on my site to create amazing practice schedules!

The trick is to do the routine five days a week. And don't try an intense practice routine if you've never done it before. That doesn't usually work! After a week or two, you'll lose motivation.

Your Practice Routine

If you have 30 minutes, you should spend 15 minutes doing free practice. In other words, play whatever you want! This could be exploring an idea, playing a song that's too tricky for you, or playing chords. Seriously, anything goes, as long as it's guitar.

Spend the other 15 minutes doing structured practice, divided into three periods of five minutes. Use a timer! It’s SUPER helpful. That way, you have a clear end to each exercise. This focuses you.

If you only do structured practice, it's hard to see the effects of your work in your playing. That's why free practice is crucial – it's when you actually see the benefits of structured practice. But without structured practice, you don't make progress. You don't give yourself your chance to learn new stuff. You get stuck in a rut!

💡The Reality of Ruts – Several great guitarists have told me they get into a rut sometimes. It happens to us all!

Let's look at the four practice areas.

Practice Area 1: Technique

Technique is vital. This means your physical ability to play the guitar, beyond music and songs. Can you pick accurately? Do you have the strength for string bends? I could suggest at least 40 technique exercises, and you'll likely find a few areas that need work.

💡Tip-Top Technique – Find tonnes of technique exercises in the dedicated section on my website!

Practice Area 2: Knowledge

The next area is knowledge. Now we go into theory world! This is another huge area and includes things like knowing which chords go together well and which scales to use in which context. A little bit of this can go a long, long way. It can revolutionize your guitar playing!

The key to mastering theory is that you must put it into practice. There's no use in learning theory from a book and not knowing when to use the knowledge. This makes a lot of guitarists give up!

💡Theory In Practice – Use theory to ignite your guitar potential with my course Practical Music Theory!

Practice Area 3: Ear Training

I also suggest some sort of Ear Training. You can do interval training, which is a little boring for some. Transcribing is great, and it's probably best to save up 15 minutes for it!

Spend that time trying to figure out a lick, chord, or song you like, and make sure to write it down. That way, you can analyze it and will have it saved for later! Another excellent ear training exercise is to Play What You Hear – imagine a song in your mind and see if you can play it on the guitar.

💡Master Transcribing – I've created a module with a ton of transcribing aids. Check it out here. :)

Practice Area 4: Song

The final area of practice is songs. You must use all your hard work in songs! You can compose your own learn the ones you love most!

Technique Work: Playing The Major Scale

Lee and I tried a technique exercise together: playing Pattern 1 of the Major Scale using alternate picking. Here are some great tricks for making the most of this one!

Make sure to play the notes on the b string using fingers 2 and 4. One reason is that the notes on the two thinnest strings and the two thickest strings follow the same pattern (2 4; 1 2 4). Using these fingers makes that easier to see, so you remember the scale better!

Another common issue with alternate picking is playing a down pick when you move down onto a new string. If you can't play the scale correctly, just use all down picks until it's natural. Then move on to alternate.

And don't play too quickly! If you make a mistake, it means you're going too fast. Slow down and make sure each note is perfect. Program your brain with this! Then speed up. Use a metronome, with down picks on the beats and up picks on the "ands." That way, you'll keep good time, your picking will be perfect, and you'll know your speed.

💡Time Trainer App – Find a metronome and loads more features on my Time Trainer app!

Without realizing, Lee was using palm mute to play the Major scale. This is quite a specific technique, so I recommend using it only in the correct context.

Economy Picking v Alternate Picking

As we discussed, Lee found it tricky to play alternate picking when changing strings. Instead, he used economy picking. Both systems work great in certain circumstances, but I suggest alternate picking here.

Creating a solid practice routine is a sure way to busting out of a rut, so start using one right away. And stick around for more Rut Busters to take your playing to the next level! Cheers. :)

lessons.title: Rut Busters ep.5 Chords In Keys?
lessons.summary: How do you work out the chords in a key and why is it important?
lessons.text:
Chords In Keys With The Captain

Today, we’re looking at the Major Scale, why it’s important and why (believe it or not) it’s not just for torturing school children! We can make music with it, and it’s fun! And really, it’s a vital part of making good music. Let’s see how.

Major Scale Suffering

We’ve all heard it a million times. Do Re Mi Fa So La Ti Do – that’s the major scale. At some point on your guitar journey, a teacher will tell you to practice it, though they might not tell you why. My teacher in high school really wanted me to learn the Major Scale, and I never got into it.

But I loved Metallica at the time, and one day I transcribed the intro solo to Fade To Black. I suddenly realized it used the same notes as the Major scale pattern my teacher had given me that week! Metallica used the Major Scale? Awesome!

My teacher didn’t tell me I could make great music with the Major Scale or use it to improvise over my favorite songs. It seemed boring and pointless until I discovered the hidden magic.

Major Scale On The Piano

Lee and I used the piano to explore the major scale. It’s really easy to see where the notes are on the piano. On guitar, it’s not so intuitive and takes practice to play. I encourage you to follow along with what we do. If you don’t have a proper piano, there are loads of free apps.

To get started, let’s play the C Major Scale. To find the note c, find one of the pairs of black notes. C is the note to the left of the three below those. Play that note followed by the next seven white notes (the C Major Scale has no sharps or flats), and you’ll hear the C Major Scale. Make sure you hear “Do Re Mi Fa So La Ti Do."

💡Building Major Scales: Learn how we make major scales with this lesson on Major Scale Construction.

Finding All The Chords In C

Now, did you know that chords come from scales? If not, all the basic major and minor chords are just three notes from a Major scale played together. Since they have just three notes, they’re called triad chords.

You can play a C Major chord on a piano by playing the note c with the white note two up (which is e) and the white note two up from that (g). Play those three notes together, and you’ll hear a C Major chord.

Great, you can play the C Major chord. Let’s find the other chords in C. Take that shape (three fingers, each separated by one key) and move it all one key to the right. That’s Dm. If you keep moving this shape up one key at a time, you’ll have Em, F, G, Am and Bdim, but we’ll leave out the last one.

We’ve only used the C Major Scale to make all these chords (C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am). So, they’re called the chords in C Major, or the chords in the key of C.

💡Chords In A Key: Ace chords in a key with my lesson on Diatonic Chords!

Soloing in C Major

Now, try playing a C Major chord with your left hand. At the same time, play ANY of the white notes on the piano with your right hand. You’re playing the C Major scale over a C Major Chord. :) Which notes sound good? Then use the piano to play notes from C Major over the top.

As another piano exercise, get together with a friend. One of you plays chords from the key of C on the guitar, and the other plays notes from the C Major Scale on the piano (white notes only).

What did you notice? When we did this exercise, Lee noticed that some notes and chords go better together than others! This is a crucial point. In short, notes found in the chords the guitarist is playing will sound great, and you can stay on them for a few seconds.

Others might sound a little strange, and you have to play “through” them, quickly changing to another note. But they all sound good, if used properly.

How do you target those good notes? Well, if you know the notes in all chords, you can deliberately change the notes you play during each chord, which is tricky. Or you can simply use your ear!

G Major Improvising

Time to switch back to guitar now and change keys! Let’s look at soloing over a real song using our knowledge of the major scale.

All the chords in the song Wish You Were Here by Pink Floyd are in the key of G. So you can use the G Major Scale to solo over that song. Again, all of the notes are good, but some will sound better than others.

Note that in this exercise, I had Lee use the same fingers that he uses to play the major scale up and down. But that was only for his sake. In the real world, this fingering is pretty irrelevant. What’s most important is that you express yourself.

Loads of songs stay within one key. But not all of them follow the rules. For example, Nirvana’s signature sound comes from using chords that aren’t in the same key.

Try soloing over these other songs in G:

John Mayer – New Light

Bob Dylan – Knockin’ On Heaven’s Door

Neil Young – Heart of Gold

Tom Petty – Free Fallin’

Guns ‘n Roses – Sweet Child of Mine (parts of it)

💡Key Tip: Any song that uses only the chords G, C, D, Am, Em, and Bm is in the key of G.

Scales And Improvising

Lee noticed that two notes of the G Major Scale often sounded strange: c and f#. Funnily enough, if you play the G Major Scale without them, you end up with the G Major Pentatonic scale. Kudos, Lee! If you realize these things, it’s a sign you’re listening to the band, not just yourself.

You can solo over any song using a major scale (in any key) if it contains the chords from that key. Loopers are amazing for this. We think they're the most important tool for intermediate guitar players! Two inexpensive options are the TC Ditto and the Boss RC-3, which cost around £80. Loopers allow you to solo over your favorite songs free of all the extra instruments and play over your own tracks. Cool!

💡Loopers: Check out this lesson to learn How To Use A Looper.

Long term, you don’t want to think about scales and scale shapes. You use those concepts to learn the alphabet and find the notes on the neck. Eventually, your fingers tend to find the right notes, the ones you imagine in your musical mind. This comes after lots of scale practice and improvising.

So we've explored a lot of theory and how to use it to transform your playing. This is just the beginning. There's lots more to come in this Rut Busters series, so stick around for me. From Lee and I, laters! :)

lessons.title: Rut Busters ep.6 What Key Am I In?
lessons.summary: Watch the Captain have a Eureka moment with chords in keys :) hope it might help you have one too!
lessons.text:
Finding The Chords In Major Keys

Hey it's Justin and Lee back for another Rut Busters! In this episode, we dig deeper into how to find the chords in a key using the guitar. If you've struggled with chords in the key, this lesson could finally unlock that door for you. :)

Quick Trick For Identifying Chords In A Key

This is a fast way to use the guitar to identify keys and the chords they contain. Remember, in a Major key, there are three Major chords, three minor chords, and a diminished chord, which nobody uses! These are called the diatonic chords.

This trick works when the root note of the scale is on string 6. And it leads us right to our first chord. This note is the root of the I chord, a Major chord.

💡Master Chords In A Key: Check out this lesson on Diatonic Chords!

Now, play the note at the same fret on the next string. That’s the root of the IV chord, which is also Major. Another two frets up on that string, you’ll find the root note of the other Major chord, the V chord. So the I, IV and V chords in a key, the Major chords, fall into a neat L-shaped pattern.

As for the minors, we can find the root of the II chord two frets up from our starting point. The root of the III chord is two up from that. Finally, the root of the VI chord is on string 5 at the same fret as the III chord. Notice the minors form their own L shape!

Overall, we have this cool visual pattern:

💡Outside The Box: Many songs use chords that aren't diatonic. Often there’s one chord that isn’t in the home key.

Use This Pattern To Figure Out Chords In A Key

Now, try to use this pattern to figure out the chords in the key of F Major. Hint: the note F is at fret 1 (or fret 13) on string 6. The answer is at the very bottom!

Jamming Exercise: You can now use the chords in the key of F to jam! Get together with a friend, or use a looper. Play chords in the key of F and solo over the top, using Pattern 1 of the Major Scale.

Using This Pattern To Figure Out The Key

If we know only some of the chords in the key, we can use this pattern to figure out the key we’re in. We don’t even need to know the note names. Grab a pencil and paper – here are some key-related exercises to test yourself! Find the answers at the very bottom. :)

1) A song has a Major chord with its root at string 5, fret 2, and another at string 5, fret 4. Which key is it in?

2) Another has a minor chord rooted on string 6, fret 5 and one rooted on string 6, fret 7. Which key is this one in?

3) Finally, Knockin’ On Heaven’s Door uses the chords G, D, C, and Am. What key is it in? Find the answers at the bottom!

💡Major Scale In Depth: Learn how to build Major Scales with my lesson on Major Scale Construction.

IV and V Chord Trick

Take a look at all the pairs of Major chords we’ve found so far. In the key of G, the IV and V are C and D Major. In F, they’re Bb and C. In A, they’re D and E. Do you see a pattern?

The IV and V chords are always, always a tone apart! So if we find two Major chords in a song that are a tone apart, they have to be the IV and V. Knowing this, we can then figure out the home key. If they’re rooted on string 5, use the pattern above to find the home key.

Other Tricks

If you find a minor chord with a Major chord rooted one semitone above it, those have to be chords III and IV. And if you have two minor chords with roots one tone apart, those have to be chords II and III.

Warning: If you only know two Major chords that aren’t a tone apart, you can’t immediately find the key. When choosing the correct scale to use for improvising, use your ear. If it sounds good, it is good.

Homework!

Find a heap of tunes you love and figure out what key they’re in. :) Can you find ones that use diatonic chords throughout? Are there any that have a chord outside the key?

Answers

Chords in key of F: F, Gm, Am, Bb, C, Dm (and E dim)

The note f is on string 5 at fret 1 (or fret 13 ;) ), meaning the Major chords are rooted on frets 1 and 3 of string 5, so they are Bb and C.

The II chord is rooted at fret 3 of string 6 (Gm), the III chord is rooted at fret 5 of string 6 (Am), and the VI chord is rooted at fret 5 of string 5 (Dm).

F# Major: the root of the I chord has to be at fret 2 of string 6, meaning F# is the root note of the key.

G Major: the root of the I chord has to be at fret 3 of string 6, making G the root note of the key.

Knockin' on Heaven's Door is in the key of G. Notice that C and D are two Major chords one tone apart, so they are the IV and V chords of the key. The note c is found at fret 3 on string 5. So the root note of the key is found at fret 3 on string 6, which is the note g. So it's in the key of G!

lessons.title: Rut Busters ep.7 Sussing Out
lessons.summary: In this lesson, we start a look at how to expand out of the usual chords when playing rhythm!
lessons.text:
Revolutionise Your Rhythm Playing

In this episode, we talk about chord embellishments and variations. This is crucial for going beyond standard chord shapes and sounds.

Lee has noticed a huge change in his guitar playing. When he started, all he wanted was the lead guitar chops. With maturity, though, he’s come to realize that the great players are those who play great chords, not those who can play lead. The key is to use chord variations.

Going Beyond The Chords On The Page

When it says Am on the page, that gives you a starting point. You can swap this chord for Asus2 or Asus4 or other Am chords like Am6, Am7, Am9, and Am13. This took us into a huge exploration of sus chords!

What Are Sus Chords?

Let’s explain this using the C Major Scale, which has the notes CDEFGAB. Major chords are made up of the root note (the 1st note in the Major scale), the 3rd note, and the 5th, all taken from the Major scale.

For example, the 1st, 3rd, and 5th degrees of the C Major Scale are C, E, and G (CDEFGAB), meaning the C Major chord uses the notes C, E, and G.

Sus means “take away the 3rd and replace with”. So sus4 means “take away the 3rd and replace it with the 4th.” Csus4 contains the 1st, 4th, and 5th degrees of the C Major Scale – the notes C, F, and G. Compare it to the C Major chord (CEG). What’s different?

Sus2 means “take away the 3rd and replace it with the 2nd.” The 2nd in the C Major Scale is the note D, so what notes does Csus2 contain?

Are Sus Chords Major Or Minor?

Whether a chord is Major or minor depends on whether it contains a b3rd or a 3rd. Since sus chords don’t have either, they’re neither major nor minor! This means we can use them in place of both. They sound atmospheric.

💡Go Deep With Sus Chords – Head to Module 5.2 of my Practical Music Theory course to look at sus chords in depth.

Sus Chords In D

Play a regular D open chord (XX0232). Now add your little finger to fret 3 of string 1. You’re now playing a Dsus4 (XX0233). Go back to the regular open D, then take away finger 2 to leave the open string. This is a Dsus2 (XX0220). Play around with these chords. They make wicked embellishments!

Now try it with Dm (XX0231). Which fingers do you need to add or remove to find Dsus4 and Dsus2? Do they still sound good next to a Dm?

Sus Chords With A Major

If we use fingers 1, 2, and 3 to play a standard A Major open chord (X02220) (with finger 1 on string 3, fret 2; finger 2 on string 4, fret 2; and finger 3 on string 2, fret 2), it’s easy to play Asus2 and Asus4. Can you figure out how?

Take off finger 3, leaving the open B string (X02200). That’s Asus2. Go back to the A Major chord, then add your pinkie to fret 3 of string 2. That’s an Asus4 chord. Try to play the sus2 and sus4 chords starting on Am this time!

Sus Chords In A-Shape Barre Chords

Now let’s move to D played as an A-shaped barre chord (X5777X). You can play Dsus4 by adding your pinkie to fret 8 of string 2 (X5778X). Dsus2 is X5775X. We play fret 5 on strings 5 and 2 with finger 1, using fingers 3 and 4 for the other two notes. This is a tricky chord.

Sus Chords From Open C Chord

What is the 3rd of the C chord? That’s right, the note E. See if you can find the Csus4 and Csus2 chords from a standard open C chord.

Strictly speaking, Csus2 is X3001X or X3003X. We need to mute string 1 so there is no note E (meaning no 3rd degree) in the chord. In practice, it’s usually okay to leave string 1 open (X30010 or X30030), unless the E note will clash with another instrument or the singer. If we do so, the proper name for the chord is Cadd9.

💡 Basic Sus Chords – Check out the most essential chords in this Beginner's sus chord lesson.

We can also play fret 3 on string 1 instead of the open string. For example, we could play Csus2 as X30013 or X30033.

There are a few options for Csus4. We can swap both e notes in the C Major chord for F notes, leading to X33011. Or we can simply mute string 1, giving X3301X. We could even leave it open to get X33010. Strictly speaking, this is a Cadd11 chord.

Sus Chords From Open G Chord

Before we explore these together, have a go at finding some sus chords in G yourself. First, what are notes 2 and 4 in the G Major Scale? Those are the notes A and C. So try to replace the note B in the G chord with A or C.

The standard grip for the sus2 chord is 3X0233, with finger 1 playing fret 2 of string 3. This is a true sus2 chord because the 3rd of the G Major Scale (the note B) is absent. Remove this finger, and you get 3X0033, which is a G5 chord. Another option is to play 3X0203, using fingers 2, 3, and 4. This is technically a Gadd9 chord, but it sounds wicked.

G Chord Alternatives

Very rarely do I play string 5 when I play the G chord. My favorite grips are 3X0003 using fingers 3 and 4 and 3X0033 using fingers 2, 3, and 4.

The first grip has a few advantages. First, it makes changing to a C chord effortless. It also only uses two fingers, meaning we can use the other two to add embellishments on frets 1 and 2.

💡Crush Your Chord Changes – If you’re struggling with chord changes, make sure you check out One Minute Changes.

With finger 1, we can play the note C (the 4th note of the G Major Scale), found on fret 1 of string 2. And with finger 2, we can play the note A (the 2nd in G Major), on fret 2 of string 3, or note E on fret 2 of string 4, which is the 6th. All these notes are fantastic for embellishing. Can you find others? :)

Intro to the CAGED System

There are only five shapes on the guitar. Every chord, every scale, and everything you learn fits into one of them. Those patterns are C, A, G, E, and D – CAGED. They take their names from the open Major chords. These five patterns link together, in the order of C A G E D.

CAGED With a C Major Chord

To demonstrate, let’s start with an open C chord: X32010. We’re playing a C chord in the C open shape.

What’s the next C chord up the neck? It’s X35553. That’s C played as an A-shape barre chord. Notice that we’ve gone from C to A in CAGED.

What’s the next chord? It’s C played as a G-shape barre chord: 875558. This one is a horrible chord and quite impractical as a full shape. It works great with a capo on fret 5, though! (CAG)

The next C chord up the neck is the E-shape barre chord: 8 10 10 9 8 8. This is extremely useful (CAGE). And finally, the next after that is the D-shape barre chord X X 10 12 13 12. (CAGED)

If we did the same with A Major, we’d find it appears in the order AGEDC (this is CAGED beginning on A). The same pattern appears with all chords and all scales.

Why Learn The CAGED System?

A huge advantage of knowing the CAGED system is that it binds our knowledge of chords and scales. And it works in all keys! It also gives us the confidence to find chords across the neck, which is useful for a whole heap of reasons.

Have fun with all these new chords, and make sure you put them into practice! If you're keen to learn more about CAGED, stick around for the next episode of Rut Busters. Take care. :)

💙Master the CAGED system and use it to make awesome music in my Practical Music Theory course.

lessons.title: Rut Busters ep.8 Unlocking The CAGED
lessons.text:
Chords In All Five Positions

Hey, it’s Justin and Lee here for another episode of Rut Busters! In this edition, we look at the CAGED system and how to create Major, minor, sus2, and sus4 chords in all five positions of the guitar. Wicked!

Quick Recap of the CAGED System

To recap, let’s play the C Major chord in all five positions. The first full C chord we can play on the neck is an open C chord: X32010. We’re playing a C chord using the C shape in the open position (CAGED). What’s the next C chord up the neck? It’s X35553. That’s C played as an A-shape barre chord (CAGED).

And the next one? It’s C played as a G-shape barre chord: 875558. This one is a horrible chord and quite impractical as a full shape. It works great with a capo on fret 5, though! (CAGED)

Then we go to the E-shape barre chord: 8 10 10 9 8 8. This is extremely useful (CAGED). And finally, we have the D-shape barre chord X X 10 12 13 12 (CAGED). Another tricky and uncommon one.

💡More CAGED – Looking for more on the CAGED system? Check out this CAGED System Intro.

If we did the same with A Major, we’d find it appears in the order AGEDC (this is CAGED beginning on A). The same pattern appears with all chords and all scales.

Exploring the CAGED Shapes: A-shape Chords

Let’s now explore each shape. The chord X35553 is a C Major chord because the root note, at fret 3 on string 5 (we play this with finger 1), is the note C. You can play this in two ways: using finger 3 to create a mini barre on fret 5, or using fingers 2, 3, and 4 to play the notes on fret 5 instead. If we keep finger 1 in place but use the other fingers to play a minor shape (X35543), this is a Cm chord. The root note hasn’t changed, but the chord type has.

Exploring the CAGED Shapes: G-shape Chords

Officially, C Major chord played using the G shape is 875558, using finger 1 as a barre on fret 5. This is like playing a G Major chord with a capo on fret 5. Try it for yourself – horrible, isn’t it? I can’t think of a single example of a real song that contains the full chord.

A great alternative is to play X7555X, using fingers 1 and 3. Other options are X75558 and XX5558. As for the minor version, there really is no G-shape minor chord. There are possible shapes, but they’re impossible to play and don’t sound good. Why bother?

Exploring the CAGED Shapes: E-shape Chords

The standard E-shape barre chord in C is 8 10 10 9 8 8. A common alternative is to play the bass note with the thumb and the thinnest three or four strings with fingers 1, 2, and 3. This leaves the pinkie to add extra notes. :)

You can change this to a minor chord by simply moving the note on string 3 down one fret to get 8 10 10 8 8 8. You can also play this with the thumb and fingers 1 and 3 (8 X 10 8 8 8).

💡Using The Thumb – Master how to use the thumb for playing bass notes with this Q&A lesson.

What about sus chords? You can play Csus4 by using a barre on fret 10 with finger 3 to get 8 10 10 10 8 8. Another option is to move the pinkie from fret 10 on string 4 to fret 10 on string 3. This gives you 8 10 8 10 8 8, which is technically a C7sus4, but it sounds cool. Another option is to play 8 X 10 10 8 8, using the thumb and fingers 1, 2, and 4.

Csus2 is a little tricky. You need to move the note on string 3 back two frets this time. Try it out. Not easy, is it? The trick here is to change the fingering and leave out a few notes. The chord is 8 X 10 7 8 X, using the thumb with fingers 1, 2, and 3 or 4. This leaves one finger spare to add embellishments.

A mini version of this C played as an E-shape barre chord is 8 X X 9 8 X. Use the thumb to play the bass note and mute string 5, and mute string 4 with finger 2. Can you find the sus 2 and sus 4 versions of this mini shape? Very Hendrix!

Exploring the CAGED Shapes: D-shape Chords

The “correct” Major shape under the CAGED system is X X 10 12 13 12, but this is rarely used. It’s horrible to play! Often we simply play the higher three notes (X X X 12 13 12), or the lowest three notes (X X 10 12 13 X, technically a power chord). Those grips are loads easier.

Another option is to play the note E at fret 12 on string 6, giving us 12 X 10 12 13. This note is part of the C Major chord. Play the bass note with finger 2, muting string 5 as you do, and fingers 1, 3, and 4 for the others. Note that this is the common D/F# open chord (2X023X) moved up!

Using The Many Chords And Their Variations

Now you can play C Major, Csus2, and Csus4 in many different ways on the fretboard! When the music says C Major, you have all these options! How do we choose?!

Each shape has its own set of tools you can use in your playing. You choose the shape according to which tools you need. Usually, the deciding factor is how easy a chord or lick is in a particular position. Even the best guitarists tend to do what they find easy rather than practicing horrible licks and chords.

CAGED Exercise: Circle of Fifths

A great exercise for getting all these grips into the muscle memory is to go through these positions for the major chords. But not in any random order – use the circle of fifths.

💡Circle of Fifths – Get to grips with the Circle of Fifths in this lesson in my Practical Music Theory course!

We start on G. Start with the open chord (CAGED), then move through each position in the CAGED system, playing the shapes you know in each position (root notes shown in bold).

The next position is the E shape (355433), followed by the D shape (XX5787). We then move into the C shape (X 10 9 7 8 7) and finally the A shape (X 10 12 12 12 10). Then we find our way back to the G shape played an octave higher than where we started (15 14 12 12 12 15). Again, notice we moved G E D C A, which is CAGED starting on G. The key to doing this is to know the notes on the fretboard and at least one root note in each shape.

The next chords in the circle of fifths are D, A, E, and so on. Keep going until you end up back at C, and you’ll have played all the Major chords in all five positions. Wicked!

How To Learn These Chords

The key to learning these chords is to use them! Find songs containing these chords or add them yourself. Practice those you'll use. If you don’t use them, there's no point in learning them. We often learn things because we think we should, wasting hours of precious practice time because we don't make music with those new ideas.

💡 Useless Learning Anecdote – I spent around 50 hours learning the Harmonic Minor Scale as a kid. And it was a complete waste of time!

Now it's time for your to explore all these positions yourself. What cool chords can you find? And again, make sure you put this into practice by including these chords in songs! Take care and see you soon for another Rut Busters. :)

Master each of the CAGED positions and discover your own chord shapes with my CAGED In Practice lessons.

lessons.title: Rut Buster ep.9 Exploring Chord Extension!
lessons.summary: In this session, we explore using chord extensions in a Blues context and expand Lee's chord vocabulary!
lessons.text:
Chords, Chords and More Chords

Hey, how you doing? It's Justin and Lee here for another episode of Rut Busters! In this one, we look at awesome chord extensions we can use to spice up our blues rhythm guitar.

Chord Extensions – The Theory

There are three core chord families: Major, minor, and dominant 7 (written 7). You can substitute chords within each family for one another.

For instance, if a song uses a Major 7 chord, we can substitute any Major chord extension for it – Maj9, Maj11, or Maj13. If it uses a minor 7 chord, you can substitute it with min9, min11, or min13. The same goes with 7 chords. The extensions used in blues are 9, 11, and 13 chords. 11s are a little jazzier, but they're all super useful.

Major 7 and Dominant 7

Do you know the difference between a Major 7 and a 7 chord? I'll give you a clue – one of the notes is different. Major 7 chords contain the 1st, 3rd, 5th, and 7th degrees of the Major Scale, while dominant 7 chords contain the 1st, 3rd, 5th, and b7th tones.

Play a C Major chord using the E-shape. See if you can turn this into a Major 7 chord by flattening one of the C notes by one semitone. One way to do this is to change the note C on fret 10 of string 4 to the B at fret 9, giving us 8 10 9 9 8 8 (root notes in bold). This chord doesn't sound great.

Jazz guitarists usually play 8 X 9 9 8 X with finger 1 for the bass note and fingers 2, 3, and 4 for the others, or the thumb for the bass and fingers 1, 2, and 3.

💡More Theory – Go deep into Dominant Chord Theory in my Practical Music Theory course.

How do you turn this into a dom 7 chord? You flatten that B note to a Bb, giving you the classic 8 10 8 9 8 8 grip. The jazzy alternative is 8 X 8 9 8 X. There are several other grips for the dom 7 in the E shape – play around and see if you can find some!

Dominant Chord Theory

Although 7 is the V chord in a key, in blues we use it for all kinds of chords! Remember, you can substitute any 7 chord for a 9, 11, or 13 chord. So these are all super useful when playing the blues.

E9 (X76777) is an ultra-common funk chord. But E9 doesn't just mean E9 – it also means E7, E11, E13, and all their many grips. There is a massive pool to choose from, and as long as we choose the right chord family, we can play whichever variation we want.

💡Master the 7 Chord – Learn a ton of Dominant 7th Chord Grips in my Blues Rhythm 1 Course.

Remember that the 7 chord is the V chord of the key. In which Major scale is E7 the V chord? Remember the shape we covered in Rut Busters 6 – if we know the V chord, we can find the parent scale by counting back two frets and up one string. The note E7 is at fret 7, on string 5, so the parent scale starts on fret 5 of string 6 – it's the note A. So E7 is the V chord in A.

E7 Alternatives – C Shape

A super cool E7 alternative comes from the open C7 chord X32310. We slide this up four frets to get E7 (X7675X). Notice that in changing from C7 to E7, finger 3 moves from the note C to E, the new root note.

A classic E13 grip is X76779. We play this by adding little finger to the usual E9 shape (X76777). We can also play X5665X.

E7 Alternatives – G Shape

The E7 in the G shape uses an open A7 alternative (X02223) moved up 7 frets (X X 9 9 9 10). You can also think of this as an open G7 chord (320001) moved up 9 frets and the notes on the thickest strings muted. In the G shape, we also have E9 as X X 12 11 9 12, and we can move this to X X 12 11 10 12, E11, just by shifting finger 1 up one fret.

💡To The 7 And Beyond – Blow open your chord vocabulary with my Dominant Chord Extensions lessons.

E7 Alternatives – D Shape

E7 using the D shape is a wicked chord (XX2434), and we can slide our little finger up one fret to get E7sus4 (XX2435). It's easy to use these together.

How To Learn New Chord Grips

Make sure to use these chords in real music. They're no use on a page! A great way to learn new grips is to focus on one position. For instance, in the C shape, learn to use E13 (X5665X, X76779) and E9 (X76777) instead of E7.

Or you could focus on the G shape, learning the E9, E11, and E7 shapes we covered. It's much better to learn a few really well. Make sure you can use them in songs. :)

Jamming Exercise: Get together with a jam buddy! One of you plays a bass line in E, and the other explores the new E7, E11, and E13 chords. Another option is to use a looper pedal or backing track.

When to Use Extensions

Sus chords are great for pop tunes that use strumming. Jazz is where we open our chord vocabulary and can use any number of chords. As we've mentioned, you can also use them in a blues context. When you first learn these chords, it takes slow practice and a lot of thinking! But with time, it'll become fluent, and you'll have an excellent chord vocabulary.

Have loads of fun with these dominant chord extensions. And remember to make music with them! See you for more Rut Busters very soon. :)

💙Ignite your Blues potential with my Essential Blues Rhythm module.
