lessons.title: Rut Buster ep.10 Hendrix Fills
lessons.summary: In this lesson I teach Lee the Hendrix Rhythm Tricks - there are follow up lessons on the site too!
lessons.text:
Hello again, it’s Justin and Lee back for Rut Busters #10. Today, we cover Hendrixisms! These are excellent embellishments for spicing up your rhythm playing, straight from the master himself, Jimi Hendrix.

This completes this mini-series on chord extensions, the CAGED system, and sus chords. Hendrix influenced a lot of music with his rhythm playing, and we’d all do well to copy him! These aren’t tricky to play, but they add so much. Let’s learn the patterns in the key of C.

E-shape Hendrix Licks

There are a couple of Hendrixisms in the E-shape. First, let’s barre strings 1 and 2 at fret 8 with finger 1, play both those strings, hammer on at fret 10 of string 2 with finger 3. Release finger 3, then play the notes under finger 1 again. That’s the first embellishment.

For the second, finger 1 now goes on to fret 7 of string 3, and finger 2 on fret 8 of string 2. Play those two, then hammer on at fret 9 of string 3 with finger 3. Release finger 3, and play the two starting notes again.

💡Movable Riffs – All of these riffs are movable! The key is to identify the root note of each. :)

In C, the root note is at fret 8 of string 6 or fret 8 of string 1 – which is where finger 1 is to start. If you start with finger 1 on fret 3, for example, you play the same riff, but in the key of G. That’s because the root note is now at fret 3 of string 1, the note G.

G-shape Hendrix Licks

Let’s now move to the G shape. For the first embellishment, barre strings 2 and 3 of fret 5 with finger 1. Play the same rhythm as before, this time hammering on with finger 3 at fret 7 of string 3. The root note is the note C at fret 5 of string 3.

For the second, now shift finger 1 to strings 3 and 4, and play the same rhythm, with finger 3 hammering on fret 7 of string 4. Finally, move the whole pattern up to strings 4 and 5, and use the same rhythm. Here’s a little challenge for you – how could you play this same riff in the key of E?

In G, the root note is the note G at fret 9 of string 3. Start with finger 1 at fret 9, and play the same riffs. Now you’re in E. :)

Make Music From These Riffs

Try playing this pattern with a metronome until it’s clean. You can also explore these riffs with a jam buddy! Another great exercise is to practice going from a chord for one bar to a fill for one bar. Once you’re super confident with the rhythm, you can play fills for more than one bar.

💡 CAGED System – Knowing the CAGED system enables you to confidently move riffs around the neck and into different keys.

Your next challenge is to play on D for two bars then C for two bars. In D, all these patterns move up two frets. I suggest you practice this over a drum groove.

Hendrix Fills Over Major and Minor Chords

Lee asked me if these fills also depend on the next chord in the song. The answer is that they can depend on them, but they don’t have to. As long as you use the right licks over the right chords, you’ll be fine. The rest can come later!

What you can do is use the exact same licks – in the same position – over the Am and C chords. In any case, use your ear. If it sounds good, it is good. :)

Notice that the root note changes. If we use the E-shape Major pattern over a minor chord, it becomes a D shape, so the root note is now on fret 7 of string 4, one fret behind finger 1. And the G-shape Major pattern becomes an E-shape minor pattern, meaning the root note is on fret 5 of string 6 and string 1, and fret 7 of string 4.

💡 Master Major Scale Theory – In my Practical Music Theory course, we cover the major scale and put it into practice, transforming your guitar playing.

In fact, you can use the same licks over any Major chord and its relative minor chord. So it really pays to know what the relative minors are! The root note of the relative minor is always the 6th of the Major scale. For example, what is the relative minor of the E Major Scale? It’s 6th of the scale, so it’s the C# minor chord.

You can also figure out the relative minor of E by finding an E note on the guitar (fret 12 on string 6 or fret 7 on string 5, for example) and counting down three frets on the same string. That’s the 6th of the scale.

Why Learn The Notes On The Guitar?

On any other instrument, you must know the notes on the fretboard. Things are different with guitar, but at some point, you’ll hit a ceiling in your playing if you don’t know them. Chords, scales, and licks all become so much easier when you do. If you don’t know the notes on the fretboard at this stage in your journey, you must learn them!

Learning The Notes On The Fretboard – Powerful Exercise

In today’s episode, Lee bravely exposed his inability to find the notes. As a reward, I gave him this wonderful exercise! Try this for five minutes a day.

Warning: this is not pleasant – sorry! But it’s powerful, and you’ll be surprised by how quickly you know the notes.

We use finger 1 throughout the exercise. First, play fret 8 of string 6. That’s the note C. Now find the C on the next string up and play it. That’s at fret 3 on string 5. Then we go to string 4, where C is found at fret 10. Then it’s fret 5 on string 3, fret 1 on string 2, and fret 8 on string 1 (the same fret as string 6). Now work backward until you reach fret 3 string 5.

💡Notes All Over The Neck – Become fluent with the notes on the neck with my Practical Music Theory course.

Let’s move on to G now. G is at fret 3 of string 6, fret 10 of string 5, fret 5 of string 4, fret 12 of string 3, fret 8 of string 2, and fret 3 of string 1.

Note that when moving from C to G, you stay at the same fret (fret 3 of string 5 to fret 3 of string 6). Why does this happen? This pattern continues until we transition from B to F. Here we need to drop back one fret (fret 2 of string 5 to fret 1 of string 6).

After G, you move on to D. The note order for the whole exercise is CGDAEBF. Put this to a metronome, playing one note on each click.

Go have fun with these Hendrix licks! Try using them to make music and move them into different keys too. And remember – always listen to what you play. If it sounds good, it is good! Take care :)

🎵 Learn more Hendrix-style embellishments with my Advanced module Mayfield and Hendrix Rhythm Fills.

lessons.text:
Hey, it’s Justin and Lee here for Captain’s Privates! Lee is coming over for a block of guitar lessons, and we thought we’d record them.

This isn’t as high-tech as the Rut Busters series, but you’ll get insight into what private lessons with Justin are like. We interact less with the audience in this series, but don’t think we’re being rude!

The Groundwork – Finding A Direction For Our Practice

First things first, we need to know where want to achieve on the guitar. As a teacher, I always ask the student questions about their guitar journey and goals. But teacher or no teacher, all guitar players should ask these questions!

The important thing when we do guitar lessons is to get to the place the student wants to go, not the place I think they should go.

1. What are three songs you can’t play now that you’d love to be able to?

This question informs the rest of the practice schedule. It’s our north star.

Lee’s first song was Little Wing. He told me he can’t play Hendrix’s chords and the embellishments. We also discovered that he can’t use Hybrid Picking.

Next, he came up with Black Dog by Led Zeppelin. He loves the guitar riff in that one. Finally, he fancies learning Bad Love by Eric Clapton. He knows the basic riff but doesn’t know how Clapton plays the trills.

There’s a clear theme in Lee’s songs: blues and rock! I can see that blues vocabulary will be crucial to his success. Again, it’s not about the teacher. If the student wants to learn a song, it’s up to the teacher to help them do so.

💡The Holistic Practice Routine – There is certainly no one-size-fits-all practice schedule. So how should you practice guitar? I call it The Holistic Practice Routine.

2. How much practice time do you have?

Lee can do 30 minutes of practice 5 days per week, and we also realized he has short gaps in the day where he could quickly grab a guitar and do an exercise. I encourage less but more often – rather than three sessions of 45 minutes, I suggest five 30-minute sessions.

3. Is there anything you can’t play because your technique is holding you back?

This is a frustrating area for guitarists, but it’s nothing that good practice can’t fix!

Lee realized he can’t pick Eric Johnson and John Bonamassa songs fast enough. We also stumbled on a huge realization: Lee can’t alternate pick! We’ll get working on this right away. While there are other ways to pick, many great players use this style, so it’s a good starting point.

Practicing scales with a metronome is a great way to develop your alternate picking. You also gain more control of the pick and get used to the feel of playing “down” on the beat, which helps you keep your solos in time. This is often what feels right, like in the Jimmy Page solo I play!

When playing scales, it’s tempting to want to play them quickly. I’d say that fast isn’t always useful by itself, but it does help us develop excellent synchronization. The faster your play, the more in sync your fingers have to be.

Transcribe Your Songs

I encouraged Lee to find one hour beyond his usual routine when he could transcribe the licks and solos of Bad Love. I insist on transcribing so much because you learn things you can never learn just by using TAB.

💡The Power of Transcribing – Seriously, transcribing is a superpower. Ready to get serious about it? Head to my Transcribing module. :)

Because you have to listen so carefully, you pick up on the phrasing, the feel, the volume of each note, the bending – and you won’t even realize it! You hear many subtleties, and your playing will reflect this. This is the best thing you can do to ignite your guitar potential.

Practice Slow

Lee commented that he felt embarrassed that he could only play accurately when he played really slow. He didn’t know that when I learn something on the guitar, I practice it super slowly. I can’t just transcribe it and play it straight away! The slower you practice at the beginning, the quicker you’ll be able to play later on.

Lee wasn’t practicing alternate picking with the Major scale. The problem is that by practicing the wrong thing, you simply ingrain everything you do wrong. It’s like writing a mental program – the more you do it wrong, the harder it is to do it right.

💡Practice Makes Permanent – Who said practice makes perfect? Nonsense! Practice makes permanent – make sure you play things correctly!

So go slow, make sure it’s correct, then speed up. If you’re struggling with alternate picking, say it out loud. You’ll be surprised at how well this trick works! :)

In an interview, Steve Vai said he spent a whole month practicing one lick for one song. Of course, we don’t see any of that hard practice, but all the great layers put thousands of hours into their playing. If it’s good enough for them, it’s good enough for us! And many guitarists who are much better than me have said that slow practice is how you play fast.

Little Wing – Tricky Bits

There’s a part in Little Wing where Hendrix plays a G chord with the thumb (3X5433) and adds a heap of embellishments. There are a lot of tricky technical bits here. The most tricky part is to mute string 5 with the thumb and string 4 with finger 2.

Each section of Little Wing has problems like this to solve. The key to learning songs like this well is to learn each part, making sure it’s comfortable before moving on.

Lee commented that he found using his thumb unnatural. He finds that on some guitars it’s comfortable, while on others it’s impossible! I’ve been playing notes with the thumb for decades. Sometimes it still feels strange, and my notes aren't always clean.

If you’re playing notes with the thumb, make sure you use the correct part of the thumb. Everyone is different, but no matter what your hands are like, we play with the side of the thumb. If you struggle with this, try playing the high notes of this G chord with the normal thumb position (XXX433). Keeping your fingers in place, play the bass note with the thumb (3XX433).

💡Thumb-Over Troubles – This technique is tricky. I played guitar for 10 years before I was able to use the thumb. To begin with, I found it difficult and believed I'd never get it! After lots of hard graft, I finally got there.

Another tip – make sure finger 1 covers only strings 1 and 2. With the mini shape XX5433, finger 1 can sit over string 3 and even string 4, even though it doesn’t play them. But if you want to use the thumb, you’ll find it way easier if finger 1 is lower down.

With this riff, you’ll go through a period when it’s frustrating. But once you learn it, you can move this shape up and down the neck.

Lick Book

We guitarists tend to repeat our favorite licks. A great way to expand our vocabulary is to create a lick book with those licks written in TAB. To find them, improvise for a whole week and write down the ones you use most.

Then improvise for another week, avoiding all the licks you wrote down, and write down the new ones. After this, you’ll have a list of all the licks you know.

From there, you can deliberately expand and vary the licks you already know. This is also super helpful for the teacher – they see your vocabulary and can help you develop it.

Scales And Alternate Picking

We moved on to the issue of alternate picking. If you find it impossible to do alternate picking, there are several remedies. Try playing a new scale position. This will break you out of your old patterns and make you think about what notes you’re playing and how.

Another is to say “down,” “up,” “down”... as you pick the scale. You’ll quickly notice if you make a mistake. When Lee said it as he played the scale, he noticed all his errors.

💡Alternate Picking Remedy – Sharpen your alternate-picking skills with this exercise based on the C Major Scale.

Installing alternate picking takes time and patience, especially at the beginning. Keep the faith! Try to keep your hand moving up and down continuously. That’s the key to alternate picking.

Great Exercise: Watch Your Favourite Players With Sound Off

This is a fantastic way to see how the best players really play. When we watch them, we’re usually distracted by the music and the crowd. But when there’s no sound, you can pay attention to the guitarist and discover things in their playing you’d never noticed before

Q&A Time

We had time for a short Q&A session at the end of the lesson!

Question 1

How’s Lee getting on with learning the notes on the neck?

Answer

He hasn’t practiced it! And it’s now going on his routine. :)

Question 2

Can you talk about transcribing chords?

Answer

This will be useful later in the Captain’s Privates series, but that’s a big topic I can’t cover right now. Head to the Transcribing section on my site for more on that.

Question 3

Do you have any Tommy Emmanuel lessons coming up?

Answer

I was going to do some with Tommy, but we couldn’t find a date and it's fallen by the wayside. I will do an Angelina lesson at some point and one on Mombasa.

Question 4

When soloing, do you pick a scale that you stick to, or do you use the chords and arpeggios? I’m unsure about when to move away from the scale.

Answer

Long-term, you don’t want to think about any of this. Ideally, you want to practice scales, licks and arpeggios enough so that you don’t have to think about them when you play. Think in terms of language and phrasing, and you’ll end up moving away from the scale.

Lee's Practice Routine

10 mins: Having fun, messing around and playing whatever he wants. 5 mins: Major Scale with a metronome. 10 mins: Little Wing practice (using my lesson!) 5 mins: Lick Book (writing down all his licks in tab!)

+ one 60-minute transcribing session every two weeks, starting with some lead lines from Old Love.

After the lesson, I typed it up into the practice routine paper (free download!) and sent him on his way.

Stick around to see how Lee progresses in the coming weeks! Take care. :)

lessons.text:
Hey, how you doing? Welcome to the second edition of the Captain’s Privates, a series of ten private lessons for Captain Lee of Anderton’s music store!

Talking Shop

Two weeks was a good amount of time between lessons. Lee did 9 days of structured practice and found it easy to maintain. With Little Wing, he had to keep going until he mastered a new part of the song, so he found it challenging to limit the time. There’s no problem with that – in any case, it’s better to practice more rather than less!

He mentioned that learning from YouTube can be a hassle when we need to skip back. Very true! The solution is to make your own tabs. Doing so also helps you learn the song and means you closely analyze your playing.

💡Free Blank Tab – No excuses! I have free TAB ready to download on the site. :)

You might wonder why I limit free practice time. The idea behind limiting the fun stuff is to make sure you follow your practice schedule. But if you do it last, you can play around as much as you want. Eat your vegetables before your pudding!

Scale Issues

After some practice, his left hand now finds the Major Scale dots quickly. He's been training his right hand to move down and up continuously as though he were strumming. He’s noticed an improvement. So have I!

Lee found it impossible to say “down,” “up,” “down,”... while alternate picking. He also commented that alternate picking doesn’t feel economical. It's definitely less efficient, but there are big rewards later on. For one thing, your time will improve loads! Most great guitarists use alternate picking.

Breaking Out Of Scale Patterns

Lee and I explored an excellent exercise for learning scales and making music from them at the same time.

Major Scale chords are built from thirds. So if you land on a good note when soloing in a Major key, the note a third up from that will likely sound good too. The following exercise takes advantage of this – it’s called Playing The Major Scale In 3rds.

Let’s play the A Major Scale in thirds. Start with finger 2 on fret 5 of string 6. The pattern is to play a note, miss one, and play the next one. The next note in A Major is B – two frets up. Don’t play that – miss it and play the note C# at fret 3 of string 5. Then play the one you missed (the note B), skip the C#, and play the note D at fret 5 of string 5.

💡Full Lesson – check out my Grade 4 lesson on Playing The Major Scale In 3rds for a full demo of this exercise!

Again, play the one you missed, then skip one and play the next. You can play up the whole scale this way. The last three notes are at frets 4, 7, and 5 on string 1, in that order. What notes are they? ;)

To come down the scale, start at fret 7 of string 1 with little finger. The last three notes are at frets 7, 4, and 5 on string 6, in that order.

Warning: at one point, little finger plays two notes in a row! That’s the trickiest part of this exercise. And make sure you play this nice and slowly. Get it right, then you can speed up.

The Benefits Of Playing In Thirds

This is a fantastic exercise, if I do say so myself! It’s slightly easier than playing the scale up and down. It also sharpens your alternate-picking skills and helps you play awesome solos! You can use the movements in real situations.

You can hear it sounds way more musical than the Major Scale. Most melodies use these thirds because they fit well with chords.

Little Wing

Lee did a great job of playing Little Wing on camera – kudos! There are parts he struggles with more than others. The trick is to isolate the tough bits. If you only play the whole song, you don’t improve the tricky parts. And whenever you come to them, you’ll feel anxious, especially when there’s an audience.

The solution is to play the song through once or twice, identify tricky parts, then spend half of your allocated time just working on those. But apart from that, Lee was surprised at his progress and felt excited to continue. That’s the power of structured practice.

💡Pro Practice – I’ve been playing for decades, and I still notice the effects of concentrated practice. This is how you get good at guitar!

Lee was struggling with the jump to the Gadd9 chord (3X5035), so I encouraged him to practice moving to it slowly.

He was scared that practicing slowly was for newbies only. Wrong. Practicing slowly is proper practice! And this is a tough chord change, meaning you can only train your muscle memory by correctly playing the chord many times.

Bad Love

In lesson 1, I put Lee on the spot by asking him for three songs he’d like to learn. He told me the first three that occurred to him! He regretted choosing Bad Love, and I underestimated its difficulty. But he did start transcribing Bad Love and learned some crucial lessons – the kind we learn when we transcribe. :)

He realized that the first bend Clapton plays is a tone bend from C to D. But then Clapton plays the octave of that note, which is at fret 22 of string 1! How does he do that? Lee couldn’t figure that out, so he moved on to the rest and figured out some of the bends and trills.

This is a tough solo to transcribe – the other instruments drown out the guitar. I could have helped Lee choose an easier one.

💡Transcribing the Blues – transcribe the blues masters with me in my special module, Transcribing Blues Solos.

It pays to have a wide blues vocabulary! If you can recognize the licks in a solo ahead of time, it makes the process a lot easier.

Notes On The Neck: Find-A-Note Exercise

Lee’s exercise for this week is to learn three notes all over the guitar neck: C, G, and D. This is part of my Find-A-Note exercise. Using finger 1, he’ll play C on string 6 to string 1 and back, then move on to G, then D.

Play thickest to thinnest (6 to 1), then come back, playing your final note on string 5. Then move to the next note name on string 6. This is on the same fret!

Here are the all notes C, G, and D in the first twelve frets (excluding open strings).

The Note C The Note G The Note D

|------------------8------------------| |------------------3------------------| |------------------10-----------------| |---------------1-----1---------------| |---------------8-----8---------------| |---------------3-----3---------------| |------------5-----------5------------| |-----------12-----------12-----------| |------------7-----------7------------| |--------10-----------------10--------| |--------5-------------------5--------| |--------12-----------------12--------| |-----3-------------------------3-----| |-----10-----------------------10-----| |-----5-------------------------5-----| |--8-------------------------------8--| |---3------------------------------3--| |--10-----------------------------10--|

For example, on string 5, C is at fret 3, and G is at fret 3 on string 6. This means that when you switch from the final C to the first G, you stay at fret 3. The same happens with G and D at fret 10.

💡Full Find-A-Note Exercise – You’ll find the whole Find-A-Note exercise in my Practical Music Theory course.

In the full version, we find the notes C, G, D, A, E, B, and F. You have to get it right. If you hit one wrong, slow it down. Practice makes permanent, not perfect!

I hope you're digging the series! Stick around to see Lee's progress. Take care. :)

lessons.text:
Howdy! Welcome back to this series of private lessons I did with Lee Anderton. Lee hadn’t had as much time to practice as he would’ve liked, but he still managed to work on everything!

Major Scales In 3rds Frustrations

He can play the major scale in thirds much better than two weeks ago. He complained he was running on muscle memory, unable to consciously keep track of the notes he was playing, even at a low speed.

When you practice a scale up and down a lot, your fingers get used to it. Eventually, you won't have to try – it’ll happen by itself. But playing scales up and down isn’t very musical. That’s why we practice playing Major scales in thirds.

You want to be able to play the scale in thirds without thinking about it. This is a good thing! You want it to be automatic – when you’re soloing, the more you think, the more you stink. And this can only happen if we practice slowly and memorize the pattern.

Thinking While Playing v Autopilot

My philosophy is that my best music comes when it isn’t planned, when I haven’t thought about scales, licks, and notes. I’ve simply listened and played, and something beautiful comes out.

Of course, to get to that stage, you need to practice a lot, but that’s the goal. Some guitarists play beautifully and think about it, but most guitarists play their best when it’s on autopilot.

💡Language-learning analogy! – The goal with a language is to be able to use it reflexively, such that the words flow out as you speak. You aren’t trying. The same applies to guitar playing.

Lee commented that he looped a chord sequence in the key of D. Before soloing, he realized he could use D Major Scale or B Minor Pentatonic Scale would work. He found that this gave him a framework – from there, he could listen and choose the right notes. This is also legit. Just remember – if it sounds good, it is good.

How To Practice Major Scales In Thirds

During the first few days of practicing the thirds exercise, Lee noticed his hands had to stretch and make unfamiliar movements. But now his hands are used to it. Playing the Major Scale up and down is now much easier too. All great signs!

He notices that when he plays wrong notes, he’s not consciously doing it – it’s as though his brain decides to play it wrong! We want to avoid errors as much as possible. When we play wrong notes, we’re programming the brain to repeat incorrect actions. This is especially true if we make the same mistake repeatedly.

The tricky part of doing this exercise in the E-shape is when little finger plays two consecutive notes. But there's a way around this! On the way up the scale, play the note on string 3 with the tip of the little finger, then roll it onto the flat side to play the next note. On the way down the scale, do the same in reverse: flat first, then roll onto the tip.

💡Full Lesson – check out my Grade 4 lesson on Playing The Major Scale In 3rds for a full demo of this exercise!

The Learning Process – Keep Going!

With the thirds exercise, I could see Lee suffering through the process that all learners go through when they’re learning a new thing on the guitar. What is that process?

When we first learn something – a chord, a song, a riff – we see a quick improvement at the start and think we’ve nailed it. But then there comes a moment of realization. The difficulty of the new item becomes apparent, and we come to terms with the jump between simply playing it and playing it really well.

At this point, all sorts of fears and limiting ideas will come: I'm not good enough, I don’t have enough time, I can’t do this. You have to push through that, continuing to practice until you reach true competency.

More Killer Major Scale Exercises

Lee told me he loves the thirds exercise. He can feel it improving his dexterity! He asked for more exercises like this, ones he can play during dead moments. So I obliged!

Four-In-A-Line: play degree 1 of the scale (in A, fret 5 of string 6) followed by the next three notes in the scale. Then go to degree 2 (in A, fret 7 of string 6) and do the same. Keep going all the way up the scale. The last run starts on the note F# on fret 7 of string 2. Finish on the top note (fret 7 of string 1), then start from there to come down.

Four-in-a-line is just as tricky as the third exercise. Lee tends to play runs too quickly and then pauses to find the next one, meaning his rhythm is irregular. Try to keep the rhythm smooth, playing slowly and staying in time.

We’ll be moving to Position 2 of the Major Scale soon – Lee is a blues guy, so Pattern 1 isn’t so useful for him. We want to explore all positions separately such that he can play licks across the neck fluently, without needing to think about the positions.

Master The Notes On The Neck

Last week, we added the Find-A-Note exercise to Lee’s routine. He’s finding this one horrible! And rightly so. It’s a tricky exercise – you have to just push through and trust you’ll get there.

To begin with, you’ll struggle to find the individual notes. But with time, you’ll see the patterns involved, and it’ll become easy.

💡Full Find-A-Note Exercise – You’ll find the entire Find-A-Note exercise in my Practical Music Theory course.

Once you learn the notes, you’ll be so thankful. You’ll be able to move licks and chords, add notes to chords, and much, much more. And if you also study some music theory, you’ll be well on your way to mastering the fretboard.

Most people falter between frets 7 and 11, but there are a couple of tricks here. First is that B, E, C and F are right next to each other, forming a box. At fret 9, B and E are at strings 4 and 3, respectively. And one fret up, we have C and F, also on strings 4 and 3. This pattern repeats around the neck – can you find the other BECF boxes?

At fret 7, you have a BEAD. B is on string 6, E is on string 5, A is on string 4, and D is on string 3. At fret 10, you have a FAD! F is on string 3, A is on string 2, and D is on string 1.

A wicked exercise is finding the notes in your mind. Close your eyes, and recite the notes at fret 5, starting with the thickest string (ADGCEA). Do the same for frets 3 and 7. Eventually, you want to be able to go up and down for any fret.

The Keys To Transcribing

Lee used Transcribe to slow the mock Albert King track to 60-70% of the original speed and managed to transcribe around 30 seconds. He didn’t write the rhythm down, but that’s no problem. Listen to the original a bunch of times to catch the rhythm! You’ll know it instinctively.

He did a great job, and I suspect he still doesn’t know what good it’s doing him! Even what he’s done up to now has lifted his guitar-playing game. When we transcribe, we listen to the dynamics, the way the notes are played. We hear things we’ve never heard before!

💡Transcribe, Transcribe, Transcribe! – If someone could only practice one thing on the guitar and they asked me what to practice, I’d say transcribing. It’s the most powerful way to unlock your musical potential. When you start, it’s horrible. You just have to persist.

Lee didn’t listen to the track before he transcribed it. In all my transcribing courses, I recommend we listen to the song at least ten times before trying to figure it out. Have it on in the background while you’re driving or doing something repetitive.

Written music gives you a good sense of rhythm. TAB doesn’t, meaning you must listen to the original if you’re using TAB. In any case, you need to listen to the original anyway! Internet TABs are often wrong – trust your ear instead.

Little Wing And Creativity

Lee focused on one part of Little Wing that he finds particularly challenging. He asked if he could simplify it a little. There’s no problem with that, unless you want to learn the song exactly as the original artist played it.

In any case, it’s best to play a simple version well rather than a complex version poorly. And if you mess up the rhythm, it won’t sound good – fancy tricks or no fancy tricks!

This took us to a crucial point: you should always question why one technique is used over another. If you know the reason behind it, you’ll understand what you’re playing and will likely learn it better too.

I asked Lee why he wanted to learn Little Wing. After some talking, we realized he wanted to create his own version of it. He also said he likes other versions of Little Wing, like Sting’s one, more than the original! In that case, there’s no need to play it exactly as Hendrix did.

The Power Of Music Theory

Lee got started on the theory course too. I highly recommend that guitarists study theory. Understanding the theory behind scales and chords opens up lots of doors in your playing. You take your musicianship to a new level. Add the notes on the neck, and you have a powerful blend.

Stick around for more of the Captain's Privates Lessons, see Lee's progress and take your guitar playing to the next level! Laters. :)

Lee's routine:

1. 5 mins/day: Scales – alternating between 3rds, 4-in-a-line and straight.

2. 5 mins/day: Notes on the neck.

a) "Find A Note" Exercise: C, G, D (revision) adding in A and E.

b) Looking at neck diagram and finding patterns

c) Mental Fretboard – recite notes from thickest to thinnest strings on dots (3,5,7) to build the note map in your mind.

3. 60 mins (twice): Transcribing – continue.

4. 5 mins/day Lee's Blues Lick Book: 10 licks in TAB – do them all the in the key of A.

5. 15 mins (3 times a week): Little Wing Practice

6. Guitarless Practice: Practical Music Theory Grade 3 (at least halfway through by next lesson please)

lessons.text:
Hi all! It's Justin and Lee back for another private lesson. We had a lot to talk about! He's made great progress with playing in 3rds, alternate picking, and transcribing.

Lee’s Transcribing Terrors!

Lee came into the studio and said he completed the transcription – but he hated it! He used Transcribe to create loops for each part of the riff and wrote down the licks in TAB before moving on to the next section. It looks like he did a good job, but he found it boring! He later said it felt like homework.

So I asked him if he knew why he should transcribe music. If I ask him to do something, he needs to understand why! And there are excellent reasons why I give him transcribing exercises.

Lee noticed that he had learned new licks and could see exactly how the guitarist played the licks. He also discovered that some bends weren’t tone bends or semitone bends, but somewhere in between! Those are good reasons, but there are LOADS more.

Why Transcribe?

I said this in Lesson 4, but I’ll say it again! If a guitar player came to me and asked what to practice if they could only practice one thing, I’d tell them to do transcribing. I know hundreds of exercises. I’ve done hundreds of exercises. And this is the best of the lot!

The transcription process involves hearing a sound and finding it on the guitar. The more you transcribe, the quicker you can find the sounds you hear.

Once you can transcribe quickly, you can express your musical ideas more effectively. You can find on the guitar the sounds you hear in your musical imagination.

💡Transcribing – Here is the most important guitar lesson you ever need! Yes, transcribing really is that crucial.

You can also hear your way through solos better. You’ll hear the right note before you play it, and with an increased connection between brain and guitar, you’ll be able to find it!

This all happens on a deep level, so often it’s not immediately obvious! You improve without realising it.

You’ll also learn the language of music. This happens when we listen to one artist repeatedly, but transcribing takes it to a new level. You absorb all the subtleties of the music and the sound of the guitar!

Major Scale In Thirds – Use A Metronome

Lee did a demo of playing the Major Scale in 3rds, and wow – he has improved a lot. He knows the pattern, plays the notes cleanly, and even uses alternate picking! He moves his hand up and down consistently, one of the most essential elements of this kind of picking.

When you’re practicing, using a metronome helps you stay in time no matter how tough the exercise is. Lee tends to speed up when he’s playing a tricky riff or scale, which only makes it worse! Try to relax into the clicks of the metronome. It should feel comfortable!

Three Notes Per String – Basic Pattern + Thirds

Each of the five positions in the CAGED system is a scale pattern that fits around a chord, and we stay within one area of the guitar. With the three notes per string system, we move around the neck more. Let’s look at one three-notes-per-string pattern in G – here's the tab:

|-----------------------------------------------5--7--8---| |--------------------------------------5--7--8------------| |-----------------------------4--5--7---------------------| |--------------------4--5--7------------------------------| |-----------3--5--7---------------------------------------| |--3--5--7------------------------------------------------|

To play the notes on the first two strings, I suggest using fingers 1, 2, and 4. Finger 1 plays fret 3, finger 2 plays fret 5, and finger 4 plays fret 7. This is a big stretch for fingers 1 and 2. But don’t use squeezy balls or fancy hand exercises – do your workout on the guitar!

💡CAGED v Three Notes Per String – While music is about what you do with scales rather than how you play them, in this article, I look at the pros and cons of each system.

Once you have the basic pattern down, try to play this in thirds! There’s a few tricky bits. Finger 1 has to play string 3 at fret 5, then string 2 at fret 5, and finger 3 has to do the same at fret 7. The trick is to use the fingertip to play the note on string 3, then lay it on the flat side to play the next note. You do the opposite on the way up.

Three Notes Per String – Slurs

One of the pros of this system is that you can play fast lines using hammer-ons and flick-offs. A lot of ultra-quick players use it. But it’s not just them! Lots of great blues players use them, and many fast lead lines in blues come from this system. So let’s practice it.

On the way up the scale, pick the first note on each string with a down pick, then hammer on to the next two notes. Concentrate on making the two notes as loud as the first, and keep even time. When you’ve reached the end of the scale, do the exact same in reverse: play the first note, hammer on the next two notes, then move to string 2.

Now it’s time for flick-offs. Place fingers 1, 2, and 4 on frets 3, 5, and 7 of string 6. Have them ready in advance! Pluck the string, then flick off finger 4 then finger 2, keeping a consistent time and volume. Then move to the next string. Play flick-offs on the way back up too.

💡Play Slow To Get Fast – Slow down Steve Vai’s music. He plays ultra-quick, but every note is absolutely perfect. Players like Steve practice slowly, get it right, then speed up.

Warning: this is nasty! Lee commented that he couldn't flick off with little finger – it felt like he was just lifting it off. That’s where practice comes in. With time, you’ll be able to play flick-offs with the pinkie.

Do not – do not! – play this quickly. Do it well at a slow pace, then speed up.

Awesome Finger-Stretching Exercise

This is a fantastic exercise for stretching your fingers, making three-note-per-string scales much easier. Place fingers 1, 2, 3, and 4 over frets 7, 8, 9, and 10 of string 6. Play the note under finger 1, finger 2, then 3, and 4. Move up the strings, and when you come back, start with finger 1 on fret 7 of string 1.

Keep your time slow and consistent – playing this one quickly is pointless. You have to feel the stretch. Also keep your fingers in place so they remain stretched. And make sure the fingers are parallel!

💡Full Exercise – You’ll get the full finger-stretching exercise, with TAB, on the website!

On the next cycle, drop finger 1 to fret 6, playing 6, 8, 9, 10. After that, move finger 1 back to fret 7 and move finger 4 up to fret 11 (7, 8, 9, 11). In the final cycle, finger 1 and finger 4 both move (6, 8, 9, 11).

Warning: this is a horrible one! But over weeks and months, you’ll see incredible results.

Make A Lick Book

Lee didn’t do his lick book this week. So for the next lesson, he’s going to write down his top 10 licks! Usually, people don’t do things I ask them to do because they don’t understand the why.

The point of having a lick book is for you to become aware of your vocabulary and why it works. You can then discover what notes your licks contain, which scales they use, and which chords they sound good with.

Then you can decide to learn new licks or develop the ones you already know. Instead of being trapped in a few licks, you’ll have a ton of variations, expanding your vocabulary.

💡Lick Book – The insanely good Blues guitarist Larry Carlton does this. He starts with one lick and develops it into hundreds of variations, creating amazing sounds. Take a leaf out of his book! :)

Why Study Theory?

Lee didn’t study any theory this week and revealed that he wasn't sure what he was supposed to be learning. In the summary lessons for each grade, I list the contents and the reasons for learning each item.

Lee was at the point of learning about the construction of the Major Scale. If you understand its construction and how to move it around the fretboard, things make much more sense.

I also believe that Lee will be more confident when talking to other musicians. When they start talking scales and theory, he’ll be able to join in!

Notes On The Neck – Practice and Persistence

Lee’s been using the JustinGuitar Note Trainer to find the notes on the neck. That’s fine if you’re commuting or on holiday, but when you have a guitar, use it!

He complained that it takes too long for him to find the notes on a guitar. He has to use octave shapes, and it’s a slow process. But that’s how it should be! Only after a lot of practice can you name the notes immediately. If you keep going with these exercises, you’ll just know the notes! Go through the hard graft now, and you’ll be rewarded later.

💡Justin’s Journey! – I didn’t know any notes or how to read music until I was 18. The head of a guitar school gave me a horrible piece of sheet music to learn as an entrance test! That’s when I got to work, but it still took a while to become instinctive.

For all his doubt, Lee played all the D notes in the first 12 frets with no issues. An enormous improvement!

This was another fun week with Lee and I think he's doing great. If you dig this series, there are plenty more episodes. Make sure to check them out! Laters. :)

New to JustinGuitar? Create a free account and access incredible practice tools to help you learn faster!

Lee's Practice Schedule

Learning the solo he just transcribed -–from memory! Get the set here if you wanna follow along.

The Finger Stretching Exercise

Learning G Major (3 Notes Per String, Pattern 1) Straight up and down In 3rds All hammer-ons (ascending and descending) as triplets, down pick on the new string (on the beat) All flick-offs (ascending and descending) as triplets, down pick on the new string (on the beat)

Lick Book – write out ten of his pet licks in TAB.

More work on Notes On The Neck.

Music Theory – continue on from Grade 3.

lessons.text:
The Captain Is Back

Hey everyone! Time for the next edition of the Captain’s Privates series. We’re up to number 5 now, and Lee is making some serious progress. Follow along with him and see your guitar level rise too. :)

Notes On The Neck + Ultimate Goal

My goodness has Lee learned the notes on the neck! I pointed to eight notes spread over the neck, and he named all of them correctly. When we first met, he had no idea what the notes were other than on the thickest two strings. A huge improvement.

The ultimate goal is to know all the notes instantly. There are some notes Lee knows instantly, and he uses those to work out the others. If he sticks with his exercises, he’ll know all the notes automatically.

Why Music Theory Is Crucial

He admitted that if he can’t see the practical application of an idea, he switches off immediately. This has been true since his school days! I reminded him that if he doesn’t understand why he’s learning something, he needs to ask me!

Some of the music theory Lee is studying relates to knowing the notes on the neck. Without knowing the notes, some music theory just won’t make sense. Though you’ll develop a relationship between the shapes and the sounds over time, you’ll lack something.

He duly asked me if he could create solos by remembering that the 3rd of the chord is one fret back and one string up from the root. I said that sometimes this would be enough if he could use it instantly. But if there are lots of chord changes, you need to know the theory.

Put Blues Theory Into Practice

Lee will see the advantages of knowing the notes on the neck when making the changes in blues solos, so let’s talk a little about theory in the context of a 12-bar blues.

Over the A (or A7) chord, we can target C# notes because it’s one of the notes in the A Major Chord (A C# E). We can target F# notes over the D (or D7 chord) because it’s one of the three notes in the D Major Chord (D F# A).

Here’s the point – you might miss some of these notes if you don’t know how to find them on the guitar. For example, the top C# (string 1, fret 9) is not even part of Pattern 1 of the Minor Pentatonic Scale.

💡 Mimic The Masters – I doubt Albert King deliberately targeted 3rds in his solos. He likely discovered it by soloing a lot and listening to what sounded best. Knowing theory helps us learn tricks that masters like him took years to discover.

And if we know the notes, we can target specific notes in all areas of the guitar, meaning we don’t have to jump across frets and strings to find the notes we know. We can forget about positions and think more about individual notes.

If you rely on knowing the root note to find the 3rd, you have to do two things: find the root note (which might not be obvious) and then use the Major 3rd shape to find the 3rd. It’s longer.

Remember, this has to be fluent when you’re playing a solo! Make the process shorter by knowing the theory and the notes on the guitar.

With some practice, Lee will know the function of all notes in the keys of A, E, D, and G and be able to use this knowledge when soloing. The greats always target chord tones!

At this stage, he doesn’t think about chord tones when playing a blues solo. And he isn’t sure about chord functions, such as why a C# works over an A and not a D. While he might not understand why, he can hear it doesn’t work, which is fantastic.

Really important – don’t think about avoiding specific notes. That way, you’ll likely play the notes you want to avoid. Instead, focus on targeting the good ones!

The Learning Process

I told Lee that if he ever needs a hand, he can call me or leave a comment on the website. It’s up to me as a teacher to justify my teaching, not the other way around. And I never teach you stuff you don’t need!

The only caveat to this idea is that sometimes you simply can’t understand the motivation for learning a new idea until later in the journey. If you haven’t progressed far enough to see the benefits, you just have to trust me when I say I’ve taught these exercises for many years and know they work.

💡Justin's Journey – At school, I learned Sonata form, counterpoint, and Bach chorales, and I had no idea why. Looking back, it was a complete waste of time.

As adults, we can choose what to learn, but we should know exactly why we’re doing so. Interval naming comes under this category. Lots of people leave me comments asking why I teach this. Trust me when I say this is useful later in the guitar journey. And in the short term, it helps you learn the notes in the keys.

Sharps and Flats in Scales

There was one thing that Lee couldn’t imagine being useful, ever! That was identifying the scale based on the number of sharps and flats it contains.

This trick is handy for sheet music because it helps you find the key right away. But it’s less relevant for guitarists today because TAB is so prevalent. And if you’re a rock and blues guitarist, you won’t use sheet music or any keys beyond G, C, D, A, and E.

However, knowing the rules for the complex keys means that the useful ones are easy for you. You’ll start recognizing guitar keys from the chords in the song almost automatically.

Make Your Lick Book

If you’re yet to make a lick book, go and do so now! Do a bunch of blues soloing and identify the ten licks you use most. Write them down in TAB.

Now, choose one of your licks and solo with it over an entire 12-bar blues. Get used to this idea of repeating licks. It’s easy to slip into playing without a structure or repeating theme, meaning you don’t tell a story with your solo. This exercise has you do the exact opposite of that.

There are great ways to expand on this, like repeating little parts of the lick. Lee did this automatically. Listen out for when the greats use their licks, how they change them and whether they repeat them. They tend to use variations of basic licks.

💡 Lick Library – I use licks as starting points or backups when I’m not in creative mode. I start a solo with my pet licks, knowing I can build on them.

Lee agreed that repeated licks in a solo sound wicked and cited Purple Rain as an example. He gets it! And this exercise is the perfect way to do this.

In real playing, we don’t want to think about scales, licks, or any of that. We want to practice those things such that they come out instinctively when we’re live. Playing one lick repeatedly means we’re more likely to play that lick when it matters.

How to Build On Basic Licks

Another great reason to have a lick book is that you can take your basic licks and alter them.

Take Lee’s lick (TAB) below or your own and see if you can expand on it. There are tons of ways to do this!

|--------------------------| |---------8----------------| |---7s9-------9s7---5------| |-----------------------7--| |--------------------------| |--------------------------|

From a technical point of view, this lick is a slide, a single note on the next string, then the same slide in reverse. We can take that pattern and start on fret 8 of string 2 instead:

|----------8-----------------| |---8s10-------10s8---6------| |------------—------------7--| |----------------------------| |----------------------------| |----------------------------|

Move this lick around the neck into different keys and see how it sounds. You can also add extra notes. The lick Lee uses is in A and doesn’t have a C#, so it doesn’t have a 3rd. Try adding the note C# (found at fret 6 of string 3).

Other options include changing the time, taking notes away, and using different fingers. That way, you find new ways of using ideas that are already natural for you. This also helps you find your own voice instead of just stealing from the greats. Learn their licks and make them your own! :)

Transcribing Tricks

Lee learned part of the Albert King solo but not all, so I wanted to ensure he knew why he should learn it.

He said it was so that he could play the solo like the original artist and use King’s licks in his own music. Those are great reasons, but there are more!

💣 Transcribing Power – When you transcribe solos and try to copy them, you learn a lot that you'll never find in TAB. You pick up on the subtleties, which will impact your solos and make you a much better player.

Have a go at transcribing some Albert King. Warning – he plays upside down! He also bends from the thinnest strings, pulling them downwards. So when replicating him, try bending from the thinnest strings.

Become a detective – transcribing requires detective work. Use the clues in the song to find out exactly how the guitarist played it. Analyze their licks and choose the parts you love, incorporating them into your own playing.

Practice Tips

Don’t confuse practice with playing. When you practice, you’re supposed to mess things up. If you don’t, it means you’re not pushing yourself hard enough! True, with technical ideas like scales, you want to play slowly and perfectly. But when exploring, making mistakes is simply part of the process.

Transcribing Eric Clapton

Lee’s homework for this week is to transcribe five Eric Clapton licks he loves. The Beano Album (John Mayall and the Blues Breakers) is a solid introduction to Clapton’s playing.

This task has two parts: first, I want Lee to find half an hour every week when he can sit down and listen to the album free of distractions. He’ll write down on paper the licks he wants to learn as they appear. Then I want him to transcribe the five he likes most.

Make Your Scales Silky Smooth

All the scales from last week sounded good, but he struggled to play the three-notes-per-string pattern with flick-offs. If you’re the same, don’t worry. Everyone finds the flick-offs exercise challenging. The key is to do it slowly, making sure all the notes are clean.

We did an exercise to demonstrate an issue that trips up a lot of blues players. I played a blues in A while Lee tried to play the three-note-per-string pattern in G. He found it sounded weird because he used a straight rhythm (with “and” in the middle of two beats). Instead, try using a shuffle rhythm, with “and” closer to the second beat.

💡 Blues Tips – If technical stuff like fingering separates scales from your real playing, you’ll never use it in context. It’ll feel detached.

If you only practice major scales with a straight rhythm, you’ll be unable to use them in the real world. Next time, Lee used a shuffle rhythm and played the same scale, starting on the note A instead of G (playing the A Dorian mode). It sounded great!

When you learn a new scale or lick, think about it in the context of what you already know and how you play. Use fingers 1, 2, and 3 on strings 1 and 2 to break out of the usual fingering. When soloing in a real context, you’re unlikely to use finger 4.

Playing scales up and down is a great dexterity exercise. But playing in 3rds is also handy for developing melodies. We can make solos with these patterns, so we should practice with the fingers we’ll use in the real world.

Hope you’re digging the series! Stick around for more Captain’s Privates Lessons to see how Lee progresses and take your playing to the next level.

💙 It's time to play like the masters! Check out my module Making The Blues Changes.

Homework

Lee's schedule for this week looks like:

Lick Book – Exploring licks one at a time Use backing track and explore different ways to repeat or modify a lick Look at ways of changing the lick to other melodic ideas.

Theory – Continue Practical Music Theory course

Listening – at least 30 minutes a week listening to Beano album (John Mayall & Blues Breakers Feat. Eric Clapton)

Transcribing – pick five favorite licks from Beano and transcribe them.

Notes on Neck – Continue!

Scales Continue 3rds practice – add in 3 notes-per-string Pattern 1 Continue legato work – focus on slow flick-offs, making sure movement is good and notes are clear. No fluffy stuff! :)

lessons.text:
Hey all! Time for the sixth installment of this series of private lessons I did with Lee Anderton of Anderton's Music Store. Life took over this week, so Lee hasn’t done much theory or transcribing. I'm sure you can all relate. But he did listen to the Beano album ten times – kudos!

Deep Listening Practice

I had Lee listen to the Beano album for homework. Clapton’s playing is relevant to our lessons, and he plays some ultra-cool blues lead guitar on this album. Lee commented that he didn’t like it the first few times, but then he started to appreciate why it’s a landmark record. It has a ton of great blues vocabulary. And just by listening, you absorb the feel.

This took us on to the subject of taste. Don’t transcribe music unless you love it! For instance, I’m not a fan of Robert Johnson’s music. I respect his playing, but it’s not to my taste, and I wouldn’t listen to it to relax.

Find what connects with you and gets you excited. Listen to it loads, absorbing the sound and feel, and transcribe it! Find ten licks you love and figure out how to play them. If you love a solo that lasts for two minutes, you don’t need to transcribe it all. Work out your favorite parts and incorporate them into your own style.

💡 Beano For Blues Cats – If you’re a blues player, I highly suggest you check out the Beano album (John Mayall and the Bluesbreakers with Eric Clapton). It’s like a dictionary. It’s just filled with insane licks.

Transcribing shouldn’t be a chore. Once you get to a certain level, it’s enjoyable. You’ll hear something you love and be able to find it quickly on the guitar.

Minor Pentatonic All Over The Neck

Lee loves practicing scales and patterns, so I set him a challenge to learn all five patterns of the Minor Pentatonic Scale for next lesson. That gives him a month!

I want him to do this in a particular way: in each position, play up to the highest note possible, down to the lowest note possible, then come back to the root note.

💡 Licks tend to work well in one or two patterns – you simply can’t play them in all positions. Don’t make the mistake of trying to learn all licks in all positions. That’s why I did, and it was a giant waste of time! Part of the journey is wisely deciding which licks can move and which should stay put.

In Pattern 2 of the Minor Pentatonic Scale in the key of A, the lowest root note is the note A at fret 7 of string 4. So we play up the scale, finishing on the note D at fret 10 of string 1. And when coming down the scale, we play on fret 8 of string 6 (the note C) before returning to the root note on string 4.

Many people learn Pattern 2 using the low C as a reference. This makes it much trickier to find the scale. And it’s unnecessary! Just remember the root note for this pattern is on string 4, and you can immediately use the scale in any key.

Pattern 3 starts on fret 12 of string 5 (the note A) with finger 3. Again, we play down to the lowest note, which is at fret 10 on string 6. The same goes for Patterns 4 and 5.

Minor Pentatonic Exercise

This is the minor-pentatonic version of the 3rds and 4ths exercises for the Major scale. I usually call this one Playing the Minor Pentatonic in 4ths, but technically you play a mixture of 3rds and 4ths. Remember it as playing the notes next to each other in the pentatonic scale.

|-----------------------------------------------------5-----8--| |-----------------------------------------5-----8--5-----8-----| |-----------------------------5–----7--5-----7—----------------| |-----------------5-----7--5-----7-----------------------------| |-----5-----7--5-----7-----------------------------------------| |--5-----8-----------------------------------------------------|

You’ll notice that you jump strings on the same fret several times. Use the rolling technique, playing the first note with the fingertip and rolling it down onto the next string, muting the previous one with your finger. Do the opposite when you play the higher note first. Modern blues uses this technique loads. It's tricky, but it gives licks a hip sound.

Three Notes Per String With 16th Notes

Last time, I gave Lee a slur exercise for the three-note-per-string pattern we looked at. Like everyone else, Lee finds the flick-offs trickier.

The danger with these patterns is that we use them only as triplets. This is how we naturally hear the scale, but we can break this habit. Use a metronome and play four notes per beat, or tap your foot on the beat, counting 1 e + a, 2 e + a, and so on.

How To Solo Over Little Wing

Lee did a cool rendition of Little Wing for us – congrats, Lee! Now let’s look at soloing over it.

The song has the chords Em, G, Am, Bm, C, and Bb as a passing chord. So what key are we in? Notice that Am and Bm are a tone apart, so those have to be chords II and III. This means we are in G. Em is the VI in G, and Bb is a passing chord. So we could use the G Major Scale to solo.

But there’s also an F in the song. The G Major Scale clashes with the F chord, particularly the note F#. At that point, try targeting notes in the F chord (F, A, and C).

Try this with the other chords too. You can play the G Major Pentatonic over the whole tune, including the F chord. But playing the chord tones changes the groove. It sounds wicked! You can use the visual chord shapes for this – you don’t have to target note names.

💡 Trial and error is also a legitimate strategy and can lead to happy accidents. A lot of my best playing has come about this way!

Think of the Minor Pentatonic as your safety net when you’re off exploring the chord tones. If it goes wrong, head back to the minor pentatonic. If you can blend theory and strict scale playing with your natural instinct for good sounds, you’ll be on your way to excellent solo playing.

Playing Patterns v Playing By Ear

We came on to the subject of playing scale patterns compared to playing by ear. Lee was complaining that he’d never learned to number the various positions of the Minor Pentatonic Scale.

This is not an issue. In fact, Jim Cregan (guitarist in Cockney Rebel and part of Rod Stewart’s band) told me he didn’t know any scales or theory. But in the intro to Make Me Smile, he runs right up the G Major Scale!

He knew the sound of the Major Scale and could play it all over the fretboard, but he’d never sat down and formally learned all the patterns.

That doesn’t mean we shouldn’t learn scale patterns. They give us a shortcut if we can’t dedicate our entire lives to guitar and learn it all by ear.

Organizing Your Practice

Lee also commented that the 30-minute periods weren’t working for him. He only did the exercises he could do quickly and found himself leaving out items like transcribing.

I find I can only do serious practice if I have a two-hour block when nobody is at home. A good way around this is to schedule one day every week when you can practice for an hour. You can also use your free time for guitarless practice, like learning theory, notes on the neck, and listening, saving your guitar time for playing.

Advice For Youngsters

And finally, some advice from two old men! Kidding. Seriously though, if you’re young and don’t have adult commitments, we recommend you practice as much as possible.

💡Justin's Journey – I used to watch the other kids play in the park from my window as I practiced. But I didn’t feel I was missing out – I just loved playing guitar!

You’re at the perfect age for learning and have loads of time. Take it from two long-time guitarists – you’ll never have this opportunity again. Make the most of it!

Keep following along with this series – there's tons more cool Intermediate–Advanced guitar tricks coming up, including harmonic analysis, melodic sequences, and modes! From Justin and Lee, take care. :)

💙 Move into Advanced guitar territory with my Advanced Grade 7 course.

Homework

These are Lee's areas for practice until next lesson.

Revision of all 5 Minor Pentatonic Patterns (Start and end on lowest root note!)

Practice Minor Pentatonic Pattern 1 – "In 4ths" (video coming shortly!)

Theory Course – get stuck in!

Transcribing – find 10 licks you love and work out how to play them!

Three-Notes-Per-String Major Scale Pattern 1 Legato (hammer-ons and flick-offs) as triplets Playing the scale with 4 notes per click (or foot tap)

Little Wing – work on exploring target tones to a backing track (or a loop you make). Aim to know where you are and what chord you are playing over at all times. This will make your soloing a little jumpy and separated for a while, but stay with it. It'll smooth out and you'll learn a really valuable skill!

+ Make some time to listen to new music – with no distractions!

lessons.text:
The Dorian Mode + Minor Pentatonic Pattern 2

This is the jetlag modes bomb lesson! With the Christmas period and a trip to LA, Lee’s structured practice has gone out the window. But he has grabbed a guitar at every possible moment and done some exercises to keep his fingers working. The enormous modal explosion kept him on his toes. :)

Notes On The Neck

We’re looking at learning the notes on the neck and using it in blues guitar. While you can target notes like the b3rd, 3rd, or b5 using visual patterns alone, it’s easier and quicker to know the note names in different keys and immediately find them on the guitar.

For instance, the b3rd in A is C. Useful C notes for blues lead are found at 4:10 (fret 10 of string 4), 3:5, 2:13, and 1:8. How about the beloved blue note (the b5)? In A, this is the note Eb; we find this at 4:13, 3:8, 2:4, and 1:11.

Knowing this means you can target notes all over the neck without knowing positions. And knowledge of the positions will boost your understanding.

Here’s an exercise you can do during dead moments in the day. Grab your guitar, choose a note, such as C, and find all the C notes on each string, starting from string 6. Or choose a fret and name all the notes on the fret from string 6 to string 1, then back up.

🎸Master the Fretboard – In Practical Music Theory Module 4.3, we dive into several excellent note-finding exercises.

Spend one month doing exercises like this for five minutes a day, and you’ll be able to instantly name all the notes on the guitar.

Why Study Music Theory?

Lee is struggling to study his music theory. He isn’t sure what it is or why he should study it! This was his problem the last time we discussed theory.

In short, music theory describes how music works. So by studying the theory, you better understand how music works. And by knowing that, you can be more creative and adapt the music to you.

💡 Car Analogy – if you really love cars, there comes a point when you want to understand how the engine works. This makes you much more adept with cars.

For blues and rock guitarists, one critical area is knowing the chords in the key. If you can figure out the key of a song from the chords, you can use the right scales and licks to accompany the song. You don’t need to figure it all out by ear.

To Lee, that feels like a long way away. But it isn’t as far as he thinks. His issue is that reading the theory course on the site feels detached and separate from his guitar playing, meaning it hasn’t stuck. That shows me I need to connect the theory to real guitar playing as much as possible!

Minor Pentatonic Pattern 2

We also explored Pattern 2 of the Minor Pentatonic Scale. This is the TAB:

|----------------------8--10--8--------------------------------------------------| |---------------8--10------------10--8-------------------------------------------| |---------7--9--------------------------9--7------—------------------------------| |--7--10--------------------------------------10--7---------------------------7--| |----------------------------------------------------10--7-------------7--10-----| - |-----------------------------------------------------------10--8--10------------|

Exploring String 1

The note D at 1:10 makes for an excellent tone bend to an E. This is part of a fundamental blues lick:

|--10b12--8---------| |------------10-----| |-------------------| |-------------------| |-------------------| |-------------------|

You can also bend a semitone to get the blue note, Eb. A classic blues trick is to curl the b3rd. In this position, 1:8 is the b3rd note. On string 1, frets 8, 9, 10, 11, and 12 are all useful in an A blues!

Bending From String 2

First, let’s look at which notes we can bend (in the key of A). One root note is at 2:10. You can bend this one tone to the 9th. If you like big bends, try bending it a tone and a half to the b3rd!

Warning – your bending on this note has to be perfect. This is because you pass through the note Bb, which is the b2 degree. Get it wrong, and it’ll sound horrible.

At fret 10, we have the note G. You can bend this one tone with finger 1, but it’s tricky. All in all, you’re unlikely to bend from this string. You’d switch positions and use a different finger!

String 3 Tricks

We can bend the note E at fret 9 one tone to F#. It sounds great, but it’s rare. And we play the note at fret 7 with finger 1, meaning it’s a horrible bend. Again, you’d switch positions.

You do have the blue note at fret 8, which can make up for the lack of bending options.

Use The Best Of Each Minor Pentatonic Pattern

Each position has its pros and cons, so take the useful bits from each one and switch positions when you run into difficulty. And you’re unlikely to use the lowest three strings from any position!

🎸 Boss the Blues – Learn these bends and more Pattern 2 licks in Blues Lead Guitar.

The way we practice blues soloing is different from how we play in the real world. During practice time, it’s great to stay in one position and solo there. You might just discover something new, like a lick or a bend. You’ll never discover these things unless you force yourself to stay in one position.

But in the real world, you want to move seamlessly between Patterns 1 and 2. Your goal must be to move between all positions as you solo.

Jamming with Vamps

Vamps are used as intro or filler music. They became popular among musicians as a tool for improvising, particularly as simple backing tracks. To create a vamp, all you need is one or two chords.

I asked Lee to play an Am vamp, and he started all tense. When he relaxed and started tapping his foot, it sounded loads better.

When you’re playing rhythm, you have to keep your time, not rushing ahead or falling back. And it’s crucial to notice how the dynamic of the jam changes. You’ll need to drop right down at some points, like during a long solo.

Try to practice this at home before you find yourself in a jam! That way, you’ll be prepared for it.

The Dropping Of The Atomic Modes Bomb!

And BOOM! The modes bomb has gone off. :) Lee created a vamp with Am and Bm, and we established that we were in G Major.

But when it came to his turn to solo, he got super confused. Should he use G Major to solo over the Am and Bm or the A Minor Pentatonic scale? Or some other scale? Don’t we use G Major over Em? So many questions – my word did he open up a rabbit hole!

Let’s demystify modes.

The A Dorian Mode

First, while the vamp is in Am, the chords come from G. It’s the only Major Scale with both Am and Bm as diatonic chords. This means that G Major is the parent major scale of the Am to Bm vamp.

Using the G Major Scale over Am (chord II in G) sounds wicked, especially for blues. It creates what we call A Dorian, which sounds different from E Aeolian (G Major over its relative minor, Em).

In fact, when we play a Major Scale over chord II of that scale, we get the Dorian sound. If you’re not convinced, record an Am vamp and play notes from the G Major Scale over it. Then try the C Major Scale over the Dm chord (chord II in C). Both sound bluesy – awesome!

💡 Remember – when we're in A Dorian, we’re still using the G Major Scale. We call it A Dorian because it has a characteristic sound common to all Major scales played over chord II.

G Major Modes In Series

The chords in the key of G are G, Am, Bm, C, D, and Em. The G Major Scale works over any progression that uses those chords, or any single one played as a vamp. When we solo with notes from G Major over one of them, we give the scale a modal name.

Using G Major in an Em context gives a classical sound. This is true for all scales over their relative minor chord. Which scale would have a classical sound when used over Am? ;) See below!

🎵 Modal Musings – Modes theory is no more than a help. The ear always wins! We have to listen for good notes and forget whether they fit a particular mode or scale.

When we play the G Major Scale over C, one note grabs the attention: F# (the #4). This is the only note different from the C Major Scale, and it gives a unique sound. We call this the C Lydian mode, and the #4 is the characteristic Lydian sound. We get a Lydian sound whenever we solo over chord IV using the parent major scale.

Again, by calling it C Lydian, we make it clear that C is the home chord while G is simply the parent major scale. The same goes for the vamp we played. It’s not a G Major vamp, it doesn’t sound majory, and G isn’t the root note.

It’s an Am vamp – an A Dorian vamp! So when you jam an A blues using G Major, you have to think in terms of A, not G.

🧐 Blues Modes – If you’re a blues guitarist, remember that the Major Scale one tone down from the root note sounds wicked over a blues. This creates the Dorian mode, which is simply the good old Minor Pentatonic Scale with the 6 and 9 added. This is essential blues knowledge.

What if we play the G Major Scale over the Bm chord? Do a Bm vamp, solo over it using G Major, and see how it sounds. You could try similar experiments same for D and even F#dim! In each case, you find a new modal sound. :)

Am Modes In Parallel

So far, we’ve spoken about the different modal sounds we create when we use G Major over its diatonic chord. Let’s change it up. What happens if we stick to an Am chord and change the scale we use to solo?

We already know that If we play an Am vamp and use the G Major Scale over it, we get a Dorian sound. We get this flavor because Am is the II chord in G Major. This Major Scale sounds killer over a blues – the one a tone below the key of the blues.

🎸 Minor Pentatonic Plus 2 –The G Major Scale with A as the tonal center (A B C D E F# G) is the Minor Pentatonic (ACDEG) plus the 6 (F#) and 9 (B). You automatically use A Dorian whenever you play A Minor Pentatonic and add B and F#.

If we wanted an Aeolian sound, we’d need to use the notes from the C Major Scale. We have an Aeolian sound because Am is the VI chord in C Major. This is a very minory sound used by bands like Metallica. It’s A Minor Pentatonic with B (9) and F (b6) added.

But Am appears in three keys! So in which key is Am chord III? That’s right – F Major! What if we play the F Major Scale over Am? We get another sound, and it's called the Phrygian mode. This is A Minor Pentatonic with Bb (b9) and F (b6) added.

So when we say a song is in Am, we have three possibilities: A Dorian, A Phrygian, and A Aeolian. They’re all minor modes with different sounds. All are the Minor Pentatonic with two extra notes added. Our choice depends on the kind of sound we want to create.

Creating An A Dorian Vamp

If you create a sequence using Am followed by chords from the key of G (Bm, Em, G, C, D), you get a Dorian sound. Over the other chords, you’ll need to target different notes from G, but the sound will remain Dorian because A is the tonal center of the song.

💡 Justin’s Eureka Moment – I found modes really, really tricky when I learned them. I tried a music encyclopedia. I tried a famous book called “Modes: No More Mystery”, which only made matters worse. Eventually, I learned a Miles Davis song in D Dorian mode. I realised that though the notes were from the C Major Scale, D was the tonal center! Hooray!

At the end of the day, modes are just a change in tonal center. It’s really simple once you understand it, but you might have to fight and struggle until it eventually clicks! Every time I try to teach modes, I find so many blocks preventing people from grasping them.

And beyond learning modes, if it sounds good, it is good. Lee was using modes without even knowing it, simply because he was listening. Never, ever, let theory get in the way of your ear!

Guitar Wisdom

Lee and I got all philosophical at the end of the lesson! He brought up the words of a great guitarist who said that his job was to “keep the shop,” to hold a steady rhythm. This is the undervalued component of a band. It’s not super flash, but without a steady groove, there is no band.

This reminded me of a Steve Ganz quote I saw on Instagram. He said something like: “Licks for show, rhythm for dough”. It’s so true. We all love jamming with guitarists that can hold down a groove!

Poor Lee, I hope he’s recovered from that modes overdose! That’s more than enough on modes for now. But if you really want to get into modes, explore the exercises mentioned in this lesson. From Justin and Lee, laters! :)

🎵 Master Major Scale modes. Phrygian, Mixolydian, Dorian… Demystify the modes with my Major Scale Modes series.

Lee’s Homework

Pattern 2 of the Minor Pentatonic Scale – Explore it over some A Blues backing tracks

A Minor Vamp Jamming – Make a vamp in Am, adding another chord or two if you like. Explore the A Dorian mode with Pete.
