lessons.text:
Hi there, it's Justin and Lee back for another private lesson. My goodness, this is our first since before Christmas!

Things are calmer now, meaning Lee will have more time to practice than he did at the end of the year. Today we look at a heap of essential blues lead techniques, along with big-picture guitar-learning strategies. Let’s get to it! :)

Lee's Confession: Playing v Theory

Let’s start with strategy. Over Christmas, Lee came to a realization about his guitar practice: what he loves most out of everything we've studied is technique practice like scales and thirds. He can happily sit for ages and play those exercises.

But whenever he's had to write or study, he's found ways to avoid it because it doesn't click for him. He doesn't see quick payoffs, meaning he swiftly loses interest.

From now on, we're going to be super practical in our approach to these lessons.

Practice What You Do or Don't Like?

My job as a teacher is to guide students to their guitar goals. There are certain points in the guitar journey where you have to learn things you don't like to reach your goals. It’s unavoidable!

But this depends on age and free time too. I don't have the time to practice areas I don't like, and neither does Lee. If your practice time is limited, don't spend it on exercises you hate. You have to feel inspired by the instrument!

🎸 All work and no play … makes Johnny a dull guitarist. Try to strike a balance between work and play in your guitar practice. On one hand, you need to enjoy the instrument. But as with any other pursuit, it's no pain, no gain!

It's also about personality. Lee has never been one for studying and retaining written information. He's all about the practical and concrete. For instance, he'd much rather build a house than do all the legal side and box-ticking!

Create Your Vision

We went back to the fundamental question all guitarists must ask if they want to build a solid practice routine: what do I want to be able to play?

Lee revealed that he wants to follow the chords better in 12-bar blues but doesn't want the theory part. He just wants to play what sounds good instinctively or by remembering which scales to use when.

🧐 What To Practice On The Guitar? – There is no one-size-fits-all practice schedule. So how should you practice guitar? I call it The Holistic Practice Routine.

I totally agree! For instance, I'd love to hear him targeting the 3rd over the I chord. Lee said he'd be happy to learn licks that target the 3rd rather than learning where to find the third in any key. He knows it's always one string up and one fret behind the root note (except on string 2).

But this is where I disagree. He'd understand the visual pattern much better by knowing the note names and being able to find them without referring to the root note. This is one of the million reasons that Lee should know all the notes on the fretboard!

The BB King Pentatonic

A great way to make the changes and switch between positions is to use the BB King Pentatonic Scale. This isn't the Minor Pentatonic or the Major Pentatonic – it's a mixture! It has the 2nd and the 6th too.

It fits over all of the chords too. The only caveat is that you have to bend differently depending on which chord you're soloing over.

Mixing Major and Minor Pentatonic

Back at the beginning of the Rut Busters series, one of Lee's main goals was to stop playing Minor Pentatonic all the time! He has learned ways to switch it up.

He knows he can use Major Pentatonic licks over the I and V chords and Minor Pentatonic over the IV and V chords.

💣 Jamming The Blues In Every Key – Take your blues knowledge and use it to play solos in any key (yes, any key) with this guide!

This is because the note C# (the 3rd of A) sounds horrific over the D chord (chord IV). Over the D, you need to switch to a D Major Pentatonic or the Am Pentatonic. But C# sounds okay over E – it's the 6th or 13th in E Major.

A great exercise is to put on a backing track and consciously make the changes, deliberately changing the scales and notes you play on each chord. Practice this a lot, and eventually you won't have to think about it.

Jumping Between Positions

In the first demo, Lee uses Pattern 5 of the Major Pentatonic over the A chord and Pattern 1 of the Minor Pentatonic on the D and E chords. Beyond the exercises, don't forget that you can stay on the Minor Pentatonic on the I chord!

Staying In Position

Another great exercise is to stay in the same area of the guitar neck. For this jam, Lee stayed between frets 6 and 10, using the Major Pentatonic for I and V and the Minor Pentatonic for IV.

💡 Put Into Practice – The most common mistake when making the changes is thinking too much and not playing enough. Granted, knowing the theory isn't easy, but you must apply it. That's how you really grasp what's going on.

Programming The Blues Autopilot

Lee is not the kind to study all the theoretical ins and outs of scales and modes. This means he'll have to practice a lot, but in doing so, he'll eventually be able to make the changes in a 12-bar blues without thinking about it.

This is great because the more you think, the more you stink. When you listen to musicians who are lost in thinking mode, you can smell it. Something just doesn't sound right. By practicing repeatedly, you program the autopilot. Eventually, you can stop thinking about notes and scales and focus on time and feel instead.

Mixing Major and Minor All Over Neck

The beauty of switching between Major and Minor Pentatonic scales is that it's pretty easy to do, especially if you only focus on the thinnest three strings. You can switch between them in all five positions.

Warning: don't try to do this in all five positions to begin with. Practice in one position until you feel comfortable playing the changes, then move on. If you try to learn many positions at once, you won't be able to play any of them well.

🎸 Use Your Ear – Keith Richards and BB King don't deliberately target the 3rd. They're relying on their years of practice to tell them what sounds good when.

Another key component to making the changes is to instinctively know where you are in a song at all times. This is simply crucial in the blues, especially in the last four bars of a 12-bar sequence. If you automatically know where you are, you can focus on your lead part rather than worrying about the chord you're playing over.

Practice Going From I to IV

A great exercise to practice with the looper is going from the I chord to the IV chord – this is the trickiest change to master.

Again, do not hit the 3rd when you're on the IV chord! One of Lee's comfort-blanket licks uses the 3rd, and I hate to spoil the party, but it doesn't sound good.

Sure, in some situations, the 3rd can sound… okay. Chuck Berry and Keith Richards often play it on the IV, and if you hear it loads, your ear gets used to it. But it's not a good note to have in the auto bag. :)

💡 Soloing Tip – To avoid a note, don't try to avoid it. Instead, focus on playing the good notes. If you repeat to yourself, "avoid the C#, avoid the C#, avoid the C#," chances are you'll hit it. Focus on hitting the nice ones, and you'll hit them!

Minor Blues

In a minor blues, we play Am, Dm, and Em instead of A7, D7, and E7. You do not, DO NOT want to hit the Major 3rd (C#, 3:6 [string 3, fret 6], 2:2, 1:8). It will sound horrific over all the chords!

Instead, stick to the Minor Pentatonic Scale. At some points, you can also add the Dorian notes – the 6th and the 9th. But you need to use your ear. If it sounds good, it is good.

Over the IV chord (Dm), the 6th (F#, at 2:7 or 3:11) will sound terrible: it clashes with the F in the Dm chord. But next door, we have the note F (at 2:6 or 3:10), and it sounds really sexy over the Dm. This is because it's part of the Dm chord (D F A). You can see this in the common Dm shape X57765. Target it! It's also handy as a passing note over Am.

But again, beyond scales and notes and scale degrees, the most essential skill is knowing where you are in the song and listening to what you play.

🧐 Music Theory – Fully understand Pentatonic scales, 6ths and 9ths, chord tones, and chord progressions and watch your playing transform with my Practical Music Theory course.

Three Notes Per String Pattern

We'll keep going with the three-note-per-string pattern in G using hammer-ons and flick-offs. Make sure every note is perfect before speeding up. Practice makes permanent, not perfect. By practicing sloppy playing, you reinforce it.

If you're a blues player, practice this pattern in the key one tone below your favorite blues key. Lee's practicing it in G because he often plays blues in A. As mentioned in Lesson 7, this gives us the A Dorian mode!

I suggest Lee does this with hammer-ons and flick-offs to play fast runs in blues. Lee loves Clapton's triplets, and this exercise will help him play them.

💣 Legato Primer – Play silky smooth licks with my Legato Primer series.

When you first practice legato playing, you have to make sure that the notes ring loud and clear. Press nice and hard. Then as you advance, you can begin playing faster. To play quick runs, you'll have to play lighter notes to achieve this, and your slow practice will prepare your fingers for it.

The BB Blues Box In A

BB King makes the changes all the time. Very few of his licks repeat across the chords: they're all adapted. He's like a jazzer in a blueser's body!

🎶 Chord Tones – I reckon BB makes the changes well because he's a singer: he's used to singing the chord tones. If you could somehow play a guitar solo with no reference to shapes, scales or chords, you'd end up playing chord tones.

Let's first look at a Major Pentatonic Pattern to describe the BB Box. If we play 3:6 (string 3, fret 6), 2:5, 2:7, 1:5, and 1:7, that's the top of the Major Pentatonic Scale in Position 1.

If we play the same pattern, but starting at 3:11, we get the BB Blues Box in A! Note that the second note (2:10) is A, and that's the root note. It's like a mix of the Major and Minor Pentatonics! Can you see why? :)

What's the difference between this scale and the Major Pentatonic Scale? We've taken away the 3rd, and we've added the 4th. But we can still get the 3rd by bending 2:12 one tone, or to the b3rd by bending 2:12 one semitone. You can also bend 1:12 one tone to get the 6th.

After some jamming, Lee noticed that the 1:10 was a funny note. He could hear that it sounded strange over A but great over D and E. That's why you need to use your ears. Only by using them will you discover these things.

Wow, that's a lot of lead blues. Get to work on the exercises. Practice them often, and you'll see a sharp jump in your ability to make the changes. And always, always remember, especially when you get to advanced levels of guitar playing – if it sounds good, it is good. Laters :)

🎸 Check out my series on Making The Changes. Through tons of example licks, scales and exercises, we'll lead you all the way to the infamous Arpeggiator!

lessons.text:
Guess who's back, back again? There are a ton of blues exercises and techniques packed into this lesson – sorry Lee! This stuff is crucial for blues players, and learning it will take you into advanced soloing. You just need practice, practice, and more practice to nail it.

Huge Soloing Discovery

Lee has recently come to a huge discovery. In his jams with Pete, he noticed that he’s naturally been seeking to structure his solos on melody rather than scales and noodling. This is a huge step!

All the great players I’ve met say that they have a bag of tricks for when they’re not feeling inspired. They start with one of these phrases and build on it, trying to connect the rest of the solo to it. If you start a solo with a strong melody, you have a strong foundation for the rest of the solo.

Lee also commented that his solos and fills sounded wicked but were pretty simple. This is no problem. Most of the best guitar playing isn’t complicated.

💡The Journey – Get really comfortable with one box. As you build up a big blues vocab, all the positions and boxes blur together. You’ll be able to switch seamlessly while staying in the same area of the neck.

Playing The Major Pentatonic On Each Degree of The Blues

Before Lee and I went further on this, I wanted to look at a soloing technique we had skipped over: playing the Major Pentatonic from each degree in the blues. This means using A Major Pentatonic over A, D Major Pentatonic over D, and E Major Pentatonic over E.

To do this, we took Lee’s pet A Major Pentatonic lick (see TAB) and moved it into different keys. In D, you use the same shape but start on 5:5, and in E you start at 5:7. Lee used this lick as a starting point for his solos.

|---------------| |---------------| |-----------2-2-| |-------2-4—----| |-0-2-4---------| |---------------|

You can take this further by using the A Minor Pentatonic as a base and moving into the A, D, or E Major Pentatonic over each chord.

To summarise, on the A7 chord, you can play A Minor Pentatonic, the A Blues Scale, A Major Pentatonic, or A7 Arpeggio.

On the D7 chord, you can play D Major Pentatonic or A Minor Pentatonic. And on the E7 chord, you can use E Major Pentatonic or A Minor Pentatonic.

🎸 Making The Changes – I have a Making The Changes Series that takes you through how to mix Major and Minor Pentatonics in a blues, leading all the way to the infamous Arpeggiator!

Awesome Blues Lick!

This is an essential Major Pentatonic box, and you can use it to make the changes. Here’s the shape in the key of A:

|-------–—-5--7-| |----5--7-------| |-6-------------| |----------—----| |---------------| |---------------|

If you move all the notes up five frets and start at 3:11, you’re in D, and the first note of the shape in E is 3:13.

You can bend the top note of this shape (1:7) one tone to the Major 3rd, which will sound great over A. Lee tried a tone bend from 2:7 over the A chord, which is bending F# (the 6th) to G# (Major 7th). This note clashes with the A7 and doesn’t sound good. What you can do is bend 2:7 one semitone to get G, the b7. This one is awesome!

💣 Push The Boundaries – Force yourself out of your usual licks by focusing on the thinnest string of this box, trying as many riffs as possible.

During the demo jam, Lee struggled to make the final E in the sequence. An easy way out of that is to jump to a chord! Or you can even take a short break. 🙂 When you’re practicing, I suggest you try hard to make the changes. If the music is too fast, slow it down.

Legato Lick

I love Lee’s style. He has lovely vibrato and beautiful phrasing. I think he could become an even better player by playing longer lines and adding repeating phrases to his solos.

A great way to do this is to develop a solo, using your bag of melodic tricks, then moving into a repeating section. The other instruments then change the harmony while you stay on that lick.

To help him do this, we’ll explore some legato licks in the A Minor Pentatonic Scale.

Four-In-A-Line Legato

Start with finger 3 on 1:8 (string 1, fret 8). Pick, then flick off to fret 5. Move to string 2 and do the same. Then continue, only picking the first note of each flick-off and any notes played individually.

|-8f5–----5—--------------------------------------------------------------| |-----8f5---8f5–--8f5—----5—----------------------------------------------| |---------------7-----7f5---7f5---7f5-----5—------------------------------| |-------------------------------7-----7f5---7f5—--7f5—----5—--------------| |-----------------------------------------------7-----7f5---7f5---7f5—----| |---------------------------------------------------------------8—----8f5-|

Make sure you practice this slowly at an even tempo. If you practice it “lumpy” (with fast flick-offs) it will also sound lumpy when you speed up!

Always use the rolling technique when you play consecutive notes on different strings on the same fret. That way, the two notes don’t ring out together. This is a perfect technique to practice when you have a spare two minutes. But if you have extra time, here’s a more thorough one.

Minor Pentatonic Exercise

This is the minor-pentatonic version of the 3rds and 4ths exercises for the Major scale. It’s great for practicing the rolling technique. I usually call this one Playing the Minor Pentatonic in 4ths, but technically you play a mixture of 3rds and 4ths. Remember it as playing the notes vertically next to each other in the pentatonic scale.

|-----------------------------------------------------5-----8--| |-----------------------------------------5-----8--5-----8-----| |-----------------------------5–----7--5-----7—----------------| |-----------------5-----7--5-----7-----------------------------| |-----5-----7--5-----7-----------------------------------------| |--5-----8-----------------------------------------------------|

You’ll notice that you jump strings on the same fret several times. Use the rolling technique, playing the first note with the fingertip and rolling it down onto the next string, muting the previous one with your finger.

Do the opposite when you play the higher note first: the finger starts flat, then rolls on to the tip. And make sure you mute the string above the one you’re fretting.

Another effect of this exercise is that it opens your possibilities for melody building. Many guitarists feel limited when they play the Minor Pentatonic scale. For instance, from the note A at 4:7, we’re very likely to play 4:5 or 3:5 next, but not 5:7. Modern blues uses this technique loads. It's tricky, but it gives licks a hip sound.

🧐 Guitar Maladies – If you suffer from going-too-fast-itis (that’s a technical term), use a metronome! :)

Positive Finger Placement

Eric Johnson did a DVD called Total Electric Guitar. He’s a total guitar nerd! In it, he talks about positive finger placement and claims that how you place your finger on the fret is crucial for getting a perfect note.

I spent a whole afternoon trying to figure out if this made a difference, and I concluded that it did! Part of the trick is using the point of the tip rather than the soft bit.

I think the mind plays a part here. Somehow, when we have a good connection with the finger, we can feel it, and it comes across in the sound. Another trick to this is the thumb. You have to move your thumb around the back when you move to the thicker strings. Otherwise, you won’t get good finger contact.

3-In-A-Line Legato

This exercise is the same as the four-in-a-line exercise except we only descend three notes each time.

|-8f5–--5—--------------------------------------------------------| |-----8---8f5–--8f5---5—------------------------------------------| |-------------------7—----7f5-7f5---5-----—-----------------------| |---------------------------------7---7f5-7f5---5—----------------| |---------------------------------------------7---7f5-7f5---7-----| |---------------------------------------------------------8---8f5-|

Again you have to play this slow and clean before speeding up. Fast and sloppy always sounds sloppy – if you want to play fast, start off slow!

When you ascend the scale, use hammer-ons. Start on 6:5 with finger 1, pick it, hammer on to fret 8, then roll on to 5:5 with finger 1, and so on.

Fast Blues Legato Lick

We also explored another fast lick that’s useful across the fretboard in blues. Let’s start at 1:5.

|-5h8f5----| |--------8-| |----------| |----------| |----------| |----------|

Make sure finger 1 is touching string 2 so that the open B string doesn’t ring out when you remove finger 3 from 2:8. You only pick twice: on the first 1:5 and on 2:8.

Try to get used to playing it for a long time, like for a whole minute. See where you can use this same lick or variations of it in your playing. Another option in the key of A is to use this same pattern with 3:2, 3:4, and 4:4.

Homework

Lee is full to the brim after that lesson! Here are his exercises for next time:

i) 12-Bar Blues with Major Pentatonic off All Three Notes ii) Mix In A Minor Pentatonic

Playing in 4ths With Rolling

Three-in-a-line Legato

We'll see Lee in a couple of weeks. I should have a better setup so we can do some recording with him. Laters :)

🎸 Check out my Advanced modules to take your guitar playing to the next level.

lessons.text:
Hey folks! In this Captain’s Privates lesson, we expand on the blues legato lines from last time and have a total geek-out on blues extended chords. Let’s get to it. :)

Practice and Real Playing

At the start of the lesson, Lee told me he’d noticed an interesting pattern in his live jamming sessions. Once the camera was rolling, he saw that he was resorting to old patterns and licks for the various chords, licks that he’s played for years. He also found it hard to move licks into different positions.

I want to assure Lee and other guitarists with this tendency that this is all normal. You just need to practice more to expand your soloing skills. It’s a matter of practicing new licks and positions until they become second nature. Then you’ll bring them out without realizing it.

🧐 Learn About Learning! – In my Effective Practice series, we cover the A-Z of skill development along with methods to optimize your practice sessions. :)

Playing In Fourths

We reviewed Lee’s progress with the fourths exercise. He worried he was muting the string primarily by lifting it off rather than muting with the tip of the finger. It turns out he was doing it totally right!

He mentioned that he still has to do it deliberately; it doesn’t happen spontaneously. Because of that, his fingers don’t use the technique when he's playing for real.

We always have to practice deliberately to begin with. Only with time do things become automatic. Keep doing the exercises and have faith that the techniques will become second nature.

Three-In-A-Line Legato

I sat down after Lesson #9 to figure out how to teach the three-in-a-line exercise. I realized that I never use these runs on the thickest strings! What’s more, if you want to play them on those strings, your hand position has to change. This makes these patterns impractical.

If you stay on the thinnest four, your arm doesn’t need to move, it feels more natural, and the licks sound better! So descend the scale using the three-in-a-line legato, then stop when you reach the root note at 4:7 (the note A). It sounds awesome!

🎸 Justin’s Journey – When I was a teen, I used to believe I had to practice every lick, chord, and scale in all positions. Now that I’m older, I realize that if you’ll never use something, there’s no point in learning it. Our time is limited: let’s use it wisely!

The trick to nailing this (and any technique) is to start slowly, at around 20% speed. Play it through a few times really slow, then speed up. You’ll be able to go faster quite easily that way. If you start at 50%, you’ll find it tricky to speed up. Seriously – play it slow! As for rhythm, count this one in triplets.

Last week, we covered a very similar exercise: the four-in-a-line legato. You’ll need the rolling technique for this, and you’ll need to count 1e+a, 2e+a, etc. The lowest note you play is 7:7. See the TAB below. :)

Lee’s Thick String Problem

Lee has noticed that he uses the thickest string as his pacifier (his words!). What does this mean? He loves starting licks and riffs from the thickest string and does this almost automatically. His buddy Pete has told him that these notes are difficult to hear in a band context.

It’s true that they don’t stand out, and they muddy the rhythm parts. Another point is that these notes and riffs sound… beginnery! The problem is that we all learn barre chords and scales using the thickest string as our reference, so it becomes our go-to for everything on the neck.

The key to undoing this is to learn licks on the thinner strings and to learn the notes on the entire fretboard.

Legato Variations

There are many, many variations of these legato patterns. One of my favorite ones is the following:

|----------------------5------8f5---5--| |---------5------8f5—-----8f5-----8----| |--7f5------7f5------7-----------------| |---–--7-------------------------------| |--------------------------------------| |--------------------------------------|

So we play descending three in a line, but the starting note moves up one note of the scale each time.

Don’t try to learn dozens of these patterns. And don’t switch positions! You’re much better knowing a couple patterns well and using them. Expand once you have those under your belt.

Theory Geek-Out Time

Lee asked a question before the lesson about why the D Major Scale works over the A11 chord!

To tackle this, we need to realize that a basic triad chord is built from the root, third and fifth of the scale. For instance, the C Major Scale is CDEFGABC, so the C chord contains the notes C, E, and G.

🎸 Chord Construction – To go deeper with triads, 7th chords, and extended chords, check out my course Practical Musical Theory.

The most common chords with four notes use the 7th in addition to the root, 3rd, and 5th. We can manipulate those basic notes to get Major 7th, Dominant 7th, minor 7th, and minor 7 b5 chords.

As for keys, each Major key has three major chords within it. These are built off the 1st, 4th, and 5th scale degrees and are called chords I, IV, and V. They also have three minor chords, which are built off the 2nd, 3rd, and 6th degrees. These are chords II, III, and VI. So the pattern is Major, minor, minor, Major, Major, minor.

If we do the same for four-note chords, the pattern extends to Major 7th, minor 7th, Major 7th, Dominant 7th, and minor 7th.

Beyond 7th Chords

If we keep building, we eventually get 9th, 11th, and 13th chords. These can all be simplified to a Major 7th, Dominant 7th, or minor 7th chord. For instance, if you see G13 (this is G Dominant 13th) in a song, you can play G7. If you see a Dm13, you can play Gm7. You can replace C Major 13 with C Major 7, and so on.

Back to the chords Lee was playing – A11 and B11. Remember, we can reduce A11 to A7, which is the V chord in D Major, hence why this scale sounds wicked over A11. As for the B11 shape that Lee plays, it’s 7X765X. He’s playing B, A, C#, and E. These notes all belong to the D Major Scale (D E F# G A B C#). So this scale also sounds great over the B11 chord.

D Major played over the IV chord in D, which is A7, is called the A Mixolydian mode (A B C# D E F# G). This is the A Major Pentatonic Scale with D (4th) and G (b7th) added. This is a typical blues mode.

Chord Extensions In The Blues

This chat about chord extensions is relevant in a blues context because A9, A11, and A13 are all excellent substitutions for A7. There are loads of grips for each. The first step to making them part of our repertoire is to learn a couple and use them in context.

Try using A9 (X4545X) instead of A7. Note that we aren’t playing any A notes! As Lee said: “Have we got any A’s in here?” While we don't fret any root notes, the reference root note is at 6:5, on the same fret as two of the chord tones.

Move this shape up five frets to get D9 (X 9 10 9 10 X) and up another two for E9 (X 11 12 11 12 X).

💡 Take It Easy – Learn a few chord grips at a time. Make sure you can switch to them easily and use them in context before you learn more. It’s way better to know a few chords well and put them to use than half-know loads of grips.

An ultra-common D9 grip is X54555, with finger 3 barring the notes on fret 5. This is also moveable, and it’s easy to switch to A9 (X4545X). Another cool option for D7 is XX7778. This chord is the common A7 open variation (X02223) moved up by five frets.

Lee noticed that he was putting his fingers down one at a time for these new chords. That’s totally normal! In this case, I suggest he plays these chords frequently in the blues. He’ll be under pressure to switch to them, which often does the trick.

Music Theory: Big Picture

Forgive me if I sound arrogant by saying this – it’s not my intention! I think music theory is a doddle. It’s like a ball of string in which all of the various parts are connected to each other.

Once you can see the entire ball, it becomes clear how all the areas are interrelated. Until you’ve understood all the concepts, it’s complicated. You have to search through the fog.

💣Nail the Notes on The Neck – Find powerful exercises for learning the fretboard in Lesson 2 and Lesson 3 of this series.

If you’re into guitar and really want to advance, you must learn music theory and the notes on the fretboard. I promise you it makes everything so much easier! It opens up the fretboard in a way that’s impossible if you don’t have the knowledge.

Many of the best players don’t have a clue about music theory. But they do know the notes on the fretboard. On any other instrument, you simply have to know them. And on guitar, it’s not super hard to learn the notes – it just takes some persistence. So go and learn them!

Stick around for more of Lee’s Privates if you want to advance as a blues and rock player. From Justin and Lee, laters :)

🎸Into 9ths, 11ths and 13ths? Build a huge repertoire of blues chord extensions.

Homework

Three Pattern Sequences (Three In A Line, Four In A Line, Variation in TAB above)

9th Shapes + Write down all Dominant 9th, 11th, and 13th shapes you know

lessons.text:
Hey, how you doing? It’s Justin and Lee back for another Captain’s Privates lesson. We hope this series is inspiring you and helping you take your playing to new heights. :)

How to Remember What You Learn

This is the first lesson since I went to Italy, meaning our last lesson was three or four weeks ago. Lee comments that he quite likes the long gaps since they enable him to practice deeply and explore what we cover.

He notices a dip when he goes three weeks without serious practice, even in areas where he is confident! So he wanted some tips to help him remember what he practices.

💡 Memory Tips – When I transcribe a new song, I don't write any of it down at first. I revisit it a week later and try to write it down from memory. Then it sticks forever.

A long time ago, a memory Olympiad came to Tassie (Tasmania) to do some talks. He could memorize the order of 15 decks of cards or something ridiculous like that! His tip was to learn something well, then leave it for a day. Revisit it tomorrow. Then do the same two days later, four days later, and so on, until you reach a year of a gap.

I did this for all the classical guitar pieces I learned as a teenager, and I still remember them! I still use this technique, albeit not strictly. If I like a song and realize I haven't played it for a long time, I'll revisit it.

I asked Lee if he had a lick book or songbook. This could be the answer. I suggest that Lee prints the chord boxes from my site and writes down the new chords we covered last week.

Extended Chord Shapes

We got to the topic of gospel slides when Lee asked if it was OK to play the A9 chord X4545X using finger 1 to barre fret 4.

🧐 Right or Wrong? – Many guitarists fret over whether their technique is correct or not. With some things, there simply is no right way. I’d never teach a rock player to use their fingers instead of a pick, but look at Jeff Beck. Find what works for you!

Using a barre is perfectly fine unless we want to play gospel slides. You'll find it tricky to slide the A9 barre shape two frets up without playing the lowest note (a classic gospel technique). It’s much easier if you use fingers 1, 2, 3, and 4 for the A9: you simply lift off finger 1 and slide.

The other issue with the barre is that you could easily play 1:4 by accident. It’s the Major 7 note, while A9 is a Dominant chord shape. It sounds horrible when you play them together!

Add Gospel Slides

Gospel slides are a cool trick we can add to our blues rhythm guitar to spice it up.

Start with that chord we looked at last week: A9 (X4545). Use fingers 1 and 2 on fret 4 and the other two fingers on fret 5. With the gospel slide, we slide up fingers 2, 3, and 4 up two frets (XX767X).

Now your fingers are on the notes A, C#, and F#, which is an A6 chord without the 5th. You can also see this is an A triad (XX765X) with the 6th instead of the 5th. So with the gospel slide, you slide from the A9 to A6 and back again. Note: it’s not an A13 because there’s no b7 note in the shape.

In fact, you could leave out finger 1 and just play XX545X to XX767X. This slide sounds very classy – all the cool blues guitarists use it!

Here’s an exercise: over a 12-bar blues chunka-chunka rhythm, use the A7 chords you already know, and throw in the odd gospel slide. You slide up on beat 2 and slide back on the “+” of 2.

🚨 Listen! – I told Lee we were changing to D the first time, but that was all. I made up the chords as I went, and Lee followed me. Bravo! Following the chords is a critical jamming skill.

Lee asked why I was using fingers 2, 3, and 4 for the shapes above. I do it because it gives me more options. We can add finger 1 to 5:4 to get the full chord shape. But we can also put it on 1:3, which is the b7.

And if we just play the thinnest three strings, we get a mini A9 grip: XXX453. If we slide this up two frets (XXX675), this is a mini A7 shape. Regardless of the names, all these shapes sound good in blues. Use them!

Gospel Slides In D Blues

Let’s look at D9 gospels now. Start with the common D9 grip X54555, barring the thinnest three strings with finger 3. Now slide the barre up two frets (XXX777). You can think of this as a Bm chord, but when D is the root, it acts as a D6. Make sure the lower strings don’t ring out when you slide.

In A, this Dominant 9th grip becomes X 12 11 12 12 12, and for the gospel part, we slide finger 3 up two frets (X X X 14 14 14). There is another slide in D: XXX987 to X X X 11 10 9. I don’t think it sounds as good as the others, so I tend to avoid it.

The beauty of learning these tricks is that you’ll hear when the greats use them. Try experimenting with new rhythms too. There are tons of options, and you might just discover something new.

Gospel Slides In Vamps

It’s a fantastic idea to use a vamp for your gospel-slide practice. That way, you can focus on finding these shapes for one chord and explore all the possibilities. You can also add all the other grips you know for the chord and see how they relate to the shapes we’ve covered. This is where the chord book comes in handy.

Minor Pentatonic Legato

Make sure every note is clear when you practice the three- and four-in-a-line patterns we covered last week in Lesson 9. You should only hear one note at a time.

You’re unlikely to bring these lines out in a solo unless they’re 100% automated. So practice them until you have that level of familiarity. You don’t need to use the whole lick either. Sometimes one little part of it will sound wicked. You can throw in short lines anywhere!

Flashy Minor Pentatonic Licks

I love Lee’s vibrato and phrasing, but sometimes I’d like to hear flashy moments. He could throw in a crazy line or two when the solo reaches a climax. This is what the greats do. Their solos build and build, and at the climax they bring out a fancy-pants lick!

So we’re going to look at a short line that Lee can use for climaxes. It’s a simple idea that you can use in tons of ways. Start with finger 1 on 3:5 (string 3, fret 5). Pick, then hammer on at fret 7 with finger 3. Flick off, then play 4:7 with finger 3. That’s pick, hammer, flick, pick.

You can also start with finger 1 on 1:5 (we covered this lick in lesson 9). See the TAB for both licks.

|---------|-5h8f5----| |---------|--------8-| |-5h7f5---|----------| |-------7-|-—--------| |---------|----------| |---------|----------|

Lee used a silent hammer-on for 2:8 – he played pick, hammer, flick, hammer. This means you hammer on the note without picking at all. If that works for you, by all means do it! I suggest you try pick, hammer, flick, pick to develop your picking skills.

Inside v Outside Picking

I noticed that Lee was starting with a down-pick, so I asked him to use an up-pick instead. This way, I could see whether he’s an inside or an outside picker.

What on earth is inside and outside picking? If you start inside the pair of strings you’re about to pick, you’re an inside picker. If you start outside, you’re an outside picker!

Try the fancy riff above, and see what picking style you naturally use. Most people prefer one or the other, so it’s handy to know which feels natural to you.

Lick Variations

You can also start with finger 1 on 1:8, hammer on to 1:10, flick off, then play 2:10 with finger 3. This is still the A Minor Pentatonic Scale.

|-8h10f8—----| |---------10-| |------------| |------------| |------------| |------------|

You can also add the blue note at 1:11 using the pinkie or finger 3. There are loads of variations on this – play around! It’s common for the picked notes to be louder than the others. Make sure they’re all the same volume. Lee noticed that he tends to pick too loudly. Great, he’s aware of it. Now he has to take action, or it will never change.

Exploring Dynamics

Lee’s picking problem took us on to the subject of dynamics. You can play at the same volume if the backing track or the band is static. But if the volume goes low, you have to go low too.

We played a 12-bar blues, and after one repetition, I dropped the volume, forcing Lee to play quieter. He did play softer, with some notes a little louder, which is excellent. But he could have played less and relaxed more, leaving longer gaps.

In slow blues, you want to play softly and delicately. Lee noticed that he has focused more on choosing the right notes than touch and feel.

🎸 BB King… is the master of dynamics in the blues. In some of his solos, he only uses one note. You can only do this if you have superior dynamics, timing, and vibrato skills.

Musical Expression In The Blues

It’s crucial that you get in touch with how you feel while you’re playing and try to express those emotions while you play. You don’t have to be miserable or morbid.

Lee came out with a terrible, apocalyptic situation that would spark the biggest blues solo in history: “I need to go into Marks & Spencer’s when they’ve just run out of hummus and prosecco on a Friday night. Then I’ll come home and play the longest blues solo ever!” Fantastic, Lee. Whatever gets your juices flowing!

We really hope you've enjoyed this Captain's Privates series. Put all of these exercises into practice and you'll be well on your way to becoming an accomplished blues guitarist. Cheers from Lee and Justin. :)

🎸Take your playing to the next level with my Advanced guitar modules.

Homework

On that note, let’s recap the practice for the next lesson:

Fancy chords and gospel slides: write them down to aid memory

Learn legato patterns: focus on solid timing

Slow blues: one jam per week, playing as softly as possible

lessons.text:
Student Highlight

Small Town Sci-Fi, aka Jonathan Suarez

I got an email from a student who had just released his first record, and I think he sounds awesome! Jonathan has made a record with cool Indie vibes. It has a little of Elliott Smith and maybe The Shins. :) There's lots of space and ethereal dreaminess, and he has a hip vocal delivery that hits home.

🎧 Listen to Psycho, the first EP released by Small Town Sci-Fi, also known as Jonathan Suarez. Great vibes and tasty guitar tones from California.

He's been a JustinGuitar student since he started learning guitar three or four years ago. He had a rough year and needed something to help him express himself. Then playing guitar got serious for him a little under six months ago.

Jonathan told me in his first email:

❝ Before, I was mostly lots memorizing chord shapes and practicing strumming patterns. But your course material enabled me to advance pretty quickly!

Recently, Jonathan recorded his first studio record, an EP called Psycho. I enjoyed listening to it – it has four cool tracks and an Elliott Smith vibe that grabs my attention. He told me that he tried learning to play from books before learning with JustinGuitar, but that didn't go well…

❝ I tried learning with books long ago, and it went nowhere. I'm not sure what I'd have done without your lessons. I recommend you to everyone that asks and some who don't!

Jonathan, I'm glad you've found JustinGuitar. I dig your music and the engagement you've shown by recording an EP and expressing yourself through music. That's always a big deal, and you sound great. Good luck with your musical journey!

Check out Small Town Sci-Fi and join the Discussion. :)

lessons.title: Sofa Showcase: Wolf Moon
lessons.summary: Jimmy Owen was a student of mine at The Guitar Institute and his duo with Kelly Lethbridge is really special!
lessons.text:
Let's welcome Jimmy Owen and Kelly Lethbridge!

In this video, I catch up with Wolf Moon – Jimmy Owen, and Kelly Lethbridge – and they give us some excellent advice for songwriting. I watched Jimmy growing as a guitar player on his social media page, and I thought his music with Kelly was top-notch.

🚨 Lethbridge Owen is now Wolf Moon! Back in the days, when we recorded this video, Jimmy and Kelly used to call themselves Lethbgridge Owen. Now, they're Wolf Moon - listen on Spotify!

I was really happy they could make it down for a Sofa Showcase, and I'm happy they did! They shared some great tips on being an artist. :)

How to Start Being a Musician

Kelly told me that when starting as a musician, you need to have a clear vision of what you want, above and beyond the technical skills. You need to be able to see your vision. Ask yourself these questions: What do you want to sound like? Where do you want to be? Where do you see yourself?

It's common for songwriters and musicians to be unsure of their vision. She told me that exposure is critical, to begin with, if you aren't sure. Working with people, being in front of cameras, and listening to different music all help you find your voice.

Get Going With Songwriting

Jimmy told me that people beat themselves up for not being fully original. He suggests it's okay to take inspiration from other songs and write similar ones to others! He added that he and Kelly always share their ideas, allowing others to expand on them. It has taken them around 10 years to find their sound.

The three of us agreed there is no set way of writing music and that we often revisit our music to refine it and change elements of it. It means we need to find our songwriting method. Even the way we write can change from song to song.

Creative or Formulaic?

We also discussed the issue of being creative or formulaic, concluding that rules and creativity are important. Song ideas often come to Jimmy as he's having a coffee! A complete idea comes into his mind, including the vocals. Other times, it's a slow process. He encourages us to listen to our musical ideas and forget the rules while admitting that some structures work well.

Kelly told me: "There are tools, but there are no rules." Wolf Moon uses tools, but they don't use formulae when songwriting. They let the music come, then try to understand what they've created. Both of them suggested listening to an enormous variety of music. That way, we pick up loads of ideas, and music comes to us naturally.

Huge thanks to Wolf Moon for coming down today. It was awesome hearing them play; I hope it inspired you on your guitar journey.

📝 Songwriting doesn't have to be a mystery. We break it all down in my Songwriting Course!

lessons.title: Sofa Showcase: Samuel Jack
lessons.summary: Samuel Jack is a super soulful singer-songwriter I've worked with, and I think he has a bright future as an artist!
lessons.text:
Welcome Singer-Songwriter Samuel Jack

I've known Samuel Jack for a few years now. The song we play, Stone Cold, is a little unusual for the Sofa Showcase series because I co-wrote it with him!

⭐️ Samuel Jack has a great voice, is an amazing writer, and works really hard. I see a bright future for him! :) Listen to him on Spotify.

Now let's chat about our song together, Stone Cold, and some advice for writing song lyrics.

Where Did Stone Cold Come From?

We chatted about the origins of Stone Cold (the song we wrote together). We were jamming at a songwriting weekend at Conversion. Samuel wanted to write a vintage love song, and he took his inspiration for lyrics from someone he loved, which helped him out.

We first decided on the tempo and found two lovely chords, then went from there. Though the bridge can be tricky to write, it was ultra quick for this tune. I came up with a bridge, Samuel sang as I played it, and it just worked!

Samuel's Advice For Writing Lyrics

Samuel said that as a vocalist, once you have the sweet spot and a melody you like, it informs the rest of the song. We agreed that being able to connect with the lyrics is vital. Samuel said he needs to be able to truly connect with what he writes. But we also agreed that the lyrics could warp the truth or even completely invent it!

Tips For New Songwriters

He gave some great advice to new songwriters and shared his process for writing tunes. He suggests we keep everything simple, to begin with. He finds some nice chords when writing songs and decides on a theme for the lyrics. He then plays the chords and sings whatever comes to his head. Then, he listens to what he's created and repeats this process until he has a song.

But if you're stuck for words, he says you can even make vocal sounds over the music. That then inspires you to create true lyrics for the song. I also shared my tips. Back in the day, I made a list of the 20 songs that affected me the most and then analyzed the structure and lyrics. I then tried to copy the same ideas in my compositions.

We both agreed that you have to listen to what you like. That's what helps you become YOU – listening to music you don't like, out of obligation, is uninspiring and makes your music inauthentic!

Thanks to Samuel for coming down! Do check him out on the following channels – his music is wicked, and his music could inspire you to write your own. Cheers. :)

📝 Up for more? My Songwriting Course makes it all easy for you! :)

lessons.title: Sofa Showcase: Klara
lessons.summary: My guest on the sofa is a student from long ago, Klara. She sings Playground House!
lessons.text:
Singer-Songwriter Klara Kjellen

Hey, it's Justin here for another Sofa Showcase! Let me introduce you to a student from Sweden, Klara Kjellen, pronounced Shillean – I can't pronounce it! I met her over 10 years ago when she came to the United Kingdom to do singing lessons and guitar lessons.

🎧 Listen to Klara Kjellen on Spotify! :)

I've been following her journey as a songwriter ever since! At the time of recording, Klara was about to release a new album, and one of her songs (These Woods) had just appeared in a Volvo advert!

How Did I Write The Fingerstyle Part?

We chatted about the fingerstyle guitar I used on the song we played today, Playground House. I decided to use a capo for this tune because the D and F#m chords feel awkward for me. With a capo on fret 2, the chord shapes change to the key of G. This makes fingerstyle loads easier.

Interestingly, it was tricky for me to find a nice Em chord for the pattern. I played the note A over the G chord, which sounded great. So I decided to play it over the Em, even though it's a strange note. And it sounded wicked! If it sounds good, it is good.

As for the chorus, I played the Em as a barre chord, leaving the thinnest string open. I repeated that trick for the D chord and did something similar on the C. That little change made these chords spooky and quirky.

With the picking, I ensured my thumb was consistent and found melody notes that worked. Fingerstyle is about the sound, not patterns or formulae.

For this tune, we decided that two fingerstyle parts were too much. It's tricky to make that work. So I played fingerstyle, and Klara played simple chords. It sounds awesome!

Klara's Songwriting Tips

As well as recording herself, Klara learned a lot from working with my guitar player on pre-production. She did a lot of demos at home before recording in a fancy studio. Klara highly recommends collaborating with other musicians, whether drummers or bass players and taking ideas from them. I agree! There is a fine line between great and terrible, and playing with someone else helps us decide if our work is the real deal or not.

📝 Songwriting doesn't have to be a mystery. We break it all down in my Songwriting Course!

lessons.title: Sofa Showcase: Davy Denke
lessons.summary: The first guest on Justin's Sofa Showcase is Davy Denke, a young singer-songwriter with a fine voice and solid songs.
lessons.text:
Jamming with Davy Denke

I met Davy Denke through YouTube, and he has helped me with my channel over the years. Together we played his tune Leaving; then we discussed some questions he had about Songwriting!

🎧 Listen to Davy Denke on Spotify! :)

Songwriting Tips – Lead Lines & More!

After jamming, we chatted about songwriting tips. Davy asked me how he could make his song more complex and extend it. For percussion, I advised him to use a looper pedal. By strumming muted strings, you can add hits over the basic tune.

Another option is to play around with the chords. When exploring lead lines for this song, I found nice triad shapes that created a lovely movement between the chords. You can also pick out notes that work well over all the chords, repeating those over the sequence and playing with the rhythm. The song is in G Major, so you can also deliberately use the G Major scale to make solos and lead lines! :)

Songwriters: Use Your Ears!

To end, I added that songwriters often use their brains and eyes instead of their ears. Lots of the stuff I've played on records has been a happy accident – I hit a note or find a line without thinking! Always keep your ears open – they beat all else. If it sounds good, it is good! :)

I hope our jamming inspires you – he started from scratch with me and is a fine example of where you can take your musicianship!

📝 Songwriting doesn't have to be a mystery. Unveil it with my Songwriting Course!

lessons.text:
10 Party Singalong Songs You Should Know!

Picture this: you're at a gathering, and someone hands you a guitar saying, "Hey, you play guitar, let's have a sing-along." You might be wondering, "What am I going to play?" Well, I've got your back! Based on my own experiences and some trial and error, I've come up with a list of songs that will get everyone singing along.

Song #10: The Joker - Steve Miller Band

First up is The Joker by Steve Miller Band. A popular sing-along, this tune can be played with really basic chords and simple strumming.

👉 The Joker Guitar Lesson

Song #09: Sweet Caroline - Neil Diamond

This one is super popular with the ladies for a sing-along, and it's a really fun one to play. It's a song that grows with you as a guitar player. You can start with simple chords and gradually add more elements as you get comfortable.

👉 Sweet Caroline Guitar Lesson

Song #08: Let It Be - The Beatles

No top 10 list would be complete without a Beatles song. Let It Be is a fantastic song to play, and everyone loves singing along to this one. You can play with simple chords, but if you want to learn the little riff at the beginning, you'll shine even brighter!

👉 Let It Be Guitar Lesson

Song #07: Margaritaville - Jimmy Buffett

Margaritaville by Jimmy Buffett is a must for any American party. This one's less well-known outside the United States, but it's a real gem. The chords are super simple, and you can even add in some riffs if you're feeling brave.

👉 Margaritaville Guitar Lesson

Song #06: Wish You Were Here - Pink Floyd

Wish You Were Here by Pink Floyd is a classic. The verses and the choruses have the same chord progression all the way through, so it's easy to pick up. Everyone loves singing along to this one.

👉 Wish You Were Here Guitar Lesson

Song #05: Baby One More Time - Britney Spears

This is one of those surprise party favorites. It's a really simple chord progression, and you'd be amazed how many people know the lyrics to this song.

👉 Baby One More Time Guitar Lesson

Song #04: Free Fallin' - Tom Petty

This one uses pretty much the same chord progression for the whole song. A key tip when you're playing on your own in a party situation is to keep things more mellow for the verses and bring it up for the chorus. That way, when it's quiet, people will be able to sing along and look at their phones to get the lyrics out for the verse.

👉 Free Fallin' Guitar Lesson

Song #03: Brown Eyed Girl - Van Morrison

This is the tune, right? Everybody wants to sing along with this one because they don't have to know the words. They can just hum along. It's also a grower. You can learn it bit by bit.

👉 Brown Eyed Girl Guitar Lesson

Song #02: Wonderwall - Oasis

Today's gonna be the day! Wonderwall is another classic tune for a singalong. It's a song with a simple chord progression that everyone loves.

👉 Wonderwall Guitar Lesson

Song #01: Take Me Home, Country Roads - John Denver

I really feel like this is the most popular song you can play if you want people to sing along. Everybody knows this song; everyone relates to it. It's just a great song with really simple chords.

👉 Take Me Home, Country Roads Guitar Lesson

Ready to Start Strumming?

That's it, folks! Ten fantastic party sing-along songs that'll make you the life of the party. So, why not grab your guitar and get the party started? Remember, it's not just about playing the right chords; it's about setting the mood and getting everyone to join the fun. Make it your own, and most importantly, enjoy the music!

If you're interested in learning more, hop over to the individual lessons, where I go into more detail about each song. I'll break down the chord progressions, share specific tips for each song, and even show you how to add your own flair to these classic tunes. Let's get strumming!

lessons.title: Neil Young Song Lessons: My Favorites :)
lessons.summary: Neil Young is one of my favorite artists, so I have plenty of song tutorials on his stuff! Here are my favorites - and my 9-year student Trent rocking 'Old Man.'
lessons.text:
This Saturday, November 12, 2022, is Neil Young's Birthday!

Neil Young is one of my favorite artists of all time. I remember getting hooked in 2003 when I saw his Greendale concert in London. Incredible.

I love teaching his songs because I enjoy covering them, and Neil Young's style is unique. It doesn't matter if you're new to guitar or a more experienced guitar player - there's always a new thing to learn from his tunes.

Neil Young Songs on Guitar - Beginner to Advanced

Next, you will find a list of my favorite Neil Young songs to learn by guitar level - from early beginners until brave advanced guitar players! But hey - I have loads more Neil Young tutorials for you, so don't miss out on the full list! :)

🎵 Beginner Grade 1 Song: Helpless

This song is a great example of Neil Young tunes requiring simple chords. Beginners wrapping up my Grade 1 course can have a go at it, as we won't need any barre chords. For that tutorial, we will also explore the capo positions to expand the possibilities for key changes so you can sing along too! :)

🎵 Beginner Grade 2 Song: Cortez the Killer (Simplified Version)

Neil Young originally plays this classic in Double Drop D, but it works great as an easy beginner song with just Em, D, and Am. :) Even if you're still working on Grade 1, you can nail Cortez the Killer if you dig it!

Intermediate guitar players can check out the tutorial teaching how to play Cortez the Killer like the original recording.

🎵 Beginner Grade 3 Song: Heart of Gold

Heart of Gold is one of Neil Young's most popular songs, and it's not too tricky. Guitar players graduating from my Beginner Course can play it just right!

And this is also a great opportunity to explore the harmonica - get yourself a G Major harmonica (Neil uses Marine Band) and experiment!

🎵 Intermediate Grade 4 Song: Rockin' in the Free World

Rockin' in the Free World is such a classic song but tricky to sing - Pearl Jam has an awesome version of it! Eddie Vedder nailed it, as always.

My lesson explains acoustic and electric guitar parts, so enjoy it!

🎵 Intermediate Grade 5 Song: Out On The Weekend

This Neil Young song is deceptively difficult to play. What a tricky rhythm! But Intermediate players getting into barre chords and alternate chord grips will benefit greatly from it.

Get ready to practice your hammer-ons and flick-offs too. Loads to work on here!

🎵 Intermediate Grade 6 Song: Harvest Moon

We'll need to get to Drop D tuning to play this beautiful ballad. It sounds lovely on the acoustic guitar - and it's a great reunion of many Neil Young tricks. :)

On the original recording, there's a little riff with 12/12 seven harmonics all the way through. That's tricky, but mindful listening will help you overcome this challenge!

➕ Want more? Explore all my 26 Neil Young song tutorials - and get verified tabs, chords, and lyrics to learn faster! :)

Student Highlight: Trent playing Old Man

Come on - it feels so good to watch my student Trent, only 9 years old, playing Old Man on the guitar. He learned it from my song tutorial! :)

Despite his young age, Trent has been into guitar and the ukulele since he was 6. He had the attitude of asking his teacher for Ukulele lessons, and... it's paying off, isn't it? :)

Trent also had a lot of influence and guidance from his father, Thomas. He's been learning with JustinGuitar since 2016!

Music is powerful; seeing young kids get into it is so cool. :) I always appreciate it when I get to know talented young musicians out there, and I'm glad I can contribute a little bit to their development!

Share an Audio-Video of YOU Playing!

I learned Trent's story because Thomas, his daddy, posted his video on the JustinGuitar Community. Over there, we have a special place where you all can share your music and guitar progress and even ask for some feedback if you want to! :)

I'm talking about our ever-popular AVOYP area, where you can share your progress with others in a super safe space. :) It takes just these 3 easy steps:

- Create a new topic with the title of the song or project you are posting. - Paste the link to your recording. - Ta-dah! Be proud of yourself. You made it! :)

👌 Up for it? Join the JustinGuitar Community, record yourself, and post your video! :)

lessons.title: Easy & Advanced Christmas Songs to Play on Guitar
lessons.summary: Spread the Holidays joy playing Xmas classics on your acoustic guitar.
lessons.text:
Learn Christmas Songs on the Guitar!

It might only be November, but it's time to get ready and learn some Christmas classics on the guitar! Let's spread the holiday joy with music, and show off all the hard work you've been putting into your play. :)

The holiday season is great for generosity, laughter, and festivities. Playing music with your loved ones will make it all extra special!

It doesn't matter if you're a beginner or more advanced guitar player or playing acoustic or electric guitar. You will likely find a Christmas song tutorial that works for you!

But ensure you start practicing your Christmas songs on time! Depending on your choices, you should start practicing right now.

🚨 Popular Christmas songs might seem easy to play on guitar. However, the most popular ones are quite tricky, especially if you want to explore fingerstyle arrangements for them!

You need time, consistency, and patience to learn to play Christmas songs on the guitar - just like any other song! If you want to sing along while playing, check out my tips on how to sing and play guitar at the same time. So, don't fret - I've got you covered. :) Here are the Christmas song lessons I recommend you explore!

5 Easy Christmas Songs on Guitar

🎄 Song #1 - Last Christmas

George Micheal is an incredible artist. This Christmas classic is so fun to sing along with - and it's so popular! You'll probably be hearing it everywhere during the Holiday season. :) Even if you're only a Grade 1 Beginner Guitar Player, you'll be able to play this tune!

You only need four chords to play Last Christmas. This song lesson keeps it all very simple, so even if you're new to guitar, you still have a chance to prepare for a solid Holiday performance!

🎄 Song #2 - Jingle Bells

You can play Jingle Bell on the guitar in loads of different ways. The chords are simple, so the melody! Most beginners should be able to nail it. But there is an F Chord in there, which you can replace with one of these F Chord Cheats if you still need to work on your full barre chord! ;)

Explore the free tutorial, and have some joy with this classic! Laughter is a fantastic thing to bring festive cheers. :)

🎄 Song #3 - Santa Claus is Coming to Town

There are many versions of this song - the original chords are complicated. But my song tutorial shows you a simple version using only open chords - which is great for beginner guitar players!

If you're up for a challenge, or a more advanced player, take advantage of the version we learn towards the end of the lesson. That arrangement gives more of a jazz tune, and it's loads of fun to play!

🎄 Song #4 - We Wish You A Merry Christmas

I've got two lessons for this Christmas classic! I recommend beginners start with the strumming option linked above: it uses easy chords (except for an F chord!) and a simple rhythm.

If you've completed Grade 2, give a go at this fingerstyle arrangement of We Wish You A Merry Christmas. It might be a bit tricky, but there's a free tab available to help you out - and you've got weeks ahead to practice! ;)

🎄Song #5 - Mull of Kintyre

Is this song the most important Paul McCartney Christmas classic? I'm not sure… but this song became the number-one hit in Britain when he released it! It pays tribute to the Kintyre peninsula in Scotland, where McCartney owns a High Park Farm.

It's a relatively easy tune to play, as it doesn't require many chords. Students from my Beginner Guitar Course should be able to play this song right in our Grade 2 - even before if they're feeling adventurous. :)

5 Intermediate & Advanced Christmas Songs on Guitar

🎄 Song #1 - Blue Christmas

Elvis was so incredible - and Blue Christmas is a fun song to cover, especially if you're up for some dramatic interpretation. :)

This song uses simple chords, but it does have barre chords, so ensure you're hip with those! This Elvis classic has a typical chord progression for Country music, so have a go at improvising if you're up for that!

🎄 Song #2 - All I Want For Christmas

Mariah Carey, our holiday season wouldn't be complete without this classic! :) This song is a crowd-pleaser, but you'll need a few advanced techniques to play it properly.

This song is perfect for more advanced guitar players, requiring a few barre chords and a diminished chord. In this lesson, we'll learn a few different ways to play the chords so you can pick which feels best for you!

🎄 Song #3 - Driving Home For Christmas

This Chris Rae tune is a great way to entertain your friends and family - a great one to play around the Christmas tree. :)

It has a lovely melody, and it's not too difficult - but it does require barre chords - no escape exit here. This tune is excellent practice for Grade 5+ guitar players.

🎄 Song #4 - Merry Christmas, Baby

An awesome live version of this song inspired me in this lesson! It's an incredible 12 Bar Blues in G and great practice for more advanced guitar players.

You'll learn different ways to play it. You can keep it simple or add some embellishments depending on your guitar skills! Start learning it early so you can develop embellishments. ;)

🎄Song #5 - Happy Christmas (War is Over)

John Lennon and Yoko are responsible for this all-time Christmas classic - a meaningful tune. It's a symbol of hope, especially during dark periods…

This song requires Barre chords, sus chords, and other cool chord extensions! It might be a tricky one to nail, but again! You have a few weeks ahead, and my free tutorial is easy to follow. :)

Learn More!

Explore my Songs page; you will find over 700 free song tutorials to play year-round, including loads more options for Christmas! And if you're really serious about learning them, remember you'll find verified tabs, chords, and lyrics that fit my tutorial with JustinGuitarTabs. :)

Go Further with My Christmas Songbook!

If you'd like to go further, check out the JustinGuitar Christmas songbook! It features 21 seasonal classics specially arranged for guitar, and I organized the songs into 4 groups:

🤭 Play on The Day: the easiest songs - not much preparation required! 👌 Learn In December: these songs are a bit harder, so start learning them earlier in the month. 😅 Learn in November: these are more difficult, demanding chords and a few quirks to practice. 💙 Chord Melody Arrangements in Tabs: these are for more advanced players who want to tackle fingerstyle guitar!

With its unique structure & timeline, you'll know when to start practicing before your holiday performance. It includes everything you need: chords, tabs, and lyrics, so your friends & family can sing along while you play!

🎄 Buy a hands-on edition of the JustinGuitar Christmas Songbook!

lessons.title: 8 Halloween Songs to Play on the Guitar
lessons.summary: Play these songs on your guitar at any Halloween party and have loads of fun!
lessons.text:
Grab Your Guitar & Let's Get Spooky! 🎃

Halloween - is a time to celebrate, dress up, and play fun songs. :) October 31 is coming up - what better way to celebrate than with a fun Halloween Playlist? Get your friends and family into the Halloween spirit by teaching them your guitar!

Here's my personalized playlist of song lessons that would fit that Halloween theme. These songs are mostly metal and rock to bring out the hardcore essence of Halloween. Learn them on time for the 31st and celebrate spookily!

Learn to play them, or listen to them through my Halloween Playlist on Spotify. And who knows, if you dig these songs - they might end up on your playlist all year long!

Halloween Fun Fact!

🤯 Did you know? Halloween is an event that dates back over 2000 years. The ancient Celts had a tradition of building fires and wearing costumes to repel ghosts on the 31st of October. Pretty cool that it stuck through all these years!

8 Halloween Songs to Play on the Guitar

A lesson is available for each of these Halloween songs. They're organized by difficulty. Whether you're a beginner guitar player or more advanced, there's something in there for every guitar level. :)

Song #1 - Bad Moon Rising - Creedence Clearwater Revival

You'll learn the beginner version of Bad Moon Rising in the lesson. This version is awesome if you're a Grade 1 guitar player. You'll need your capo at the 5th fret - so make sure you have one!

You'll discover how to play it in its most basic form. As you gain confidence and improve your guitar journey, you can revisit it to add some SUS chords, strumming patterns, and accent patterns! So it's fun, even if you're more advanced in your guitar journey.

Song #2 - Time Warp - The Rocky Horror Show

Time Warp is perhaps my absolute favorite classic - and the most iconic song from The Rocky Horror Picture Show. If you've somehow never seen this movie, it's a must-see! This is a great tune for Grade 3+ beginner guitar players - and it'll get the people dancing!

Song #3 - Don't Fear The Reaper by Blue Oyster Club

I love this song - it's so easy to play & it has a great ring. This will sound even better if you have someone to play the cowbell for you! An excellent rock riff to get stuck in. This tune is great practice for Grade 3+ beginner guitar players.

Song #4 - Fade to Black by Metallica

Fade to Black is how I first understood the usage of the major scale. I was in my early teens, and I was a big Metallica fan! It was an instrumental song, central to developing my connection to music theory. In this lesson, perfect for Grade 3+ guitar players, we look at both of James Hetfield's guitar parts.

Song #5 - Sweet Leaf by Black Sabbath

Sweet Leaf is an intricate, experimental, layered song, as you can expect from a group like Black Sabbath.

For this particular lesson, I kept it as simple as possible. You'll explore some of the verses, and any novice Grade 3+ guitar player new to power chords can still play the riffs!

Song #6 - Hells Bells By AC/DC

An all-time rock classic here - loads of fun to play and some exciting parts here.

You can play it individually, or even better, have a guitar mate join you! Great groove and some fun, flashy Angus stuff. This one is suited for Grade 4+ guitar players.

Song #7 - Enter Sandman by Metallica

Yup - another Metallica song - I can't help it. Metallica songs are so great to learn on the guitar - and they're all a bit spooky. The full song is suited for Grade 4+ guitar players. It's a blast to play on guitar! Some tasty stuff to add as you learn to play, but enough for intermediate players to enjoy it as well!

Song #8 - Seek and Destroy by Metallica

Seek and destroy is a three-series lesson - so you'll be sure to have all the details you need to play this metal song! Seek And Destroy is a terrific song from Metallica's first album, Kill them All. It remains my all-time favorite of their records. Very raw and worth a listen! Lots of cool riffs in there for Grade 5+ guitar players.

Halloween Song Just For Fun!

No lessons for these tunes - but they're too fun not to include! These will be great tunes to blast while receiving trick-or-treaters or carving out your pumpkins. :) Give them a listen and get into the Halloween spirit!

Mr.Crowley by Ozzy Osbourne

Thriller by Micheal Jackson

This Is Halloween by Danny Elfman

Monster Mash by Boris Karloff

Tubular Bells by Mike Oldfield

Abracadabra by Steve Miller Band

Werewolves of London by Warren Zevon

Want to go further? Grab my Lessons & Songs app and play along with the songs you love!

lessons.title: JustinGuitar's Top 10 Blues Albums
lessons.summary: Getting into the blues? Here's my Top 10 Blues Albums list. Classic stuff to feed your ears!
lessons.text:
I wish someone had given me this list when I got into Blues.

And that's why I'm writing it here for you. :) My Top 10 Blues Albums is perfect if you want to know some great Blues music and guitar players. But, obviously, I probably didn't include your favorites. Also, feel free to drop your suggestions in the comments below. These are only my personal opinion, and I can't wait to know yours!

I always get asked about my favorites, and with so much music around, I think having a list of great albums to check out can be helpful. I hope you enjoy these fine recordings as much as I do! By the end of this post, there's a cool playlist you can listen to - and some guitar lesson recommendations too.

Now let's see the list.

1. B.B. King - Live At The Regal

Live At The Regal is a live album by B.B. King from 1965. It's undoubtedly one of the fines Blues albums ever recorded, and it's incredible on every level. I don't know anyone who doesn't like this album, but I know many awesome players who mentioned this record as a great influence: John Mayer and Mark Knopfler are just two of them!

BBs playing is right on it, and the audience interaction is a window to the world at a very different time. Powerful. I don't have any song lessons - yet! - on tracks from this album, but you can listen to it on Spotify.

2. Stevie Ray Vaughan - Texas Flood

Steve Ray Vaughan was an incredible guitar player, one of the greatest to grace our planet, and influenced many. He released Texas Flood in 1983, featuring some of the finest Texas Blues you'll ever hear. From the raw power of Pride And Joy to the subtle jazz fringes in Lenny, this is one of the all-time great Blues albums.

3. Blues Breakers with Eric Clapton

This John Mayall album featuring Eric Clapton was released in 1966. It blew my mind when I first heard it. Clapton is full of energy, and the band's power is incredible - you can feel it. The album features incredible lead solos and a brilliant cover of Freddie King's song Hideaway.

This album is also known as The Beano because Clapton is reading a British children's comic of the same name on its album cover. :)

4. Albert King - Born Under A Bad Sign

Albert King's unique style is full of incredible string-bending techniques. He played his guitar upside down with the thin string at the top - string bending is a bit easier this way, pulling down. He's worth exploring! King was a huge influence; most later, blues players copied his licks. I have a full course exploring Albert King Style on guitar!

5. Robert Johnson - Complete Recordings (1936-37)

Robert Johnson sold his soul to the devil at the crossroads and started a legend, and his playing has been even more influential. He is the Blues, and though all his recordings are a bit scratchy (it was a while back), his genius still shines through. Essential listening!

6. Freddie King - Let's Hide Away and Dance Away

Freddie King is one of the great 3 Kings - with Albert and BB. He was a Texas Blues pioneer and hugely influenced young Steve Ray Vaughan. Let's Hide Away and Dance Away album is all instrumental and features great writing and incredible playing. It was released back in 1961.

7. T-Bone Walker - The Original Source

I love T-Bone's playing. As well as being a brilliant player, he was one of the first showmen who played behind his head. He did the splits and rocked the house! The Original Source track box set spans his incredible career - it's mandatory.

8. Jimi Hendrix - Are You Experienced

I always wonder if Jimi should be Blues or Rock - he's both. Even though there are no 12 Bar forms on the Are You Experienced album, it's certainly Blues-based and hugely influenced many blues guitar players. Well, all guitar players, I guess. :) It's a must!

9. Robben Ford - Talk To Your Daughter

This album is slightly different from the others on this list, with slick production (maybe overdone.) Still, Robben is an incredible player and tears it up on this album. With one foot in traditional Blues and the other in Jazz Be-Bop, he makes a unique and brilliant blend!

10. Howlin Wolf - His Best

The guitar player for Howlin Wolf (vocals and harmonica) is a fellow called Hubert Sumlin, who's one of the finest blues guitar players of all time. You'll hear plenty of his great work on the Chess 50th anniversary collection.

Top 10 Blues Guitar Spotify Playlist

What are your thoughts about my Top 10 Blues guitar albums? :) You can also check out this Spotify playlist I put together for you! Awesome songs to listen to - featuring some from those albums and some from other incredible Blues artists too!

Want to Play the Blues?

My Blues Guitar Studies is the best place to develop your Blues in a very practical way, and I have a great list of awesome Blues songs for beginner guitar players too. There are so many songs you can play after you've learned a Blues piece :) If you're unsure how to get started, learn this 12 Bar Blues Progression for beginners and play the Blues today.
