lessons.title: JUSTIN Ear Training Exercises (S9)
lessons.text:
The key to learning music well is to use your ears. Don't forget that music is about sound and listening so this part of your guitar study will help you a lot more than you will realise initially.

REMEMBER to stop the vid right after the chord you are trying to identify because...

The Last Thing You Hear, Stays In Your Ear!

Take it slow and don't expect results too quickly, it will take some time develop your listening skills.

Chord Quality Recognition (CQR)

It's going to get a little tricky now, because we are going to include sus chords in this exercise. You will need to play these chords a lot on your own and really try to listen deeply. When you have listened a lot, they will become very obvious because they have a very distinct sound!

Sound Pallete: Major or Minor, 7, Maj7 and also Power Chords (5th) and Sus chords.

Single Sound Recognition (SSR)

This exercise is also going to be tricky because we are including ALL chords we have covered so far in this so you have quite a few choices. Think of this as a little test. Can you do it?

Chord Pallette: Every chord we have covered in this beginners course! including slash chords and sus chords!

Chord Progression Recognition (CPR)

Now the progressions are a little longer: can you work them out? These are based on real songs. All I have done is remove the strumming patterns which are best studied separately. Good luck!

1. |__________|__________|__________|__________| 2. |__________|__________|__________|__________| 3. |__________|__________|__________|__________|

You'll find the answers here :) but no cheating.

lessons.title: Consolidation Test & Practice
lessons.text:
Well done! You made it to the end, well, almost...

Now it's time to consolidate all you have learnt, so you are ready to go on with the next course, and get into the intermediate stage. So, use the chart to make sure that you feel confident with all the stuff we've covered in this course.

It is MUCH better to get really good at these things and be able to use them well to play some songs, than playing more advanced stuff badly. Really it is. Ask anyone that has to listen to you!

When you discover things that you don't know, make a list out of them and work out a practice schedule that gives each problem area a five- minute practice slot and then work on it until they are fixed. Then choose some more things to work on, until, eventually, you are on top of this whole list.

Good luck, take care and I really hope you have enjoyed the course. I look forward to helping you learn lots more cool stuff in the years to come.

Justin.

Chords

You should instantly know ALL of the following chords and know any fingering variations for each that you can use, depending on the situation:

The Basic Eight Shapes: A, D, E, G, C, Am, Em, Dm.

The Dominant Shapes: A7, D7, E7, G7, C7, B7.

The Sus Shapes: Asus2, Asus4, Dsus2, Dsus4, Esus4.

F Chord and variations: F, Fmaj7.

Basic Slash Chords: D/F#, G/B, C/G.

You should be able to change between any two chords at a speed of 60 changes per minute (one change per second).

You should also be able to locate and play any power chord on either the fifth or sixth string and be able to play them without the open strings ringing out.

You should be familiar with some chord variations (for A and G and others) and know when you might use them.

Rhythms

You should be able to play RUST strumming patterns 1, 2, 4, 8, 9 and 16 confidently and fluently at a range of different tempi while tapping your foot.

You should also be able to play basic fingerstyle and be able to make to make up your own patterns.

Scales

You should know the minor pentatonic scale and be able to play it with one note per click with the metronome set at 120 beats per minute, using all down-picks, all up-picks and also alternate picking.

Improvising

You should be starting to experiment with using the minor pentatonic to improvise. Don't expect too much at this stage; just be able to play about and make up something easy over a blues.

Theory

You should understand and be able to use the following concepts:

The note names of the open strings.

Tones, semitones and the note circle.

Sharps and flats.

The names of all the notes in the first five frets of the guitar

The principal elements of rhythm

All the note names on the thickest two strings.

How to use a capo.

Songs

You should be able to play at least ten songs all the way through without stopping. This might seem a lot, but it should be possible now with all the hard work you have done. The strumming should be solid too and you should be able to play in time with a metronome!

Would be great if the songs could incorporate most of the concepts covered in the course, so some suggestions that would make a great first repertoire...

Three Little Birds (great song, very easy, uses A, D and E)

Knockin' On Heavens Door (very easy again, uses G, C, D and Am)

Killing Me Softly (lots of nice easy chords)

Everybody Hurts (easy fingerstyle)

Pink Bullets (use of bass note strumming)

Fly Away (easy use of Power Chords)

Fast Car (medium fingerstyle and strumming)

Basket Case (medium use of Power Chords)

Have You Ever Seen The Rain (Use of slash chords)

Before You Accuse Me (12 Bar Blues Style in A)

I wish you many years of guitar playing fun and hope you enjoy the rest of the material on the site :)

Where to next???

The Intermediate Method :)

modules.label: Module 0
modules.title: Before You Begin: Guitar Basics
modules.intro:
Welcome to the JustinGuitar Beginner Course!

Our first module gets you ready for a successful guitar journey. :)

In the following lessons, we will learn basic skills you'll forever need as a guitar player! If you get those things down, you'll build up your abilities without the bad habits that are so common for many beginners. A few things might not make sense immediately, but trust me and the process. It'll all come together at some point!

What You'll Learn

In this first module, we'll learn how to (really) hold the guitar and the best way to position your fingers on the fretboard. We'll compare the many guitar picks and the best option for beginners!

Then, you'll learn how to hold your guitar pick! We'll get into strumming with your fingers, too, but I recommend you take some time to learn how to play with a guitar pick. That might be important at some point, and starting early is better.

💡 Don’t rush through the lessons! Make sure you always get a lesson down before moving to the next one unless I say otherwise. :)

To prepare for our first songs, we'll learn how to read chord boxes! You'll need that to play your first chords at the beginning of our next module, and then you can crack on playing real music.

Build a Strong Foundation!

These lessons work just like private guitar classes. If you stick with the course, you'll get as far as you want as a guitarist! Whether you want to play campfire songs, perform in live concerts, or write your music, the foundation we're building in these first lessons will be useful later in your journey. Take it easy, be proud of your accomplishments, and have fun!

You can skip the first lesson if you know how to tune your guitar, but ensure you tune your instrument before each practice session. You must get used to the right sound of the notes.

👉 Ready? Let's go and learn how to tune your guitar!

lessons.title: How To Tune A Guitar For Beginners
lessons.summary: Don't start playing if you don’t know how to tune your guitar! Get used to the right sound! :)
lessons.videoChapters: 00:00 Lesson's intro 00:18 What is the best guitar tuner? 01:45 How to use a guitar tuner? 04:28 How to tune your guitar after restringing 05:16 How to mute the strings for an accurate tuning 06:20 Retune your guitar twice!
lessons.text:
You should never play with an out-of-tune guitar! Never.

The first thing you need to do before playing is to get your instrument in tune! I recommend tuning your guitar before each practice session so you get used to the right notes. We don’t want to get into the wrong stuff, right? ;)

Tuning your guitar is easier than you think! Later in our journey, we’ll explore how to do it by ear - a great skill to develop! Right now, as a beginner, we’ll learn how to tune a guitar by using a clip-on tuner or an app. If you need help putting on a new set of strings, check out my Guitar Maintenance lessons.

How to Use a Guitar Tuner

Tuners work better if the guitar is almost in tune! If you just changed your strings, you may need to use your ear a little bit. The goal is to get closer to the note so that the tuner can do its job!

Be also aware that you may have to tune your guitar twice because sometimes the neck can move back and forth. That might change the tension of the strings, which is not a problem – just go back and do some fine-tuning.

You may struggle to pick individual strings well enough to get an accurate tuning, and that’s normal when we’re learning! Here’s my trick to help you get an accurate tuning in your guitar:

Use your thumb instead of a pick! Strum a string with your thumb, and then rest your finger on the string below.

Tuning the guitar is not hard - and I’m sure you can do it!

The Best Tuner for Beginners

There are a few different ways you can tune your guitar. You can use a stand-alone tuner or use the tuner inside my app on your phone. The clip-on tuner is usually accurate and the best one for beginners. They are relatively cheap, easy, and quick to use. If you’d rather use a guitar tuner app, be careful not to use one that’s not accurate!

Here are my favorite clip-on tuners for beginners:

The TC Electronic PolyTune Clip is more expensive than other tuners but much more accurate. It has excellent battery life. It’s small and easy to use. It also shows you the tuning of all strings at once.

The Snark Tuner is excellent for beginners. The downside is that it’s a bit too big. Well, it’s good enough for the price. It does the job!

The D’Addario Micro Tuner is fantastic if you want to leave it on your guitar all the time. Accurate and easy to use - reasonable price too!

🎸 Tuning an electric guitar? If you’re using an app, you’ll have to amplify it so it works well. You won’t have to plug an electric guitar if you’re using a clip-on tuner! ;)

If you prefer to use an app, check out the free tuner built into my Lessons & Songs app! That one is great for beginners, and I kept it free for everyone - even if you don’t learn with my app. :)

Ok - so is your guitar in tune? Let’s learn how to hold your guitar correctly.

lessons.title: How To Hold Your Guitar
lessons.summary: There's a right way of holding your guitar! Make sure you start off on the right foot.
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Where do you hold a guitar?

02:25 Tip: Watch out your wrist!

02:59 Tip: Guitar posture matters!
lessons.text:
Learning how to hold your guitar may seem an obvious thing, but it’s not.

There’s a right way of holding your instrument, and as a beginner, you must ensure you don’t fall into any bad habits from the get-go. In this lesson, we’ll learn the proper way of holding your guitar to improve your playing. Now let’s get stuck in!

Step-by-Step: Holding a Guitar

The following steps will teach you how to hold a guitar from a right-hander’s perspective. If you’re left-handed, do the opposite.

Step 1 - Rest the guitar on your right leg.

I recommend you sit the acoustic or electric guitar on your right leg. Resting the guitar on your left leg is more like a classical approach. It can bring some benefits, but not for most beginners.

Step 2 - Use your right arm to stabilize the guitar.

If you’re playing an acoustic guitar, you should have your arm resting on top of it. If you have an electric guitar, your arm will come slightly over the top of it. Let it rest on the front of the instrument.

🚨 Extra Tip! You don’t want the weight of your whole arm on your shoulder while you’re playing. Get comfortable and make sure your strumming arm feels relaxed. Strumming is a bit tricky, and these small details will help you out in the future. ;)

Step 3 - Make sure your fretting hand isn’t holding up the guitar.

Your fretting hand must be there to press the strings! Make sure your guitar is stable without using your fretting hand. You should be able to move your hand up and down the neck quickly!

Step 4 - Don’t lean the guitar back towards you.

Leaning the guitar towards you is a natural movement for beginners, but it’s a bad habit. When you do this, you work harder to bring your wrist around the neck. It causes unnecessary tension in your hand, which you should avoid at all costs.

Step 5 - Be aware of your posture.

Finally, try not to lean your body over too much. When you’re playing, the natural tendency is to hunch over to check out what your hands are doing. It can happen sometimes, but be aware of it and make an effort to stay as upright as possible while playing.

Alright - now I’m confident you know what’s the best way of holding a guitar! I promise you: your whole guitar journey has just got easier - and free of any back pain!

In the following lesson, we’ll learn a trick to help you minimize finger pain. Let’s go!

lessons.title: Positive Finger Placement
lessons.summary: Want to avoid finger pain when playing guitar? Don't skip this lesson.
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 How to avoid finger pain when learning guitar?

01:13 How hard do you need to press on guitar strings?

02:55 Where do I place my fingers on a guitar?
lessons.text:
Howdy - believe it or not, there’s a right place to press the strings on the guitar fretboard.

I call it Positive Finger Placement. If you pay attention to it, you’ll be able to play chords way more easily, with minimal effort, making your guitar journey less painful. :) As you’ll need to apply less pressure to play chords, you’ll minimize your finger pain and sound better too.

Of course, all beginners will get sore fingers at some point - Nitsuj did - it’s part of the process! But learning how to make the best sound with a small effort will make your guitar sessions way more comfortable. So, before we even learn any chords, we’ll learn exactly how to place your fretting fingers on the strings!

Placing Your Fingers on the Fretboard

You must place your finger in a proper position on the fretboard! When pressing a string, get your finger as close to the fret as possible without actually touching it. Like this, you won’t have to press down too hard to produce a good sound.

Want to try it out? Here’s a simple test for you!

Choose any string to play. Place your first finger as close to the fret as possible, and pick that string. How much pressure do you need to get a good-sounding note? You should not have to press very hard at all if your finger is right next to the fret!

Now, move your finger to the back of the fret. Place it nearest the nut, away from your body but within the fret. Do you see how much pressure it requires to get that same note to sound good? Don’t let the finger sneak over the fret, though, or you’ll mute the sound.

Try this exercise in other frets and strings. Make sure you experience the difference between how much pressure you need to apply when pressing the string. A good-sounding note depends on where you place your finger! Do you understand now why do you need to use Positive Finger Placement? ;)

Next, we’ll learn all about reading chord diagrams!

lessons.title: How To Read Guitar Chord Boxes
lessons.summary: Guitar chord boxes are visual tools that show you how to play a chord. Let’s break it all down!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Read a chord chart - The vertical lines

00:45 Read a chord chart - The horizontal lines

01:23 Read a chord chart - The dots

02:21 Read a chord chart - Which strings to play
lessons.text:
Learning to read chord boxes - or chord diagrams - is essential to any guitar player!

A chord box shows you how to play a chord. Before you can imagine, you’ll use chord box diagrams to play your favorite songs. Fun, eh? :)

Let’s take a look at the image below. It’ll help you get familiar with the symbols we use in a chord box diagram.

What do the lines mean?

The vertical lines in the diagram represent the six strings.

The line on the furthest left is the thickest string.

The two lines at the top of the box represent the nut.

The rest of the horizontal lines represent the frets.

What do the dots mean?

The dots represent the strings you should place your fingers on, and the numbers inside the dots show which finger to use.

Number 1 is the index finger.

Number 2 is the middle finger.

Number 3 is the ring finger.

Number 4 is your pinky.

Numbering the Strings

We usually use numbers to refer to the strings as well. For example, you might hear the 3rd string rather than the third thinnest string in my guitar lessons. Some people prefer to name the string by pitch, but that can be tricky later in our Beginner Guitar Course. My preference is to stick with calling them Strings 1 - 6! So, you must memorize that:

The thinnest string is string 1.

The thickest is string 6.

Which Strings to Play?

When reading a chord box diagram, observe that some strings have an X and others have an O above them. That tells you if you should or should not play a string! You should memorize that:

The O stands for open. It means that you play an open string – with no fingers holding it down.

The X means that you should not play that string at all.

You’ll always play the strings that have fingers on them.

🚨 Piano Fingering vs. Guitar Fingering - If you’ve played the piano, make sure you don’t get confused! Piano finger numbering is entirely different from guitar finger numbering. Guitar players generally don’t use their thumbs to fret a string.

Guitar Tabs vs. Chord Diagrams

We use tablatures - or tabs - to writing music for guitar, while chord diagrams only tell us how to play a chord. We’ll learn more about tablatures later on in our course. For now - no need to worry about it!

🚨 Chord Diagrams for Left-Handed Players - I recommend that left-handed guitar players get used to reading right-handed chord boxes. Unfortunately, most available resources only present the information in one way – usually right-handed. That said, if you do find a left-handed chord box, be aware that the thinnest string is on the left. It’s a mirror image of the right-hand diagram!

Next - we’ll explore a tricky topic for beginners: guitar picks.

lessons.title: How To Hold A Guitar Pick
lessons.summary: The right pick matters! Let's choose the best one for you and learn how to hold it.
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Should beginner guitar players use a pick?

00:31 What is the best guitar pick for beginners?

02:09 The best pick for acoustic guitar

03:51 How to hold a guitar pick
lessons.text:
You don’t have to use a guitar pick, but I recommend you do. :)

Using a guitar pick may be challenging at first, but I guarantee: it’ll help you out in the long run. In this lesson, we’ll learn how to hold a guitar pick properly and which one is the best option for beginners!

Later in your journey, you’ll decide if you prefer using a pick or your fingers to strum the guitar. For now, we’ll make friends with the pick - and make sure you have the best one to learn how to strum the guitar.

The Best Guitar Pick for Beginners

You should start your guitar journey with a very thin pick – as thin as you can find! Thinner picks are flexible and don’t get tangled up in the strings. They’re much more forgiving than the thicker ones. The downside is that thin picks are less accurate when it comes to picking out individual notes. But, as a beginner, don’t worry about that. The thinner, the better.

I recommend the Dunlop Nylon .38 as the best thin pick for beginners. A 12-pack is enough for your beginner journey. Unless your sock monster is playing guitar, in which case he’ll steal them all!

📏 Make sure you start with a standard size pick. For most of my life, I used a smaller pick called Dunlop Jazz III. I don’t recommend them for beginners. - they’re too small and way too stiff.

The Best Pick for Picking Individual Notes

I recommend that you also buy a thicker pick - we’ll need them when learning to play riffs - and that will happen soon! The Dunlop Tortex Orange is my to-go - ideal for picking out individual notes!

🚨 Yes, I know I mention Dunlop a lot, but it’s not an endorsement. They make great picks. :)

How to Properly Hold a Guitar Pick

Yep - there’s a right way of holding a guitar pick too! We’ll learn the most common way to hold the pick, but be aware that many amazing guitarists will do it in other ways. Also, keep in mind that this is a starting point, and you can change it later if you find a good reason to do it.

When learning to hold your guitar pick, keep in mind these three things:

Pay attention to your thumb. You want the pick to come out from the side of your thumb, not the tip.

Place your guitar pick well. A centimeter or so of the pick should be coming out from your finger.

Hold your pick as lightly as you can without it falling out of your fingers. The light grip will help keep your arm relaxed.

🚨 Remember: tension is the biggest strumming enemy.

Follow the two steps below to master your pick position:

Step 1 - Place the pick on finger 1. Its point should follow the direction of your finger - the pick should point out the top of it.

Step 2 - Place your thumb on top so that the pick is coming out of the side of your thumb.

💬 Did you give it a try? Let me know in the Discussion section how it was! :)

We’ll revisit this topic many times in our beginner lessons, and we’ll learn many tricks to sound better with a pick. As an Intermediate player, manipulating a pick will be a recurrent skill to develop so that you can play individual notes fast!

Again - you’ll likely feel that using a guitar pick is challenging, and it might be! But don’t give up - learning it now will be beneficial for many things as you advance in your journey.

Next, we’ll learn how to strum the guitar without a pick.

lessons.title: How To Strum Without A Pick
lessons.summary: Learn to strum a guitar without a pick and actually sound good!
lessons.text:
Have you just started your guitar journey?

The best way of learning how to strum is by using a good guitar pick for beginners. But I know you’re curious about strumming with your fingers - and that’s ok too! Strumming with the fingers sounds great - but there are a couple of different ways you can do that, and we’ll explore some of them!

As long as you get the hang of strumming with a pick as well, you’re good to give it a try. Let’s take a look at some tricks to help you out.

Is it better to strum with or without a pick?

There’s no right or wrong here - it depends on your taste. As we’ve learned in our previous lesson, using a pick will help you develop many guitar techniques. Also, when using a pick, most people tend to do it the same way. When you don’t use a guitar pick, you have many options for using your fingers to strum. So, it’s easier to learn the rules when using a pick than when using your fingers.

When strumming without a pick, you can use many fingers simultaneously and explore how much you move them no matter your arm’s movement. That might be a big advantage depending on the song you’re playing. It might also help you explore some dynamics too! We’ll learn more about that later in our course. :)

Without a pick, there are more variety and modifications available to you, and your fingers can add tonal variations to get particular cool sounds.

💡 I tend to do at least 50% of my practice without a pick. Still, I’m pretty comfortable when I have to use one. Set this as your goal. ;)

How to Strum the Guitar With Your Thumb

Strumming with your thumb gives you a rounder sound, and strumming with a pick gives you a brighter sound. Things to keep in mind when learning how to strum the guitar with your thumb:

With the down strums, use the fleshier part of your thumb. On the up strums, your nail may catch the string. That results in a brighter sound that doesn’t always make sense, so be careful not to sound awkward.

Work on getting your thumb’s angle right! You don’t want your thumb to get caught on the thinnest string on the up strums. You can flat your hand out slightly, so you don’t get too much of your nail on the up strums.

Keep your fingers open and strum from your elbow, just like you would when strumming with a pick. You can also anchor your fingers on the guitar and strum using your thumb more independently of the arm.

When playing the guitar with your fingers, there’s no one rule fits all kind of thing. You should explore the possibilities and see what works better for you!

How to Strum the Guitar With Your First Finger

When you strum with your first finger, you generally get a more pleasant sound. Your nail hits the downbeats, and your flesh hits the upbeats. It’s the opposite of strumming with your thumb. Also, be aware that guitarists that strum with their first finger tend to use less arm movement.

If you want the flesh to hit both the up and downbeats, you’ll need to flatten your whole hand. That position will give you a softer and more delicate sound - it might be the one you were looking for!

How to Sound Brighter Without a Pick

But how exactly do you get that brighter sound that you get with a pick without using one? Put your thumb and first finger together as if you’re holding a pick between them! It’s simple - when you strum this way, your nail hits both the up and down strums, mimicking the sound of the pick.

You can also strum from your elbow, just as you would if holding a pick. That’s great for when you drop your pick mid-song, which happens from time to time no matter if you’re a beginner or now!

Explore Your Strumming Options

Whether you’re strumming with your first finger or with your thumb, the key is to experiment. You have to find the right angle and what works best for you. Your fingers shouldn’t get caught on the up strums, and the sound should feel right.

As you get more comfortable with strumming, you can try mixing things up. For example, you can hit the bass note with your thumb and then strum with your first finger.

Play around and explore your guitar - that’s the best way to develop and customize the way you sound. Don’t get too caught up with the right and wrong ways to do this. Always remember – playing the guitar has technical aspects, but it’s a creative adventure. Put your personality all over it!

💙 Enjoying the course? Please help me to keep it free!

Okay - so you have the basics to start playing guitar. In the next module, we’ll learn the A & D chords and play your first song. Yeah!

modules.label: Module 1
modules.title: A & D Chords: Play Your First Song!
modules.intro:
Today's the big day! :)

You'll learn your first guitar chords and start playing your first songs on the guitar!

Let's start your guitar journey by learning the A and the D chords and how to change faster between them when playing a song! A & D are essential guitar chords you'll encounter in many songs, no matter their style.

We'll also learn a few basic skills, and you'll meet the One Minute Changes Exercise - my trademark trick to help you boost your chord changes practice. If you'd like to dig deeper into that exercise, you can try my Beginner Guitar App - it's fantastic to keep track of your progress.

What You'll Learn

Besides getting into the A and the D chords, we'll also learn some fundamentals of rhythm. In addition, you'll get familiar with some basic strumming vocabulary, such as a bar of music and beats. With those lessons, you'll have all the knowledge you need to play your first actual song, and I'm sure that will be pretty fun. You'll probably suffer from finger sores in the early stages of your guitar journey, so we'll check out extra tips to help you handle that!

A full practice routine will be available for you by the end of this module! Don't forget to log in to your account and add it to My Practice Assistant. It'll help you track what you have to practice and for how long so you don't waste time wandering around. ;)

You've Got This!

If you struggle with something in these early days, don't forget: we all struggled. The first few weeks of learning guitar might be tough, especially if you go too hard at it. My advice? Keep your journey fun, forgive your mistakes, and always remember: you're not alone! I'll walk you through all the steps you need. If you encounter some challenges, you can leave your questions in your comments below, and the JustinGuitar team will get you some help in no time. :)

Don't forget you can follow this course along with Nitsuj as well. See how he handles his struggles - it might help you handle yours! It's quite funny, and I'm sure you'll learn loads from him. :)

Now grab your guitar, and let's strum your first chord!

lessons.title: How To Play The D Chord
lessons.summary: The D Chord is the first grip we learn in the Beginner Guitar Course! Are you ready? :)
lessons.text:
Ready to play your first grip? Learn how to play the D chord on guitar.

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, the D chord is the very first chord grip we learn! Why? Well, it's an essential grip for all guitar players, and you'll find it in many songs - no matter the music style you're playing.

You'll be happy to hear it's not too tricky to play; you need fingers 1, 2, and 3 to play it. Here's how to D chord looks on a chord diagram. Take a good look at the chord diagram, and make a mental note of where each finger goes!

Now, grab your guitar, and let's get started! :)

The D Chord in 3 Easy Steps

The D chord uses three fingers, so let's learn how to play it in three easy steps! The best way to learn a new grip is by putting your fingers down in this order. Ready? Here we go!

Place your 1st finger in the 2nd fret on String 3 - it's the 3rd one up from the bottom.

Place your 2nd finger in the 2nd fret on String 1 - the bottom, thinnest string.

Place your 3rd finger in the 3rd fret on String 2.

💡 You might need to stretch your 3rd finger to get it close to the fret. That might be tricky, but don't worry - it gets easier with practice.

We'll check out a few tricks to make it all easier in the following few lessons, but for now, remember to keep your fingers as close to the fret as possible. Using a positive finger placement will help give you a better sound.

How To Strum The D Chord

To play the D chord, we only strum the first four strings starting from the bottom. If you're comfortable reading chord boxes? You'll notice that, in the diagram, the 4th string is marked with an O.

This means we play the string, but there are no fingers on it - it's an open string! Strings 5 and 6 are marked with an X, meaning we don't play those strings. Finally, please give it a strum! Strum down softly on the thinnest four strings with your thumb.

Congratulations! You just played the D Chord. How does it feel? :) Don't worry if it sounds rough; that's normal at this early stage! Now, let's look at how to get that D Chord sounding nice and clear.

D Chord Perfect Practice

Here is a 4-step process to help you solve common beginner problems you might have when learning a new chord:

Step 1: Finger Placement

Place your fingers on the correct strings in the right frets. Use the chord box diagram to guide you if you need it.

Step 2: Strum the Chord

Press down on the strings and strum the chord. If it doesn't sound great, no worries! We'll fix it.

Step 3: Individual Strings

Play the strings one at a time. Each note should ring out true and clear. If they don't, we must find and fix the problem. Follow these steps, and let's find it together!

Start by playing the open 4th string. If it sounds muted, it's probably because your 1st finger is touching it.

Next, check the 3rd string. If it's not ringing clear, ensure your finger is near the fret and that you're pressing hard enough. It might hurt a bit at first. Also, ensure that your 3rd finger isn't touching the 3rd string. The slightest touch will stop the note from ringing out. We all struggle with this, so if you find keeping each finger on its string hard, don't beat yourself up over it. Time and practice will fix this!

Check the 2nd string, which you play with the 3rd finger. The challenge here is getting your finger up close enough to the fret. You'll probably find it harder than you expected. But don't worry! Your fingers are amazingly flexible. You'll soon wonder how you ever found it hard!

Finally, let's try the thinnest string. For many people, the underneath of the 3rd finger often touches the string. To avoid this, play each string with your fingertips.

Step 4: Strum Again

Strum the chord again. Does it sound better? It should! If not, go through the steps again to check your finger position. You'll know when you've got it. The chord should ring out clear and true.

Tips & Tricks

Fingernails: Keep your fingernails trimmed. Long nails make it hard to fret the strings with your fingertips!

Painful Fingers: Your fingers probably hurt, right? Same for me, when I started. For now, don't press too hard on the strings while you're practicing your finger placements. Also, try to practice often for shorter periods rather than less often in long, marathon sessions.

🚨 Time and practice will make your fingertips stronger! Make sure you've seen these tips on how to avoid finger pain.

Thumb Position: Keep your thumb behind the neck, and don't let it rest in the palm of your hand. It'll help build the muscle between your thumb and 1st finger, handy for barre chords. You'll thank me later on your journey! :)

Don't forget: memorizing chords is super important! Visualize it. Sometimes, chords have alternative fingerings - but not the D chord. Some play it differently, like the acoustic legend James Taylor, but I don't recommend you try it (we're not quite there yet!).

Practice Schedule

The best way to practice is with My Practice Assistant. It's free - make sure you've logged in, and you can organize and keep track of your practice schedule through your dashboard. You'll find your first practice routine at the end of this module.

Moving Forward

We'll develop all the skills to play chords as we go along. So don't worry if you have questions right now. We'll explore them shortly! Don't forget that you can get some help at the JustinGuitar Community. I do my best to answer them all - or you'll get help from one of the JustinGuitar official mentors! :)

Ready for the next step? Time to learn how to play the A chord!

lessons.title: How To Play The A Chord
lessons.summary: Here's an easier way of playing the A Chord - an essential grip for any guitar player!
lessons.text:
Learn How To Play The A Chord On Guitar

In the first lesson of our Beginner Guitar Course, we learned how to play the D chord. Now it's time to learn how to put the A chord into action! Pretty exciting, right?

First things first, check out the diagram below - this is what the A Chord looks like:

A Chord Finger Position

To play the A chord, we use fingers 1, 2, and 3 - all in the 2nd fret. Remember the positive finger placement when playing any chord - always keep your fingers as close to the fret as you can. It'll help you get the best sound when strumming the chord. Take a look at how I do it:

Place your fingers on the strings one at a time, in the following order:

1. Place your 1st finger in the 2nd fret on the 3rd string.

2. Place your 2nd finger in the 2nd fret on the 4th string.

3. Place your 3rd finger in the 2nd fret on the 2nd string.

You'll probably find all three fingers in the same fret a bit of a squeeze, but don't worry, it will get easier with practice! As for the strumming, more about that later in this course.

How To Strum The A Chord

Counting from the bottom up, we play only the first five strings. By now, you should know how to read chord boxes. Let's take another look at the A chord diagram below:

Notice how your fingers line up 2-1-3 from top to bottom? The 1st (thinnest) and 5th strings have an O at the top. These are open strings - we play them but don't fret them with our fingers.

Now, go ahead and give the chord a strum. Strum down softly on the five thinnest strings with your thumb. And voilà! Congratulations, you just played an A chord. :)

💡 The 6th string (thickest) comes with an X. It means that we don't play that string at all!

Get Your A Chord Sounding Good!

It can take some time to get the A chord right. Just like everything else, this takes practice and patience! The good news is if you put in the time, you'll jump to it quicker and more effortlessly than you probably think.

When practicing this chord, here are some things to look out for:

● Make sure Finger 3 is not touching the thinnest string.

● Make sure your fingers are pressing hard enough on the strings to sound all the notes out clearly.

● Remember that Finger 1 will have to press a little harder than the other two fingers because it's further from the fret.

● Make sure the neck of the guitar is not resting in the palm of your left hand. You want to position your thumb roughly in the middle at the back of the guitar neck. Try to squeeze the neck between your thumb and your fingers.

● Make sure your forearm is not touching your leg!

Sore Fingers?

You and everyone else! Rest assured if your fingers are hurting at this stage of your guitar journey, it's totally normal. Some tips will help you get through your practice without hurting so much, but you'll have to deal with a certain amount of pain!

Until your fingers toughen up, the soft pads of your fingertips flatten out and touch the strings where they shouldn't. Sometimes no matter how hard you press down, you still won't get a good note. Don't worry about it. You'll need a few more hours of pain to get to where it no longer hurts.

And if your notes sound wonky or unclear, and if you feel like you're never going to get it, that's normal too! Everyone struggles with this stuff. I know I did when I first started! Stick with it - it just takes practice.

Tips And Tricks

Mini Barre: Sometimes, we play the A chord using a mini barre with one finger across all three strings. It's cool, but I strongly recommend that you DON'T use this technique at the early stage of your guitar learning.

The fingering we learn here is much better for positioning, chord changes, and toughening your fingers.

How Does the A Chord Sound?

Use this audio clip to check if A chord sounds good! :)

The Traditional Fingering for the A Chord

The traditional position for the A chord uses Fingers 1, 2, and 3, all in a row, on the second fret. I taught this position for years, but the way I teach now is just way better.

The position I teach now allows you to get two fingers up close to the frets. It's much easier to get a good sound like this! You can change chords faster and more efficiently from this position, especially when using an anchor finger. We'll talk more about anchor fingers in the next lesson.

Easy Songs with Two Chords

If you've learned how to play the D and the A chords, you can already play some fun songs. That's right, all you need is two chords! We'll talk about this later, but if you're up for an extra challenge, check out my song tutorials!

Follow along and learn an anchor trick for faster chord changes!

lessons.title: How To Use Anchor Fingers
lessons.summary: Anchor finger is a simple but effective trick for fast chord changes!
lessons.text:
In this lesson, we’ll learn a little secret to faster chord changes. I call it Anchor Fingers, and it's the detail that will allow you to play your first songs in no time! By using anchor fingers, you get faster to the following chord. Cool, eh?

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, I expect you to know the D and A chords - those are the grips we'll use for this lesson! There are other moments where you'll be able to apply anchor fingers - and these lessons will guide you through all you need to know. :)

Now let's learn that trick!

What's an Anchor Finger?

When you change between two chords and keep a finger on the same fret or string, we call that finger an anchor finger. Anchor fingers make chord changes faster and more efficient!

It's not always possible to 'anchor fingers,' but you should always take advantage of it when you can. It really helps you speed up your guitar playing, and it's the secret to nail playing easy songs even in the very early guitar stages. :)

Now, let's give it a go and see how an anchor finger can help you change from the D to the A Chord.

Fast Changes Between A & D Chords

Here's a step-by-step you can use to change faster between the A and the D Chords! Follow them slowly:

First, place your fingers on the strings to form a D chord. You won’t strum the chord for this exercise, so there’s no need to press down on the strings.

Once your fingers are in position, raise your 2nd and 3rd fingers off the strings. This leaves your 1st finger anchored in the 2nd fret.

Now slide your 1st finger back slightly within the fret, keeping your finger on the string the whole time.

Now, replace your 2nd and 3rd fingers in position to form an A chord. Repeat this process by going back and forth between the D and the A chord.

A Little Reminder :)

Keep your 1st finger touching the string throughout the chord change. Focus on getting your fingers in the right position each time. Over time this exercise will help you build up speed when changing chords. Once you’ve mastered chord changes using an anchor finger, let’s move on to the next lesson and meet the best beginner exercise for learning chord changes!

lessons.title: One Minute Changes Exercise
lessons.summary: This is the best exercise to help you get faster at changing from one chord to another.
lessons.text:
Now it's time to learn a game-changer exercise for beginner guitar players. :) In this lesson, we’ll discover the One Minute Changes Exercise, the best trick I can give you to help you play songs nice and easy! Seriously, this exercise works better than any other method I know for learning to change chords fast. I first started teaching this as a game for kids, but I now teach it to anyone learning guitar - even more advanced players struggling with fast changes!

While the Chord Perfect Practice we've learned in the previous lesson helps you with chord accuracy, the One Minute Changes Exercise is about speed when switching between chords.

So, if the chords sound a bit wonky as you go through this exercise, don’t worry. Our focus here is on getting the fingers into the basic chord shapes fast and on time.

Let's see how!

Exercise for Fast Chord Changes

The idea of One Minute Changes Exercise is simple. Follow this three easy steps:

Step 1

Pick two chords and see how many times you can switch back and forth between them in one minute.

Step 2

Your goal is to reach around 60 chord changes per minute. That’s one per second! It'll take you a few sessions to reach your goal - keep track of your results with My Practice Assistant or download my Beginner APP!

Step 3

Do this exercise every time you put a new chord into your practice routine.

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you'll do the One Minute Changes Exercise with the A and the D chords. Further, we'll revisit this idea and learn how to prioritize items in your practice sessions.

FINGER PAIN? THIS EXERCISE HELPS IT TOO!

There are two common obstacles for any beginner guitar player: finger pain and changing chords fast enough to play a song. The One Minute Changes Exercise helps you get past both of them. If your fingers hurt after this exercise, that’s ok. It means they’re getting tougher! Also, remember you can take a break before moving on with your practice session.

ARE YOU STRUGGLING TO PLAY YOUR FIRST SONG?

Nothing gets in the way of playing a song more than slow chord changes! The good news is that the One Minute Changes will help you with that too. Focus on the chord changes that you find the hardest - or the ones in the songs you want to play!

KEEP TRACK OF YOUR PRACTICE!

The key point in this lesson is to focus on only one chord change during one minute. It's essential to keep track of your practice sessions, so you'll see where you have to put more effort on. There are many ways you can monitor your progress! When I was first learning, I used an old kitchen timer - My Practice Assistant is way better than that. :) It gives you statistics about your progress - a great motivator and practice optimizer! Make sure you’ve logged in to use My Practice Assistant - it's free.

My Beginner Song Course App also has this exercise, and it's very cool and interactive! It's another excellent way to keep track of your progress while you learn to play guitar with actual songs!

If you don't want to use an application to monitor your progress, all you need to have is a countdown timer. I just recommend you take note of the number of changes you're doing, so you know what to do next!

WHEN TO MOVE ON?

It can take you some time until you reach 60 chord changes per minute. It's completely normal - I still remember how much I've struggled with changes using the G chord, for example! Before you move on to the next lesson, try to get up to 30 chord changes per minute between D and A chords.

lessons.title: Bars & Strumming On 1
lessons.summary: Let's learn a simple strumming pattern and get started with rhythm.
lessons.text:
Are you ready to start learning about rhythm? :) If you're following my Beginner Course, this will be your first strumming pattern ever!

Rhythm is challenging for most of us - and I even have a full lesson explaining why strumming is so hard! At the beginning of your guitar journey, you'll probably find that this is as tricky as chord changes - but don't worry. We'll learn slowly to build a solid foundation.

So, before we get started with your very first strumming pattern, let’s define some of the terms we use when talking about rhythm!

WHAT IS A BAR OF MUSIC?

Most songs have a regular and consistent pulse or beat. It's the reason why, when you listen to music, you might begin to tap your foot or nod your head along with the tune. A bar (or a measure) divides musical rhythms into a consistent form. A bar is a specific space of time!

When musicians count out “1, 2, 3, 4” before starting a song, they're counting the beats of a bar!

A time signature specifies how many beats are in a bar. The most common time signature in music is 4:4 - four beats in a bar! You might also see it written as 4/4.

In these early stages of our Beginner Course, we'll play songs with four beats in each bar. Later on, we'll look at other time signatures and understand more about the theory behind them!

THE EASIEST STRUMMING PATTERN EVER

Ok, now we’re ready to give it a go with your first strumming lesson. Remember, the goal is to build a solid foundation. To start with, we'll only strum on the first beat of each bar. Like this, you'll have plenty of time to make your chord changes.

It’s a simple process! Grab your guitar and follow along with the video lesson. Here are some tips:

If you’re playing the same chord in the next bar, make sure you're strumming only on Beat 1. If your chord changes are slow, try lifting your fingers off the strings earlier. It'll give you a bit more time to set up for your next chord!

At this stage, the most important thing is to strum the chord right on the beat. Not before, and not after. Even if you can’t let the chord ring out for as long as you want before making the chord change!

You’ll get better at this as your chord changes speed up. Keep up with your One Minute Changes Exercise, and keep track of your progress. It’ll help with this lesson too!

We'll explore more strumming patterns later in this course. You’ve got enough on your plate right now to keep you busy. :)

TIPS TO HELP YOU PROGRESS FASTER

It takes some time to develop a good sense of rhythm. There are a few tricks that can help you progress faster:

Counting “1, 2, 3, 4” out loud as a song plays helps you get used to feeling the beats!

If you can, tap your foot along with the music. We’ll go into more detail about this in the next lesson.

If you have music experience with another instrument, you may find it helpful to work with a metronome. But if this is all new to you, a metronome is not necessary at this stage.

We’ll get more into the metronome later on in the Beginner Course. For now, congratulations - you’ve completed your first strumming lesson! Next up is how to strum only the correct strings. That's a thing!

lessons.title: How To Strum The Correct Strings
lessons.summary: Strumming only the right chords can be tricky! Learn how to handle it.
lessons.text:
Have you ever tried to play a chord and it sounded awful? Sometimes, that happens because you hit the wrong strings. When you start on guitar, it's normal to struggle to play only the right notes that make up a chord, and this lesson is all about that!

We'll learn about when strumming the wrong string is a problem and how to avoid it! Your goal should be playing only the right strings, but don't worry too much if that's too hard at this stage of your journey. For this lesson, let's use the two chords we’ve learned so far in our Beginner Course: D and A.

How to Strum the D Chord

As you might know, we only play the first four strings when strumming the D Chord. You don't play the thickest two strings and that is not always an easy task! You'll often play them by mistake - but that's not the end of the world!

Even though it’s wrong, playing the 5th string doesn’t sound too different. You might even think it sounds good! Sometimes, you’ll hit the 6th string as well, ending up playing all the strings. It doesn’t sound great, but it’s not terrible. If you mess up and play the wrong string at this stage of your guitar journey, it doesn’t matter that much. It’s normal, and we've all been there.

You should always aim for hitting the right strings and be aware of this issue. Later on in our journey, we'll develop techniques and mechanics that will help you out.

Now let’s look at the A chord.

How to Strum the A Chord

When strumming the A chord, you play only the first five strings. You don’t play the thickest string. Sometimes, you’ll make a mistake and hit the thickest string - an E! Look how interesting this is:

The thinnest string (1st string) is also an E - and it’s part of the A chord. So, the A chord already has an E in it! So, if you play the thickest string by mistake, you’re only adding an E, and there’s already one in the A chord! :) Although it doesn’t sound as good, it still sounds ok.

We won't be getting into a lot of Music Theory in this guitar course, but check out the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course if you want to have a deeper understanding of how music and guitar work!

Practice Routine: Hitting The Right Strings

Playing strings that aren’t part of a chord changes its sound. Sometimes, you'll get away with it. Sometimes, it'll sound awful.

Your ultimate goal is to play only the correct strings, but no need to stress out about it now. At this stage, you have a lot to learn and other priorities. Chord changes and strumming patterns, for example, are already a lot! It’s more important to focus on that and have fun when playing a song, for example.

The time to focus on hitting the right strings is when you’re working on your Chord Perfect Exercise. That is the time to concentrate on playing only the right strings of the chord.

Your goal should be to hit only the right strings, but this won't happen at the early stages of your journey. Like everything else, this gets easier as you play more and get comfortable with your guitar. It’ll all come together with time and practice, so there’s no need to worry about it right now.

Ready to move on to our next lesson? We'll learn 3 awesome tips to avoid finger pain and improve your practice sessions. Let's go!

lessons.title: How To Minimize Finger Pain
lessons.summary: Are your fingers killing you? Here are 3 ways to deal with finger pain!
lessons.text:
If you’re in the early stages of your guitar journey, you're probably handling some level of finger pain. It's normal - I've been there too! Painful fingers are part of the process of learning how to play guitar - especially when you've just started it. Playing guitar hurts - who knew. :) There’s no way to avoid finger pain completely, but here are three things you can do to reduce it.

TIP 1 - PRESS DOWN ON THE STRINGS ONLY WHEN NECESSARY

The first tip to minimize finger pain is to press down on the strings only when you play the chord. When you're practicing the finger placements of a chord, rest your fingers on top of the strings.

When you're working on your Chord Perfect Practice, that’s when you need to press down on the strings.

TIP 2 - POSITIVE FINGER PLACEMENT

The second tip is to play with your fingers as close to the fret as possible. Like that, you’ll get the best sound with the least amount of effort. We've talked about this before! It's what I call positive finger placement.

Positioning your fingers in the right place on the fretboard is essential to minimize finger pain. If your fingers are far away from the fret, you’ll need to press down harder on the strings to get a full, clear sound.

TIP 3 - PRACTICE IN SHORT SESSIONS, BUT PRACTICE OFTEN

Practice in short sessions, but often. At this stage, an hour-long practice session does more harm than good! Faster, more regular practice sessions don’t hurt as much. They’re also much more useful for the early learning stages!

Start with 20 minutes a day, four days a week. That's the perfect schedule to help build strength and stamina in your fingers without destroying your fingertips. If you're having a bad time organizing your practice sessions, take a look at the Effective Practice module.

Trust the Process!

Part of this process is to grin and keep going. We all go through it. I promise that it gets easier over time and with practice.

Good luck! See you in the next lesson. :)

lessons.title: Super Easy 2 Chord Songs
lessons.summary: Here are 7 awesome songs you can play with only the A and the D chords.
lessons.text:
Looking For EASY 2-chords Songs To Play On Guitar?

Look no further! To start playing songs on guitar, you don’t need to know a whole ton of chords and strumming patterns. If you know only two chords, there are already songs you can play! In this lesson, we'll explore 7 tunes that only use the A and D chords.

💡 More beginner-friendly songs available on the JustinGuitar Lessons & Songs app! The karaoke-style is a super fun way to get your learning songs FASTER. And, it'll help you improve your rhythm. :)

7 Super Easy Guitar Songs

1. DANCE THE NIGHT AWAY - THE MAVERICKS

If you haven't played your first song yet, Dance the Night Away is a great one to get started! It's easy and fun to play along with. If you find that it's too fast, try slowing it down the first few times.

Dance The Night Away is a great song to grow with as you improve your guitar skills. This song tutorial includes more advanced information - try it when you're ready for more challenges!

2. BORN IN THE U.S.A. - BRUCE SPRINGSTEEN

The chord changes for Born in the USA are slightly slower than in Dance The Night Away, so you might find it a bit easier. But that also means you get less practice with the chord changes.You'll need a capo on the 2nd fret to play Born in the USA. The good news is that you’ll play along with The Boss! I've also got a song tutorial on this tune. Check it out if you want to get fancier.

3. YOU SOUND GOOD TO ME - LUCY HALE

If you dig the style, this modern pop-country track is a great, easy beginner song! You'll need a capo on the 4th fret, so your chords might feel a bit cramped. It’s a tight squeeze up there! Check out this song tutorial for more advanced tips on how to play this song.

4. GIVE PEACE A CHANCE - JOHN LENNON

John Lennon originally played Give Peace a Chance using the D and the A chords. But Lennon tuned his guitar down a semitone, which means it’ll sound weird if you try to play along with the original.

If you're a big fan and want to sound just like the original recording, you'll need to tune your guitar to Eb. When you're ready to grow your playing on this, check out this song tutorial on how to play Give Peace a Chance.

5. FEELIN ALRIGHT - JOE COCKER

The hit Feeling Alright by Joe Cocker is a fun song for beginners! You'll need a capo on the 3rd fret. There are a few piano fancy-pants rhythms, but don't get put off by it. Find the count, and follow along!

6. BLOWIN' SMOKE - KACEY MUSGRAVES

Blowin’ Smoke is a lovely country/pop tune. It's a simple and fun song to play - and you don't need a capo! Learn how to play it with this song tutorial. :)

7. BOYS 'ROUND HERE - BLAKE SHELTON

If you dig songs about trucks, dirt roads, kickin' up dust, and prayers to the man upstairs - this one is for you! :) You don't need a capo to play along with the original record. Have fun!

Spotify Playlist

Here's a Spotify playlist of the songs listed above for you to check out! :) You might discover some new bands to love (or not!).

Play Songs You Love!

Other songs use only the A and the D chords, but you'll have way more options after learning the E chord.

You should practice with songs that you love and that inspire you. It's tricky with only a few chords, but you can explore new music, too. You might find an artist you dig and want to get to know better. Practice sessions are way more fun and productive if you enjoy what you’re studying.

Know any other songs that use only A and D chords? Login to your FREE website account and share in the discussion area!

lessons.title: How To Use Justin's Song App
lessons.summary: My App is the best way of practicing songs and keep yourself accountable when starting your guitar journey!
lessons.text:
I hope you’ve been having a good time following my Beginner Guitar course thus far. :)

Now I’d like to introduce you to my Lessons & Songs App. You don’t have to use it to learn with me, but the App can really accelerate your progress and stop you from falling into some bad habits.

💡 You can get a free trial, so try it for yourself. And even if you don’t subscribe, keep using the tuner - it’s always free! Download your free trial here. :)

The lessons on the website and the App are the same. But, in the App, you get an incredible collection of songs to play along with, like a guitar-a-oke! 🎸

The songs collection is organized to match your beginner journey so you can practice the skills you’ve just learned. For every module of our Beginner Course, I’ll suggest songs you should work on, and you can also choose from over the 600 available tunes! The App will give you a backing track, minus guitar, so you can play along with your favorite music.

How can my App help you?

I’ve been teaching for over 30 years now, and I know it: beginners will always go through the same sticking points. First, it’s finger pain. Then, the chord changes, then the rhythm. :(

Unfortunately, the App won’t really help you with the finger pain. But the App can be a game-changer for your chord changes and rhythm! Let me explain how.

If you only play on your own, you might end up developing the habit of stopping between chords - which is a really, really bad habit. You should NEVER stop the rhythm.

Playing with the App trains your rhythm skills! The backing tracks don’t stop, so it’s like playing with a metronome all the time - but way cooler and way more fun! Have I mentioned that you’ll be able to practice with the songs you LOVE? :)

When your first start, you might struggle to do your chord changes in time. But don’t worry: just stick to the exercises you’re learning (One Minute Chord Changes and Perfect Chord Changes), and you’ll soon be speeding up those transitions. The App will give you the extra push you need to progress faster!

It really works - check out the reviews and feedback we get! The JustinGuitar Songs & Lessons App has helped hundreds of thousands of guitarists lift their game. Let it lift yours as well!

Coming Soon

The App does not link with the website. So, though the courses are the same, the practice you do on one is not logged for the other, and favorite songs and lessons also do not sync. Yet. But we’re working on it.

We’re also working on some simplified super-beginner songs to fit the first grade! We’re listening to your feedback, and we noticed that a complete backing track can sometimes be tricky for beginners. So, we’re bringing back some simplified versions more like what the old App version used to sound like!

In Use

I hope you will love the App and have a pain-free experience! The layout is logical, and it’ll guide you along the path. You can jump around and explore as much as you like, but I would strongly suggest you stick to the proposed route! :) You’ll make the fastest progress and have the most fun that way.

If you hit “LEARN” at the bottom, it will guide you right through the learning path and into the Practice Assistant, which will tell you exactly what to practice and for how long. It will also show you the songs that match up with that module.

Play. And then play more!

You should also use the App for playing additional songs at any time you like! Just hit that song tab at the bottom. You can search for a specific song, check the recommendations, or filter songs by artist, grade artist, and style. We even have some backing tracks for exercises!

When you’re learning a new song, you can slow it down by swiping up and down on the screen! That should help you out a big deal and, as you progress, you’ll be able to speed that playing up. ;)

💡 Don’t forget that the tuner is always free, even if you don’t subscribe. :) You should always tune your guitar before your practice sessions, eh? ;) For more info on using the tuner, please see the video on the tuner screen.

Try the App for Free! See it for yourself. :) Wishing you an incredible guitar journey.

lessons.title: Module 1 Practice Routine
lessons.text:
Welcome To Your First Practice Routine

We've learned many things, and now it's time to set an effective schedule to improve your guitar skills. Consolidating your knowledge is as important as learning new things.

Log in to your JustinGuitar account to make the most of your time and track your progress! My Practice Assistant is a fantastic resource - and it's free to all users. :)

In this lesson, we'll set your first practice routine with everything we've learned so far. Focusing on the right skills at the right time will make you improve faster. Using My Practice Assistant will keep you accountable and motivated!

💡 Use the pre-made practice routine for Module 1 by clicking on the 'Practice' Tab under the video. Save the routine, then access the items in your Dashboard.

20-MINUTE BEGINNER GUITAR PRACTICE SESSION

Yes, you read it right! Only 20 minutes per day will make you improve faster. Short sessions help with focus and regular practice help build your muscle memory.

At this point of your guitar journey, some level of sore things is normal. If that's your case, short but regular sessions will help you better than long ones! If you're struggling with painful fingeIt'scheck out these 3 tips to avoid finger pain.

If you've been following the Beginner Course, you should know how to play D and A, move faster between chords, and a simple strumming pattern. It's a lot to practice! The secret is to have fun, and that's why we'll dedicate a timeslot to practice songs you like.

Here's what I suggest as your first practice routine:

1' Technique - Tune Your Guitar 3' Technique- Chord Perfect Practice D Chord 3' Technique- Chord Perfect Practice A Chord 2' Technique - Anchor Finger A & D Chords 1' Technique - One Minute Changes A to D 1' Technique - One Minute Changes D to A 10' Repertoire - 2 Chord Songs

HOW TO CREATE A PRACTICE ROUTINE

If this is your first time using My Practice Assistant, you need to create a routine to add the practice items. Don't forget there are a timer, statistics counter, and metronome to help you out.

Everything you need is there! Awesome, eh? Learn how to use My Practice Assistant with me. :)

WHEN TO MOVE ON?

So now, the big question is: Are you ready to move on to the next module? :) Well, here's how you'll know:

● You've memorized both the A and D chords.

● You can make at least 30 chord changes in one minute.

● You had a go at playing a song.

Ready? Let's go!
