lessons.title: Module 2 Practice Routine
lessons.summary: In this lesson, we check out what I recommend you practice for the next week or two.
lessons.text:
Congrats! You made it to our second guitar module.

Now it's time to set an effective practice schedule to improve your guitar skills. For this stage, we'll have a 20-minute practice session. This plan will cover everything we've learned in Module 2!

Here are some guitar practice tips to remember:

I recommend committing to 4 practice sessions a week

Don't over-practice - it can lead to finger pain

Make sure to have a light touch with your fingers when practicing chord changes - don't press the strings too hard, and aim for the correct finger placement

Use the right pick - thinner picks are more suitable for beginners

Don't forget about tapping your foot - this is really helpful!

💡 Make things easy and use the pre-made practice routine for Module 2. Click on the 'Practice' Tab under the video, save the routine, and access the items in your Dashboard.

My Practice Assistant

The best way to practice the guitar is to use My Practice Assistant, which is available for free to all users! My Practice Assistant is a fantastic tool to keep you accountable and motivated. :)

Make sure you log in to your JustinGuitar account to make the most of your time and track your progress. Once logged in, go to your dashboard. The link is on the top right of your screen - you can access it here. Select the Practice tab, and off you go! Of course, you can edit your routine as you wish. :)

20-Minute Practice Breakdown

Here is my recommendation for a typical 20-minute practice session at this stage:

-' Technique - Tune Your Guitar 2' Technique- Chord Perfect Practice E Chord 1' Technique- Chord Perfect Practice D Chord 1' Technique- Chord Perfect Practice A Chord 2' Technique - Anchor Finger E, A & D Chords 1' Technique - One Minute Changes A to D 1' Technique - One Minute Changes A to E 1' Technique - One Minute Changes D to E 1' Riff - Peter Gunn Theme 10' Repertoire - Songs for Module 2

YOU'LL BE READY TO MOVE ON WHEN...

You memorized the E chord - as well as A and D chords, of course! :)

You are comfortable using an anchor finger for these chord changes

You can get around 30 chord changes in one minute between all chords learned so far

You had some fun with the Peter Gunn Theme

You had a go at playing a song (or two) using all three chords.

Now good luck and see you soon!

modules.label: Module 3
modules.title: Capo, Minor Chords & Up Strums
modules.intro:
What are minor chords? When should you strum up?

You have so many questions, don't you?

But I hope your fingers aren't hurting too bad! If you've just started with your guitar lessons and your fingers are sore, don't worry - it's part of the process. The finger pain should start to lessen in the next few weeks! You'll forget all about it with the news ahead. :)

Module 3 of my Beginner Guitar Course is one of my favorites! Here, we'll learn about minor chords - some say they sound pretty sad. We won't be getting too deep into theory, but check out the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course if you're into it.

Let's take a look at what else is on today's menu.

What You'll Learn

We'll start by learning to play Am and Em and get a taste of the theory behind minor chords. We'll then get into up strums and backbeats! By the end of this module, you'll know when you should strum up and when you should strum down on the guitar.

💡Understanding up strums is a light-bulb moment! Make the most out of it. :)

Module 3 also answers all your capo questions! We'll dig into that weird guitar accessory and understand exactly when you should use a guitar capo. You'll also get why they're not only for beginners. ;)

And then, a super reward: we'll learn how to play the classic riff Seven Nation Army by The White Stripes. You can play it using only one finger, and it's a fantastic beginner guitar exercise!

Excited? You should be!

By the end of these lessons, you'll be comfortable playing the 5 essential open chords. That's big! But before we get started, here are a few reminders. :)

Accuracy Over Speed

With all these new techniques to learn, I know it's tempting to rush over things as fast as possible! Learning guitar is hard; it requires practice and patience, and everyone learns at a different rate! Take your time and focus on perfecting the skills you struggle to play. It'll make you a much better guitarist later on! :)

💡 Make sure you set up a balanced practice routine if you haven't already. Use My Practice Assistant for free and stay focused on the essential.

Playing Guitar is Awesome!

Keep your guitar journey as enjoyable as possible. Don't worry if you can't do things straight away - don't be too hard on yourself, and enjoy the process.

Focus, but let loose. You should feel comfortable and relaxed when you're with your guitar. The more pleasure you get from your practice sessions, the more likely you'll stick with learning guitar. And I promise: playing guitar is awesome! So at the end of your sessions, you should feel good.

I'm here to guide you throughout this guitar journey, but you're doing the work! Be proud of everything you've learned so far.

I'm proud of you. :)

Ready for the next step? Let's learn some Minor Chords. I can't wait to hear if you find minor chords sound sad!

lessons.title: What Are Minor Chords
lessons.summary: Do minor chords sound sad? This is actually a decent definition, but here, we delve a bit deeper into what makes a chord minor.
lessons.text:
I'm sure you heard about Minor Chords before - but what exactly are they? Some people will say Minor Chords sound sad - do they?

In this lesson, we'll learn all about Minor Chords on guitar. If you're following our Beginner Guitar Course, you'll soon get to know how to play the Am Chord and the Em Chord. But before we get strumming, let's look at some essential takeaways on Minor guitar chords. :)

What Are Minor Chords

You might think we're playing 6 notes when we're playing a chord, especially when we're strumming all six strings, but that's not true. A Major chord only contains 3 notes - the 1st, 3rd, and 5th notes of a Major scale. To get a minor chord, we simply flat the middle note (the 3rd) by a semitone (or one fret.) So, there's only one note difference between Major and Minor chords. Learn about the music theory behind chords and notes here!

Sometimes, changing a Major chord into a Minor chord on guitar is as easy as lifting off a finger. It's the case of the E chord. Other times, you'll have to use alternative fingerings when going from a Major to a Minor chord.

How Are Minor Chords Written

We write minor chords in a specific way. Let's take the A chord as an example. You'll see it written as a Minor chord as either: A Minor, Amin, or Am. Unless otherwise specified, they mean the same thing. If there's no other indication and you just see an A, it's the Major chord grip.

How to Figure Out Chords by Ear

You can most of the time recognize their different sounds - especially if you play a Major chord followed by a Minor chord. Many will say that Major chords sound happy, while minor chords sound sad - and that's not far from the truth! Giving chords a personality will help you recognize them. I recommend you listen to them a couple of times and try to incorporate their feeling.

Sometimes, it's tricky to hear the difference between the Major and Minor chords, especially if you're just starting your guitar journey. The good news is that you can train your ear, and I help you do that on this Ear Training course! Learning to distinguish chords and figure out songs by ear is powerful in many senses. Give it a try. ;)

Now, let's move on to the next lesson and learn how to play the Em chord.

lessons.title: The E Minor Chord
lessons.summary: The Em Chord is an easy one, but there's a very common beginner mistake you should avoid!
lessons.text:
The E Minor Chord is one of the easiest chords you'll learn - most beginner guitar players have no problem with it at all. But there are some tricks to make it even easier and prep you to play many other minor chords on the guitar!

For now, you should have a good idea about what minor chords are, so now let's get strumming and check out how we play the Em Chord and how it sounds. :)

How To Play The E Minor Chord

It's time to lift off one finger! Follow this 3-step guide below to play the Em Chord on guitar:

Start with positioning yourself for playing the E Major Chord. You should already be familiar with it! :)

Lift your 1st finger (index) off of the 3rd string, and strum your guitar. To play the Em chord, you should strum all the strings.

You've just played the E Minor chord! Do you hear the difference between the E Minor and the E Major chords?

Use the chord diagram below as a reference for your finger placement for the E Minor chord:

Here's how the Em Chord looks like when I'm playing it:

Em Chord: Mistakes to Avoid!

I know I said that the E Minor chord is super easy and straightforward to play, but it's essential not to mute the 3rd string with your 3rd finger. If your 3rd finger touches the 3rd string, it won't sound like you're playing the minor chord but the regular E chord.

To avoid this mistake, make sure you know how to position your fingers on the guitar fretboard. The correct finger placement on the string will make your life way easier. :)

How Does E Minor Sound Like?

If you're wondering how the E minor chord should sound like, play this audio example as a guide. It should sound just like it! :)

Alternative Guitar Fingering

To start with, you should get a good sound Em Chord using your 2nd and 3rd fingers. With practice, make them your go-to fingers for the E minor chord. Don't forget to take the time to include this chord on your 1-Minute Changes Exercise routine - even if you feel it's an easy grip!

Once you're confident with the chord changes using regular fingering, you can experiment with alternative fingers as well. You can do this with the 1st and 2nd fingers or the 3rd and 4th fingers. Here are some images showing this alternative guitar fingering for the E Minor chord:

As you practice, you'll find out which fingering is most comfortable for you! It'll depend on the chords you play before and after the E Minor chord. Change your fingering based on the song you're playing on the guitar.

That sums up how to play the E minor chord on the guitar. Next lesson, we’ll explore how to play the A Minor chord! :)

lessons.title: The A Minor Chord
lessons.summary: Why is A Minor Chord so familiar? Find out now - and learn how to take the best out of it!
lessons.text:
So, it's time to learn one more minor chord grip. :) The A Minor Chord is a popular one, and you'll find it in many songs.

If you already learned how to play the E Major chord in my Beginner Course, this lesson will be a breeze! :) You'll find some similarities between them. Let's check it out!

How to Play the Am Chord

The A Minor chord uses the exact chord grip as the E Major chord. Take a look at the guitar chord box below:

Follow the 3-step guide below to play the Am chord:

Place your 1st finger (index) in the 1st fret on String 2 - it’s the 2nd string up from the bottom.

Place your 2nd finger in the 2nd fret on String 4

Place your 3rd finger in the 2nd fret on String 3.

Here's how the A Minor chord will look like on the guitar:

How to Practice the Am Chord

When you're learning how to play the Am chord on the guitar, play each string individually to make sure you're getting a clear sound. Remember to position your fingers correctly to get a good sound with the least amount of pressure - that'll avoid finger pain too!

Be careful not to mute the thinnest string! If it doesn't sound good, check if your 1st finger is not muting it by accident. When your strum the Am chord, you should avoid playing the thickest string.

Here's how the Am chord should sound like on guitar:

Common Chord Change With A Minor

A very common chord change is to go from A minor to E major chord. You'll find this transition in many popular songs, so practicing it is super helpful for your guitar journey!

Here's an easy way to change between Am and E on the guitar:

First, move all your fingers from the A minor chord down a string. As a reference, use your 1st finger to get your other fingers placed. Make sure your 1st finger (index) is on the 2nd string. Try going back and forth between the two chords. It should feel (almost) effortless. :)

And there you have it! Now you should know how to play two minor grips: Am and Em. Up next, a much-needed reminder on how to hold your guitar! :)

lessons.title: Holding the Guitar
lessons.summary: Learn how to hold your guitar properly and avoid developing bad and hard-to-break habits down the line.
lessons.text:
In this lesson, we'll review the correct way you should be holding your guitar. Often, beginners hold their guitar neck up with their fretting hands. You don't want to get into this habit! You must pay attention to how you’re holding and gripping your guitar.

So, grab your instrument, get comfortable, and let's get started! :)

Get Your Guitar In Position!

Follow this simple 4-step process to get your guitar in position:

Using your strumming arm, anchor your guitar in a place where it feels comfortable.

Rest your guitar on your leg with the cutaway.

Stabilize your guitar and keep the neck in place - your guitar shouldn't be wobbling!

If needed, take your time to adjust yourself until your guitar is stable.

You should feel minimal pressure from your arm. Here are some key things to keep in mind:

Don't hold the guitar with your fretting hand - never! Your fretting hand will be already busy with all the chord grips and changes, so no need to give it one more challenge! :)

Your guitar should be stable - whether your fretting hand is on the guitar or not. Again, the fretting hand doesn't hold the guitar.

Rest your guitar on your leg with the cutaway.

You want the grip of your skin on the guitar itself. Any pressure should come from here.

Remember, it's essential you feel relaxed and loose. That is one of the main things that will help your strumming feel and sound good!

Still unsure how to hold to your guitar? Check out this step-by-step lesson and some other mistakes to avoid when holding your instrument.

Types Of Guitar

All guitars have similar guitar anatomy, but their shape might vary. Some guitars can be neck-heavy or body-heavy. Their design can cause the neck of the guitar to either droop down or shoot straight up.

These shapes can be tricky for beginners. If you're already using these types of guitars - don't worry! Having good posture will make it work. Use my tips and adjust your position until it feels right.

If you're using Flying V guitars, invest in a good strap! Their funky shapes are also not ideal for practice. Other types of electric guitars are more suitable for beginners.

So, what's the best guitar for beginners? Check out my detailed recommendations and tips on how to choose the right guitar for you!

lessons.title: Counting Ands
lessons.summary: When should you strum up on the guitar? The answer is here!
lessons.text:
When it comes to strumming and keeping time, counting the beats is essential. To play rhythm guitar, you must learn how to count (and feel!) the beats and the off-beats - which we call 'ands.' That is key to playing a solid rhythm guitar.

In this lesson, we'll learn all about the 'ands' and explore how you should practice counting the beats! :)

Counting the Beats: What is an 'And'?

So far, you should already be familiar with strumming down on the beat and counting the four-beat bar. Like this:

1 2 3 4 D D D D

When you play consecutive down strums on the beat, your strumming hand naturally moves up on the off-beat. So, the 'ands' happen between each down-strum. Generally speaking, each beat gets a down strum, and the off-beat gets an up strum.

We usually write the 'ands' as a little + between the beats. We don't call it plus or cross - we always say 'and.' Take a look:

1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + D U D U D U D U

Later on, we'll explore how to play these up-strums. For now, let's focus on counting them!

How To Practice Counting The Beats

First, focus on saying the count of "one and two and three and four and" out loud. Get used to saying it with an even rhythm. Keep repeating it to get it stuck in your brain. Trust me - it'll be worth it later! :)

While you're saying the counts out loud, start moving your strumming arm up and down with the beat. The down-strum happens on the beat - and the up-strums movement happens on every 'and.’ Try this without actually holding your guitar. Keep your strumming hand moving evenly, even when it's not playing anything!

Once you feel confident with this strumming movement, the next step is to tap your foot on the beat - and keep counting out loud! If you need a refresher on how to tap your foot for guitar playing, check out this lesson.

The goal is to ingrain the rhythm within you. Practice counting the beats out loud over and over again - sometimes there's no way around it. You'll have to trust me on this one - I wouldn't lead you astray! :)

lessons.title: All About Up Strums
lessons.summary: All you need to know about up strums so you build a solid strumming foundation.
lessons.text:
You’ve mastered the down-strum. Now, it’s time for its partner in crime - the up-strum. It’s simple enough but still takes some practice to get comfortable with them.

Some people will say that strumming up is harder than strumming down - but I disagree. Down strokes are just different - don't be afraid of exploring them!

First Things First!

You should know by now that up strums happen on the "and" counts. If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, we covered counting ands in the previous lesson.

If you're not sure what I'm talking about, click here and learn how to count the upbeats. :)

Beginners, Thin Picks Are Your Friends

Before we get started, I recommend getting a skinny tiny pick. That will make a big difference. In this lesson, I’m using this 0.38mm pick, which is ideal for beginners.

🚨 Avoid thicker picks when you're learning how to strum the guitar - they can make strumming very difficult!

In the future, you'll find that a thicker pick might sound better. However, it requires a much softer play, which can be tricky for beginner guitarists. For now, the thinner the pick, the better! :)

How to Count Up Strums

Up Strums happen in between each down strum. When counting your strumming pattern, you’ll play upstrokes during "and" counts. Use the image below as a guide. Here, the up strum is the U and the and.

How To Strum Upwards

First, let's focus on your strumming hand. Strum your guitar on muted strings. Hit all the strings on your way down, then all strings on your way up. Keep your hand steady, and move your strumming hand to the beat. During the up strum, you’ll want to pull slightly away from your guitar.

Typically, you won’t play all the string on the up strums. You'll want to pull away from the thickest strings. While you strum upwards, play the thinnest 3 or 4 strings. That will give a better sound and groove than it does when you hit all the strings. You should be able to hear the difference! ;)

How To Practice With The Metronome

To practice, you'll want to make sure your four down-strums stay even. A metronome will help you do this. Don't have one yet? Use my very own free online metronome! :)

Set your metronome somewhere in the range of 60-100bpm. I recommend setting it at 80bpm. Your up-strums should fall right between the metronome clicks.

You might prefer playing at a slower tempo (60bpm) or a faster tempo (100bpm). Start with whichever tempo is easiest for you, then work your way toward whichever is hardest.

Eventually, you want to be able to practice your up strum at any range - slow or fast! That will prepare you to play strumming patterns at any speed.

And there you have it, the art of the up strums! Next lesson, we'll cover strumming patterns with ups. :)

lessons.title: Strumming Patterns With Ups
lessons.summary: It’s time to practice your up strums! Here are a few different rhythm patterns for you to work on.
lessons.text:
Strumming patterns with up strums are some of those guitar skills that take repetition to master! On the surface, it doesn't seem like it'd be that tricky. But it's normal to find these strumming techniques difficult!

Think of it this way - strumming should be so continuous, it becomes automatic - and the only way to get there is through repetition. If you struggle with strumming, make sure you add extra time to include this lesson in your practice routine.

Let me show you two very easy strumming patterns to practice with up strums! We'll explore some strumming mechanics to get this right. The essential thing to remember here is to keep moving your strumming hand! :)

EASY GUITAR PATTERN #1

For our first pattern, we're going to play an up strum after beat 2. Wrap around your finger for a muted guitar neck - this will help you focus only on the strum patterns. Remember to keep your strumming hand moving - even if you make a mistake! Use this visual below as a guide. Here, the up strum is the 'U' and happens once in the pattern.

1+2+3+4+ D DUD D

Before you move on to the following strumming pattern, make sure you're feeling confident with this first one.

Ready? Let's go!

EASY GUITAR PATTERN #2

For this second pattern, you'll add two up strums in the guitar pattern. Here, the up strum happens after Beat 2 and Beat 3:

1+2+3+4+ D DUDUD

This pattern is the precursor of the most common guitar pattern of all time - the old faithful. We'll explore this later on! For now, repeat this pattern until it feels automatic. I promise - this will set you up for success later on.

How To Practice New Strumming Patterns

When focusing on a strumming pattern, I recommend doing exactly that – focus only on the strum pattern! Don't worry about fretting any chords or switching between yet.

When you practice, count the beat by counting ands. Remember that the up strum isn't going to strum all the strings, and it should happen on the 'and' count.

Always pick a tempo that feels comfortable for you. You want your arm to feel nice, steady, and reliable. If you choose a tempo that's too slow or too fast, you'll likely run into some problems.

My Advice About Strumming

I want to remind you to relax. Make sure you keep your strumming arm as relaxed as possible. Do your best, but take breaks as often as you need to. Practice takes time - no need to rush things!

At these early stages, be forgiving with yourself and don't think too hard! If you want to learn a little more about rhythm and guitar, check out why strumming is so hard!

lessons.title: All About Capos
lessons.summary: Are they just for beginners? How can I use a capo? What's the best capo available?
lessons.text:
At this point in your guitar journey, you might be asking if you need a capo. Is a capo necessary? Actually... what even is a capo?

First, let's get something out of the way – capos are not just for beginners! :)

Some players seem to think they’re made only for beginners - but that's not true. They're a useful tool even for more advanced players. Neil Young uses a capo all the time, and he's a great guitarist. One of my favorite ones!

In this guitar lesson, I'll tell you all about the theory behind capos. You'll learn awesome tricks to expand your guitar possibilities. :)

WHAT IS A GUITAR CAPO

A capo is a super handy device that you clamp along your guitar's fretboard. It allows you to use the same chord shapes to play songs in different keys. It comes in handy to play barre chords, playing tricky songs, and changing the key of a song.

Capo pronunciation changes depending on what part of the world you live in. I say it cap-o; others say kay-po. But who cares? Not me! Whichever way you say it, people will know what you're talking about.

WHAT'S THE BEST TYPE OF CAPO FOR GUITAR

Different types of capos exist, but they'll all pretty much get their job done. What's important is that your capo puts the right amount of pressure on your guitar strings. Too little pressure won't serve the capo's primary purpose. Too much pressure can stretch your strings, knocking them out of tune.

The Kyser capo is a common one. It's got a nice big handle which makes it easy to place and move. For some people, it can get in the way of their fretting hand. If that's the case, opt for a smaller capo, like the G7th capo.

The G7th Capo is a touch more expensive and smaller than the Kyser capo, but it doesn't have a handle on it. Either way, a good capo should last you a solid 20-30 years - as long as you don't lose it!

HOW TO PLACE A CAPO ON THE GUITAR

Like when you place your fingers along the fretboard, you want to clamp your capo as close to the fret as possible. You want your capo placement right before the metal bar - and never directly on top.

Right behind the fret is the correct placement of the capo. If it's too far away from the fret, you'll get a lot of buzzing. The sound won't be uniform and sharp across all the strings - it won't sound pretty!

Why And When You Should Use A Guitar Capo

There are many reasons why you should use a capo. First, using a capo allows you to play complicated chords. You’ll play the same chord sounds - but simpler chord shapes.

You might want to use a capo to simplify some songs that would otherwise use barre chords. A capo is an excellent option for many tunes - such as Walk of Life by Dire Straits.

Capos are also great to play along with original recordings - which is so much fun to do! If you use my Beginner Song App, you'll have loads of play-along song options to practice with your capo!

If you like to sing along with your guitar, capos are great for changing the key of the song to suit your voice. You'll have to move the capo and adjust the placement until it feels right with your singing. This process will be more of a trial and error. Where you place the capo will depend on the tone of your voice.

If a female singer wants to sing something by a male singer, she might opt to move the key up. Using the capo will allow her to hit the lowest notes in the song — vice versa for male singers, who might need to move the key down.

As you can see, there are loads of reasons why you should consider using a capo. I hope I opened your mind about this awesome device! Give it a try - you won’t regret it :)

Next, we'll learn how to play Seven Nation Army by The White Stripes - an awesome riff for beginners!

lessons.title: Seven Nation Army
lessons.summary: Have fun with this easy riff for beginners! You only need to use one finger. :)
lessons.text:
White Stripes' "Seven Nation Army" Riff Is Awesome For Beginner Guitarists!

And a great one to get your fingers moving. :)

Seven Nation Army by The White Stripes is a super popular song! Everyone seems to know it, and that catchy and recognizable riff can quickly get stuck in your head. In this super easy beginner riff lesson, we'll learn how to play Seven Nation Army by The White Stripes.

Playing this riff is a great way to improve your finger agility at this stage in your guitar journey. It took Nitsuj some time to get it right! Like most things on our guitar-learning journey, practice is the cure here. :)

IS SEVEN NATION ARMY HARD TO PLAY?

Learning Seven Nation Army with my left hand has been super enlightening! Going through this course with Nitsuj made me realize how tricky this little riff can be. You need only one finger to play it, and the notes are all on one string. But there's quite a bit of coordination involved.

It's normal if you can't play along with the original recording to begin with - don't let that discourage you! It's a great practice riff for beginners, and little improvements will go a long way. You'll also be able to revisit this song as you advance in your guitar playing.

🎸 Intermediate Seven Nation Army Lesson: if you're at Grade 3 or above, head to my Intermediate Seven Nation Army lesson for the power-chord and barre-chord versions of this riff!

HOW TO PLAY THE RIFF IN SEVEN NATION ARMY BY THE WHITE STRIPES

We're going to jump around with the 1st finger on the 5th string quite a lot. There’s a lot of moving up and down the neck. You’ll want to use the little finger of your picking hand as an anchor and rest it on the guitar. That’ll allow you to keep your fingers in the right place.

🚨 Don't worry if you can't play this riff perfectly - Nitsuj struggles too! Practice it loads and try to get the right groove and feel.

Try to avoid picking the other strings when you're playing this riff. To guard against this, touch the 6th string with the tip of your 1st finger to mute it and try to lay the rest of your 1st finger across the remaining strings to mute them, too. If you accidentally hit them, they won't make a sound. :)

THE WHITE STRIPES SEVEN NATION ARMY RIFF: TAB

Follow the Tab below to help you learn this riff. You’ll learn how to read guitar TABs in Module 4, so don't worry if you're not familiar with it. For now, focus on the numbers on the second-bottom line - these are the frets you play with your fretting hand.

💡 Get full tabs, chords, and lyrics for the full Seven Nation Army song and 600+ song lessons! Start your free trial over at JustinGuitarTABS .

Add this lesson to your practice schedule! Join my site for free to use My Practice Assistant and optimize your guitar time. :)

lessons.title: Songs For Module 3
lessons.summary: The best songs to practice the skills you've just learned.
lessons.text:
I know - you're eager to practice guitar songs with the chords and strum patterns you've learned so far!

Good news - There are loads of songs you can play with only the E Minor and A Minor chords. Let me show you some easy guitar songs awesome for practicing at the early stages of your guitar journey! :)

3 EASY SONGS ON GUITAR USING ONLY EM AND AM CHORDS

Here are three easy songs using only the Am & Em chords. Click on the song names to access the specific song lesson, where we'll dive in together about the technical details. These options will be fantastic to work on your strumming mechanics and up strums.

1. Sing – Ed Sheeran. This one's great for switching back and forth between Em and Am chords. Keep the rhythm simple here. Pick one of the strum patterns with up-strums you've learned in this module, and play from there!

2. Moves Like Jagger – Maroon 5. A bit faster and groovier than "Sing." This song is fun to play along with. Note that the original song uses Bm and Em, which we'll explore later. You can use a Capo and play either Am and Dm with Capo at fret 2 or Em and Am with Capo at fret 7.

3. I Belong to You – Lenny Kravitz. If "Moves Like Jagger" is a bit much for you, take it slow with this iconic Lenny Kravitz tune. This song has a much slower tempo than the others. It'll give you some freedom when it comes to experimenting with your strum patterns. Yep, it's still just using Em and Am chords!

MORE AWESOME GUITAR SONGS FOR MODULE 3

So far, if you've been following my Beginner Guitar Course, we've learned the chords A, D, E, Em, and Am chords. It's worth practicing with one or two of these chords as well. Here are easy song lessons with these different chord combinations that might also interest you. :)

1. Use Me – Bill Withers. A little different from the others, Use Me switches between E minor and A Major rather than A Minor. This one is a funky song!

2. Kinky Afro - Happy Mondays. Another A and Em all the way kind of tune! It's a great play-along song for beginners. :) Play this song along with my guitar Lessons & Song app.

3. Call Out My Name - The Weeknd. A classic pop hit with Em and Am chords - all the way. This one is in 6:8 time - it might be tricky for some. I'll walk you through it in the video lesson :)

4. Cortez The Killer - Neil Young. Cortez the Killer is one of my all-time favorite songs. To play it, you'll use the Am, D, and Em - so it's an excellent way to practice a 3-chord song!

SPOTIFY PLAYLIST

Not familiar with these songs? Give them a listen on this Spotify playlist - you might find one you really dig & want to learn that on guitar! Enjoy. :)

REMEMBER, PLAY THE SONGS YOU LOVE!

Not into these songs? Don't worry - What's important is to play the music you love and find inspiring! At these early stages, play songs that motivate your guitar playing. It will encourage you to practice more often. You'll be more inspired to get it right if you like what you're hearing!

Of course, you should explore new music too. You never know what you'll discover. You might find a song in a different music genre that you is lots of fun to play :)

If you're feeling inspired, check out my Beginner Song APP. It has loads of play-along options. Try it out for free. :)

lessons.title: Module 3 Practice Routine
lessons.summary: Get a 20-minute practice session for Module 3!
lessons.text:
Congrats - you made it to our third module together! :) At this stage, your finger pain should start to lessen, so you should begin to really enjoy playing! Now it's time to set an effective practice schedule to improve the guitar skills you’ve learned. For this stage, we'll have a 20-minute practice session. This plan will cover everything we've learned in Module 3!

Here are some guitar practice tips to remember

I recommend committing to 4 practice sessions a week.

Don't over-practice - it can lead to finger pain.

Keep your strumming arm nice and relaxed.

Don't forget about counting the beats out loud. :)

Use the right pick - thinner picks are more suitable for beginners.

💡 Click on the 'Practice' Tab under the video, and save the pre-made routine for Module 3. You can edit and access the practice items in your Dashboard.

MY PRACTICE ASSISTANT

The best way to practice the guitar is to use My Practice Assistant, which is available to all users! My Practice Assistant is a fantastic tool to keep you accountable and motivated. :)

Make sure you log in to your JustinGuitar account to make the most of your time and track your progress. Once logged in, go to your dashboard. Select the Practice tab, and off you go! Of course, you can edit your routine as you wish. :)

20-MINUTE PRACTICE BREAKDOWN

Here is my recommendation for a typical 20-minute practice session at this stage:

-' Technique - Tune Your Guitar 1' Technique- Chord Perfect Practice Am Chord 1' Technique- Chord Perfect Practice Em Chord 1' Technique - One Minute Changes Am to E 1' Technique - One Minute Changes Em to D 1' Technique - One Minute Changes Am to Em 1' Technique - Anchor Finger E, A & D Chords 2' Technique - Strumming 2' Riff - Seven Nation Army 10' Repertoire - Songs for Module 3

YOU'LL BE READY TO MOVE ON WHEN…

You've memorized Am and Em chords (as well as all chords learned so far!)

You can get around 30 chord changes in one minute between all chords learned so far.

You had some fun with the Seven Nation Army Riff!

You had a go at playing a song (or two) using both our new chords.

Aim to feel confident, but remember that there are still early days. Everything improves as you keep practicing, so don't be hard on yourself! :) See you on Module 4!

modules.label: Module 4
modules.title: Metronome, Stretches & THE Pattern
modules.intro:
Short Pinky? Uncontrollable Fingers?

Get ready for a nice finger stretch exercise and some challenges!

I can't believe we're already in Module 4! As we progress in our Beginner Guitar Course, your skills improve, and you become more confident with your instrument. I hope you enjoy the ride and feel more confident with your chord changes.

We'll explore important things for your guitar journey in the next lessons! First, you'll meet the metronome and develop your rhythm abilities further. By the end of this module, you should be comfortable playing one of the most common strumming patterns ever. From Nirvana to Sheryl Crow to The Beatles - you can play it with that one. We'll also get into a stretching exercise for your fretting hand.

😅 Short pinky? You can start thanking me if you've got a short pinky as I do. :)

Before We Get Started

We need to pay some attention to your guitar pick! In this module, we'll get into a slightly harder strumming pattern, and the weight of your pick will make a huge difference for you. For beginners, it's usually a good idea to stick with a lightweight guitar pick. It's much more forgiving and comfortable to use, so you'll sound better.

Also, make sure you keep the nails on your fretting hand short. It isn't easy to play stringed instruments with long fingernails simply because they get in your way. You want them short so that you can press the strings down with your fingertips. A good rule of thumb is that you shouldn't see any white parts of your nail from the back. If your nail is hitting the fretboard itself, it's too long.

What You'll Learn

In terms of new grips, you'll learn how to play the Dm chord. It might be harder, but take it easy, and you'll get there! Make sure you follow a consistent practice routine, and always prioritize the hardest chords for you.

Module 4 also introduces the metronome, but as I said, the goal is to strengthen your rhythm skills! Make sure you've got an accurate metronome, and remember: it'll all come together at some point. ;)

The riff on this lesson is a classic from Eric Clapton! That means you're becoming an advancing beginner, eh? Are you enjoying the ride as much as I am?

Now, grab your guitar and get ready. We'll soon be missing a down strum. ;)

lessons.title: Beginner Finger Stretches
lessons.summary: Develop your finger strength and flexibility with this fast and effective exercise.
lessons.text:
This is not a speed exercise, but an exercise to help you out with finger strength and flexibility, two skills you need to play fast! :) This exercise also helps you develop the muscles in your hand, which will help later on when learning how to play barre chords!

If you've got short fingers - my pinky is real short, so I know - you'll really benefit from this exercise. It'll improve your playing down the road, but you might see some benefits right away.

Let's get started!

Step-by-Step Finger Stretching Exercise

We'll use only down-picks for this exercise. If it helps, use your pinky finger to anchor down your picking hand. Here's what you have to do.

Starting on the 5th fret, place your 1st finger down on the thickest string and pick.

Next, leave your 1st finger down and place your 2nd finger one fret higher and pick.

Then, add Finger 3 and pick the string. You have to keep Fingers 1 and 2 in position.

Lastly, add Finger 4 while keeping all the fingers in position.

Now it's time to check if all your fingers are in the right position. The palm of your hand should be more or less parallel to the guitar fretboard. Let's continue:

Hold the fingers in position for a second and make sure you feel a bit of a stretch, but no pain!

If this feels too much of a stretch, you could try moving it up the fretboard to start on Fret 8.

Repeat the process on the next string down, and continue.

When you’re comfortable doing this whole exercise at Fret 5, start moving it down the fretboard until you’re able to do it starting from the 1st fret.

Make The Most Out of This Exercise

This is an important exercise that will help you develop finger dexterity, finger flexibility, finger independence, and much more. You'll be developing the muscles in your fretting hand, and that will be handy later on in your guitar journey. Here are a few extra tips to make the most out of this stretching exercise for beginners:

1 - This is NOT a Speed Exercise

Take your time and do this exercise slowly. Think of it as yoga for your fingers. Your movements should be steady and deliberate. Focus on doing it properly rather than quickly.

2 - Keep Your Fingers Parallel to One Another As Best As You Can

The natural tendency will be for the fingers to start slanting in one direction or another. This is totally normal, so don’t get too frustrated if you find yourself doing this at first. It will get easier the more they do the exercise.

3 - Keep Your Fingers Roughly Where They Should Be

That means to have your fingers sort of lined up and ready to place on the string as you work through the exercise. No flailing fingers!

4 - This Is A Finger Stretch Exercise, Not A Finger Pain Exercise

Yes, you should feel a good stretch while doing it, but if it gets to be too painful, either take it more slowly or stop and rest for a bit. It really shouldn’t hurt very much.

5 - Be Forgiving :)

This finger stretching exercise can be really easy or difficult, depending a lot on your anatomy! We’ve all got different hands and fingers, so even if you have to work a bit harder at this than some others might, remember – you’re doing just fine!

Now let's put that stretchy fingers to good use and learn how to play the Dm Chord!

lessons.title: The D Minor Chord
lessons.summary: The Dm is pretty different from the D Chord, but I made it all easy for you! :)
lessons.text:
The Dm Chord doesn't look like the D Chord. Differently of the Am and Em, it takes more than one finger change to change from D Major to D Minor. Take a look at the Dm Chord guitar diagram:

Now let's get strumming!

How to Play the Dm Chord on Guitar

There are two different fingerings you can use to play the Dm Chord on guitar. If you're a beginner, I recommend using Fingers 1, 2, and 4 to play the Dm chord on the guitar. We tend to avoid using our pinky in the early guitar stages, but we need to develop that 4th finger! There are a few benefits related to this fingering, and we'll get back to it in just one second.

Many teachers and guitar players usually play with the 3rd finger instead of the 4th finger. Especially if you're a beginner, using the 3rd finger to play the Dm chord might be a bit of an awkward stretch. If you use your 4th finger, you'll strengthen it up, and that will help you out later on in your guitar journey.

No matter the option you go for, you won't strum the thickest two strings when playing the Dm Chord. Just like with the D Major Chord, the 4th string is open, and then you’ve got fingers on the thinnest strings.

🚨 Be really careful here! All of your fingers are placed squarely on their strings, and they shouldn't be muting any of the neighboring strings. As a beginner, you might find that your 2nd finger on the 3rd string might accidentally creep up and mute that open 4th string.

Like all other things when learning guitar, the Dm chord will require some practice. The One Minute Change Exercise and Perfect Chord Practice are your best friends here! If you're wondering which fingering you should choose, try both and see...

What Works Best For You?

When learning to play guitar, you'll need to make decisions that only you can take! It's no different when choosing the best fingering. You should play around with finding what’s comfortable for you as far as your hand and arm position is concerned. Some people might find it easier to slant their fingers to one side, while others will feel better with having them squarely in front of the strings.

Try wobbling your arm around with your fingers in place on the strings, and then slowly start to relax your arm and see where it naturally falls.

What works best for you?

Next, meet the metronome! Click, click, click, click…

lessons.title: Meet The Metronome
lessons.summary: Let your metronome be your best friend and thrive in your guitar journey! ;)
lessons.text:
Click, click, click, click…

It's time to make friends with the metronome!

A metronome is an essential tool - and not only for beginners! If you start practicing with a metronome in the early stages of your guitar playing, you'll benefit a lot from it. Ultimately, you'll be able to play in a steady, consistent rhythm - one of the vital skills for being a great guitarist.

But there are a few tricks to get the best out of a metronome. This guitar lesson is all about that! :) We have a few things to check out, so let's get started.

What Is a Metronome?

A metronome is a device that many musicians use, not only guitar players! It's a fantastic tool that helps you develop your sense of rhythm and play at a consistent tempo.

The metronome gives a regular click in a regular interval of time that we call tempo. Tempi is the plural of tempo, and we measure tempi in beats per minute - or BPM. So, for example, 60 BPM has one click per second.

But you're probably wondering…

Why Exactly Should You Practice With a Metronome?

If you practice with a metronome regularly, you’ll develop your inner sense of rhythm! Over time, you'll have the ability to play at a consistent tempo even when the click is off. What separates the great musicians from the meh musicians. :)

Practicing with a metronome might feel too easy or too tedious at first, but trust me, it will come in handy later.

Practicing with a metronome will have such a positive impact on your playing! We can often tell who are the guitar players who practice with a metronome and those who don’t.

Even the most advanced players practice with a metronome, and that's a great habit to get into from the very beginning of your guitar journey. So now, let's take a look at how to choose the best metronome for your practice!

First Rule: Different Tempi!

I love old-school stuff, and you have to agree that those old tick-tock pendulum-type metronomes are very classy! Take a look:

You’ve probably seen one of those in a music room, but they are not very practical for real-world use. :)

Those pendulum metronomes usually work in only one tempo. But my first recommendation is to choose a metronome that clicks in different tempi! So, yes, that means you’ve got to go digital, and in this modern era, your best option will probably be a metronome app on your smartphone.

Most apps are loud enough to hear over your instrument unless you are playing loud through an amplifier. When playing acoustic guitar, I try to rest mine as close as possible to my ears. If you're going to rock out, you'll have to use a single earphone to hear the click clearly!

If you don't want to download anything, use the JustinGuitar Metronome. But there's another thing you should look out for when shopping or downloading a metronome!

Second Rule: Accentuate the Beat!

Most metronomes allow you to set an accent on the beat, and that's a pretty big deal! As a beginner guitar player, you should be practicing songs in 4/4 - meaning four beats per bar. So if you set the accent for the first beat of every bar, you’ll always know where Beat 1 is, and you won’t get too far off track!

Third Rule: Accuracy

There's no point in practicing with a metronome that is not accurate. Make sure you choose an app that you can trust and keeps a steady time! You should hear precise clicks on each beat.

The JustinGuitar Time Trainer Metronome

I always wanted a metronome with all of the features I needed in one place while being accurate and reliable. However, I couldn’t find one that ticked all the boxes for me, so I had one made. Thus, my Time Trainer Metronome was born!

As the name implies, it has some excellent training features designed to help you develop your internal sense of time.

It includes a countdown timer which you can use to time your practice sessions. Like that, you ensure you’re spending the right amount of time practicing the right things.

The Time Trainer is available for Apple iOS and Android, and it costs less than a beer. :) Go check it out - you won't regret it! If you don't want to download an app, you can use the free metronome available here!

Now grab your guitar, and let's learn one of the most common strumming patterns ever! Seriously - you'll be able to play most of the songs you like with that one!

lessons.title: THE Strumming Pattern
lessons.summary: Is this the only strumming pattern you'll ever need? Maybe!
lessons.text:
The Old Faithful Strumming Pattern

If you only wanted to learn one single strumming pattern in your entire guitar journey, it'd be this one!

If you're a beginner guitar player, you need this strumming pattern. On the other hand, if you're a more advanced player and already play some popular songs, you probably know this strumming pattern. :) In that case, breaking it down can understand what you're playing, and you might end up sounding better!

I call it the old faithful because bands have been playing it so much and for so long! So that means that this pattern is way likely to work for that song you love and want to play!

The old faithful is not tricky to play, but it does require some practice. We'll break it down in easy steps, so you'll be playing it in no time.

🎸 This is a practical class, so grab your guitar and let's get playing.

Strumming for Beginners: Step-by-Step

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you know we're learning how to strum the guitar step-by-step. I've figured that the best way to help beginner guitar players that struggle with rhythm is to break it down, so you build a strong foundation. When you get the strumming basics down, you become more comfortable with your instrument. Your playing will feel - and sound! - much better. :)

In our previous module, we learned a basic strumming pattern with up strums. This pattern is a slight variation on that one, but we'll be skipping a bit. That means you won't play Beat 3.

And now it's time for the life-changing trick: you should keep your strumming hand moving, even if you don't hit any strings. You'll skip a down strum, but your hand will still move consistently, just like a pendulum.

You might have heard it before - I say it a lot, especially when explaining why strumming is so hard for some of you.

If you look at most guitar players, they always keep their hands moving even when not strumming. Of course, there are exceptions to this rule, and sometimes you'll opt for not moving your hand. But for now, while learning guitar and building your foundation, keep your hand moving even when you don't need to strum the guitar.

And don't forget: aim to move your arm as evenly and smoothly as possible, and you might consider using a metronome. The JustinGuitar Time Trainer is also fantastic for developing your rhythm skills! ;)

Now it's time for some playing. Ready?

How to Practice A Strumming Pattern

Grab your guitar and play along with me! In this lesson, we'll learn the old faithful strumming pattern until we get it sounding great. We'll follow these three easy steps:

Strumming Pattern Step 1

Start off with a simple pattern of four down-strums per bar. Then, while you strum, you should count aloud – 1, 2, 3, 4…

Strumming Pattern Step 2

Now, it's time to add some up strums. We'll play the backbeat after beats 2 and 3. Take a look:

1 2+ 3+ 4 D DU DU D

Strumming Pattern Step 3

Finally, skip the down strum on beat 3, keeping the up strum after it. Continue to count aloud!

1 2+ + 4 D Du u D

Skipping a down strum might be easier said than done. :) If you have a hard time, know you're not alone, and many students struggle with rhythm in the early guitar stages. So just stick with it - we'll be working on strumming patterns through the entire course!

🚨 Don't forget: the best way to practice a new strumming pattern is by focusing only on that. Don't add any chords before you're comfortable playing the strumming pattern.

Now check out a few extra tips to get this all down!

Using a Metronome

When you’re practicing this on your own, it’s a good idea to use a metronome. Set it somewhere between 80 and 100 BPM - a good practice is not too fast, but not too slow.

If you don't already have a metronome app, don't forget to check out the JustinGuitar Time Trainer Metronome - available for Apple and Android devices. If you don't want to download anything, check out this online metronome.

Let's Play Some Songs!

With a couple of open chords and this strumming pattern in your pocket, you can play and sing along with thousands of popular songs! And guess what? That's the best thing you can do to improve your guitar skills and develop your musicianship.

There are a few things you can try! Check out my songbooks and try to figure out the songs you like on your own. You'll have the chords and lyrics right in front of you, and then you can even play along with the original recording. That's ace!

If you'd like more help, you can explore my song tutorials. You can choose from over 600 free lessons - but at this stage, stick with the ones from the Beginner Guitar Course (Grades 1, 2, and 3.) Right now, we're in Grade 1, and playing slightly harder songs can be a fun challenge to try. By you don't want to get into bad habits or get unmotivated, so don't give a step that's bigger than your legs. :)

Choose wisely, and you'll be a pro in no time.

Now let's learn how to read guitar tabs so we can nail that Eric Clapton riff by the end of this module!

lessons.title: How To Read Guitar TAB
lessons.summary: Reading guitar TABs will open up a world of possibilities for your beginner guitar journey! :)
lessons.text:
You've probably heard about TABs before, right?

TABs is how we write down guitar music!

TAB is short for tablature, and it's a way of writing music that is specific to fretted instruments like the guitar. In this lesson, we’ll learn how to read guitar tabs. TABs are the most common way of writing music for guitar. Not a perfect tool, but it’s very easy and popular.

Let's learn all about it right now!

What is a Guitar Tab?

A guitar tab - or guitar tablature - is a way of writing music specific to fretted instruments. It’s a perfect system for musicians who don’t read traditional, standard music notation. TABs often give you more information than notation does too.

A TAB has six horizontal lines that represent the six strings on the guitar. Here’s an example:

The TAB above is an ASCII TAB, the most popular form on the Internet. It’s the one I use on my website!

Reading Guitar Tabs

As I’ve mentioned before, the six lines represent the six strings of the guitar. The top line represents the thinnest (1st) string. The lowest line represents the thickest (6th) string.

Bass at the bottom, treble at the top

Take another look at the image above. At the end of the lines, I add the letters T.A.B. - Treble (T) And (A) Bass (B). A trick to help you remember:

The Bass Strings are at the bottom. They are the fattest strings with the lowest sound.

The Treble strings are at the top. They are the thinnest strings with the highest sound.

Here's another way to think about it. A tab ‘stave’ shows the strings of the guitar as you’re looking down on them when you’re playing. :)

Step-By-Step Example

Follow the three easy steps below to play your first guitar tab:

The numbers on the lines show you on which fret to play a note. If there’s no number on a string, don't play it.

A ‘0’ means that the string is ‘open.’ You’ll play that string, but with no fingers on it!

When you see numbers aligned vertically, play all the numbered strings at the same time.

In the example above, you'd play an E chord shape first - press down the strings on the fretboard as shown. You should strum all the strings! Then, you’d play the strings 3, 2, 1, 2, and 3 in turn.

You might find TABs confusing when you first see them, but it doesn’t take much practice to master them. For beginners, reading TABs is far easier than learning traditional notation. But you're probably wondering...

Where's the Rhythm?

These types of TABs don't offer rhythmic information. Sometimes, I add rhythm notation into my TABs too, but that's not a standard practice. I recommend learning how to read rhythm as part of your study, but we won’t cover it in this Beginner Guitar Course.

💡 The absence of rhythm makes this kind of TAB easy to write. Writing the ‘licks’ that you’re learning can help your guitar development. :)

🚨 Because TABs are so easy to write, many inexperienced players post their TABs online. Most time, the TABs aren't accurate. Make sure you choose TABs from a source you trust.

Now let's take a look at how a more professional TAB looks like!

Tabs With Standard Notation

More professional tabs include standard notation (the ‘dots’) and the rhythm. Take a look at this example:

This example is still pretty simple. Professional TABs can include all kinds of other technical information. It takes much longer to create them, and you’ll need some knowledge of notation and rhythms. And also to be a whizz with the software you’ll choose to use!

Here are a few examples of technical information you can find in a tab:

String bends. An arrow pointing up from a note.

Slurs (hammer-ons and flick-offs). Curved lines going from one note to another.

Slides. Straight lines between two notes.

Picking directions. Shown above the notes.

Finger tapping. Usually, a+ above a note.

We’ll learn more about tablatures later on!

MY SHORTHAND FOR INDIVIDUAL NOTES

I’ve got a shorthand to represent individual notes that is really useful! You’ll often see it in my lessons, but it’s not something used by other teachers. It’s a handy way of specifying a note when you don’t need to write out a full TAB. Here is an example:

S5/F8 - It means String 5, Fret 8.

Now let's take a look at the difference between tabs and traditional notation.

TABS VS TRADITIONAL NOTATION

The big advantage of TABs is that it tells you where to play a note, not just the note itself. As you can see below, the same note (an E) appears in six different places on the neck. The standard notation shows the same dot, but the TAB shows you where to play it.

Standard notation can make simple things look complicated.

For example, in blues music, rhythm is very free. Writing it down ‘correctly’ is difficult - and reading it even more so! For blues, plain TABs without notation or rhythms are the easiest way to communicate an idea. But you’ll have to do some listening to understand how to play it. :)

Look at the example below. It looks terrifying, and it's a tricky rhythm to explain. It's a ‘loose and free’ improvised solo on a slow tempo blues. Take away the notation and the rhythm, and it doesn't look so complicated!

Now you're probably asking yourself...

Should You Learn Standard Music Notation?

Well, my most common answer is no. I wouldn’t recommend that you learn traditional notation. It’s essential to know it for playing some styles, like jazz. But for most guitar players, music notation is not particularly useful. Learning it can be a massive waste of time! Standard music notation and guitar playing can be a nightmare because you can find most notes in more than one place on the fretboard. But TABs tell you which note to play and also where to play it. :)

I’ve always wanted to play classical and jazz guitar. Reading music is an essential skill for those styles. Even so, it’s easier to master music notation when you’ve reached a good standard of playing. I read music well, but I still prefer to use TABs for writing or reading solos.

At the beginning of your journey, learning to read music sucks all the fun out of playing. So, wait until you have a reason to know it!

TAB Alternatives

Other guitar notation systems have appeared over the last 30 years or so. TAB is still by far the easiest one to understand. I’d suggest avoiding other systems. It's frustrating to learn a new system that you’re unlikely to find anywhere else.

Now it's riff time! Howdy, grab your guitar - we'll play an Eric Clapton classic. :)

lessons.title: Sunshine Of Your Love
lessons.summary: This classic riff might be a bit difficult, but it’s a great challenge and beginner workout!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Introduction

01:27 Close-up Fretting

03:16 Playing Tips

05:50 Conclusion
lessons.text:
Learn How To Play The Guitar Riff Of "Sunshine Of Your Love" by Cream!

In this lesson, you'll learn how to play the riff for Sunshine of Your Love on the guitar. This song is by Cream, and it's an excellent tune for beginner guitar players! Many cool, exciting things are going on in this riff - we'll explore the chords, rhythm, and what to do with your fretting hand. :)

This is an exciting lesson for many guitar players - if you're an Eric Clapton fan, this might be your first guitar riff ever featuring the great master. This riff is very recognizable, but it's a bit difficult. You love a challenge, don't you? And the reward is fantastic, I promise! Let's get started and see what's up. :)

💡 Curious about how to play the full song? Check out the full lesson here. However, this lesson has advanced guitar techniques and suits Grade 4+ intermediate players. Maybe it's something you want to add as a dreamer song in your repertoire!

Rhythm & Picking

We’re doing things differently from the original recording; we're playing the riff on another part of the neck, which is easier for beginners. Now for the rhythm, it's a tricky one to count aloud. So many sure you take some time to listen to the original recording a few times before playing it.

For the picking, you're only going to be using down picks. The challenge will be string jumping, part of Clapton's signature style. If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, this will be the first time you play a guitar riff on three different strings! But rush it, and start with a slow tempo. :)

When it comes to your fretting hand, you'll play on the thickest three strings with your 1st, 2nd, and 3rd fingers lined up in a row. The trick here is to keep your fingers relatively in place on the fretboard. Your fingers shouldn't be flailing about too much! Finding it too much of a stretch? It just takes some practice, and you'll soon get it down. ;)

Sunshine of Your Love - Guitar TAB

The best way of learning a guitar riff is by ear! It might take longer, and you might even get some wrong notes, but you'll be improving your ears. Ultimately, you'll become a better musician. :)

But I know getting TABs down can be confusing and time-consuming, so here's the guitar tab to play Sunshine of Your Love by Cream on guitar:

Want the Tab for the full song? Check out JustinGuitar TABS - you'll enjoy over 600 songs with accurate chords, lyrics, and tabs to follow along with and rock on!

lessons.title: Songs For Module 4
lessons.summary: So many songs to choose from. :)
lessons.text:
Songs to Practice the Dm Chord! :)

Let's work on your chord changes?

We've been learning guitar together for some time now, so you already know I consider playing songs a big deal. Playing guitar is all about having fun and playing songs you like - and even writing your own music! To develop your musicianship and practice the techniques we've just learned, you should choose songs you love and inspire you to pick up the guitar.

Here are a few recommendations of songs you can try using the Dm Chord!

6 Songs With Dm On Guitar

Here are 3 songs to practice the Dm Chord on guitar!

505 - Arctic Monkeys

All Your Love - John Mayall

Chocolate Jesus - Tom Waits

These next 3 songs have full lessons and are also available on my Lesson & Songs App - try it out for free and learn by playing songs! ;)
