Fallin’ - Alicia Keys

A Girl Like You - Edwyn Collins

Spotify Playlist

Check out this Spotify playlist for Module 4, and give a listen to the original recording! It might inspire you to try something new on your guitar. :)

Do your best to find songs that you really like! Got some suggestions? Let me know in the comments below and I might make a lesson on it!

lessons.title: Module 4 Practice Routine
lessons.summary: Here’s a 20-minute practice schedule including all your new guitar skills.
lessons.text:
It's Practice Time!

Time to get the best out of your practice time.

Here’s a breakdown of what a typical 20-minute practice session should look like to practice everything you’ve learned so far.

-' Technique - Tune Your Guitar 2' Technique- Finger Stretch 1' Technique- Chord Perfect Practice Dm Chord 1' Technique - Whichever chord you find most difficult 2' Technique - Two sessions - whichever changes you find most difficult 2' Technique - Old Faithful Strumming 2' Riff - Sunshine Of Your Love 10' Repertoire - Songs for Module 4

Don't forget: choose songs you like! You know enough chords, so there are a bunch of cool songs to choose from.

💡 Click on the 'Practice' Tab under the video, and save the pre-made routine for Module 4. Edit and access the items in your Dashboard.

You’ll be ready to move on when...

You can get around 30 chord changes in one minute

You’ve memorized all of the chords you’ve learned so far – A, D, E, Am, Dm, Em

You’ve got the Old Faithful strumming down consistently and comfortably on muted strings, preferably with a metronome

You can get through the Sunshine riff

You’re able to play at least one song decently well most of the way through

See you in Module 5 - we'll get a taste of music theory, learn to play the C Chord, and so much more!

modules.label: Module 5
modules.title: Basic Theory & Strumming Development
modules.intro:
Welcome to Module 5!

Have you wondered about the C Chord? It's time to learn it. :)

You've probably encountered the C chord when looking for songs to play, haven't you? It's a common grip, and it's finally time to learn it. In this Module 5, we'll also get deeper into strumming patterns and learn the best strumming pattern exercise you'll ever try. :)

Let's check out what else is on the menu!

What You'll Learn

When learning the C Chord, we'll get into deliberately muting neighboring strings when playing a chord. That will make loads of difference when you play this new grip.

We'll also explore how you can create your strumming patterns and how you can incorporate that into your practice routine. Following my tips will give you a deeper understanding of rhythm. Stick with this course, and we'll learn how to play any strumming pattern by ear by the beginning of Grade 4! ;)

It's also time to get into some music theory. We'll understand the note circle and how to apply it to the guitar fretboard. That's a pretty practical guitar lesson - you'll be surprised! If you'd like to dig deeper into theory, check out the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course - a course made by a guitar player for guitar players.

🚨 Following my Beginner Guitar Course? Make sure you are comfortable with all you've learned so far before hitting this new module!

By the end of Module 5, you'll know how to play one more riff, Come as You Are by Nirvana, and loads, loads of songs.

Ready? Let's check out how to play that C Chord.

lessons.title: The C Chord
lessons.summary: Learn how to play the C chord on the guitar and a nice trick to mute the thickest string.
lessons.text:
Ready to meet the C Chord?

It's not the easiest one, but it's a must!

The C Chord on guitar can be challenging for some hands because of the finger stretch involved. But it’s a very commonly-used chord, so essential to learn.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to play the C Chord on guitar! You'll learn which strings to strum, the correct finger placement and strings, and some awesome tricks to get the C Chord sounding good! :)

Let's get playing.

How to Play the C Chord on The Guitar

Follow these three easy steps to play the C chord on the guitar:

Place your 1st finger on the 1st fret of the second string.

Then, your 2nd finger goes down in the 2nd fret of the 4th string.

Finally, your 3rd finger reaches around to the 3rd fret of the 5th string.

Don’t worry if it feels a bit tricky already - it’s normal. :)

Use the image below to help guide your finger placement:

Wondering How the C Chord Should Sound Like?

Here’s an audio snippet:

The Right Finger Placement to Play the C Chord

To play the C chord on guitar, slant your hand at an angle. It’ll prevent you from having to stretch too hard, and your grip will feel more comfortable.

When you put the third finger down, try to mute the thickest string - we don’t want to play it anyways! However, make sure you’re not muting the 5th string! Your thumb should not come up more than halfway up the back of the neck when you make the chord. Doing this will open up your hand and help you make that 3rd finger stretch.

Thumb Muting?

Some players like to use their thumb to mute the thickest string, but this can be tricky when you’re doing certain chord changes - I don’t recommend it for beginners.

However, play around and find the method that works best for you. Everyone has different shaped hands and lengths of fingers, and the C chord always looks a little different for everyone. Some people have their fingers more or less angled, and there is a huge variation in thumb placement between others.

Don’t worry if you don’t get it on the first few days you're practicing the C chord. Be patient - and don’t give up! :)

CHANGING CHORDS INTO THE C CHORD

Now, the next challenge will be changing into this chord. When you’re doing your C chord practice, make sure you take your whole handoff, then place it back correctly.

Removing your hand and then helping its way back again will help you later on. It will feel challenging at the beginning - but a few weeks of practicing, and this will feel like all the other chords you’ve learned so far.

Add this lesson to your practice routine schedule! Use My Practice Assistant and learn guitar faster. ;)

lessons.title: Guitar Strumming Tips
lessons.summary: Learn how to play ANY guitar strumming pattern with these essential strumming basics.
lessons.text:
Are you still struggling with strumming?

Don't worry. This is more common than you think, but here is how you'll master it!

For many beginner guitar players, chord changes will be the hardest struggle. But for many - maybe even more! - the big problem will be to play a nice, relaxed, and consistent rhythm. To master guitar strumming, you must first understand what's happening with the movement in your arm. And this lesson is all about that!

We'll go through all the strumming basics and exercises I've been teaching in live workshops for years, and you'll learn an exercise that will help you play the strumming pattern you want. You’ll be able to work out song rhythms and improve your confidence when making your own strumming variations!

Ready? Let's go :)

Before You Start: These 3 tips will help you succeed!

Before we dive into strumming, let's review some important beginner guitar reminders.

Use a thin pick - they are more flexible and easier to use! Thin picks are more forgiving in your early strumming practice!

Relax your strumming arm and rest it comfortably over the top of your guitar. Make sure you're feeling nice and loose!

The strumming motion comes from your elbow, not your wrist! Be mindful of this to prevent pain :)

Now let's get started.

Learn Any Strumming Guitar Pattern

You'll start by playing four beats per bar using down-strums. Once you start strumming, focus on keeping the rhythm consistent. Aim for a flow of consistent motion with your strumming arm. Keep this same motion throughout the exercise without stopping.

Once you can keep it steady with four beats per bar, you can move on to manipulating the rhythm and strumming pattern. This is the fun part ;)

To manipulate the guitar rhythm, start playing around with different random strumming patterns. The basic four down-strum also has four up-strums. These up strums are the "ands" that come between your four counts. Now it's time to start strumming on these up-strums. To help guide yourself, you can try counting the beats out loud.

💡 So now, you've got eight strums to work with - pretty cool, right?

Make sure you keep that initial four beats per bar strumming motion. Then, determine which up strums and down strums you'd like to include in your new pattern. Experiment with different ones - be your own strumming boss! :)

For the beats you're not playing, lift your pick off of the strings. Your strumming arm is making the same motion, but no sound will come out of the guitar.

I'll repeat this again - KEEP YOUR ARM MOVING! I promise - it'll help you experiment with different strumming patterns and keep a steady beat.

How to Practice Any Strumming Pattern

The key with guitar strumming is to feel completely comfortable playing a specific rhythm. Strumming should come so to you that it becomes almost mindless. After all, how are you ever going to sing and play at the same time if you can't get this down? More playing, less thinking :)

To practice, try to carry on a conversation while practicing your strumming without breaking the pattern. Strumming should come so to you that it becomes almost mindless.

I recommend practicing strumming patterns on muted strings. Doing this is super helpful - especially for beginners. Muting the strings will help you only concentrate only the strumming! Tapping your foot is also a great way to keep your guitar strumming timing consistent.

Pick a few strumming patterns that you like and focus on playing those well. These will be useful to have as you progress and learn to play more songs!

Free PDF Available!

Log in and get a PDF I created just for you! :) It's 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + printed a bunch of times, so you do this exercise several times. It's super helpful to help you make up your strumming patterns or even take notes from my song lessons.

Don't forget to track your progress! Add this lesson to your practice routine schedule.

lessons.title: Exploring Strumming
lessons.summary: Explore strumming and create your own strumming variations with these awesome tips.
lessons.text:
At this point in your beginner guitar journey, you can start making up different strumming patterns. How exciting is that? :) The best way of learning and creating new strumming variations is by picking a strumming pattern from a song you love.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to level up any strumming pattern you want! Let's explore some strumming exercises, best practices, and awesome tips to improve your guitar strumming!

Explore New Strumming Patterns

Some songs have specific strumming patterns. Others have a looser structure - and you can apply whatever strumming pattern you like to it! These songs are the best to explore different strumming options on the guitar.

It's key you remember that you can add in extra strums and leave others out. It really doesn't matter! Experiment with it - and let loose! :) This is how you'll learn to create strumming variations.

Always make sure you relax your arm! Keep going until you get that nice flow of strumming arm movement at all times. This is the foundation of all strumming - that continuous arm movement.

Generally, every four or eight bars, a slight rhythmic strumming variation should happen. This is an excellent time to start manipulating your strumming. Your strumming pattern should stay the same most of the time, but this change will make it pop! It'll make your sound more exciting to listen to and musically engaging.

How To Practice Strumming With A Metronome

To practice, find a few patterns you like, then just put in your own twist! Remove strums, and add strums - see how it feels and sounds.

Practice with the metronome as often as you can. This will develop a sense of time and help you stay on tempo. It might feel weird at first, but you want to feel relaxed with the metronome. If you don't have a metronome on hand, use my free metronome tool on the website.

When you strum to the metronome, it should feel like you're not chasing the time but anticipating the following tempo. The metronome clicking sound should feel comfortable. Relax as you strum into its clicking sound - just let it happen naturally! :)

Add Dynamics To Your Guitar Playing

You'll want to be aware of your rhythm dynamics, which is how hard and how soft you strum. Start experimenting with playing really loudly and really softly.

A quick exercise you can do is to begin strumming on muted strings as soft as possible. Gradually increase the volume until you're playing as loudly as you possibly can. Then, make your way back down. We'll talk more about using dynamics to improve your guitar playing later on. For now, start being mindful of this!

Strumming Should Feel Automatic

I recommend you keep a record of strumming patterns you really like. Spend a bit of time working on those to make them stick with you! You'll be able to revisit your strumming patterns later on.

If you're a beginner guitar player, practice your strumming for two minutes each practice session with the metronome. Stick with a few patterns, and add more as you practice. These strumming patterns should feel so consistent that they almost become automatic. I recommend you add this lesson to Your Practice routine - and track your progress as you go!

Good luck, and have fun exploring strumming patterns. Next lesson, we'll take a look at some basic musical theory! :)

lessons.title: Understanding Music Notes
lessons.summary: Understand music notes with these music theory basics all guitar players should know!
lessons.text:
Learning the basics of music theory is essential.

And even beginner guitar players can benefit a lot from it!

A little theory goes a long way, and understanding what you're doing will help you improve your guitar playing. It also helps you connect your skills with your musical imagination! :)

In this lesson, we'll take a look at The Note Circle. You'll also have a better understanding of sharps, flats, and enharmonic equivalents.

Let's start from the very beginning.

What Is The Note Circle

The Note Circle is a circle that shows all 12 notes that we use in western music. Pictured below, you can see you've got your basic A-G notes. Between those notes, you've got some sharps and flats.

The Note Circle Explained In 5 Steps:

Each step around the "clock face" of the Note Circle is a semitone.

On your guitar, each fret represents one semitone.

We call two intervals between two notes a tone.

One full lap around the note circle is an octave.

Depending on what you play, you’ll either play one octave higher or lower.

Now, check out your guitar’s fretboard - see the double dots on the fret? These signify the 12 frets on most guitars. Use the double dots to help you navigate the note circles on your fretboard.

I recommend you spend some time studying and memorizing the Note Circle. Then, quiz yourself by picking two notes and trying to determine how many semitones are between them. If you have to peek at the Note Circle to do this at first, that's fine! It'll sink into your head before you know it.

🤐 I should mention that Americans tend to call a semitone half steps and tones whole steps. To me, that is a bit confusing. I prefer using the other terms - it makes much more sense musically!

What are Sharps

A sharp (#) raises the pitch of a note by one semitone or one fret on your guitar. An easy way to remember this is if you sat on something sharp, you would jump up!

What are Flats

A flat (b) lowers the pitch of a note by one semitone or one fret on your guitar. Remember this - if your car tire is flat, it goes down.

What are Enharmonic Equivalents

If you look at the Note Circle, you'll see that you can also write each sharp as a flat. For example, an A# is the same as a Bb. This means that A# and Bb are enharmonic equivalents.

The reason behind why the same note has two different names is more complex. We'll explore that later on. But, for now, what you need to understand is that they are on the same note.

The H In German Music Theory

In Germany and some other European countries, the note B note is traditionally called H. Today, most music teachers in Germany teach the regular B, but others still use the H. If you're a German music student, I don't recommend learning it as H. Since the rest of the world uses B, it makes more sense to use it. It’s always best to learn music in a universal way.

Now, if we could only get the Americans on board with the metric system… Just kidding! :)

If you want to learn more about guitar music theory, check out my Practical Music Theory Course. It's one of my favorite courses to teach - c'mon, music theory is a superpower! 🪄

lessons.title: Your Own Songbook
lessons.summary: Learn how to your make own songbook and easily access songs you love to play!
lessons.text:
Want to know what’s the BEST guitar songbook for beginners?

Easy - it’s the one created by YOU! :)

There are many reasons why you should create your songbook. I mention this often, but playing the songs you love will improve your guitar playing faster! It motivates you to practice and inspires you to play. The goal here is to have a personal reference book to access songs you love and play with confidence easily!

In this lesson, you’ll learn how to make your own songbook and some handy tips to keep in mind.

Here we go!

How To Create Your Songbook

There are a few options to make your own songbook repertoire. I recommend having a display folder with clear pockets where you can put pieces of paper inside.

Every time you learn a song and dig it, you can print it out and put it in this display folder. First, print out the song sheet with the guitar chord and lyrics above.

Once you combine a few songs, you'll have this personal songbook you'll love to play! These songs should become part of the ones you practice regularly.

Saving your song sheets as PDF files can also be super handy. That way, you have a backup of all the songs you love. Also, if you forget your songbook, you'll be able to access them anytime digitally.

Why You Should Create Your Songbook

An important part of the process is having a collection of songs you can play with confidence. Whether you're playing by yourself, with family and friends, or performing for a gig, this will help you improve your stage performance and musical confidence.

Once a week or month, go through your songbook and practice all the songs. That way, you'll be prepared for any upcoming event!

Creating your songbook is awesome when you meet other musicians, and you're not sure what to play. Just grab the book, and you’ll have a selection of what you can currently play.

Make sure the lyrics are nicely printed so others can look at them and play along with you. And if you’re at a party or gathering, everyone will be able to sing along!

Having a physical printout version will also help you remember them. In a way, it almost frees a bit of hard drive in your mind.

Play The Songs You Love 💙

I recommend don't have too many songs in your repertoire. That can be overwhelming and make it difficult to decide which one to play. Keep around 20 songs you love playing at the moment! You can also build your own virtual song repertoire on your JustinGuitar dashboard. Make sure you sign in to your account and add the songs as choosing them, so you save time and play more! ;)

If you want a songbook right in your pocket, try out my Lessons & Songs App. You can save songs into a playlist and play along with REAL backing tracks.

lessons.summary: Learn the riff for Come As You Are By Nirvana - a great exercise for beginner guitar players!

lessons.text:
What's Better Than Learning While Playing Songs?

Learning While Playing NIRVANA! 🤘

Come As You Are by Nirvana is a classic 90s grunge track you're probably familiar with, aren't you? What's awesome about Come As You Are is that it has a powerful riff perfect for beginner guitar players!

In this guitar lesson, we'll only learn the riff. It sounds like the original recording, and that's cool stuff! There's more to this riff; if you're feeling adventurous, check out the full song tutorial here.

When playing this song, you'll be practicing:

Picking

Fingering

Rhythm

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, I suggest you stick to this lesson and consider it a practical exercise to use the techniques you've learned so far. Grab your guitar, and let's get playing!

How To Play Come As You Are Riff

For this riff, you're going to use all down-picks. The challenge will be going back and forth between the two thickest strings. Make sure each pick is precise and the correct one!

You'll start by playing the open thickest string twice. Then, Finger 1 goes on the first fret of the thickest string. Follow with Finger 2 on the second fret of the thickest string. This whole sequence happens on beat 1.

You'll play an open A from the second fret, then back to the second fret on the thickest string. Follow by playing twice on the second fret of the thickest string. Finally, Finger 1 plays on the first fret to the open.

🚨 If you're a more advanced guitar player, you could add in an F sharp Power Chord. That's Grade 2 stuff - you don't need to rush things out, but you can still get a taste of what's waiting for you. :)

This power chord happens on the second fret of the thickest strings and the fourth fret of the fifth string. Only do this if you're confident playing the simple version! It's a bit of a challenge, and there's nothing wrong with keeping it simple for now. :)

Come As You Are Riff: Use Your Fingertips

At some point in the riff, you'll have to leave a finger down on one string and pick another open string next to it. Make sure that you're using your fingertips while you're fretting. If not - you might mute the open strings you're trying to play.

Focus on getting the right strings right out clearly. It might take a bit of practice - so don't rush it! The key is to use your fingertips and let the notes ring out together.

Come As You Are Riff: Counting The Rhythm

You might find counting the rhythm for this riff a bit challenging. For now, it'll be easier to learn by listening to the original recording. Get the sound in your ears rather than thinking in numbers.

The actual tempo riff is a little faster than what I showed in the video. But take your time - and practice at a slower tempo if you need to. With time, you'll feel more confident, and you'll be able to speed things up!

🔑 Think of this riff as an exercise. It should be fun, and it's great to practice your guitar picking. :)

Come As You Are Riff Tab

Need extra help? Use the tab below to guide your playing.

💡 Inspired to learn this full song? Get the tab, lyrics, and chords for this Nirvana song and 600+ more with the JustinGuitarTabs! Try it out for free. :)

Don't feel you need to know how to play this song perfectly before moving on to the next lesson. Have some fun with it! Now, time to get into some new songs. :)

lessons.title: Songs For Module 5
lessons.summary: Here are some songs for you to practice the concepts and techniques you've learned in Lesson 5 of this beginner's guitar course.
lessons.text:
Look at that! You've almost completed Module 5!

Ready to put your C chord into practice?

We've just learned how to play the C Chord, so now it's time to play some songs with it. If you're looking for songs to practice with, you'll notice that many need a G Chord too. We'll be learning that at the beginning of the next module, and then the list of songs you'll be able to play will grow a lot. Often, the G chord is also involved when there's a C chord. :)

So, for now, hold on a bit. In the meantime, check out the song tutorials below!

3 Easy Songs On Guitar With The C Chord

Here are three easy songs that will put your C chord into play:

1. Eleanor Rigby - The Beatles

This song is just C and Em chords. It's a beautiful song with a couple of quickie things. Some variations happen that you might not anticipate during chord changes. You'll be able to apply many different strumming patterns for this one.

2. Pearl Jam - Black

They are one of my favorite bands, particularly in my teenage years! This song uses the C chord alongside other chords you've learned throughout the course, particularly the D and Em chords.

3. Love Again - Dua Lipa

This one came from a student suggestion in our Community! This pop song is a simple four-chord song with the same progression repeating throughout: Em, C, Am, and D. Each chord gets half a bar in 4/4 time. Many ways to have fun with it too!🙂

4. Daft Punk - Get Lucky

This one has Am, C, Em, and D. This song is a different genre than I usually include. It's kind of like a disco, and it's super catchy! Here we are doing a simplified strumming version, but it's the same chord sequence throughout the song. It'll be great to work on jumping from the C chord to the minor chord. This particular chord sequence is quite common, so you can use it for other songs.

MORE AWESOME GUITAR SONGS FOR MODULE 5

So far, if you've been following my Beginner Guitar Course, we've learned the chords A, D, E, Em, and Am, and now the C chord. You've now got an excellent base under your belt.

Here are two more easy songs involving the C chord and these different chord combinations that might also interest you. No lessons yet for these tunes, but they are still great options for you to check out :)

I Only Want You - The Eagles of Death Metal

Tonight's The Night - Neil Young

Putting New Songs Into Practice

You can either pick one of these signs for your practice or choose a different one to try out every time. It's really up to you. And who knows, maybe one of these songs will end up in your songbook!

The most important thing is that you practice songs you enjoy listening to! So don't worry if you're not digging my options - you can always add your song preference. If you're looking for song inspiration, check out my Beginner Song App where I have more than 600+ songs to play along on the guitar! :)

Module 5 Spotify Playlist

Get inspired and listen to my song recommendation on my Spotify Playlist for Module 5. Hope you find something you like. :)

Now, let's look at an effective practice routine you can follow to practice all your new skills!

lessons.title: Module 5 Practice
lessons.summary: Now that you've completed Lesson 5 of the JustinGuitar Beginner's Course, you can work on perfecting the techniques you've learned. Here's the practice schedule.
lessons.text:
Module 5 Complete. Well Done! 🎉

Feels good, eh? :)

At this stage, you’ve learned so many fundamentals. It should all start to come together and make sense. Let’s set up a new practice schedule to improve all the guitar skills you’ve learned. For this stage, we'll have a 20-minute practice session. This plan will cover everything we've learned in Module 5!

Here are some guitar practice tips to remember:

I recommend committing to 4 practice sessions a week.

Don't over-practice - it can lead to finger pain.

Study a bit of music theory - a little theory goes a long way!

Get confident playing and anticipating metronome clicks

If you’re really digging playing a few songs, add them to your songbook

Use the right pick - thinner picks are more suitable for beginners.

💡 Under the video, click on the 'Practice', and save the pre-made routine for Module 5. You can edit and access the items in your Dashboard.

MY PRACTICE ASSISTANT

The best way to practice the guitar is using My Practice Assistant - a fantastic tool to keep you accountable and motivated. :) Make sure you log in to your JustinGuitar account to make the most out of your time and track your progress. Once logged in, go to your dashboard. Select the Practice tab, and off you go!

Of course, you can edit your routine as you wish. :)

20-MINUTE PRACTICE BREAKDOWN

Here is my recommendation for a typical 20-minute practice session at this stage:

Finger Stretch: 2 minutes

C Chord Perfect: 1 minute

Perfect Chord You Struggle: 1 minute

OMC Am to C: 1 minute

OMC C to Em: 1 minute

Strumming (Any pattern, focus on timing): 2 minutes

Come As You Are riff exercise: 2 minutes

Song work: 10 minutes

YOU'LL BE READY TO MOVE ON WHEN…

You can get around 30 chord changes in one minute

You’ve memorized all of the chords you’ve learned so far – A, D, E, Am, Dm, Em, and C

You’re feeling more confident with rhythm and are fairly consistent with keeping the hand moving, preferably with a metronome

You can get through the Come As You Are Riff. Not perfect, but have some fun with it!

You’re able to play at least one song that uses the C Chord most of the way through.

Keep up what you’re doing! You’ve gotten so far already. I'm proud of you.

If you feel unmotivated from the guitar sometimes, know it's normal. We've all been there! Make sure to take breaks and enjoy your practice sessions. The guitar should be a source of pleasure, not pain. Well, some finger sore sometimes. :)

See you on Module 6, where we’ll finally explore how to play the G Chord - with only two fingers! 😯

modules.label: Module 6
modules.title: 6:8 Time, Fast Changes & Alternate Picking
modules.intro:
Welcome to Module 6

It's time to learn the last chord from Grade 1!

Wow! You’ve made it this far - be proud of your progress. I certainly am. 👏 Even if you’re still struggling a bit or if it all feels a little clunky, no worries. It was the same for me, years and years ago. It's the same for Nitsuj - are you following his battles and victories?

Your playing will continue to get better and better over time. It doesn't stop getting better and feeling better! As more you relax into it, the faster you'll learn and sound good.

Now it's time to introduce new lessons into your practice arsenal - if you've ever had any questions, don't hesitate to reach out in the comments below. The JustinGuitar gang is here to help! :)

Let's see what's on the plate for Module 6!

What You'll Learn

This module is different - and we'll start with a beginner alternate picking exercise! 😯

Yes, you've read that right. Things are about to spice up, aren't they?

It's also time to finally meet the G Chord! We'll take a look at a few different grips, and we'll explore when to use each one of them. I can't be impartial here: I love the 2-finger grip we'll learn! I wish my teachers had taught me that way too. :(

But anyway. I learned the hard say so you don't have to. ❤️

Back to lessons - we'll learn all about time signatures! Have you heard about them? So far, we've been playing songs in 4/4, but now we'll start exploring 6/8 songs too!

😅 Once you get one 6/8 strumming pattern down, you can easily make variations. That means it only takes one pattern to play many 6/8 songs out there. :)

In terms of music theory, we'll learn the names of the open strings on the guitar fretboard. That's more practical and cool than you think. :) And, last but not least, you'll know how to force chord changes, so you don't stop in the middle of a song! :)

But...

🚨 There's no new riff in Module 6!

That's because we need to focus on consolidating the skills you already have. You're almost an advancing beginner now, and we need to get your foundations well set. ;)

Ready for some Beginner Alternate Picking Exercise? It's a sort of workout - let's do it!

lessons.title: Beginner Alternate Picking
lessons.summary: Learn how to alternate between up picks and down picks.
lessons.text:
Alternate...Picking?

That means exactly that - alternating the way you pick individual strings.

And it might be more challenging than it sounds!

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, we've been only using down strums up to this point. Now it's time to conquer alternate picking - a technique that you'll need to play the riffs and solos!

We'll start simple and make sure we get a solid foundation! Firstly, you must understand the pick angle’s importance and how that will influence how fast you can play! And guess what? Pick angle also affects strumming, so that lesson will help you out even if you're not planning to play songs that require alternate picking strings.

As we go through this course, we'll incorporate more lessons on alternate picking and ways to improve your technique. So don’t rush - getting the basics down in a reliable way is the best thing you can do to thrive in the Intermediate Foundation!

🎸 Improving alternate picking is an ongoing process for most guitar players - including myself! :)

The Right Angle For Your Pick

When it comes to alternate picking, the angle of your pick is essential. Try this:

Hold the pick completely flat against the string and try to pick it down and up. You might find it’s pretty challenging to get a good rhythm going without the pick. You're just catching on the strings and making things all lumpy.

If you start picking notes across different strings and your pick is parallel to the strings, that will cause you many problems. You’ll be likely to catch the wrong notes by accident and the one you want to hit!

Awful, isn't it? Now let's fix that! Thy this:

Instead of holding your pick flat, try holding it at an angle. You should hit the string with the edge of the pick than with the flat side of it. You’ll find that the guitar pick glides much more easily across the string.

Eventually, you'll be able to build up more speed this way. For example, you might use one edge of the pick for going down and the other for going up.

Life is much easier now, eh? :) But we won't stop there!

Here's The Secret: In and Out

Once you're comfortable holding the pick at an angle, it's to unveil the secret! Instead of thinking about alternate guitar picking as down and up, you should think in and out.

Let me explain:

👉 In - the pick goes towards the guitar. 👉 Out - the pick goes away from the guitar.

Again, this isn’t something that you’ll be using a whole lot as a beginner guitar player, but it’s a great habit to get into. It'll make you a better intermediate guitarist. ;)

I didn't learn this way but really wish I had.

How to Practice Alternate Picking

The best way to practice is by taking it slow! Remember accuracy over speed. Speed will come over time if you get things right!

This is all you have to do to practice alternate picking as a beginner guitar player:

Pick a string and get comfortable picking it back and forth. Be aware of the in and out, up and down movement.

You can vary the strings you choose, so it doesn't get boring! Also, picking on the thicker strings will feel different from picking on the thinner strings. :)

⚡️ Extra Tip: A powerful exercise is to alternate between picking with the pick parallel to the strings and then picking with the pick angled to the strings. That will help you better understand the difference between the two movements. Observation and practice are key to master that angle!

Wants to go further? If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, just be patient - we'll get there very soon! :) If not, feel free to check out my Technique Guitar Lessons: more advanced guitar lessons are available over there.

Thanks, Troy!

Much of what I know about alternate picking comes from the most extreme picking nerd that ever lived - a dude based in New York called Troy Grady. He's got a fantastic website called Cracking The Code, which delves deep into picking and the different approaches to playing fast and clean.

Cracking The Code is not for beginners, but it's super exciting. The depth to which he (still) studies guitar picking is insane, in a beautiful way. :) So bookmark his site, and when you're done with the basics, check that out! I am still learning a lot from his adventures, and you probably will too!

Now let's check into the G Chord… HACKED!

lessons.title: The G Chord... hacked!
lessons.summary: This is the ultimate G Chord hack. I struggled with it for years, but you don't have to! :)
lessons.text:
Following my Beginner Guitar Course?

That's the last essential open chords you need to learn!

And the good news doesn’t stop here. :) Even if you're a random student (nice to meet you, by the way!) that just wants to nail the G Chord, you'll love this guitar lesson.

🍀 The G Chord is one of the toughest ones for many beginner guitar players, but it won't be for you!

I've found you an incredible trick that makes just so much sense it should be the rule. We'll learn how to play the G Chord using only two fingers, and that's awesome because:

💡 It's easier to play, and it sounds better, cleaner, and brighter.

We'll also learn the traditional three-finger G Chord, and you'll be able to choose which grip you want to use. But here's a heads-up: the traditional G Chord gave me a ton of problems back when I was a beginner.

I just couldn’t deal with it.

I even went out of my way to find songs that didn’t use that chord. :) It was a little too stretchy for me, and I couldn’t get my fingers to bend the way they wanted me to. It was just a mess.

So now, I'll encourage you to learn the G chord that I wish they had taught me when I first learned how to play guitar. Then, stick to the end of this guitar lesson, and you'll know the traditional version as well!

We have a few things to check out, so let's get started.

The G Chord: 2-Finger Grip

For this simplified version of the G chord, you just need Finger 2 on the thickest string on Fret 3 - and let it lay slightly flat, so it mutes String 5. Finger 3 goes down on Fret 3 on the thinnest string.

That's it! Boom! 🪄

You’ve got two fingers down and one muted string. The muted string will happen pretty naturally, so you almost don’t even need to worry about it.

And the rest of the strings are open! Take a look at the diagram:

The G Chord: 3-Finger Grip

The full version of the G chord uses one extra finger. Your index finger goes to the Fret 2 on String 5 - the one we've muted in the 2-finger version.

That means you have to be sure you're not muting the 5th string with your 2nd finger! I’ve always found that the addition of the 1st finger makes the chord harder to play, but you should give it a try and decide for yourself. Take a look at the diagram:

Chord changes are harder with this grip too! With the two-finger version, chord changes are a breeze! :)

How to Practice the G Chord

I’m sure you already know! :) It's time for your Chord Perfect Practice Exercise. You can start with the 2-finger version, but you practice a bit with the full version to register it in your mental chord bank.

Now… have you heard about Time Signatures?

lessons.title: About Time Signatures
lessons.summary: Everything a beginner needs to know about time signatures is here!
lessons.text:
What is Time Signature?

And why you need to know that as a guitar player!

Alright, let’s get into counting and know what a time signature is.

Every song has a time signature, and they usually maintain one time signature for the entirety of the song. A time signature is just the way we describe the feelings of the beats in a bar. :)

Of course, it involves some music theory, but this guitar lesson will be about the practical understanding of time signatures. If you'd like to learn more about music theory, check out the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course.

Now let's get started!

Time Signatures - What's 4/4

Songs in 4/4 have for beats per bar. When we count beats, we say "1, 2, 3, 4." When playing songs in 4:4, we tend to accentuate the first beat of each bar.

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, all the songs we've learned so far are in 4/4. But, we’re about to change that!

Time Signatures - Meet 6/8

6/8 is another time signature, and it's a pretty common one! 6/8 songs have six beats per bar, and when we count them, we say "1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6." When playing in 6/8 time, we tend to accent beats 1 and 4, so it's two groups of three pulses.

The > is the symbol we use to show an accented beat. For example, a primary 6/8 looks like this:

> > 1 2 3 4 5 6

Now let's check out the next time signature!

Time Signatures - Meet 3/4

Another typical time signature you might encounter is 3/4 time. That one has just 3 beats per bar, and it gives that familiar waltz feel. If we divide 3:4 time with 'ands' between the beats, we also end up with 6 pulses in a bar, but the accents’ placement differs from 6:8. Here's how we'd found a 3/4 time:

> > > 1 + 2 + 3 +

They are pretty similar, and you don't have to overthink any of this. You're much better off just listening and feeling the rhythm for these things. :)

Getting Used to 6/8 Songs

You'll find different time signatures in many diverse music styles! The 6/8 time is more common in pop music, so we'll focus on that one for now.

The best way to get better acquainted with a time signature like 6:8 is to just listen to songs that use it. While listening, count out loud along with the music, “1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6,” just so you can hear the beats and the accents.

Here are some songs you can listen to using 6:8:

• This Year’s Love David Gray

• Everybody Hurts REM

• Fade Into You Mazzy Star

• Nothing Else Matters Metallica

• Hide Your Love Away - The Beatles

• Kiss from A Rose Seal

How to Practice 6/8 Songs

When playing 6/8 songs, think of six down strums to a bar of music.

When we learned 4/4, each beat was a down strum with your up strums representing your and beats, remember? It's the same here, but now we have six down strums per bar.

Practice with a metronome set to somewhere around 130 BPM. You'll play one down strum per beat while counting out loud. Once you’ve got that down, work on accenting beats 1 and 4 with the stronger accent on beat 1.

Like with 4/4 time, the most important thing is keeping your hand moving all the time, no matter the strumming pattern. So try to train your arms to get that consistent movement down.

If you want extra help practicing rhythm, check out the JustinGuitar Time Trainer Metronome. Next, we'll learn the most useful 6/8 strumming pattern for beginners

lessons.title: A 6:8 Strumming Pattern
lessons.summary: The ONLY 6/8 strumming pattern you need to worry about is here!
lessons.text:
Digging 6/8 Songs?

It's time to learn how to play them!

You should be familiar with the concept of time signatures, so you should have started getting a feel for 6/8 songs. Now it's time to practice some strumming patterns in that time signature!

As always, I recommend you start pretty easy. If you haven’t practiced strumming one down strum per beat, go ahead and give that a go. It’s always helpful to count out loud as you get started. That will significantly help you nail accenting the beats!

In 6:8 time, we should accent Beat 1 and Beat 4, though to a lesser extent than Beat 1! Now let's check out that cool strumming pattern. :)

6:8 Strumming Pattern for Beginners

To play this 6/8 strumming pattern, we'll skip beats 2 and 5 and hit some up strums in between! It's a helpful pattern to get down - you should be able to use it in most 6/8 songs out there.

To help you understand it, we'll explore three strumming pattern variations, and I've even included music notations if you dig that! It's ok to be curious about that stuff, but don't worry or overthink that just now.

Here are they:

🎸 Check out the video lesson to play these strumming patterns along with me. :)

Extra Strumming Tips for Beginners

No matter the time signature, there are a few things that will make your strumming sounding better. Here are a few tips for you:

Ensure your strumming arm keeps moving even when you don't play a beat!

The metronome should be your best friend! Find a good tempo that works for you!

Don't add any chords until you're comfortable with the strumming movement.

Once you get comfortable with the strumming pattern we've just learned, try to vary it up a bit. You can add additional up strum after the 6th beat - it sounds great!

You should get creative and explore what feels and sounds good to you. :)

Now let's get into some theory and learn the open string note names on the fretboard!

lessons.title: Open String Note Names
lessons.summary: It's time to learn the open string note names on the guitar fretboard.
lessons.text:
No More Thickest or Thinnest Strings!

It's time to learn the real name for open strings on the guitar. :)

In the early stages of the beginner guitar journey, it's okay that we call the guitar strings by numbers or whatever. But you should know they've all got a name, and learning them will help take you further!

We'll probably still refer to those notes in other ways (especially when learning songs or grips!), but all players must know the note names, and that's what we're doing today.

If you'd like to know more about the theory behind music, check out the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course. It's a music theory course for guitar players made by guitar players. :)

Now let's get started with some mnemonics to help up remember the open string note names on the guitar.

Mnemo… WHAT?

Have you all heard of or used mnemonics before? They’re handy little words that we can use to help us remember words or concepts in a specific order.

We'll use mnemonics to memorize the names of the strings on a guitar. After some practice, the names will become familiar, and you'll be able to ditch those mnemonics. For now, let them make your journey easier!

Here's one of the most common English mnemonics for the open string note names:

Eddie

Ate

Dynamite

Good

Bye

Eddie

If you look at the first letter in each word, they are E, A, D, G, B, and E. These are the names of your strings - thickest to thinnest. :)

What About the String Numbers?

I should mention that when numbering strings, we tend to go in the opposite direction. So we usually call the thinnest string the 1st string and the thickest string the 6th string.

You’ll notice that the thickest and thinnest strings are E. Calling them by their string numbers helps distinguish the high E (thinnest) from the low E (thickest).

Make Up Your Mnemonics

Don’t you like the dynamite mnemonic? No biggie – just make one up yourself! :)

It can be anything you like as long as each word starts with the strings’ names in the correct order. Get creative, find something meaningful to you, and go with that. Whatever you choose, remember that the goal is to commit the string names to memory.

If you want to make up your mnemonics, let me know in the comments below! That's always super fun. :)

Now let's learn how to force those chord changes, so you don't stop when playing songs!

lessons.title: Forcing Chord Changes
lessons.summary: Can't change chords fast enough to properly play a song? Let's fix that!
lessons.text:
Is your strumming sloppy because you stop playing to change chords?

Here's what you need to know!

The one thing worse than misplaying chords in a song is sloppy rhythm. This lesson is for you if you struggle to change chords fast enough to keep strumming when playing a song.

First, you should know that this is a common problem for many beginner guitar players. Many people tend to fumble their fingers around a bit to get to the next chord in time for that perfect strum.

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you know that consistent strumming makes the real difference when playing songs. And that even non-musicians can notice a sloppy rhythm - so let's check out a few ways of forcing chord changes so you don't stop a song in the middle of it.

4 Tricks to Get Faster Chord Changes

Practice with a metronome. That helps you build a solid rhythm foundation and develop your inner sense of time, so you don't have to worry too much about your strumming hand.

Take some time to practice the chord changes that are harder for you! The One Minute Changes Exercise is your best friend. :) Push your fingers out of their comfort zone! The timer can add some pressure, but it gets easier with practice. Use My Practice Assistant to keep track of your progress!

Keep your hands moving. Even if you miss a chord, keep going with the rhythm. Skip a chord if needed, but don't stop the strumming hand from moving. I promise - most people won't notice if you miss a chord!

Play with the Lesson & Songs App! When you play along with my song app, you have to keep playing the song - the backing track won't stop if you miss a chord. That is excellent for getting you to force chord changes. ;) You can try out the APP for free, and then there's a subscription fee - check out the details here.

Now… let's play some songs?

lessons.title: Songs For Module 6
lessons.summary: Songs you can play to practice the techniques and chords we've learned so far.
lessons.text:
It's time to grow your repertoire!

Here are some songs to choose from.

At this point in your guitar journey, find songs you love to play and push yourself. It's SO important to make the most out of everything you've learned so far. This includes playing all the essential 8 open chords, 6:8 strumming patterns, and those chord changes.

I want you to take a moment and be proud of what you've learned so far. Learn guitar is HARD - and you've made so much progress already! Stay motivated - and keep going! :)

Check out these song tutorials to practice the G chord and put into practice everything you've learned so far on your guitar.

4 Easy Guitar Songs Using the G Chord

Here are songs using the G chord songs mixed with chords you're already familiar with:

Hey Joe - Jimi Hendrix. This song uses all of the 5 major chords. So you'll be able to practice some solid chord changes, specifically the G to D and A to E chord change. This song is also great to recap all the material you've learned so far!

This Year's Love - David Gray. A beautiful song to work on the 6:8 strumming pattern and using all our chords you're familiar with. It uses the guitar strumming pattern you learn earlier in this module.

Mad World - Gary Jules. Just a super cool song with plenty of G in it. In this song lesson, I show you some fancy things you can have a try at too.

Country Roads - John Denver. Using the G, C, D, and Em chords. It also has a sneaky F major 7, but use Am chord for a simple alternative. This song is available to play along with my Lessons & Songs App - which is a fun way to learn it!

More Guitar Songs Using the G Chord

Here are some more options to add to your G chord repertoire. I hope you find something you like :)

Wish You Were Here - Pink Floyd. Learn a simplified version of this iconic guitar riff, and explore the rhythm too.

Heroes - David Bowie. I'm still sad that he's no longer with us. He was a hero. This is a fabulous song using only the G, D, Am, and Em chords.

Heart Of Gold - Neil Young Great. A song by an iconic guitar player. Some fancy riffs going on, but you can leave them out.

How To Save A Life - The Fray. A lovely song with the classic G, C, D, and chords.

Get Inspired And Play The Songs You Love

Find songs you really dig - it'll inspire you to keep practicing! :)

If you need inspiration and more song options, I have a few options for you. First, check out the main songs page of my website. Filter the songs by the chords you've learned so far, or by the genre you prefer. With lots of beginner song options - you're set to find something you like for your guitar skills! If you're already using my Lessons & Songs App - you can filter songs this way too!

Spotify Playlist Module 6

Here's the Spotify Playlist for recommended songs for Module 6 guitar players. Some of these are classic rocks songs - hope you dig then. :)

Keep your motivation strong, and keep practicing consistently! You've already got so much guitar knowledge - and there's more fun stuff on the way.

lessons.title: Module 6 Practice
lessons.summary: Get ready to set up an effective practice routine for all the skills you're learnt in Module 6 :)
lessons.text:
Congrats - you completed Module 6!

You can play loads of songs, can't you? :)

At this stage, you've learned all 8 essential open chords, meaning you can jam too many songs, which is so much FUN.

Now, it's time to perfect those guitar skills with a 20-minute practice routine. Feel free to tailor this routine to your needs—focus on practicing what challenges you the most.

This routine covers everything we've learned in Module 6. Here are some guitar practice tips to remember:

I recommend committing to 4 practice sessions a week.

Don't over-practice - it can lead to finger pain.

Start getting familiar with your guitar rhythm.

Play around with alternate fingerpicking and explore different options.

Play the songs you love - so many options now that you've learned the G chord. :)

Use the right pick - thinner picks are more suitable for beginners.

Stay motivated - you're almost finished Grade 1!

💡 Under the video, click 'Practice' and save the pre-made routine for Module 6. You can edit and access the items on your Dashboard.

Make the Most Out of Your Practice Time

If you don't already know, the best way to practice the guitar is to use My Practice Assistant, free for all users! My Practice Assistant is a fantastic tool to keep you accountable and motivated. :)

Log in to your JustinGuitar account to make the most of your time and track your progress. Once logged in, go to your Dashboard, select the Practice tab, and off you go! Feel free to edit your routine items to suit your needs.

20-MINUTE PRACTICE BREAKDOWN

Here is my recommendation for a typical 20-minute practice session at this stage:

Finger Stretch: 1 minute

Alternate Picking String (Focus on pick angles, wrist, and arm movements): 1 minute

G Chord Perfect: 2 minutes

Perfect Chord You Struggle: 1 minute

OMC G to C: 1 minute

OMC G to D: 1 minute

OMC C to D (or most challenging one): 1 minute

Strumming 6:8: 2 minutes

Song work: 10 minutes

YOU'LL BE READY TO MOVE ON WHEN…

You can get around 30 chord changes in one minute.

You've memorized all the chords you've learned so far – A, D, E, Am, Dm, Em, C, and G.

You've explored alternate picking on a single string. You've also experienced the dramatic differences that picking angles can have in your guitar playing.

You've tried strumming in 6:8, preferably with a metronome. Even if you still find it tricky, you should be able to anticipate the click and tempo.

You can play at least one song (using the G chord) most of the way through. Hey Joe by Jimi Hendrix is a top song choice because you'll put into practice all the five major shapes!

The key here is to stay motivated! Loads of fun stuff to learn in Module 7, so keep going. Up next, you'll learn more about dynamics, grooving, and how to make your guitar sound better.

modules.label: Module 7
modules.title: Air Changes, Dynamics & Consolidation!
modules.intro:
Congratulations!

You've made it to the end of Grade 1 :)

I'm proud of you! If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you know how to play all the essential open chords for beginners. :) You should be comfortable with the most common strumming pattern for 4/4 of the songs so you can play easy tunes and even some riffs.

Not bad, eh? :)

Now it's time to consolidate all the techniques we've learned. By the end of this module, you'll have all the basics you need to become an advancing beginner player. From there, things get more and more exciting!

But before we talk about Grade 2, let's check out what's on the menu for Module 7 - the last one of the white grade!

What You'll Learn

Before introducing new skills, we'll explore the chords you know and tricks to improve your playing. You have eight chords in your pocket, but which chord changes are worth practicing? The answer is in the very next lessons!

We'll also explore ways to make you sound better and get into the groove! A good strumming pattern is about feeling good, and that's easier to say than to do. But I've got you covered here. ;)

I'll also answer some of the questions I get the most about music theory, ear training, and practice routines. Having goals in mind is a big deal when it comes to playing guitar. And we'll talk about that too!

Now, let's get started! And don't worry - by the end of the module, you'll know if you're ready to pass Grade 1!

lessons.title: The 8 Essential Beginner Chord Grips
lessons.summary: Before moving on to more advanced lessons, let’s review the eight chords we’ve covered so far.
lessons.text:
SO MANY SONGS YOU CAN PLAY!

Here are the eight essential grips you need to become a campfire guitar player :)

Do you know that incredible feeling of sitting around a campfire, grabbing the guitar, and playing hits your friends will sing along with you? You basically need these eight open chords!

Of course, you can - and should! - stick around and get into some chord variations and even barre chords. But true is - there are hundreds of popular songs you can play using only those eight grips.

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you'll already be familiar with many things we'll explore here. If you're struggling with some of these grips, you might learn something that will help you out! This guitar lesson is an excellent revision of many techniques we've learned so far.

Let's check that out?

Chord Perfect Practice

This exercise is the best, and you should use it whenever practicing a new guitar chord. It's very simple, and it consists of checking out all notes in the chord to make sure they all sound clear.

When you find a string that's not sounding well, you should work specifically on it. Observe your finger position and try to figure out what's going on.

Many guitar players will struggle with the same problems - so let me show you the most common ones and how you can fix them!

1. The D Chord

Many beginner guitar players find the D Chord the hardest one of these. The best way of getting it down is by practicing it, so just stick with it!

Take a look at the diagram:

Here are a few problems you might encounter and my advice to get it right:

Ensure you're using your fingertips. If the fingers flatten out, the 3rd finger will probably mute the thinnest string.

Get the fingers as close to the frets as possible, especially that 3rd finger. It's the positive finger placement, remember?

You shouldn't play the thickest two strings! This can be difficult, so try and do your best here. If you can't perfectly avoid the thickest strings, don't let that stop you from playing songs.

Now let's check out the A Chord.

2. The A Chord

We've learned two different fingerings to play the A Chord! I recommend you stick with the following one. It sounds better, and it's easier to play. Take a look at the diagram:

Here are a few common beginner mistakes when playing the A Chord on guitar:

Don't play the thickest string. It’s not the worst if you do, but better to learn not to. Tune your ears to be aware of what the chord should sound like. That way, you’ll know when something is off.

Be sure you can hear the thinnest string ringing out. If you can’t hear it, you might be accidentally muting it with your 3rd finger.

Ready for the E Chord?

3. The E Chord

You might find the E Chord is easier to play than A and D! Take a look at the diagram:

You should play all the strings when strumming the E Chord! So, focus on the correct finger position on the guitar fretboard, and you'll nail it.

Be careful to not mute any string by accident, and there you go - a perfect E Chord. :)

Remember, you can use anchor fingers to switch faster between chords! Now let's check out the Am Chord!

4. The Am Chord

The Am Chord looks a lot like the E Chord - you only need to move down a string! Take a look at the diagram:

Just like in A Major Chord, you shouldn't play the thickest string when strumming the A Minor Chord. That's your big challenge here!

Now, let's check out the Em Chord.

5. The E Minor Chord

Here's an easy one, right? But there's a common mistake many beginners make. Before we explore that, take a look at the Em diagram:

Yes, it's probably the easiest open chord ever. But if you accidentally mute the G string (3rd string) string, you'll sound like playing E Major, not E Minor. Be aware of that!

Want to go further and understand the relationship between majors and minors? Check out the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course! :)

Now let's get strumming the Dm chord.

6. The D Minor Chord

The Dm can be a bit tricky for many of you, but practice will help you out. :) Take a look at the D Minor diagram:

I recommend you use the 4th finger to play the second string! It's ok to use the 3rd finger, but you do eventually need to make your pinky stronger, and this presents an excellent opportunity to do so. It also brings chord change benefits. :)

Don't play the thickest two strings at all. It just sounds wrong!

We're almost there! Let's check out the C Chord.

7. The C Chord

I love teaching the C Chord! It's an excellent grip to practice a few little guitar tricks. Take a look at the diagram:

When playing the C Chord, you must make sure your fingers aren't square on the strings. Keep them at an angle!

Your 3rd finger can be flatter than the others, so it mutes the thickest string. The C Chord doesn't include the thickest string, so if you make your 3rd finger slightly flatter, you'll mute that unwanted note. :)

#guitartricks, eh? Muting the thickest string is essential when playing the C Chord. That trick is the difference between sounding great and sounding… beginner.

Last but not least, the G Chord!

8. The G Chord

You've probably learned the G Chord using three fingers, haven't you? Me too - and I struggled so much with that. I recommend you stick with a 2-finger version. It's easier to play, and it sounds better too! Take a look at the diagram below:

You should lay your 2nd finger down flat when playing this grip, so it mutes the 5th string.

Now let's learn the best chord changes to practice, so you optimize your guitar time!

lessons.title: Best Chord Changes To Work On
lessons.summary: Too many chord changes to practice? Focus on those ones!
lessons.text:
Get the most out of your time!

Here are the best chord changes to practice.

So, you've got some open chords in your pocket but aren't sure which chord changes you should master? This lesson will help you out!

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you're familiar with the One Minute Changes Exercise. But you've learned eight chords so far - that would be 56 chord changes to practice. Are they all worth it? Not really!

Optimize Your Time!

Speaking for personal experience, I know that we don’t always have as much time to dedicate to practicing as we’d sometimes like. That means we have to prioritize!

Some chord changes aren't essential to practice, such as D to Dm or E to Em. You might see those chords next to each other in some songs, but it's not common. When those exceptions happen, you should practice them.

Daily, you might want to focus on chord changes you're likely to encounter, like A to D or C to G!

💡 You could make a graphic with the chord changes you want to practice. You can also try out my Beginner Song App or My Practice Assistant, excellent tools to keep track of your progress.

Check out a list of 25 chord changes all beginner guitar players should practice!

My 25 Most Important Changes

A,C

A,G

A,E

A,Em

A,D

A,Dm

C,G

C,E

C,D

C,Dm

C,Am

C,Em

G,E

G,D

G,Dm

G,Am

G,Em

E,D

E,Dm

E,Am

D,Am

D,Em

Dm,Am

Dm,Em

Am,Em

Now it's time to get faster chord changes. Let's air change!

lessons.title: Air Changes (aspire to this!)
lessons.summary: Save time using air changes and play sounds without interrupting the rhythm. :)
lessons.text:
Ready for a new approach to chord changes?

It's time to air change!

When learning a new chord, I always recommend you practice by placing your fingers on the strings one at a time in finger-number order. That's great to develop muscle memory and automatize the chords in your head.

When it comes to chord changes, the truth is - putting your fingers down at the same time should be your ultimate goal! That will save you time between chord changes, and ultimately, you'll sound better and more relaxed.

My trick to do that is by air changing! Let's dive into it. :)

Air Chord Changes for Beginners

Essentially, we change the chords in the air, forming the shape of the chord grips before the fingers even make contact with the strings. By getting them into position ahead of time, you can more quickly and easily plop them all down on the strings and strum the chord.

These air changes become essential when you develop your guitar skills. If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, it's time to make air changes your goal. For now, practice forming the chord grips in the air, placing the grip on the strings, and then strumming the chord.

Once you’re comfortable with the concept of air changes, you can incorporate it into your One Minute Changes Exercise and Chord Perfect Practice. Many of you will find you already change chords in the air, and that's great. :)

💡 A good chord pairing to try air changes is G to C. All of the fingers change when switching between these two chords, so it's a great but fun challenge.

Don't feel at all frustrated if you find this very difficult. Nitsuj surely did! That is the kind of thing you should aspire to, but it's likely to take you some months of work and something you'll work on for some time to come!

Now let me tell you a little secret.

lessons.title: Open Strings Between Changes
lessons.summary: Sometimes hitting the open strings between chord changes helps the tune sound easy and relaxed. It’s not “wrong” if it sounds good!
lessons.text:
Sometimes, open strings will sound between changes

And that's ok!

Open strings ringing out between chord changes is probably something you’ve heard - and you've done! - loads of times without even noticing it. That means some strings are ringing out in between fretted chords, usually with a lighter up strum!

Open strings ringing out before chord changes can work as accidental embellishment, which sounds pretty cool. They can help make chord changes feel less clunky and jerky and give more groove to your playing.

Hitting the strings between changes doesn’t always sound the best, though. You have to train your ears to decide when it's a good idea or now. :) And you shouldn't overthink it too much - just be aware it's something you can take advantage of when playing songs.

If It Sounds Good, It Is Good :)

Now might be a good time to remind you that music is never wrong as long as it sounds good! If you like the way it sounds and if it’s not disrupting the rest of the band, if you’re playing with one, go for it.

🎸 It might not be right, but if it sounds good, it's good!

Now let's make your STRUMMING feel fantastic.

lessons.title: Feel Good Strumming
lessons.summary: When playing music, the technical side is often less important than the way it makes people feel. Learn to get into the vibe!
lessons.text:
You know the biggest secret of strumming!

Keep… your… hands… moving!

If that's not the first time you land at JustinGuitar for a strumming guitar lesson, you've heard it before: the big secret to nailing strumming patterns is to keep your hand moving consistently.

As a beginner, that can be pretty difficult. Your arm might get tired quickly, or maybe you’re worried about the strumming pattern and can't move your arm steadily. The result is your strumming sounding more tense every time you practice!

That's the opposite of what you want! You want your strumming to feel relaxed and effortless.

Here's how you should try to fix that!

Play a pattern you’re already comfortable with, along with a metronome. You should feel relaxed in your hand, arm, and shoulder, but also your mind! Don’t underestimate the impact a busy or worried mind can have on your playing. Get out of your head!

Easier said than done, though, eh?

To get your head into a more relaxed and chill space, you’ve got to get into a happy headspace. What I like to do is to force myself to think happy thoughts. :)

Also, I make myself smile! I know it sounds crazy, but I promise you – it does work. You’ll feel yourself loosening up and not worrying so much about whether or not your strumming is perfect. Ultimately, your strumming will loosen up. Even if the song you’re trying to play is sad, you still want a relaxed strumming arm to get through it.

When practicing this, the chords you play don’t matter, although a Major Chord might help with the happy place thing - check out the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course if you didn't get that joke!

And don't forget - the technical side of playing guitar is important, but people listen to music because of how it makes them feel.

Especially at this consolidation stage, you might find that you can relax your strumming when no chord changes are going on, but when there's more to think about, the tension creeps in. Stay aware when you're playing songs that you need the strumming to be relaxed and feelin' good, and focus on getting one thing right at a time.

👉 When you're practicing chord changes, you're practicing chord changes. 👉 When you're practicing with a metronome, you're practicing with a metronome.

Different skills require extra attention.

Now let me teach you something that will change your playing!

lessons.title: Dynamic Improvements
lessons.summary: Dynamics refer to how loudly or softly you play throughout a song. Learn to do that well and take your playing to the next level!
lessons.text:
Dynamic Changes

Not to be too dramatic, but this might transform your playing!

Simply put, dynamics refer to how loudly or softly you play. And once you get that skill under your belt, you become a better guitar player.

Let me explain.

Often, a song contains different dynamics. They rarely keep one volume straight through the whole tune. When you're playing music on the guitar, you must consider its dynamic changes, so your playing gets more attractive to the audience.

Dynamic changes involve making creative decisions about where to be quiet and loud in the song. Depending on how you choose to do this, it can really impact the mood you’re going for!

When we're beginner guitar players, we can use the same strumming pattern for an entire song. But think about it - that can get really monotonous and boring! Not only for you but your entire audience.

If you understand the principles behind songwriting, you can apply dynamic changes to the songs you’re playing! But, of course, that starts with understanding the basic structure of a song!

Typical Song Structure

Most songs follow this basic structure:

Verse – Verse – Chorus – Verse – Chorus – Bridge – Chorus – Chorus

If you choose a song at random, you’ll find that it likely follows this pattern. Of course, there are exceptions, but this is a good starting point for what we’re talking about today.

Storytelling with Dynamics

Use this structure to guide you. Think of your song as a story you’re telling your audience, with the bridge serving as the story’s big climax. You’ll notice that the bridge will either be very loud or very soft, depending on the song’s storytelling.

When you introduce dynamics into the typical song structure, you’ll usually find choruses are more prominent and louder than the verses. This is because the chorus is the leading hook of the song! It’s the part that people remember, so you want it to be loud and noticeable as a guitar player. That encourages people to sing along with you!

On the other hand, the verses are typically softer. That encourages the audience to listen closely and carefully until… you ramp back up into the chorus!

Changes in dynamics can happen abruptly, or they can happen gradually, slowly building up from soft to loud or vice versa. So again, it depends on the journey you want your audience to go through. :)

How to Practice

When practicing dynamic changes, you want to be able to play the softest you can possibly play and the loudest you can possibly play.

The best way to practice that is by trying it out. First, you should get comfortable with the extremes! Then, try going from loud to soft gradually and then from mild to loud.

If you’re playing with a band, practice these changes with your bandmates. The whole crew should be on the same page as far as the dynamics of a song. It’s definitely something that needs to be addressed, discusses, and agreed upon as a band.

Everything is Relative!

When it comes to playing music, never forget that it’s an art form! There are rules and guidelines, yes, but at the end of the day, the music you play is an expression of you.

Play the song how you like it best and/or how you think your audience will best receive it. Don’t be afraid to experiment with different dynamic changes until you find something that sounds good to you.

Remember – you’re trying to convey an emotion to your listeners. You want them to walk away from your performance feeling something. So even if you screw up a few chord changes here and there, their lasting impression will be more about how your song made them feel.

Now let's learn how to memorize some easy songs. :)

lessons.title: Memorize Easy Songs
lessons.summary: Learn how to memorize easy songs on guitar so that you have something to play anywhere you go!
lessons.text:
In this lesson, you'll learn some quick tips on how to memorize guitar songs. In reality, you're not going to carry your own songbook everywhere you go. So, you need a backup plan in place!

At some point, you might even find yourself at a party with someone that would love to hear you jam! It's in those special moments that it's fantastic to know some easy songs from memory. Here's how to make sure you've always got a few songs ready to play on guitar! I'll also give you some guitar song suggestions that are super easy to memorize!

How To Memorize Easy Songs On Guitar

First, you want to learn a couple of simple songs. They should only have a couple of chords with simple strumming patterns. It's also a good idea that the chords included are some that you enjoy playing. But most importantly, pick songs you really love - they will always be more memorable to you!

The goal is to build an internal song repertoire of 4-5 songs. To memorize them, focus on remembering the chord order and progression. Make sure only to pick very repetitive songs with simple verses.

Why You Should Memorize Songs On Guitar

I know it can be tempting and seem more impressive to show off complex songs to your peers. But it's more pleasant for everyone - and less stressful for you - if you can easily play songs from memory. In addition, you want to be able to play them with confidence.

This way, you won't find yourself scrolling around your phone trying to find chords online. Of course, in the long term, you'll eventually memorize more difficult guitar songs. I know it's tempting, but for now, keep it simple!

Easy Songs To Memorize On Guitar

Here are some of my party favourite songs that are great to memorize, with different chord options! Note: the link for 'Get Lucky' is to a ukulele, not guitar, lesson.

Easy guitar songs using 2 chords:

Dance The Night Away - The Mavericks (one bar each, D to A)

Songs for Module 1 with super easy 2 chords songs!

Sing - Ed Sheeran (four bars each, Em to Am)

Songs for Module 3 (Using the Am and Em Army!)

Easy guitar songs using 3 chords:

Johnny B. Goode - Chuck Berry (12-bar form, A D E)

Wild Thing - the Troggs (A D E D, half bar each)

Songs for Module 2(A, D, and E)

Easy guitar songs using 4 chords & repetitive patterns:

Get Lucky - Daft Punk (one bar each, Am C Em D)

Knockin' On Heaven's Door (G D Am G D C, half bars on G and D, whole bars on Am and C)

Now, these are only some of my favorite easy songs to memorize. These easy options are also great to start memorizing. If you're looking for more song options, use the filter tool on my website. Choose the chords and fave artists to filter through our massive song repertoire. Loads of songs - with each their own song lessons - available for you to get inspired!

Want even more easy song options?! Download my Lessons & Songs App and choose from hundreds of songs suitable for your guitar level.

lessons.title: Why do Ear Training?
lessons.summary: Many beginners don’t like interval training but trust me – it’s super helpful and we can do it together!
lessons.text:
Ear Training Takes You Further!

And it's so rewarding :)

When you think about it, we listen to music with our ears, so nothing makes more sense than training our ears. But, unfortunately, many guitar players don't seem to pay much attention to that, so they can never reach a further stage in their guitar development.

Ear training is one thing where it’s hard to convey its value to people who have never done it. But think of it as some superpower - just like Music Theory! And it also rewards you with that gratification feeling!

I won’t lie – a lot of beginners don’t like doing this! But if you bear with me, it’ll all be worth it. I created a practical ear training course that can take you further. Let me show you. :)

The JustinGuitar Ear Training Course

I developed an ear training course that's fast and effective! You'll feel like having a private session with me - and I'll give you all the tools and exercises you need to thrive in your journey! Your ears will be stronger before you even realize it.

One of the primary things we'll go over in the ear training course is interval training. This helps you hear the distance between two pitches. Later on, when you’re figuring out tunes - transcribing! - interval training is super helpful.

When You Should Start

The JustinGuitar Ear Training Course is there for you. You can start if and when you want to, but I recommend getting started with it early on in your guitar-playing journey. :)

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, the end of Grade 1 is excellent! You can already play guitar, so you can dedicate some time to develop your ears.

Hear Music Differently

As a beginner, ear training will help you hear music differently. Think of it as an artist who has to look at the world differently to capture it on a canvas. :) You'd be able to pick out under and overtones of colors and seeing lines and angles in a two-dimensional way rather than three-dimensional!

To master an artistic craft, you have to be able to understand it in a more in-depth way than you’d previously done. For musicians, ear training is a part of that process. The more you train up your ear and the stronger it gets, you’ll start to hear things you hadn’t before, even in songs you’ve listened to thousands of times!

You’ll hear the different parts and voices in the music, focusing on specific elements within the song and hearing how they all come together.

🎤 Speaking of voices - if you’re a singer, ear training will help you stay on pitch and harmonize better.

How to Practice

For interval training, we usually start by identifying intervals and relating them to popular songs, like the Wedding March. The more you practice listening, the better you’ll get at recognizing standard intervals.

As with everything we've learned so far - start slowly and take it at your own pace! The earlier you start, the better. Ear training is always a good thing to be aware of, regardless of how advanced a musician you are.

Click here and get started with the JustinGuitar Ear Training Course now!

lessons.title: Why study Music Theory?
