lessons.summary: Music theory is the reason behind everything and it helps us make sense of music. So I’ve got a music theory course just for you! :)
lessons.text:
Learn Music Theory The Way I Wish I Did :)

In a practical and helpful way!

My first experience with music theory was just awful. I was a 15 years old punk rocker, and they showed me classical music that I couldn't connect with at all. Unfortunately, that's still the reality in the classroom.

Many music schools and private teachers will start students off with some music theory with no practical application! That can put people off from music altogether or create a tension between practical and theoretical knowledge.

So I decided to change that, and I created the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course - a course wrote by a guitar player for guitar players.

I tend to take a practical approach, enabling you to make music faster and easier. Think of it as some sort of shortcut! By learning the theory behind music, you'll be able to make it yourself. :)

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you may have noticed that music theory hasn’t been much of a thing so far in this course. I may have mentioned it here or there, but it hasn’t been the primary driver of learning how to play the guitar.

That's because I wanted to get you playing first of all. That's what guitar is all about, isn't it? But as you become a more intermediate-ish guitar player, music theory will be handy. Later on, it can be another superpower you add to your pocket.

Why Should You Start Learning Music Theory?

The short answer for that is: you'll be able to understand what you're doing. Only that should be enough reason for you to stick with music theory, but there's a world of awesome stuff that will come with it! In addition, music theory gives you skillsets that will quickly teach you how to make music, particularly when composing and improvising.

Learning music theory includes learning how to manipulate chords, for example. That means that you'll be able to learn just one chord and then change it into another one. :)

► By understanding the basic chord structure, we can apply the concept to your practice routine. Like that, you don't have to memorize thousands of chords, their names, and all of their possible variations!

Another fundamental concept is learning which chords belong in a particular key. By knowing that, you'll know which chords relate to each other, so you don’t have to guess which ones sound good together.

When you’re writing a song, you choose a key and work within it. That will save you tons of time and headaches. It’ll also keep you from throwing some wonky chord into your tune by accident – unless wonky is what you want!

But it's crucial that you always take the time - and put in the effort! - to ensure that you know how to apply your knowledge in the real world.

Music theory can be what separates you from an eternal advancing beginner to an intermediate guitar player. But to do that, you have to practice the concepts, and that's what I want to inspire you to do from day 1!

Check out the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course and learn to make music!

lessons.title: How to PASS Grade 1
lessons.summary: We’re finally at the end of Grade 1! :) Let's recap on what you need to know before you move on.
lessons.text:
You're almost a Grade 1 Guitar Player! :)

You did that!

It must be awesome to see your guitar progress through all these weeks. All thanks to your hard work and passion for learning. :)

As we wrap up Grade 1 of the JustinGuitar Beginner Course, let's recap what you've learned so far. This lesson will give you an idea of what you should be confident doing before moving on to Grade 2. Focus on practicing the things you struggle with the most.

Use this information to guide your practice in the next few weeks. If you're not there yet, set them as goals you want to accomplish. Then, track your progress by adding them as practice elements to your practice routine.

Let's first check out 5 things you should focus on to pass Grade 1.

How To Pass Grade 1

#1 You should be able to tune your guitar with a tuner.

If you've been playing for a little while, I'm hopeful that you know how to tune your guitar. It's super important you get this fundamental guitar skill figured out on your own.

#2 Memorize and play the 8 essential beginner chords on the guitar.

The goal is to say the chord's name and play it straight away - without even thinking! These 8 essential beginner chords are A, D, E, Am, Dm, Em, C, G.

Aim to play all 8 chords perfectly. Mute the strings that should be muted, and make sure they all ring out correctly. You should be able to play them from memory, in any order, straight away. Get the right sound from these chords at least 50 % of the time.

#3 Play 30 chord changes in 1 minute.

This makes for 2 seconds on each chord. It might seem like a lot - but it's totally possible. Eventually, you'll be able to do 60 changes per minute, but 30 changes is a realistic goal for now. If you're not there yet, keep practicing using the one-minute changes exercises. Each time you change chords, you're counting 30 chord movements in 1 minute. Do this with any chord pairing you've learned in the beginner course so far.

#4 Play The Old Faithful strumming pattern consistently at 80 beats per minute.

Put your metronome at 80 beats per minute and play along. You should stay with the metronome and play the strumming the old faithful pattern on the right counts. Now, we've talked a bit about adding variations. That's totally fine! Make sure your hand keeps moving if you're adding and removing strums here and there.

Remember, your strums should be automated and continuous. An excellent way to test this out is to distract yourself by looking at something else and see if the strumming pattern continues.

#5 Memorize 5 easy songs.

We've already talked about memorizing easy songs with simple chord progressions. Aim to play comfortably 5 songs that you know from memory that you can play at a party anytime. I recommend simple repetitive chord progressions so that it's consistent all the way through. That way, it's all you need to play the whole song through.

See if Nitsuj is ready for Grade 2

Practice frustration - it's part of the guitar journey. Sometimes things don't go as quickly as you think! Still fumbling on some of the chords, but Nitsuj is super satisfied by his progress at the end! Is it good enough to tackle Grade 2 ? Let's find out ... :)

Watch here - Nitsuj Module 7 Practice 10

Grade 1: Optional Courses & Tips

I highly recommend you complete the Ear Training Grade 1 and Music Theory Grade 1. A lot of people skip over these courses, but it's worth your time and effort. These courses can really improve your guitar skills and musical sense. It'll set your tone for the skills you develop in the next grade and make you a better musician. It's an excellent idea to check them out, but it's not mandatory to pass Grade 1.

To check up on all of these guitar skills, it's a good idea to record yourself playing the guitar and practice. That way, you can see what you need to work on. For some, this might be intimidating - but you don't have to post it anywhere. So instead, keep it for yourself - later on, when you're more advanced - it'll be awesome to look at where you started.

Grade 1: Key Reminder For Guitar Players

When learning the guitar, always be kind and forgiving with yourself. I know it can be frustrating at times, but remember, this is a fun journey! The idea of this test is a list of things you want to do. Think of it as a self-assessment tool and as guitar goals you'd like to accomplish :) Watching yourself progress should be an incredible and rewarding feeling!

Next up, we'll check out more about Module 7 practice and how to consolidate your guitar skills. You'll learn all the practice tools to pass Grade 1 with confidence :) See you there!

lessons.title: Module 7 Practice
lessons.summary: I'm going to give you some suggestions, but you have to figure you're own routines now...
lessons.text:
Helping you out with your practice schedule is tricky because, at this point, all students have different struggles. There's no one-size-fits-all here, so I'll give you a starting point to help you figure out what you need to practice - and for how long!

By the end of this guitar lesson, you'll have great guidelines to practice all the skills we've learned in Grade 1 of my Beginner Guitar Course - and we've learned a lot. :)

💡 Under the video, click on the 'Practice' and save the pre-made routine for Module 7. Edit and access the items in your Dashboard.

Starting Point

The following practice routine should address the most common beginner guitar problems at this stage. Use this as a starting point for your practice routine is:

2" Chord Perfect on (what's the struggle)

2 x 1" OMC Worst 2 (if needed)

2" Strumming (working w metronome)

2" Strumming 6:8 (working w metronome)

2" riff fun!

10" Song work

The thing is - when it comes to Nitsuj's practice, we've had to adapt this routine a lot. He does have a particular skill set, but…

You Have to Adapt!

You HAVE to adapt this practice routine to what YOU need! I can't be physically there with you, so you'll have to make the calls here.

In private lessons, a good teacher would see what you are struggling with and create a routine to help you out. But here, you'll need to use the starting point I'm offering you and trust your instincts.

Be honest with yourself and what you want!

One thing I do recommend is not being too critical at this point. If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you've done around 8 hours total of practice time. That's not enough to become a master guitar player. So trust - and enjoy - the process!

We'll get there. :)

Nitsuj's Approach

So, Nitsuj has memorized the chords and has a good sense of time and strumming. :) So, for him, the best and most effective approach was playing songs! That could be the case if you're following my lessons to consolidate some old knowledge.

He ended up doing ten sessions for consolidation - probably could have done with a few more, but he needs to crack onto the Grade 2 stuff to refine that journey before you get to it! ;)

My Practice Assistant

If you've not explored it yet, I suggest you get familiar with editing the routines in My Practice Assistant. Use that awesome tool to stay motivated and keep track of your progress. It makes a huge difference!

Digging the Lessons? Donations keep them free!

My Beginner Guitar Course is free, so people who can't afford it can access high-quality guitar education. If you can afford it, please consider donating. I also invited you to learn why I run JustinGuitar this way. :)

See you in Grade 2. :)

lessons.title: Consolidation Practice Tip
lessons.summary: Nitsuj has some awesome practice tips for you!
lessons.text:
In his consolidation practice, Nitsuj was pretty solid on the basics, so chose to do songs mainly - but when struggling to get some changes as good as he hoped, he stumbled upon Perfect Fast Changes - basically a mix of Chord Perfect and One Minute Changes - and I've incorporated it more into the next grade too! :)

If you choose to practice songs but have some struggles with a particular change, try this Perfect Fast Changes Exercise! Do one or two minutes of work on a particular change, as fast as you can, but making sure every chord sounds right - if it doesn't, slow it down. :)

I hope this helps some of you.

lessons.title: Grade 1 Feedback Please!
lessons.summary: Help me improve this course and get the chance to a video meeting with me. :)
lessons.text:
Well done! You made it through Grade 1 😎

In our colour system, this is the White grade – the start of your guitar adventure. We’ve covered the basics: your first open chords, strumming patterns, and a few campfire-ready songs. By now, you should be feeling confident enough to impress your friends (or at least annoy your neighbours in a fun way 😉).

Share Your Thoughts

Now it’s your turn: how did Grade 1 treat you? What did you love? What made you pull your hair out? Both praise and constructive feedback are welcome – we can take it! 😎 Fill in this short form to share your thoughts, and I’ll use them to make the course even better (and maybe sneak in a few more fun surprises).

Need a hand or have questions? Submit an inquiry via the contact page! Our support team is here to help you and find you the resources you need to succeed in your guitar goals!

Grade 1 consolidation, and then you’re off on your Grade 2 adventures!

modules.label: Justin Learning Left Handed!
modules.title: Nitsuj Grade 1 Practice
modules.intro:
Never thought I’d be a beginner again, but I simply couldn’t resist the temptation to try out my own beginner’s course!

So, meet Nitsuj, my own left-handed counterpart (it's Justin backwards in case you hadn't noticed!).

For Beginner’s Lesson 1, it took Nitsuj four separate practice sessions to get comfortable enough with the material to move on to Lesson 2.

For most of you, I suspect it will take two to four weeks of practice with about four practice sessions per week before you’re ready to move on. It’s much better to take your time and get your fundamentals down super well before going further in the course. Otherwise, the rest of it will all be a struggle and you’ll constantly be playing catch-up!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 1 - Practice 1
lessons.text:
Judging from Nitsuj’s first practice session, not to mention the moaning about finger pains, it seems as though he found Lesson 1 to be a bit more difficult than he was expecting!

Despite his discomfort, remember – finger pain is normal! It’s just something you’ve got to get through, and over time, it absolutely will get better.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 1 - Practice 2
lessons.text:
Much to Nitsuj’s dismay, his finger pain hasn’t subsided quite yet, but I could have told him – it will take a bit more than one practice session to get through it!

Things seem to be progressing nicely, though. Chord changes are getting better, and Nitsuj almost makes it through his first left-handed song.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 1 - Practice 3
lessons.text: A breakthrough! After just a few sessions, Nitsuj is feeling significantly more comfortable with his left-handed practice routine. Sometimes, it just takes getting over that initial hump of awkwardness and discomfort.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 1 - Practice 4
lessons.text:
Four practice sessions in and Nitsuj is ready to move on to Module 2!

Don’t feel bad if it takes you a few more practices before advancing. Especially in these early stages, it’s super important to get your basics down as best you can!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 2 - Practice 1
lessons.text: Lesson 2 brings with it a new chord for Nitsuj to master – the E chord! Still complaining about finger pain, Nitsuj carries on despite the awkward finger stretches and clunky (though less clunky than before) chord changes.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 2 - Practice 3
lessons.summary: Yes there is a practice session missing! I misplaced the video file and wiped the SD card!
lessons.text:
Goodness, Nitsuj really has seemed to improve quite a lot between this session and the last!

Oh, wait… that’s because I've accidentally deleted his second practice session.

No worries! Things are coming together nicely and those chord change exercises are proving to be super helpful.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 2 - Practice 4
lessons.text: Eight total practice sessions in and Nitsuj’s fingers are still sore. This just goes to show that in order to get good at something, you’ve got to keep working through the mucky and less-fun bits! It will all be worth it in the end.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 2 - Practice 5
lessons.text: Even for a dedicated and excited guitar student like Nitsuj, it can be difficult to find or make time for a 20-30 minute practice session. Still, it’s important not to lose your momentum! It’s best to get into a practice habit and schedule it regularly as best you can. Yes, sometimes life gets busy and time gets away from you, but consistency really is key.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 3 - Practice 1
lessons.text: Hello, from Abbotsford! Just because Justin’s got some fancy workshop to attend out there doesn’t mean Nitsuj can’t get his practices in. He’s working on some strumming some fun patterns with his left hand today.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 3 - Practice 2
lessons.text: Is jet lag a decent enough excuse to miss a practice? How about a general lack of sleep? For some, maybe. For Nitsuj? Certainly not! Here goes Practice 2 in Canada, sleep-deprived and all.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 3 - Practice 3
lessons.text: Man, Justin’s work and travel schedule are a lot for Nitsuj to keep up with. The good news is that the jet lag has subsided a bit finally! Minor chords are coming along nicely, as well as the strumming exercises.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 3 - Practice 4
lessons.text: In Nitsuj’s own words, he’s feeling pretty confident with his progress through Lesson 3. His chords are sounding much better and the strumming? Well, it’s improving, which is the best any student - beginner or otherwise - can hope for!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 3 - Practice 5
lessons.text: And we’re back in the UK! After taking a few days off to catch up on work, life, and SLEEP, Nitsuj is ready to tackle his strumming practice with his favorite thin pick. It’s amazing what a difference a few small changes can make.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 4 - Practice 1
lessons.text: Finger stretching exercises – yikes! These are not the easiest to do, but Nitsuj knows well enough that they’ll certainly be helpful in the long run. Let the fun begin!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 4 - Practice 2
lessons.text: Just as Nitsuj thought he was getting the hang of everything, some of these exercises have proven to be quite humbling! All good, though. No one ever said progress is easy, but it certainly can be rewarding.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 4 - Practice 3
lessons.text: Practice may not make perfect (whatever “perfect” even means), but in Nitsuj’s case, it’s helping to make better. Things are getting easier, even though those finger stretches are still - expectedly, to be fair - a little achy and uncomfortable!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 4 - Practice 4
lessons.text:
It’s finally starting to get easier, though there’s definitely still room for improvement.

Just a reminder, don’t feel bad if you need to spend a bit more time on a particular lesson or exercise. The better you master each concept the easier future concepts will be to learn. Otherwise, you’ll just be struggling to play at a more advanced level with a less advanced skill set.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 4 - Practice 5
lessons.text: This is the last practice for Lesson 4 of Justin’s Beginner’s Course! Nitsuj is finally feeling confident enough in his playing and his mastery of Lesson 4 concepts to move on to Lesson 5, though this cold weather seems to have frozen his fingers stiff. Gotta love winters in the UK!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 5 - Practice 1
lessons.text: Nitsuj is taking on the C chord in Lesson 5, as well as continuing his finger stretches and his strumming exercises. He’s also working on getting that Nirvana riff firmly under his belt.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 5 - Practice 2
lessons.text: Justin’s busy schedule has been threatening to cut into Nitsuj’s practice schedule, not to mention there’s a bug in the air – flu season is no joke! Still, you’ve got to make time for practice and progress.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 5 - Practice 3
lessons.text: Nitsuj is back and in better spirits than he was in his previous practice session! Feeling a little better and feeling more natural with his left-handed guitar playing, things seem to be moving along nicely.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 5 - Practice 4
lessons.text: After waiting an entire week between practice sessions, Nitsuj’s fingers are a little softer and weaker than before. They’ll need to be broken in and toughened up again. This is just one of the many reasons why consistency is so important when it comes to learning an instrument. Of course, life gets in the way sometimes! No worry – just pick back up from where you left off.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 5 - Practice 5
lessons.text: Nitsuj is on his last practice of Lesson 5! What a journey it’s been so far. He’s finally getting used to playing with his left hand, so much so that he finds himself naturally sitting down to play with his left hand rather than his right. Onward to Lesson 6!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 6 - Practice 1
lessons.text: Nitsuj is starting off strong with that G chord – so far, so good! Those chord changes could use some more work, but that’s why we keep practising.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 6 - Practice 2
lessons.text: Practice needs to happen, sometimes even at the expense of a grumpy dog’s feelings! Sorry, Ziggy… must get this session in.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 6 - Practice 3
lessons.text: Justin did loads of practice earlier in the day, so it’ll be interesting to see how these tired and fatigued fingers handle Nitsuj’s practice session. Can’t be too bad… can it?

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 6 - Practice 4
lessons.text: Going back and forth between right-handed and left-handed playing can be a little tricky, but fortunately for you all, this is likely not a problem you’ll ever have! This is purely a Justin/Nitsuj problem!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 6 - Practice 5
lessons.text: This is Nitsuj’s last practice session for Lesson 6. It may be a very late and awkward time to mention this, but here’s a pro tip: Make sure your guitar is in tune before you start your practice! It seems like such an obvious thing, but it makes such a huge difference to your practice, especially when you’re working on your chords. If the chords don’t sound right, you’ll know it’s because you need to fix something!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 7 - Practice 1
lessons.text:
Time for Nitsuj to consolidate the first grade. This practice session will be a revision. Let's see what he needs to work on before moving on to Grade 2!

It's always best to focus your practice on what challenges you the most - it's the best way to progress!

Nitsuj decides to add Heart Of Gold into his song repertoire. Maybe something he'll perform later on as well :) Turn out it's not as easy to play as he expected ...

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 7 - Practice 2
lessons.text:
Nitsuj is dealing with some obstacles today - laptop has died, no charger and can't find Ipad. But - that won't stop him!

He's determined to keep going - so he'll have to go app-less for this lesson! With the notes he took in the last lesson, he will tackle the techniques that needed the most work.

Some major improvement happening with his chord changes - Nitsuj is pleased with his progress. How'd you think he did? :)

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 7 - Practice 3
lessons.text:
Good morning - or good evening - fellow guitarist! Wherever you are in the world, Nitsuj hopes your doing well and progressing in your guitar journey. :)

Today, Nitsuj is mostly playing songs. More thinking needs to be done on what needs work. Strumming is better - but he noticed his arm still needs a bit more relaxing.

Starting the practice with Eleanor Rigby, a Beatles classic!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 7 - Practice 4
lessons.text:
Today, Nitsuj is focusing on keeping things consistent. This is an important factor to keep in mind when you're setting up your practice routines!

Even if one day you might nail a skill and practice it flawlessly, check up on it and see if it's consistent! :)

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 7 - Practice 5
lessons.text:
For this practice, Nitsuj is continuing his quest to get his songs sounding decent. We're not aiming for perfection, but a place where it feels comfy, relax, and it sounds good to the ears!

And, learning brand new songs is always a bit rocky - and that's the process of the guitar journey! Keep at it; we'll get there! :)

See you next practice :)

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 7 - Practice 6
lessons.text:
Nitsuj has never spent so long on one stage! But that's normal - the consolidation process takes a bit longer. And when you're working on feeling confident and comfortable with a skill, you really want to take your time. No need to rush! :)

Synchronizing the hands is the challenging part here :) Things are coming together. How'd you think it went?

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 7 - Practice 7
lessons.text:
Nitsuj's fingers are feeling a bit sore today - but that's not stopping him from practicing!

He comes up with new practice elements throughout the lesson, and it seems to be pretty effective! What are your thoughts on this new exercise?

And .. Time to start practicing on Grade 2 elements! Some exciting stuff up ahead. See you next practice!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 7 - Practice 8
lessons.text:
Off to a rough start, Nitsuj realized he might require a tuner upgrade. Perhaps even a guitar upgrade?! What do you think? :)

That would be a nice treat for all Nitsuj's hard work. Grade 7 consolidation stage is finally coming to an end! Excited for what's ahead.

I hope you're having a fab day wherever you are.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 7 - Practice 10
lessons.summary: Nitsuj's final practice session in Grade 1 - he passes today :)
lessons.text:
Practice frustration - it's part of the guitar journey. Sometimes things don't go as quickly as you think! All you can really do is channel that energy into something good.

And that's exactly what Nitsuj does in this practice session! Still fumbling on some of the chords, but Nitsuj is super satisfied by his progress at the end!

But is it good enough to tackle Grade 2 ? Let's find out ...

modules.label: Justin Learning Left Handed!
modules.title: Nitsuj Grade 2 Practice
modules.intro: There are 8 practice sessions in Lesson 8 but I've not finished editing them yet - but will get them ready asap!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 8 - Practice 1
lessons.summary: Let’s see how Nitsuj does with his first Grade 2 practice session.
lessons.text: Nitsuj has finally graduated from Grade 1 to 2! After a quick break, let’s see how he gets on with the new stuff. He’s got some chords to look after, scales, strumming patterns - it’s getting to be a lot to keep up with!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 8 - Practice 2
lessons.summary: Nitsuj starts off on this practice session on a bad note - with an injured finger!
lessons.text:
Nitsuj got off to a rocky start with this practice session. It’s a hard lesson learned, but now he knows to watch out for wonky guitar strings! One of them got him pretty good right on his (left-handed) fretting hand.

Still, it doesn’t seem to have slowed him down too badly…

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 8 - Practice 3
lessons.summary: Another day in quarantine, another practice day for Nitsuj.
lessons.text: In the middle of a global pandemic, Nitsuj is looking forward to all of the practice time he’ll be putting in while quarantined! Way to look on the bright side, eh?

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 8 - Practice 4
lessons.summary: Nitsuj struggles his way through a practice session with finger pain.
lessons.text:
Still having not learned his lesson, Nitsuj seems to have underestimated how formidable finger pain can really be! To his credit, Nitsuj pushed his way through to complete a full 30-minute practice session, but…

Who do you think won this round, Nitsuj, or the pain in his 3rd finger?

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 8 - Practice 5
lessons.summary: With his fifth practice session in the bag, Nitsuj just might be ready to move on to Lesson 9.
lessons.text: With coronavirus making its way across the globe, Nitsuj’s home life seems to have gotten a bit busier than usual (even if he is staying in the house all day). Still, always the diligent student, he’s managed to siphon off some time for a quick practice session. After all, he’s ready to move on to Lesson 9!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 9 - Practice 1
lessons.summary: Is Nitsuj ready to tackle that F chord, his first barre chord?
lessons.text: Armed with everything he learned in Grade 1, Nitsuj is finally ready to tackle the beast head on - the F chord, in all of its fully-barred glory. Maybe he psyched himself out a bit too much, though. It didn’t go nearly as badly as he thought it would!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 9 - Practice 2
lessons.summary: Nitsuj presses on with his F chord practice, determined to master the barre.
lessons.text: After experiencing some technical difficulties on the most Monday of Mondays, Nitsuj pressed on and completed his practice session. His F chord seems to be improving, but what of the finger pain that’s bound to accompany it?

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 9 - Practice 3
lessons.summary: Nitsuj is giving his fingers a break from the acoustic and switching over to an electric guitar - and a new one at that!
lessons.text: With everything going on in the world, from the global pandemic to Nitsuj’s F barre chord woes, he decided he was due for a new guitar. While it’s always nice to treat yourself, new guitars offer their own bit of struggle! They certainly take some getting used to, assuming they’re up to your level of snuff straight out of the box. However, practising the F barre chord on an electric guitar rather than an acoustic could help Nitsuj bridge the barre gap a little easier. With thinner strings, they require less finger strength to produce a good sound. While it’s still important and advisable to strengthen your fingers on an acoustic, practising chord shapes on an electric will help your fingers get into their correct positions more readily.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 9 - Practice 3 (NEW GUITAR!)
lessons.summary: Nitsuj is unboxing his new guitar! Any guesses what it could be?
lessons.text: Presenting - Nitsuj’s first (unsponsored) unboxing! Buying a guitar while in quarantine presents its own set of challenges, but the guitar is finally here. Let’s see what he’s got…

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 9 - Practice 4
lessons.summary: Nitsuj is working hard on his Lesson 9 practice, but he’s sticking with the electric for a bit longer.
lessons.text: Going against Justin’s Lesson 9 recommendation that students alternate between an acoustic and an electric guitar each practice session, Nitsuj is going for his second consecutive day on his electric guitar. Can you blame him, though? We all love to play with our new toys.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 9 - Practice 5
lessons.summary: Nitsuj is back on his practice grind after taking a week off! Let’s see how he does.
lessons.text: After taking a whole week off from his practice sessions (because sometimes life gets in the way of practising), Nitsuj is back at it. Usually, a week off from practising won’t completely destroy your progress. In fact, it can even be helpful to give your fingers a break every once in a while. Not just that, but it helps to get out of your head a bit, too, especially if you’re one who tends to overthink things here and there.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 9 - Practice 6
lessons.summary: What’s it like going back to an acoustic after playing an electric for a while? Nitsuj is about to find out.
lessons.text: Today’s the final Lesson 9 practice for Nitsuj! Back on the acoustic guitar, did Nitsuj’s electric practices help him with his chord shapes and changes?

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 10 - Practice 1
lessons.text:
Nitsjun has not been practicing for nearly 1 week. But he's back at it and ready for another fully loaded guitar session!

In this module, Nitsuj is tackling the Weak Finger G chord, mini A chord bar, and C major scale with alternate picking. He's also gonna be improvising some bits to improve that F chord. Loads of fun ahead, right? :)

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 10 - Practice 2
lessons.text:
It's normal not to always be in the mood to practice the guitar. Realistically, we're not always going to feel our best. Especially when a lot is going on, and you're just feeling kind of off.. blah? Nitsuj is definitely feeling that way today!

But that won't stop him, and it shouldn't stop you! Push through those feelings, and let the guitar be that distraction from everything else. Sometimes, playing guitar is that relief you need to get out of a bad headspace.

Channel that energy, and who knows - maybe it'll help you nail a technique you've been working at. :)

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 10 - Practice 3
lessons.text:
Today, Nitsuj is back on the electric guitar! He'll practice the F chord and F chord changes and see if he can graduate from C to F. And, you'll watch Nitsuj struggle with his second finger. Sometimes, things are harder than expected. This only means it'll be something you'll have to focus on and explore in your next lessons.

Starting with a 5 minutes song revision of This Year's Love by David Gray. Nitsuj hasn't played that one in ages. How do you think he did? :)

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 10 - Practice 4
lessons.text:
In this guitar session, Nitsuj will spend a bit of this lesson revising Wonderwall by Oasis. First, he'll muck around a bit without the song app to see what happens.

Today, Nitsuj is dealing with a sore wrist. So, he's feeling pretty stiff - but that won't stop him from putting in the work. However, if you're ever feeling any major pain and tension while practicing - please take it easy on the guitar. :)

Nitsuj is definitely noticing skill improvement and feeling like he's heading in the right direction of his guitar journey!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 10 - Practice 5
lessons.text:
Today, Nitsuj is testing out a guitar strap to see if it helps relieve some wrist pain! Finding the right comfortable position to play guitar is key and something we learn in the earliest guitar lessons.

Being comfortable playing the guitar starts with having a relaxed yet straight posture. And, sometimes, it takes some adjustments to make it feel right. Guitar straps definitely provide a bit of posture relief. So, if you need to, explore to see what feels best for you!

Nitsuj starts with a 5 minutes revision of House Of The Rising Sun by Dire Straits.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 10 - Practice 6
lessons.text:
Nitsuj has come a long way - Module 10 is almost completed! The wrist soreness is finally feeling a bit better. :)

Today, he's feeling like trying something new. Sometimes, it's nice to switch up our practice songs. It helps you revisit some techniques and keeps you inspired.

For this session, Nitsuj starts with Wish You Were Here by Pink Floyd.

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 10 - Practice 7
lessons.text:
For the last practice of Module 10, Nitsuj tries to incorporate that new A mini barre chord in his guitar playing. He's also determined to ring out that F chord. How'd he do? :)

And, just a reminder, we're not looking for perfection. Learning the guitar is hard - and it's normal to still struggle with certain things at this stage! Practice is the only way to improve those tricky skills. The more you try, the closer you'll get to having those skills under your belt. Nitsuj is a perfect example of this!

Next practice, Nitsuj will tackle Module 11 with loads of fun stuff to put into practice. :)

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 11 - Practice 1
lessons.text:
Nitsuj has been busy for the past week. He hasn't even touched his guitar 😲

Sometimes life gets in the way, and as Sinatra said - that's life!

So he might be a little rusty on this first lesson practice for Module 11. Nitsuj is starting with 5 minutes revision with Dreams by FleetwoodMac. Let's see how he feels practicing that F chord. Not bad - How'd you think he did?

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 11 - Practice 2
lessons.text:
In this practice session, Nitsuj is having a go at revising Wonderwall. Then, he's tackling a R.E.M classic - he's even singing along to this one. The fingerpicking is coming along - he's getting there!

When you practice new songs, it's important not to aim for perfection. The key here is to keep going and keep that strumming hand moving!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 11 - Practice 3
lessons.text:
Day 3 - Nitsuj is starting with 5 mins of revision practice. Trying to work on getting in some groove into the strumming pattern. But this is tricky when your hands have a mind of their own! So if you're feeling that way lately - Nitsuj can relate!

Moving on, 3 minutes of fingerstyle - an interesting exercise on electric guitar! How'd you think it sounded?

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 11 - Practice 4
lessons.text:
Module 11 - day 4.

Nitsuj is back on the acoustic today. If you're lucky enough to have both kinds of guitar - it's a good idea to switch up your practice on both acoustic and electric. You'll learn to manipulate them differently - and this will help you as you advance and get into more complex techniques.

Which kind of guitar is your fav? Log in and share your answers in the comment. :)

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 11 - Practice 5
lessons.text:
It's sizzling hot in the UK - so Nitsuj is cooking in his studio. No such thing as perfect weather, right?

Let's start with House of The Rising Sun, then following with a Clapton classic - Wonderful Tonight. Nothing like playing the classics tunes. And - it's already the last practice of Module 11! Nitsuj's Sus chord still needs more work (and other stuff too), but we will keep at it in the next practices.

How's your practice coming along? :)

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 12 - Practice 1
lessons.text:
It's Rock TIME! That's what Module 12 is all about. And Nitsuj is excited to put all those techniques into practice, including those power chords! So many fun songs to tackle.

He'll start with some fingerstyle to make up for the last lesson. Then, we'll venture into some Metallica with Enter The Sandman. Sounding pretty crunchy! What do you think?

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 12 - Practice 3
lessons.text:
For Nitsuj, apparently, rest is for the wicked! So he did not have a rest day between last practice, but feeling ready to play some power chords! Adding some distortion to Enter The Sandman, Nitsuj is really taking it up a level.

Module 13 practice is coming together pretty quickly. Power chords still need some work, but we're getting there! :)

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 12 - Practice 4
lessons.text:
In this practice, Nitsuj first has a bit of a go with Wonderwall and Wish You Were Here. Then, we try out Fly Away by Lenny Kravitz. It's hard not to sing along to the chorus of that one, eh? :)

Reminder to recognize the progress you made when your practicing the guitar! Sometimes, it can get frustrating - Nitsuj gets it!

Learning the guitar is hard. Whether you think your practice went well or not, you're still putting effort in is helping you advance, be proud of that! :)

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 13 - Practice 1
lessons.text:
Confession - Nitsuj hasn't practiced in weeks! Exciting things are cooking, so bear with the rustiness!

It's blues weeks - time to get into some blues!

5-minute revisions Nitsuj will muck around with power chords. Why? Because that's what he struggles with the most.

It's a good idea to focus on practicing what challenges you the most. This is the best way to grow as a guitar player!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 13 - Practice 2
lessons.text:
Nitsuj is back with you for Module 13 - day 2.

Still playing the electric guitar today, he's dedicated to nailing those power chords. Sounding pretty fuzzy. What do you think?

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 13 - Practice 3
lessons.text:
Nitsuj gives the acoustic guitar another try this practice! After playing the iconic Go, Johnny, Go By Chuck Berry, he realized he should focus on his strumming pattern.

Those moments are perfect for muting the strings and focusing on the strumming and the accents. It's one of the best ways to reduce distractions around you and fully concentrate on the strumming rhythm!

lessons.title: Nitsuj Module 13 - Practice 4
lessons.text:
Nitsuj is starting with 5 minutes revision with power chords. Loads of blues songs in this practice - the backbone of music today! Country, rock, and metal all have some blues influence!

I hope you're having a fab day wherever you are. Are you enjoying this blues course as much as Nitsuj? How's your blues progress going? :)

modules.label: Module 8
modules.title: Your First Scale, Pick Tricks & 8th Note Strumming
modules.intro:
Welcome to Module 8. You're now an advancing beginner! 👏

You made it through Grade 1 of the Beginner Guitar Course - that's a big accomplishment! So let's start Grade 2 with a round of applause for all your hard work!

🎸 By now, you should feel more confident with your guitar playing! You can even play easy songs you love.

Looking forward, we have loads of new stuff to learn - so I hope you're feeling up for the challenge. :)

As you complete Module 8, you might find some skills easier to learn and others more challenging. Throughout Grade 2, you'll be able to personalize your practice to suit your needs.

What You'll Learn

We'll start Grade 2 by checking out the Stuck 3&4 chords. This incredible set of chords, also known as the Wonderwall chords, is a favorite for many advancing guitar beginners!

Learning these chords will also be perfect for the riff we'll learn: an easy version of Wish You Were Here by Pink Floyd - a great exercise to practice combining strumming and fingerpicking.

As an advancing beginner, it's time to introduce a new exercise to practice your chord changes: Perfect Fast Changes. This combination of two exercises will improve your chord speed and accuracy.

You'll learn your very first guitar scale - the Open Em Pentatonic Scale! This scale is super handy - you'll often use it to improvise later in your guitar journey.

We'll check out a new All-Down 8th Note Strumming Pattern - a cool way to get easy high-energy strumming into your playing.

We'll spend some time looking at pick manipulation. This is a skill many people struggle with, especially when it comes to holding a pick. You'll understand how to mute your guitar strings - deliberately! This technique is super effective in tidying up your guitar playing and sound.

And last but not least, a quick theory crash course on notes in the open position will help you better understand your guitar fretboard.

But Before You Start …

It's time to get yourself a thicker guitar pick. With all these new techniques, you'll need a sturdier pick! So make sure you have one on hand! Start exploring the difference it feels in your hand and for your guitar playing!

💡 The Jim Dunlop orange tortex pick is a great thickness for your current guitar stage. We'll need a thicker pick for the next lessons, so ensure you have one with you.

Take a few minutes to complete our quick Grade 1 consolidation survey! This is a great way to reflect on what you've learned so far, see how confident you feel with your skills, and give us feedback to help improve the course.

👉 Now grab your guitar, and let's get started with the Stuck 3&4 chords! :)

lessons.title: The Stuck 3&4 Chords
lessons.summary: Explore and learn to play 9 guitar chords ALL guitar beginners should know :)
lessons.text:
Learn 9 Fancy Chords All Guitar Beginners Should Know

Why do beginner guitar players love these chords so much? To play them, you can keep two fingers in the same position when switching between these awesome grips.

Even better, they sound super cool, and they're useful for many chord changes now and later in your guitar journey. Many call these The Wonderwall Chords because they are played in that Oasis classic. They're also common chords in other 90's rock ballads. So chances are you're already familiar with their sound.

If you don't memorize all these new chords immediately, don't worry! This is a lot of new information, and it'll take practice & time to get familiar with these new chords.

👀 Completed Grade 1? We'd love to know how the consolidation went! If you have a few minutes, complete the Grade 1 consolidation survey! This is a great way to reflect on what you've learned so far, see how confident you feel with your skills, and give us feedback to help improve the course. :)

Stuck 3&4 Chords

The Stuck 3&4 chords get their name because fingers 3 & 4 are stuck on the thinnest two strings. Now, they don't have to be - but this is true most of the time! But this will also depend on what song and the specific sound you're going for.

You'll often find those two fingers staying in the same place - on the thinnest two strings of the 3rd fret. These chord shapes will give a unique sound known as the drone effect. This drone effect is what we call two notes ringing out together.

Why Is Your Little Finger Hurting?

You'll use your little finger a lot more with these chords. Expect some pain level, and take enough breaks to let it heal a bit between your practice sessions.

Suppose you haven't already - you still have time to set up your practice sessions with My Practice Assistant. This free tool helps set up practical practice sessions to prevent overplaying.

💡 Don't be in a hurry - you'll learn BETTER and FASTER if you give yourself time to heal.

Nitsuj found his Finger 3 was hurting a lot during this practice session. Finger 3 overcompensates for the weakness of Finger 4 by pressing harder than it should - so be mindful of this. Nitsuj knew what was going on and still struggled with it. It's normal if you struggle too! Stay aware, and don't hurt yourself. :)

Because of the shape of these chords, you should find that the muscle between your thumb and index finger can get a bit pumped. This is GOOD! It means you are growing that muscle.

You'll need to get that muscle strength for next week's lesson. So work on it - but not until it's painful! Let's look at those nine awesome chords - starting with the 'Big G' chord.

The 'Big G' Chord

This is the best introduction to the Stuck 3&4 Chords and is the 'daddy' of them!

Try not to press too hard with fingers 3&4 (but aim to get the notes clear).

You can use this any time you see a G Chord written!

For obvious reasons, you'll often hear people describe it as the 'Four Finger G.'

G5 'The Rock G' Chord

Note the muted 5th string here - same as the previous easy G we learned earlier!

If you're studying Music Theory, you'll notice the '3rd' is missing, hence the name G5!

This grip is *usually* much better than any other G when playing with overdrive/distortion.

I generally prefer this sound to the "Big G," but they all have a place.

Cadd9 Chord

It's exactly like the Big G but with fingers 1 & 2 moved down a string.

Make sure you mute the thickest string with the tip of Finger 2 (it shouldn't be hard!).

D sus4 Chord

Don't worry about the name. We'll get more into that later.

This chord is commonly substituted for regular D if the other chords are Stuck 3&4 grips.

Sometimes, it sounds cooler to go to regular D (use finger three as an anchor).

A7 sus 4 Chord

And another big scary name chord, but not hard to play. It's an A chord variation when holding the Stuck 3&4.

The stretch between Finger 2 and 3 is the tricky part of this one!

Try not to play the thickest string.

A7 sus 4 Chord (Variation)

In Wonderwall, we have this other version with the Open G string.

It's got the same name as it's just doubling a different note than the last grip.

It might look easy, but ringing the open string out can be tricky!

E min7 Chord

There are a few ways of playing an Emin7 chord. This is the Stuck 3&4 version.

The stretch between Fingers 2 and 3 makes it the most challenging chord here (I think!).

D add11/F# Chord (Whaaaat?)

This is often a transition chord when moving between G and Em (as in Wonderwall).

Moving between the Emin7 and this is a great finger exercise for independence!

F 6/9 Chord

I just added this one because it's a fun one in the Stuck 3&4 grips, but it's less common.

Just like Cadd9, fingers 1 and 2 moved down a string.

Don't play either of the thickest two strings.

Mute string 5 with the tip of finger 2.

I wouldn't practice this one much until you find it in a song!

The Stuck 3&4 chords are perfect for our next exercise: Perfect Fast Changes.

lessons.title: Perfect Fast Changes
lessons.summary: Want FAST & PERFECT chord changes on guitar? Here's a new exercise to improve your guitar skills!
lessons.text:
Brace Yourself, A Brand New Chord Exercise Is Here.

If you're following my beginner guitar course, you should be familiar with the One Minute Changes exercises. In this lesson, we explore a new exercise to improve your chord accuracy and the speed of your chord changes!

When Nitsuj was doing his left-handed lessons, we noticed that these two exercises weren't cutting as the lessons became more advanced. And this is how the Perfect Fast Changes (PFC) exercise was born!

💡 This is a great time to practice the 9 fancy chords we explore in the previous lesson. At this stage, you should be up for a bit challenge! :)

Perfect Fast Changes Guitar Exercise

This new exercise is a magical combination of the two previous chord exercises. With the One Minute Changes, you're going back and forth between two chords. You practice how many chord changes you can squeeze in a minute. No matter how clean or messy those chord changes are, the goal is to build speed and muscle memory.

With the Chord Perfect exercise, you're focusing on getting every finger down in its proper place. You focus on ensuring that each note rings out beautifully as you pay attention to your chord shape. Now with the Perfect Fast Changes exercises - you're combining the two!

Follow these four steps to put this exercise into practice:

1. Choose two chords you find tricky to switch between.

2. See how quickly you can change between while getting each chord as close to perfect as possible!

3. Focus on both speed and quality, but if you need to sacrifice one for the other at first, focus on quality over speed.

4. Build up your speed as your progress.

🚨 It's normal not to have as many chord changes as your One Minute Changes. You might not beat your record right away, but the speed will come as you keep practicing constantly. :)

How To Practice With A Slow Strum

Strum your chords slowly. This way, you'll be able to hit each note of the chord. Then, you can check that all your fingers are where they should be. Suppose your fingers are NOT where they should be - slow down! If you're getting some muted or buzzing strings, slow down some more.

Keep slowing down until you can at least get the chords down correctly. Then, you can start building up your strumming speed.The word 'perfect' can be scary, especially for beginner guitar players! The key here is to get the chords as best you can. And remember, you'll get better and better the more you play.

Give yourself a break and trust the process, but don't be afraid to challenge yourself! Pick some chords that you need to work on. The goal with practicing is always to improve what's more challenging to you. It's not the most fun part of learning guitar. But it'll help you as you progress in your guitar journey.

Up for more? Discover your very first pentatonic scale.

lessons.title: Open E Minor Pentatonic Scale
lessons.summary: Learn how to play the E Minor Pentatonic scale with valuable tips and visuals!
lessons.text:
The E Minor Pentatonic Scale - the first pentatonic scale you should learn on guitar.

With all the guitar skills you have under your belt, you're ready to explore your first scale: the Open E Minor Pentatonic Scale! You're ready for it, BUT it doesn't mean it won't be tricky. Learning scales is a vital guitar technique to help elevate your guitar playing! In this lesson, we'll explore how you can approach this and some valuable tips to help you out.

Practicing scales for guitar beginners is a great skill to add to your repertoire. It helps with your pick accuracy, riffing and gives you material to improvise your riff too! First things first, let's check out some visuals to guide you! :)

How To Play Open Emin Pentatonic Scale

The Scale Box is like a chord box. The difference is you play the notes one at a time. You'll start with the lowest-sounding note, then work up to the highest-sounding note. Then, you'll head back to the lowest notes, playing them one by one.

Take a moment and visualize the diagram below: it'll help you see the visual relationships between the notes.

Open E Minor Pentatonic Scale TAB

Check out the TAB below - it shows you the order of the notes. As you can see, the lowest line is the thickest string and the fret numbers. Usually, the lowest line does not designate the fingers to use. But for the but the E minor pentatonic scale, they are the same!

Don't worry about the traditional notation at the top of the TAB. It comes free with the tab - so I included it ;). If you need extra help, check out the video for a slowed-down playthrough of this scale.

How To Practice Scales On Guitar

Using only your second and third fingers to fret, you will start on the thickest string. Then, you'll work your way over to the thinnest string. Finally, head back over to the thickest string.

As with most things, start slow. Learning this scale will likely be tricky for you - this differs from anything else we've done in our beginner guitar course! There's a similarity between scales and riffs, so this will help you play and improvise riffs later on!

So far, we've focused on strumming and strumming patterns. So, we haven't done a whole lot with picking techniques. For now, only use down picks. We'll get more into up picks later!

With scales, we're only playing one note at a time, so don't worry about any of your chord shapes right now! And don't get down if you're picking the wrong string. It's a common struggle for most beginners. Keep going! You can do this :).

3 Tips to Practice Playing Scales

TIP 1 - Memorize The Shape

Memorize the scale shape as you learn them by taking a mental image of the diagram. They'll come in handy later in your playing as you get more advanced.

It's OK to look at the diagram the first few times, but you don't want to rely on it! You want to play the scales without being glued to a TAB sheet or scale box. Committing the shape of the scale to memory is very important. Getting it clear in your mind from the start will help you remember it forever!

TIP 2 - Play The Scale Slowly!

Do it slow enough to get it perfect. Take your time, and get the shape exactly right! Even if it takes you a few times, don't get discouraged. Learning the guitar is hard, and you don't need to rush things.

Play the scale as slow as you need to. Make sure you're not skipping strings or picking the wrong ones.

TIP 3 - Practice With A Metronome

Focus on playing it slowly for the first few times to get it right. Once you feel confident picking every string, set your metronome at a target of 80 bpm. You'll want to pick 1 note for each click of the metronome.

At first, this might feel too quick for you - that's normal! Slow it down, and find a speed that works for you. Playing with the metronome induces panic, building the habit of playing in time. You'll develop your internal sense of time, and this will help you jam with other musicians!

PRACTICE MAKES PERMANENT

It's super important to get this right! Think of this scale as a learning tool. Take your time and get it right. Remember - practice does not make perfect - PRACTICE MAKES PERMANENT. Practice things right, even if that means going at a slower pace.

If you make a mistake and you keep practicing it, you'll have to spend some time correcting it later! So, practice this scale and all other skills correctly and lock it in your brain! Doing this will save you from having to break many bad habits later. :)

Next lesson, we learn how to mute unwanted strings.

lessons.title: Muting Strings Deliberately
lessons.summary: In this lesson, explore how to mute unwanted string when playing guitar and elevate the sound of your scales!
lessons.text:
Elevate Your Guitar Sound ... By Muting Your Strings!

You heard that right - String muting can improve the sound of your guitar playing. Especially with scales! We've encountered muting strings as a practice technique. We mute the strings with our fretting hand while working out a strumming pattern with our other hand.

Or, we mute one string at a time during our chord practices. Many of the chords learned through my beginner guitar course also require you not to play one or two open strings. The easiest way to achieve this is usually by muting those strings.

So, deliberately muting string is a technique that will help elevate your guitar sound! In this lesson, you'll learn how to mute unwanted strings - THE RIGHT WAY! :)

💡 Know how to play the E minor Pentatonic scale? It's the perfect time to learn how to mute your strings deliberately.

Why Mute Your Guitar Strings?

But first, you need to understand why we mute strings. When playing scales, if you don't mute any strings, many open strings will ring out when you don't want them to!

All that sound can be messy and impact the flow of your scale. To fix this, you can deliberately mute the strings you don't want to play. And, as you already know, it doesn't take much to mute a string. A slight touch will do! Too often, we accidentally mute strings when we play - which I know can be frustrating. Now, we want those mute to happen on purpose.

Muting is often used to fit the tone of a song. Sometimes you don't want a full-on strum with all the strings ringing out. It might not suit the mood of the tune you're playing.

🎵 Don't forget, music is a subjective art form. It's up to your musical judgment to see what sounds better for a song.

Now, how should you be muting your strings on purpose? There are two main ways to mute your strings - either with your fretting hand or your strumming hand.

How To Mute Strings On Guitar

Muting with your fretting hand is something you're already doing. So great news, you should already understand how it works! It happens when you fret a note on a string but lay your finger down slightly flat. This way, it barely touches and mutes the following strings.

The muted strings are either above or below the string you're fretting. As you get better at palm muting, you'll start to see how your strumming hand can pick up your fretting hand.

While you play a scale, mute with your strumming hand using the heel of your hand. It should be resting on the thicker string while it's not playing.When you get to the thinnest string of the scale, your picking hand should already mute the other four or five strings. It might feel a bit awkward at first - that's normal :).

The goal is to balance how much you want the string muted and how much you want to ring out. It can be tricky - so don't get discouraged. Again - this will get easier with practice! So don't worry too, and try not to perfect it right now.

How To Practice Muting Strings

It's an excellent idea to practice muting strings, but I don't want you to overthink too much about this yet. Muting strings is HARD. But it does get easier with time! As you practice, you eventually won't have to think about it - the string muting will automatically happen.

For now, be aware of this technique and what it can do. Incorporate it into your practice routine, and be mindful of the difference it can make in your sound!

Don't feel like you must get all your string muting perfectly before moving on. This skill can take months of practice to get right! You don't want to get stuck on Lesson 8. Think of this guitar technique as a long-term project.

Next lesson, learn an easy high-energy strumming pattern!

lessons.title: All Down 8th Note Strumming
lessons.summary: Learn a high-energy strumming pattern using only downstrums and explore accenting the back beats!
lessons.text:
Learn An Easy Strumming Pattern With All Down Strums

We already know how to downstrums on beats 1, 2, 3, and 4. You're also familiar with adding upstrums on the 'ands.' This strumming follows the natural movement of your arm when you're strumming, so it's pretty easy!

But what if you want to make things feel faster and have more energy without speeding up? This lesson will teach us a high-energy strumming pattern that will add speed to your sound without changing your tempo! And, you'll learn some tricks to make it more dynamic, which will help develop your overall guitar technique. :)

All-Down 8th note Strumming Pattern

This easy strumming pattern is very effective. It's also often used in pop music. Coldplay often uses this all-down strumming style. It allows you to double the number of possible strums in a bar! You'll start with four downstrums in a bar. Then, you'll want to add a downstrum for every 'and' of the beat. This will give loads more energy to our strumming. You'll feel it picking up! Later on, we'll start exploring by adding upstrums in there too.

💡 Remember about counting ands? We usually add upstrums on those 'ands,' but now you'll play only downstrums.

Accenting the Back Beats

Now, strumming eight identical notes can be tedious. It's also time to introduce the idea of adding an accent to your strumming. This means you'll be playing some beats louder than others! To add some groove to your strumming, you'll want to play some strings louder than the others.

To accent the backbeats, strum louder on Beats 2 and 4. You can also play all the other strums quietly. Give it a go, and see the dynamic difference it makes! It should add more momentum to your strumming and pulse to the pattern. With practice, you'll be able to accent back beats with all the other strumming patterns you've learned. Keep it simple with the eight-down strums and make it feel nice!

How To Pick The Right Strings

Let's go through how to pick the right strings for a few common chords for this strumming pattern. First, with the A chord, you want to pick from the 5th string down. You can mute the thickest string by reaching your thumb around the fretboard.

Make sure that string does not ring out! With the C chord, it's easier to mute the thickest string with finger 3! Playing the D chord might feel trickier - you're picking from the fourth string down.

It won't be perfect at first - and that's okay! Developing picking string accuracy happens with progress. Your picking hand will eventually find the correct string to play. That's a skill that will come with practice. For now, be aware of your string accuracy, so you can encourage this idea to grow. :)

Strumming Pattern Practice

First, get familiar with playing this way! It might feel a bit awkward at first. Keep going at it until it feels good.

To practice this strumming pattern, pick any chord you like and start strumming. Go slow and easy. Don't overthink it - you already know how to strum; you're just doing more of it now.

Once you're feeling comfortable, start practicing the strumming pattern with a metronome. This is where it can get tricky for beginner guitar players. With more notes in the bar, it can be easy to get off tempo. Find a speed that's not too fast or too slow, and set your bpm between 60 and 80.

The ultimate goal is to play this all-down strum pattern on any chord. For now, try to make it feel good. Get your groove on. Then, you can start thinking about the string accuracy and chord progressions you play!

Now - let's explore how you can improve pick manipulation!

lessons.title: Pick Manipulation
lessons.summary: Learn how to manipulate your pick when it shifts and explores different picks!
lessons.text:
Pick Manipulation: here's what you need to know.

When you first start playing guitar, using a thinner pick is more forgiving and is great to hold tightly. But, now that you're an advancing beginner, you're starting to play scales and picking out notes individually!

It's the perfect time to start exploring with slightly thicker picks. Thicker picks are also great if you're playing songs that move between strumming and picking notes. In this lesson, you'll learn valuable tips on manipulating your guitar pick while you play. You'll also explore how to experiment with different types of picks. :)

The Right Guitar Pick Matters

If your pick is too thin, you'll struggle to pick out the notes. But, once you move on to a thicker string, it'll be harder to hold on to the pick. It might move around in your fingers or fall on the floor.

Thicker picks make bigger contact with thicker strings - which unintentionally makes it move in the wrong direction. At this stage in your guitar journey, experimenting with all different pick thicknesses is encouraged!

💡 Be aware of the different pressure you have holding them. Thicker picks need a lighter hold to have dynamic control!

Thicker picks are better for picking, while thinner ones are better for strumming. However, thicker picks will move around in your handly and are harder to hold. Be aware of these nuances, and see what you prefer in your strumming and picking style!

Picking Manipulation When Strumming

How do you deal with the pick suddenly pushed in, and you can't play with it? Or what if your pick starts rotating? You'll have to find a way to manipulate your pick back into its correct spot!

When you're playing a song, you don't want to make an obvious stop to put your pick in the right place. You'll have to explore and see what works best for you. Get used to fiddling with the pick. The key is to keep strumming and playing even if your pick moves around.

Here are some options I recommend to manipulate your pick if it starts shifting:

When your pick shifts around, your middle finger will usually get involved to fix it. Use your middle finger to flick the pick back in place.

Lightly hold your pick and let the pressure of the string move the pick around. The pick might start pointing away from you, but keep playing. Use your thumb and finger to gradually shift it back to its original position. Keep going until it's back to its correct position.

Sometimes, you might have no choice but take a little beat break to turn your pick. Do it quickly, and get right back into the pattern. Don't stop the whole song even if your pick has gone in a funny direction!

How To Practice Using A Pick

To practice, I recommend you start rotating the pick in your fingers. Get comfortable with your pick, twirl it around your finger, and even change the pressure of your grip.

Experiment with all three different pick thicknesses. It'll help you understand what manipulation options work for you. Do this incrementally, and try different picks with scales, practice songs, and chords exercises.

Start with the thinnest pick and gradually move to the slightly thicker ones. What's important here is that you become more aware of your pick manipulation. This process can be tricky - so don't get discouraged if you don't get it right away. Part of your guitar journey is to balance what you can do and what you find fun!

Let's check out some easy songs for advancing beginners!

lessons.title: Songs For Module 8
lessons.summary: An awesome song repertoire with loads of easy songs for you to practice the Stuck 3&4 chords!
lessons.text:
New Guitar Skills ... New Guitar Songs.

And I have an awesome song list perfect for advancing beginners! :)

For Module 8, break up your song practice into two parts. First, work on a song you already know for 5 minutes. Then, spend 10 minutes working on a song that uses the new Stuck 3&4 chords. This way, you'll be able to improve skills learned in Grade 1, as well as put into practice your new 3&4 stuck chords.

Now, which new song are you going to pick? That's up to you! These are all great options for practicing, but pick a song you enjoy! It's always important to play the songs you love, especially at your current guitar stage - it'll help you stay motivated. :)

9 Easy Songs For Advancing Guitar Beginners

Here 9 songs perfect to practice stuck 3&4 chords on the guitar. Some of these song lessons are pretty old! So don't mind the quality. But the material is still great to learn these awesome songs.

Wonderwall by Oasis (Simplified)

Wonderwall is THE classic song known for 3&4 chords. But the original chords and the strumming can be tricky for beginners. If you want to learn this song, it's a good idea to simplify it! Strum only on the beat, and don't get too fancy with the strumming variations! Learn it using the JustinGuitar Lessons & Songs App.

Every Rose Has Its Thorn by Poison

Maybe it's just my generation, but I can't hear these chords without thinking of this song! Every Rose Has Its Thorn - Poison is a great song for familiarizing with the Stuck 3&4 chords. Most of the song uses G, C, and D Chords. You also have an Em chord coming at the bridge. You can play regular chords for that part, but it's a fun variation!

Brown Eyed Girl by Van Morrison

Brown Eyed Girl by Van Morrison is a real classic and a party favorite! The original recording doesn't use the Struck 3&4 chords. However, they work great in this song. We might check out the riff later too! ;)In the song lesson, swap out some regular chords to play the stuck 3&4 chords.

Free Fallin by Tom Petty

Free Fallin uses a standard D, the 'Big G,' and an Asus4. When you play the Asus4, remember to lift the little finger off and let that E string ring out! This tune is an awesome way to play the Big G, and I love Tom Petty!

Good Riddance (Time Of Your Life ) by Green Day

Good Riddance by Green Day is a pop-rock classic! It uses the 3&4 stuck chords, in combination with picking out notes one at a time while strumming. You'll learn more about that guitar technique later on.

Patience by Guns N Roses

An awesome 90's ballad. This song has many slash chords (the name has nothing to do with the band or guitarist!). We'll be looking at slash chords later in this grade, so it might be a good one to take an early look at!

You Shook Me All Night Long by AC/DC

Now we're talking! My favorite band! :) If you're a rocker and want to put your 3&4 stuck chords into action - this is the song for you! Many beginners will find it pretty tricky to follow the record - so once again, simplify it. This lesson is super old, but it still rocks!

Shallow by Lady Gaga

What a song! This Lady Gaga song uses the Struck 3&4 grips and some variations. It also has some tasty fingerstyle in it! And sorry, no lesson for this one, but it's something I'll look into.

Spotify Playlist Module 8

Give these awesome original recordings a listen, and get inspired to rock out on your guitar with my Spotify Playlist for Module 8.

Know other awesome songs that use the stuck 3&4 chords? Log into your JustinGuitar account and leave a comment below! Maybe you'll inspire a fellow guitar player. :)

lessons.summary: One of the best-known guitar riffs of all time and SO MUCH FUN to play! :)
