lessons.text:
Beginners can play this iconic Pink Floyd riff!

Develop your guitar skills by practicing 'Wish You Were Here.' :)

Learn how to play a beginner version of the Wish You Were Here riff by Pink Floyd on the acoustic guitar! This ballad is an all-time party favorite - people love to sing along to this song. It's also an excellent riff exercise to practice those stuck 3&4 chords. There are loads of good stuff there, which will be great for you to explore!

2️⃣ Grade 2+. Wish You Were Here is excellent to practice all the things we learn in the JustinGuitar Beginner Course - Grade 2.

To play the riff for Wish You Were Here as a beginner, you'll need to:

Use a slightly thicker pick

Fingerpick individual notes

Listen to the rhythm by ear.

In this lesson, we'll focus on learning the riff as a practical exercise to use the techniques we're learning in this course! Check out the full song tutorial here if you want to learn the entire song.

How to Play the 'Wish You Were Here' Riff

This simplified riff version is almost the same as the original. The original has a few more subtle things: extra strums, hammer finger techniques, and fingerpicking variations. But my simplified version makes it so much easier to play for beginners! And it sounds just as cool.

This riff has a mixture of picking out notes individually and then strumming. I recommend using a thicker pick - it'll help ring out those individual notes!

'Wish You Were Here' - Guitar Chords

The Wish You Were Here chords start with the stuck 3&4 Chords in open G. Then, you'll play an open A string and an open D string. In the intro, only use down picks for now. As you progress and feel more confident with the chords, you'll be able to get fancy and add some picking variations.

There is an Em 7 in there - and there's no way around this stretchy chord. E minor 7 chords will be tricky! Getting that stretch between those two fingers is hard work! So it's normal if the transition isn't flawless at first!

And it might be tempting - but don't use your thumb to reach over the fretboard and mute the thickest string. Doing this will cause more problems and muscle pain - and you'll need your muscle intact for an upcoming barre chords lesson.

So, make sure you keep your thumb right behind the neck of your guitar fretboard - and keep it there!

Wish You Were Here Rhythm

You might find counting the rhythm for this riff a bit challenging. The best way to learn this is by listening to the original recording. So please give it a few listens to understand how it rhythmically flows.

Don't worry too much about the rhythm! This song is in 16th note counting, which we deal with in the intermediate course. For now, focus on knowing where things fall on the beat! If you need to, tap your foot to help guide you - it'll be easier than counting out loud!

I hope you enjoy learning this awesome Pink Floyd tune! If you want to have a bit of a laugh, then go and check out how Nitsuj's attempt! You can watch him fumble my way through this song, and maybe you'll relate to some of his struggles :)

'Wish You Were Here' - Free Tabs for Beginners!

Here are free guitar tabs to help you learn Wish You Were Here faster! But long-term, you'll need to memorize the song rather than play it from paper. :)

💡 Get full tabs, chords, and lyrics to follow along with over 700 song lessons! Check out JustinGuitarTabs and start your free trial right now. :)

👉 Have some fun with it! When you're ready, let's get into some practical Theory with notes in the open position!

lessons.title: Notes In Open Position
lessons.summary: Let's check out some music theory and learn notes in the open position!
lessons.text:
Music Theory Can Be Fun and Practical!

In this lesson, you'll learn about notes in the open position :)

Learning notes in the open position gives you a deeper understanding of how and why you play chords a certain way. It also helps unlock your fretboard possibilities!

In Grade 1, you learned about the note circle. Now, it's time to figure out where the notes are on your guitar fretboard.

The first 3 to 4 frets on the guitar are in the open position. To learn open position notes, you'll need a combination of the note circle and the names of open strings notes. Now, let's check exactly how you can do that! :)

What Are Open Notes On Guitar

You should already know open string note names. If you need a reminder, check out these common English mnemonics for the open string note names:

Eddie

Ate

Dynamite

Good

Bye

Eddie

To locate the notes of your fretboard, you have to count up from these open strings. Each note on the circle is a semitone, which is one fret on the guitar. Two semitones make one tone, which is two frets on the guitar.

On the note circle, you'll remember that some of the white notes have sharps and flats between them and some of them do not. For example, E to F is a semitone apart, or one semitone/one fret. However, F to G is a tone apart - two semitones / two frets. It makes sense, right? :)

For now, we're only going to be worrying about the white notes - no sharps and flats yet!

How To Practice Open Notes On The Guitar

This theory isn't something you need to practice over and over again! Learning this is more like studying - look at it long enough until you've understood and memorized it.

Use this diagram you can use to guide you - but you shouldn't be glued to it. Try to visualize the open notes in your mind - or even better - locate them on your guitar as you learn each one.

Focus on knowing the white notes in the open position. Spend some time practicing this by adding this lesson to your practice routine. Run your fingers through the notes, and play the white notes up and down. The goal is to figure out all of the notes you might want to play in the open position.

If you feel that you can easily name and play all of those notes, move on to a more practical exercise. You can spend extra time on chord changes or improving your guitar rhythm. Always focus on practicing the skills that challenge you the most. :)

Diggin' music theory and want to learn more? Check out the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course. A practical. fun, and fast music theory course for guitar players to help connect your skills to your musical imagination! :)

Now - it's time to wrap up Module 8 and to set up an effective practice schedule.

lessons.title: Module 8 Practice
lessons.summary: Set up an effective 30 mins practice routine and edit your guitar practice to your needs!
lessons.text:
Module 8 Complete ... Another One Bites The Dust!

IMPORTANT - an apology

The practice item "L8 Songs using Stuck 3 & 4 chords" plays with no volume in My Practice Assistant. Please set your own 10-minute timer and play along with songs on the JustinGuitar App or other audio sources.

Now, let's up your practice sessions. :)

We'll be aiming for 30 minutes per practice session from now on! :) If you struggle to practice for that long, separate your practice into 2 x 15-minute sessions. The key here is to make sure that you work on all the things on the list.

And if you do practice for a bit longer, that's fine too! You might be feeling the vibe of your songs and want to keep at it. Go for it! :)

The more you practice, the faster you will progress. But, don't go crazy and over-practice! That can lead to wrist and finger pain - which is no fun!

💡 Set it up using the pre-made practice routine for Module 8. Under the video, click on the 'Practice' Tab. Save the routine, then edit and access the items in your Dashboard.

Practice For Your Guitar Needs

By Grade 2, you should know your guitar self enough to what works best for you. Feel free to add to or change things up! Your guitar journey has to stay inspiring, and enjoying your guitar practice is essential to stay motivated! :)

So, don't be afraid of changing things. Throughout the next few weeks, you might find you want to skip over certain skills and focus extra time memorizing certain things. I encourage you to edit your routine to fit your needs!

30-Minute Practice Breakdown

Here's my recommendation for a typical 30-minute practice at this stage:

Exploring Stuck 3&4 Chords (either OMC / PFC): 3 minutes

Em Pentatonic Scale Practice: 2 minutes

OMC G to D (4 finger G): 1 minute

Perfect Fast Changes (PFC) G to D: 1 minute

New Strumming Practice: 3 Minutes

Riff Fun: 3 Minutes

Open Note Study: 2 minutes

Song work (new songs): 10 minutes

Song repertoire revision: 5 minutes

When Will You Be Ready To Move On?

Put these skills into practice for at least 2 weeks. If you practice 4 times a week, you might even be spending 3 to 4 weeks on it - and that's fine! Don't rush things - there's some essential guitar material in there you learn correctly. To optimize your practice schedule, you can always use My Practice Assistant to track and follow your progress.

When you're ready to move on, you'll be able to:

Play all the new Stuck 3&4 chords from memory - and remember their names!

Play the Open Em Pentatonic Scale up and down with the metronome at 80bpm. Aim for one note per click.

Play the all-down 8th note strumming with a metronome at 80bpm with confidence.

Had some playing Wish you Were Here Riff.

Learned at least 2 songs that use the new Stuck 3&4 Chords.

Learned the notes in the Open Position - if not from memory yet, you're able to figure them out quickly!

It would be awesome if you can play at least one of the new songs all the way through. Do this either with the beginner course app or with the song's original recording!

I hope you're enjoying Grade 2 so far. See you for Lesson 9 very soon - where you'll learn the dreaded F chord. Nitsuj is battling with it now!

modules.label: Module 9
modules.title: The F Chord Journey & Pinky Workout
modules.intro:
WELCOME TO MODULE 9! 🙌

Are you up for the challenge? Time to learn the F chord!

This module gives you a first taste of the F Chord and some awesome F Chord Cheats! Some of you will find it easy, and others, like Nitsuj, might find it a bit of a battle! And that's fine - we all learn at different speeds! Take your time if you need to. :)

For now, we're not looking to master the F. You'll start working and a bunch of tips to make your playing more effortless! Here's what you'll learn in this module.

What You'll Learn

We'll start Module 9 by tackling the F Chord. A struggle for most guitar players - but many ways and cheats to play it! And they might call it the F chord for a reason, but I promise I made it easy for you! :)

This lesson will go perfectly for the exciting riff exercise! You'll learn the Californication riff by Red Hot Chili Peppers - and an iconic tune to practice some F chord variations.

We'll check out a helpful technique to mute your chords on purpose, a simple movement that is useful for many reasons!

Then, we'll learn how to can create your chord book. Why? Well, no one knows your playing style better than you! And I made free downloads for you to print out on paper. :)

Next, we'll learn the C Major Scale - an awesome scale to learn to improvise on the guitar! It'll be useful for all the fun songs planned for this module.

Finally, it's about time you learn about the 16th Note Strumming Pattern. The goal here will be to explore - and have fun with some new patterns!

You'll learn an awesome exercise to strengthen your pinky finger! Not a finger we use very often so far, but it needs to be in top shape when it's his turn to play!

You'll end with a bit of music theory to better understand what chords are in a key. Nothing too complex- just enough to understand this fundamental guitar basic. :)

👉 Ready to learn and have some fun? Let's get started with the F chord! :)

lessons.title: The F Chord
lessons.summary: The F chord is a struggle for most beginner guitar players, but together we can do it :)
lessons.text:
THE F CHORD ...

It's Finally Your Time To Learn It!

You've made it to the F chord! Your first barre chord and the most notorious chord of them all.

MOST beginner guitar players will struggle with this! It might take you weeks, if not months, to master this chord. It's a process - so be patient with yourself! The key is to get the finger placement right and to make the F chord ring out clearly. Then, you'll learn how to change chords to and from them and incorporate them in songs!

You'll want to effortlessly shift in and out of the F chord, like with your open chords! So, you've got to give your hand some time to strengthen and get familiar with the positioning.

This is why I'm introducing it pretty early on in Grade 2. The sooner you start working on this one, the better!

In this lesson, you'll learn everything you need to know to start playing the F chord. We'll look at the thumb position, wrist position, hand rotation, and much more! I'll also give you 6 valuable tips that will make the F chord a bit easier. :)

What Is a Barre Chord?

You know what they say - you never forget your first barre chord, especially when it's the F chord!

Barre chords get their name by the way you grip them. With them, your first finger lays down, barring across the strings.

Your first finger acts as the nut of your fretboard, moving it up to whichever fret you're barring across. This makes it easy to move up and down your fretboard.

Barre chords are awesome - they let you do much quicker chord changes and allow you to play loads of songs!

How To Play The F Chord

To get you started, here's how to position your hand. Place your 1st finger barring across the 1st fret. Your 2nd, 3rd, and 4th fingers are playing individual notes. Look at the chord shape in front of the barre - it should be the same as an E chord shape. The only difference is the fingering.

Use the diagram below to help guide you.

Try playing an E chord using your 2nd, 3rd, and 4th fingers. Then, move the entire shape up one fret and barre the 1st fret with your 1st finger.

Now, when you add the barre on the 1st fret, you're shifting everything in your Open E Shape chord up by one fret. An E chord moved up one fret becomes an F chord.

With the F chord, there are a few positioning challenges that you might encounter. Things might work better depending on your finger length and strength. How you interact with your guitar will also determine the best position!

6 Tips To Play The F Chord

TIP 1 - Curve your first finger

You're fretting three of the middle strings. So, your first finger only needs to hit the thickest string and the thinnest two strings! This is great because it's challenging to play all six strings using only one finger!

Don't lay your 1st finger down completely flat and straight on. It should be leaning it slightly over to its side. Stay aware of where your knuckles and the fleshy parts of your finger sit on the strings. This will make sure you're getting the best sound out of those barred strings.

Now, you'll want to experiment a bit and position your finger wherever you find you get the best sound. Try and find a position so that your hand position is the most relaxed. This might look different from someone else's barre chord positioning. Don't compare yourself to others - and find what feels best for you. :)

Try not to place the first finger so high up that it hangs over the top of the fretboard by more than 1cm (half an inch). Your first finger should only be just over the edge of your fretboard.

TIP 2 - Roll the barre slightly onto the side

When practicing the F chord, place your barre down first. Then, add the other fingers onto the strings. If you notice your fingers leaning over a bit while doing this - that's alright! Your fingers aren't used to this shape yet. Once again, it's all about finding a position that feels comfortable and makes the best sound.

Once you've got all your fingers in place, pick out each string individually to see that each one is ringing out. Then, strum the whole chord.

Yikes! Sounds off? Don't panic!

Your first F chord attempts might sound terrible - it likely WILL sound terrible! But this will get better with practice and patience. You've got to build up some muscles in your hand for this chord to sound good - and this takes time!

If you find your hand muscles a little sore, especially between your 1st finger and thumb - that's normal! You're growing your strength - and that's a good thing!

TIP 3 - Explore different hand positions

Here's how to find the perfect hand position. Place your fingers on the strings in position (2nd, 3rd, and 4th fingers first, and then the barred 1st finger). Then, relax your hand and your arm.

Pay attention to where you're tensing up, where it hurts, and where it feels awkward. Avoid soft fleshy bits of the finger. These are too soft to put the amount of pressure you need. Wobble your arm around and try to find the place that feels most comfortable. Then, press again and see if it's working on getting cleaner chord sounds.

Explore doing this - it will take you a few tries until it feels right. We all come in different shapes and sizes. So, you've got to focus on what works for your needs!

It can take time to find the right place for you! The beginning stages of most things can be a struggle. Remember that it will get better through time and practice! :)

TIP 4 - Angle your wrist

Pay attention to the angle created at your wrist. Once you've got your fingers in position on the strings, you may notice that your wrist is almost at a 90-degree angle. This isn't great - it can be bad for your tendons. This can create pain and lead to carpal tunnel syndrome!

To soften that angle, try bringing your elbow back. Doing this will help relieve some of the arm strain and pressure from your hand by pulling back on the strings.

Try and use a mirror or a selfie camera to see make sure you have the right position!

TIP 5 - Pull your arm back

With barre chords, you'll want a good amount of pressure on the strings with your fingers. To do this without straining the muscle, try pulling away from your fretboard with your arm. That little contribution can help add more pressure!

Pulling back just a little bit can make a huge difference - give it a go!

TIP 6 - Rotate your wrist

When fretting your F chord, take a look at where your thumb is on the neck of your guitar. Use your hand to create a lever. This helps press the strings down harder and with less effort!

Now, move your thumb higher up your guitar neck. This will make it more in line with your 2nd finger. Doing this will naturally rotate the wrist towards you.

It'll help add more pressure against the strings - and this means your 1st finger doesn't have to work so hard!

How To Practice the F chord

I know - there's a lot to think about when it comes to the F chord!

The most important thing to remember is to be patient with yourself! Practice makes permanent - so make sure you're learning this barre chord the right way. So, don't rush the process - and make sure your positioning is correct!

If you're lucky enough to have both an acoustic guitar and an electric guitar, I recommend that you alternate between your guitars to practice the F chord.

On the electric guitar, it's easier to get your fingers in a nice position and to figure out the positioning mechanics. With the acoustic guitar, you need a lot of strength to get the notes right out.

So, by alternating between the guitars, you get the strength element from using the acoustic guitar. With the electric guitar, it's easier to practice the correct position.

Now, here's a quick recap to help you practice: Position fingers first, then barre the strings Explore the best position of the barre to avoid soft fleshy bits of the finger Roll the barre slightly onto the side Check your wrist angle! Pull back slightly with your arm to help get pressure. Check the thumb position and explore the lever effect. Make sure you regularly relax your arm to find the perfect finger position for your anatomy!

I know I've said it already - but be patient with yourself! This is NOT one of those chords that you'll pick up immediately. Even once you can play it well, you've got to be able to play it within a song.

So, you'll be working on the F chord for a little while. Don't give up! If you need a little motivation - and a laugh - check out Nitsuj's attempt to play the F chord!

Up next - I have some exciting F chord cheats that are super helpful! :)

lessons.title: F Chord Cheats
lessons.summary: 3 ways of playing the F chord - WITHOUT a barre :) Awesome chord substitutes for you to explore!
lessons.text:
3 ways of playing the F Chord

And they're NOT barre chords :)

While you're still learning the F chord, I need to show you some helpful F chord cheats! These are F chord cheats - but it doesn't mean they won't be a challenge! Think of these as your get-out jail chords. ;)

These chords are a great substitute for the F chord most of the time, but you'll have to put your ear training to use to know what sounds best! If you're struggling to play a big F at some point, these will be great to substitute it!

In this lesson, you'll learn how to play these 3 F chord hacks:

F Major 7

F Major 7/C

The Mini F Chord

These 3 chords are great on their own, and you might prefer a specific one depending on the chord changes or song.

So - grab your guitar, and give these a go!

How To Play the F MAJOR 7

This chord is a good substitute for the traditional F chord most of the time. But - you'll have to use your ears! Sometimes, it won't sound right in a particular tune. To help guide your finger positioning, use the diagram below. :)

For this chord, you're only playing the thinnest four strings. Use your 3rd finger to help to mute the 5th string. If it rings out - it's not always the worst thing in the world! Don't play that low E string, though! It'll sound not very good.

Also, be careful not to mute the thinnest string with your 1st finger.

You may notice that this shape is like that of a C chord shape - they're both a little stretchy! That's actually a good chord change for you to practice - C to Fmaj7.

How To Play the F Major 7 With A C Bass

This one is an excellent, old-school chord that sounds a little fuller than the last one! It builds on the Fmaj7 chord - this time, you're fretting the 5th string instead of muting it.

You've got the full E chord shape going with your 2nd, 3rd, and 4th fingers. But instead of the barre on the 1st fret, you're only playing the 2nd string with the 1st finger. Mute the thickest string, and leave the thinnest string open.

Again, practice changing between this chord and a C chord. Take your time and make sure you get it right! Here's what it should look like on your fretboard:

Those numbers under the chord box are showing the function of the notes. Don't worry about it for now! You'll learn about that stuff later on!

How To Play The Mini F Chord

This F chord hack is possibly the most useful of all 3. It might seem simple - but this one is also a challenge!

The mini F uses the thinnest four strings. Unlike the F major 7 chord, you're fretting the thinnest string rather than leaving it open.

To play the mini F Chord, create a mini barre with your 1st finger. Use it to play the thinnest two strings. Lay it down first, and then place the 2nd and 3rd fingers down. Again, you're going to avoid hitting those thickest two strings. Use your 3rd finger to help mute the 5th string.

Check out the diagram below - see how your 1st finger is only 'barring' two strings?

Sometimes, you'll see players adding a bass note by hanging their thumb over the top of the neck. Don't worry about this for now! It's much too tricky for beginners, and you'll do fine with sticking to your four fretted strings.

A good chord change to practice with the mini F chord is D to mini F. This change will involve all of your finger changing. It's something you'll want to add to your OMC exercise!

Extra Tips

You've got to listen! When substituting one of these chords out for a full F chord, listen to which one sounds the best. If it doesn't sound great, try a different one.

Also, these chords are helpful on their own. So, even if you can play the regular F chord, these are still great to keep in your chord arsenal. Practice them - and practice them as soon as you can!

Even better - Start working on these using My Practice Routine. You'll be able to track how fast you can change in and out of these chords - and see proof of your progress throughout the weeks! That's always encouraging. :)

You can start with some of the suggested chord changes in this lesson. Then, you can see what some other common F chord changes in songs you'd like to play.

💬 Join The Discussion!

View this post on Instagram A post shared by JustinGuitar (@justinguitar)

Remember - you might find these Grade 2 lessons more challenging than Grade 1 - but that's good! As you advance in your guitar journey, it's normal to spend more time on lessons. If you're not blowing through them like you were in previous lessons - don't worry about it! It's part of the journey. :)

Next lesson, let's explore how you can mute your strings with your strumming hand!

lessons.title: All Stop Mute
lessons.summary: Muting your strings is useful for many reasons! Learn how to mute your strings with a simple movement.
lessons.text:
Muting your strings is useful for many reasons!

All you need is a simple movement :)

In this lesson, you'll learn how to easily mute all your strings with your strumming hand. This can be useful stylistically - and is excellent for rock and reggae. It can also be helpful if you accidentally hit a wrong note somewhere!

How To Mute ALL Your Guitar Strings

To mute your string strings, use the outer part of your strumming hand - the edge of your palm.

A slight twist of the wrist is all you need to mute all the strings in one go! It's a small but significant movement.

Work on it slowly and try to feel out your anatomy and mechanics. See what works best for you. Also, this is an excellent time to pay attention to your hand placement over the strings. If your hand is at the right angle, this should be easy to do!

When To Mute Your String

Muting your strings is particularly useful if you're playing rock or with distortion. You'll need to know how to mute the strings quickly!

It's also great when your practicing chord changes and accidentally hit the wrong strings. It's a good way to reset your strings back in place - so you can quickly move on!

As I said, this is great for when you make a mistake and need the wrong notes to stop ringing out! There's nothing worse than the wrong note going on for a full bar.

And, it's great when you play riffs! Again, if you hit the wrong note somewhere or might want a shorter note - use this technique to mute your strings!

Muting In A Strumming Pattern

You'll find that this type of mute is pretty common in reggae and ska music, too. For this style of music, you don't mute after beat 1. You mute right after you strum the chord - which makes your chords shorter and more staccato. We'll be exploring this more a little later - but no harm in exploring it on your own. Especially if this is the style of music you dig - try incorporating it in a strumming pattern and seeing how it sounds!

This technique is something you'll want to start working on! It's a good one to practice with your Perfect Fast Changes exercise. You'll be able to practice muting your strings and improving your chord changes at the same time.

Next lesson, let's check out how you can make your own chord book! :)

lessons.title: YOUR Chord Book
lessons.summary: We’ve all seen those massive books of guitar chords, but building your own is way better!
lessons.text:
Got quite a few chords under your fingers?

Time to put together your own chord book! 🙌

I know there are tons of chord books on the market, but there is some value to building your own.

There's nothing better than personalizing a product to your needs! After all, you know yourself better than anyone else.

So, let me show you why and how you can create your own chord book! :)

Why You Should Build Your Own Chord Book

First off, most of those chord books are chock-full with chords you may never use. When making your own chord book, you can fill it with chords that you need to know for songs you're actually going to play.

Sometimes it's not necessary or beneficial to learn every variant of every chord out there. Unless you're Ted Greene, author of the legendary Chord Chemistry book. An exciting read for musical theory fanatics like :)

The process of putting your chord book together is helpful in many ways. You'll be able to put all the chords you want in there and writing them in the way you like to play them!

You're creating a visual representation of it in your mind, committing it to memory, and making sense of it. How awesome is that? :)

While making the chord book, you can even write down what the notes in the chords are. This becomes especially helpful when you go on to study more music theory.

For now, you can start recognizing patterns in the notes. This will help you understand how each note functions within the chord. Then, you'll be able to see how you can manipulate the notes in a chord to get a specific sound!

How To Create Your Guitar Chord Book

To start, download some blank chord box paper in the DOWNLOADS tab above. I included a few variations so you can choose the style that suits you.

Print out seven pages. That way, you can have one page for your A chords, one for your B chords, one for your C chord, and so on!

Later on, you can add pages for your A# and Ab chords and whatever else you would like.

Organize it all in a binder and keep it handy!

Great Guitar Chord Books To Buy

Later in your journey, you will almost certainly want to get some chord books. These are great to explore new chord forms you might not think of on your own.

Here are some excellent chord books I recommend:

The Mickey Baker Jazz Guitar book is a classic,

Reaching For The Uncommon Chord by Allan Holdsworth,

Joe Pass Jazz Chords book

So many options out there! Try and avoid the ones marketed at 1001 chords you must know and other clickbait titles. They're most often full of silly chords to make up the numbers!

Next up, let's have some fun with the C major scale for beginners :)

lessons.title: C Major Scale
lessons.summary: Wanna learn scales for beginners? Start here. Let's check out the C major scale in the open position.
lessons.text:
Major Scales For Beginners

A skill worth your time and effort!

When used correctly, scales are super helpful in advancing your guitar playing! Practicing scales is great for practicing picking individual strings.

At this stage in your guitar journey, scales should be part of your practice routine. Add this as a practice element in your practice assistant, and track the speed of your scale playing!

In this lesson, we’re going over the C major scale n the open position. Once you’ve got this down, you can improvise around it on your fretboard. This means making up melodies and guitar! How fun is that? :)

Scale Box For C Major Scale

Use these visuals to help guide, and position your fingers on your guitar!

How To Play The C Major Scale

For the C major scale, as with any scale, you’re going to start and ending, on the lowest root note - C. You can find C on the 3rd fret of the 5th string - it is highlighted in red on the diagram.

For this scale, the finger numbers match up with the fret numbers. So, for example, your 3rd finger plays in the 3rd fret.

Using all down picks and going very, very slowly, play the scale ascending. This means your going up from the root note. Once you get to the top, make your way back down to the low open E string. Since you always end a scale where you started it, come back up from the low E to your C root note.

Follow along with the TAB below. NOTE. Read the TAB as a repeating pattern of four bars, one that takes you from the last note back to the first note. When you are ready to stop make sure to play fret 3 of the 5th string - the root note - to end.

How To Practice Scales On Guitar

I've said this before, but practice makes permanent - not perfect! Practice as perfectly as possible, no matter how slow you need to go!

That way, you're committing the right things to memory rather than the wrong things. You're building code in your brain, so you need to be sure everything is in there.

This isn't a speed game! You can always speed it up later.

For now, focus on getting the notes in the scale right and picking the correct strings.

6 Tips To Practice Guitar Scales

Are you struggling with your scales practice? Here are 6 tips to help you play your C major Scale!

Break up the scale in chunks, and practice the scale going up only. When you feel comfortable with it there, you can work on coming back down.

When you're learning the scale, it helps to close your eyes and picture the scale in your mind. This will further cement it in your memory.

Pay attention to what the scale sounds like. When learning music, sometimes we get caught up in techniques and rules. Don't forget that we're learning to play MUSIC! :)

Listen and train your ear to hear what a major scale should sound like. It will also help you spot mistakes!

Once you're comfortable with the scale, work on your timing. Try playing along with a metronome. Start at a slow bpm, and pick the note on the metronome's click.

Keep an even tempo. Find a speed you're able to do that while playing the scale correctly. Sometimes going either too fast or too slow can trip you up, so see what works for you!

Got any more tips to play scales? Share with the JustinGuitar community in our discussion tab. Make sure you log in to your account first. Now, let's explore the 16th note strumming pattern for beginners! See you there :)

lessons.title: Ups To The All Down (16ths)
lessons.summary: Let's explore the 16th Note Strumming pattern. It's about time, huh? :)
lessons.text:
At Last - the 16th Note Strumming Pattern

Time to elevate your strums!💪

Up until now, you've learned strumming patterns using all down strums on the 8th notes. Now, we’re going to start incorporating some up strums! It’s about time, huh?

If you're confident with the 8th note strumming, you're ready for this next strumming step! The goal here is to start exploring this new technique. So, don't be afraid to experiment with more complex or advanced strumming patterns.

Write it down patterns you try and like! Get it down on paper so you can visualize it and keep up with it. For now, I’ve got three patterns to elevate your strumming pattern. Make sure to relax into them! This learning process should be fun and easy! :)

You'll want to aim for a consistent pattern. But, if you add in a few extra strums here or there, it’s usually fine. It can be pretty nice to add in some variation. Especially at the end of a section just before a chorus. We'll explore this a bit more later!

16th Note Strumming Patterns

In the video, I talk you through three suggested patterns. They're good starting points if you want to explore different types of strumming!

Remember the numbers and '+' will be downs, and 'e' and 'a' will be up. And, if you want to add an extra strum here or there - go for it!

Strumming Pattern 1

Play all the down strums, but adding an up strum after beats 2 and 4. Start nice and slow, and then you can speed it up. Make sure you're fully relaxing that strumming arm.

This one is almost like a bounce of the backbeat! :)

Strumming Pattern 2

Putting an up strum after the and of 2 and 4. This one will be useful for many songs.

Now - if you hit an extra strum in this pattern, that's fine! Aim for a consistent pattern, but the goal here is to experiment!

Once again - keep that hand moving consistently.

Strumming Pattern 3

An extension of Pattern 2, you're now also adding an upstrum after beat 3. Make sure it feels nice and relaxed. Slow your speed down if you need to.:)

16th Note Strumming Practice

The aim of all these strumming patterns is to push yourself out of your strumming comfort zone. It's a good idea to start without a metronome. For now, you don't want to focus on the speed but just trying out new strums. You can add this as an element to your practice routine. That way, you'll be able to track and measure your progress.

To start, I recommend muting your strings to practice. This way, you'll be able to concentrate on the strums fully.

And, don't worry about counting! The goal of this lesson is really to explore and have fun. As you play around with different variations of the 16th note strumming patterns, you'll start building a sense of its rhythm.

REMEMBER - Keep your strumming hand moving consistently! :)

Next up - let's check a workout - for your pinky!

lessons.title: Pinky Workout
lessons.summary: To play guitar, your pinky finger should be strong and controlled! Here's the pinky finger workout you need.
lessons.text:
Let's put that pinky finger to work 💪

And grow its strength!

We don't often use the pinky finger (4th finger). But when it's time to shine, you want it to be strong and controlled!

You don’t want it flailing around the moment you pull it off of the string. You want to produce a solid note with it. Let me show you how you can train it with a helpful pinky finger exercise! :)

Pinky Finger Guitar Exercise

Starting on the thickest string, place your 3rd finger on the 7th fret.

Then, place your 4th finger on the 8th fret beside it.

Do the same thing on the 5th string, continuing until you get all the way down to the 1st string.

From there, make your way back up to the thickest string, this time going from 4th finger to 3rd.

Repeat the process going from 2nd finger to 4th and then 1st finger to 4th.

Remember that this is NOT a speed drill! You’re focusing on your pinky finger's ability and control.

To goal is to strengthen up your pinky. And at the same time, you'll toughen up the pad of the finger. Your pinky finger should be as hard and calloused as your other fingers!

Exercise TAB

The music TAB for this exercise looks way more complex than it is. For extra help, watch the video! It'll make more a lot more sense. :)

Next lesson - I have a special treat. Learn the iconic Californication riff and impress yourself - and your mates!

lessons.title: Californication Riff
lessons.summary: Californication by the Red Hot Chili Peppers is an awesome beginner riff! A great riff to practice the F chord.

lessons.text:
Are you a Red Hot Chili Peppers fan? 🌶️

Learn The "Californication" Guitar Riff For Beginners!

Alright - let's have some fun! Californication by the Red Hot Chili Peppers is a great tune for this module. In this lesson, we'll focus on the bare-bones version of the riff. There’s still plenty for you to get out of it. Loads of fun stuff for you to put into practice!

It features the Am and F barre chord shapes, and it will help you practice picking out individual notes.

How To Play Californication Riff

For the first part of the riff, you will be using the Am chord shape. From there, you’re going to play the F barre chord shape. Go ahead and fret the thickest string with the 1st finger, but be very careful not to mute the rest of the strings!

🔑 This is an effective way to practice curving your 1st finger in the barre chord shape. You should be familiar with this from the F barre chord lesson.

This is very tricky to do! If you’re struggling with it, don’t worry - it's a GREAT practice. Practice the riff slowly at first. Don’t get frustrated if it takes some getting used to! Be patient, and you'll get there. :)

You’ll have to figure out what feels comfortable for you and your hand. If you want, you can work in the chords too - C, G, F, and Dm. But the goal of this exercise is to nail that riff!

Californication Riff TAB

For extra help, follow the TAB below to help guide you through the guitar riff.

lessons.title: Songs For Module 9
lessons.summary: Check out these easy songs to practice the F chord - The Rolling Stones, Coldplay, RHCP, and much more!
lessons.text:
Looking for Easy Songs to play the F chord?

Rolling Stones, Coldplay, RHCP, and much more!

Throughout Module 9, your focus has been the F chord. We've also learned loads of cheats to work around this tricky chord. So, time to put it all into practice with some fun songs!

If you've nailed the full F Barre chord, then there's no harm in using it! But, the F mini barre grips are useful too - don't forget about those!In your guitar journey, you'll have discovered songs you want to play but avoided - because of that F Chord.

Now is the time to have a go at them. Now more than ever, pick songs you want to play and enjoy listening to! It'll inspire you to practice and learn them, especially when dealing with the F chord.

6 Awesome Songs To Practice The F Chord

Californication - Red Hot Chili Peppers

You learned the riff in the last lesson, so it makes sense to check out the rest of the song, right? :)

You can use the Mini F for this song. But you can swap it for the F Maj7 if you need to!The guitar solo modulates to another key and needs an F#min and a Dmaj7. You might have to skip that bit or come back to it later!

Can't Always Get What You Want - The Rolling Stones

I love this song! The original version is usually played with an open tuning.You can play it with the C and Fmaj7/C for the verses and a sneaky D chord now and then. Simple version lesson coming soon!

House Of The Rising Sun - Animals

This is a great one for D to Mini F shape, and we'll be revisiting this song a bit further down the way for some fingerpicking, so it's a good one to have a look at now!

One - U2

This one uses the Fmaj7, not the regular F! It's a great song to practice this chord. You'll be able to revisit this one later using Sus chords!

The Scientist - Coldplay

In the original recording, this Coldplay song uses an altered tuning. So, if you want a simple version, check it out here!

Dreams - Fleetwood Mac

Oh man, someone suggested this in the comments, and I LOVE this song! How could I have forgotten it? :) It's Fmaj7 to G for the majority of the song. I wish Nitsuj had been working on this - going to add it in!

Spotify Playlist Module 9

Here's a Spotify Playlist for Module 9 songs. Listen to the possibilities, and get inspired to nail that F chord on your guitar! So many to choose from. :)

Know other fun songs to practice the F chord? Log into your JustinGuitar account, and leave a comment in the discussion area! Share and inspire the JustinGuitar community! :)

lessons.title: Chords In Keys
lessons.summary: Let's tackle a bit about music theory. Understand what are chords in keys! :)
lessons.text:
Wondering What Are Chords In Keys? 🤔

Let's dive into a bit of music theory!

If you're an advancing beginner, you might be wondering: What do chords in the key mean?

Here's the basic idea when we're talking about chords in keys. All of the notes in a chord come from one specific scale. Typically, this is a major scale; minor scales have a different theoretical approach.

If you look at all of the notes on a major scale, we can combine those notes to form chords. All of those chords that we use in that scale are in the same key of that scale. For more theoretical details, check out my Practical Music Theory Course! :)

Now - to better understand this, let's look at the key of the C major.

Chords in the Key of C

All chords in the key of C will only use notes from the C major scale.

Major Chords: C, F, G Minor Chords: Dm, Em, Am

Songs containing a combination of those chords are said to be in the key of C. Makes sense, right? :)

When playing a song in the key of C, you'll want to use notes from the C major scale in the melody lines and solos. One of the many reasons why it's essential to practice your scales.

Work out the notes in the chords and compare them against those in the C major scale. Try writing out the notes in the scale and the chords. If you're a songwriter, listen to songs using the key of C to get familiar with the actual sound of the key.

Get Started With Improvising

Knowing this is super useful when you're improvising a guitar solo! Use the chords that are part of the signature key of the song - and you'll have a solo that sounds great and makes sense!

Think of Californication by Red Hot Chili Peppers. It's in the Key of C - and you guessed it - their awesome solo only uses a combination in the C Major Scale!

A fun exercise is trying to figure out the solo by yourself! Even if you don't get it right 100%, it's a fantastic way to develop your musicianship.

And that wraps up Module 9. Let's implement all those skills and set up an effective practice schedule!

lessons.title: Module 9 Practice Schedule
lessons.summary: Ready to work on everything you learned in Module 9? Let's set up a new practice schedule!
lessons.text:
Congrats - You Completed Module 9 🎉

Now - let's set up an effective practice schedule! :)

As you progress in your guitar journey, think about what you practice and adapt the routines to what you need! We all have different strengths and weaknesses when to comes to learning to play guitar.

Your practice routine should focus on what challenges you the most! This is key to efficient practice sessions.

I'm here to give you starting points from what I know about teaching. I've also added some stuff from my lefty (Nitsuj) experiences. Feel free to change things around and personalize them to your needs! And, to optimize your practice schedule, you can always use My Practice Assistant to track and follow your progress.

Also, KEEP IT FUN! :) Find ways to make the routine work for you! Like working out at the gym, you have less chance of sticking with the program if you're not enjoying it! Find what inspires you - and keep going. :)

💡 Under the video, click on the 'Practice' Tab, and use the pre-made practice routine for Module 9. Save the routine, then edit and access the items in your Dashboard.

30-Minute Practice Breakdown

Song repertoire revision - moved to first place to serve as a warm-up: 5 minutes.

Attempting F Chord: 2 minutes.

F Chord cheats practice - work on the ones you need for songs. Use the perfect idea to pick out notes one at a time & check you have all the notes ringing out clearly: 2 minutes.

PFC - Fmaj7 to C or change these to suits songs you want to play! : 1 minute.

PFC - Fmaj7 to G: 1 minute. PFC = D to F: 1 minute.

C Major Scale - SLOW and CAREFUL!: 2 minutes.

Pinky Finger Workout: 2 minutes.

Californication Riff: 4 minutes.

New Song work using F chord variations: 10 minutes.

When To Move On?

Here's when you'll know you're ready to move on to Module 10:

You have memorized the F chord cheats.

You play the C Major scale from memory.

You explored the pinky workout.

You had some fun with the Californication riff.

You added a song with an F chord to your repertoire.

You've attempted the big F barre or cheats if those are harder for you! :)

modules.label: Module 10
modules.title: Alternate Picking, Hammer-Ons, and Improvisation!
modules.intro:
Welcome to Module 10! 🚀

How's Grade 2 been treating you so far?

By now - you should be starting to have fun with your F chord. Plenty more awesome stuff to learn in Module 10. I hope you're going to dig all of it!

At your guitar stage, it's time to start exploring improvisation and how to make up your guitar solos! How awesome is that?

You'll also learn new tricks that will elevate your guitar playing! So get ready to impress yourself - and your mates! Here's a quick overview of what you'll learn. :)

What You'll Learn

We'll start Module 10 by exploring a chord variation for faster changes! I call it the Weak G Finger - and it's a super useful chord grip that needs little movement from your fingers.

We'll check out a said ''bad habit'' - the 'Mini' A Barre Chord. This A chord variation only requires one finger - your first finger! It's often my default A Chord, so I'm excited to show you its ability!

We'll tackle the F chord .. again! ! It's normal if it's still a work in progress - it is a tricky chord! At this point, it should be playable - so we'll look into some essential F Chord changes to practice.

You'll learn all about feeling your frets to develop playing without looking at your fretboard. Developing this skill will be a total game-changer in your guitar playing!

Then, we're back with some scale practice. This time, we're checking out alternate picking and improvisation using the C major scale. Very exciting if you're looking forward to making up your guitar solos!

And - it's time to switch up your sound with hammer-on and push strumming for beginners! These fun techniques will be awesome to add under your belt.

Everything you learn will go perfectly with the riff exercise I have lined up. You'll learn La Bamba's guitar riff by Ritchie Valens. A timeless tune that makes everyone want to dance!

👉 I told you - the real fun starts now. Let's check out the Weak Finger G Chord!

lessons.title: Weak Finger G
lessons.summary: The Weak Finger G chord is a super useful chord for faster chord changes!
lessons.text:
A G Chord Trick to Make Your Chord Changes Faster?

I Call It The Weak Finger G!

In previous lessons, I mentioned the two-finger G chord hack for beginners. Now is a great time to explore that a bit further! In this lesson, you'll learn a super helpful chord grip to get under your fingers. This G chord variation will allow you to make your chord changes even faster!

As you know, the typical G chord has three fingers on strings - the 1st, 5th, and 6th strings. Or, you can get crazy with the Big G - the regular G with an added note on the 2nd string.

For this Weak Finger G version, we're focusing on the 1st and 6th strings. So, for many chord changes, it'll require very little movement from your fingers. This is awesome to make quicker transitions!

How To Play Weak Finger G

This chord variation works any time you have a G chord. But, there will be times where one 'grip' of the G will sound better than another in a song. You'll have to use your ears and decide which one YOU like the sound of best! Check out the diagram below to help guide your finger placement.

Here's how to play this two-finger G chord hack.

Place your 3rd finger on the 3rd fret of the thickest string.

Using that same 3 rd finger to gently mute the 5th string.

Place your 4th finger on the 3rd fret of the thinnest string.

🚨 Feels like an awkward stretch? Don't worry - you'll get used to it! This grip is excellent for developing finger independence. This skill is helpful to play many songs. And, it'll prepare you for more complex techniques later on in your guitar journey!

Things To Watch Out For

If you place your 3rd finger down first and then try to add your 4th finger, you might find that the 3rd finger gets pulled down. It can cause the string to bend, which then knocks the note out of tune.

If you place your 4th finger down and then the 3rd, the opposite might occur. Be sure to keep your fingers planted firmly and squarely on the strings to prevent this! Again, it might feel awkward at first, but it'll get easier - I promise :)

Also, be careful to mute the 5th string with your 3rd finger. In the classic G, you would normally fret this string . Since we're opting out of that note, we can't have the open A string ringing out. To prevent this, we can gently touch and mute the string with our 3rd finger.

Finally, this may go without saying, but pay attention to where your fingers are placed on the fretboard. You want them as close to the fret as possible!

When To Use This

Many of you may think this is just a "cheat" or a "hack," but I'd say not necessarily! It may not even be an easier version of G for some of you.

You might prefer to play the classic or full Gs, and that's fine!

I do find myself using this weak finger G pretty often. It'll depend on the chords immediately before and after the G.

It may be easier to use this particular grip because it wouldn't need your whole hand to change position!

For instance, some chord changes need each of your fingers to reposition themselves. With the two-finger G, you can cut the distance your fingers need to travel. This allows cleaner, quicker, and easier chord changes.

Chord changes where the Weak Finger G Chord comes in super handy: C to G G and A minor G and F

With these chord changes, practice keeping your finger movements as small as you can.

These chord changes are great for your Perfect Fast Changes exercises!

As we advance

Once you practice this chord grip, it's up to you when you want to use it!

Even if you never use it, at least you know it's available to you. Having the option can open up a world of possibilities for you.

When you play songs, you might prefer a specific chord grip over the original artist's one. I encourage you to use whichever fingering makes the most sense for you. It all depends on your anatomy, skill level, and the emotion you're trying to convey with your playing.

Don't ever forget - music is about art. I teach you the basics and all the tips and tricks. But, the key is to experiment and find what feels and sounds best for YOU.

Up next - we're exploring a bad habit .. the mini A barre chord. Is it a bad habit? Let's see!

lessons.title: First Finger A Chord
lessons.summary: Let's explore the mini A barre chord.  Play this A chord variation using only your 1st Finger!
lessons.text:
Learn the mini A barre chord

Using only your first finger!

Coming hot off of that weak G, I figured we could re-imagine the A major chord while we're at it.

This mini A barre chord is is my default A Chord. Some might think it's a bad habit, but it might be an easier option for certain chord changes!

In this lesson, you'll learn how to play this A chord variation. The more grips you can play on guitar, the better! It's how you discover fingerings and patterns that work best for you.

How To Play The Mini A Barre

For this A chord, you won't be squeezing three fingers into one fret! What a relief, right? :)

You're going to use only one finger - your 1st finger. To play it, lay your 1st finger down across the three strings, forming a mini barre.

Try this mini A barre chord and give it a solid go for a few days! Then, see how you feel about it. It may be tricky at first, but you'll get the hang of it after a few days of practice.

🚨 Now, some people will find this very easy. Others will find it difficult. Don't fret over it too much (see the pun there?!). Your grip ability has a lot to do with your individual ability. Whichever grip you prefer is up to you and okay! I always encourage keeping an open mind and trying new techniques. :)

Things To Watch Out For

Like the A major chord, you won't play the thickest string for this chord. Leave the 5th string open, and the barre chords will be the 4th, 3rd, and 2nd strings.

Now - you've got some options when it comes to the 1st string. We include the thin E chord in the classic A chord, but I'm not a huge fan of that twangy open string ringing out! I prefer muting the 1st string with my 1st Finger. I slightly angle it to mute the string, but I don't fret it.

If you choose to leave the thinnest open E string, rotate your hand around from the knuckle. Rotating it will leave a gap between your mini barre and the open string.

Be aware of the big E (thickest string)! Up until now, you haven't been playing it often. Make sure you don't strum it by hanging your thumb over the top of the neck to mute the thickest string. If this is too much of a stretch for you, don't worry about it! Leave the thumb out of it for now.

This thumb technique is not for everyone and doesn't always work on every guitar! Later in this grade, you'll learn more about this thumb over the guitar neck technique. :) For now, focus on barring those strings!

When To Use The Mini A Barre Chord

As with the weak G, you might find that the mini barred A is easier at certain times. So - depending on the chords surrounding the A, you can decide if you want to use this barre.

Right now, it's important to explore alternate ways of playing. Doing this will give you a better understanding of the instrument! Different options of grips mean more flexibility and freedom. It will come in handy when you want to create or execute a particular sound.

See what feels good for you! And remember, it's going to feel awkward at first - like it did for the regular A a couple of weeks ago! Explore chord variations for guitar, and have fun. :) Also - don't forget to add the chords variations you really enjoy to your own chord book.

Keep an open mind and try new things - it's an awesome part of learning. Now, let's dive into some F chord changes.

lessons.title: F Chord Changes
lessons.summary: Time to start working some F chord changes! Even if your F chord is still a work in progress!
lessons.text:
Essential F Chord Changes 🎸

All beginners should know!

Oh yes - we're back at it with the full F barre chord, and it's time to start diving into more details.

Barre chords are tricky at first. Once you're comfortable with them - they open up many guitar possibilities! By now, you've practiced your first barre chord - the dreaded F chord! It's normal if it's still a work in progress! But at this stage, it should be at least playable!

In this lesson, you'll explore some chord changes that will be useful for many songs! You'll be able to add them as PFC exercise for this module's practice schedule.

Struggling With The F chord?

The F Chord is a major beast to slay. So - don't worry if you still find it challenging. :)

There are many ways to approach the F chord. Some put their fretted fingers down first when playing the F barre chord, and others place their barre down first. Try it both ways and see which way feels more comfortable!

Here's what works for me:

Placing your 1st finger down roughly in position.

Place your fingers down, and then readjust your barre.

Do this before committing to any finger placement. Then, you can move things around.

This approach seems to help frame and position the chord on the neck. Other than that, you've just got to keep at it.

🚨 Remember - be patient with yourself! You'll get through this hurdle! :) It's much nicer on the other side of it. I promise!

F Chord Changes

It's a great time to think of chord changes to and from the barred F chord.

Often, you have to change the position of your entire hand to make the changes rather than moving some fingers around. Once you introduce barre chords, it changes things up! It breaks you out of the first position / open chord comfort zone.

Here are common chord changes to practice the F chord:

C to F

G to F

Am to F

How To Practice The F Chord

Take the time to look at yourself as an 'objective observer'. Pay attention to the way your hand and your arm move with the neck and the strings.

Observe what you're doing things and the way you're doing them. This will allow you to see if there's a better way.

Focus on improving your positioning, skill, and finger independence. Get your fingers used to moving into the general chord shapes. It'll all come together before you know it.

Finally - don't be too hard on yourself! It's all part of learning by doing. The sooner you start working on these changes, the better! Incorporate these changes into the songs you're learning - it'll help absorb them.

Next lesson - we're exploring how to play guitar without looking! This awesome exercise to help develop your guitar skills. See you there. :)

lessons.title: Feeling The Frets
lessons.summary: Learn how to play guitar without looking at your fretboard and elevate your musical senses!
lessons.text:
Playing The Guitar Without Looking 👀

An awesome way to build your musical sense!

I should have realized this a long time ago. But during my Nitsuj practice, I made a discovery. When I'm playing, I noticed I could feel the frets with my fingers. - without even looking!

Doing this will get your fingers in the perfect position - without trying too hard. So this exercise is awesome to practice and build your guitar intuition! It'll feel funny at first, so being open to the full experience is essential. :)

In this lesson, you'll explore how to play guitar without looking! This exercise is loads more effective if you do it along with me. I encourage you to play along with the video instead of attempting it on your own later.

Grab your guitar, and let's give it a go! :)

Why Should You Play Without Looking

Playing an instrument is about skill, technique, and know-how. It also involves more than your sense of hearing. After all, your fingers are the ones doing all physical work - not your ears!

You may notice that your favorite musicians aren’t standing on the stage staring at their hands. Yet, somehow - they’re hitting all the right notes? How are they doing this?

They can perform this way because they feel the frets beneath their fingers! The frets act as guides along the fretboard. Since they’re raised, you don’t have to look at them to find them.

How to Play the Guitar Without Looking

To play without looking, start with your fingers in the C chord position. From there, remove your 2nd and 3 fingers, leaving your 1st finger on the string.

Now, pay attention to what you’re feeling with your 1st finger. Try to focus here on a specific fingertip.

Here's what you should ask yourself:

Do I feel the string beneath your finger?

Do I feel any of the nearby strings?

Am I touching the fret?

How much pressure am I placing on the string?

Is my hand tense or relaxed?

Think about that for a while - then slide your finger around until you can only feel the fret.

Take note and remember this feeling! The fret might only feel like a slight change in pressure. Even though it's subtle - you will be able to feel it. Your guitar is built to make the frets noticeable under your fingers.

After that, do the same with each finger. You may even want to do it with your eyes closed - this will remove any distractions from your other senses. Try to isolate the touch as much as possible!

This exercise should be fun! Not having to look at your fingers is a game-changer. Moving on, let's check out some alternate picking for C major.

lessons.title: Alternate Picking C Major
lessons.summary: Mastered and memorized the C major scale? Let's check out some alternate picking!
lessons.text:
Alternate Picking the C major scale

Using a combo of up and downstrums! :)

We've done loads of chord work so far in this module. Let's switch it up now with some scale work! Everyone's favorite, right?

But first - only attempt this once you've mastered the C major scale. If you've been following Grade 2, we learned the C major scale using all down picks.

Before attempting this, make sure you play the scale with accuracy, even if that means keeping the tempo down for the moment! Make sure you have the C major scale memorized. You'll need this before you get into improvising your guitar solos. And that's where the real fun happens! :)

C Major Scale Alternate Picking

Alternate picking involves alternating between down and up picks. This is different from using all down or all up picks - it's a combination of both strums.

When starting, go slowly! Remember - this isn't about speed. It's about building certainty in your mind. Funny enough, going slow will help you progress faster. Slow and steady wins the race here. :)

Speed and knowing the notes in the scale will come with practice. But - try to keep your tempo consistent, whichever speed you choose.

You should know the C major scale by itself so well that your fretting hand is working automatically. It shouldn't need too much attention or effort on your part!

How To Practice Alternate Picking

Practice this new strumming picking slowly. You want to get it right straight from the start. This way, you don't form any bad habits for later on! Bad habits are hard to break. It's tough to unlearn stuff once you've locked them into your head - it'll only make things more challenging as you progress.

Here are some tips to help you with this C major scale alternate picking:

Say the words out loud "down' and "up" as you're picking to focus on what you're picking hand should be doing.

Use anchor notes within the scale or markers. It's great for keeping you on track as you progress through the scale.

Readjust if necessary once you get to it. And this is better than continuing to play the scale using the wrong picks.

Finally, practice deliberately and keep in mind the particular thing you are practicing. In this case, you should be hyper-focused on your alternate picking.

Ideally, you won't be making mistakes - so you shouldn't need to check that you're still doing it right. But in reality, you might have to readjust here and there! It's one of those things that seems intimidating at first. Once you get going with it, you'll get it down faster than you think.

Next lesson, we're learning some major scale improvisation - Major Scale improvisation!

lessons.title: Major Scale Improvisation
lessons.summary: Learn how to improvise using the major scale and explore how to make your own guitar solos!
lessons.text:
Get Ready To Learn How To Make Your Own Guitar Solos

And have a blast on your guitar!

If you weren’t having fun in your guitar journey already, you’re about to now. :)

You’ve been working hard on scales and picking, now let’s put it to good use and have some fun making up your solos. Improvising is super exciting, and it helps you to unleash your skills as a musician. You’re moving on up in your guitar journey, so be proud of that.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to make up your guitar solos through major scale improvisation!

Improvisation With The C Major Scale

You've learned the C major scale, and it'll be perfect to start improvisation. For now, don't worry about the alternate picking. If you can do it - go for it! If you're not there yet, use all down picks.

Within any key, some chords belong to it, meaning the chords are composed of the notes found in the key. For the key of C, the chords are:

C, Dm, Em, F, G, and Am

The C major scale is your home base for now! If a song is in the key of C, all the notes in the C major scale will sound good. So you can play them over any of the chords in the same key.

Of course, loads of exceptions exist! But for now, stick with songs that stay in one key. It'll make more sense when you're learning how to improvise on the guitar.

7 Tips For Guitar Solos Improvisation

Improvising on the guitar can be intimidating! You’re breaking free of any protections on your ego and stepping out on your own. You’re transitioning from someone who can sort of play the guitar - to a real musician. How awesome does that sound? :)

So let yourself be vulnerable and put your feelings aside. You’ll do great! Follow these 7 tips to help you improvise guitar solos.

Tip 1 - Use The Thinnest strings

To start, only use the thinnest three strings for your guitar solo. Do this instead of using the whole scale at once!

You can also start with the notes on the thinnest string. Then, add in one string at a time. It'll give you a chance to understand the music theory you learned and put it into practice. :)

Listen to how each note rings out over the chords. Identify which combination of sounds you enjoy. Finally, pay attention to the emotion you convey as you play.

Tip 2 - Improvise with a few notes

For now - don’t worry about playing MORE stuff. I know it's tempting, but don’t use too many notes yet!

Not all guitar solos are about shredding! Think of some of your favorite guitar solos and note how they use time. It’s not always about speed.

Some of the best solos are slow and deliberate. Soloing is your chance to sing with your guitar, and there’s plenty to explore there!

Tip 3 - Use repetitions

Less is more at this stage. Take your time and use repetitions.

If there's a little riff that you like playing, try repeating it a few times as the chords beneath it change. Repetitions change the whole feel and sound of the riff!

Repeating chord sequences in your guitar solos will also make more sense to your listener!

Tip 4 - Let your riff breathe

Speaking of timing, don’t underestimate the impact of a rest. Leave some space here and there. Let your riff breathe!

The gaps in the melody are almost as important as the notes when it comes to phrasing.

Think of rest like a comma or period in a sentence. The placement will make a difference in the message and tone.

Or, think of it like a person who talks non-stop without even taking a moment to breathe! If they paused - it would make their message much more clear!

Tip 5 - Leave gaps in the melody

Leaving gaps in the melody is a useful way to let notes from the previous phrase ring out. And - it gives you a moment to think about your next move! Think about the direction you want the melody, and try to execute your idea.

Finally, don’t be afraid of your gaps. While it may feel like you’ve been resting for a long time, it doesn’t feel as long to the listener.

Tip 6 - Record yourself

A good way to know what listeners are hearing is to record yourself. I encourage you to do this!

It'll help put your playing into perspective. Do this with audio or video to step outside of yourself and hear things you may not be hearing!

If you’re using video, you can see your positioning. It'll help you adjust your posture and playing!

Tip 7 - Sing over the backing track

The last tip I’ve got for you is to sing over the backing track. Singing will help you understand natural, melodic, and interesting lines of phrasing. Doing this will do a few things for you:

It will help you hear the notes in the key.

It'll give you a bit more freedom to experiment with different sounds. And without fear of hitting a wrong note.

It'll force you to breathe.

So now is the time for exploration! Grab your guitar and have fun improvising your guitar solos!

Improvising With A Backing Track Or Jam Buddy

Now that you know the theory behind it, time to let loose! Experiment with different sounds, and find something that you love. You’re developing your songwriting skills - and allowing your creativity to grow!

Log in to your account and access the backing track through the Resources Tab. The mp3 download is also available in the tab above.

Let the JustinGuitar Community know how it goes in the discussion section. You can also share a video of yourself trying this out. Have fun experimenting! :)

Next lesson - let's take a look at a strumming technique to make your playing more exciting! See you there :)

lessons.title: The Rhythm Push
lessons.summary: The strumming push is a rhythmic technique that adds excitement to your guitar playing!
lessons.text:
What is A Strumming Push?🤔

Easier felt than explained!

The rhythmic push is a technique on guitar that adds excitement to your strumming pattern. Here's the best way to describe it: It's comparable to someone coming up behind you and gently pushing you on the back.

Your feet won't move, but your body will move forward. You want to feel that movement when you're doing chord changes on the guitar!

So this involves changing chords a bit earlier than what you're used to. This will keep the song moving forward!

The rhythm push helps to move the melody forward. You'll do this without actually changing the timing or the tempo of your strumming! It gives the feeling of a forward movement.

How To Do A Strumming Push On Guitar

The rhythm push occurs when you change the chord on the "and" of beat 4 instead of on beat 1. You're changing the chord on your upstrum right before the bar line. This will happen half a beat earlier than you would expect. Sometimes, you'll do this before beat 3 - but this is less common.

So what does it do musically? Since the chord change comes just a little earlier than you're expecting it, it'll create:

a sense of movement

urgency

excitement to the song

So it's worth exploring at your guitar stage! It can be a very effective rhythmic device. To make it work, you need clean and quick chord changes!

Check out the diagram below. Remember that numbers will be downstrums. The + will be upstrums.

How To Practice Strumming Push On Guitar

To practice the push, start listening for the push in your favorite songs. Once you do this, you'll notice that there are plenty of songs that use it.

Think about how the music makes you feel and how much of that is because of that rhythmic push.

Grab your guitar, and practice the strumming pattern on its own on muted strings. This will help you get a feel for the rhythm and strumming pattern.

Then, pick a chord combination you're comfortable with. D and G is a good one, or any of the ones you're working on in your Perfect Fast Changes exercise.

Practice the rhythm going back and forth between the two chords. Keep your changes as clean as possible! Also, the timing of the change matters here. If you need to - start slow and increase the speed as your progress.

The rest of the strumming bar is yours to experiment with. Try different push rhythm patterns! As long as you're still changing chords on the "and" of 4, you'll still achieve the rhythm push effect.

Next, let's explore hammer on for beginners on guitar!

lessons.title: Beginner Hammer-Ons
lessons.summary: Explore hammer-ons for beginners and develop your finger's independence and dexterity!
lessons.text:
Hammer-Ons Exercise For Beginners 🔨

Add some flair to your playing!

Hammer-ons are fun to work into tunes here and there! Whether you’re playing some backing chords or you're doing a guitar solo.

This technique can add interesting ornamentation to your guitar playing. We'll explore more about this concept in Module 11. For now, let's explore this technique with a helpful hammer-on exercise for beginners.

How To Do A Hammer-On Guitar?

Hammer-ons are when you pick one note and then hammer a second finger down onto the same string to get a second note - without picking a second time!

To do a hammer-on, the technique is simple. Start by playing one note on your guitar. While it’s ringing out, you hammer down a second finger onto the same string. It'll allow you to hear a second note without having to pick the string a second time.

For this to work, you’ve got to hammer that second finger onto the string! It takes some force and some finger strength. The hammer-on technique will develop finger independence and dexterity. These are useful skills for guitar beginners, especially with what we have lined up in the next module!

While the idea is simple, putting it into practice might take some work! So don't get discouraged if you don't get it right away :)

Hammer-On Guitar Exercise

Here are 7 steps to practice the hammer-on exercise:

Start with your 1st finger in the 5th fret of the thickest string

Pick the string

Then, hammer on your 2nd finger one fret higher

Get it accurate and be sure to use the tip of your finger

Don’t be afraid to hit it hard - but you don't have to go crazy.

Experiment and find the right amount of hit you need to apply

Repeat this on each of the strings. Work your way down to the thinnest string. Then, come back up to the thickest.

Try hammering between different fingers, repeating these steps. Do this between:

1st to 2nd fingers

2nd to 3rd fingers

3rd to 4th fingers

And then ONLY if you have time you can try these few below but don't be in a hurry.

1st to 3rd fingers

2nd to 4th fingers

1st to 4th fingers

How To Practice Hammer-On For Beginners

This is not a speed exercise! Focus on what you're actually here to practice. For now, you’re working on building up your finger strength and independence. Your second note should be as loud as the second note as you can.

To help with this, you might want to pick softer than you normally would. This will make it easier to match the first note’s sound and intensity. Accuracy and strength are more important than speed. If you need, slow down your tempo to help you! And remember - you're hammering down - not pressing the strings.

For your Module 10 practice, I recommend you schedule 1 minute of hammer-ons in your practice schedule. It'll be a good element to add to your practice assistant. This way - you'll be able to measure your progress with this tricky technique.

Now - are you ready to learn an awesome riff? Have some fun, practice your skills with La Bamba Riff!
