lessons.text:
Up For A New Riff On Guitar?🎶

Learn 2 ways to play "La Bamba" with the C Major Scale!

La Bamba by Ritchie Valens - a super cool riff that never seems to go out of style! It’s a classic tune that’s always a hit at parties! Even if the only line you know is “La la la la la la Bamba!”

In this lesson, you'll learn two different approaches to play the La Bamba riff. The first uses all single notes, and the second option adds a few. There are plenty of other things to focus on here.

This riff will help you with your string crossings, timing and rhythms, and chord changes. But best of all, it helps you see how you can transform a scale into a hit song! So, what are you waiting for? Grab your guitar and let's get into it!

How To Play La Bamba Riff

For this riff, you'll play all down picks, not alternate picking. It's possible to play it with alternate picking, but using all-down picks will give it LOADS more energy! :)

The first three notes are what we call a pick-up. To quickly recap, they lead into the first bar of a song. The riff starts on the “and” of beat 3.

La Bamba heavily relies on our new best friend, the C major scale. The chords in the song are C, F, and G. Using your weak finger G chord will make those chord changes easier!

You'll also notice it feels a bit different than playing a regular scale. When you're practicing scales, the notes go straight up and down. But, when you're playing a real riff - they jump around a bit more.

💡 If you got a jam buddy, take turns with one of you playing the chords! The other can play the riff over the top.

La Bamba Riff Tab Easy

For extra help, use this guitar tab to help guide you with the simple version! Once you get it down, you can move on and add a harmony note to a couple of notes as part of the riff. It'll make it more interesting, and it's super fun, and we love having fun eh? :)

💡 Get full tabs, chords, and lyrics to follow along with over 600+ song lessons! If you haven't already, start your free 7-day trial over at JustinGuitarTabs. :)

Elevate Your Sound With Harmony Notes!

For the second riff option, you're still playing all down picks for the strumming! When you graduate to this version, you'll push a bit further and pick two notes!

When working with harmonies, you’re playing at least two notes at once. It'll give La Bamba some more depth and interest. For this riff, a few of the notes are harmonized. To play them, fret the two fingers, and pick only the two strings you need.

Your picking hand is staying consistent. Just let the pick come down a bit further than you normally would to hit two strings at a time. Here's the Tab with the additional harmony notes - notice the difference between the easy version? :)

Time To Practice Your Rhythm Push!

If it’s your turn to play backup, this will be a great song to practice your rhythm push! The chord changes to the G come at the end of the previous bar, and it'll add lively energy to the song.

Once you're comfortable with everything, put it all together! Try to get the riff to match the speed on the record. This might take a bit of time - but keep practicing. :)

Next lesson - let's explore 5 chord progressions you NEED to know. :)

lessons.title: 5 Common Chord Progressions
lessons.summary: Explore 5 common chords progressions using the Key of C on guitar!
lessons.text:
5 Common Chord Progressions for Beginners

As we're closing Module 10, we're slowly working towards being songwriters, not just guitar players! How awesome does that sound? :) As you progress in Grade 2, you learn the musical elements that make up songs and understand the concepts and guidelines of those musical elements.

In this lesson, you'll learn 5 common chord progressions you'll probably be able to recognize in popular songs! It'll be a good Ear Training exercise, and these chord progressions are awesome for future songwriting!

Chord Progression Using The Key Of C

Chord progressions are a series of chords that sound great together from the same key. Since music has evolved - certain chord progressions sound particularly good! They are a helpful starting point in songwriting and improvising!

These 5 common chord progressions will be in the key of C... again! :) Here are the individual chords in this progression:

C, Dm, Em, F, G, Am

These chord progressions work in numbers. Assigning a number to each chord in the sequence will let you use the same pattern in various keys. Then, you'll reassign each number to a chord in whichever key you're playing in.

In the key of C, it looks like this:

1 = C

2 = Dm

3 = Em

4 = F

5 = G

6 = Am

7 would be Bdim, but don't worry about this one for now!

5 Common Chord Progressions

Learning these 5 common chord progressions will help you recognize the movement of the chords and which ones work well together! :) Paying attention to patterns in chord progressions is a great way to get into songwriting or music appreciation! Here they are:

1-5-6-4 C, G, Am, F

6-4-1-5 Am, F, C, G

1-4-5-4 C, F, G, F

1-6-4-5 C, Am, F, G

2-5-1-6 Dm, G, C, Am

Have Fun & Explore

Now - it's your turn to explore these progressions and see how they sound to you! Experiment by playing them slow and fast. Explore how you can use them on your guitar!

💬 Can you recognize a song in any of them? Join the discussion and let me know! :)

If you can - practice these different chord progressions with a real human! Have your jam buddy play a particular one - and play the other! It'll be memorable this way - and loads of fun to do! :)

👉 Next, we'll explore new songs to practice for Module 10!

lessons.title: Songs For Module 10
lessons.summary: Here are song recommendation for Module 10. The focus here is working on the Weak G Finger and A mini barre!
lessons.text:
Song Options For Module 10🎶

More options than ever! :)

You'll want to focus on songs that use weak finger G chord and A mini barre for this song practice. But as always, aim for songs that you enjoy. This way, they can be part of your repertoire later on - and it'll keep you motivated.

By now, you have loads of song options. Any songs with mostly the chords combination of C, F, G, or Am, G, and F will be great options for your song practice. This is when the weak finger G will be the best grip option.

However - the grips you choose always depend on your comfort level. So use the tools, skills, and chord grips that feel the best for your needs!

6 Song To Practice The G Chord On Guitar

Dreams - Fleetwood Mac

Dreams by Fleetwood Mac uses F to G for almost the entire song - so it's a great choice to practice your weak finger G! There's just a quick change in the progression for the instrumental interlude - using Am.

Nitsuj has been practicing this song loads because there are so many variations in it to test out. He practiced chord changes to the weak finger G alternating between Fmaj7, F mini barre, and F full barre. However, the F full barre was less successful than the others - check it out here if you want a laugh.

All Along The Watchtower - Bob Dylan

This Bob Dylan hit is played with Am, G, and F throughout the song. This song will be nice to work on your weak finger G. No lesson yet - but an awesome tune to check it!

Jambalaya - Hank Williams

This Hank Williams classic is a cool C, F, and G chord song try-out. There are some fancy bass note-picking patterns to explore if you are feeling adventurous! I have a 2 chord option (C/G option), but it might be a little too simple for you at this stage.

Little Talks - Of Monster And Men

Little Talks is a cracker if you want to push yourself with some super-fast chord changes! Nitsuj found it too fast and ended up slowing it down to be able to play along. So feel free to tone down the tempo if you want to play it! This song is a good test to see if you're burning through this stuff!

Dance The Night Away - Mavericks

Dance the Night Away is a song we explore in Lesson 1! It's just D and A for the whole song, so a great one for working on the A mini barre! Explore how this particular chord change feels like your A chord variation. :)

What I Like About You - Romantics

For some unknown reason, Nitsuj kept stumbling into this when exploring the E A D A progression. He never learned it properly ( and never have I ) - but maybe you'll be up for the challenge. It's a catchy one, so you might find it cool to check out :)

Spotify Playlist Module 10

Get familiar with and inspire your song choice with this Spotify Playlist for Module 10. Discover a cool tune to inspire your next guitar practice. :)

The I V VI IV Progressions

There are loads of songs that base themself around the I V VI IV progressions. You play these songs in the key of C with C, G, Am, and F chords.

If you have never watched this video, check out the Axis Of Awesome Four Chords - I use it for loads of songs. Just a heads up, they curse early in the video (1 bad word) - so be aware if you're playing it around children!

Know other songs to practice these new chord variations? Log into your JustinGuitar account, and share in the discussion area! Maybe you'll inspire other members of the JustinGuitar community! :)

lessons.title: Module 10 Practice Schedule
lessons.summary: Here's the rundown of your practice schedule for the next few weeks!
lessons.text:
Another Beginner Module Completed 🎉

Now - Let's update your guitar practice schedule! :)

You learned loads of exciting stuff in Module 10 - from improvising guitar solos to playing the guitar without looking. Now - it's time to solidify and develop those skills.

When setting up your practice sessions - think about what challenges you the most and focus on that. Feel free to adapt your routine to fit your needs. Keep it fun, enjoyable, & practice elements you want to keep playing. :)

💡Click the 'Practice' Tab to use the pre-made practice routine for Module 10. Save the routine and access it in your Dashboard.

30-MINUTE PRACTICE BREAKDOWN

Here's a starting point to guide your practice sessions:

Songs repertoire revision: 5 minutes

Attempting F Chord / Changes: 2 minutes.

Weak Finger G / mini A barre chord: 2 minutes.

PFC C to Weak Finger G chord: 1 minute.

C Major Scale Alt Picking: 2 minutes.

C Major Scale Improvisation with a backing track: 2 minutes.

Push Strumming (optional): 1 minute.

Hammer-Ons: 1 minute.

La Bamba riff: 4 minutes.

Song work using the Weak G Finger: 10 minutes.

PLUS Explore progressions in your own time!

When To Move On?

You'll know you're ready to move on to Module 11 when ...

You have memorized the Weak Finger G chord.

You have memorized the mini A barre chord.

You're able to play the C major scale using alternate picking, keeping your rhythm consistent.

You've learned at least one song using the Weak Finger G chord.

You had some fun with La Bamba! :)

Optional but useful: You're able to use the Push strumming pattern in a song

modules.label: Module 11
modules.title: Fingerstyle & Songwriting First Steps
modules.intro:
Howdy again! :) Welcome to Module 11.

Sus Chords, Fingerstyle, Songwriting, and much more!

For this module, I want you to let go and let loose! Rather than learning a bunch of new chords and techniques - let's focus on making music. And now's the time to use your fingers instead of your pick. :)

The following lessons will focus on fingerstyle; we'll learn basic fingerstyle patterns and how to train your fingers so you won't even have to think about fingering when playing fingerstyle!

We'll also get into Songwriting. Trust me - it's much better to start learning and thinking about these things sooner than later. Contrary to popular belief, you can start exploring and even writing your music as a beginner. It's a super fun thing to get into. :)

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

In this module, we'll continue our study of chords - by looking at suspended chords and exploring the chords' grips.

After you take your first steps to fingerstyle, you'll learn an awesome fingerstyle version of Happy Birthday. It'll be perfect for playing chords and the melody simultaneously. And we'll appreciate it at your next birthday party.

You'll see how small changes can add interest, especially when playing a chord for an extended time.

We'll check out some Reactive Listening™. This technique allows you to hear your guitar combined with the backing track you're playing over.

You'll get a bit of a taste of Songwriting. Together, we'll write a song using the dice method. If you haven't written a song before - it's a nice trick to get you started!

👉 Let's get into it! We'll start with some chord freedom. :)

lessons.title: Chord Freedom
lessons.summary: Exploring chords is a great way to discover new sounds and feels on your guitar!
lessons.text:
Open up your ears .. and your guitar playing 👂

and explore chord freedom for beginners!

To kick off Module 11, we will explore some of the open chords you're already familiar with.

I've done a series called "The Chord Shape Explorer," where I dive deep into the five chord shapes on the guitar. That's more for Grade 3 students, something to look forward to later!

If you're a beginner guitar player, I want you to be fearless with exploring chords! In this lesson, you'll learn how to open this chord exploration door - so consider this an introduction to chord exploration. You'll explore how to play it by ear with this new empowering tool.

Why You Should Explore Chords

The idea is that you use your ears when you play chords - not your mind or eyes. The goal is to realize that there's a lot you can do with simple chords.

Right now, I recommend using your ears - it'll tell you whether you like the sound or not. You can look at the complexities and theories later.

Have some fun with it! This lesson won't be part of your practice routine - this idea is bigger than that. Every time you're learning a song or playing around on the guitar, try some new stuff. :)

It's a guitar game-changer, and the reality of making music is that it's a lot freer than you think! The most creative songwriters and musicians do things differently - in their way. And the only way they got there is by being creative and exploring new ways of doing things!

How To Explore Chords On Guitar

Let's start by exploring the D chord on your guitar. By now, you must be very familiar with the sound, but we're going to switch it up a bit.

Try pulling one finger off of the strings at a time. Start with the 1st finger & strum the D chord minus the 1st finger. Listen to the difference and ask yourself these questions:

Does it still sound like a D chord?

What's different about it?

What mood or emotion does it evoke?

Could you possibly use it as a substitute for a D chord in a song?

Do the same for each finger in the chord and take notice of which ones sound good to you! To help you, close your eyes to hear better without focusing too much on what your fingers are doing.

Another thing you can try is moving one finger up or down a fret. You can even try moving the whole chord shape up or down on the fretboard. The reality is that you can more or less do whatever you want as long as it sounds good to you!

👂 Remember - if it sounds good, it is good.

Repeat this process with some other chords. Have fun with it, and maybe even try writing a short riff based on the new chords and sounds you've discovered.

No Limits Here!

There are no limits to chord exploration. Explore chords in any way you like. If you're playing a song cover, some of the experiments won't sound great, so you'll need to try another one. It's that simple!

The key thing here is whether you like the sound of it or not! I encourage you to explore this idea every time you're learning a new tune. So don't be afraid of it.

Have you made some chord discoveries? Log into your account and share with others on the discussion board. Inspire others to explore your new findings. :)

I hope you enjoyed this lesson! Up next, we're tackling sus chords for beginners - new sounds to add to your chord repertoire. :)

lessons.title: Beginner Sus Chords
lessons.summary: Explore sus chords and how they can spice up your guitar playing!
lessons.text:
Are you bored of your chords? 😴

Spice up your playing using beginner-friendly sus chords!

Here's your ultimate guide to suspended chords. We'll learn how to make the most out of sus chords and their theory. Then, we'll look at some relatively easy chord grips you should start exploring as embellishments.

💡 I was anticipating sus chords would be super easy, but when Nitsuj had a go at this, it was loads harder than I thought. So don't freak out if you struggle a bit! It gets easier, and you'll soon be making the most out of your sus chords. If you're struggling, it's normal! It just means that you'll need to practice a little bit mote. :)

First, let's start by understanding what they are. :)

What Are Sus Chords On Guitar?

"Sus" is short for "suspended." With sus chords, you're taking away the 3rd and replacing it with… something. Without getting into music theory, here's the basic idea.

Major chords consist of the 1st, 3rd, and 5th notes in a key. For instance, the notes in the D major scale are

D E F# G A B C#

The 1st note in the key is D, the 3rd is F#, and the 5th is A. These three notes make up the D major chord.

Now, the 3rd note in the chord is pretty crucial! The chord changes from major to minor when this note is flattened by one semitone (or one fret).

But what happens if you take the 3rd away? Well, it's neither major nor minor. It becomes its own thing.

Let's take a look at the D chord. If you take away the 3rd, the open E string rings out. E is the 2nd note in the D major scale. Since the E (2nd) replaces the F# (3rd) in the chord, you get a Dsus2 chord.

Following the same pattern, Dsus4 replaces the 3rd with the 4th, a G.

How To Use Sus Chords On Guitar

You can apply sus chords to music in a few different ways. They are new sounds you can add to your musical repertoire at the most basic level.

Sus chords can be ornaments when used sparingly within a song. They can replace the root chord or become part of a melodic riff. There are many ways to get creative with these! You might find that moving one finger while holding the rest down is challenging. It's completely normal if you find this tricky at first!

When playing them on your guitar, don't be afraid to experiment with different fingerings. You might find a way of playing sus chords that work better for your needs and anatomy.

Sus Chords Diagrams

I suggest you explore sus chords with A and E shapes, both major and minor. Sus chords work with C and G, but they're more challenging. So keep them alone for now. Only tackle them if you're up for the challenge.

Maybe you've been playing them already - so feel free to start adding them as ornaments to your songs! Don't be afraid of getting creative and seeing what you come up with. There's no limit here! To help guide you - follow the easy sus chords diagrams below. :)

Dsus2 & Dsus4

Asus2 & Asus4

Esus4 (Esus2 shown but not recommended at this point!)

3 Easy Sus Chord Exercises For Beginners

Now it's time to learn a helpful exercise to help you practice your sus chords. I suggest you first explore sus chords with A and E shapes, both Major and Minor. Sus chords work with C and G shapes, but that's a bit more challenging. Follow the sus chord exercises below:

Sus Chord Exercise 1 1 2 3 + 4 + D D D U D U 3 3 3 4 3 2 Sus Chord Exercise 2 1 2 + + 4 D D U U D 3 3 4 4 3 Sus Chord Exercise 3 1 2 + 3 + 4 D D U D U D 3 4 3 4 3 2

Take it slow, and try not to get discouraged if they feel strange at first. It's part of the process of learning a new skill and sound!

Experimenting will be key to getting used to sus chords! Now that you know what they sound like, you'll also start to recognize them in your favorite songs. Stay aware of them and keep your ears open to them!

There are loads of awesome examples in 90s rock acoustic ballads. If you're not familiar with the song Dead or Alive by Bon Jovi - give it a listen. There's a nice line of sus twiddles with the D chord in there. Another great one for sus chords is the iconic Bryan Adams riff for Summer Of 69.

Hope you dig and have loads of fun with sus chords! Next lesson, let's revisit the F chord. See you there :)

lessons.title: Shifting The F
lessons.summary: Let's tackle some common F chord struggles and ways to help you improve this tricky barre chord!
lessons.text:
Let's revisit that F chord!

I have some helpful tips and exercise to help you :)

Getting the B stringing out clearly is one of the most common struggles with the F chord. Pressing those strings down near the nut is definitely a challenge!

Experiencing this usually means you're not pressing the barre hard enough. You might need to build up some finger strength! And you'll develop that as you practice.

In this lesson, let's check-in on the F chord and see how it's coming along. I'll give practical tips and exercises to help you improve this tricky chord. :)

Common F Chord Struggles

For the F chord, you’ve got your 1st finger barring over the 1st fret. Barring down with your finger pressing down all the strings is a common challenge. It could mean that the nut on your guitar is a touch too high.

Your guitar nut raises the strings further away from the fretboard, making them harder to press down. The closer to the nut you are, the harder it will be. To try this, shift the F chord up to the 5th fret. It'll be easier to get a solid grip further away from the nut.

You might find that it’s a little more difficult for you to play up there. Since you’re engaging different muscles in your hand, practice it for a few days.

It's common to play the chord on the 5th fret correctly but still struggle on the 1st. You might need to take your guitar in to have the nut sanded down a touch. A good guitar setup can make a world of difference!

🚨 A cheap guitar with a good setup is often better than an expensive one with a bad setup. It can affect the sound of the instrument. Most importantly, it can affect your playing.

Shifting the F chord Exercise

To practice shifting the F chord, slide your fingers up to either the 3rd or the 5th fret. Choose whichever feels more comfortable with your wrist. The barre should be easier to press down.

When shifting the F chord to alternative frets - we're getting into barre chord territory - which is intermediate-level material. This lesson is an introduction to what's to come! That way, you'll know what to expect.

So - keep working on these barre chords. They're essential to play loads of songs! As you advance, you’ll be using them more often. In some cases, you may even prefer them over the open chords.

Explore the F Barre Chord Shape

At your beginner guitar stage focus on open chords and F chords and making them strong. It'll make it easier as you progress. But, it's also time to be fearless and explore moving your barre chord around.

Watch the video to see how you can move your barre chord around the Note Circle. Sound pretty awesome, right?

So - keep working on the F chord changes and putting big barre chord F in a song or two. But start becoming aware of a different approach to barre chords.

Got any F chord tips? Login to your account and share them on the discussion board. And you can visit the JustinGuitarCommunity for advice from fellow guitar students following the course.

Next lesson - you'll learn an awesome trick I like to call Re-ACTIVE Listening. See you there! :)

lessons.title: Re-Active Listening ™
lessons.summary: Learn re-active listening - and try fun exercises to develop your musical listening skills and guitar improvisation!
lessons.text:
Re-ACTIVE Listening ™ 👂

Learn guitar improvisation without overthinking!

Playing guitar using your ears is a lot freer than you think. Music is about feeling and expressing yourself. Knowing the theory behind which notes to play and when is helpful ... but, it’s not always the best option.

When you're playing a guitar solo, you don't have time to think about much. So instead of thinking about the correct theory to use, we listen!

We’ve touched on improvisation in previous lessons, so now it’s time to build on that skill. In this lesson, you'll learn this little trick I call Re-ACTIVE Listening.

What is Re-Active Listening ™?

When we use the reactive listening approach - we're listening to what we play combined with the note that we're playing over. We use our ears to decide if it's a great note choice or not. Then, we change notes until we're playing to a better note option.

Focus on listening to what you're doing and its impact on the music you're playing over. When improvising, some notes sound better than others when played over certain chords. You might notice this happens even if you're staying in the correct key.

If you play a note over a chord and it doesn’t sound right, it's simple. Change notes until you find a note that does sound good. You've heard me say it before, let me say it again - If it sounds good, it is good!

The statistics say that if you're not on a chord tone - a scale step in either direction will USUALLY get you to a chord tone. A lot of this will become easier with time and experience. But, I have some exercises that can help you train your ears and get there faster.

So grab your guitar and play along with me! :)

3 Exercises For Re-Active Listening ™

I’ll start by playing a chord. Your job is to find the note on a specific string that sounds best when played over that chord. Take your time if you need to. Try not to overthink this - it’s all about listening! Here are 3 exercises to get you started on re-active listening.

Re-Active Listening Exercise 1

a) Play the F chord b) Find the best note on the E String

Answer: F

Re-Active Listening Exercise 2

a) Play the C Chord b) Find the best note on the E String

Answer: E or G

c) Find the best note on the B String

Answer: C

Re-Active Listening Exercise 3

a) Play the Am Chord b) Find the best note on the B String

Answer: C

c) Find the best note on the E String

Answer: E OR G!! just not the F (1st fret!)

These are great exercises to do with a fellow beginner guitar player. You can even do it virtually over zoom or facetime! Take turns alternating between who plays the chords and who improvises. Mostly importantly, have loads of fun trying these exercises :)

Now - it's finally time to learn fingerstyle on guitar! So - come along and let me guide you through your first steps. :)

lessons.title: Introduction to Fingerstyle Guitar
lessons.summary: Ready to take your first steps with fingerstyle? Learn the basics of this guitar technique and transform your playing!
lessons.text:
Beginners: Start Your Fingerstyle Guitar Journey Here!

Fingerstyle opens up a whole new world of guitar playing. Going from strumming to fingerstyle can transform the style of your playing! This technique will open so many creative doors for you.

We'll get more into fingerstyle in Grade 3, but this easy lesson will get you started on fingerstyle basics, and you'll even be able to play some easy fingerstyle songs. Get ready to take your first steps, grab your guitar and let's go!

Guitar Fingerstyle Basics

Fingerstyle involves plucking individual strings in a chord instead of strumming them. When using fingerstyle, we use our thumb, 1st, 2nd, and 3rd fingers to pluck the individual strings. For now, we don't use the 4th finger. You'll learn more about that later on.

Assign each of those fingers to one of the three thinnest strings. The thumb handles the three thickest strings; its job is to move between them to play the bass notes of whichever chord is being played.

Should You Anchor to Fingerstyle?

The 4th finger on your picking hand isn't completely useless here! Many people find it helpful to use it as an anchor for their hand by resting it on the guitar's body. Personally, I don't!

I've got a short little finger, which creates unwanted tension in my hand. Of course, tons of brilliant musicians anchor (almost all of my favorites!). So this choice will be personal preference - always go with what feels comfortable for your needs.

Where it feels smooth and relaxed, that's where the sound will be the nicest! And to get there, you have to experiment with your guitar playing and practice.

Should You Use Nails To Fingerstyle?

It's up to you if you want to use nails to fingerstyle. There is no wrong way to do it - but your choice will affect your sound differently.

When picking with nails, you'll get a sharper, crisper, and louder sound from the strings. When picking without nails, you'll get a softer, rounder sound.

So your choice will depend on what sound you're going for. Of course, make sure you're consistent! If you've got all short nails but slightly longer ones, that string with the long nail will ring out over the rest.

😩 Pro tip for playing with nails: make sure there are no nicks or snags in them. Keep a nail file handy for this! The worst thing is to have a snagged nail get caught on a guitar string and ripped off. Ouch!

How To Get The Fingerstyle Sound

It's important to start slowly when playing fingerstyle. Ease into it! Pay attention to the quality of sound you're getting from the strings. Be careful to let the notes ring out, and find a good hand position to get the sound you're looking for.

Make sure you don't have too much movement in your hand. The movement should come from your fingers! It'll give you nicer contact with the strings. And, it'll prevent you from grabbing and pulling your strings - which is never great.

Now you might be wondering - what about the bass note? The thumb will play the bass note of the chord. The string of the bass note changes with the chord. The bass note will be the same whether the chord is major, minor, sus, 7, or 13#5b9 :)

Root on String 4: D and Mini F

Root on String 5: A and C

Root on String 6: G and E and full F Barre

The Fingerstyle Exercise

We'll be doing an entire module on fingerstyle in Grade 3, but this is enough to get you started. Think of it as your introduction exercise to fingerstyle. :)

For this exercise, you'll be playing in 6/8 time. That means there are six beats per bar. Your thumb will handle the bass notes while your fingers take care of the rest. And remember, the bass notes will change depending on the chord.

✓ Practice fingerstyle using this super easy pattern (play each one on the beat):

1 2 3 4 5 6 T 1 2 3 2 1

Pick a chord and practice this pattern with it. Think about the way your fingers are touching the string. Go up and down the chord, slowly practicing the pattern. Focus your attention on keeping your volume and tone consistent. And make sure you have an even timing throughout.

👉 Next, let's learn to play Happy Birthday in Fingerstyle! :)

lessons.title: Happy Birthday Finger Style
lessons.summary: For your first dive into finger style, we'll learn how to play Happy Birthday on the guitar - a classic unlike any other!
lessons.text:
Learn to play Happy Birthday on the guitar - Finger Style! 🎂

In this easy guitar lesson for beginners, we'll learn how to play a finger style arrangement of Happy Birthday on the guitar! This tutorial is part of my free Beginner Guitar Course - Grade 2 and introduces finger style guitar to my students. :)

🥳 I can assume most people know Happy Birthday by heart; it's pretty universal and you might sing it in many different languages. The melody dates all the way back to 1893! How crazy is that?

When you learn how to play Happy Birthday, you can make your friends and family's birthdays extra special! People will appreciate it even if you're fumbling through it on the guitar. :)

In this lesson, we'll be working on a chord-melody concept, meaning that your thumb will play the chords' root notes, and your fingers will play the melody line. Ready? Let's get stuck in.

Happy Birthday: Guitar Chord & Melody

To play Happy Birthday on the guitar, you'll need the C to the G chord, simple chords, but also an F Chord.

💡 Happy Birthday is a great song to learn this idea of a chord melody. A chord melody is when you're playing a melody line and a bass note simultaneously, and it's often done in classical guitar. You'll learn more details later on in your guitar journey. :)

For this lesson, the chords aren't the main focus; we'll focus on coordinating your fingers. Focus on using your first finger and your thumb, or try it out with your second finger in your thumb. Use the finger combinations that feel best for you!

Finger Style Tips For Beginners

When starting off with fingerstyle, take it slow! The fingers on your strumming hand aren't used to this movement yet, so they might struggle with their dexterity and finger independence. Give them time to get used to doing what you're asking them to.

When you're learning a fingerstyle pattern, learning it in chunks is useful. To do this, learn the first few notes, practice them up, and get confident playing each bit. The finger style pattern should feel smooth under your fingers!

Ideally, you'll do it from memory because the more memorization you do, the better you'll be able to concentrate on the important stuff. Rather than being stuck in a particular guitar tab, memorizing patterns will help you:

Get your guitar tone nice and clear;

Make sure your fingers aren't grabbing and pulling strings;

Get your hand in the correct position.

At your beginner stage, focus on keeping your fingerstyle simple. Don't overcomplicate things, and do what feels most comfortable to you!

Happy Birthday: Free Guitar Tab

Follow this free guitar tab to learn how to play Happy Birthday:

If you need extra help, you'll find a free PDF file and a Guitar Pro file in the Resources tab. Fancier possibilities will come as your advance; this fingerstyle is a little taste of what's to come! For now, keep it simple and have loads of fun learning how to play Happy Birthday!

👏 Module 11 is almost complete! Next, let's check out new song recommendations to consolidate your new skills.

lessons.title: Songs for Module 11
lessons.summary: Discover 9 songs for easy fingerstyle & sus chords. I hope these inspire your next song guitar practice. :)
lessons.text:
SONG OPTIONS FOR MODULE 11🎶

Time flies when learning is fun!

You have many new guitar techniques under your belt .. and many more to come! We've been introduced to loads of new guitar concepts, and the skills you're learning are increasingly complex. So it's normal you're still finding some of these newer techniques a challenge!

In the most recent lessons, you've learned fingerstyle and sus chords. They both work together, but when it comes to your song practice, it's better to tackle them separately. Spend most of your time working on one of these techniques.

When you feel comfortable, move on to the other. Or you can divide your second practice session into halves. It's completely up to you! You'll soon be doing practice consolidation for Grade 2, and then you can pick and choose the things you want to work on. You'll be in the consolidation phase for a little while, so there's no need to be rushing techniques right now.

💡 Remember - choose songs that you enjoy. Make sure it's songs to work on your fingerstyle or sus chords & always focus on techniques that challenge you the most. :)

5 Songs To Practice Fingerstyle

Here are 5 song recommendations to practice your fingerstyle. I included different genres, so there's something in there for everyone. Some of these songs are also available guitar-oke style on the JustinGuitar Lessons & Songs app. :)

Everybody Hurts by REM

This is an ace song. You'll need some power chords for the bridge, which you'll learn shortly. You can make this super simple, or if you're ambitious, you might like to add in the little rundowns and stuff :)

House Of The Rising Sun by The Animals

You may have already learned this song. The original recording uses a pick to play it, but it works GREAT as a fingerstyle song. It's a tad fast at the original tempo, so slow it down if you need it!

Hallelujah by Leonard Cohen

I love this song! It's original by Leonard Cohen, but the Rufus Wainwright version kills me every time. Most folks like the Jeff Buckley one. It's got quite a few fast changes, so this won't be the one to start with! The lesson for this one is an oldie - but still great to learn the song.

This Year's Love by David Gray

Another one you may have looked at before! This song is a wonderful option for an acoustic fingerstyle song.

Nothing Else Matters by Metallica

This uses fingerstyle in 6:8. But there's more going on, and most of you will find this very tricky!

4 Songs To Practice Sus Chords

You can practice sus chords as ornaments in songs you already know. This is something you want to develop over time anyways! You might enjoy playing some classic riffs that use sus chords too.

Summer Of 69 by Bryan Adams

This Bryan Adams classic is probably the most famous sus chord riff! There are a few barre chords in the song later on. But, we'll cover them with Power Chords which we'll be learning in Module 12!

All You Have Is Your Soul by Tracy Chapman

I was not familiar with this Tracy Chapman song until someone suggested it in the comments on a previous lesson. It's a superb track. No lesson yet, but I will do it sometime soon!

All I Want Is You

This U2 hit needs an F# minor for the chorus, but the sus riff is super nice :)

Who Says - Selena Gomez

Ok, this is super pop, but it is D Dsus2 D Dsus4 for pretty much the whole song! Here, the sus chords come on the 'and' and after 3, even on the 8th note.

Not my cup of tea, but a beautiful message to the song. If it's you dig it - then check it out - it's PERFECT for working on your D sus shapes! This was a song recommendation by Davey, one of my students. Thanks for sharing this tune with us!

Spotify Playlist Module 11

Ok - you now have so many song options - why not give them a listen first and see which one inspires you? Check out this Spotify Playlist for Module 11 and energize your next guitar practice!

Have more song recommendations to practice these techniques? Log into your JustinGuitar account, and share them in the discussion area. Help inspire the JustinGuitar Community to discover new tunes! :)

lessons.title: Introduction To Dice Songwriting
lessons.summary: We’re going to write a song together from start to finish in just 30 minutes… this should be interesting!
lessons.text:
Songwriting For Beginners - Let's Make That Dream A Reality 🎶

Write your first song today!

In this lesson, we're going to write a song together - a complete song, start to finish in just 30 minutes!

Think of this lesson as a crash course to what it's like to write a song. There's nothing to be afraid of when diving into the world of songwriting. So be fearless when you're diving into this wonderful music world!

Let's get this out of the way - the first few songs you write won't sound so great! Speaking from experience, this is how my first song went! Everything from the lyrics to the melodies was boring! But as with most things, it will get easier over time, and you will become a better songwriter with practice.

So be open to this trial and error process. Let's dive right in. :)

How To Create Your Lyrics

For this experiment, I crowdsourced lyrics from you all on my Instagram - and wow! You all came up with some interesting lines! Thank you to all who contributed, and I hope I did justice to your lyrics.

In a proper songwriting session, you'd have to spend a bit more time on the lyrics than I did. For the sake of this video, I'm pretty happy with how they turned out.

When applying pre-written lyrics to a song, you've got to be aware of pacing. Here are questions you should ask yourself when creating lyrics:

How many syllables can you fit into a line?

Can you carry a lyric over from one line to the next?

Does it make sense musically?

Do you need to re-write the lyric to shorten or lengthen it?

How To Create Music

To create music, take the chords you already know. Pick a few of them and arrange them into a chord progression. There are a few go-to chord progressions that you'll often find in popular songs.

When you're looking to create a fresh sound, try songwriting with the dice method. :)

Here's how to approach the dice songwriting method:

Assign each chord in a key a number, 1-6.

Then, you roll your dice! Whichever number comes up is the chord number you'll play first.

Roll the dice again to get the second chord in your progression.

Continue until you've got a few lined up, and give it a go on your guitar.

There's a very good chance a few chords may sound out of place! If something doesn't sound great to you, the great thing about writing music is that you can change it. After all, it's your song - you're the boss here. You've all the creative licenses in the world.

When playing your chord progression, think about rhythm and strumming patterns. Think about the tone you're after or the emotions you're trying to convey with the song. Experiment with different patterns until you find something you're happy with.

Putting Lyrics And Music Together

Now, the fun stuff. Sing your lyrics over your chord progression and hear how it all comes together. Don't be afraid to try different melody lines, too.

If you sing your song, but the chords don't sound good, switch up the chords. It's all up to you! The more you explore, the better!

Learn Music From The Best

Here are 5 ways to improve your songwriting skills:

Take a song you love and dive into it.

Pick it apart.

Look at the chord structure.

Study the melody lines, the tempo, the dynamics.

Try to feel the emotion & and the storytelling in the lyrics. What is the meaning behind the words?

Take note of the things you like and the things you don't like.

Listen for what works and contemplate why it works. Do the same for those things that don't work for you. Take at the complete structure of the song - all of it!

Once you've done that, pick another song and do it all over again! Study songs in different genres. Check out songs from the same artist at other points in their career. You can learn so much by doing this and focus on listening.

Song Structure Outline

Need inspiration? Follow this common song structure to help you develop your song.

Verse 1 Start the story. Verse 2 Develop the story but KEEP THE SAME MELODY. Chorus Keep it simple and hook the listener. Verse 3 Drop it down - SAME VERSE MELODY Chorus SAME AS LAST TIME. Bridge A significant change in pace and chords. Chorus SAME AS LAST TIME. Chorus SAME AS LAST TIME (or with minor variations!).

I hope you have as much fun with this lesson as I did. This process should be fun! Don't hesitate to share your songwriting creations with the JustinGuitar Community!

lessons.title: Module 11 Practice
lessons.summary: Ready for your Lesson 11 practice schedule?
lessons.text:
Module 11 Completed 🙌

Time to set up a new practice schedule!

In module 11, we introduced you to loads of more complex techniques. From fingerstyle to sus chords, you’ve got loads under your belt. Most of these lessons were a taste of what’s to come.

Nitsuj had an extra one 1-minute on flicks-offs. But he decided it wasn’t very effective. This is a perfect example of how you should tweak your practice to your needs. And, if you haven’t already – check out Nitsuj lessons & have a laugh at my attempt to play left-handed. Now, remember - edit these suggestions to suit your guitar journey and what you need.

These are just suggestions, and you can change them depending on your needs. Have fun, and approach your practice sessions with excitement and an open mind. 😊

💡 Make things easier and get yourself a pre-made practice routine for Module 11! Click the 'Practice' Tab under the video and save the routine to access it in your Dashboard.

30-Minute Practice Breakdown

Here are some suggestions to break down your practice sessions for Module 11.

Song Repertoire Revision: 5 minutes.

F Chord Chord Changes: 2 minutes.

Exploring Sus Chords: 3 minutes.

C Major Scale Improvisation: 2 minutes.

Fingerstyle Exercises: 4 minutes.

Happy Birthday guitar riff: 4 minutes.

New Songs: 10 minutes.

When To Move On?

Think of this as an introductory module. So work on as many things as you can and explore. You'll be ready to move on when:

You learn one fingerstyle song.

Explore using sus chords in a song or riff.

Learn Happy Birthday to a level where you could get through it at a birthday party!

Once you’re happy and confident with your progress .. get ready to ROCK! :) That’s right – next module, you’ll be learning power chords!

modules.label: Module 12
modules.title: Rock Power Chords & Techniques for Beginners
modules.intro:
Are you ready to rock? 🤘

In this module, you'll learn all about Power Chords!

This module will focus on building those power chords, and you'll also get the chance to let your creativity shine and learn how to create your guitar riffs! How awesome is that?

Power Chords are known for electric guitar, but they also sound super cool on acoustic! They're great when you encounter a barre chord you don't know. So they are valuable skills even if you don't dig rock or distortion!

WHAT YOU'LL LEARN

This module will explore power chords with the Root 5 and 6 Shapes.

You'll then meet the A minor pentatonic scale. This scale is essential if you dream of playing Blues guitar down the line!

We'll follow with an easy guitar technique: Palm muting! You'll learn how to 'chugg' your strings - which can make a massive difference in your guitar playing!

Overdrive, distortion, fuzz... have you heard about them? We'll learn what you need to know about guitar effects and how to understand distortion!

You'll rock out to the iconic Enter Sandman riff by Metallica! And fantastic exercise to build finger independence. Finally - you'll play awesome new songs to put your power chords into practice!

👉 Now grab your guitar, and let's ROCK! :)

lessons.title: Power Chords
lessons.summary: Learn how to play power chords on the guitar! Get ready to rock with the Root 5 Shape and Root 6 Shape.
lessons.text:
Are you ready to rock? 🤘

Your Ultimate Power Chords Guide for Beginners!

Power chords are awesome musical elements to learn on guitar. They're considered the foundation chord for rock music. If you're a fan of punk/rock music - you'll have loads of fun with them! But - learning them is useful in any music genre, many popular songs you know use them!

Power chords are also fantastic to play if you encounter a barre chord that you don't know. They'll be easier to play & will extend your chord freedom.

In this lesson, you'll take your first steps and learn how to play power chords on the guitar! We'll start by exploring the Root 6 & 5 Shape, and I'll give you handy exercises and songs to develop these awesome chords.

So grab your guitar & get ready to rock! :)

What Are Power Chords On Guitar?

Power chords are made from the root note and the 5th of the chord. Sometimes, they're also made of the octave of the root. Similar to sus chords - power chords are neither major nor minor! When you play them, you won't be using any open chords.

The note under Finger 1 is the ROOT NOTE- this is what gives the chord its note name! The shape of power chords always stays the same, which means you can easily move them around your fretboard.

We call them "5th chords," and C Power Chord is usually written as C5.

💡 Watch the video & listen to my opening power chords.Hear that awesome crunch and distortion?! That's the signature sound of power chords! :)

Root 6 Shapes

I would recommend you start by learning the Root 6 grip. If you're confident with your F Barre chord, your placement of Finger 1, 2, and 3 will be easy.

You might struggle to get Finger 1 to lay down and mute strings 1,2 and 3 - that's very common! To help you, touch them lightly, so they don't ring out. It's okay if they make a click, but be careful not to press your power chords too hard!

When you start moving the shape, you might find that Fingers 3 and 4 want to pull apart. Aim to keep them together - touching - 3rd fingers on top of the 4th. It'll help you when you move the grip around your guitar fretboard!

Instead of having the standard 3 note version - play the Root 6 Shape with just 2 fingers.

For this next version, play the root note with your Finger 1. For the other note, play them with Fingers 3 or 4. Choose whichever feels the best & most comfortable for you! :)

🤔 Did you know? Kurt Cobain played his power Chords with his first and 3 fingers. Kurt often accidentally let it press a little too hard, and he would also get the note on string 3 ringing. It's one of the subtle trademarks of his playing style! But for now, I recommend you simply let your Finger 3 lay flat to cover strings 5 and 4.

Root 5 Shape

You'll apply the same rules to the Root 5 Shape, but with the root note on string 5. Here, the big difference is that the tip of Finger 1 mutes the thickest string. Finger 1 is the big player here - it's muting strings 6, 2, and 1 all at the same time. It might take a few tries to get it right - but keep practicing; you'll get there!

So - make sure to mute your thickest string. Use the diagram below to guide you.

The 6 Essential Notes For Power Chords

To play power chords, you need to have memorized and play the notes on the bottom two strings. Make sure you can quickly find any note on strings 5 & 6. It's one of those things that you are going to have to learn sooner or later. It'll help with so many skills as you advance in your guitar journey.

So - start by learning the 6 key tones - the notes on frets 3, 5, and 7. With your knowledge of tones and semitones - you can easily find notes you need. Remember about the sharps and flats between the 'white notes' - revisiting the Note Circle will help if needed! :)

Power Chords Guitar Exercise

To slide your power chords, maintain the shape of the grip by slightly losing your grip. Make sure to keep contact with the strings and keep fingers 3 and 4 together.

Exercise

Repeat this exercise to help get this skill down! Play these chords as even 8th notes - and try your best to keep your power chord grip shape! :)

C D E F E D C B (8th notes, 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 +)

4 Sliding Power Chords Song Exercises

Cocaine by Eric Clapton. Play them with this chord sequence → EEDE E D E D CCCCB.

Anarchy In The UK by Sex Pistols.

Song 2 by Blur. To play this song, follow this chord sequences → F# E A A B C#. I played it detuned and with 2 finger grips.

Seven Nation Army by the White Stripes. You should be familiar with this one from Grade 1. Adding some power chords will elevate your sound!

To cross your chords - keep your same grip shape. You might quickly lose contact with the strings - that's okay! Maintaining contact with the string will help keep the open strings from ringing out. You'll have to experiment here - and try it for yourself! :)

2 Crossing Power Chords Song Exercises

How could I not include some Nirvana?! Here are two songs to practice crossing your power chords.

Mollys Lips by Nirvana.

Smells Like Teen Spirit by Nirvana.

More Songs To Practice Power Chords

There are SO MANY awesome songs to work on your power chords - it's up to what you like. More on that in a lesson coming up!

The best way to learn power chords is by playing songs with them. Exercises are helpful as a starting point, but once you get the basics down - practice power chords by playing songs you dig! It's going to help you solidify this skill.

For inspiration, look through my song lesson playlist. Narrow down the music genre to what you dig by using the filters. Most importantly - find power chord songs you love. Play them as much as you can - and unleash your inner rocker!

Next lesson - learn the first scale beginners should learn to play blues guitar ... the A Minor Pentatonic Scale!

lessons.title: The A Minor Pentatonic
lessons.summary: The Minor Pentatonic is THE scale to learn if you want to start exploring Blues lead guitar!
lessons.text:
Dreaming of playing blues guitar?

Meet the A Minor Pentatonic scale!

Learn the first scale guitar beginners should learn to play blues guitar! It's commonly used in improvising, which we're going to get into shortly!

You'll need to play further up the neck - so it'll feel slightly different from what you're familiar playing. It'll present you with a few challenges - but practice will make that all better!

In this lesson, you'll learn how to play the A minor pentatonic scale and how to feel comfortable playing up and down the scale.

Is the Minor Pentatonic Easy To Play?

You might be wondering ... is the pentatonic easy?

The A Minor Pentatonic is pretty easy to play. The visual shape of the scale BOX should not take you long to learn and memorize. That's because there are consistently two notes on each string & the picking is consistent.

💡There's a little clue in the name. Penta means five, and the pentatonic scale has five notes scales in the key of A.

The 'root note,' which gives the scale its note name, is under the first finger on String 6. With Finger 1 on the 5th fret, you will be playing A Minor Pentatonic. Move Finger 1 up to the 10th fret, and you'll be playing D Minor Pentatonic!

To learn this scale, you'll want to focus on the geometric shape created by the scale. Many people call the A minor pentatonic scale boxed one. I call it pattern one; others call it to position one. Call it what you want - it's all the same thing!

Here's how the fingering for the Minor A pentatonic shape. Use the diagram below to help visualize it.

Finger 1 is playing all those notes.

Your third finger on the following three strings.

You've got a little finger on the thinnest two strings.

Notice how it forms a box?

The most common way to practice this scale is using Finger 4 on the thinnest two strings - and that's fine for playing it up and down. When it comes to playing blues solos - you are likely to find that you use Finger 3 on those strings. You might want to start exploring that fingering, too - some even find it easier! :)

Minor Pentatonic Strumming For Beginners

When you first start learning this scale, keep your strumming to all down picks. Once you're comfortable with that - you can venture into alternate picking.

Once you can play the scale and you've got it to memory, then you might want to start thinking about doing alternate picking.

The easiest way to think of alternate picking here with this scale shape is that you're going to use. A down pick on the notes with the first finger and an up pick on all of the others.

You'll likely explore other options as you progress, but this is a solid way to start!

Want some pentatonic motivation? Check out some John Mayer tunes - he's a phenomenal scales player and plays the minor pentatonic scale so well! He's a great inspiration for what you can achieve. :)

A Pentatonic Scale Practice Tips

Remember - doing it slowly, much better. It's better to be slow and accurate than it is to be faster at making mistakes. Every time you make practice a mistake - you have to do it like a hundred times to reprogram your brain to do it the right way!

When learning scales, arpeggios, and more complex shapes, you want to do them slowly enough. This way - you'll train your brain into doing it right! Don't risk doing it wrong and fast.

Here are things to focus on when you're practicing your A Pentatonic Scale:

Don't be in a hurry! PRACTICE makes PERMANENT, not perfect - so PRACTICE PERFECTLY! :)

Play it with the down picks first of all to get that shape right. Then, start exploring with the alternate picking.

Use metronome if you want! Or concentrate on making sure you're tempo is consistent!

Keep that rhythm nice and even as possible!

The minor pentatonic scale will be in your practice schedule for this module. Start by practicing it up and down - then work on the alternate picking.

Start Exploring String Bending

Scale fingering and practice is a good starting point to playing blues guitar. But as soon as you get into playing blues and rock - you'll encounter string bending!

String bending is where you push the string up to change the pitch of the note. As a starting point - use your third finger of the thinnest two strings.

This recommendation might be controversial, but you might want to explore string bending at the early stages! We're not going to be covering string bending until after the beginner's course. But it's something you might find helpful practicing now to prepare.

Got questions about this lesson? Log in & check out the comments section in the discussion area. You'll find advice from beginner guitar students - and maybe you'll add some of your tips to help others!

Next lesson - we're checking out palm muting. An essential technique for rockers! ... . See you there!

lessons.title: Palm Muting
lessons.summary: Palm Muting technique is essential for any guitarist that wants to rock out!
lessons.text:
Let's explore palm muting!

A rock guitar technique you need to know about :)

Palm muting is helpful for many guitar styles - particularly in acoustic rock songs! If you think of some Nirvana songs we're all familiar with - you'll recognize the sound it creates!

In this lesson, you'll learn how to introduce palm muting into your playing. This guitar technique is easy to learn - and will help with improving your picking too!

So get ready to add some spice to your rhythm playing and make a massive difference to your sound!

How To Do Palm Muting On Guitar

To mute with your palm, use the outer part of the palm of your hand. You'll want to rest it lightly on your strings. This will create that muffled sound.

Let a note ring out for some time. As soon as you get the palm mute - it'll fade out more quickly and become more of a thud!

Where Should You Position Your Hand To Mute?

This is a question many students ask! Your hand position depends on loads of different elements. The type of pick-ups, how much gain you use, how hard you pick, and the placement of the hand will all alter the sound of the palm mute!

You'll need to experiment and get used to how the changes affect the sound. This way, you'll also know how much mute you need for a specific sound.

You'll find that with a bit of practice, this will become automatic! Exploring it is part of learning how to manipulate this technique for your needs. :)

Palm Muting For Strumming Pattern Accents

To add accents to your sound, you will commonly 'chug' on one string. Then, you'll push through further and play more string for the accents.

Once you're confident with the basic palm muting technique, try adding the accent on beats 2 and 4 of your strumming patterns.

🚨 Feeling adventurous? Check out Basket Case by Greenday for some creative inspiration! All The Small Things by Blink182 is also a great song to practice palm muting.

You can also 'open up' for your strumming pattern accent. This means you'll play the notes without the palm mute, which can sound super cool in the right place!

Hope you have fun with this new technique! Give it a go with your power chords to see how it all sounds together. :)

Next lesson, we're checking out guitar effects for beginners! See you there!

lessons.title: Understanding Distortion
lessons.summary: If you want to rock, you're going to have to get dirty! Here's what you need to know about guitar effects. :)
lessons.text:
Gain, Crunch, Overdrive, Distortion, Fuzz ...

Here's your introduction guide to using guitar effects!

Most beginners will want to experiment with guitar effects at some point in their guitar journey. If you want to play rock or blues - you'll want to add some dirt to your sound - this is where guitar effects come in!

If you're new to this, check out bands like Metallica or Black Sabbath - they have a much heavier, crunchier sound to their guitar playing. They achieve this by using distortion - and it's the perfect time to learn all about it. In this lesson, you'll learn a rundown of the basics of guitar effects, 4 different pedals and we'll explore and 3 types of gain: Overdrive, Distortion, Fuzz.

Let's get stuck in. :)

What Is Guitar Distortion?

Guitar effects allow you to manipulate your electric guitar sound. This can be built into your amp - or accessed through a pedal.

A CLEAN sound is what that word means - it's not supposed to sound messy! But rarely is a perfectly clean guitar sound very pleasing. Even the most 'perfect' clean sound - like a mid 60's Deluxe amp - has a kind of grit that makes it feel good. The guitar you use - specifically the pickups you use - will play a big part in the amount and type of gain you get.

Single coil pickups are generally 'thinner' and can be noisy. They cut through the sound and have a great bite.

Humbuckers are bigger pickups and 'buck the hum.' They give a lot of grain - it's what I'm using in the video.

The type of pickup depends on your preference! Be aware that the gear you choose will make a big difference in your sound.

Built Into Amp Or A Pedal?

A nice valve amp will deliver sweet dirt but not usually a heavily distorted tone.

Pedals are convenient, easy to swap around, and commonly used (often with valve amps!).

If you are a beginner and new to all this stuff, I recommend getting a Boss Katana amp. This amp has many kinds of dirt built-in. You'll develop a taste for what you like, what you don't and what you want more of! It also has the advantage of having almost every other effect built in too. Loads of free Katana presets are available throughout the website. :)

If not a Katana - see if you can get your hands on a multi-effects device. Pick something that has everything you need to explore!

4 Different Guitar Overdrives

Here are 4 pedals overdrives that are worth checking out!

Tube Screamer Mini

The tube screamer is an all-time classic dirt box, and this mini one sounds fantastic and is a super great value! This is Overdrive!

Buy a Tube Screamer Mini Here

Boss DS-1

The first and another classic Distortion box.

Buy a DS-2 here (probably better for beginners and cheaper!)

Nobels ODR-1

Best bang for buck pedal ever? I know loads of pro players with the best gear that still use one of these bad boys!

Buy an ODR-1 Here - but note they've gone up in price since I last checked. They cost more than the previous 2 pedals here, but it's still a great option!

Dan Drive Austin Pride

Seems I have no budget Fuzz pedals - so this is my favorite of all time. Incredible sound, extremely versatile, looks super superb - mega on every level. Matching price tag.

Contact Dan about making you a Fuzz pedal here!

The Knobs

Most of the time, you'll find 3 knobs on a dirt box. Some will have more Tone controls, like a Top and Middle, but Fuzz boxes can have a lot more!

Here are 3 three of the most common knobs:

Gain / Distortion / Crunch This will set how much dirt you get from the unit.

Tone This will either take or remove the high sounds or high mids. It'll drastically change your whole sound! This will have other names sometimes, like Spectrum or EQ.

Level The gain might make the pedal louder, so you might need to adjust the overall level. Or, you might want it to get a lot louder for your guitar solo!

Brief History of Distortion

Here's a quick breakdown of guitar effects throughout the years:

In the early '50s, people started experimenting more with sounds. They would turn up amps louder than they were designed to go. This was when OVERDRIVE-ing the amps started!

In 1960, a song was released by country crooner Marty Robbins called Don't Worry. There was something wrong with the mixing desk, and the lead guitar came out sounding funny. The song became a big hit, and everyone wanted the sound. So - his friends made an effect box to replicate the sound - the Gibson Maestro FUZZ.

1965, Keith Richards used it for Satisfaction. This started the whole Fuzz effect obsession for guitarists!

Vox Tone Bender was born - which became the sound of Jeff Beck, The Yardbirds, and Led Zeppelin.

1969 - Fuzz Face (that Jimi Hendrix sound!) and the Big Muff distortion pedals were born - the birth of the term distortion!

1970's amps get bigger, people want more distortion

1977 - 3 amazing new stompboxes that use HARD CLIPPING were born. This includes the MXR Distortion +, The RAT pedal, and the BOSS DS-1 Distortion.

1980's amps like the ubiquitous Marshal JCM800 had the DISTORTION built-in.

By the 90's - there was a crazy amount of new distortion types and digital emulations of distortion. And now, it's forever growing.

For the detailed history of guitar effects, check out JHS Pedals on The History Of Distortion.

Next up, we're checking out one of the greatest rock riffs of all time .. Enter the Sandman by Metallica!

lessons.title: Enter Sandman
lessons.summary: Ready to rock out to some Metallica? Learn the iconic Enter Sandman riff – one of the greatest guitar riffs of all time!
lessons.videoChapters: 00:00 Demonstration 00:17 Lesson Intro 01:31 Enter Sandman: Riff 1 04:27 Enter Sandman: Riff 2 05:07 Enter Sandman: Riff 3 06:27 Enter Sandman: Riff 4 07:02 Enter Sandman: Riff 5 07:20 Learning Tips Part 1 09:12 Enter Sandman: Riff 6 10:08 Learning Tips 2
lessons.text:
Learn the "Enter Sandman" Riff by Metallica!

In this lesson, you'll learn a simplified version of the first riff. This is an awesome exercise for beginners! But this is about more than simply learning the riffs – we'll also explore how to approach learning tricky songs as a beginner.

At this stage in the journey, you'll find lots of songs beyond your level. And I don't want you to feel intimidated. You can simplify songs to suit your level. We'll dig into a process for this after learning the Metallica riffs.

So, are you ready to rock? Grab your guitar, and let's get going with the first riff!

Enter Sandman by Metallica: Riff 1

Fingers 2 and 4 stay put all the way through the first riff. Finger 4 goes on 5:7 (string 5, fret 7), while finger 2 goes on 4:5 (string 4, fret 5). This will feel stretchy! Make sure fingers 2 and 4 are right up next to the fret, and keep them in place while you play the other parts.

This is a great exercise for working out your little finger. You'll build finger independence by holding down fingers 2 and 4 while manipulating the others. But if this feels too stretchy, use finger 3 on 5:7 and replace 4:5 with the open G string (the notes are the exact same). This way is loads easier! It just sounds a bit different.

Here's riff 1 in TAB:

Finger 3 plays 6:6, and finger 1 plays 6:5. For the easier version, play 3:0 instead of 4:5, and use fingers 2 and 1 to fret the notes on string 6.

Enter Sandman by Metallica: Riff 2

Let's check out the second riff. We start by strumming the open E string with all downstrums and some palm mute. The rhythm is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. After the downstrum on beat 4, finger 1 goes on 5:5. Pick, then slide up to 5:7. We return to a downstrum on the E string on beat 1. The rhythm for this is:

4 e + a 1 D 5:5 5:7 D

Keep finger 1 down on 5:7, using the underside of the finger to mute strings 4, 3, 2, and 1. Keep playing the same rhythm on the open E string, then play 5:7 with finger 3 followed by 4:7 with finger 1.

💡 Palm Mute – It's crucial you use the correct amount of palm mute. You should still be able to hear the chord.

Enter Sandman by Metallica: Riff 3

Then we grab an F power chord (13XXXX), strum it, then flick off both fingers to reveal the open strings (00XXXX). If you find this tricky, you can simplify it by just playing 6:1 and flicking off to 6:0.

The rhythm for this is:

1 + 2 + 3 + 4 e + a D D 5:7 5:5 D D D 6:1 6:0

On the third and four reps, we add 6:5 on beat 3.

Enter Sandman by Metallica: Riff 4

The next part starts with an E power chord (02XXXX). Use finger 1 to play 5:2 and mute the other strings. Then we play 5:7, 6:6, 6:5. Here's the rhythm:

+ 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + E5 E5 5:7 6:6 6:5 E5

The E5 is pushed: we switch to it on the "and" of 4 instead of beat 1. I also tend to mute the strings a little on beat 4.

Enter Sandman by Metallica: Riff 5

Time for riff 5.

+ 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + G5 6:0 F#5 6:0 F#5 G5 F#5 E5

Use palm mute throughout, except for the E5 chord. This is the full riff, but you can simplify it by only playing the bottom notes (6:3 for G, 6:2 for F#, 6:0 for E).

☑️ Listen, Listen, Listen to the original recording. Not only will you learn the order of the song, you'll get a much better idea of the rhythm and pick up further nuances.

Enter Sandman by Metallica: Riff 6

This one is the hardest riff in the song, and it's tricky for most beginners. Try it out and see how it feels to you.

Barre the four thickest strings at fret 2 with finger 1. Then put finger 3 down at 4:4. Pick strings 6, 4, and 3, then put finger 2 on 5:3 and lift it off to reveal 5:2. Then pick string 4.

When you pick 5:3 and 5:2, lightly touch the thumb of your fretting hand against string 6 to mute it. Most beginners will find this one really tough. One cheat is to pick 6:2 instead of string 4 at the end.

Approaching Enter Sandman As A Beginner

I highly recommend you learn riff 1. It's great for finger independence. You'll find it tricky to play notes with fingers 1 and 3 while keeping 2 and 4 stable. That's what NITSUJ spent most of his time on!

If you're a big Metallica fan, watch my full lesson on Enter Sandman. See which parts you can play and which you need to simplify.

💡 Justin's Journey – Nowadays, I'm pretty pedantic when it comes to learning songs. I want to get everything spot on! But when I was starting out, I was the opposite. I was out in bars, playing Dire Straits songs completely wrong! I was playing Rolling Stones riffs in the wrong tuning. But I still enjoyed myself, and it sounded good. That was all that mattered!

How To Approach Difficult Songs As A Beginner

At this stage in your journey, you'll come across many songs that are beyond your level. If you really love a song, use your enthusiasm to keep you inspired. Being motivated is one of the most important elements at this stage.

🧐 Justin becomes Nitsuj – After playing guitar for so many years, I'd forgotten what it was like at the beginning of the journey. So I did an experiment to test out my Beginner's Course worked and walk a mile in my students' shoes. See how Nitsuj got on. ;)

Some examples of simplifying songs are using power chords instead of barre chords, and two-note power chords instead of three-note power chords.

Don't be afraid to explore! Simplify other songs you dig if they feel too difficult. Your love for a song will motivate you to make it work no matter what.

Have loads of fun with Enter Sandman by Metallica. Come and tell me how you've simplified the song – I'd love to know. See you for more guitar real soon. :)

🎵 Next lesson, you'll have a go at writing your own guitar riff. :)

lessons.title: Writing Riffs
lessons.summary: Have some fun, be creative and explore how you can create your own guitar riffs!
lessons.text:
Create Your Own Guitar Riff

Time to explore and let out your creativity!

In previous lessons, we looked at song structures and putting chords together. We even start improvising with the major scale. Now - it's time for you to learn how to create guitar riffs!

This particular lesson won't be part of your practice routine. But - it's incredibly fun! Especially if you're jamming with another musician or someone you met on the JG community.

Time to get creative. Let's get stuck in. :)

Understanding the basics

First, let's quickly look at the difference between riffs and licks. If you've been following my beginner's course - I know you're familiar with riffs! If you're new to all this - riffs are a short musical motif that gets repeated around in a song.

Now - you've most likely heard the term lick before. I tend to think of licks as words. If you're making up a blues solo - you'd have many different licks put together, creating a specific musical sentence.

That's the basic idea of a riff - a little short musical idea that repeats around a lot in a song. There are hundreds of examples of guitar riffs you're going to encounter in your journey - so feel free to learn from them at any point. Enter Sandman is a great example!

Create A Riff Using The Pentatonic Scale

By now, you should be familiar with the A minor pentatonic scale - it's a great starting point for creating riffs! You should be primarily concerned with the bottom few notes and strings. Start with those notes and have a go at creating a little riff for yourself!

Keep in mind that repeatable musical idea that you might want to play around with. Don't be afraid and explore! I encourage you to do this, particularly if you want to venture into songwriting.

No Rules Here!

Scales are an excellent place to start - but you can go anywhere with your creativity! Remember - if it sounds good - it is good! You can make up anything in this experimental stage. Here are some things that might be fun to explore:

Mix two pentatonic scales. Go higher in one, and lower in the other.

Try approaching every note from a semitone below.

Play a riff your love backward.

Develop the dynamics of your riff - Make some loud, others quieter.

Play around with your guitar effects - add some distortion, see how it feels!

Have fun with it - no rules when you're exploring! Hope you have fun with this lesson.

Have some helpful tips you'd like to share? Go to the discussions sections and share them with the JG community. Maybe you'll find some valuable tips for yourself :)

Module 12 is already coming to an end - how crazy is that? Up next, I've got some awesome power chord songs to practice all that you've learned so far. :)

lessons.title: Awesome Power Chord Songs
lessons.summary: Check out these awesome song recommendations to practice your power chords!
lessons.text:
Practice your Power Chords with these songs, and get ready to rock. 🤘

Many great songs use Power Chords, and playing them is the best way to practice them. Why do boring exercises when you can play awesome songs? :)

The key here is that it's fun! So research if you need to, and find stuff you dig. If you want to learn a song that's a riff and got some Power Chords in there - got for it!

💡 Some of these songs are available guitar-oke style on the JustinGuitar Lesson & Songs app. May app is an awesome tool to make you learn songs faster with chords & lyrics!

If you enjoy a song, or if you have a band that you love, even better! You'll be motivated to keep up with your practice sessions. Always play what you love. :)

6 Songs to Practice Sliding Power Chords

The following songs will help you practice sliding Power Chords up and down your guitar neck!

3 Songs to Practice Crossing Strings With Power Chords

The following songs will help you learn how to cross strings when playing Power Chords:

Molly's Lips by Nirvana | Guitar Lesson. This song is super easy: just 2 chords, but crossing strings.

Smells Like Teen Spirit (Nirvana) Lesson. I've got a free Katana Patch for this song!

Pretty Fly For A White Guy (The Offspring) Lesson. This song is tricky but loads of fun!

Songs To Practice Palm Muting With Power Chords

12 More Songs To Practice Power Chords

Rolling In The Deep by Adele | Guitar Lesson. This is a cool choice if you dig pop!

American Idiot by Green Day | Guitar Lesson

Iron Man by Black Sabbath | Guitar Lesson

Hells Bells by AC/DC | Guitar Lesson

Teenage Dirtbag by Wheatus | Guitar Lesson

Here are more suggestions for songs I still don't have tutorials for! You can request a lesson for your favorite song if you want me to do it here. :)

Hit Me With Your Best Shot by Pat Benatar

Blitzkrieg Bop by Ramones

Brainstorm Riff by Arctic Monkeys

Lonely Boy by The Black Keys

Spotify Playlist Module 12

Here's the Spotify Playlist for Module 12 with all of these Power Chords song recommendations. Give the original recordings a listen and discover how awesome Power Chords sound!

👋 Up next, it's time to say goodbye to Module 12 and set up a new Practice Schedule.

lessons.title: Module 12 Practice Schedule
lessons.summary: Ready to set up an effective practice schedule to rock out your power chords?!
lessons.text:
Congratulations - you completed Module 12! 🙌

It's time to set up a new practice schedule.

Make sure you tweak the recommended practice schedule so that it fits your needs! Remember - we all have different struggles. :) Some people will find power chords really simple and find the A minor chord tricky to learn. Others might experience the opposite. So always focus on what challenges you the most - that way, you can effectively develop your guitar skills.

To optimize your practice sessions, enter your practice elements with My Practice Assistant. This way - you'll be able to track your progress and switch up your sessions accordingly. Look forward to practicing! Music should be fun. We play guitar one our previous spare time, so it's important to enjoy it! 😊

💡 Use the pre-made practice routine for Module 12. Click on the 'Practice' Tab under the video, and save the routine. Edit and access the items in your Dashboard.

30-Minute Practice Breakdown

Here are some suggestions to break down your practice sessions for Module 12.

Songs repertoire revision: 5 minutes.

A Minor Pentatonic Scale: 2 minutes.

Power Chord Here, you'll experiment with different fingers, muting, placement: 3 minutes.

5th root and sliding (ex: Cocaine / Anarchy In The UK, Song 2): 2 minutes.

String Changes and Shifting (ex: Mollys Lips / SLTS): 3 minutes.

Palm Muting Work (ATST slow): 2 minutes.

Enter Sandman Riff / Song: 3 minutes.

Song work (new songs): 10 minutes.

When To Move On?

Well, now we're into tricky territory! Even if you don't love rock, these are all valuable skills for many other music genres! There's loads of good stuff to learn here, which will help you later on.

So - take your time, be patient and learn a few songs. Focus on getting comfortable with power chords. You'll get there by playing songs or practicing exercises - whatever is best for you! Power chords will make your life a lot easier when you get into barre chords.

You'll be ready to move when you:

Memorize the notes on the thickest two strings.

Play R6 and R5 Power Chord shapes. Mute the unwanted strings effectively.

Explored Palm Muting.

Memorized the A Minor Pentatonic Scale.

Had a go at Metallica's Enter Sandman riff.

Learned at least a couple of songs using Power Chords!

The next lesson is all about Blues - so it might also help to do a bit of listening to some great Blues Tracks! (my Spotify playlist).

So - I hope you enjoyed this module and let your inner rocker shine! Next module, you'll get your first introduction to blues guitar! Exciting stuff ahead - see you soon :)

modules.label: Module 13
modules.title: Blues Guitar & Easy Improvisation
modules.intro:
Dreamin' of Playing Blues Guitar?

Together - let's make that a reality!

In this module, get a taste of the blues! Let me introduce you to all the basics you need to play blues guitar - perfect for guitar beginners!

Learning the Blues unlocks so many genres of music. Loads of music we know have a Blues influence! From rock to country, even metal music elements of it!

Some of the most iconic guitar players are Blues guitarists. Here are just a few Blues legends:

Albert King

BB King

Muddy Waters

Stevie Vaughan

Robert Johnson

Chuck Berry

The list goes on and on!

I should mention that I'm teaching this lesson on my acoustic guitar. But the Blues works great on acoustic and electric guitars!
