💡 Other than very early Blues on a resonator acoustic - the Blues is typically associated with electric guitar. For lead guitar, it's usually easier on electric. If you're lucky to have both, practice on each one and feel the difference it makes.

Introduction To Blues Guitar

Here are some of the skills and techniques you'll learn in Module 13:

How to play 7th Chords - useful in many styles!

How to play a Shuffle Rhythm

The 3 most important 12 Bar Blues Progressions

How to play a Beginner Solo

How to improvise a solo over a 12 Bar Blues

How to Play a Blues Shuffle Riff

Other Beginner Blues Module will be available for Grade 3, and I have loads of other Blues lessons throughout different course levels, mostly for Intermediate guitar players. So, as you progress and complete this module, you'll have plenty to move forward with later on!

👉 Let's get stuck in starting with the open 7th Chords! :)

lessons.title: Open 7th Chords
lessons.summary: Dominant chords, also known as seventh chords, are awesome to play Blues guitar and many other styles!
lessons.text:
Seventh Chord Grips & Variations ...

All beginner guitar players should know!

Dominant Chords are commonly called 7th chords. Some might say they are the 6 essentials grips to play blues guitar - but they're also useful for many other guitar skills! Checking out some blues before will be a perfect vehicle for practicing them!

In this lesson, you'll learn all about the seventh chords. I'll take you through each of them & a couple of different variations to some of these dominant chords. Most of these are easy to remember and play, but there's a couple of tricky ones in there! They might take a little longer to learn - but are worth having under your guitar belt. :)

First, let's quickly take a look at the theory behind the 7th chords.

What Are The Seventh Chords On Guitar?

You might be wondering what the 7 means in these chord names.

You've most probably seen G7, C7, or B7 written down in a piece of music. The 7 is adding the flat seventh degree of the major scale. It might make more sense to you if you've already ventured into a bit of musical theory.

An easier way to think of it is that the 7 adds a note that is one tone lower than the root note for an octave higher. For example, if you're trying to play a G7 chord, you would add whichever note is one tone below the root note, G. So, for a G7 chord, you'd add in an F.

💡 Think about the note circle, which you should already be familiar with. If you want to get more into the theory of chords and how they're constructed then do check out my Practical Music Theory course! :)

The E7 Chord

Start with a regular E, lift-off Finger 3, and you're there!

The E7 Chord (alternate fingering)

Keep regular E and Add Pinky on fret 3, string 2

Try not to press too hard with Fingers 3 & 4 (but aim to get the notes clear)

I like the sound of this one a lot, but it's a tad harder!

The A7 Chord

If you use my suggested A chord fingering, lift-off Finger 1!

Careful not to mute String 3 - that's the important note!

The A7 Chord (alternate fingering)

Use finger 1 mini-barre and add finger 2 or 3 on fret 3 of the thinnest string.

Sounds particularly good after the B7 in a blues in E!

One of the reasons the A mini barre is better with finger 1 (some find Finger 2 easier, but not for this!)

The D7 Chord

A mirrored D chord!

No variations here for now.

The G7 Chord

A bit stretchy for most, but you'll get there.

You can choose to add Finger 2 on the 2nd fret of String 5, but I think it just muddies it as it does in a regular open G!

Very bluesy sound in this grip!

The C7 Chord

This uses all four fingers, but it's not as easy as it looks!

Start with regular C and then add in the pinky.

The B7 Chord

Not many people like this one because it's a bit tricky under the fingers!

Changing to and from it can be hard, but as usual, practice is the answer.

How To Practice 7th Chords On Guitar

To practice 7th chords - and any other new chords - you first have to memorize them! You don't want to have to look at a chord book to play them. So make sure you spend some time studying the diagrams to memorize all the chord shapes.

Then, I recommend spending a bit of time practicing each one of the chords. Make sure that you can get all the notes ringing out nice & clear. Some of these are slightly stretchier than others. Be patient with yourself if they aren't perfect right away!

For your first practice sessions of Module 13, you might want to play all the grips through. Get used to how the different shapes feel on your guitar neck!

Then, you can spend some time doing One Minute Changes between them. Focus on the ones that challenge you the most! Here are some common changes that will be helpful to practice:

E7 to B7 chords

B7 to A7 chords

G7 to C7 chords

C7 to D7 chords

Once you're confident with that, practicing doing Perfect Fast Changes exercise between them. This will be an excellent way to develop these grips. You'll want to make sure the chords are ringing out nicely and that your fingers aren't muting any open strings!

I hope you dig this lesson - and that you learned a whole bunch of new chords to explore! See you next lesson where we'll take a look at the shuffle grooves and strumming! :)

lessons.title: Shuffle Grooves & Strumming
lessons.summary: Learn all about shuffle grooves & strumming. Explore how you can get that bluesy sound to your guitar playing!
lessons.text:
Understanding The Shuffle Rhythm ...

An essential part of learning blues guitar!

So far, all the rhythmic things we've been talking about have been even eighth notes. We've divided a beat. It's been cut exactly in half. We're keeping the distance between the beats exactly halfway. But - now that you're venturing into the blues - it's time to switch that up!

In this lesson, you'll learn the mathematical way to understand shuffle grooves. You'll also explore how you can vary it to make it feel good with your playing!

Grab your guitar & let's get stuck in. :)

What Is The Shuffle Rhythm?

A 'shuffle' is a feel.

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, this feeling will be different from the standard timing you've previously learned. With shuffle rhythm, the 'ands' are moved a little later while the beats remain in place. This timing gives your guitar sound that groovy feel!

The most common approach is to explain it as a triplet. First, you'll need to divide a beat into three sections instead of two. That single beat is now divided into three, with the middle note missing.

At first - this might feel a little jerky! A bluesy shuffle is more than this triplet explanation. The shuffle grooves is a feeling that is flexible - and that you can easily move around!

💡 Wondering what's the best way to learn the shuffle rhythm? I recommend you start with this triplet idea. Then, you want to learn the type of blues shuffle from a Blues master you have the most connection with. Learning the blues really starts with listening to it!

The Shuffle Zone

If you want to hear pure blues musical genius - check out Jacob Collier explaining his love for 57% Swing. His knowledge of music is so far beyond mine! I set the time to the bit about swing percentages - but I recommend watching the whole interview!

Collier has this awesome way of thinking of shuffle rhythm in percentages. This shuffle zone is a way to visualize how to get a bluesy sound to your guitar playing. Check it out below!

7 Tips Play Shuffle Rhythm

Here are 7 tips to remember when you're learning shuffle rhythm & strumming on the guitar.

Listening to the blues is the best way to get it! Here's a must-hear Blues Spotify playlist!

The shuffle zone idea is not just for chords and strumming, but notes and riffs too!

With shuffle strumming - make sure you're strumming gently! On your electric guitar, turn down your volume if you need to!

You can use two down strums or down-and-up to get that groovy sound.

You will probably find that down/up strumming feels best for many simple shuffle strumming. Explore this idea and have fun!

Accent beats 2 and 4 if you can. Work on it with muted strings to focus on the groove!

Make it feel good. The key thing here is finding the feel - keep playing until it feels good!

There is a physical part of this - the practice. For Nitsuj - he felt this was tricky! So - be patient with yourself, and keep practicing until it feels right! :)

Notation

If you read rhythmic notation, you might find this helpful!

I hope you enjoy this lesson & it inspires you to go and listen to some great blues music! That shuffle feels it's going to be an essential part of playing blues guitar later on. :) Next lesson - we're checking out the 12 bars blues progression!

lessons.title: 12 Bar Blues Progressions
lessons.summary: Time to learn how to play 12 bar blues progressions using those open 7th chords!
lessons.text:
Learn How To Play 12 Bar Blues Progressions

And three of the most important variations in different keys!

When it comes to playing the blues, there are three standard chord progressions to look at. Now, there is some debate over some of the terms and formats - but who cares? As long as you learn, you can call it whatever you like!

In this lesson, you'll learn the 12 bar blues and three different variations. You'll explore these variations in three other keys.With practice, you'll memorize all these different patterns, and it will be easier to play. It just takes practice to get there - like everything else! :)

Three Blues Bar Variations In Different Keys

Here are the 3 variations in 12 Bar Blues Progression that you'll explore.

The Standard 12 Bar Blues

The Quick Change 12 Bar Blues

The Slow Change 12 Bar Blues

Each of them uses those I, IV, and V chords. Since you'll be playing them in different keys, you'll use different chords each time. You'll also be using 7th chords - so make sure you're feeling confident with those grips. If you feel need it, practice them a bit before testing out these progressions!

🚨 In previous lessons, you learned that we name chords off of their scale degree. For example, the I chord is the first chord in the key or the same as the root note in the scale. In the Key of C, the I chord would be the C chord. The IV and V chords are the fourth and fifth degrees in the scale. In the Key of C, the IV chord is F (C - D - E - F), and the V chord is G (C - D - E - F - G).

We're going to be working in the Keys of A, E, and G. This way, so get ready to put those 7th chords into play!

Now that you know a bit of the theory - let's take a look at those 3 variations!

The Standard 12 Bar Blues

To learn this progression, go through it and play your strumming on the beat. Then - have a go at adding that shuffle strumming!

I I I I IV IV I I V IV I V

At first - this might seem like loads of new chords to learn! Remember, but what you're going to find is that you develop a feeling for when it's time to change chords.

This might take a few weeks or months to happen, but you will eventually develop that feeling. It'll help you with all sorts of other awesome blues songs in the future!

The Quick Change Progression

This is all about that change to the IV chord in Bar 2 - that's what makes it a quick change! The Quick Change is all about that change to the IV chord in bar 2 - that's what makes it a quick change!

As soon as you're hip with the progression, start putting a bit of that shuffle rhythm you just learned!

I IV I I IV IV I I V IV I V

🎶 This chord progression is very common! A great song example is Before You Accuse Me by Eric Clapton.

The Slow Change Progression

Some call this bar a standard Blues without a turnaround. You'll learn more about what that's all about in grade 3. Personally, calling it Slow Change seems is a more straightforward explanation.

I I I I IV IV I I V V I I

How To Practice 12 Blues Bar

When you start practicing, focus on playing the progressions as they are. Memorize them before worrying too much about the strumming and rhythm.

The 'feel' of it all will come to you naturally the more you practice! As you get better with your shuffle feel, you should play the Blues with confidence!

Also, feel free to mix it up! Try playing the progressions in different keys - you don't have to stick to the pairings I've given you in the video.

💡 Remember - the blues are made for improvisation! It's all meant to be flexible and free-flowing. Once you've got the basics down, you have laods of creative freedom here.You'll find a list of Blues classics with 12 Bar progression in the blues songs for beginners lesson ! :)

What's your fav progression between the three? Log in and share the one you dig the most in the discussion area! Next lesson - you'll learn how to get started on your first beginner Blues solo!

lessons.title: Beginner Blues Solo
lessons.summary: Get started with blues guitar solos on your guitar! This one uses the A minor pentatonic scale and is loads of fun! :)
lessons.text:
Blues Soloing For Beginners

Get started with practice, tips, and much more!

This is where we get into the GOOD stuff - the real bluesy stuff!

In this lesson, I've got a blues solo for you to learn. You'll get an idea of how a blues riff can sound like on your guitar! You'll complete it with an intro and a turnaround. How exciting is that? :)

For this solo, we'll be playing in the Key of A mostly working with the A minor pentatonic scale. When you're learning this riff, play it as is! I know it's tempting - but hold off on adding in any flourishes, inflections, or vibrato.

Play it straight the way through as a tempo you're comfortable with no stops. Once that you built that consistency, start experimenting with different sounds and effects. I encourage you to do it! :)

There's a PDF of the TAB available free in the downloads tab. If you can - give the guitar pro a go. It's a awesome tool to manipulate original tracks so you can play along!

Guitar Pro Download

If you are working with the Guitar Pro file, you can easily slow down the track. All you need to do is use the speed button in the top right next to the tuning fork icon.

Guitar Pro is free to download for registered users - but you need Guitar Pro software to use it. If you don't have this awesome software yet - you can use this link with promo code JUSTINGUITAR to get 20% off. :)

Beginner Blues Solo TAB

Here's the tab for you if you don't need the PDF of GP file !:)

Blues Guitar Solo Tips

I recommend practicing each of the chunks individually. Do this before piecing it all together! :) Once you're confident with all the bits - have a go at playing it through. Try to keep the tempo as even as possible.

Speaking of tempo - the full speed for this is 94 beats per minute. Using a metronome, start around 60 bpm and work your way up from there!

Ideally - you'll want to play it with a backing track - or another human being! But first - you need to be able to play this solo on your own. Try to recognize if there's any bit where you might be slowing down because the backing track won't stop.

If certain bits are wobbly - practice them until it feels good! Then, go back and practice the whole thing. That way, you won't have to play it from beginning to end over and over again. If there's a bit that's difficult - focus on that bit. :)

At this stage - don't worry too much about the picking. You can use all downpicks if you'd like. Incorporating some upstrokes is fine too! The essential practice elements here are getting the notes right and the right strings. Make sure your open strings aren't ringing out all the time and that they are accurate.

💡 A fantastic exercise is practicing playing with someone while they play rhythm guitar 12 bar blues shuffle riff. One person would play this solo set - then improvise a couple of rounds. Then, you could swap over!

Up next - learn how to improvise your blues guitar solo! Cheers. :)

lessons.title: Easy Blues Improvisation on Guitar
lessons.summary: Blues guitar is all about improvisation! Here are some guidelines and tips to get you started on this journey :)
lessons.text:
How To Improvise Blues Guitar? 🤔

Blues guitar is all about improvisation, which is essential to creating blues solos!

If you have no idea how to get started with Blues improvisation, this lesson is for you. :) And good news ... Improvising a guitar solo is easier than you think! There are many fun ways to personalize it, and I have a few tricks up my sleeve for you! :)

Improvising Blues solos is one of the things I love the most when I'm playing my guitar just for fun. If you dig the Blues, I recommend you give it a try too - it's a rich learning experience, and you'll discover many new things.

A great start is to improvise on a set Solo, which we covered in our previous lesson. If you missed that out, check it out. You'll be able to download the free GuitarPro file and TAB to start jamming today.

So get ready to learn 7 tips on Blues Improvisation for beginners. These tips will help you add your special touch to your Blues solo. We'll take a look at each of them, but before, let's make sure we're on the same page. :)

The Blues Lick

I'm sure you've heard the word lick before! It's a very common word in the Blues vocabulary. Think of 'licks' as words that you put together to make sentences. These sentences will tell your Blues story.

Many Blues licks use bending strings - but that's a bit out of scope for this beginner's lesson. Bending strings can be challenging, and we’ll explore them later on. For now, you’ll still have loads of fun improvising a Blues solo without getting out of tune because of string bending. :) You want to think about listening and how you're going to phrases the story you want to tell your guitar.

💡 If you listen to the Blues, you'll notice that many Blues guitar players use similar bases for their solos. From Eric Clapton, Albert King, and Stevie Ray Vaughan - they've all got a poll of certain blues phrases and words that they utilize. The good news is you can have loads of fun improving without doing any string bending!

Now - ready for the 7 tips? Let's get stuck in.

Tip 1 - Leave Space

Since licks are words, they won’t make any sense if you don't put space between them. Leaving space is a fantastic tip, and many beginners miss it.

When you leave some 'space' on your solos, you'll have more time to think about what you might play next. It'll make you sound better because you'll have the opportunity to connect with what you want to express.

Don't panic if you feel you're leaving too much space! What feels like a long, dragging pause for you won't feel as long for the listener. When you play licks after licks without any space between them, you'll sound busy - and probably boring for the listener!

Keep in mind that, in the real world, you'll likely have a backing track or a jam buddy to help fill those spaces too.

Tip 2 - The Play/Rest Approach

Rests between licks are like commas and periods between phrases. They work like punctuation in writing.

Play and rest for at least 1 whole bar. Try playing for 2 bars and resting for 2 more! It will feel like forever, but this should make more sense to you as you start jamming. Resting is key for improvising Blues solos!

Resting between licks will create an impact on the chords after. Listen to Blues music to hear how your favorite Blues guitarist does this. Here are my 10 favorite Blues albums to feed your ears. :)

Tip 3 - Repetition

What's the best way to send a message? Repetition! If you want a tune to stick in your audience's ear, repetition is the way to go.

It gives a sense of cohesion to what you're playing, and you can try adding in slight variations on the theme. Don't be afraid of repeating ideas!

Don't forget that you'll be playing over a backup chord progression. The same lick played over different chords could give it a whole new sound and feel! Again - try it out, see if you like it.

Tip 4 - Repetition

See what I did here? ;)

Tip 5 - Listen to The Whole!

Alright, now that you're a bonafide soloist, it's easy to forget that there's a whole band behind you.

Try not to get so focused on your solo that you lose sight (or sound?) of the band. Remember - you're playing a song, not a solo. You'll want to ensure that the backing chords work well with the notes you're playing over them and vice versa.

Tip 6 - Wrong Notes?

There's no such thing as a "wrong" note in music. You might even want to veer off of the scale you're playing. Luckily, sometimes that works!

If you like the way it sounds, then do it again. Listen before shutting your ideas down. :)

Tip 7 - Practice It Until It Happens

Be conscious of these tips. Ease into it, and be mindful of what you’re doing. With practice, they will become natural.

Practice improvising around a Blues solo set you already enjoy. Take some of its ideas - steal the rhythm and change it up to make it your own. I recommended finding someone to jam the blues with; you’ll learn so much faster, and it’ll be more fun!

How To Practice Improvisation On Guitar

You need to practice this stuff to develop confidence with improvising. Much like learning a language - or any skill - the idea is to think about it and practice deliberately.

If you can - find someone to jam with! Whether it's IRL or someone you meet online, playing and improvising with another human is effective. You'll learn much faster - and you'll have a blast! :)

🚨 Remember - practice makes permanent! Improvising the Blues is like learning a language, and it takes practice to get fluent. The goal is not to have to think about it. You need to practice to make it happen. You can do it if you put your time into it.

Got any more improvisation tips? Log in and share them in the discussion sections and help other your fellow guitar friends.

Hopefully, this lesson will inspire you to have loads and loads of fun with the blues! Next lesson - we're checking out a 12 bar shuffle riff. See you there! :)

lessons.title: 12 Bar Shuffle Riff
lessons.summary: Learn to play the 12 Bar Shuffle Riff that is the foundation of loads of iconic blues guitar tracks!
lessons.text:
Learn an easy 12 Bar Blues Shuffle Riff

And jam along with me!

This shuffle riff is part of your blues foundation. It'll be perfect for soloing over if you’ve got a jam buddy! :) Once you've learned this, you'll be able to change it up here and there to suit your Blues guitar preferences!

Funny enough - there's no proper name for this 12 blues bar shuffle riff. This super common riff is the foundation for TONS of blues tracks, and I'm sure you'll recognize it straight away.

For this riff, you'll play in the Key of A using the standard 12-bar Blues progression from our last lesson.

Let's Get Started!

Grab your guitar and play along with me! We'll do it slowly TOGETHER.

But not too slowly! The sweet spot for this seems to be somewhere above 60 beats per minute. Use my metronome if you need to!

Slower than this, and you might make it more difficult on yourself! Think of riding a bike very slowly - it's crazy hard! You can build up speed once you're comfortable with it.

As mentioned earlier, we'll be using the standard 12-bar chord progression. Later on, you can try it with the other two variations.

💡 You also want to make sure you can play it right the way through without any stops. Otherwise, your jam buddy trying to solo over you might not be too pleased!

Blues Shuffle Playing Tips

Absorb that great blues' feel' by playing along with original recordings. Check out some Blues Masters songs suggestions here.

Experiment with how much 'shuffle' you're using, too. Find a groove that feels nice to you and go with it.

When counting, try to think of it a little differently than we've done up to this point. We're going to be counting the bars rather than the individual beats. This will make it much easier to hit your chord changes! You won't get confused trying to count out shuffled beats.

🚨 Pay attention to your picking hand! It can be challenging to pick the right strings. If you need to, looking down at your picking hand - it'll get easier with practice! Keep at it. :)

Blues Shuffle Riff TAB

Here's the rhythm part from Beginner's Blues Solo - the Shuffle Riff in A!

Next lesson - we're checking out blues songs for beginners! Loads of iconic tunes from Blues master for you to explore! See you there. :)

lessons.title: Blues Songs For Beginners
lessons.summary: Check out these Blues songs for beginners. Loads of songs you can play with the 12 bar blues progression!
lessons.text:
Looking for Blues Guitar Songs For Beginners? Look No Further!

Loads of options to play with the 12-bar blues progressions. :)

Some blues are more played in a particular key. But - it doesn't matter! Have a listen and see if you can move it to a key that you'd like to practice. You can play any of the blues in any key - if it sounds good, it is good!

There is plenty of stuff to explore here - the most crucial thing is improvising and memorizing the 12-bar blues form. These skills will allow you to access all these fantastic songs - and loads more.

💡 Make sure to give a listen to the great blues masters. Watching live sessions, and spending a bit of time studying their style is a fantastic way of expanding your musical knowledge. :)

Blues Guitar Songs For Your Guitar Practice

Some of these amazing Blues songs are available on the JustinGuitar Lessons & Songs app. If you like the idea of learning songs guitar-oke style and would like to optimize your learning - the app is definitely something you'll want to check out!

Standard 12 Bar Blues Songs

Boom Boom Boom - John Lee Hooker

Kansas City - Jimmy Witherspoon

Sen-Say-Shun - Freddy King

Keep What You Got - Lonnie Johnson

Ramblin On My Mind - Eric Clapton (Bluesbreakers)

You Can't Lose What You Never Had - Muddy Waters

Quick Change Blues Songs

Crossroads - Eric Clapton (note that the original by Robert Johnson is not a regular 12 Bar Progression) (Key of A)

See See Baby - Freddie King (Key of Bb)

Sweet Home Chicago - The Blues Brothers (Key of A)

The Sky Is Crying - Elmore James (Key of D)

Slow Change Blues Songs

Johnny B Goode - Chuck Berry (Key of Bb)

Scuttle Buttin - Stevie Ray Vaughan (Key of Eb - he's tuned down a half step)

Boom Boom - John Lee Hooker (Key of F)

One Chord Songs!

Mannish Boy - Muddy Waters (amazing groove on this one!)

I'm A Man - Bo Diddley

Practice Tips

I suggest finding a tune or two that you dig and working on them in whatever key you like. Try a few and explore them on your guitar! Find a key that feels good for your singing range if you want to sing along!

Listen to the original blues records before trying them out - you'll want to understand the feel & groove of the song. And you'll learn faster by going for it - making mistakes and learning on the way. This is how you'll develop your skills and sense of blues.

We haven't talked much about transcribing yet, but it might be worth starting to look at! Especially if you're really diggin' the blues. :)

Spotify Playlist Module 13

Want to listen to these tracks? Check out this Spotify Playlist & listen to some of the tracks below you dig! Most of them use the Blues progression. But you can always switch it up and play them the way you'd like!

If you dig the Blues guitar, I hope these songs will inspire your next guitar practice. Give a listen to the legendary original recordings and see what you can do with the 12-bar blues progression. :)

I hope you're feeling inspired to try out some of these awesome songs. See you soon to set up your Module 13 practice schedule. :) Cheers!

lessons.title: Module 13 Practice
lessons.summary: Ready to unleash your inner Blues guitar player? Let's put all these beginner Blues elements into practice!
lessons.text:
Congrats! You Completed Another Module 🙌

Are you feeling the blues yet?

ENJOYING YOUR PRACTICE is the most important thing. Some exercises will be hard work - but it might help you play something you enjoy! Keep that in mind. :)

You need to look forward to practice, so always adapt the routine to fit what you love doing. :)

You'll be starting with five minutes of repertoire revision. Feel free to choose what to work on - whether that's fingerstyle, power chords, or songs you did earlier in the Grade 2 course. Revision is more about warming up and keeping things fresh in your mind!

Spend some time working on those dominant seventh chords. Most people find the C7 and B7 the most tricky - but focus on the chords that challenge you! Your first few practice sessions can be just about memorizing the chord shape.

💡 Your pre-made Module 13 practice routine is waiting for you! Click on the 'Practice' Tab under the video and save the routine to access it in your Dashboard.

30-Minute Practice Breakdown

Here are some suggestions to break down your practice sessions for Module 13 - and what Nitsuj followed. Remember that the Blues is a very free form. Let yourself be creative and explore it in different ways! :)

Songs repertoire revision (Power Chords for Nitsuj!): 5 minutes.

7th chord work, memorizing and fingering. Once you nail this, add this time in other areas!: 2 minutes.

Blues in G: 2 minutes.

Blues in E: 2 minutes.

Justin's Beginner Blues Solo in A Key: 3 minutes.

Blues Improv in A: 3 minutes.

Blues Shuffle In A: 3 minutes.

10 Song Work (5 strums, 5 shuffle!): 10 minutes.

+LISTENING to Blues masters as much as you can!

🚨 Don't leave out the listening bit! Listen to Blues masters while you learn this stuff - it's part of the journey! Absorb the feels and grooves as much as you can & unleash your inner blues players!

You're Ready To Move On When You Have ...

Memorized the main 7th Chord grips.

Explored playing a Blues in G.

Explored playing a Blues in A.

Had some fun with the set Beginner Blues Solo.

Tried your hand at improvising a Blues Solo.

Learned the Basic Shuffle Groove!

BUT... The Blues is not to everyone's taste - and this module is a taste of it. If it's not your thing - learn the chords, explore the shuffle strumming, and then move on!

Good luck with your new practice sessions & have loads of fun! Remember - you can always add your new practice routines to My Practice Assistant & track your progress. Cheers. :)

modules.label: Module 14
modules.title: Beginners: Get a PRO Upgrade!
modules.intro:
Welcome to Module 14! 🙌

Your last module before you graduate from Grade 2. :)

How amazing is that? :) We've got super exciting things to check out - so I hope you're ready!

We'll learn new chords and new concepts. Then, you'll consolidate everything you learned in Grade 2.

Now's the time to choose what you enjoy playing on your guitar! This way - you can focus on skills you'll need and keep your practice sessions exciting. :)

What You'll Learn

We'll start by taking a look at Slash Chords. These are chords with a bass note other than the root note. They are awesome to play in many songs!

It's also time to stand up and get a pro update. :) We'll learn how to play the guitar without looking, a skill that might not seem like a big deal, but learning to play without staring at your hands is liberating.

Then, you'll see how to mute some bass notes with thumb muting. You'll see how these techniques relate to learning how to play standing up!

You'll learn how to interact with guitar players with different playing approaches to jamming for beginners! I'll walk you through the do's and don'ts when you meet with other guitar players. :)

You'll look at how to add backbeat hits to your playing. An awesome technique when you play solo, and that sounds particularly good on acoustic guitar!

You'll develop your song repertoire and look at home recordings. There are many reasons you should properly record your playing - loads of benefits here!

Finally, you'll come across super-cool songs you'll be able to play - so I hope you're excited about this adventure! :)

👉 Ready to get stuck in? Let's start with the essential slash chords!

lessons.title: Essential Slash Chords
lessons.summary: Slash chords are variations on the chords you already know. You’re simply changing the bass note of the chord. Tons to get into here!
lessons.text:
I’m sure you’ve seen some Slash Chords before!

And they have absolutely nothing to do with the Guns N Roses guitarist.

Slash Chords are great! They're not hard to remember, and can really add some fun to your playing. . :) We call them Slash Chords because there's an actual slash on their name! For example:

👉 C/G - You can read that as a C slash G, or a C over G chord.

But what exactly are slash chords? Well, I'm glad you've asked!

👉 Slash chords are the same open chords you know, but with a different bass note.

Before you get too scared, keep in mind that if you don’t know how to play a specific Slash Chord, you can just play the chord in front of the slash. But, in today's lesson, we'll learn 10 Essential Slash Chords All Beginners Should Know, and that'll save you loads of headaches. Now let's get started!

10 Essential Slash Chord Grips

Before we get into the following chord grips, be aware that you can explore different fingering options. Choose the ones that feel the most comfortable for you! Sometimes, you can choose a certain fingering (or even play a Slash Chord instead of regular grip) to make the chord changes easier!

How to Play G/B - Option 1

There are many different ways you can play G/B on the guitar. The following diagram shows you the simplest way of playing it. It's not the most common grip, but it's perfect for giving you an idea! Take a look:

How to Play G/B - Option 2

Now, take a look at this way of playing the G/B chord! I'd say this is the most common way.

How to Play G/B - Option 3

Another common variation is moving your pinky down to the thinnest string. It's still the same chord but with a slightly twangier sound.

How to Play D/F# - Option 1

If you can grab the 2nd fret with your thumb you get a big fat D/F# - take a look:

How to Play D/F# - Option 2

If you can't grab the thumb over, here's another fingering option for playing D/F#. I don't like this one - it feels awkward - but it might work for you. Give it a try!

How to Play D/F# - Option 3

Without using the thumb, this is the D/F# variation that I play the most!

How to Play D/F# - Option 4

Depending on the circumstances, you can play D/F# without using your first finger. Sometimes, that makes chord changes easier!

How to Play G/F#

The G/F# is a ton easier to play than D/F# if you are going from G to Em. Sometimes, it sounds better, sometimes it doesn't. You just have to use your ears and decide what you like best!

How to Play C/G - Option 1

The C/G chord is one of my favorite slash grips! I love this one, and I often play it instead of a regular C, just because it sounds so big. Take a look at the diagram - this is an easy one! ;)

How to Play C/G - Option 2

If you are alternating the bass notes, it might work best to move Finger 3 over and not add the root back with Finger 4. Listen and decide, no rules here.

How to Play C/E - Option 1

If you have a C and you're going to play an F, this C/E makes for a lovely transition.

I've just noticed a MISTAKE here - the rote in String 5 should be finger 3. To be fixed as soon as possible!

How to Play C/E - Option 2

There are times that the C/E on just the thinnest four strings will sound sweeter.

How to Play C/B

This is a common substitute for the G/B as it has a similar sound.

How to Play Cadd2/B

This C chord variation is super useful in the right place - just gotta use your ears!

How to play A/E

Just play a regular A chord and forget to mute the thickest string! :) But it's better if you mute String 5 with the tip of your 2nd Finger!

How to play D/A

This one is like if you were playing a D and accidentally played the A string too! It sounds great, and you'll find it in loads of songs from rock bands like AC/DC!

How to play F/A

Not a super common chord but sounds great in the right place. It's not too hard either!

4 Slightly Harder but Cool Slash Chords

Up for a challenge? I've got a few more Slash Chords for you!

How to play A/C#

This A/C# sounds really nice coming from A or Bm or going to D.

How to play Am/G

You'll commonly find Am/G between Am and F. It sounds great! An Am7/G can be a substitute for Am/G, and it's identical to C/G. :)

How to play G/F

You'll easily recognize this chord from the song Hand in My Pocket by Alanis Morissette.

How to play Am/F#

We also know this chord as F#m7b5 - a super cool one found in Kashmir! :)

Practice with Actual Songs!

The best way to learn a new grip is by playing them on real songs! Actually, don't feel like you should learn all these new chords at once. You've just checked out the most common ones, but there are many others out there. You should learn the ones that you need to play the songs you like. Here are a few awesome songs with moving bass lines that you can try:

The Needle And The Damage Done - Neil Young

Like A Rolling Stone - Bob Dylan

Sunny Afternoon - The Kinks

Tears In Heaven - Eric Clapton

Mister Bojangles - Jerry Jeff Walker

Norwegian Wood - The Beatles

🎶 Check out JustinGuitar TABS and get chords, lyrics, and tabs to follow along with my song tutorials!

When Should You Use Slash Chords?

With music, there are rules and theories that you should know, but at the end of the day, it all comes down to what sounds good. So, use slash chords whenever you’d like to. If you like the way a tune sounds with a G/B rather than just a G chord, then play it that way! There are also instances where the slash chords can be easier to change from or into, so take advantage of that too.

Slash chords can add some nuance and texture to your playing. They can make it all sound more interesting for your audience. Sometimes, changing the bass note is key to making a song sound exactly like the recording. Other times, they don’t make much of a difference at all! The secret? To experiment!

Now, let's learn how to play guitar without looking at your hands the whole time!

lessons.title: Playing Without Looking
lessons.summary: It seems like such a simple thing to avoid, but most beginners struggle with looking up while playing, rather than staring at their hands the whole time!
lessons.text:
Playing your guitar while looking down at your hands is...

Not cool.

Imagine watching a musician that performs staring at their instrument the whole time. What kind of vibe would you get from them? Probably that they’re not super confident, or that they’re not a great musician! On the other hand, a guitarist looking up and out into the audience is engaging, entertaining, and in control of their environment. They look like they’ve really got it together! :)

Apart from the bad messaging, looking down while playing can have other bad impacts:

You won't be able to sing well if your throat is being squished and constrained.

When you look at your hands, you’re more likely to pull the fretboard closer to you. This can put your wrist in the wrong position, and that will impact your entire playing.

So, it's time to stop looking like a beginner, but most important: it's time to break a bad habit that can be really damaging later on in your guitar journey! In this lesson, we'll learn how to play the guitar without starring at your fretboard the whole time. If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you should be feeling pretty confident with the basics, and this lesson won't be too hard. Just take the time to do the exercises I'll suggest here - they'll be a game-changer in your guitar playing.

If you're still not convinced, check out the 10 reasons why you shouldn't be looking down when playing the guitar!

10 Reasons to Keep Your Head Up

When playing guitar, it’s easier to get lost in the moment. Your brain is focused on trying to process loads of information - think about RAM! If you don't have to stare at your hands, your mental space will be more free for other things, like:

1. Connecting with the feeling of the song 2. Listening to and complementing other musicians 3. Paying full attention to particularly tricky passages

Keeping with the metaphor of your brain being a computer, let’s talk about programming. Looking away from your hands and relying less on your sense of vision serves to reprogram your brain and your fingers. In doing this, you’re:

4. Forcing your fretting hand to develop muscle memory much quicker than it would otherwise 5. Forcing your picking hand to find the correct string faster 6. Developing a mental map of your instrument, understanding where you need to be and when, and getting there easily

On that note, after some time and practice, you’ll notice that once you stop looking at either hand to make sure each finger is in its proper place:

7. The fingers will find where they need to be by utilizing your sense of touch instead of vision 8. You won’t panic as much about upcoming chord changes 9. You’ll be able to better engage with the audience and take in any “scenery” (that may be sitting in the front row)

And last but not least…

10. You’ll look cooler, which simply cannot be understated! :)

Now I'm sure you’re sold on keeping your head up! But, how exactly will you practice this new skill? Well, there are a few exercises that will really help you out. Let's take a look at them!

How to Play Guitar Without Looking

The following exercises will help you learn how to play your guitar without looking! We'll use certain chord progressions in this lesson, but feel free to do this same practice with other chords you know.

🚨 When doing these exercises, just use the chords you’re super familiar and comfortable with - never use new chords!

Don’t worry about playing this in time, either. That’s not what these exercises are about. Now, let's get started!

Playing Guitar Without Looking - Exercise 1

Let's start with a simple chord progression: G - C - D - C. Do the following:

Place your fingers on the fretboard to play the first chord. Remember - no peeking!

Feel the frets and the strings with your fingers. Ensure everything is in its proper place.

Once you’ve locked your fingers down, glance at it to check that you’ve done it correctly - don't practice mistakes!

Finally, looking away again, go from the first chord to the next chord in the progression and repeat steps 1-3.

Playing Guitar Without Looking - Exercise 2

This next exercise will help to expose any mistakes you’re making. To practice, play a song that you’re already confident with - something that comes super easily to you. Do whatever you can to keep your head up, and don't look at your hands for the duration of the song! If that means wearing a blindfold or playing in a pitch-black room, then so be it! Whatever you do, don't look at what your hands are doing.

Notice the mistakes you're making. You should work on them using Exercise 1.

🎯 Apart from correcting your mistakes, the point of this exercise is to learn to trust yourself. You can’t be afraid of making mistakes. They inevitably arise, and you should be able to focus on them and resolve them. In the long run, this will make you a much, much better guitar player. I can’t emphasize this enough.

These two exercises work very well together, so I’d suggest working on a particular chord progression with Exercise 1 and then taking it to the next level by practicing it with Exercise 2. You can play a song with Exercise 2 and then go back and practice any tricky chord changes more in-depth with Exercise 1. Both of them are super helpful, and they grow with you. As you advance as a guitar player and learn more difficult chords, you can always revisit these exercises.

Bonus Tips

Before we move on to the next lesson, here are a few more things to consider. :)

Forcing your fretting hand to develop muscle memory much quicker than it would otherwise. Yes, this will feel different than what you’re probably used to! That’s normal and expected, and it will take some getting used to. Over time, you’ll feel less anxious and more confident in your playing, but remember that time is a critical factor! But don’t worry - you’ve got plenty of time to learn and master this stuff. :)

When doing big jumps from one fret to another, you will need to look down briefly. Even the pros do this! One tip is to aim your gaze at where you’re going, not where you are. For instance, if you’re playing in the 4th fret and need to jump up to the 12th, you’ll want to look at the 12th fret, not the 4th. Your finger is already in the 4th - it doesn’t need any additional attention while it’s there!

Enjoying my Beginner Guitar Course? Donations keep these lessons free! If you can, please donate. Thank you! 💙

lessons.title: Thumb Muting
lessons.summary: Your thumb is for so much more than just chilling behind your guitar neck! It’s got potential and we're ready to explore it.
lessons.text:
Meet your new best friend: Thumb Muting!

This little guitar trick will make you sound so much better.

You've probably noticed that I often have my thumb over the top of my guitar neck. In this lesson, we'll learn why that is and exactly when to do it!

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you know that - up to now - I recommend that you always keep your thumb behind the guitar neck. The reason is that it helps you build up the muscle between your thumb and your first finger. You'll appreciate that when getting into barre chords.

But at this point, as an advancing beginner, your thumb is ready to start exploring and moving around a bit! Your thumb is not there just for grip support but also to play around with the thickest strings. :)

💡 By hanging your thumb over the top of your guitar, you can use it to mute or even fret the string.

Naturally, you'll need some time to get used to this.

How to: Thumb Muting for Beginners

You’ll have to explore your hand’s positioning to find what feels comfortable for you. There’s not really a right place that will work for everyone! It all comes down to your personal anatomy and your guitar.

You will notice that the grip you’ve got on your neck becomes tighter and firmer than it would be with your thumb behind the neck, but that’s generally fine. Also, it will take some time to build up sensitivity in your thumb. Your other fingers are used to interacting with strings and frets by now, but your thumb is only just learning!

Be patient - it’ll come together.

6 Moments When Using Your Thumb Can Help Your Guitar Playing

A Chord Shapes

Use your thumb to play A, Am, A7, Asus, etc. Any open A Chord shapes that you encounter! With most variations on the A chord, you should be able to reach your thumb over to mute the thickest string. You don’t play it anyway! So, this only ensures that you don’t accidentally hit it with your pick. Just the slightest touch here will do the job. After all, you’re not fretting any notes.

Open D Chord Shapes

When playing an open D Chord, you shouldn't hit the thickest two strings. That can be a tricky task when strumming a song, so use your thumb to reduce the chances of hitting the wrong notes. With D Chord Shapes, that 6th string is always terrible. You can get away with the 5th ringing out, but not the 6th. That said, you can attempt to mute the 6th and the 5th strings simultaneously with your thumb, but you run the risk of fretting the 6th string.

But on that note, maybe you want to fret the 6th string! The thumb is great for hitting that 2nd fret for a D/F# chord.

Open G Chord Shape

Some people (who are not me!) use their thumb to fret the thickest string for a G chord. It’s never really worked for me, though, apart from a few exceptional instances. Depending on the song, it can make more sense to utilize the thumb here. Stop This Train by John Mayer, for example, springs to mind.

In other cases, you can use the thumb when, say, changing from a G to an A chord. The thumb can be at the ready, waiting to mute that E string for the A chord.

Open E Chord Shape

For this chord shape, there’s not much need for the thumb, is there? Since that’s the case, this is a good shape to experiment with your thumb placement, paying careful attention to your hand looks and feels like as you adjust the position.

Keep in mind that there won’t be a hard and fast way to play these chords every single time. Your hand placement will depend on several different factors, many of which will be circumstantial and variable. You’ve got to stay adaptable!

Playing Single Note Lines

You’ll be able to use your thumb when you’re playing interesting melody lines. Your thumb will either mute the thickest strings or give yourself something of a bass line. This is a super funky style, and guitarists like Lenny Kravitz & John Frusciante are particularly adept at it. At this stage in the game, though, it’d be best left for later.

E Shape Barre Chords

🚨Grade 4 Alert! You've probably noticed I used my thumb to play the bass note of E Shape Barre Chords, too, such as the F Chord. Depending on how big your hand is in relation to your guitar neck or how long your fingers are, this will come more or less easy for you. Try it and see how it feels for you, but I suspect that 99% of you will be like, What the….?!

Now - who's up for some jamming?

lessons.title: Jamming For Beginners
lessons.summary: Jamming with a buddy can feel a little awkward at first, but it’s truly one of the greatest things you can do to improve as a musician.
lessons.text:
Jamming is one of the reasons why you wanted to learn the guitar, isn’t it?

Jamming is one of those things that can seem intimidating, especially for beginners. But it doesn’t have to be! When you play with others, you develop your musicianship, regardless of your skill level. So, besides being super fun, jamming is also one of the best exercises you can ever do!

In this lesson, we’ll explore how and why you should get jamming with fellow players, and we’ll check out some common mistakes you should avoid. Let’s start with them!

Jamming for Beginners - 3 Mistakes to Avoid!

Jamming is fun, and once you get into it - it happens pretty naturally. But you should do a few things to make sure you don’t get frustrated or stuck in your first jamming sessions. Here are three common mistakes you should avoid:

Mistake #1 - Not Getting Prepared!

One thing that seems to catch new players up is not being prepared. This doesn’t mean more practice or skills, but getting ready for that specific session with your jam buddy.

Before you and your buddy meet up, discuss some tunes or ideas you’d like to work through. Then, practice your part as much as you can on your own so that once you’re with your buddy, you two can just focus on the collaboration aspect.

Keep reading to learn more tips about getting ready for a jam session!

Mistake #2 - Not Paying Attention.

Another thing you’ll have to get used to is listening to another guitar player! Suddenly, there’s more than one instrument for you to pay attention to, and music is just as much about active listening as it is about playing.

What are you listening for? Well, of course, you want to make sure you’re both playing in time, lining up the beats, and keeping your tempo as steady as possible. Also, if something sounds a little wonky or if the two parts don’t really sound great together at a certain point, you can always go back and fix it. In fact, you should! Conversely, if you hear something you really love, make a note of it and maybe build off that sound.

Mistake #3 - Playing The Same Thing.

A common mistake involves trying to play the exact same thing as the other person. Music is about individual parts coming together to create a greater whole. It sounds pretty metaphorical, doesn’t it? :)

The purpose of bringing in a buddy for this isn’t so you two can just play the same thing simultaneously. It’s about creating! It’s about experimenting with sound and seeing what you can achieve together that would not have been possible on your own.

Now let’s take a look at some tips to help your jamming flows perfectly! Don’t miss out on the gold tip. ;)

6 Jamming Tips for Beginners

Tip #1 - Decide Songs In Advance!

You already know that you should prep things in advance for a specific jamming session. Deciding on a jam session setlist before the jam session is a massive time-saver, and it’ll help you know your friend’s playing style and musical preferences.

Before the session, try to find some common ground. Throw out a few songs you would like to work on, preferably ones you already play with confidence. In return, see what your jam buddy is tossing your way! Discuss why you love a particular song, artist, or style, and try to settle on some songs that will help both of you to learn something while still enjoying yourselves.

Once you’ve both settled on three, four, or five songs, work on them on your own before meeting with your buddy. Again, this will save time during the jam session because you won’t have to sit there figuring out your individual parts. The jam session is all about collaboration!

As you get more advanced, you’ll find jam buddies that you really vibe with, so this prep step won’t be as significant. For now, though, I highly recommend it!

💬 Up for meeting new friends? Check out the incredible JustinGuitar Community and learn with and from my guitar students! You’ll meet fantastic musicians from all over the world. :)

Tip #2 Gold Tip: Explore Your Guitar Capo!

Let’s say the two of you want to play the same chords in the song, but you want to make it a little more interesting than just two guitarists playing in unison. A great thing you can explore is one of you playing the open chords and the other playing the same ones further up the guitar neck using a capo.

If you’re unsure how to do this, spend some of your pre-jam prep time working out where those chords fall along the neck. It can really sound amazing once you get it right and add some depth to your playing.

⭐️ That’s a trick that we use in studios all the time, and it definitely should have a place in your jam session! Check out my Creative Capo lesson if you want to learn more about it. :)

Tip #3: Start Slow!

That’s an easy tip! :) When you first start jamming, I’d recommend that you and your buddy play a little slower than you usually do on your own. That’s because it’s pretty common to inadvertently start picking up the tempo, especially if you’re nervous or anxious at all. This will also give you time to really listen to the other guitarist, as your attention may feel divided before you get used to doing this.

Overall, just slow down, try to relax, and let the music take over!

Tip #4 - Learn & Teach.

What’s the best way to learn something? Teach it to someone else! That’s one of my favorite parts of being a musician. Sharing what I’ve learned with other musicians and learning from them in return is magical. But you’ve got to be open-minded and open-hearted here!

Back when I first started jamming with other people, I was fortunate enough to find more experienced musicians who were happy to help me out along the way. This has proven invaluable to me and my playing, so I’d encourage you to seek out similar experiences!

Remember, it’s a give-and-take. Be kind to your buddy! It’s all for the greater good of the music you’re creating together.

Tip # 5 - Share Solos

Speaking of giving and take, you don’t want to be that guy who hogs all of the solos! When you’re jamming with a buddy, it should be an enjoyable and beneficial experience for you both. That means taking turns throughout the session, with one of you on rhythm and the other on lead.

💡Typically, a good solo will go for four to six rounds of a 12-bar blues progression before swapping.

Even if the person you are jamming with is much better or worse than you, you’ve still got to let them have a go. Over time, it’ll pay off as you’ll both improve significantly!

I should mention that I actually really dig playing rhythm parts too. Not all the fun is in the solos! There’s plenty to experiment with and explore in rhythmic bits, and what you do there can impact the overall feel and tone of the song.

Another thing - if you’re into what your buddy’s playing, ask them about it! You’re there to learn from each other and create together. The better you understand what your buddy is doing, the better you can complement them. Of course, it never hurts to learn new styles and techniques and add them to your repertoire.

Tip #6 - Set Arrangements

Finally! Looking for songs arranged for two guitars is one thing I enjoyed as I got better at reading tab and notation. To start off, you can search online for different set arrangements to help you on the right track.

You’ll find loads of classical stuff, but there are also many Beatles arrangements and other pop, jazz, and folk songs. Not so much Blues and Rock, unfortunately. :) Just search for guitar duets or arranged for two guitars.

Don’t have a jam buddy? Check out JustinGuitar Jams! It feels like playing with a real band!

lessons.title: The Backbeat Hit
lessons.summary: Ready to add some groove to your guitar? Learn how to add percussive hits to your strumming patterns!
lessons.text:
Add Some Groove To Your Guitar ... With The Backbeat Hit!

The secret is adding percussive hits to your strumming patterns.

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you should be confident with your strumming! Now is the perfect time to crank things up a bit!

Adding in a percussive hit while strumming will spice things up. This technique mimics a snare drum hit and typically happens on beats 2 and 4.

In this lesson, you'll learn how to add a backbeat hit even when you play guitar on your own! This works particularly well on an acoustic guitar. But - I've heard plenty of electric guitar players make it sound pretty groovy.

Ready to get your groove on? Let's get stuck in.

How To Play Percussive Strumming on Guitar

First - you've got to get the 'hit' down.

To do this, you need to practice and experiment until it feels natural. It'll feel awkward a first - but stick with it! It's part of the wonderful guitar learning journey. :)

Here are the two main steps to nail this guitar technique:

Step 1: Your arm will move similarly to how it would while strumming. Rather than strumming the strings with your pick, the palm of your hand will mute them - all six of them!

Step 2: Immediately when your palm mutes the strings, your pick comes down and hits the strings. The hit itself is both the pressure from the hand and the pick hitting the strings. The two together give you that 'smack' sound.

🚨 In the early stages of learning this technique, think of this as two separate movements rather than one. Before you try to put it into a strumming pattern - make sure you're confident doing one smooth movement with the palm mutes!

5 Minute Practice for Awesome Rhythm On Guitar

For your first 4 or 5 practices sessions - spend 5 minutes just going through the motion. The goal is to find that point where the edge of your hand mutes all the strings. Don't be in a hurry! No need to rush through this technique. It's more important to make sure you get it right!

💡 Enter this as a practice element using My Practice Assistant. You'll be able to track your progress and see how this technique improves each session. Remember - practice makes permanent, so practice perfectly. You don't want to keep practicing the mistake over and over again.

I recommend starting with really simple patterns. Try it out on your guitar with the two easy patterns below. :)

Pattern 1

The easiest way to practice this is by strumming beats 1 and 3 and doing a percussive hit on beats 2 and 4. With this pattern, you're practicing switching between strums and hits. - which will be useful for many songs.

If you want to add more strums in on those downbeats later on - go for it! Experimenting leads to new guitar discoveries. :)

Pattern 2

I'm sure you've heard this super common pattern before! It's featured in the popular song Proud Mary by Creedence Clearwater Revival. Personally - I think it's one of the best sounding patterns.

You'll play even eighth notes with the percussive hit on beats 2 and 4. That means a down-up strum for beat 1, a hit on beat 2, and an up strum on the "and" of beat 2. The pattern repeats for beats 3 and 4.

Unlike Pattern 1, which has you transitioning from a hit to a down strum, you're going UP this time. It may feel strange at first - it takes a bit of practice and getting used to!

How To Get That Groove On Guitar

Is your technique feeling good, but your music missing some groove?

It's essential that these backbeats FEEL good when you play these patterns! Remember, you're playing music - you want people to dance! There's no real way for me to explain to you how to get into the groove (maybe Madonna can help, though? haha).

You've got to go for it and explore with different patterns. Relax into them, and pay attention to how it feels to play them. You should feel loose and easy, but don't fret if this doesn't happen right away. Guitar skills develop with time and repetition! :)

Next lesson - we're taking a look at different goals when you're developing your song repertoire!

lessons.title: Developing repertoire
lessons.summary: Develop your song repertoire by setting goals & learn my best tips for memorizing guitar songs!
lessons.text:
Looking For Some Tips To Remember Guitar Songs?

Learn how to develop your song repertoire with set goals!

You're almost at the end of Grade 2 - so I know you've checked out loads of songs! But which of those are you able to play now from memory? I can't even begin to count how many songs I've learned in my time as a guitarist.

The number must be somewhere in the thousands! If you're anything like me - or Nitsuj - you're probably struggling to remember them all! It's a good idea to develop a song repertoire at any level in your guitar journey. It's even better if you can do it from memory. :)

Let's develop your song repertoire and explore some of my best tips for memorizing guitar songs.

Why You Should Memorize Songs On Guitar

The kind of repertoire you develop will depend on your specific goals. If you want to play in a band, you'll need to find songs that work well in a band. And - you'll need to have them memorized.

Having a printed book is practical and can make things even more fun! It allows you to bring it along, play music with your friends and family, or have a sing-along at Christmas. A printed repertoire book helps with the memorization process and is useful at any guitar level.

Printing Your Songbook

You might be thinking that no one has paper lying around these days. But trust me! Having a printed repertoire book is worth the effort. A repertoire book consists of a set of songs that are your go-to songs. Having songs printed with chords and lyrics on the same page will help you memorize the songs.

Seeing it on paper can help you get familiar with it again, especially if you memorized a song but haven't played it in a while. And - if you've got a jam buddy who doesn't know the song, the printed music will come in handy! :)

💡 Back when I was doing private lessons - all my students had a repertoire folder. They had songs they knew in the front, and in the back, they had songs they were still working on.

Now, it's important to set specific goals to motivate your learning process. Depending on what kind of guitar journey you're hoping to have, your approach will be different.

3 Song Repertoire Goals

GOAL #1 - THE MEMORY SONGS

Print out at least 5-10 songs that you know and dig. Make sure they are super easy for you to play!

These should be crowd-pleasers in case someone at a party asks you to play a few tunes. Song requests happen more often than you think.

You'll want to have them memorized. You don't want to be looking for sheet music at a party! The simpler these songs, the better - it'll make things easy for yourself in these spontaneous situations!

GOAL #2 - THE OPEN MIC GOAL

Here's an excellent way to do this: pick a date in the future and promise yourself to play an open mic night by that date.

Playing an open mic is a step from playing in front of your friends. Playing in public in front of people can be scary - but it's a fantastic way to develop your stage performance!

For this goal, you've got to have a solid two or three songs in your repertoire that you can play perfectly. You should feel confident playing them.

So - you might want to spend some extra time on the songs you want to perform. Raise the bar for yourself and your playing. Work on the dynamics, tones, and song's musicality. These will be your go-to songs, so they need to be performance-ready!

And - it should go without saying that these should be songs that you love!

💡 If you're motivated to perform - see if a local bar or coffee shop will let you play for their guests. You can also find plenty of virtual open mics online, like on the JustinGuitar Community. Our Community hosts fun and safe online open mics events, and it's a great hub to meet fellow guitarists. :)

GOAL #3 - THE 10-SONG SET

This is an excellent goal for someone aspiring to play in a band. Develop your song repertoire to have ten songs you can play all the way through with the record. These songs should be in the proper key and at the original recording speed.

This goal encourages you to learn a song as it is. The bridge, the chorus, the arrangement, the chord progressions.

When you play with the record, you'll start picking up more subtle nuances and the time feel. You can explore those differences and figure out ways to better mimic the sound on the recording.

🚨 Feel free to make up your own goals! Part of graduating from Grade 2 is deciding which of these goals work for you and how you will move forward.

The next lesson will be helpful to MANY of you. I'll show you some tips on how to play the guitar standing up! See you there. :)

lessons.title: Stand Up
lessons.summary: What's so hard about playing the guitar standing up? Learn why and 10 tips to help you stand up and play!
lessons.text:
Learn How To Stand Up When Playing Guitar

I've got LOADS of tips on how to start standing up when you play. :)

I often get asked how to transition into playing the guitar standing up and what's so difficult about it. Playing standing up is different in many ways than playing sitting down.

First, your guitar neck will be all wobbly the first time you try and stand up to play. When you sit down, your arm is resting on your guitar - so you're going to want to make sure you've got a guitar strap to do this.

And - your neck is going to feel a lot looser when you stand up for the first time! It's normal this feels awkward at first. In this lesson - we'll look at why this feels different, and I'll give you 10 tips to make this change a bit easier for you. :)

9 Reasons Why Playing Standing Up Is Different

If you already gave this a go - you might be wondering why it feels so different.

Beginners guitar players tend to have their guitar leaning over to see what they're doing. If you're used to looking at your fingers when you play - you'll have to adjust to this new position.

Here's why playing the guitar standing up might feel different than sitting.

Your neck moves around.

Your neck is likely to be at a different angle. It might even be at a better angle!

Your view is very different - and hard to angle the neck!

There's more focus on the side fret markers rather than front ones!

If your picking hand is not anchored, it might pick the wrong strings.

The thumb position on the neck will change. Placing it over the top often feels better!

If you stand up - you're likely to move differently.

Tapping your foot might move your whole body. Personally - doing this technique makes me sway. See what feels good for you!

More technical guys tend to have it higher - more feel players have it lower - but there's a balance for the rest of us!

10 Tips For Playing Guitar Standing Up

If you're planning on performing in front of people one day - or expanding your guitar mobility - you'll need to practice doing this! To help you get started, follow these 10 tips to practice playing the guitar standing up.

Secure your strap correctly & get strap locks if you can!

Practice how you intend to play!

Experiment with strap height. Whether I'm sitting or standing, my guitar strap is at the same height. Slash / Hetfield style looks cool - but you'll have to practice that way too!

Playing a gig? Make sure you practice standing up for long periods, not just short practice sessions. You need to get your muscles strong enough to last the gig!

Try putting the guitar on the left leg when seated - how does it feel? What is different?

Use a lightweight guitar. For example, my Gold Top weighs a ton, and it's more challenging to use at gigs.

Get a comfortable (wide) strap.

Explore fretting hand position (When is thumb over better? Bends, bass notes, blues?)

A Kneel seat option can be helpful if you like to play low but standing for long periods gets uncomfortable.

Relax your arms, explore your anatomy, and see what works for you. We're all made different, and you want to find what is best for you!

Again - SECURE YOUR GUITAR STRAP! :)

💭 Have any more helpful tips? Log in to your account and share your thoughts in the discussion area. You might help a felow guitar player out and learn some cool tricks. :)

Next up - learn how to get started on home recording - an awesome way to assess your guitar playing!

lessons.title: Home Recording
lessons.summary: Explore why and what you need to start recording yourself playing the guitar at home!
lessons.text:
Learn How To Record Yourself Playing The Guitar

It's loads of fun & a GREAT way to improve your playing!

There are SO many benefits to recording yourself playing music! It helps you develop your musical creativity, and you'll learn loads about yourself in the process.

Of course, you can record yourself with your phone. It'll get the job done, but in this lesson - we'll go deeper than that. I'll walk you through how and what you need to record individual tracks. At first, it might seem scary - but it's so much fun once you get into it!

So get ready to learn how to record yourself playing & the essentials tools you need to record yourself at home. Let's get stuck in. :)

Why You Should Record Yourself Playing

First - it's FUN to record yourself! Whether you're in a proper studio or at home with a laptop. Recording can be a whole musical experience - especially if you're into songwriting and composing.

Recording yourself playing is a great tool to listen to your musical creations. It's hard to understand what you're audience hears while you're playing - this is why it's so exploring this is valuable!

When you record yourself, you're able to listen to yourself as a third party. This lets you have an outside opinion on your playing. You'll be able to tell if your timing is offbeat, if your dynamics are too loud, or if your groove needs work!

You might sound better than you thought - and sometimes - it's the other way around! Either way, it's a great learning experience and an effective way to assess your guitar playing.

Recording yourself also gives you the option to collaborate with other musicians. With the technology available these days, it's easy for you to record a part & send that over to a jam buddy. Then, they can record their part yours - and musical creations can be born!

To help you get started recording yourself, you'll need to invest in some gear! Let me walk you through the 5 essentials tool you need to record yourself.

🚨 It's very, very easy to spend a SMALL FORTUNE on recording equipment. The sky's the limit with this stuff - please do your research before purchasing anything. :)

5 Tools To Record Yourself

Here are 5 essential tools you'll need to record yourself.

#1 Daw Software

A DAW is a digital audio workstation. This is a type of recording software and is what can give a studio-like finish to your recordings.

Apple computers usually come pre-installed with the free software GarageBand. Garage band is an excellent program for beginners! I recommend it - especially if you already have it pre-installed on your Apple computer. You can create some high-quality recordings with it! If you're looking for something more professional, try LogicProX. This is Apple's upgraded recording software.

If you're using a PC, the go-to recording software is Audacity. I haven't used it - but it's got many loyal users, and its feature list is impressive. The best part - it's completely free and open-source.

#2 Audio Interfaces

Once you've got the software, how do you get your recording into it? You'll need an audio interface to do that. :)

Your microphone or guitar cable plugs into the audio interface. This would then connect to your computer (via USB). You can also plug your headphones into this to listen back to what you've recorded.

For home recording beginners, a two-in-two-out interface is a good option. This way, you can plug in either your acoustic or electric guitar and your microphone.

#3 Microphone

It's easy to spend a lot of money on microphones! So make sure you do your research.

Find something that works best for your budget and personal needs. If you play electric, you can plug it directly into your audio interface. You'll still need a microphone to record your voice.

I recommend looking for something called a "large-diaphragm condenser microphone." Rode makes some great ones, and it's a good bang for your buck! You might want to start your microphone search there.

There are a few mic accessories you'll need. Most importantly, a microphone stand, suitable cable, and a pop shield/reflector protection.

Plugging an acoustic guitar into an audio interface won't give you a sound like a microphone. If you play a lot of acoustic, you'll want to look for a microphone that's suitable for voice and guitar recording.

#4 Headphones

Whatever you do, don't use Bluetooth headphones! There will always be a bit of a lag with these! Adding instruments and play in time, more chance of running into problems! I recommend you go with a pair that has a cable.

When looking for headphones, you might want to look for ones that have a closed back. This means that the sound won't bleed out the back of the headphones and into the microphone. This is important when you're recording acoustic guitar and voice!

#5 Knowledge

Audio recording is its own art form. There's plenty to learn about the recording processes and how to use effects and production.

In your beginner stages, you'll need to spend some time learning with your equipment and software. See what works for you, learn as you go, and grow as a musician.

💡 You might enjoy the Production Basics course. My studio assistant Adam made it for me during Corona lockdown! It's a great learning tool.

Low Budget Guitar Recording Setup

Technology has progressed since I started recording with a four-track cassette! You can get great quality recordings done with budget gear.

Here are some recommendations for you to get started. :)

DAW Software: Garageband for Apple computers & Audacity for PC.

Audio Interface: Focusrite Scarlett

I don't own one of these, but I know many people who use them and love them. Great bang for your buck, easy to set up, and easy to use!

Microphone: Rode NT1a

You might first want to know that the condenser mic was a Rode - I confirm that they make great budget gear. Their NT1a is no exception! They often bundle it with a vocal pack. This is awesome because it includes stuff you'll want to buy anyway.

Yes - cheaper options exist. But - try not to cheap out on your microphone. A good mic will make a massive difference in your recording!

Headphones: AKG K52

Again, work within your budget, but do your homework!

Microphone Stand: Hercules MS432B

For microphone stands, I wouldn't go cheaper than this! A bad mic stand can affect your recording session.

If you want something that's very long-lasting and durable, I would consider going for a K&M brand stand. They're more expensive - but they are of excellent quality.

Cable: Stagg SMC6

You can find it cheaper than this, but you'll be repurchasing it soon after. Many good cable options available exist - buy the best you can afford and look after it!

Vocal Pop Shield: Neewer Pop Shield

I used a pair of women's tights stretched over a coat hanger as my pop shield for a long time. And yep - it totally worked! Budget-friendly options exist that are WAY better than doing this!

My Pro Recording Setup

Many of you are curious about what I have in my recording room! Here's what I'm currently using to record myself.

Audio Interface: Universal Audio Apollo

I love Universal Audio gear - their audio interfaces are as good as it gets. Their plugins for effects are also incredible. This interface is well worth the investment if you're more serious about recording.

I use an 8Xp as my main interface and have had smaller units too. You can't go wrong here - they don't make anything less than excellent! If your budget allows, definitely look into UA.

Vocal Microphone: Shure SM7B

I have quite a few microphones that I use for different things. I particularly love the sound of this mic for vocals.

With microphones, the most expensive option isn't necessarily the best option. It might be worth renting a studio with many different ones that you can try out before buying.

My London studio was above legendary producer Hugh Padgham's Sofa Sound Studio. He let me borrow and try out whatever I wanted from his incredible collection. I even bought an incredible Neumann U87 from him - it was probably used on many famous recordings! It's fantastic - but for my' ropey at best' voice, the SM7 works a treat!

Acoustic Guitar Microphone: Neumann KM184

My taste for acoustic microphones changes quite often. I have a few different ones, but the KM184 is a regular favorite. It almost always sounds amazing! It might be too amazing and clean at times!

Headphones: KRK 8400

I love these KRK headphones. I've had mine for a long time - it might even be more than 10 years now!

They've got an in-line volume on the cable. They close tightly enough, so I get minimal bleed when recording quiet acoustic parts.

Got any recording suggestions? Log into your account and share in the discussion area. You might also find some neat recommendations there!

I hope you have a blast getting started with your recording journey. See you in the next lesson, where we'll look at setting up your Module 14 practice sessions. :)

lessons.title: Module 14 Practice
lessons.summary: Time to set up effective practices routines for the FINAL module of Grade 2! :)
lessons.text:
And There's Grade 2 Completed 🙌

You. Did. That. Congrats, pat yourself on the back!

You've heard me say this loads of time - practicing things that you enjoy every session is SO important! :)

For your new practice routine - make sure you work on stuff that you LOVE playing! Find the things you love doing and work on them. I want you to look forward to your guitar practice. So - feel free to change up your practice routine to make sure it's stuff that you dig. In Grade 3 - we'll start to get a little bit more specialized. So - now's the time to think about the things that you really love doing!

💡 Under the video, click on the 'Practice' Tab and save the pre-made practice routine for Module 14. Access and edit items in your Dashboard.

30-Minute Practice Breakdown
