Here are my recommendations for your practice sessions for Module 14. You can choose to practice a little bit longer or for a little bit shorter. Adapt your routine to suit your personal needs. :)

Songs repertoire revision: 5 minutes.

Slash Chord Work: 3 minutes.

Playing Without Looking Exercise 1: 2 minutes.

Playing Without Looking Exercise 2: 2 minutes.

Exploring Thumb Muting: 3 minutes.

Percussion Hit Practice On Beat 2 & 4: 3 minutes.

Stand Up Playing: 2 minutes.

Song Work (revision and new!): 10 minutes.

PLUS: Jamming

PLUS: Recording

🚨 I suggest you practice these elements for a few weeks. Then, move on to Grade 2 consolidation and work on anything you love doing for a few months before heading into the Grade 3.

Additional Practice Elements

There are two optional elements I'm adding to your practice. This will push your sessions beyond that 30 minutes. So - it's not something you need to be doing every session.

First - get into jamming! I encourage you to find someone to have a jam with! It's a great experience - meeting other musicians is a wonderful thing.

Then - have a go at recording yourself playing the guitar! If you have a bit of free time - have a shot with Garageband or Audacity.

Figure out the plugging, your interface - see how it works! I've had a recording studio for 30 years, and I still find when I plug things in for the first time, something doesn't work!

There are always minor problems that can happen, so you need to experiment and solve your way through. You'll learn in the process.

So ... when will you be ready to move on?

This time - it's a bit different. We're at the consolidating stage for everything you learn in Grade 2. I discuss that separately here - so check it out when you're ready! You'll learn what you need to know before moving on to Grade 3!

Good luck with your new practice sessions & have loads of fun! Add your new practice routines to My Practice Assistant & track your progress. Cheers. :)

lessons.title: Rut Busting & Consolidation
lessons.summary: How to avoid getting into a rut and giving up guitar and what to consolidate before you move onto Grade 3!
lessons.text:
Woohoo - You're Almost A Grade 2 Graduate!

You should be proud of that.

You put in the work - learning the guitar isn't an easy process. I first want you to recognize your progress and where you started. Look how far you've come! Now - let's take your skills to the next level!

As we wrap up Grade 2 of the JustinGuitar Beginner Course, the essential things to work on are what EXCITES you!

I want you to look forward to these consolidation practice sessions for these next few months. Grade two has already started to open up room for creativity and exploration. Part of this growing process is to taste everything and realize what you prefer. You might not dig everything you learned - so focus on what you enjoy playing. :)

As individual guitar players in this journey, we all have different musical preferences. Celebrate your differences when it comes to consolidation! This will prevent you from getting stuck in a rut which can lead to giving up the guitar.

Let's first check out four guitar elements you should explore before you move on to Grade 3.

#1 Chords

We've explored loads of chords in Grade 2. The key here is to be able to remember them when you play songs!

The seventh chords and sus chords might not be as essential as mastering major and minor chords! Until you grasp chord manipulation - you don't want to try to memorize too many grips - it might be overwhelming.

Don't put too much on your plate yet! We have an awesome chord explorer lesson coming up, which will help put everything in perspective.

Here are chord elements you should have explored:

Stuck 3&4 Grips: "Big" G, G5, Cadd9, Dsus4, A7sus4, Emin7, Dadd11/F#, F6/9

F Chord & F Chord Cheats: Fmaj7, Fmaj7/C

Weak Finger G

A with mini-barre

Suspended Chords: Asus2, Asus4, Dsus2, Dsus4, Esus4

Power Chords: Root 6 and Root 5

Dominant 7th Chords: A7, D7, E7, G7, C7, B7

#2 Scales

Spend some time sing and improvising scales. Play scales shapes up and down instead of collecting them. Use them as much as you like and make music with them!

Here are the 3 scales to explore:

Open E Minor Pentatonic

Open C Major Scale

A Minor Pentatonic Scale

#3 Strumming

Once you have the basic techniques down - it's all about timing, feel, and getting your groove on!

Spend some time playing an easy pattern over and over again. Aim for it to become so automatic it feels great to play! At first - it might look easy - but the more you do it, the more you notice the small things that need work.

Some of the strumming you should check out include:

All Down 8th Note Strumming

Adding Ups to the All Down

The Push

Palm Muting

#4 Techniques

Most of the techniques covered in Grade 2 are essential to your journey.

But - always think about your goals and what tools you need to achieve them! Explore them all, but don't waste time on techniques you'll never use!

String Muting

Pick Manipulation

All Stop Mute

Alternate Picking

Hammer-Ons

Re-Active Listening

Fingerstyle Basics

👀 Grade 2 Feedback: How did it go?

Take a minute to share your thoughts in this quick Grade 2 survey! Let us know what clicked, what was tricky, and how confident you feel—your feedback helps us make the course even better

Grade 2: Optional Courses & Tips

I recommend you take a look at Ear Training 2 and Music Theory Grade 2. The knowledge you'll learn through these courses will elevate your musical sense. It'll help develop your sense which leads to a more realized understanding of music - but it's not mandatory before moving on to Grade 3.

Having a hard time self-assessing? Remember - we have a whole course on how you can record yourself at home! It's a great way to see what skills might still need work. You'll also be able to visualize your progress with physical proof. As you advance in your guitar journey, it'll also be fun & humbling to see where you started! :)

⚙️ As always - use My Practice Assistant to optimize your learning progress! This fantastic tool will help you stay motivated, keep track of your progress. It's really effective to prevent you from falling into that rut. :)

Digging My Lessons? DONATIONS Keep Them Free!

My Beginner Guitar Course is free. Part of my vision is to make high-quality guitar education as inclusive as possible. If you can afford it, please consider donating. Check out why I run JustinGuitar this way. :)

Best of luck with your Grade 2 consolidation. Have loads of fun, explore, and be kind to yourself! See you in Grade 3. :)

modules.title: Chords For Beginners
modules.intro:
Chords are best learned as you need them, in songs as part of a module and I STRONGLY suggest that beginner guitarists learn chords as part of my Beginner Course, that way you'll learn not just where the fingers go but how to use them, practice them and lots of tips and tricks.

But I'll add the chords here for reference anyways because I figure it's likely that some people will be looking for a specific chord, and I'll add links to the related lessons too!

lessons.title: The 8 Essential Beginner Chords
lessons.summary: A, D, E, C, G, Am, Dm and Em are the essential eight chords that every guitarist must know!
lessons.text: The chords covered in the White grade of my course are these 8 Essential Chords with which you'll be able to play a LOAD of great songs and have a lot of fun with. You'll find all of these summarised in Module 7 of my Beginner Course, so better to learn them there, but for reference here they are!

lessons.title: Open 7th chords
lessons.summary: E7, D7, A7, B7, C7, G7 Open Chords are shown here!
lessons.text:
Dominant 7th chords have a cool sound and are used in many styles. The names are abbreviated to "7" so you never need to write out Dominant 7.

These are all covered in Stage 5 of my Beginner's Course, so best learning them there, and you'll also get context because we learn how to use them in Blues!

The Open Chords for beginners include B7 (of which there is no regular easy B chord!) and there are a couple of different suggested fingerings for both E7 and A7 - use whichever is easiest for you - or use the one that sounds best to your ear if you can play both easily!

lessons.title: The F Chord
lessons.summary: The F chord is the beginner nemesis and best learned as part of the Beginner Course, but here it is presented with extra tips and options to make it easier!
lessons.text: The F Chord is famous for being a bugger to learn. Check the lessons on the Beginners Course so you work out which one is the one for you for where you are at right now...

lessons.title: Open Suspended Chords
lessons.summary: Suspended Chords (sus) are wonderful for embellishing open chords and can really help a beginner player sound awesome!
lessons.text:
I've loved the sound of suspended chords since I started playing and worked out how to play the intro to Dead Or Alive by Bon Jovi! I'd worked out the main chords and was trying to figure out how Ritchie was doing the 'twiddle' in the verses and just by messing around figured that I could add my little finger on the thinnest string to my D Chord and it sounded ace!

I would recommend that all players learn how to use Sus chords, they're included in my Beginner Course.

Note there is no lesson on the Esus2 because it doesn't sound as cool, it's not as easy to use at the others. I've just included it here for the sake of completion! It kinda looks like a B Power Chord but with the E bass note.

lessons.title: Power Chords
lessons.summary: Power Chords are used in rock and are covered in detail in my Beginners Course, but explained here for those not on the program!
lessons.text: These are the starting point for barre chords, learning these first will make the transition to full barre grips a load easier! They again are part of Beginners Course... The cool thing is that the shape remains the same, you just have to move them around! Click on the chord shapes to get the full lesson and learn how to use the root notes and all that! It's real important...

lessons.title: Open Slash Chords
lessons.summary: Wondered what D/F# means and how to play it? Slash chords are mostly easy to play and sound awesome, particularly as linking chords.
lessons.text: No they have nothing to do with Slash from Guns 'n' Roses - they are chords with a bass note other than the root. These are all covered in the Beginners Course and are all very common and sound cool. There are many thousands of possibilities, but these are the ones you are most likely to find in the real world because they sound good!

modules.title: Chord Adventures
modules.intro: In this series, I plan to share some adventures in chord shapes! We'll look at a specific concept each lesson and explore a series of shapes and fun things to do with them!

lessons.title: Lush Acoustic Chords w Drone Strings 1
lessons.text:
My Chord of the Day series on Instagram is pretty popular. Still, trying to do things super quick, I felt like I was leaving good stuff out... so I thought I'd try this new format using a chord progression and a specific concept.

We start with a TL;DW (Too Long; Didn't Watch) version: a cut-down lesson less than 2 mins long which outlines the chords but without all the detail. Then we dig into the whole concept, the drone strings (Open E & B Strings), the function they provide to create dissonance, and why it makes Chord Lush.

Some chords work better than others, but the ones that do work can be WONDERFUL in the right place.

These look like barre chords, but they are a lot easier because there is no actual barre! They sound so much richer than either open chords or barre chords because of the clashing notes.

Who would have thought that clashing notes makes chords beautiful... but it does! :)

lessons.title: 12 Awful Stretchy Guitar Chords
lessons.summary: Why do these stretchy guitar chords sound so awesome?
lessons.text:
In this lesson, we'll learn 12 awful stretchy guitar chords - and why they sound so awesome! If these stretchy guitar chords don't tear your fingers apart and you're able to play them, you'll have loads of fun! :) But before we get into that, let me talk about… the pinky finger.

Short Fingers? Me Too!

I struggled a lot with my pinky finger when learning guitar. My pinky is really short, and playing these stretchy chords always feels awkward to me.

The good news is that, just like many other things, it only takes practice to develop the strength and dexterity of your fingers.

Moonlight in Vermont by Johnny Smith was one of those songs I thought I would never be able to play, but I did! Finally, I was able to do it - and I'm sure you are too! Here's an awesome finger stretching exercise you can try.

Now let's check out what is so special about these stretchy chords!

Why Do These Stretchy Chords Sound So Good?

Most stretchy guitar chords have many dissonances - meaning the distance between the tones and semitones is unusual and kind of clash. That will be a common theme for many of these grips!

Let's take a look at them!

Stretchy Chord 1 - Aadd9

What's interesting about this chord is the dissonance, tone, and semitone distances that clash together! This happens between the B to the C#. This clash is what makes it sound fantastic.

Stretchy Chord 2 - A11

In this chord, you have a semitone gap in the middle tone. You can add some variety and play many different base notes on this chord!

Stretchy Chord 3 - A11 (G/A)

This is a dominant A chord - and it's neither major nor minor! To make this reach, you might have to put your fingers down in a particular order to get into position. Sometimes, you have to try and explore ways to make the stretch!

Stretchy Chord 4 - A6

This particular chord is played in Moonlight in Vermont by Johnny Smith. This is a close-voiced chord, which means the tones are voiced together as close as possible! Very similar to an A triad from a C shape barre chords - but we have a tone gap between the 5th and 6th strings. It has a lovely sound to it and a useful chord in jazz and solo.

Stretchy Chord 5 - A9

This chord is intriguing - yet painful. Pretty cool I discovered this one during the lesson. That's the beauty of exploring chords! This would be a dominant 9th chord. This one hurts so good - if you know what I mean! :)

Stretchy Chord 6 - Amin6

Ouf - this one is stretchy! It feels like doing yoga for the fingers - but more painful. But it's quite a lovely chord - it has a melancholic tone to it which can be perfect for slower songs! You might need a little break before venturing into this chord.

Stretchy Chord 7 - Amin9

This chord has a root note on the thinnest string, and you won't be playing the thickest string on this one either. It has a semitone between the B and the C, and a tone between the G and the A.

Stretchy Chord 8 - Badd11

In this chord, there's a semitone between the D sharp and the E. This dissonance is what makes it sound so beautiful! This one is an excellent substitute for guitar ballads. Think of it as a regular B major chord which a little bit of dissonance in it. You can find this chord in the song ''Always With Me, Always With You'' by Joe Satriani. Give it a listen and see how amazing this chord can sound!

Stretchy Chord 9 - Dadd9

This a great sounding chord - the harmony between the clashes sounds lovely altogether!

Stretchy Chord 10 - Dmin9

This is as stretchy as I possibly can go - Good luck with this one!

Stretchy Chord 11 - Gadd#11

For this chord, you won't be playing the two thickest strings. Think of this as a G triad with a sharp 11th. Having that harmony at the top makes it sound fantastic!

Stretchy Chord 12 - Amin7

A minor 7th chord - not too bad if you have a slightly longer pinky. If you want to get clever, you can drop the first finger - and you'll have a minor 6.

I know I said we'd check out 12 grips... but I've got an extra one! Take a look:

Stretchy Chord 13 - Amin13

For this chord, you won't be playing the thickest string. There's a nice semitone 6 and the flat 7th. This chord can be an excellent substitute for a minor 7th chord!

How to Use These Chords?

I love these dissonant, clash guitar chords, but putting them on songs is probably not the best idea. Most of them require loads of practice and are pretty hard to manage when you're on the stage. Imagine changing from and to these chord grips!

What I want to inspire you here is to explore them. I encourage you to play with these grips and see what you get from them. If you're into jazz, they're the perfect chords to try.

Want to understand more about the theory behind chords? Check out the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course.

modules.title: CAGED System
modules.intro:
Understanding The CAGED System will deepen your understanding of the instrument in many ways. You'll be able to play all over the fretboard and see better the relationships between chords, scales and arpeggios. It's a big deal!

At The Intermediate Stage I recommend understanding it more than playing it, most times using the E & A Shape Barre chords is enough, but explorers will sure enjoy the other 3 Shapes.

lessons.title: CAGED Logic
lessons.text:
This lesson explains where the CAGED system came from. It's important to realise that the CAGED system was not 'made up' by anyone, it is just the basic logic that follows the tuning and construction of the guitar!

This video should help you understand how it came about and how the irregular tuning of the 2nd string (B) makes it all possible...

Chord Boxes

So we start with good ol' E Chord.

We move it down toward the ground, which in these chord boxes is over to the right by one string. And when we do, we move the note on the second string up one fret (shown with the arrow) and you get our A Chord...

Now we'll move our A Shape over to the right, move the note on the second string up a fret... and we get D Shape! Note that we added the note F# to the thickest string (you know the two outside strings are the same note right, so we just copied the one off the thinnest string).

Now we'll move all that over again, move up the note on the second string and add a note on the thickest string - we got ourselves a G Chord. Note that we added the note G to the thickest string (we just copied the one off the thinnest string again).

Now to get to the C we use the most basic form of G Chord - just cos if we stick with the shape we got then you might not recognise the C Chord :) We'll move it over, move up the note on the second string and we got C Shape!!

Now when we move this one over to the right and move the note on the second string we get an F chord, which is just E Shape again but up one fret, and the cycle begins again!!

Maths View

If I write all the chords in fret number, look at the numbers going diagonally down, left to right. Notice that they stay the same until they hit the 2nd string they go up a number? * with the exception on last note of of the C which doesn't follow the pattern because of the multiple choices of grip for the G chord.

E: 0 . 2 . 2 . 1 . 0 . 0 A: 0 . 0 . 2 . 2 . 2 . 0 D: 2 . 0 . 0 . 2 . 3 . 2 G: 3 . 2 . 0 . 0 . 3 . 3 C: 3 . 3 . 2 . 0 . 1 . 0 F: 1 . 3 . 3 . 2 . 1 . 1

lessons.title: The CAGED System Introduction
lessons.summary: Introduction to The CAGED System which breaks the guitar neck into five areas of study. Great learning accelerator!
lessons.text:
The CAGED system was not 'invented'. It is a fact. It is how the guitar works and comes directly from the tuning of the instrument combined with western harmony.

I've been meaning to add this lesson for some time, so after harassment from certain members of the forum and seeing the question asked a few times I have decided to use some time off this afternoon to get it done :) hope it makes sense to you...

You should find that after understanding this system that a lot of things make more sense and I will try and point out the most important things as we go and link to relevant lessons.

The Birth Of CAGED

As I mentioned before the CAGED system comes from combining the notes on the guitar neck with the notes of a chord. For this example, I will start with an F chord as it fits well on the neck but works with all other chords too. I will ask you to do it yourself later with other keys.

Finding the notes

A major triad consists of the first, third and fifth notes of a major scale. If you are not sure how this works you will just have to trust me, and read up on some theory later.

In the key of F Major (F G A Bb C D E F) the triad notes would be F A and C. Lets start by finding them all on the guitar fingerboard. Notice that every note can be found on every string. On some strings the octave is shown to to help make the shapes clear later.

I would suggest if you do this yourself that you work out where each note is found on each string and then double check them. Mistakes in this kind of exercise can be a real pain.

Once you are sure you understand this bit, it's time to move onto the next lesson - CAGED - Seeing The Shapes.

lessons.title: The CAGED System E Shape
lessons.summary: The first and most common chord grip of the CAGED System is the E Shape, you probably know it already!
lessons.text:
To start exploring how these dots join together and form chord shapes we are going to start looking at one area of the neck at a time and see how they resemble chords shapes you (hopefully!) know.

Finding the shape

Now let us look more closely at the first group of notes, found at the top of the neck. I have made them green now and moved them onto a smaller neck diagram below. But make sure you can see where they came from on the full neck diagram on the left.

Now some of you might recognise it as a regular F Barre chord!

Notice that it is still only using the notes F A and C but they form a useful and common shape. Also, notice that the 'root note' is on the thickest (6th) string.

Add a Barré

Look at it more closely and I have put a big black barre over the first fret so you can clearly see the shape of the chord in front of the barre... Imagine that barre is the nut of your guitar. Do you recognise the Open Chord shape?

Hopefully you recognise the shape is the same as your old friend the open E chord!

This shape is often called the "E Shape barre chord". You know it is the chord F but the parent shape of the chord is the common open E chord shape.

Position 1 vs E Shape

This shape is sometimes also referred to as Position 1. Mainly (I guess) because it is the first shape that many people learn.

So be sure to understand the "E shape" and "Position 1" mean the same things depending on who teaches them. I personally much prefer E Shape, and I think of position as the fret I am playing in... (more on that later too...).

Remember too that every shape on the guitar that DOES NOT use open strings is moveable. Just think that the root note (in this case F) is on the thickest string. Know that you can move this shape up and down and it forms any other chord. For example - this same shape moved up to the 5th fret becomes the chord of A but still uses an "E Shape".

This shape is usually played like this:

Because E is the first shape, and called Position 1, sometimes (although rarely) the CAGED system is called EDCAG.

Let's look at the other shapes in the next lesson - CAGED - More Shapes (D).

lessons.title: The CAGED System D Shape
lessons.summary: Next in the CAGED System module is the D Shape which is a funky little shape indeed!
lessons.text:
The D Shape

If we look a little further up the neck we can see the next group - this time I have made it in blue - but be sure that you can still see the shape in the diagram on the left.

Notice too that I have left one note as a red one - it's not a mistake - it is a note of the chord and does fit the CAGED system but it is easier to see the chord shapes if you ignore it for now.

Remember too that you only have to play one of each note to get the chord - any old F, A and C will do - you don't have to try and play them all - but more on that later in Triads :)

Notice that it is still only using the notes F A and C but they form a useful and common shape. Also notice that the 'root note' is on the 4th string.

Add the Barré

Look at it more closely and I have put a barre over the third fret so you can clearly see the shape...

Imagine that the big black barre is the nut... do you recognise the small chord shape?

It's the shape of the good old open D chord :)

That is why this shape is often referred to as the "D Shape" barre chord. You know it is still an F chord but the parent shape of the chord is the common open D chord shape.

Position

This shape is also referred to as Position 2. Be sure to understand the "D shape" and "Position 2" mean the same things depending on who teaches them.

Remember too that every shape on the guitar that DOES NOT use open strings is moveable.

This one can be quite hard to play - quite a finger stretcher - but possible :) like this: (The barre to 5th string is optional depending on whether you intend playing that note.)

More about the red note

A quick note about the notes on the 5th and 6th strings. Sometimes an open D chord is played in a way where the lowest note alternates between the root on open D string and the open A string. The note A is a chord tone and is sometimes included as part of the chord like this. Look at the red note. Maybe you have played the chord D/F#? otherwise known as a D chord with the 3rd in the bass. The reason it sounds so cool is that the chord tones are still the same but the bass note has changed to a note other than the root ;) So the red note is actually a chord tone and part of the "D Shape" but not one we use practically when playing chords!

Well there are another 3 shapes to do - so let's crack onto the next lesson - CAGED - More Shapes (C).

lessons.title: The CAGED System C Shape
lessons.summary: C Shape is the third shape in our CAGES System module, and it's a very useful shape to learn!
lessons.text:
The C Shape

Moving onto the next shape we have a few more red "unused notes". These will be explained more a little further down the page.

Check out this next shape - this time in purple.

Still we only use the notes F A and C but they form a useful and common shape. Also notice that the 'root note' is now on the 5th string.

Add the Barré

Now lets look at it more closely and I have put a barre over the fifth fret so you can clearly see the shape...

Imagine that the big black barre is the nut... ignore the red dots... can you see it?

It's an open C chord shape!

This shape is often called the "C Shape" barre chord. You know it is the chord F but the parent shape of the chord is the common open C chord shape. Hopefully, you are getting the idea now :)

Position 3

This shape is also referred to as Position 3. Be sure to understand the "C shape" and "Position 3 " mean the same things depending on who teaches them.

Remember too that every shape on the guitar that DOES NOT use open strings is moveable. And this one is no exception.

It is usually played like this:

More on the red dots

Now as you may know there are many ways of playing an open C chord. Sometimes (especially back in the 50's and 60's) it was played using your 3rd finger on the 6th string and your 4th finger on the root note. Think about it - they are all chord tones, and it sounds pretty cool. Most of the time we want the root note to be the lowest note though - that why it is the way that you have probably learnt it :)

Also see the red note on the thinnest string. Try playing an open C chord and adding that note in - sounds cool eh :) - I use it in my arrangement of the Beatles song Yesterday - it can really make a nice change from the "usual" C shape :) - but it is very hard to play as a barre cos we don't have enough fingers :))

When playing a C- shape barre, these two options become difficult - unless you have five fingers! :)

Only two shapes to go now - CAGED - More Shapes (A).

lessons.title: The CAGED System A Shape
lessons.summary: The A Shape of the CAGED System is a very common barre chord form, second only to E Shape.
lessons.text:
This next shape - this time in yellow - is the second most common shape - also known as position 4. Make sure that you locate it on the big neck diagram on the left.

Still we only use the notes F A and C but they form a useful and very common shape. Also notice that the 'root note' is on the 5th string - just like it was for the C shape - but now the notes are higher (further up) than the root note.

Add la Barré

Look at it more closely and I have put a barre over the eighth fret so you can clearly see the shape...

Imagine that the big black barre is the nut... see it?

It's the shape of an open A chord! Easy :)

This shape is often called the "A shape barre chord". You know it is the chord F but the parent shape of the chord is from the common open A chord shape.

Position

This shape is also refered to as Position 4 - and is a very widely used barre chord, the only more popular one is the E shape. Be sure to understand the "A shape" and "Position 4" mean the same thing - depending on who teaches it.

Remember too that every shape on the guitar that DOES NOT use open strings is moveable. And this one is no exception.

It is usually played like this:

There are quite a few different ways to play this as a barre chord - if you are not sure it may well be worth checking out the CAGED chord shapes in the chords and scales part of this site.

As with the other shapes, the red note can be included too, but as it is not the lowest root note the way shown above is the most common :)

Only one to go now - CAGED - Last Shape (G).

lessons.title: The CAGED System G Shape
lessons.summary: The G Shape chord is not commonly played but is the final part of the puzzle and makes sense in so many ways beyond the chord shape (for scales and arpeggios!)
lessons.text:
The G Shape

This last shape is probably the least used and can be very hard to play as a barre chord - this time in orange :).

Still we only use the notes F A and C. Also notice that the 'root note' is now on the 6th string.

Check out the barré

Look at it more closely and I have put a barre over the tenth fret so you can clearly see the shape...

Imagine that the big black barre is the nut... can you see it?

It's the same shape as an open G chord!

This shape is often called the "G shape barre chord". You know it is the chord F but the parent shape of the chord is from the common open G chord shape.

Position

This shape is also referred to as Position 5. Be sure to understand the "G shape" and "Position 5" mean the same things depending on who teaches them.

Remember too that every shape on the guitar that DOES NOT use open strings is moveable. And this one is no exception.

It is a very hard chord to play as a full barre chord but if you are going to try it is usually played like this:

Red dot rock fever

If you look at the red dot now and add that to your regular open G chord you will get what I often refer to as "rock G" as it is mostly used in rock music.

Well, that is the CAGED system for now, at some point I will revisit and explain how scales and arpeggios fit into the same system!

lessons.title: Jimi Hendrix Style: How to Use Your Thumb to Play the Bass Notes of Chords
lessons.summary: When you get the thumb playing the bass note it allows you a lot more freedom with the rest of your fingers for embellishments and fun!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Lesson Welcome

00:36 D/F# with Thumb

02:30 E Shape Major Chords

06:04 Why Use The Thumb?

06:53 E Shape Minor Chords

07:20 Hendrix Fills

07:54 John Mayer Chords

08:41 Practice Tips

10:18 Warning for Beginners
lessons.text:
This Jimi Hendrix-Style Technique is AWESOME!

Many guitarists struggle with using their thumb to play the bass note of chords, and I did, too - for a long time. It's a great technique, but it isn't easy. I love Jimi Hendrix, and he constantly used his thumb in chords and riffs, so I wanted to copy him! It took me at least two years to figure out a way, but I persisted, and with some practice, you'll get there too. :)

🚨 Don't try this if you're a beginner. Nitsuj tried it, and it was simply impossible. It's also detrimental to your guitar development - learn Barre Chords first to develop the muscle between your thumb and index finger, then come back here. :)

Let's start with a simple open grip: D/F#.

The D/F# Guitar Chord With Thumb On Bass Note

When playing open chords like D, you'll find your thumb either stay behind the neck or comes up enough to mute the thickest string.

To play the F# bass note (at fret 2 of string 6) over the D, bring it further up and squeeze the thickest string at fret 2 with the flat part. You pull it down and towards you to pinch string 6. It's a good idea to lightly touch it against the A string to avoid the muddy sound of several bass notes. You'll often find D/F# between G and Em. Once this grip feels comfortable, try playing the super-common sequence G, D/F#, Em, D/F#.

Let's move on to E Shape Barre Chords.

E Shape Major & Minor Barre Chords With Thumb On Bass

It's super common to play E Shape Barre Chords with the thumb. The technique differs from the D/F#, where you can only see part of the thumb. In the E Shape Major and minor grips, you can see all of it and part of my palm. You grip the guitar like a bat - I can lift it with my fretting hand!

E Shape Major Chord: Step by Step

Let's check out how to play a G Major barre chord, starting with fingers 1-4. Finger 1 barres 1:3 (string 1, fret 3) and 2:3, finger 2 frets 3:4, and finger 3 go down on 4:5 and mutes string 5 (XX5433). Make sure the fingers sit at an angle and touch one another. Grab this mini version first, then get the thumb involved.

You should be able to wrap your hand around the neck and place your thumb on the bass note at 6:3, just behind the fret. Press the string down with the side rather than the flat part. The final grip is 3X5433.

I grip the neck and can lift the guitar and play it mid-air! It's a different technique from the D/F#. :)

Grip Options

The most common grip is the one we learned above, but other options exist. You can fret two notes at once with Finger 3 - 4:5 and 5:5 - if you place it between strings 4 and 5. This gives you 355433, which is the full E Major shape.

🧐 Another Option: If you move finger 3 to 5:5, your pinkie can play 4:5. This is another way of getting the full Major grip.

E Shape Minor Chord with Thumb on Bass Note

Once you've nailed the Major grip, it's time to look at the trickier Em Shape Barre Chord.

Let's look at playing Am this way. Finger 1 barres strings 1, 2, and 3 at fret 5, finger 3 frets 4:7, and the thumb wrap around to play string 6 at fret 5 (5X7555). To play the full shape (577555), use the pinkie or play two notes with finger 3, as we did above.

Why Use These Alternate E Shape Barre Chords?

You might think these grips are unnecessary. After all, we can play the simple barre grips instead, right? Not so fast - there are some excellent reasons for having these alternate grips in your arsenal!

General Guitar Playing

A great reason for using these grips is to relax your hand during songs with lots of barre chords. After two or three minutes, the muscle between the thumb and finger 1 gets tired. Switching to these alternate versions gets you the same sound while letting that muscle relax.

This grip also frees up your pinkie, meaning you can add melody notes two frets above the root note. Over G, for example, we can easily play 3:5, 2:5, and 1:5 with the pinkie.

💡 The Pinkie: this finger can go down on several scale degrees: the 4th (string 3), 6th (string 2) and 9th (string 1), which are super cool Major Pentatonic notes. Maybe you can even see Major Pentatonic Pattern 1 under the grip. ;)

The thumb can also reach bass notes that are impossible to fret with ordinary barre grips. Over G, you might play A (6:5) to get G/A, a common funk chord.

And it can be easier to change to this grip than the regular barre - once you're used to it! For example, if you switch from open C to the standard F Barre Chord, your whole hand needs to change shape. But to switch to F with the thumb, you move fingers 2 and 3 down a string and wrap the thumb over the top. It's loads easier!

Hendrix Fills For Rhythm Guitar

We can adapt the Major grip to mimic Jimi Hendrix's awesome rhythm fills. Put finger 1 down at 3:2 (the 2nd scale degree of G) and finger 2 on 2:3 (the 5th of G), with the thumb grabbing 6:3. This is your basic shape - you can add extra notes with fingers 3 and 4 at 2:5, 3:4, 3:5, and 4:5.

Hendrix created a lot of riffs with these notes - experiment and saw what you can find. :)

💡 Play Like Jimi: His riffs are so cool that I made a mini series full of Hendrix fills. :)

John Mayer

If you want to get into fancy stuff, John Mayer is the guy to check out. Neon is an excellent example. He has unbelievable thumb skills and can play flexible voicings that I'm physically incapable of reaching!

► Free John Mayer Song Lessons! John Mayer's songs are full of awesome riffs, cool rhythms, and interesting voicings.

The key is to experiment and see what you can do. I've given you a general method, but everyone's hands are different, and you might play these grips differently.

It'll probably feel uncomfortable when you start, but it's a matter of practice. It took me a couple of years to figure out a way, so be patient and expect it to take some time. Half an hour a day for a few weeks should get you there. :)

🔥 Check out my Advanced Guitar Lessons and master your instrument!

modules.title: Triad Chords
modules.intro:
Triads are smaller chord grips that are useful in many, many ways - for 'chips' in soul and funk, for making chord solos, as a second guitar part while another person strums and for making riffs. Very versatile.

The videos in this section are due an update for sure, but the info is still useful, so I'll leave it here until I get to refilming them!

lessons.title: Triad Chords [1/3]
lessons.text:
Triads are a very useful little trick, fantastic as a second guitar part, but also for creating riffs too. To hear some great 'real world' examples check out "Brown Eyed Girl" (Van Morrison) for some cool use as a second guitar part, "So Far Away" (Dire Straights) uses a whole heap of shapes for the main riff or "Substitute" (The Who) that uses the very shapes shown in the lesson to make the main riff. Maybe you should try and work them out?? hint hint...

I break the lesson into three parts, each with a video. Try and get each bit down before moving onto the next.

Part 1

This first step is to learn the three shapes of triads on strings 1,2 and 3. The shapes are shown below. Make sure that MEMORISE the shape and the ROOT NOTE. Without this knowledge you will never use them well. The shapes are shown below. Learn them well.

Note that these triad shapes can be called Major (ie. G Maj), or just the note name (ie. G) or sometimes using the term triad (ie. G Maj Triad). Doesn't really matter, they are but simple major chords!

lessons.title: Triad Chords [2/3]
lessons.text:
Now that you know the shapes you need to learn to move them around to make any chord you want. For the whole demo in this lesson I am using the chord sequence: G . . . C . . . G . . . D . . .

Now it is important that you know the root notes because knowing the root notes tells you where to place the triad shape. All you have to do is place the root note on the note that you want and it will be the correct shape.

For example: Triad shape 1 - root note is on thinnest string. The note G is at the 3rd fret. So place the root note from the shape at the 3rd fret. To make it a C Chord, find the note C on the thinnest string... at the 8th fret. And put the chord shape down. Got it. Easy peasy!

lessons.title: Triad Chords [3/3]
lessons.text:
Now the fun begins ;) You have to now be able to find all three shapes in one area! This means you REALLY have to know your root notes and shapes. This will probably take you a little while and some practice.

In area 1 use G (shape 1), C (shape 3) and D (shape 2)

In area 2 use G (shape 2), C (shape 1) and D (shape 3)

In area 3 use G (shape 3), C (shape 2) and D (shape 1)

It is also good to just play around and use whichever one falls under your fingers. You should be able to move between them quite freely, but this will requite you to know the notes on the fingerboard very well.

So where to next???? minor problem....

Now you know your major shapes, you have some homework to do!!!

Make sure you know these major ones well first... then YOU have to work out the minor shapes. Find the 3rd of each shape (that will be the note B in a G triad) and flatten it by one semitone (fret). This will give you the three minor shapes on strings 1 to 3.

If you are struggling with this then you might want to check out Practical Music Theory, that will help with finding the notes, and understanding the chords!

You should then be able to play pretty much any song using your triads. Try it. Be able to find any major or minor chord in and area of the neck and find the next chord nice and close!!

Then once you have that down you should try and find the major triad shapes that live on strings 2,3 and 4. Then find the minor shapes of those!

Advanced ideas...

Then you might want to find then on strings 3,4,5 and 4,5,6 - although you probably won't use those ones as much, you still should learn them if you are an advanced player!

modules.title: Practice Better & Finger Gym Exercise
modules.intro:
Module Introduction

Welcome to Module 15! You're an advancing beginner, and we're about to get ready to become an (excellent!) Intermediate guitar player. :)

I hope you're as excited as I am. You already know how Grade 3 works and what we'll take from it. So now, let's check out what's on this module's menu and get started. We have a bunch to do!

What You'll Learn

The Holistic Practice Routine - we'll learn how to set up effective guitar practice routines. You'll learn to optimize your time, avoid frustration, and make sure you practice all you need to practice.

The Finger Gym - that's the most effective exercise to develop your finger strength and agility. It is like going to the gym, but you'll exercise the muscles you need to play the guitar!

Chord Link Bass Notes - this is a cool rhythm trick! You'll learn to use single notes to link chords. It sounds great, and you won't believe it's a beginner trick. :)

A Capo For Two - starting our new Duet series, this lesson will teach you how to jam with a friend playing the same open chords. But one guitar player will use a capo! So cool.

Mindful Listening - this powerful and simple practice helps you become a better guitar player. It helps you connect with your musical imagination and develop your musicianship.

Guitar Tone: Controls & Knobs - we'll understand the principles of getting the perfect guitar tone. You'll learn all about the proper controls on your instrument and how to choose the best string gauge for your guitar!

Transcribing Real Songs - yes, it's time to learn how to write songs. It won't be super easy, but it'll be super fun! We'll make it as simple as possible in 4 easy steps. :)

You'll get a suggested practice routine, a Spotify playlist with the songs to develop your new skills, and extra tips by the end of this module.

👉 Excited? I am! Let's see what are the 6 Essential Guitar Areas You Should Practice.

lessons.text:
The Holistic Practice Routine

There is certainly no one-size-fits-all practice schedule. So how should you practice guitar?

I call it The Holistic Practice Routine. It's a system that I've developed over the years that breaks guitar practice down into six areas. It also considers that we all have different needs and that our practice routine should reflect them.

Understanding how guitar playing works and how each area of practice interacts with each other is the biggest deal here. It's fine if you decide not to use the system we'll learn in this lesson, as long as you understand each of the basic principles of guitar playing and apply that knowledge. Now - what are they? I'm glad you asked!

But before we get stuck in and learn the 6 essential things that I suggest you practice, remember that you can, and should, adapt your practice schedule. If you're following this free beginner course, we'll soon get into setting your guitar goals and managing your practice time effectively.

For now, just remember to adapt your practice schedule to fit your guitar needs - don't forget to think about the big picture!

💡 The Whole Body Approach Using the analogy of our own body, you wouldn’t want to go to the gym and work on just your weakest arm or your favorite arm. You wouldn’t get it looking super buff without working on the rest of your body at the same time, would you? Would look pretty strange! When it comes to guitar practice, it's the same. You won't become a better guitar player if you only practice the things you enjoy or the things you're really struggling with. You must understand how the different parts work together to put them effectively in your practice routine.

So, what are the essential areas of guitar practice?

I see them falling into six categories, and we'll explore them one by one - but not in order of importance! The last ones are probably the most important, but we'll learn in an order that will help you make sense of it all! Also, don't forget: we're all different guitar players with different practice needs. You might adjust these according to your guitar goals. As general advice, just make sure you don't overdo #1. Now let's reveal those fundamental areas every guitar player should know.

6 Guitar Areas You Should Practice

Depending on your big picture, you should manipulate the amount of time you spend in each practice area. Think about your goals, the music you love, and your strengths and weaknesses. You might potentially drop some of these areas if they are not relevant!

#1 - Technique

The Technique category works out the physical mechanics of your playing. It's like going to the gym! Are your fingers flexible and fast enough? Can you synchronize your movements? Are you able to bend in tune? Are you picking accurately? Those are all things that you can improve when practicing your Guitar Technique.

🎸 If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you'll always get a suggested practice routine in Grades 1 & 2, which works great for guitarists learning from scratch with me. For this Grade 3, we'll keep that very same structure, as we're still working on some structural learning bricks. :) But, as we get closer to our Intermediate grades, I'd recommend you start working on adapting my suggestions to your particular needs!

Always keep in mind that, as different guitarists that we all are, we'll have different needs for Technique practice. Our anatomy, our guitar background, the music we want to play - many different things influence the Techniques you should practice. So, no need will be able to forever tell you what to do! Only you can make decisions.

That said - don't skip the basics. There are a few Technique things that most players will benefit from - as exercises to help you develop your pick accuracy or the synchronization between your hands. As a rule of thumb, ensure you know why you're practicing a certain skill. If you don't really know WHY you're exercising something, you're unlikely to benefit from doing it.

#2 Knowledge

Knowledge includes theory but also the application of it. Guitar Knowledge includes things you should know that will help you in the real world: keys, scales, arpeggios, modes, licks, chord grips… There's a lot of things you can put in this spot, so you need to choose wisely!

Knowledge helps you sort out your guitar fretboard and manipulate chords and grips. When sorting out your effective practice routine, you'll need to find a balance between knowing things and actually being able to play them.

So, make sure you focus on playing - and sounding good. At the end of the day, playing guitar is all about expressing ourselves through the music we love!

#3 Repertoire

Your repertoire is really what it all boils down to - what do you want to play? The other practice areas will help you play the songs you put here! Without songs to play, you can't really perform, express yourself or even entertain friends at a party.

🎸 If you stick around with our Beginner Grade 3 course, we'll soon learn the 3 Types of Songs You Should Practice (To Become a Better Guitar Player).

Then - when setting up your practice routine, make sure you include the Technique and Knowledge content you need to play your repertoire!

#4 Ear Training

Many guitarists often neglect Ear Training, but it is one of the most important and rewarding areas to study. Ear Training can be as fundamental as hearing a song and finding it on your guitar. But how to even get started with Ear Training?

Well, transcribing is one of the best ways to train your ears! That means you'll work on a song and figure out its chords and rhythm. If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, we get started with transcribing right at the beginning of our Grade 3! Transcribing songs is easier than you might think, but there is a steep learning curve when you start. You just have to start off with easy songs and an effective pathway - just like we do in our lessons!

Ear Training develops the relationship between your 'inner ear,' your musical imagination, and your hand, which increases your ability to express yourself. A great test is to try and play Happy Birthday on guitar without any external help. Start on any note, and off you go. Can you sort that out?

💡 Learning a song from a songbook or my song lessons is great practice. Still, nothing is as good to develop your musicianship as learning songs by using your ears!

When you sort out music by yourself, you develop an important ability that you wouldn't be able to do otherwise! So, please - don't neglect Ear Training. If you ask me, the great guitar players that we know from a few decades back play the way they do because they had no choice but to develop their musicianship and sort out music on their own. I bet you can imagine there weren't many tabs or sheet music back in the day! :)

#5 Time

The longer I play, the more I think that Time is really where the whole thing is. All the greats have amazing time feel, solid time, and 'in the pocket' grooves. Solid time makes people tap their feet, nod their heads, get involved with the music. Rhythm is what makes music a universal language! If you don't get your time right, your audience will have trouble connecting with your playing. When your time is good, you get people's attention.

Beginners should make their strumming patterns feel good, and Intermediate guitarists can work on their riffs, scales, licks. Advanced players should ensure that they get their septuplet subdivisions right on.

​​💡 Explore your weaknesses! Does your strumming feel wonky? You might want to revisit some basics. Can't get it feeling good? Practicing with muted strings might help! Want more tips? Check out these 11 tricks to help you get better strumming patterns!

Now, let's talk about #6. The last is we'll explore what might be optional for many guitar players - but it's probably my favorite one!

#6 Improvisation

Improvisation is important for those that want to do it! If you're a songwriter and not interested in lead guitar, it may not be as relevant, so that you might drop it. But if you want to play Jazz or Blues solos, this needs to be a priority as this is where you will put it all together with your band or a backing track.

How much improvisation you practice really depends on what type of guitarist you want to be and how much that skill matters to you! Later on in this Beginner Course, we'll talk about goal setting and how to plan your practice routine now to become the guitarist you want to be in the future.

Ok - that's pretty much it; those are the six areas of guitar practice you should be exploring. The way you'll organize them within each other will vary according to your guitar affinities.

🚨 Many guitar players spend far too long practicing their technique! They develop incredible chops but have nothing to say, no understanding of what they’re saying, and no songs to say it in! Practicing your guitar technique is important, but it’s just part of your development. Without the other elements, you’re unlikely to feel satisfied.

Now, you're asking...

How should you organize your practice?

Well, if you're following this Beginner Guitar Course, you'll find a suggested practice routine by the end of each module, just like we did in Grades 1 & 2. For Grade 3, you'll get suggestions of two elements for each of these six areas. Each element has 5 minutes of duration, which means you'll get an an-hour routine.

You can adapt the routine to fit your guitar needs!

What if you can't practice for a full hour? 🥺

Nothing to be sad about! An hour is quite a lot - and sometimes I do not have a full hour to practice either! So, if you can't do an hour's practice a day, which is quite a lot, break it down into two practice sessions. You can do half an hour on one day and the other half on the next day.

💡 Try and remember to spend as much time on the fun playing as you can, though! At this stage, it's important to spend as much time on the fun playing as you do on focused practice.

Make sure you make time to just play your guitar. Sometimes, instead of dedicating your practice time to a set schedule, you'd be better off just playing songs or doing whatever. You should enjoy your instrument!

Particularly as we leave the beginner levels and reach the intermediate stages, it's important to focus on getting some fun with your guitar time. If you stay super focused on a routine without doing the fun stuff, you're likely to get bored - and that's the last thing you want!

Keep that fun element in your practice routine even if you're through the Intermediate stages. Suppose you plan to be a professional guitar player; in that case, you might need to practice like 8 hours a day. But, if that's not your case, if you don't aim to be a professional musician, just balance between developing your guitar skills and having fun!

Getting a better understanding of these areas will help you wisely use your guitar time. As you develop as a musician, you'll naturally adjust your time to fit your needs. Sometimes, you'll find yourself transcribing for a few hours a week because you really enjoy it or because you really need to develop that skill! For now - just make sure you focus on finding what works best for you.

💡 Practicing a bit every day is better than practicing a lot at once and then spending days without any practice at all. ;)

If you struggle with your practice's regularity and consistency, try the 5-minute practice trick! I'm sure you can find five minutes every day, so try and sit with your guitar for at least those five minutes.

Keep Your Motivation High!

As we go through our Practice lessons, at the beginning of each module of this Grade 3 course, we'll learn my secrets to keep motivation high and stick with your practice schedule. For now, trust the process, and remember that this Holistic Practice Routine is here to help you!

Now, we'll get into Chord Manipulation! Let's turn your D Chord into something AWESOME.

lessons.title: D Chord Shape Explorer
lessons.summary: Tired of playing that same old D Chord? Learn how to turn one chord into many - no diagrams required. :)

10:20 What about the D Minor Chords?

12:08 Tricks to developing your musicianship
lessons.text:
Are you still playing that same basic D Chord? Let's change that up!

It's time to learn how to manipulate open chords and turn one grip into many. You won't need to memorize new chords, but understand how you can turn the ones you already know into many others! That will spice up your guitar playing and help you unleash your guitar neck!

By the end of this lesson, you'll have a better idea of what happens when you lift fingers off, place fingers down, move things around a bit. Most importantly, you'll know how you can use those little tricks in songs!

💡 If you're following my Beginner Guitar Courses, you know the drill: if it sounds good, it's good!

Once you get the very basics of guitar playing down, you shouldn't be afraid of exploring your instrument and taking the things you already know further! :) The best way to learn your fretboard is when you're playing tunes for real! Is there an open chord on a song you're playing? Just lift off or put some finger down - you'll surprise yourself! :)

We'll work on the D Chord for this lesson, so you'll get used to that idea. Then, in modules further into Grade 3, we'll work on the other shapes of the CAGED System and get a better understanding of what that all actually means!

Note: Explorer lessons for all five CAGED shapes can also be found, grouped together, under All Courses here.

Chord Shape Explorer: The D Chord

We won't focus on learning chord names in this lesson or get too deep into theory. Our goal is to develop your listening skill and step out of your comfort zone. Changing a regular open D chord into a variation can be as simple as adding a finger or lifting a finger off. It'll give a new sound to it - take the time to listen. :)

💡 Different chords, different possibilities. Every grip has its own personality - and they aren't substitutes for each other.

Now let's look at some great D chord variations for beginners and how you can use those same tricks on other chord shapes.

5 Ways of Playing the D Chord

Here are some alternatives to your regular open D chord on the guitar - again, don't worry about names or diagrams. Just experiment with your fingering, and pay attention to the sounds.

Dsus4 Chord: To play this chord, add your little finger down on the 3rd fret of the thinnest string. This is a common variation you can use anytime.

Dsus2 Chord: To play a Dsus2 chord, lift off your second finger. This grip is super common too!

D6 Chord: Lifting off your third finger. Sounds super cool! It might not work every time - but it's still worth exploring. It is unlikely to find this grip in a chord book because it is uncommon.

Dadd4 Chord: To get a Dadd4 Chord, all you need is lifting off your first finger. You won't get an unpleasant chord, but it definitely sounds different.

D/F# Chord: Add an F Sharp note as the bass note of your D Chord! You'll use your thumb to do this one but feel free to re-fingering it however it feels best for you.

Check out the video lesson to keep manipulating the D Chord and find new sounds you'll love! The more you explore, the more you'll get into the idea that you can expand your chord grips by simply lifting off your fingers here and there. The most important thing here is exploring and experimenting with the guitar shapes.

🚨 If you're able to stretch your little finger a bit, you might find the Dsus#4, and a sharp four chord is a kind of thing called the Lydian Mode, which may sound like Greek to you, eh? :) Modes of the Major Scales are topics we'll cover way further down the line. For now - just explore the sound of the chord you've found. :) If you'd like to dive into (practical!) Music Theory, check out this course.

What about the Dm Chord?

You can apply all these experiments we've been trying with the D Chord to the Dm Chord as well. Start by placing your fingers on the D Minor chord position, and have some fun exploring its notes. Move your fingers here and there and see what you've got. If it sounds good, it's good.

The big point of this lesson is to inspire you to explore your guitar neck and the chords you already have under your fingers. Spending that time just playing around your fretboard and trying to break free from only playing chords you find in a songbook or because someone else taught you.

Up next? Gym time! Let's exercise your fingers stronger. :)

lessons.text:
This Finger Gym is NOT a speed exercise. Still, it'll transform your playing.

If you ask me, you're about to learn the best exercise for your technical development on the guitar.

It's not an easy exercise, but if you stick with it, you'll see an overall improvement in your playing skills. You'll get a stronger fretting hand, and you'll get more dexterity too!

Some of the finger combinations we'll learn in this exercise are very difficult to execute at first. But, if you persevere, your finger independence will increase, making everything and anything easier to play on the guitar. :)

💪 This exercise is the guitar equivalent of going to the gym. It will improve every aspect of your playing if you do it regularly - just don't go too mad with it at first. You don't want to hurt yourself.

Also - don't try to rush things up. The Finger Gym exercise is not a speed competition; it's not a speed training. When first getting started, make sure you've got access to a metronome - we'll use it to ensure we get our time right!

Getting Ready for the Intermediate Stages

This Finger Gym Exercise is part of the final grade of my Beginner Guitar Course, and it'll prepare you to get full on in techniques like hammer-ons and pull-offs. It's a great practice to develop and polish your fretting hand technique, and you'll see improvements fast. I'd recommend it to any guitarist wanting to play better.

Again - this is not a speed exercise, but it'll get you playing faster once you get things right in the first place! So, keep in mind: accuracy goes over speed in this exercise!

Hammer-ons for Beginners

Hammer-ons are when you pick one note and then hammer a second finger down onto the same string. You'll get a second note without picking a second time! To practice hammer-ons on the guitar, do this exercise:

Start off with your first finger on the thickest string at the fifth fret. Play that note.

Hammer down the second finger one fret higher, so the sixth fret.

We'll try other combinations, and they'll be harder. :)

You'll see you really have to hammer it down to get a good-sounding note. Check out the video lesson, and you'll see that we can get the note without picking it, just hammering your finger down.

🚨 If you don't hammer your finger on the guitar and just put it down, you won't really get a good note! So, use the tip of your finger to hammer down, and don't do it too fast. Slow movements and accuracy are the way to go!

Also - ensure you've got the right angle position. When you get to the thinner strings, keep your fingers curled up. For this exercise, the bottom of your hand should be parallel to the fretboard, not with an angle. Take a look:

Sometimes, we play with a certain angle there - but it's not the case during this exercise, so get your finger placement right.

Hammer-ons and pull-offs are part of the Legato Technique, which ultimately allows you to play faster. But for now - no rush! Learn slowly and stay away from bad habits. Before practicing flick-offs, make sure you understand the hammer-ons and practice them properly!

🎯 Your goal with this exercise is to get the notes sounding even. If you can't do it - slow things down! The Finger Gym Exercise teaches you how to control your fretting fingers. If you don't keep your time even, you will practice a reflex action and not learn to control the muscles.

Once you can play the notes evenly, I'd recommend getting your metronome on! Download my Time Trainer Metronome app if you're looking for a precise metronome with incredible training modes and tools! When practicing with a metronome, set it no faster than 80bpm.

Ready? Let's go for more. But…

Before We Move On

My teacher John McMillan first showed me this exercise back in the day. I was doing all those different pairings, as well as groups of three and four fingers. I was practicing not only the hammer-ons we've just learned but also flick-offs.

Pull-offs or flick-offs? 🤔 People call this Technique pull-offs, but here at JustinGuitar, we'll call it flick-off. It just makes more sense - the movement your finger makes is more like a flick-off than a pull-off. Calling for the right action might help you do it right, so be aware the movement is a lot more like a flick than as a pull!

Previously, I'd also recommend you get into practicing some flick-offs within this Finger Gym exercise. However, I've realized that the best way to approach this exercise is by focusing on the hammer-ons. Practicing the finger combinations that we've just learned will give you the finder independence and the strength we're looking for! :)

🚨 Be careful to not misunderstand the Finger Gym Exercise goal! We're not learning to play legato here - we're only working on our finger dexterity and agility. You can do better exercises to learn Legato Techniques on guitar - and we'll get into that later on our guitar journey!

This Finger Gym exercise is a fantastic way to develop the strength in your hand and the dexterity of your fingers. You'll be able to control your movements more efficiently!

I'm sorry! :)

For anyone who's done this exercise with me before, I'm sure you've learned a lot and got some great finger strength. However, now I know that this Finger Gym exercise is not the best way to practice your flick-offs. So, trust me, and practice hammer-ons and pull-offs with exercises that allow you to keep your fretting hand relaxed.

How to Practice Hammer-ons?

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you'll find a practice routine by the end of this module. When it comes to practicing the Finger Gym exercise, follow these general guidelines:

This exercise works your finger dexterity and hand strength. It's like going to the gym, but for guitar! Do it slowly and carefully, so you don't hurt yourself.

I'd recommend doing just 5 minutes a day, maybe 10 if you work hard on your practice. But really, you will be better off doing other guitar exercises as well than overdoing just this one!

Remember to practice what you can't do, not what you can! Focus on the harder combinations for you, and don't rush things out.

Keep your time even. That's crucial in this exercise. When working with a metronome, 60 bpm is a very good time! You can play along with me too - but, in this particular case, the sound of my guitar might distract you. So, you're better off with a metronome! :)

Try to do this exercise regularly! It's the regularity and accuracy that will help your technique improve. Regularity is the key to maintaining your guitar technique too!

Don't over practice, ok? That can lead to permanent problems and a real pain! Be careful, and remember: this is NOT a speed exercise. Accuracy over speed!

What Next?

OK - so we've made it through the first Technique lesson of our Grade 3. Next, we'll look into our first Rhythm lesson for this Orange grade. If you're still (!) not following my free guitar courses, you might want to check out this lesson on How you should practice guitar. ;)

Now, let's learn a super cool and easy trick to add interest and movement to your guitar playing!

lessons.text:
This guitar trick makes you sound like a pro.

I call it Bass Note Chord Links, which adds loads of movement to your playing!

This is one of my favorite guitar tricks to teach advancing beginners, as it can help you sound more interesting. You'll add a couple of notes in when you play so that you link up the bass notes of your chords. Sounds complicated? But it's not - and this guitar lesson got your back! :)

This rhythm trick has a country vibe and sounds awesome on the acoustic guitar, but it works well in all styles. Let's get stuck in and check out those bass note chord links.

Get The Trick: Bass Note Chord Links

Not a big secret here - we're looking for two bass notes that will link from one chord to the next. You'll put these notes on beats 3 & 4! There are no real set rules here, but we should explore some common patterns next. Seriously - they'll make you sound like a real pro! Here are 8 common patterns you should explore:

C to G

G to C

A to D

D to A

Am to Dm

C to A

G to E

C to F

Check out the video lesson to learn how each one sounds. But the best way to discover and understand what's happening here is by grabbing your guitar and exploring all we're learning!

Let's ensure we understand what's happening with these Bass Notes Chord Links and how you can use this guitar trick in real life! Let's use the chords C and G to learn how to apply this trick! You'll probably recognize this sound. :)

Chord Pattern #1 - C to G

This is probably the most common combination to learn. It works both G to C and C to G. If you start on a C chord, the bass note will go from C (within the C chord) to B to A to G (within the G chord). So, you're moving down the C Major Scale - or the G Major Scale, depending on how you'd like to look at it! These notes are in both.

💡 Level this up even more! :) You can play alternating bass chords, just like we've explored when learning Slash Chords in Grade 2. So, for example, here you'd have a C/G, C, then the walk down. It sounds great, eh? Check out the video lesson!

This particular chord change is a big trick! You'll hear it in different music styles and tempos, but it doesn't have a bit of a Country, slow vibe. I dig it - don't you? :)

🎸 Changing from the A chord to the D chord is another common pattern all beginners should explore! You'll need a little bit more hand movement, but I promise - it is worthy. Check out the video tutorial to learn more about the most common patterns to apply this rhythm trick!

Exceptions: Chromatic Scales

All we've been doing so far is using the Major Scale to link Major Chords or the Minor Scale to link Minor Chords. But, you'll notice that, sometimes, the chords are too close together, or there's another reason why the scale-wise steps won't work.

You won't have enough notes to apply this trick if you've got a chord change like C to A, either Major or Minor. So, you will have to use a Chromatic Scale, which means you'll introduce a note not originally in the scale you're playing. The big deal here will be to use your ears and decide what sounds good to you.

Did You Get The Trick?

You need to find two notes between the chords that link one chord to another! The Major Scale for linking Major Chords most commonly needs two-tone steps notes, while the Minor Scale for Minor Chords needs a tone, then a semitone. But again - no real rules here, so explore. If it sounds good, it's good.

🚨 When you're going to an F chord, you can use a Chromatic Scale. So, if you're going from the C Chord to the F Chord, you can go G/F# to F. That doesn't work so well for me if going to the C, though - and I'd do it differently! Try to apply this guitar trick to that chord change pattern, and let me know how you sort that out in the Discussion section. :)

I'd encourage you to try to make up some of your chord link patterns. Try exploring some of these in songs you know already - usually, a better idea to build on a song you know than try to get it going from scratch!

As with most rhythm things in guitar, your first step should be getting the notes right and accurately. But once you can technically execute the movement, you want to stop thinking about the mechanics of playing. Your goal is to relax and get into that vibe. That will make you sound great, but getting there takes time and effort. And practice makes permanent!

👉 Following my Beginner Guitar Course? Up next is our first lesson on guitar duets!

lessons.text:
How can beginners jam together and sound just like professional guitar players? The answer is here!

And it's a pretty easy one - we'll use a guitar capo on a trick that I call A Capo for Two, and yep, it requires open chords only. You'll find famous artists playing like that - it's simple, most beginners can do it, and it sounds incredible!

🎸 This is the first lesson of our Duets series, and it's part of Grade 3 of my Beginner Guitar Course. Hope you enjoy it!

This tutorial will explore how two guitar players can play together even as beginners. You can get two acoustic guitars - it's great - or combine acoustic and electric guitars as well. The classic version is two acoustic guitars playing together, but creativity and musical expression are the only rules here.

To take advantage of this guitar trick, you'll need to follow some general guidelines. Let's start by exploring them. :)

Jamming for Beginners: Before Getting Started

This guitar trick works around what we call the CAGED System - something we'll explore in many lessons in Grade 3 and further on in our Intermediate stages. For now, we need to get you started with the fundamental idea of what the CAGED System means. Here's a simplified explanation:

What's the CAGED System?

There are only five ways of playing chords on the guitar: the C, A, G, E, and D shapes. I'm sure you've encountered them before. Let's take a look at your guitar fretboard! If you start off with a C chord, you've got the notes C, E, G, C, and E. So, it's an open C Chord with a C Shape.

💡 We get the shape’s name from the chord in the open position!

The important thing here is to realize that there are different ways of playing those same notes - C, E, G, C, and E - somewhere else on your guitar fretboard. For example, you could play an A Shape - you'll play those same guitar notes, but the position on the guitar neck would look similar to the open A chord. Your first finger would work as a guitar capo on the 3rd fret. :) Check out the video tutorial to visualize this better!

You'll hear it - it still sounds like a C Chord, but it's slightly different because the top notes sound different. Join the video lesson to keep exploring this concept - we've got 5 different ways of playing the C chord on the guitar.

As we advance in our guitar journey, we'll explore more about the CAGED System and how to put it into practice. For now, we're only getting into it so that you understand the basics and how you can use that to play along with other guitar players and sound like a pro - even if you're still a beginner!

Get the Trick: A Capo For Two!

The CAGED System allows you to play all the same open chords you know in different places of your fretboard using a capo. So, the trick here is to get a friend to jam with - one will be playing the chords in the open position, the other will be playing the same chords, at the same time, but down the neck - and using a guitar capo! That sounds beautiful.

💡The way your guitar fretboard works is cool, eh? Once you understand how it all comes together, you've got the fretboard freedom you've been looking for. Just stick around, commit to your guitar practice routines, and trust the process. You've got this!

So, I call this trick A Capo For Two - seriously, it's the coolest beginner jam trick I know. :) The challenge will be to find the right place to put your capo on your guitar neck. If you're doing a song that has loads of chords - that'll be trickier! Here is some general advice for you:

Trial and error work pretty well here! You already know how one guitar will play (the usual open chord position) - so, experiment with the second one. Move the capo around and pay attention to what you like the most. You'll learn a lot about root notes, tones, semitones… in a practical way!

You should know the root notes on the thicker strings at this stage of your guitar journey. If you still haven't memorized them, check out the 6 Essential Notes here. Preferably, you'd also know the notes on the 4th string - but there's a cheat for that, and we'll learn it in the video lesson. :)

Getting to know the root notes and finding the shapes on the guitar neck is another level, eh? If you'd like to go further in your guitar journey and become a musician, I'd recommend you dig into it and get the time to know how your instrument works. If not, if you just want to have some fun, all you have to do is memorize some common patterns. It all comes down to how far you plan to go in your journey.

To help you out, here's a cheat sheet for you!

Open Chord Shapes Cheat Sheet

This chart should help you make sense of things, and understanding your guitar neck will be easier! All you've got to do is check the open chords and see where they all line up on a certain capo position. The top row of chords in the grey cells are those you may be aiming to play - call them your target chords. All chords shown in the rows below, and right of a capo position, are the 'chord shapes' you need to hold to play the target chords.

This chart only considers open chords because this lesson is part of Grade 3 of my Beginner Guitar Course. If you're a more advanced guitar player, feel free to add barre chords as well!

What about the Minor Chords?

You can apply the things we learned here to play Minor Chords, but it usually takes more complicated fingerings, and this A Capo For Two trick works less. That's because there are no C Minor and G Minor open chords. To understand the reason behind that, check out my Practical Music Theory course.

So, for now - I'd recommend starting with Major Chords and visiting Minor Chords later in your guitar journey.

A Capo For Two - Real-Life Examples!

You'll find the trick in so many awesome tracks! Some of my favorites are:

Handle With Care by The Traveling Wilburys

Wildflowers by Tom Petty

Wild Horses by The Rolling Stones

Choose songs you love but have easy chord progressions - and, for now, prioritize songs with Major Chords only. We'll get fancier about all of this later on!

Practice. :)

The best way to figure out this stuff is just to do it. If you have a friend who also plays guitar and you can sort this stuff out together, even better for you! With someone else, you'll learn together and have loads more fun!

Following Grade 3? Next, we'll learn a simple secret from the greatest musicians!
