lessons.text:
Give it a chance, and this Music Meets Meditation lesson will help you elevate your musicianship.

Ultimately, you'll become a better guitar player.

Have you been my student for a while now? :) You might have noticed that I'm big on Meditation, and I believe that is a valuable practice for many different areas of your life. However, my goal in this lesson is to help you understand how we can take advantage of what I call Mindfulness Meditation to develop your guitar skills.

You might have explored this mindfulness idea before, but to make sure we're on the same page, let's start with the basics!

What's Mindfulness?

Mindfulness is a meditation practice that comes from Buddhists. The basic idea is to be very present in a particular moment. Usually, the most common way to learn to be mindful is by focusing intensively on your breathing. You'd focus only on your breathing for a given period. If you do that regularly, you'll improve your concentration, so you're less distracted by external stimuli.

💭 I got into mindfulness in 2016 mainly as a tool that'd help me clear my mind. I've got a super active mind - a monkey one; it just doesn’t stop! Getting into Meditation was amazing and improved my day-to-day life a lot - I was sleeping better and feeling way more relaxed! On top of it, I've discovered Mindful Running. Instead of concentrating on your breathing, the fall of your feet becomes the sole focus of your attention.

I've done Mindful Running for a while, which inspired me to think about how we could bring mindfulness into guitar practice. And that's how we've got into today's lesson. :)

What's Mindful Listening?

Back in the day, before all this technology and social media distractions, music had a more dominant place in our lives. I'm sure that students from my generation or older will remember that listening to a new album that was out was a pretty big deal!

💭 I remember sitting in between speakers, back in Tasmania, listening to new music that was out. I'd order a new album from the store, wait months for it to arrive, and then spend weeks listening to that one record. I'd really absorbed it and appreciate its value to my life. I'd be so immersed by the things going on in a song! I'm sure that helped me become a better listener and musician!

But that's not the reality anymore, and we don't really make time to listen to music like we used to do back then. Like, not just having something playing in the background, but really listening closely to the music.

Mindful Listening used to be something natural to most music lovers, but unfortunately, that's not the reality anymore! And, sadly, because that's an incredibly important habit on many different levels. Many of the great players I admire often talk about the importance of listening (for real) to music. But, with music being so available these days, taking time to really appreciate the songs you love is a big deal and something we should all practice more!

How to Practice Mindful Listening

Start by getting a playlist ready in advance - add in the songs you'd like to absorb. Then, find a quiet room to get comfortable and get yourself still. While listening, start by letting your focus wander over the music and see where it lands.

Now, try to get into that aspect and drill deeper into it. It might be the guitar tone and then how it sits in the track or the sound of the pick hitting the strings. It might be the drum groove and then the high-hat, the locking in of the high-hat and the acoustic guitar, or the pattern it makes.

It's not really important where your focus ends up. Still, I think it can be helpful to try to guide yourself deeper into wherever your focus drifts.

💡 Some experience in Meditation will be a big help to get yourself started! I used the app Headspace for a few months to get going and found it really helpful! These days I use the Waking Up app almost every day and that takes things a bit further along, but perhaps isn't as beginner friendly if you are completely new to it all! But there are loads of resources available that you can explore.

Practicing mindful listening has opened up some albums that I was already very familiar with, and I've discovered new layers to explore. I now sometimes listen to something with a very specific aim.

For example, I wanted to explore Angus Young's vibrato. So, while AC/DC is probably not the music we usually associate with Meditation, I went in a mindful state with all of my attention centered on this one thing. Another thing I got into was exploring the 'pocket' of funk grooves and trying to focus on the relationships between the instruments and how tight (or loose) they were. Music production, focussing on reverbs and textures, and exploring guitar layers are also fascinating journeys.

Explore!

You can choose to get into the zone and let stuff happen or explore something specific. No matter what you choose to do, just let yourself get absorbed into the music. It's all good - there are no rules, just fun things to explore.

📚 If you'd like to go even further, I'd recommend checking out the book The Music Lesson by Victor L. Wooten. This is a really deep and compelling book - so insightful. Many life lessons are hidden in a search for spirituality through music. It contains some of the best explanations of how music works at the big picture level.

Many guitar players neglect developing their listening abilities, but I truly hope you won't be one of them. You don't have to call it Meditation. Call it Deep Listening or something like that - as long as you find time to really listen to music and pay attention to its elements.

If you want to be a musician, getting in touch with music deeper will help you connect with your instrument. Whether you go for the full experience or not, don't neglect your musical imagination or your listening skills.

Yeah - wow! Sharing all of this was something new to me, but I hope you enjoyed this guitar lesson. If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, we'll get one of these Understanding lessons in each module of this Grade 3.

Up next - we'll get into guitar tone and learn the basic settings! Ready? Go!

lessons.text:
The perfect tone starts with your instrument but goes way further. Learn all the secrets here!

Often, someone will comment in my song tutorials: Hey, Justin, how do you get this perfect guitar tone? Well, my friend - that's not an easy answer. There's a lot of tone in your guitar… it all starts there! And then - so many possibilities and stuff to explore.

🎸 Guitar Tone is a big topic - and we want to get that very right! So, we'll need more than just one lesson to get a good answer to that big question. For today, we'll focus on the tones in your instrument! Follow this Beginner Guitar Course to continue this series. We've got loads to discover. :)

The tone really is a big deal. The amps and effects play a big role in your guitar sound too. In fact, a cheaper guitar plugged into an awesome amp is likely to sound good - but the opposite is not true! If you have a great guitar, but your amp isn't good, you probably won't get an incredible sound.

So, what's the best guitar for you? 🤔 The one that feels good to you. When I'm shopping for a new guitar, its feeling is the main feature. You have to enjoy the way your guitar looks, and it feels against your body. Trust me - that all makes a difference. Learn more about how to shop for your perfect guitar!

Ok - you've got your instrument. What next? How to get a great guitar tone? That passes through a series of things - and we'll explore each one next. Let's go!

Guitar Tone: Your Strings Matter!

The truth is that the perfect guitar tone starts with your strings! Yes, that's right - the strings you choose will modify the tone you get. I always thought that fat, thicker strings would mean a big tone - but that doesn't seem to be true! I've lately been playing an SG guitar, and that made me realize the science of thicker strings = fatter sound was wrong.

💭 My SG has 8-gauge strings - and that's crazily thin. Still, it sounds massive. :) Apparently, Angus Young uses ultralight strings - the same for Billy Gibbons (ZZ Top) and many other great guitar players.

So, don't assume that thicker strings will sound more massive than thinner strings. They might in some circumstances... but not in my real-world experience... try it and see for yourself. Always trust your own ears over other people's words!

The Best String Gauge for You

10-gauge strings are usually my go-to, but you should experiment and see what works best for you. When I get a new guitar, I have to work out and experiment with different stuff before deciding. And that's part of the process of getting the perfect guitar tone!

The string's brand probably makes some difference in your tone, but experiment and try different ones too. D'Addario is my go-to, but different strings will work differently in different guitars. Try and see it yourself. :)

🎸Playing an acoustic guitar? That's not the focus of this lesson, but I should mention that each of my acoustic guitars has a different string type on it! Whether it's a phosphor, bronze, or 80/20 string, you'll have to experiment and see what's going to work best with that particular guitar.

Sometimes, using an 8-gauge string or a 9-gauge string is too easy, and I won't be able to play vibratos or specific techniques the way I'd like to. So, also keep in mind what you'll be playing and which strings will help you get the sound you're searching for. So - try and listen. Luckily, you already know how to restring your guitar!

The Best Guitar Pickups

A pickup is this little thing on your guitar that picks up the sound from the strings' vibration. There are different pickups, and they'll sound different on each instrument. So, for this lesson, we'll take my main electric guitar, a customized Gray Guitar, and we'll explore its pickups - but consider this information relating it to your instrument!

This guitar has a Humbucker - a splittable humbucker that sounds like a single-coil pickup. It also has a classic pickup, very common in strat guitars. So, the humbucker is essentially two single coils stuck together. You can get pretty noisy when you have that, especially with an amp - I'm using a Kemper Profile today!

💡In a nutshell, you'll find that a single coil has a lot of noise attached to it, and a humbucker doesn't! They sound very different too, and having a guitar with both is quite common now, particularly more contemporary guitars.

This setup ends up very versatile, but your goal is to understand the pickups and doing. That's how you'll be able to get the perfect guitar tone!

🎸 Radio Shop is a great company from Wales with awesome pickups. They're not a budget pickup, but it's one of those upgrades that can be game-changing. ;)

So, it might be worth doing some research on that, but that's the different types of pickups generally. Also, be aware that the pickup position changes the final tone - check out the video tutorial to listen to it and understand pickup positions!

What About That Volume Knob?

The volume button in your guitar will also change the tone you're getting. You should tweak it until you find the perfect spot: it's the one that clears your sound (or that gives you all the distortion if you really want that!)

The amount of volume you send to the amplifier affects everything, so explore that little button to see what will work best in a specific situation. Be aware that the sound you send to the amplifier has a big impact on the final result of your tone - so get things right with your instrument first!

And The Tone Knob?

The tone knob on your guitar will define how much treble you get. That will make you sound fat or scratchy. The default here is to have it all up, but experiment with dropping back and boosting tops on your guitar amp!

💡One of the tricks with tone control is to back the tone off to 6 or 7. Then, you'll turn the treble up on the amp. You'll end up with the same sound, but then you can boost your treble by turning the tone up.

Check out the video lesson to learn more tricks - we'll also get a good look at my Gibson SG. That's a lot to consider, eh? :) But again - the word here is experiments.

It's a good idea to go to your local music store to try out a bunch of different guitars, especially if you're in the market for buying a new one. Let's face it - aren't we all, all the time?

Ready for more? Let's transcribe your first song!

lessons.text:
Learn to work out songs on your own.

That's what you're aiming for as a guitar player, right? :)

And I agree - transcribing is a pretty big deal! It's probably the big goal of most guitarists, even those who want to play as a hobby! And I have to tell you: transcribing is not easy, but it's super possible, even for beginners.

So, come with me, and learn how to transcribe songs for the guitar! We'll take it slowly, and I'll make it as effortless as possible for you! We'll learn how to work out songs on the guitar in 5 easy steps and explore how to incorporate transcribing into your practice routine.

🚨 Following Grade 3 of my Beginner Guitar Course? We'll get fancier about Transcribing in each module! By the end of the course, you'll be confident transcribing power chords, open chords, and easy guitar riffs too. :)

Using backing tracks and made-out examples is effective to some level. Still, to learn how to sort out songs on your own, there's nothing as working with real examples - and that's what we'll do here! By the end of this lesson, we'll check out a special curation of songs I'd recommend you explore.

🎸 Transcribing as a pro takes time! You might find it very hard initially, but stick with it, and you'll get all the benefits from it. Always picture the big goal: transcribing helps you develop your ears! Long term, you'll be able to have a sound in your musical imagination - or listen to a song on the radio - and easily be able to reproduce that music on your guitar. How awesome is that?

Now let's get stuck in and learn how to transcribe songs on the guitar!

4 Easy Steps to Working Songs Out

No matter which song you're trying to work out or which guitar level you are, I'd recommend following these easy steps when transcribing a song:

Step #1: Listening

You will never sort out a song on your own if you don't have it in your musical mind. The best way of absorbing a song into your mind is by listening closely to it and soaking in it. Generally, listen to a song 5 times before working it out.

As you get better, you might need fewer listening sessions. Still, to start with, you'll find that some mindful listening will help you out! Just be sure not to get distracted by other things when learning a song you're planning to transcribe.

You should look for things you already know when listening to the song. Is there a familiar sound? Is it possible that you know one of those chords? Can you identify changes in the chord progression - maybe from the verse to the chorus?

Step #2: Jam With It!

The best starting point is to have a go at working out the song in real-time. :) But don't expect too much from your first try! You might stumble upon the key center or a few of the chords, but don't get discouraged if you don't. It takes time and effort to learn how to transcribe!

🎸 Understanding some Music Theory basics will help you out! If you know what chords in keys mean, for example, you might be able to associate chords with certain progressions. Check out my Practical Music Theory course and get started with it now!

Here's the deal: grab your guitar and jam to the song you're trying to work out.

Step #3: Pause!

That's an easy trick:

⏸ The last thing you hear stays in your ear! ⏸ The last thing you hear stays in your ear! ⏸ The last thing you hear stays in your ear!

So, get used to pressing the pause button several times when transcribing a new song. You'll listen to just the first chord, pause the music and try to find the sound on your guitar. Play that song bit again and see. Sometimes, you'll listen multiple times to the same bit.

💡 A player that always starts from the same place (and not where it just stopped) is very helpful. I use Transcribe! - it's awesome software, and you can get a 30-day trial here.

Learning to pause the song at the right moment when transcribing is a skill. :)

Step #4: Scribe

Transcribing a song means you'll write it down. But, long term, it'll be much better not to write anything down! As you get more confident with transcribing, you might find that you don't want or need to write down as much. Still, as a starting point, I'd recommend writing down the chords as you figure them out. That gives you more brainpower to dedicate to listening!

Don't worry too much about beats, bars, or strumming patterns yet - go for the chords. :)

🚨 One common beginner mistake is trying to get in too much too soon when learning to transcribe. If you can work out most of a song but a few notes are missing, just gloss over it!! Leave the embellishments and more complicated stuff for later when your ears are fine-tuned! I'm pretty sure most of what I learned in the first few years of transcribing wasn't that accurate - but the process will still strengthen your ears!

How to Practice Transcribing?

Transcribing is different from the other skills we're learning in this course. We'll have it on our set practice routines, but my general advice is to practice transcribing in some big chunks of time! So, you might want to do it once a week for a full hour, for example, instead of small chunks every day.

Now let's look at some easy songs for beginners learning to transcribe!

6 Easy Songs to Transcribe - Power Chords

We'll start as simply as possible, so all songs here use Power Chords. As we advance in this course, we'll get into more complex songs using Power Chords and then dig into open chords and guitar riffs!

You'll find a few hints with each song. But try hard on your own before getting that extra help - it might seem hard, but it pays off. If you already know how to play one of these songs, pass to the next song. Here's the list:

Song #1 - Molly's Lips by Nirvana

This song is very easy. Just go for it - you'll do it on your own!

No? Click here to reveal two tips!

There are just 2 chords, one with Root 6 and one with Root 5. Same fret! The first chord is a G5

Song #2 - Blitzkrieg Bop by Ramones

I still remember working this out when I was about 13 years old! :)

Here are your tips!

There are nearly just 3 chords! The end of the chorus hits a B5 chord but only for a bar each time. The rest is just 3 chords!

Song #3 - All The Small Things by Blink 182

Ignore the first couple of chords for the intro - they're tricky! For this song, you'll start transcribing from the verse.

Two tips for you!

The chords are F, G, and C - in what order? The first chord is a C!

Song #4 - Fly Away by Lenny Kravitz

You have the same riff throughout the song - the Power Chords stay the same! The guitar drops in and out, but it's pretty easy!

Do you still need some help? Here!

The chords are G5, D5, C5, B5, and A5 - but in what order? This song starts on an A5 chord.

Song #5 - Polly by Nirvana

Oh - we've got something new here! This song has two chord progressions, one for the verse and one for the chorus.

I know - your tips!

The chords are D5, C5, G5, Bb5, and Open E5. The first chord for the verse is Open E5. The chorus starts with D5.

Song #6 - Go With The Flow by Queens of the Stone Age

This is a fun one! Give it a go - there are only 4 chords.

Your tips? Yep - here they are. But do you still need them? Are you sure?

Two of the chords are open E5 and Open A5 Power Chords. The other two chords are D5 and C5.

Try to make this happen, and transcribe your first songs today. That will improve your skillset, and you'll ultimately become a better, more autonomous musician.

🤔 Have questions? Log in to your JustinGuitar account and drop a comment in the Discussion section. We'll get you some extra help!

What Next?

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you've got a lot on your plate right now. We're about to finish Module 15, which opens Grade 3 - our last beginner stage. I'm proud of you - it's been a long journey, and I'm sure you're having fun!

We have a bright future ahead of us, as we'll keep working hard to develop our musicianship and build a closer relationship with our guitar.

But before we get into more new stuff, it's time to consolidate everything we've learned in these previous lessons. How? Practicing!

👉 Get your Suggested Practice Routine here - and off you go. :)

lessons.text:
Yeah - we've made it!

It's time for your first Practice Routine in Grade 3.

Now, our goal is to consolidate everything we learned in Module 15! But, differently from what happened in Grades 1 & 2, you should now adapt your practice routines to fit your guitar goals. As we get ready to reach our Intermediate stages, you should see Grade 3 as a bridge that will take you further in your guitar journey.

🚨 Did you miss out on Grades 1 & 2 of my Beginner Guitar Course? Not to worry - following this practice routine will be very easy and intuitive anyways! And - just to let you know, Grade 3 wraps up our beginner stages. Check out this JustinGuitar Course Map to learn more about our learning pathway!

We all have different needs and battles at this point in our guitar journey! Our background also changes our struggles and strengths. As we learned, there are 6 essential guitar areas I'd suggest you practice on guitar, and that's how this suggested routine works! But, as well, remember that we've learned you should now adapt your routine to your reality and guitar goals.

So, the point of this practice routine suggestion is to give you some general guidelines that include everything we worked on in Module 15. Before working on it, or setting something else, ask yourself:

How much guitar practice can I commit to?

What are my guitar goals?

How do I want to pursue the guitar?

What guitar schedule fits my lifestyle?

Great! Now let's check out my suggestion to organize your guitar practice effectively.

6 Areas to an Effective Guitar Practice Routine

You already know I'd recommend practicing these guitar areas. So, that's how this schedule works as well. If you need a refresher, remember that we've got a video lesson for each one of these topics. And before you ask me…

How Long Should You Practice For?

Ideally, you'll get between 30 and 60 minutes of guitar practice a day. As we'll be exploring more next module, breaking your practice into small 5 minute chunks will help keep you focussed, though some areas will be better done once a week.

💡 Practice makes permanent. Practice perfectly and regularly!

And super important - keep your guitar time equally as fun! Make sure you leave some time to muck around on the guitar! Don't lose the fun part. If you need, make half of your practice routine a set practice and half an hour of fun.

Module 15 Practice

Here's a summary of my practice schedule recommendation for Module 15:

5' Technique - Finger Gym 5' Technique- Link Chords Using Scales 5' Knowledge - D Shape Explorer 5' Knowledge - What You Need 5' Repertoire - A Capo for Two 5' Repertoire - What You Need 5' Time - Feel Good Strumming 5' Time - Play Along With Great Songs 10' Ear Training - Transcribing 10' Improvisation - Revision + Jam Tracks

Let's talk a bit more about each one of them!

Section #1 - Technique - 2 x 5-minutes

Finger Gym + Link Chords Using Scales

Practice the Finger Gym exercise for the first slot of your technique section. Think of it as going to the gym, but for guitar playing. Consistency and regularity are key things here!

For the second technique slot, begin to explore linking chords using bass notes on the 3 and 4. Start by using some of the eight common patterns then branch out and start creating your own.

Section #2 - Knowledge - 2 x 5-minutes

D Shape Explorer + Music Theory

Your first slot goes to exploring the D Shape. Try practical exercises, but also experiment with these grips. Lift different fingers and see what sounds best to you! As you venture into your chord manipulation, write down what you dig. It might be helpful later on. :)

For the second part of this Knowledge section, you could focus on Music Theory - that really takes you further! If music theory is not for you - focus on a different skill like transcribing, ear training, or having fun with your guitar!

Some advice? Be open-minded about Theory. Some people ignore it (even experienced guitar players), but Theory unleashes your guitar fretboard. ;)

Section #3 - Repertoire - 2 x 5-minutes

Songs You Love + Duets

Spend this section partially playing the songs you love. You should really have sorted out your repertoire from earlier grades, but if you have not - now's the time! Which songs have you learned in the beginner courses that you really love? Keep the songs you dig and want to have in your bag at all times. Take some time and have a real think about this!

🎶 Need some extra inspiration? I've got over hundreds of free song tutorials for you! Check them out. ;)

Now, it's time to duet! Try to find yourself a guitar friend so you can jam together. You already learned about this in A Capo For Two, so you know the drill: jamming and dueting with another musician can help accelerate your learning.

If you don't have a jam buddy, record yourself playing one part and then play it again using a capo. Or play along with me in the video lesson!

🎸 Looking for a jam buddy & other like-minded guitar players? Join the JustinGuitar Community. Make friends and find somebody to jam with, even if it's virtual! It's great fun. :)

Section #4 - Time - 2 x 5-minutes

Feel Good Strumming & Song Practice

Great guitar players play with a confident, steady, and feel-good time feel. So, your focus here is making your timing feel comfortable and relaxed - but still solid!

Playing along with songs is great; you can even mute your strings, so you focus on the groove. This is excellent practice, and it'll make you feel more comfortable with your guitar playing.

I'd recommend jamming with groovy records! You don't even need to play the chords - focus on getting a natural groove going. This will shape you as a musician.

🎶 Need song inspirations? Check out my Spotify playlist! I'm constantly adding in new stuff and great songs to play along with.

Section #5 - Ear Training - 2 x 5-minutes

Transcribing

If you really want to train your ears and learn how to work out songs on your own, you'd need to spend an hour a week working on that. Just follow the 4 Steps to Transcribe Songs and all the tricks we learned in that lesson, and you've got this. Good luck!

Section #6 - Improvisation - 2 x 5-minutes

Revision + JamTracks

We covered this in the beginner course - and now I want you to take it further! Have a go at revising some of your Pentatonic Lead or Major Scale stuff. Your choice here depends on what improvisation you got going, especially if you enjoy it. Make sure to spend some time improvising over music, my videos, original recordings, and my JamTracks.

When to Move On?

Most students will need to practice this Module 15 routine for at least two to four weeks. No rush here - take the time you need. Make sure you fully digest the material before moving on to the next course.

Learn to find your way through your practice routine! Figure out what works for you and keeps you motivated - that's super important. Fiddling around to sort out a routine that works best for you really pays off! Don't forget to keep track of your progress too! Whether using paper and pen, my Lessons & Songs App, or your Dashboard - keeping track of your progress is key to success.

💬 How are you getting on with Grade 3? Please leave your comments and feedback in the Community discussion area.

Set yourself up with a pre-made practice routine for Module 15. Under the video, click on the 'Practice' Tab. Save the routine, and access the items in your Dashboard. You've just got really busy, eh? See you in Module 16.

Welcome to Module 16!

The second installment of our Grade 3. :)

We've got lots of fun stuff coming up. Here's what you'll learn:

We'll continue our Effective Practice series! We'll learn to use the proven Pomodoro Technique to supercharge your guitar practice. It is a five-minute miracle!

We'll learn how to move easy chord shapes up your guitar neck. It's the super cool and practical application of the famous CAGED System.

Fingerstyle loves! We'll look at Rolling Chords, which means you play the notes of a chord one at a time to accentuate the highest note. This is very important when you're playing chord melodies!

We'll explore Greensleeves. It's a classic Folk song, great to practice your Chord Melody techniques.

Our Duet series will feature what I call Harmony and Melody Split. You'll learn how to work out a melody on your own for songs that you already know. It's easier than you might think!

We'll also talk about how to flex time when you're playing on your own. This is really fun stuff! :)

We'll learn all about basic amp settings! You already know how to make the most of your guitar settings - now it's time to explore your guitar amp.

Want to go even further? You should explore Theory as well. Understanding music is key to becoming a great guitar player!

👉 Now, let's start and learn how to supercharge your guitar time. :) Happy trails!

lessons.title: Supercharge Your Guitar Practice with Timeboxing!
lessons.summary: Learn how to use a countdown timer to increase your focus and optimize your time!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Why Timeboxing

00:58 5 Benefits of Timeboxing

08:57 Extra Tips for a Successful Practice Routine
lessons.text:
Supercharge Your Guitar Time!

You might have heard about timeboxing before. It's basically specifying the amount of time you'll spend doing each item on your practice routine. And yep - you should use a countdown timer to control that!

When I first heard about this technique, I thought it was a real joke. Timeboxing your practice using a timer didn't seem to make any sense - it just seemed too technical and too organized! Too rigid to be good for music, just silly, you know?

Well - how wrong I was. Timeboxing your practice will supercharge your guitar time in many different ways. Especially if you're that kind of person who gets easily bored, or does an exercise for a little bit and, you know, starts skipping around!

Timeboxing your practice will also be a powerful tool as you become a more advanced musician. You'll definitely come to a point where timeboxing and thinking exactly about your practice schedule will be extremely valuable.

💡Using a timer helps me practice more effectively and cover all the things I need! That keeps my focus and motivation pretty high. :)

So, I've got to tell you. Ultimately, this technique allows you to practice insanely better and develop your skills way faster. It's super powerful. But why exactly? I've got loads of reasons - let me outline the main ones.

4 Benefits of Practicing with a Timer

Timeboxing your guitar practice supercharges how much stuff you get done in your practice time! I've got a very limited amount of time to practice guitar (pretty busy running this website), so that's a hell of a benefit to me!

Using a countdown timer to practice the guitar and even do other stuff on my workdays helps you make more of your time, but the benefits don't stop there. Here are some more benefits of practicing with a countdown timer:

#1 - Improve Your Focus!

Learning the guitar involves a different range of skills! The biggest benefit of timeboxing your practice is your ability to focus on the skills you're practicing at a given moment.

💡 You should have a reason to add a certain thing to your practice schedule! Always make sure you know how, why, and for how long you're practicing something. If you're not sure about the areas you should be practicing, check this out.

Having clear objectives will help you make the most out of a practice item! For example, don't add scale practice to your practice routine without knowing why you were doing that. Is it to work on the synchronicity between your hands or improve your alternate picking skills? You could also be practicing scales to increase your fretting hand accuracy and much more!

You should pay attention to the whys when adding a new exercise to your practice routine, pay attention to the whys. That's the first step to making your five minutes, timeboxed practice count!

Then - you'll want to keep your attention right there. Don't allow yourself to be distracted by other parts of the practice or by random thoughts. Your goal is to be absolutely zoned in your practice.

💡 This is very much like Mindful Meditation, where you focus on your breath. You develop the ability to send thoughts away, which you want to do for your guitar practice!

I've often felt like guitar practice was a kind of therapy or meditation. And I suspect that if you have good focus developed during meditation, you'll easily transfer that skill set over to guitar practice. If you've not tried meditating before, it might be helpful in many other areas of your life. ;) Give it a try!

Focusing on the task in your hands is an incredibly powerful tool. If you can do just that. You'll be much more aware and present in what you're doing. :)

🚨 Know that, sometimes, you'll need not focus! Automating strumming or fingerstyle is a great example. You'll need to spend some time on getting the pattern right - and for that, you'll need loads of focus. But then, you should practice the pattern while trying to let your mind wander, doing things like watching TV or having a conversation.

Using a timer could work as a little wake-up call in cases like this. But I wouldn't recommend using timeboxing to practice a new strumming or fingerstyle pattern. Generally speaking, timeboxing is absolutely incredible for everything except the guitar skills you should practice without focus, over and over again, and for a longer period.

#2 - Keep Your Motivation High!

The second benefit from timeboxing your practice might be the key to sticking with the guitar in the first place! Using this technique helps you keep your motivation high - and there's science behind that! :) Ticking your Done box helps to release Dopamine.

💡 Dopamine's a little chemical. It gets released in your brain as a reward, so it makes you feel good. Every time you practice and tick the box, you get a small but useful Dopamine hit. That helps your brain learn that practice is good and maintain your motivation and desire to practice more. It really works!

Try doing little five-minute slots rather than doing one hour of random practice. Like that, you've got six times that you're going to tick that box and get the little Dopamine hit. :)

#3 - Use Your Time Successfully!

The third benefit is probably obvious by now. :) When you timebox your guitar practice, you use your time effectively. If you're time-poor like I am - we've got many things to do! So, if you've got a limited amount of time, making the most out of it is a big deal!

When you're time boxing, you really focus on that little sprint of effort. You're much less likely to delve into procrastination or spend your time just wondering about things that you shouldn't be wondering about. :)

#4 - Be Happier!

The fourth benefit of timeboxing your guitar practice is the effect that it might have in your personal life! Developing the ability to be more present can benefit relationships, sports practice, studying - whatever you're doing! It happened with me - and it might happen with you too. Give it a chance.

How to Get Started with Timeboxing

If you're using one of my beginner courses, you've probably been time boxing already. :) I specify how long you should be practicing and what for. My Practice Assistant and the interactive exercises in my app help you make them happen, but the technique is timeboxing! If you're new to the idea of timeboxing your practice, check my Holistic Practice Routine method. In that lesson, we explore my suggestion to approach all the available guitar study areas!

Once you understand what you should practice on guitar to be the guitarist you aim to be, it's time to divide that into blocks and use a countdown timer to keep track of your practice.

⏰ When I first started using timeboxing, I used a kitchen timer. It looked like a tomato, you know, Pomodoro technique. :) I'd turn it around for five minutes, let it go, and it would ring a little bell at the end. :)

Now I just use my phone's timer or even my Time Trainer Metronome app. It has an easy-to-use countdown timer, so we can do all our technical work for just the right amount of time. :) But make sure you got notifications turned off because you don't want to be distracted in the middle of your practice routine!

Now - you know the drill!

Timeboxing your practice is very easy and super simple too! Set it for short periods when you start working with a timer - 2 minutes is a great duration! You'll follow these simple steps:

Decide on what you're practicing first hand. Taking notes and organizing your schedule is a good idea - more about that later!

Start the timer. Using your phone? Notifications should be off!

Work on the one skill you've chosen to practice.

If any other thoughts enter your mind, push them out. Don't let them invade your practice time!

Every time you've got distracted, renew your focus on the task at hand and begin again if needed.

💨 Practicing with a countdown timer is a bit like a sprint! When you know where the finish line is, you feel better about giving it your all until you get there, and you know you can have a rest at the end. ;)

The major benefit of using a timer is that your mind knows that it only has to use this intense concentration for a finite period. Your focus becomes insane!

Struggling with Distractions?

You might find it difficult to practice like this when you first start, and that's okay. It's totally all right getting distracted in the early stages. It's actually a good thing! You're training yourself every time you get distracted, and you bring your attention back to what you should be doing. You're strengthening your attention! In the early stages, you might find you can never concentrate for five minutes, always getting distracted by stuff. But it's okay - you're not the only one. Just train yourself to don't let yourself get distracted.

Learning to focus takes practice! After a while, you'll find you can concentrate for quite a while without other thoughts getting in the way. Build it up slowly, be confident with a 2-minute focus and build it up over a month or two.

🚨 I rarely use this approach for exercises that require longer than 5 minutes! I know I can concentrate much longer, but five focused minutes is usually enough to practice one thing.

And since most times exercises involve Technique practice, let me talk about guitar fatigue.

6 Extra Tips to Achieve Success

Please, don't skip this section, especially if you're used to practicing until you hurt yourself or feel you practice a lot but never really improve! :)

#1 - Avoid Physical and Mental Fatigue.

Another interesting benefit of using a countdown timer when you practice is giving you an endpoint. I've mentioned it before but wanted to talk more about it. Practicing in short bursts also helps you avoid fatigue, which is important both physically and mentally.

When practicing something physically demanding, like learning barre chords, you must take breaks to avoid injury. Mental fatigue is a lot less likely if you take regular breaks, too, especially if you 'refresh' between blocks. At the very least, I stand up and walk around the room or have a quick drink. Something to release the focus before diving back in.

#2 - Use a Holistic Practice routine.

Another major benefit of using a timer is to stop yourself from practicing a particular thing too much. It's easy to practice what you enjoy but leave out things you find difficult - which is unlikely to bring great results. :( It's easy to get excited about particular skills while ignoring other areas of practice!

For example, people often work far too much on technical exercises and nowhere near enough on transcribing, repertoire, aural training, or music theory. Other people spend all their time playing songs and not doing any technical work - both of which are as bad as each other. The only forgivable one would be someone who transcribes all the time, that person would end up a good player, but that's a whole other story…

💡 If you missed my Holistic Practice lesson, check that out too and learn more about the 6 guitar areas you should be practicing!

Even if you don't use a set practice routine, a timer can still be super helpful for the other reasons mentioned in this lesson.

#3 - Stop Procrastination.

My tip number three is to stop procrastinating! :) And it's easier than you think: just do it! Gamifying your guitar practice might be fun and a great boost in your routine, so you might want to try tools like my songs app.

But a notebook and pencil will do - just remember that ticking the boxes off gives you extra satisfaction, so try and gamify your guitar practice. :) Even if you don't use time boxes, short bursts of focus will help avoid procrastination. You'll still focus and practice way better!

#4 - Don't Multitask!

Humans can't think of more than one thing at one time. Our brains can only really focus on one thing at once, so don't even attempt to have multiple things going on simultaneously unless that's the objective! So, when practicing, focus only on what you're doing. Don't try to multitask, and do not let your attention flit around.

🚨 If you're doing the fingerstyle practice while watching tv and you're deliberately trying to distract yourself, of course, that is okay! But other than stuff like that, don't try to multitask.

Working on 5-minute blocks will really help you with this, and not just for guitar! Many students told me that this kind of practice helped them in many areas over the years. ;)

#5 - No More Disruptions. :)

When you're doing your 5-minute practice block, don't answer the phone or allow yourself to be interrupted! Unless, of course, you're a fireman, or there's an emergency at home, of course. :)

🔕 Don't forget to turn off notifications on your phone, particularly if you're using it as your countdown timer.

Tell your family that, if they see you focused, you'd like them to come back in 5 minutes. Not many things can't wait for 5 minutes. Sometimes, you'll get to pause your practice session - but try and do your best not to!

#6 - Don't forget the playtime.

If you're following my guitar courses, you already know it: having fun with your instrument is as important as practicing and doing new lessons. That's why we learn how to play real songs in our very first module.

It's very important to schedule time to jam and play anything you want! Have fun with your guitar: play the riffs you like, muck about, connect with your instrument - exploratory, curious practice is as important as timeboxing! You'll learn much more doing this than you might first think!

I hope this helps you make the most of your... precious time. :) Next - a special lesson for fingerstyle lovers!

lessons.text:
Today we'll learn how to move your open chords all over the guitar neck!

It's a very cool trick that adds another level of creativity to your playing. You'll be able to take the same easy, open chords that you've learned as a beginner and move them all up the fretboard. It's a super creative and useful tool, with many get-out-of-jail-free cards to explore. :)

​​💡 Struggling with barre chords? You'll learn little tricks in this lesson that will help you get around that. And it just sounds very cool!

But even if you're completely hip with your barre chords, you'll still benefit a lot from moving easy chord shapes all over the guitar fretboard. Rather than just sticking with the same old chord shapes, you'll explore new sounds and probably surprise yourself with how cool and different some chords will sound when you move chord shapes around.

Exploring the 5 CAGED Shapes

In this lesson, we'll go through each of the 5 CAGED Shapes: C, A, G, E, and D - all chords you learned in our beginner guitar course.

🚨 We won't get into the theory behind the CAGED System or movable shapes, just their practical applications. If you want to dig deeper and understand music much better, check out my Music Theory Course for Guitarists. The first two grades are free!

As general information, keep in mind that movable guitar chords are chord shapes that you can place at any fret of your guitar using the same fingering. At the same time, you can only play open chord shapes in specific frets. Get the difference? :)

So, we'll explore the CAGED shapes and look at the minor chords! We'll learn the most common ones and the placements that are particularly useful for getting out of tricky chord situations.

💡 This lesson is part of Grade 3 of my Beginner Guitar Course! It will give you a lot of information about how to move the chord shapes we learned so far, but don't hesitate to try other chord shapes you might know too.

If you know chord shapes like Dominant 7th Chords or Minor 7 Chords, go ahead and explore them too! You can just move them around the neck and see what you can find because it's super fun. When it comes to guitar playing, you already know: if it sounds good, it's good!

Now let's get started and check out how to play easy chords up the neck. Bring your guitar. :)

Moving Easy Chords

Let's explore the chords and see what happens when moving them around. We'll explore each one a bit and see where they go!

The C Shape

You'll find the first useful grip when moving the C Chord that you know two frets up the guitar neck. You'll find a D chord. It sounds great, doesn't it? In theory, there's something else going on there - but don't worry about it. Just explore the sounds and know that you're playing a D root note there.

Be aware that, when moving the C Shape around the guitar neck, we're moving the lowest note of the chord with us. That doesn't happen all the time, though! Still, it's a really nice trick to know - it'll be particularly useful for when you've got a song with G, D, and C, for example. :)

💡 Get this cool trick with the C Chord Shape! You can always add your little finger down on the same fret as the third finger on the thinnest string. That sounds great, just on a regular C chord as well - you don't have to move it around to do it!

Trying things like that on the D chord you've just found can sound really nice! Sometimes you'll find there is a little bit too much going on. Sometimes, adding that little finger down is a great substitute for a D chord almost any time. Check out the video tutorial to explore this trick with me and when it sounds good or not!

Playing the same chord sequence on different sections of your guitar neck can take a song to the next level! Experimenting with how you can move shapes around the neck to make song sections sound differently from each other is just really cool. Especially if you're a songwriter, this trick will supercharge your creative process. Try and see it. :)

The A Shape

The next shape we'll explore is the A Chord, but this one works a bit differently from what we just learned. In this case, we're not playing the root note; the root note here is the open string, and it'll usually be a drone A root note! So, generally speaking, if you're moving the A chord around, you'll get a slightly different effect than when moving the C chord. :) But there's a couple of super nice little tricks that you can use with this one as well!

If you move your A chord up one fret on the neck, you'll find a weird but cool chord. It has a Spanish-y music vibe. That gives me a lot of musical ideas hope it does the same for you! Keep going up the neck to find some more good, interesting sounds. Use the video lesson to guide you.

💡 What else will you find? Use the video tutorial to find out, but don't forget to explore your fretboard on your own as well. That's how you really learn - by connecting and spending time exploring your instrument!

Now go ahead and try to find standard chords as well. Just mucking around your guitar will teach you so much, particularly if you want to be a creative musician. Rather than just playing other people's songs, you'll be able to embrace your musicianship and take your guitar journey so much further. Don't be afraid of exploring your guitar. Don't like a chord you've just found? Just skip it! Stick with the good surprises. :)

The G Shape

I've never found moving the G Chord around my guitar neck very useful. No matter where I move it, I just don't connect with the sounds I get - but maybe you'll. :) The best-case scenario for me is moving the G chord up to the 10th fret.

🎶 There's one tune by Gomez that contains this little riff, which is like a G7 chord that they moved up the neck. It's wrong, as wrong as it could be, but actually, it sounds great. :)

That was a good example of how powerful and creative moving chord shapes can be. Even if you end up on the wrong fret, you can still accidentally find something that sounds cool and then just follow that idea through. That's how we create great stuff!

The E Shape

Just like happened with our A Chord, you'll also get a drone root note when moving your E Chord around the neck. The trick with this particular chord shape is not always playing that lowest root note! Instead, you'll pretend your root note is something else. It can be pretty fun and a useful trick to have under your fingers. Check out the video lesson to explore it with me!

💡 Moving the E Shape up the neck and manipulating its bass note is also a very useful trick. For example, it can save you from playing a B Barre Chord, and it also sounds lovely on certain songs.

Again - explore and discover your fretboard. :)

The D Shape

This is probably my favorite CAGED shape to move around the neck. The D Chord can sound lovely, and it takes me to very creative places! Old Man by Neil Young is a great example of how moving this shape around sounds great. If you don't know that song yet - give it a shot!

💡 Explore the D Shape with me! :) If you haven't already, check out my D Shape Explore lesson.

Exploring the D chord up the neck is whole loads of fun. It sounds great - just grab your acoustic guitar and explore your instrument. You'll love it!

Moving Minors?

You can move Minor chords up the neck too! In fact, playing an Am shape on the 3rd fret is a common Bm escape. It won't work all the time, but when it does, it's a great-sounding chord substitute, so you skip that barre chord. :) But don't stop there! The Am chord has loads to give you - explore it and see it.

💡 Dm and Em are great Minor Chords to move up the neck as well! E x p l o r e. :)

Here's one more trick: the Em gets you out of the F#m or G#m pickle! Can you guess which fret?

What Now?

Rather than just exploring all shapes a little bit as an exercise to moving your hand around, go further! I'd recommend exploring one shape before moving on to the next one. You can even choose a favorite one and spend more time exploring it! You'll benefit a lot from listening and concentrating on the sounds you find! Exploring the instrument key to becoming an Intermediate Guitar Player. :)

💡 A great idea is to have little chord boxes of your favorite grips. Your own chord book is the best chord book you'll ever buy.

Now - if you're feeling overwhelmed about the number of things you've just learned, don't worry about it. All you have to do is some exploring on your own, so just grab your guitar and explore the shapes on your own. Make it fun - have fun! Happy trails. :)

Next - we'll learn a fingerstyle technique to upgrade your rhythm game! Coming soon.

lessons.summary: This acoustic guitar technique consists of playing a block of notes of a chord, but one at a time. It really brings out the melody of a song!

lessons.text:
Rolling chords is a very tasty technique to get under our fingers!

This lesson is not on how to play Greensleeves on the acoustic guitar - yet. Actually, it's about a technique we call Rolling Chords. Greensleeves is really a great song to practice that, but first things first: let's make sure we learn this technique the right way, so we stay away from bad habits and make the most out of our guitar time. :)

Rolling Chords To Accent The Melody

The Rolling Chords is an acoustic guitar technique that consists of playing a block of notes of a chord, but one at a time. It really brings out the melody of a song! Really think about the idea of playing blocks of notes: we'll roll through the notes from lowest to highest. Get it?!

💡 Rolling Chords is great for accenting the top note of a chord. You'll very commonly find this technique in chord melody arrangements. Here's a great example: Yesterday by The Beatles.

There are a few different approaches to learning finger style like this. This lesson will give you my best tricks and guide you to find out what works best for you - one of these approaches should. :)

Before You Start

Here are a few things to keep in mind before checking out the different approaches to play the Rolling Chord Techniques:

Make sure you start with all the fingers on the strings and then peel them off.

The Rolling Chord technique can be a bit tricky as you first start. But once you have it down, it shouldn't feel so clumsy. Stick with it, and you'll get there!

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, we'll be practicing fingerstyle a log in the next modules. You're about to learn a lot more, so make sure you take time to really explore what you're learning now. Combining your knowledge will get loads easier down the road. ;) Just trust the process.

Now let's take a look at the different options you've got to play Rolling Chords on the acoustic guitar!

Approach 1: Peel It Off

Place the chord shape you want to play - I'm using an A chord in the video lesson! For your strumming hand, think about peeling your hand away and fingers off, starting with the lowest note. Try to get that peeling feeling!

🚨 You’ll probably find you accent the thinnest string heavily too, which is ok. One of the things you want from a roll is to accent that note - but don’t let it get too out of control.

Once you have the feeling, you should aim to decrease the hand movement but retain its feeling in the fingers. This is likely to take some practice, but trust me - that's how most of my students learn faster. The process is literally just doing this over and over and over again!

Learning to play fingerstyle is like programming your mind and your ear into what it should sound like and feel like. Make sure your hand stays pretty consistent, and don't learn wrong patterns here.

Approach 2: Start Slow

Another approach is to play the notes slowly and then gradually speed it up until it becomes a ‘roll.’ Some people might find this easier, but be careful. You should make sure to keep the notes evenly spaced. You don't want it to sound lumpy.

💡 A Slow Roll can also be a useful technique to have in your bag! So, it’s worth working on different speeds.

Be careful not to let the back of your hand move much. If you need to do that, then maybe switch to Approach 1 and see how you go that way.

Approach 3: Split Notes and Fill

Sometimes a full roll can be a little over the top. Splitting the bass note and the top note (melody) are separated - the melody note is coming ever slightly after the bass note. Then if needed, you can fill in some more notes with the other fingers afterward.

🎥 Check the video tutorial for the close-ups on each of these approaches. Which's your favorite? Let me know in the Discussion section!

Don’t Overuse This!

Rolling Chords is a very useful technique when playing chord melody, but it can get tiring and lose its beauty when you put it on every chord. ;)

How to Practice

Try rolling and splitting many different chords and different strings within the chords. Get creative as you want, but remember that it’s always better to start simple and get it right before trying anything too fancy!

Time to practice what you've just learned. And yep, with Greensleves. :) Coming soon.

lessons.text:
Learn how to play a chord melody arrangement of the traditional folk song Greensleeves!

This tutorial is an easy introduction to playing chord melodies, meaning that you have a melody line and the chords played simultaneously. It's a particularly good skill to develop - it's loads of fun!

💡 If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, Greensleves has the perfect chord melody to practice the Finger Rolling technique we've just learned. If you've missed that lesson, check it out! You'll get a much better understanding of the fingerstyle technique behind this song.

Before we get stuck in and learn how to play Greensleeves on the acoustic guitar, I'd recommend printing out a copy of its tabs and making notes on things that you need to remember! You might want to explore different fingerings and that sort of thing! Just head over the Resources tab under this video, and off you go. :)

Greensleeves - Chords

We'll start off with an Am chord. You'll play just the third string, probably with your driving finger. Then, you'll play the middle four strings: thumb, one, two, and three.

💡 You'll probably use a roll there. If you don't know how to do a roll, just play the chords as a block. Check out my lesson on the Rolling Chords technique to learn more!

The following chords are all easy, open chord shapes - check out the video tutorial for the entire chord progression. But then, you'll encounter an F Chord! You've got a couple of options there:

Play the regular F Barre Chord - just do it! It's actually a great song to work on your full F Barre Chord.

Play an F Barre Chord Cheat. :) You'll use your thumb to play the bass note, but many of you will find that really difficult.

Check out the video lesson to explore both options with me and find out what works best for you.

Learning to Play Greensleeves

When learning songs like Greensleeves, which require a certain concentration level to manage both hands, building up a mental picture of the song is the way to go! As you first start learning, having the chords and tabs right in front of you will help you learn faster, but you must lose staring at the page as soon as you possibly can!

Greensleeves isn't that hard of a piece to play on the acoustic guitar. And trust me: longer-term, it's much easier to play it from your memory than from a page! Get each chunk of the tune done, and just move on to the next one when you feel confident with the chunk you've just learned.

I'm sure you know the melody of Greensleeves right away - everyone seems to recognize this popular folk melody! I'm sure being familiar with the melody is already going to help you a big deal! Listen to it as many times as you need to have it solid in your musical mind.

I really hope you enjoy learning this tune aside from the technical benefit of practicing your Rolling Chords technique. :)

Next, we'll learn how to play any melody on the guitar! Ready? Let's Do It!

lessons.text:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to learn the melody of any song and play it on your guitar!

This is awesome if you've got a jam buddy - one guitarist can play the chords to a song while the other plays the melody. :)

🎤 This Melody & Harmony Split Trick that we're about to learn is great if you don't have a singer. The guitar playing the melody will sound just like the voice of the song - it's very cool!

If you don't like singing or think you can't sing a song, this is a great approach to jamming and can open up a whole new world.

🚨 This lesson is part of my brand-new Beginner Grade 3! If you're learning to play with me, you should have all skills you need to learn how to duet like this. :) If you're new around here, I'd expect you to be hip playing open chords and basic rhythm. :)

You'll rarely find melodies written out in tabs. Still, you’ll often find them in traditional notation in “lyric and chord” songbooks. So, if the melody isn’t necessarily in beginner songbooks, how will you learn it? The answer is in this lesson, and it really improves your musicianship! :)

😅 No! You won't need to learn how to read traditional notation. It's far from that. This lesson is very practical!

Ready? Let's get stuck in!

How to Learn Melodies on Guitar

Learning to play melodies on your acoustic guitar is actually nowhere near as hard as you might expect! Follow the following 5 easy steps, and you'll know how to play any melody on guitar.

Step #1 - Listen Up!

You first need to listen to the song's melody and really pay attention to it - focus on where it goes up and down. You've got to listen carefully to the song's melody, not just like have the music on in the background!

Ideally, you want to really try and get the song's melody into your musical imagination, in your musical mind. You should be able to hear it without the music on. ;)

Try to get the song's melody in your musical imagination before starting. It can help if you pick a song you know well and sing to yourself in your musical mind.

Step #2 - Know the Chords First!

Before you start working out the melody to a particular song, I'd strongly recommend checking out the chords first of all! That's because you'll find most melody notes within the chords!

💡 This is a practical lesson! If you want to learn more about the theory behind all that, please - join my Theory course now! Understanding how music work is key to developing your musicianship - and I want to get you there. :)

Knowing the chords help because usually, the melody note will be a chord tone. And the notes joining the chord tones are likely to be scale tones in the song's key. Not always, but most commonly. :) It'd also be super helpful if you know the chords in the key - also covered in my Understanding Music course.

💡 If you've followed my free Beginner Guitar course, you learned about Chords in Keys in Grade 2. Need a refresher? Check this out!

When you know the chords in the key, it becomes easy to figure out what key you're in and the Major Scale, where you're likely to find the rest of the melody notes.

Step #3 - Open Or Closed

A common problem is not knowing if you should start in the open position (using open strings and up to fret 5) or a close position further up the neck.

I'd recommend that you start in the open position! It's just a bit easier, and it doesn't involve memorizing scale patterns. As you advance, you get more familiar with Major Scale Patterns, which allows you to find the melodies easier. This might be helpful later, but I'd recommend that you start in an open position at these early stages.

As you progress, you are likely to use both open and close positions, sometimes in the same arrangement! But starting in an Open Position is probably a good starting point if you’re new to this. :)

Step #4 - Starting Note

The first note of the melody is super important! Finding that note should make the rest a lot easier, but beginnings will need some guesswork here. :)

The starting note is probably going to be a chord tone. So, if you know that first chord, things will get easier!

💡 Don't worry- you'll find a list of easy songs to practice below! And I'll give you the starting note to help you get going.

Step #5 - Write it out

This last step is particularly useful for beginners! It’s always better to learn things by memory, but when you start out with this, you’ll probably find that it really helps to write the melody down as you figure it out.

💡 Don’t worry about notation or rhythm! Just TAB your melody out to help you work things out.

As you get more advanced, you might write things down to help you remember embellishments like slides or vibrato. It can be very useful to move the melody up an octave.

How to Choose Easy Songs

To start with, I'd suggest you try and work out easy melodies! Here are three things you should watch out for:

#1 - Range

The range of the song can make things harder! If it's really high, you won't be able to play it in an Open Position!

#2 - Large Jumps!

Songs with large jumps in the melody, meaning the distance between the melody notes is further than a couple of tones, are generally harder to work out!

#3 - Embellishments

Embellishments can make things harder, too, RnB stuff particularly. Still, even some older, simpler stuff, like Wish You Were Here, can be kinda tricky!

🚨 You might find it tricky to learn the melody for more modern pop music. The melody often becomes much more rhythmic and less melodic, making it harder to define the melody. Sometimes, the words are more spoken than sung!

While it’s totally possible to learn to play melodies with loads of embellishments, it’s probably not a great starting point.

BONUS! Go Further.

3 awesome things happen to you when practicing to play melodies on the guitar! Let's talk about them. :)

Bonus #1: Sing with Confidence!

People often are not confident singing when they don’t know the melody!! It's very hard to sing a melody well if you don’t know what it is!

Learning to play the melody on guitar will, for certain, help you sing it better and sort out any strange tuning moments. :)

Often when people sing out of tune, it’s because they’re uncertain of the melody at that particular point!

Bonus #2: Leading to Chord Melody

As an awesome bonus, once you know how to play the chords and the melody, you can start putting them together into chord melody arrangements! A great example is the Greensleeves arrangement we learned in a previous lesson. :)

Bonus #3: Learn Solos

As you get better at hearing and learning melodies, you’ll find that it’s also a lot easier to pick up lead guitar lines as well! Why not try some easy ones right away? :)

Because you’re used to working out the voice on the guitar, you’ll also be able to pick out other instrument melodies like harmonic or even piano lines!

8 Easy Songs to Try

Here are 8 songs to get you started playing a melody on the guitar!

1 - Let It Be by The Beatles. The first part is all based around a C Major, and you can play the entire melody in an Open Position.

2 - House Of The Rising Sun by The Animals. Start off on the second fret, fourth string to the third string. Then, play the open string and the first fret on the second string. We put it just with the chords now! Did you get the idea?

3 - Hallelujah by Leonard Cohen. This one is a very easy one! You'll probably be able to work out the entire melody on your own.

4 - Ain't No Sunshine by Bill Whitters. A great one to play the melody and combine with the chords. Super fun practice!

5 - Three Little Birds by Bob Marley. Great song, also good for beginners. We'll play a bit together in the video lesson, and you should be good to do the rest on your own. :)

6 - Breakfast at Tiffany's. This is one of my favorites. It works great in Pattern 3 of the Major Scale. :)

7 - Yellow by Coldplay. Lovely melody - try to sort it out!

8 - Wish You Were Here by Pink Floyd. This classic might be a bit harder, as it gets loads of embellishments. Still, if you're feeling confident, give it a go! It sounds great! :)

Advanced Shizzle!

Here are a few things to pay attention to once you feel comfortable with a melody and play it confidently:

Listen out for places where a slide up or down to a note will sound cool. You can either take it from the actual melody or try things out for yourself.

Pay attention to how long notes are held for. Try to replicate the actual melody as an exercise, but remember you can totally make it your own and play it however you like.

If you can use vibrato, think about where this will sound good. Hint! It’s not going to be every note. Usually just the notes you end on but make sure it’s appropriate. Commonly vocal vibrato starts small and gradually gets wider. Rock Guitar vibrato goes crazy right away!

For a second verse, it can sound really cool for a second verse to play the melody up an octave. That gives movement to the arrangement but means you’ll have to learn it in two places.

As you get better at this, you might find that you can ‘hear your way around’ playing a melody without working it out. How cool is that? If you get to that place, congratulations - that’s a great jewel in your musicianship crown!

💡 Following Grade 3? You'll get a personalized practice schedule by the end of this module. If you're not following the program but struggle with practice routines and consistency, check this out.

Now, it's time to grab your guitar and join me in the video lesson to learn more.

Next - The falling leaf… Coming soon!

lessons.title: Flexing Time: The Falling Leaf
lessons.summary: Let's talk about flexing time to manipulate dynamics and add movement to your guitar playing!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 When to flex time

00:50 The Story :)

03:47 The Lesson!
lessons.text:
Play like a falling leaf…

Today, we'll talk about something very important. I call it Flexing Time!

It means we'll manipulate dynamics and speed to add movement to your guitar playing. It adds contrast and a kind of an emotional connection with the things that you play.

Now, this is primarily something for when you're playing on your own. It works great when playing chord melodies, or maybe just you and a singer too. But it doesn't work so well in a band scenario because everyone would have to be flexing the time at the same moment.

💡 This can happen with a band is really super tight! Rolling Stones & Led Zeppelin are great examples of bands who used to manipulate time organically, as a whole group.

But that's a lot harder to do and requires loads of listening. The band will really need to be in sync!

The Story :)

I have a bit of a story for you. I learned it from a particular teacher back in the day! If you've seen the video in this lesson, you might notice I'm holding a classical guitar. It's because the first time I encountered this idea, I'd been studying classical guitar at the Tasmanian Conservatory of Music.

I was probably in my third year, and there was some problem with the teachers. I think a new teacher took over as the director of the Conservatorium. He changed the entire board, and he got his wife a gig teaching guitar!

The head of the strings department, Christian Vidovich, an incredible cellist, reassured me that this lady who was about to take over was really, really good. He told me I'd learn a lot from her!

The first lesson arrived, and I was a little bit apprehensive. The teacher sat down and said: "you haven't done any Bach Lute Suite. You should have a go at doing this." Then she plopped down this Bach Lute Suite in E minor, which was really difficult.

She said I should learn it before coming back the following week. So, I tried to get it under my fingers, which was very challenging! In fact, this was like 25 years ago, and it's still really difficult to play!

😅 I'm struggling with it a bit! But hopefully, I can play just the very first bit well enough to demonstrate what I'm talking about. Let me have a go at playing it for you. Check out the video lesson to see how that goes! :)

When I played it back for my teacher Amanda Dahan after having that one week to practice, she just looked at me and said: "Yeah, well. You've got the notes mostly right." I was a bit disappointed. What did she mean? I've got the notes right, so what else was left to do?

At that point, I didn't even know I trusted her as my teacher. I wasn't sure how that would work, but then she picked up her guitar. She played that same thing, and it was beautiful - so much better than what I'd done! Ok, so there was something really missing in my playing! What was it?

She explained that I needed to think about the dynamics and the speed. Amanda told me that I needed to put some feeling into my playing. Not just trying to play mechanically what's written on a page!

💡 Today, I think I understand this with classical guitar. It's your interpretation of the song that really matters!

You have to really learn to find your feeling and put it into the music. Otherwise, you won't have the chance to express yourself within the music. And I think now is the time to start dabbling with classical music if you haven't!

As we wrap up our beginner lessons, it becomes essential to start exploring your musicianship. That's how you'll become a great guitarist!

The Lesson!

Ok - so, I asked my teacher exactly what she was doing there! She mentioned the falling leaf: "think about when the leaf falls. There's this little moment where the leaf stops before it kind of accelerates! So, it's really quiet, and then it goes down and gets louder and faster. Then, it goes back up and soft, and it goes down, it gets louder, it gets softer."

Wow, eh? :) Thing is - when you apply that to music, it suddenly gives it this real dynamic sense. Particularly going faster and louder, and then slower and softer! It really is a powerful thing.

This falling leaf metaphor is really beautiful for thinking about expression in music. It works great for classical guitar, but not only!

💙 I really want to give a shout-out to Amanda Dahan! She's the teacher who taught me this idea and lots of other stuff. She turned out to be a really great teacher, and I learned an awful lot from her!

Music = Expression!

Part of the game of playing guitar, and probably any other instrument, is to manipulate the way you express that to allow yourself to get through any particularly tricky passages.

💡 Most Baroque music is really difficult to play, but you can experiment with this trick with other styles as well. In this video lesson, I demonstrated it to you using my arrangement for Yesterday by The Beatles. Can you spot how it sounds different?

Using this dynamic movement doesn't have to be super obvious or extreme! You don't want to go from very quiet to very loud, or you can end up sounding a bit awkward.

The point here is to find ways of expressing yourself through music. When you can get in touch with that sort of thing, your musical game will step up hugely!

Following Grade 3? Next, we'll learn all about your guitar amp!
