lessons.text:
Understand your amp and the best Settings for the perfect guitar tone!

New to guitar and amplifiers? You might be wondering about the best guitar amp for beginners or even how to adjust your amp to get the best sound possible. So many Settings are available!

I'm glad you're here - this lesson will answer the most common questions about basic amp settings and (great!) guitar tone.

💡 Understanding your guitar amplifier is your second step into getting the perfect guitar tone! The first one is to understand how to make the most out of the sounds available in your instrument. :) Great guitar tone starts here.

Ok - so, if you know how to control the knobs and pickups on your guitar and send a good sound to your amplifier, it's time to explore it. But again: first things first. The amplifier you have in front of you makes a huge difference!

Different Amps, Different Sounds.

Different amplifiers can sound very, very different! So, a Marshall amplifier sounds very different from a Fender amplifier, which sounds very different from a Vox.

When you're a beginner guitarist, you're unlikely to know what those differences are. Still, later, you might be able to recognize a sound on a record and know the best amp type to get that sound!

My suggestion for beginners is to get a device with lots of different guitar amp sounds within it. Boss Katana is a really good budget if you're just starting out!

Some new companies now make amp simulators for phones and computers. You'll need some sort of audio interface to plug, but something like that will give you a range of different sounds to explore. As a beginner, this really is a great idea!

Justin, what's your favorite amp?

I get this question every single day! I'm quite specific about what works for me - and I'd recommend you explore what works for you! But my favorite of all time is the Tone King Imperial in terms of amplifiers.

For me, the Tone King Imperial amp has a kind of Fender sound, but it just seems to refine it in a way that I really really like!

However, my day-to-day guitar playing is nearly always through a Kemper Profiler. I've been using it for a few years now. It looks like a toaster, but it can sound like many different guitar amplifiers, and that's a big deal to me. :)

💡 I mostly use profiles by Michael Britt. For sure, it's not a budget option, but it's unlikely you'll need anything else!

Check out the video lesson to explore some different profiles with me. It's super fun to understand how a little thing can change your entire tone! Also, it should be a part of your journey as a guitar player to learn to recognize and emulate a tone.

All Amps Have The Same Controls.

No matter which amp you choose to use, all got the same knobs. Every gear is different, so your first step is to understand how each control affects your instrument and interacts with each other.

Gain

Gain is a really big deal - it defines how much distortion we've got! Because every amp is different, you need to experiment and sort out your gear and how much gain you get from different things.

Bass

Bass is important too! Interestingly, when recording, you very often lose a lot of the bass on the guitar sound. That's why the bass is about your listening experience as much as anything!

If you're working with a digital audio workstation, a really useful experiment would be to record your guitar without touching anything. Then, muck around software to get a feeling for what it sounds like when you boost or cut down your bass.

Middle

If you want to make your guitar sound louder in a band, you often need to boost the middle knob - not the volume knob!

If you do that, the bass frequencies of your guitar upset the bass player. However, if you boost just the middle range of your guitar, you should be fine.

💡 Mids are really important in Heavy Metal, especially in the 90s. They did a thing called a Scooped Mid, where they turn the bass up, turn the treble up, and then turn the middle down.

That kind of sound was a real popular one. Do you like it? Let me know in the Discussion sections. :)

Treble

Treble is an easier one to get a grasp of what it's doing! It sounds like somebody's closed the door and is practicing guitar in another room. You open the door, and that it sounds like that - you know what I mean?

It's like you've got socks over your ears, and a bite of the sound has disappeared.

Presence

Presence is higher than treble. No amps will have a Presence knob, but if you've got one - remember you have to try! Mock around with the gear you have, and think about the sound you're getting. What's going on?

Reverb

I'm definitely a reverberaholic. For most of my life, I've always loved the sound of reverb, and I rarely buy amps that don't have reverb!

😅 That's not quite true - haha. Actually, loads of the amps I've got behind me don't have reverb. But I'd always prefer to play where I can hear reverb.

I'd definitely be adding it on later in the studio when playing with an amp without reverb. Often, producers will want you to play without reverb to add it later. That might make sense at a recording studio, where you've probably got access to better quality reverbs than what you might have built into your amplifier!

Experiment!

If you want to be a great guitar player and make the most out of your own gear, you've got to take your guitar and your amplifier and experiment! Spend some time doing nothing but mucking around with the controls on your amp and on your guitar too.

You'll fine-tune the detail on stuff like that as you become a more experienced guitarist. For now, just try to experiment with different types of amplifiers.

Hopefully, your ear will pick up the sounds that you like, and you can further refine the sound that you want to become your sound further down the line!

Following Grade 3? New lessons coming very soon!

Congratulations on completing one more module! :)

Now it's time to practice everything we learned so far and ensure you've got it all down. In this lesson, you'll get a suggested practice schedule, but remember you can - and should! - swap any items for things that are more important to you right now.

💡 Not sure what exactly you should be practicing on guitar? This guide will help you understand your needs way better.

Module 16 Practice

Here's a summary of the following practice section suggestions:

5' Technique - Finger Gym 5' Technique - Rolling Chords 5' Knowledge - Moving Easy Chord Shapes 5' Knowledge - Music theory 5' Repertoire - Chord Melody 5' Repertoire - Duet Work 5' Time - Flexing Time Musically! 5' Time - Play along with great songs 10' Transcribing - Transcribing Melodies For Duets 10' Improvising - Optional!

Section #1 - Technique - 2 x 5-minutes

Finger Gym + Rolling Chords

The first slot should probably be the Finger Gym again unless you're totally cool with your fretting hand. Of course, you'll be training your fretting hand when practicing skills like playing chord melodies, for example. But Technique time is important too, so make sure you dedicate enough time to it. :)

In this slot, explore Rolling Chords. A good idea could be to use your second Technique slot to put your skills to practical use! It might be that you actually write your own composition! Why not try doing something creative with your Technique practice?

Section #2 - Knowledge - 2 x 5-minutes

Play Easy Chords Up The Neck + Theory

The first section could be moving Easy Chord Shapes Up The Neck. We're talking about just literally taking your chords around and manipulating them where you find a good spot!

The second slot could be some Theory. Understanding Music is key to mastering your guitar! What do you need to learn to play the songs you love?

Section #3 - Repertoire - 2 x 5-minutes

Chord Melody + Duet Work

You could work on your own solo guitar arrangements! Explore Greensleeves or even Yesterday - but it doesn't have to be one of my song lessons!

The second part could be duet work. You could be playing a melody, preferably with someone else. That helps you learn a lot faster, so try to find a jam buddy if you can.

Section #4 - Time - 2 x 5-minutes

Flexing Time + Songs You Love

First, explore the Falling Leaf idea. See if you can find things that you play on your own where learning to flex the time a little bit will be valuable!

Trying to put your own expression in, feeling where it's going to speed up and where it's going to slow down. Explore where the song gets louder and softer, that kind of thing. :) Thinking about the dynamics and the performance aspect of things you're going to play is very important.

The second slot would be playing along with songs that you love. This is a really big deal - you can even try and pretend that you're in the band!

Section #5 - Ear Training - 10 minutes

Transcribing

This could also be once a week for an hour! For this module, I'd recommend transcribing melodies that you would use in the duets. By learning to play melodies, you're also transcribing!

If you can figure out how to play the melodies of some songs that you've learned already, remember the thing about the chord tones, and off you go. :)

Section #6 - Improvisation - 10-minutes

Blues Improv

This one is optional. If you're working on improvising, playing the Blues is great stuff! You might want to revisit this lesson.

When to move on?

You should practice this routine for at least two weeks before cracking into Module 17. Don't forget: practice makes permanent!

Under the video, click on the 'Practice' Tab and save the pre-made routine specially curated for Module 16. Access and edit the practice items in your Dashboard. Ready for Module 17? See you soon.

modules.intro:
Welcome to Module 17!

Lots of super fun stuff is coming up for you, advancing beginners.

Here's what's on the menu:

Goals & Destinations - We'll start by looking at Goals and Destinations because if you don't know where you want to go, you're very unlikely to get there! That's a big deal and will help you further your guitar journey!

C Shape Chord - We'll also check out the C Shape Chord and all the different variations you can get by lifting your fingers off and adding fingers to your C Shapes.

How to Pick Individual Strings While Strumming - Learn how to target individual strings while strumming! It's a super-effective technique you'll use for the rest of your guitar journey.

Thumb & Finger Strum - We'll also learn this cool thumb and finger strum technique! You'll dig it even if you mostly like using a pick. ;)

Introduction to Triads - You'll learn to use triads as a second guitar part for duets! This lesson is a great introduction to triads, and I'd recommend it to everyone who can't find triads on their fretboard.

Your Ultimate Guide to Reverb - Learn how to make the most out of Reverb and understand the difference between Spring, Plate, Pre-Delay, Hall, Shimmer... all types of reverbs! Learn when and how to use each and much more - including the best reverb pedals!

Meet The Musician In You - Learn how to channel your emotions through guitar playing and become a complete musician.

Very Easy Riffs to Transcribe - Stop learning riffs from tabs and start using your ears instead! Start with easy riffs, and off you go!

So, loads of big deals happening in this Module, eh? Let's get stuck in and learn it all! Happy trails. :)

👉 Ready? Start by setting your Goals & Destinations. Let's go!

lessons.text:
Are Your Guitar Goals SMART?

Deciding where you'd like to go on your guitar journey is really important!

Over the years, I have heard from hundreds of students that have lost motivation because they didn’t feel they were getting anywhere. Do you feel like that too? Well, this lesson is all you need then! :)

We'll learn how to set goals that make sense to your guitar journey. We'll break your long-term guitar dreams into actionable, motivating goals so that you achieve your guitar success faster.

💡 This lesson is part of my Beginner Guitar Course - Grade 3! Check the free program here.

But before we get stuck in and learn all about smart guitar goals to optimize your practice time, let me talk a little bit about how we learn to play guitar at JustinGuitar.

Beginner Course - Intermediate Method

I think there are many basic skills that all beginners should learn. And that's how I set up my Beginner Guitar lessons. After that, when reaching the Intermediate stages, the students should decide where and how they want to carry on. That's how my Intermediate Guitar Method works.

In Grade 3, the end of the beginner level, you'll notice that I start to encourage you to adapt your practice routine to fit your needs. Defining your guitar goals will help you decide what to study, what to practice, help keep you focussed on the things that matter and ignore things that are not going to help you get where you want to go.

Practice Smart! :)

Using S.M.A.R.T. goals to organize your guitar journey might really help you out. But what's that even about? S.M.A.R.T. goals are used in many things depending on circumstance - project management, etc. Now let's learn how to apply that concept to our guitar studies in this lesson.

SMART goals help you go further! When setting your goals, that's what you're looking for:

S - Specific

The more specific you can make your goal, the more likely you will plot a great path to get there! Let's say you want to play Jazz - what type of jazz?

M - Motivating

You need to set goals that inspire you to play! That’s a crucial part of the whole goal-setting thing!

💡 Don't you know what to practice? Check out the 6 guitar areas you should be practicing (to play better!)

If something doesn’t inspire you, choose something else to focus on. Choose your battles! :)

A - Achievable

Make sure you’re setting achievable goals. You’re much better off setting smaller goals that you can actually complete than ones that take a long time or might not be reachable. Though it’s fine to have a dream, these SMART goals are the steps toward it - keep them achievable!

R - Relevant

Most goals are stepping stones toward an even bigger goal - if you have a big long-term goal, then bear that in mind when you’re setting your smaller goals. But stay flexible!

T - Trackable

Don't forget to track your progress and make all your goals time-bounded! Tracking your goals is important for watching your progress and defining when you’ve achieved your goal.

Think!

It might sound like a strange thing to suggest, but please spend some time thinking about the things you most enjoy about the guitar. That's an important first step in goal-setting! Some good questions to ask are:

What gives you the most satisfaction when you practice?

What songs do you enjoy playing the most?

What do you escape from when you practice?

Reflecting on these questions can help you refine what you should be working on and help with your goals. Ideally, everything you practice will help you reach your goals or destinations.

But always try to remain flexible and fluid! Music is an art, and there are no rules in art. It’s mostly feelings. And it’s ok for feelings to change.

Big Picture (Long Term - 5 to 10 years)

A rough idea of where you would like to take the guitar is a really great starting point. Doesn’t have to be super specific, and it can change, but having something written down is a good idea.

Some Big Picture goals that might (or might not) apply to you:

Become a rock star and tour the world

Make a living playing guitar

Play regularly in a band

Record an album of original songs

Become a full-time guitar teacher

Some slightly less ambitious ones:

Play a live gig

Play for friends at a party

Teach guitar as a side income

Impress that pretty girl or boy you like

Entertain my kids with music

These are all reasonable goals, some I'd hope most guitarists would want to achieve.

Break It Down!

Once you have a long-term goal in mind, you need to think about the steps you need to achieve that goal! To do that, you should break them down into medium or short-term goals. It depends on how ambitious your long-term goals are!

Work out the things you would need to do to get there. Then, work out what things to practice to get your journey underway. Just try it - everything takes practice - even working out what to practice. :)

Medium-Term Goals (a month to a year)

Here are some medium-term goals you might want to consider:

Improvise on a blues

Get confident with strumming campfire songs

Develop a solo repertoire

Write a song

Play a jazz standard

Improvise confidently using the major scale

And you can break that down even more!

Short term goals (up to a month)

Here are short-term goals that you can achieve as fast as up to a month. :)

Learn a dozen Blues licks and how to use them

Nail a particular strumming or fingerpicking pattern

Learn a solo guitar arrangement for X song

Understand song structure and its application

Learn the basic Jazz chords

Learn Pattern 1 Major scale and improvise within it

Scale patterns at X speed.

Which Method?

Picking a good guitar teacher and methodology is very important to your guitar success! Having a good teacher will make a big difference in your learning journey. A good teacher understands the various paths available to reach your big picture goal. They'll show you the right way to get there, and a great teacher might even show you cool shortcuts. :)

A common mistake is a teacher teaching what they're into instead of what their student needs. This is a mistake I made many, many times when I started teaching. Beware of teachers who do not understand where YOU want to go. It's about what YOU need to do to get there - this is important!

💡 Having concrete goals will help both you and your teacher. And these goals come from you. So take 30 minutes, reflect, dig a little deeper, and find out your guitar goal before setting it.

Need individual guidance? Check out the JustinGuitar Approved Teachers!

Ask Why!

If you're not clear about the purpose of practicing a specific guitar exercise, don't practice it! It's as simple as that. If anyone, including me, suggests practicing anything, question it! When you have an answer that makes sense for your needs - then start working on it.

COMMON GUITAR GOALS

Everyone's goals will be different, but some common big picture kind of goals might be:

To be able to play some easy songs with my mates at a BBQ

To play regular gigs with a band

To make a living from playing guitar

To be the greatest guitar player ever to walk the face of the Earth

Each of these requires completely different paths and different skills. And many guitar journeys will take similar paths. For example, you'll need to learn your minor pentatonic scales if you want to play Blues guitar or Rock. But - it might not be a necessity to a classical guitar player! This is why this decision part is so important - it all depends on you! Help yourself reach your guitar goal by knowing where you're going.

💬 Join the discussion. What does your guitar goal look like? I'd love to know! Log in and leave a comment in the discussion area!

It's a great feeling to realize that you have achieved your goal. It'll help you stay motivated. For many aspiring guitar players, this is the hardest thing to do!

SOME USEFUL GUITAR PHILOSOPHY

The more you know, the more things you realize you don't know. Socrates told a story once and described knowledge as standing in a circle. Inside the circle are things you know. Outside this circle is what you don't know.

The more stuff you learn, the more the circle gets bigger. As it grows, you realize the endless learning possibilities.

Once you get into the habit of forming and achieving goals - you'll find it spreads into your whole life. This is a great thing!

I meet many people that feel they never get anywhere in their life. Mainly because they never set out in a particular direction. Then the problem comes in deciding which direction YOU want to go in. Only YOU can determine that, and it's often the most challenging learning process.

It is simpler to get what you want if you know what it is. The other option is just bumbling around until you stumble on it! You will become better just for having given this some thought! So do it now - grab a pen and write down things you want to do - see if you can define a big goal.

Need individual help? Contact a JustinGuitar Approved Teacher!

lessons.title: C Chord Shape Explorer
lessons.summary: Explore the C Chord Shape and learn new variations to play the C chord on the guitar. It's easy - and it sounds beautiful!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 C Chord Shape Explorer - Welcome!

00:43 Variation #1 - C Major 7

06:51 Variation #2 - C7

07:24 Variation #3 - C sus 4

08:06 Variation #4 - C/G

08:57 Variation #5 - Guess the Name!

09:21 Go Further!
lessons.text:
Upgrade your basic C Chord!

Discover new C Chord sounds to explore on your guitar. It sounds beautiful!

It's time to learn many different ways of manipulating that easy C Chord we learned as a beginner! That helps you sound more interesting, and you'll be able to easily use these tricks as embellishments! A great one is to create a little bit of melodic movement within the chord itself.

💡 This lesson is part of my Chord Shapes Explorer series - included in my Beginner Course - Grade 3. If you've missed the previous lessons, check them out now.

D Chord Shape Explorer

Moving Up Open Chords

And much more to come!

Note: Explorer lessons for all five CAGED shapes can also be found, grouped together, under All Courses here.

Now let's get to a close-up and explore the C Chord Shape!

Exploring the C Chord Shape

Place your open C Chord on the guitar - we'll start by looking at what happens when we lift our fingers off!

By the time you reach this lesson, you should be pretty comfortable playing your regular C Chord. However, consider revising this lesson if you're struggling to get your C Chord sound great. ;)

Variation #1 - C Major 7

Ok, so the first finger you're lifting off is your first one. You'll get a Cmaj7 - and just switching between that and the regular C Chord sounds awesome already. It adds loads of movements!

🚨 Make sure you're aware that C Major 7 and C7 are different types of chords. They sound very different! C7 is more like a Blues chord, while Cmaj7 sounds folkier. :) You can't substitute one for the other, so use your ears to judge when to use what. Check out my Theory course to understand this better!

So, lifting off your first finger gives you a lovely C Chord! This little variation works particularly well if you hammer that second finger down after playing the chord. ;) You can try that too - but don't worry about fancy pants names for now! If it happens to sound cool, great. If it doesn't sound cool, just move on and try something different.

💡 Did you know? If you lift off a finger from a chord very quickly, you're changing the tonality - that only happens if you left your finger off for ages! So, be careful to not end up playing an Am Chord or something when doing the trick you've just learned. Check out the video lesson to learn more - with examples!

A real common variation with the C Chord is to put your little finger down on the third fret of the thinnest string. You're still playing just a C Chord, but you've doubled an Open G note. So, it's still a C Chord, just not your regular one! :) Inspiring, eh?

If you wonder why there are two very similar variations of the C Chord, a lot of it has to do with a thing we call Voice Leading. Voice Leading is when you go from one chord to another - it's how the note on each string is moving.

🚨 A great example of Voice Leading is when you're moving from the D chord to a regular C chord. Check out the video tutorial to hear it.

Sometimes, you'll just find that putting your little finger down just changes the chord in that subtle way that sounds nicer with the melody. Generally speaking, you're playing the guitar with a singer, so you want to find the nicest chord that fits in that occasion.

But sometimes, you might use these variations in a Chord Melody approach. If you're playing a melody, you might have a specific reason why you want to accent that particular note!

Variation #2 - C7

The C7 chord we've seen before is a very common variation of the C Chord Shape! It generally works okay going to the F Chord.

But again, sometimes, if you've got a regular C and you play a C7 chord, it might sound really cool, or it might sound a bit sour. Experiment and see - if it sounds good, it's good!

Variation #3 - C sus 4

Another option that we've got is adding your little finger on the third fret of the fourth string. This makes it a C sus4. If you don't play the thinnest string, if you do play the thinnest string, you've got a C add4. :)

However, the names here don't really matter. Today's goal is to get you to explore your guitar fretboard and discover new sounds. This gives you a boost of creativity, confidence, and motivation. What a trio! :)

💡 Of course, Theory matters too! Understanding how music works will help you master your guitar playing. :)

Variation #4 - C/G

If you just move your third finger down to the thickest string and put your little finger where the third finger was, you've got a C/G. It means your bass note is now G!

💡 Slash chords sound great are super fun to explore: learn 19 easy slash chords for beginners!

This C/G chord has a cool, old-school kind of rock and roll vibe! Experimenting with this variation can be fun if you dig and play songs like that. :)

Variation #5 - Guess the name! :)

Another common variation doing the same sort of thing involves moving your third finger over. This is kind of a common Country trick - you'd be picking that note, then picking the fifth string, then the sixth string.

💬 Can you guess the name of this chord variation? If you've followed my Theory course - you might get it right! Let me know in the Discussions section. :)

Go Further!

One interesting thing about using the C Chord Shape here is playing the C Major Scale within the chord shape. It might feel tricky to do this if you're a beginner, but it's a nice thing to explore as your skills grow.

In this C Chord Shape, you've got the full scale available there, which becomes really interesting, especially if you're getting into Chord Melody.

The best thing you can do at this stage of your beginner journey is exploring your instrument! Finding melodies within chord shapes is a high-value skill to develop your musicianship.

Your goal is to get those melodies into chord embellishments and variations as soon as you can. Long term, you'll use all of this to embellish your playing very easily and instinctively. :)

Following my new Grade 3? A new lesson is coming out very soon!

lessons.title: How to Pick Individual Strings While Strumming
lessons.summary: How to pick out individual strings while strumming your guitar and exercises to help you practice. Easy enough for beginners, and such a cool technique!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Demo

00:35 Welcome

01:40 Exercise 1

02:30 Strumming Mode!

06:58 Exercise 2

10:56 How to Use This Tricky!
lessons.text:
Pick or strum? Both!

Learn to target individual strings while you strum. :)

You've asked for it - so here it is! A comprehensive lesson to teach you how to pick out individual strings while strumming on the guitar. It sounds great and definitely a fun skill to learn as an advancing beginner.

💡 Missed my brand-new, free guitar course? Check out Beginner Grade 3 right now - this lesson is just a little piece of it!

Particularly when doing chord embellishments, you want to target specific notes within a chord while strumming your guitar. It definitely takes a little bit of practice, but it's something that most advancing beginners should be able to handle!

Learning how to target the individual picks, particularly with the up strums, is a very big deal! The following exercises will help you get started!

The Best Exercises

For the following exercises, we keep returning back to the bass note of the chord we're playing. This is very important in this technique, and you'll use it in different ways. Great examples are when you're alternating bass parts or when you want to pick out the bass note of a chord individually.

We'll be focusing on the thinnest strings to start off with because, most commonly, that's where you'll put chord embellishments if you're picking out the melody of a song, for example.

Exercise #1

We'll start simple, and you can use the tab available in the tutorial to follow along with me. Remember that you should have that relaxed feeling when you strum! So, this exercise should feel nice.

When you're strumming a song, you should be able to maintain that kind of relaxed feel. You're just trying to get some accuracy within that simple framework!

Of course, you can change up the pattern we've used in this lesson! Whenever you want, just make up your own pattern. But at the beginning, it's worth having a set pattern so that you practice this new skill!

Exercise #2

If your confidence is growing and you find the first exercise easy, here's another little variation you might like to try. This time, you'll first up pick on the third string. Check the video for more information!

An even bigger challenge would be to change between those two things, so start with the thinnest string the first time around and your open G string the second time around.

Explore!

This idea of picking out notes individually while strumming your guitar is a very cool tool to add to your regular strumming patterns. Once you get confident with it, experiment with different songs and see!

This really is a great thing to add to your guitar vocabulary, especially when you get into advancing beginners and early intermediate guitar stages.

If you're at that point, learning about chord embellishments and experimenting with chord shapes will give you loads of food for thought and things to get creative with. Happy trails!

Learn more! Check out awesome lessons to get out of the beginner plateau. :)

lessons.title: How To: Thumb & Finger Strums
lessons.summary: Learn how to strum the guitar using your thumb and index finger to sound more groovy! This strumming technique might be exactly what you’re looking for. :)
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Strumming Technique Demo

00:40 Lesson Welcome & Song Examples

01:31 How to Thumb & Finger Strum

02:57 Percussive Hit

05:15 Applying This Technique

06:54 Using the Palm of Your Hand

08:59 Alternating the Bass Note & Extra Tips
lessons.text:
This is THE Strumming Technique You’ve Been Looking For. :)

If you’re interested in a sort of percussive strumming and picking out melodies of a song, this technique is what you need! You’ve probably heard it in songs like Blackbird by Paul McCartney or one of Neil Young’s classics.

To strum your guitar like that, you’ll use your thumb and fingers simultaneously. It’s easier than you think, but it does require some practice if you’re a beginner.

💡 Learning to play? This lesson is part of my free Beginner Guitar Course. Don’t miss out on those lessons! ;)

The big deal with this technique is that your thumb will always play the chord’s bass note. This strum will happen on beats 1 and 3, and you’ll do an up strum with the flesh part of your fingers on the ands. Use your nails to hit the strings for the other down strums.

You’ll notice that the fleshier part of your fingers gives a more rounded sound, while your nails will give a brighter, loud sound. You’re looking to keep a consistent time and strum on the right beats! Check out this lesson if you’re not hip with counting the beats.

The Backbeat!

Once you’re comfortable with the strumming pattern we’ve just learned, it’s time to incorporate that percussive feeling into your playing. That will give another dimension level and add loads of interest to your sound!

As I’ve mentioned, you’ll probably notice that the beats where we use our nails are brighter. That’s for emulating the groove feeling usually added by the drummer when playing with a band. When playing on your own, that’s a very cool trick to sound more dynamic and rhythmically interesting.

💡 Revisit my The Backbeat Hit lesson if you need some easier, beginner advice on how to accentuate the backbeat of a song.

Your challenge is to build a memory of those movements, which might require some practice. So, let’s take a look at how you can get there faster!

Thumb & Finger Strum Practice

I’d recommend spending some time practicing this strumming technique without any chords. Mute the strings so the chords won’t distract you! Practicing each guitar skill at once is very important.

Make sure you relax your movements. You don’t want to sound tense, and the only thing that will help with that is practicing!

🎯 When learning a guitar technique like this, feeling good and relaxed are your ultimate goals.

Spend some time practicing it with muted strings. Really, don’t worry about the chords - just about getting the groove right! Make your guitar playing feel nice to you. That’s how you’ll make it sound nice to your listeners. :)

Adding a Chord Progression

Once you feel comfortable with your strumming hand, it’s time to add on the chords! Check out the video tutorial to see how this thumb and finger strum technique works with a very common chord progression.

💡 Don't know what I'm talking about? Learn all about chord progressions and how to make the most out of them here!

We’re using one of the most common chord progressions you’ll encounter: C, G, and Amin in this lesson. Now, give it a go and see if you can make that sound good. :)

Start with a slower tempo and increase it as you feel confident. This strumming technique really works with different styles, tempos, and feels. Explore and see what sounds good to you!

Go Further!

It’s a little cool trick to use the palm of your hand to add an even stronger percussive feel to your guitar playing! You’ll do that on the backbeats, which means that it happens at the same time as your first finger strums down.

🎶 Feeling adventurous? Check out my lesson on how to play Blackbird by The Beatles. This Paul McCartney classic is definitely a more Intermediate tune to learn on the guitar, but it's a great song to practice this thumb and index finger strums technique.

You can vary the intensity of the palm hitting depending on the effect you’re looking for. Check out the video lesson for a few examples!

An extra tip is to experiment with alternating the bass note of the chords you’re playing. This is very common in Country songs, and it’s usually simple and easy enough for beginners to handle. :)

Later on, you might use this technique to pick out individual notes when strumming. If you’d like to add melodic elements to your playing, that’s great.

Interested in learning more? These Advancing Beginner Lessons will help you out!

lessons.title: How to Use Easy Triads on Guitar
lessons.summary: In this lesson, beginners will get to know how to use Triads (and Arpeggiated embellishments) to duet on the guitar!

05:49 How Triads Work (Minor Chords)

06:47 Rhythm Pattern

lessons.text:
Play Arpeggiated Triads on Guitar!

Triads are easy to play, and they sound super cool. It's especially awesome if you have a friend to jam with you, but not only. Beginners who learn to play Triads get more confident with their fretboard, which is a big deal when moving towards the Intermediate guitarist stages!

💡 This lesson is part of JustinGuitar Course - Grade 3. The full program is available for free here.

We'll learn how to find Major and Minor Triads on the guitar and the best rhythm pattern to play them. Once you're confident with the basics, we'll learn some embellishments you can try, such as arpeggiating triads. We'll explore my favorite tips and tricks to get you even further!

Using Triads to Duet on Guitar

Triads work great in duet situations - you'd have one guitarist playing the chords and the other using these triads. In my opinion, it works best with an acoustic guitar doing the strumming and an electric guitar playing the lead part. Still, it totally works with two acoustic guitars or two electric guitars.

🚨 If you don't have a guitarist to jam with, consider dueting with JustinGuitar Songs & Lessons App. You'll find hundreds of awesome backing tracks of easy songs!

I'm using the electric guitar for this tutorial, and I'm also using a little bit of digital delay. That combination is an all-time classic! Check out the video to listen to it. :) Now, let's get to a close-up and check out how little Triads work.

Finding Major Triads

Triads won't be any hard if you are familiar with the F Chord! As you progress toward the Intermediate levels, you'll learn that you can move that F Chord shape up the neck. Yes, just like Power Chords!

The big deal here is that you're confident with the notes on your thickest two strings. If you're not, you'll have to use your ears to sort out the fretboard position that sounds good!

For example, to play a C Triad, you'll stay in the same fret of a C Power Chord. Your first finger moves to the thinnest two strings, while your second finger goes down one fret above it on the third string.

💡 Get The Trick! Moving around the fretboard is easier than you might think, and this trick will help you a lot. The trick is to remember that you want to look where you're going to land your chord shape. You shouldn't follow your fingers up with your eyes! The best way is to look at the point where you're going to play the next chord. You always want to look and stare at where you're going to play. Don't follow your hand because, by the time your eyes kind of get to the right fret, your hand's still likely to keep moving. :)

That is a really, really big tip when you're jumping around on the guitar neck. Make sure you've got this, ok?

Finding Minor Triads

Minor Triads are very popular too! Luckily, it's even easier to find Minor Triads than the Major ones. For example, start with an A Chord and find your A Major Triad Shape. The minor one is the first finger playing the same fret of the thinnest three strings. :) Easy, eh? Check out the video to learn more!

Rhythm Pattern

Rhythm is a very important part of playing Triads on the guitar. You have an infinite choice of rhythmic patterns here, and you can vary them all the time! Still, I'd recommend starting off with a simple pattern as a beginner. Once you're confident with the basics, applying patterns as that old faithful one will be very fun!

Embellishments

Don't rush to get here, but you should try some embellishments once you're comfortable playing easy Triads. It usually takes one finger! You don't have to worry about the Theory behind that; just use your ears (and the video lesson) to experiment with some fun add ons. :)

💡 Learn the Theory behind Triads and go even further! Together, we'll apply that theory and reveal your guitar fretboard. :)

Understanding Music Theory is very useful, but your ears should tell you much quicker than your Theory thinking mind would. Don't be afraid to use and trust your ears. Check out my Ear Training lessons for helpful exercises to develop your musicianship.

Practice!

Triads are a great way of playing with other musicians, which is really valuable. If you don't have a friend to jam with, check out JustinGuitar Songs & Lessons App. If you're using the app, you'll have the backing tracks and the chords on your screen. Try to find your Triad grips straight away while you're looking at the different chords present in the song you're playing. ;)

Want some more? There are 12 Easy Triad Grips to learn. Go for them!

lessons.summary: This lesson will help you enhance your musical connection and find a way to express your feelings through music!

lessons.text:
How to Enhance Your "Musical Connection"

Here's some food for thought that will help you develop your musicianship and how you express your emotions through your instrument!

Music is a fascinating thing. It can reach deep inside us and connect with our emotions in a very powerful way. It can change or enhance our mood, fire us up or soothe our hurt.

I’m not sure anyone yet really understands the science of how this works - I know they will get it one day. But I have some ideas on how these connections happen, and even if there’s more to it (which there almost certainly is), it makes for very interesting food for thought.

Spending some time thinking about how music works and how you might deepen your own connection with music can significantly impact your playing. I would encourage you to spend some quality time with an open mind and get curious about musicality!

The Universal Language?

Music is known as the ‘universal language,’ but it has no words, and there is no musical phrase that says “I am sad,” “I am happy,” or “I love you.” Interesting that the same musical phrase might say any of those things!! How on earth might that work?

We almost certainly need to learn how to express our emotions THROUGH music. I first started thinking about this when I was studying classical guitar, where the music is set, but somehow people express their own personality as they play music someone else wrote. When you watch two masters play the same piece of music, it’s different, and some versions will connect more than others. I felt that learning to channel my feelings through the instrument when I played was the thing that mattered most.

When a player has complete freedom of note choice and choice of tone, the available palette of expression becomes HUGE. There are so many choices to make! The note, the context, the dynamics, the sound, so many nuances, and how you feel when you MAKE THOSE CHOICES. It’s your personality that will guide these things. You can’t help it.

Musicians who find a way to connect their feelings to music will always connect with others. We can somehow FEEL that person when they play in a way that we won’t feel when a performer has not made that expression connection yet.

What About Technique?

For sure, there is a kind of ‘technical ability to control the instrument’ that comes into play here; being able to control the sound of the notes and the dynamics, understanding the sound they are making, and how to control it. If you’re playing a ballad, but the notes are all buzzy, your bends are out of tune, and you’re using an inappropriate tone, it probably won’t touch anyone’s soul!

Get Sad :)

For some unknown reason, it seems that learning to express sad feelings is easier to start off with than it is to express happy feelings. I often encourage people to sit on their own and dwell on the saddest moment of their life and then try and play how it feels - to channel that sadness out of the instrument. It can be very powerful and unleash all kinds of emotions. Try it! What does it feel like?

Even when strumming a simple song, you should connect to a feeling that will come through. To me, Jack Johnson has one of the happiest vibes of any songwriter. Putting on his music makes life seem better, a little sunshine no matter how dark the skies. Can you tap into that feeling when you listen to his music? Can you then try to capture that feeling and express the same when you play a song?

Who Do You Bond With?

I’ve spent many hours wondering why we all connect with different music and with different musicians. And it’s a very strong connection for many people; they find themselves with a very strong bond to a particular artist, me too!

My best guess is that we somehow connect to the performer's personality (or the producer's!) and feel a connection to some character trait. Either they possess something in their personality that we wish we had (confidence, individuality, courage?), or we feel they are some kind of kindred spirit that ‘feels the same as we do.’

Thinking about this really helped me connect with music and my own musicianship. Knowing what music people like can speak a lot about their personality, and I suspect it also relates to the ‘tribe’ feeling that many of us get with people who like the same music.

I would encourage you to explore the artists you deeply connect with and see if you can find your own answers to how or why you relate to their music. I found it helped me understand myself on a philosophical level too.

Some personal examples… I most likely love Elliott Smith because I feel he was his own man, a deep artist, and perhaps I care too much what others think of me and my music. I feel a deep connection with Neil Young, and I suspect it’s for his rebellious nature, confidence in his art, and more. Lately, I’ve been listening to Taylor Swift, likely I’m longing for the youthful freedom and wide-eyed wonder that now seems so long ago…

Give it some thought - it’ll likely take you to some interesting places and make you a better guitarist!

lessons.text:
Everything you need to know about Reverb, the most common guitar effect ever!

Learn how to make the most out of Reverb and understand the difference between Spring, Plate, Pre-Delay, Hall, Shimmer... all types of reverbs! We'll learn when and how to use each of them and talk about the best reverb pedals for beginners, plug-ins, and tips to use Reverb on the guitar - but not only! Reverb also works great on vocals, and it's a common trick I always use!

In this tutorial, we'll mostly use Boss RV-6 Reverb Pedal, but we'll also explore Neunaber Reverberator, Strymon, and Specular Tempus. Incredible reverb pedals to choose from!

So, let's get stuck in your ultimate guide to Reverb! :)

What is Reverb?

Reverb is an effect that occurs naturally in your everyday life. When you enter a hall or church, you'll notice your voice sounds different, a bit echoey. That's reverb! A footstep or a clap sound will last longer with reverb rather than the original sound. The sound waves bounce off, reflecting surfaces when you hear them back.

Reverb effects can add the illusion of space to an instrument sound, giving you a much bigger ambient and atmospheric soundscape. It's one of the reasons why recording studios have so much soundproofing: you're trying to remove as much of the natural reverb as you can. Then, you add the reverb later by using pedals or plug-ins.

Historically, you might have gone to a room that had naturally great reverb. There are studios, like Abbey Road or Ocean Way, where bands have a room with beautiful natural reverb. Now, we have loads more options! We can even have different reverbs on different instruments to create these clashes and interesting mixes of atmospheric conditions, naturally or not.

Abbey Road is known for its natural reverb! In this image, you see Studio 2, where bands like The Beatles, Oasis, and Pink Floyd recorded iconic albums!

Reverb can make your sound pretty interesting, and there are quite a few different ways to get that sound. I usually use plug-ins, but you'll find plenty of amps with multi-effects and reverb pedals!

💡 If you've seen my song lessons before, I usually use a reverb plug-in for acoustic guitar and/or for my voice! Reverb is definitely one of my favorite guitar effects.

Before we get into the different types of reverb and how to use each one, let's look at the history of reverb and how we got here!

History of Reverb

The first type of reverb ever was the one you get in a room. Columbia's 30th Street Studio is a famous example of naturally occurring reverb in the room where Miles Davis recorded his legendary album Kind of Blue. Definitely worth checking out!

Kind of Blue by Miles Davis is a great example of music recorded with natural reverb! If you're a more advanced guitar player, don't miss out on my So What guitar lesson. ;)

The record producer Bill Putnam is credited with the first artistic use of reverb. He used an echo chamber in his 1947's recording of "Peg o' My Heart" by the Harmonicats.

The first real artificial reverb machine was the EMT plate, a giant metal plate suspended in a box. I had one in my old recording studio - but they weigh 200 kilograms, so not the kind of thing you'll be lugging around on your pedalboard. But they sound incredible!

Now, it's time to explore the settings you'll usually find on a reverb pedal and the different reverb types you can explore.

Reverb Settings

You'll encounter different settings on different reverb pedals. We'll walk through the most common ones in this lesson and understand how to use them. Then, we'll explore the different types of reverb!

💡 I'm using the Boss Reverb RV6 pedal for this lesson. This is my favorite option for demonstrating the different reverb types. Its controls are pretty simple - great for new guitarists!

When starting with guitar effects, you want pedals without too many parameters. The pedals I like are the ones with an infinite number of different parameters and variables to play around with. But you should avoid that when starting out - it can be overwhelming!

A great trick to start is setting all your reverb controls roughly at 12 o'clock, which is usually a good starting point for a usable reverb sound. If you set everything at 12 o'clock, you can hear the reverb effect straight away. Check out the video tutorial to hear the difference. :)

Effect Level Control

Effect Level (E. Level), also called Mix or Blend, controls how much reverb you'll add to the primary sound of your dry guitar.

💡 When a guitar has no effect, we call it dry! We're making it wet when we add effects to your dry guitar. :)

So, the Effect Level control tells how wet we are making the sound and how much reverb we're adding to it.

Tone Control

The tone control is also common, and you'll find it in most pedals. Generally, when you turn the tone control clockwise, you make the sound brighter. If you turn it back the other way, you'll find the type of sound you usually find when entering a cave. It's a low-frequency reflection.

💡 On budget pedals, the tone can get too sharp and sound too digital. Be careful with it!

I prefer a brighter reverb sound than a low one, particularly with electric guitars. If you're in a band, you don't want too many bass sounds on the guitar. If you're playing on your own, it doesn't really matter, but I tend to go to the brighter side. :)

Time Control

Time Control tells how long the delay effect lasts.

💡 Remember, the Effect Level is how much reverb you get versus the original sound. Then, the Time Control is how long it lasts!

Generally speaking, very long reverbs will create an atmospheric sound, where you'll play a few notes that will last a long time. You're probably better off going for the digital delay in those cases, but explore it and see.

Reverb Types

There's no such thing as the right reverb type to use. It should really be a creative tool, but sometimes a reverb type will be more useful and adequate than others. For example, the spring reverb, which we'll explore later in this lesson, is perfect for adding a surf vibe to your sound.

Plate Reverb

Plate Reverb sounds like an EMT plate, which was basically a big metal plate with transducers. I really like plate reverb on voices and acoustic guitar; if you've heard my acoustic guitar in any videos, it had a plate reverb! I use it all the time, not through my Kemper or amp, but as an effect plug-in.

Spring Reverb

Spring reverb is the sound built into many of those early amplifiers. It adds a great sound effect to your guitar when playing notes fast. Check out the video tutorial for a real-life example of spring reverb!

Modulate Reverb

Modulation adds like a chorus pedal to the delayed sound. It's like adding a little bit of unicorn magic fairy dust stuff into your sound!

Hall and Room

If you've played in places like a school hall and there was no one there for your soundcheck, you know what this reverb type sounds like! :) It sounds like one of those wood-paneled floors with loads of echo, whereas if you were playing in a smaller room and no people in there.

💡 These terms for different reverb types, like Cathedral, Canyon, and Cave, describe their sound. It's very clever technology because it allows you to get reverbs that simulate different spaces.

You can get all sorts of reverbs that change the character of the sound you're playing. When you play in a very active room with lots of natural reverb, you'll have to pay attention to your guitar effects so it's not overwhelming. With time and experience, you'll find it easier to adjust to different situations!

Shimmer Reverb

Shimmer reverb adds a pitch-shifted reverb to your sound. It adds artificial overtones, like a unicorn fairy magic. Great on atmospheric stuff!

💡 The Strymon BlueSky is responsible for popularizing the Shimmer Reverb. If you want to explore this reverb type, consider that pedal! It's expensive, but a flagship!

Not my favorite one, but definitely worth exploring!

Delay + Reverb

Delay is like an echo. So, this effect is not really a reverb but a digital delay. It might be handy to have it on a reverb pedal, but I tend to use a reverb pedal for reverb and then a delay pedal for the delay effect.

Pre-Delay

Pre-delay adds a gap before the reverb starts. I don't tend to use it a lot, but it does have a place!

💡 You won't find a Pre-Delay in this Boss pedal. For this tutorial, we're exploring this effect with Neunaber Immerse Reverberator.

Without pre-delay, the reverb starts right away. With pre-delay, there's a gap before the reverb starts, and when it starts, it's kind of a bloom afterward. I'm not exactly this effect occurs in real life, maybe in a tunnel where the reverb occurs somewhere else.

Reverb Pedal Recommendations

There are plenty of reverb pedals to explore, and their prices will vary a lot! This Boss Reverb RV6 might be your best choice if you're on a budget, but if you're up for paying more, here are a couple more options to consider!

Neunaber Immerse Reverberator

This Neunaber's pedal is great, particularly awesome for plate reverb. It has a really rich sound! Their spring reverb is pretty good, and their shimmer is less drastic than the Boss one. Great pedal if it fits your budget!

💡 I use Logic, Apple's recording software. So, I tend to use many different plugins, and each one does a particular thing. I use UAD - Universal Audio, EMT250, a replica of the M2250.

BlueSky Reverberator

The BlueSky Reverberator is a legendary pedal! It's great for shimmer reverb, it has a little bit of pre-delay to it, and it sounds very rich! The spring effect on this one is incredible - it sounds so springy!

Specular Tempus

This is a reverb and delay machine, a super creative pedal that has loads of different parameters to play around with. So, if you're looking to get really creative and try to explore things, this is a great option!

Q&A - Reverb Effect on Guitar

I asked you to drop your questions about reverb on Instagram, and I have some answers for you! Let's take a look. :)

Q - Is there such a thing as too much reverb?

The answer is definitely yes! It hurts me to say that because I love reverb, and I'm definitely a musician who puts too much reverb on things. :) Sometimes that's okay, but sometimes it's not! You'll have to use your taste and judgment to experiment with what works best.

Q - How to choose the best reverb pedal for you?

It does come down to budget! If it's to pick one right now, it would be the Specular Tempus, but that's an expensive pedal. The Boss pedals usually have a good price and sound great, so they are definitely an option if you're on a budget. There are cheaper ones out there, as cheap as 30 or 40 pounds, but I haven't tried them. Reading shoppers' reviews might be a good idea before buying a pedal! :)

💡 The Boss GT 1000 is what I usually take on workshops and events. It's like all of the Boss pedals ever in one box! Very practical.

If you're looking for various effects, you can get one pedal with more built-in options. The Boss Katana has an incredible amount of effects built into it - it's an incredible option if you have the budget!

When I started playing guitar, we had to buy individual pedals for each effect. Now, we can get one of those amps with many built-in effects, which is very useful.

Q - Am I weird for playing completely dry?

Definitely not! A dry sound can be really cool! When I record, I mostly record dry and add the effects later so I can take effects off again if I want to. Recording dry is a really good idea, so you can add the reverb later.

It also works for vocals! I like the sound of a dry voice because it sounds more intimate, but I tend to put reverb on my voice when recording song lessons. It hides some flaws and makes my voice sound a little bit nicer! I'm still not super confident as a singer, I can sing okay, but sometimes a bit of reverb seems to really help me out!

💡 Interested in learning more about Boss Katana and even getting some free presets? Explore these lessons!

What Next?

I encourage you to explore the effects on your own! The more you do that, the more you'll start to recognize guitar effects in real life, and the easier it will be to copy sounds you hear.

But don't forget: great guitar tone starts here!

lessons.text:
Stop Learning Riffs from Tabs (use your ears instead!)

As part of your journey as a guitar player, you'll come to a point where you need to start working out songs on your own. Using tabs, sheet music, or song tutorials to learn is great, especially if you develop your ears to tell if you sound right.

But most important than learning to play riffs and songs from tabs, you should be able to just translate to the instrument the sounds you hear in your musical imagination! But how to get songs out of your fingers? It might be easier than you think!

💡 New to JustinGuitar? This lesson is part of my free Beginner Guitar Course - Grade 3. Check out the full program here!

In this lesson, we'll explore some songs I suggest you should work out on your first attempts at transcribing. We'll also learn some tips to get you through them, but stop the video lesson before listening to them if you're feeling confident! Try working out these songs on your own, and if you need extra help, come back here for some tips on hand positions and starting notes.

5 Easy Riffs to Transcribe

Let's get started and check out 5 easy riffs that even advancing beginners can transcribe!

Easy Riff #1 - Satisfaction by The Rolling Stones

Satisfaction by The Rolling Stone has only three notes. It's really simple, and you could even play it with one finger if you wanted to. An extra tip? You'll play this riff somewhere at the first frets of your guitar neck. Have a go at it!

Easy Riff #2 - Redemption Song by Bob Marley

The riff played at the beginning of Redemption Song by Bob Marley is an easy one to transcribe! It's really naked, and there's nothing else going on there, so you should be able to hear the riff really clearly. It's at the first frets of your guitar neck, so don't try to find it at the middle-end of your fretboard!

There are quite a few hammer-ons in the original recording, but you can ignore that for now. Just go for the melody. ;)

💡 Being able to sing a song and have it clear in your musical imagination will be really helpful when transcribing! So don't forget to listen to the songs you're trying to work out on the guitar; you should be really familiar with them.

Easy Riff #3 - Another One Bites The Dust by Queen

Another One Bites the Dust by Queen is pretty easy too, but if you just look at the riff part. That's actually played by a bass guitar in the original recording, and it's relatively easy to sort it out.

💡 An extra tip, not just for this song but all of the songs, is that you want to learn how to stop! I use a specific software called Transcribe!, which always plays from the same place each time after you stop a song. Very useful.

The last thing that you hear stays in your ear, so if you can play a record from the same place, it'll be easier to get the sound of what you're trying to transcribe clearly in your ear. Check out my 4 Easy Steps to Transcribing for extra help!

Easy Riff #4 - Black Night by Deep Purple

The riff of Black Night by Deep Purple is also an easy one to transcribe! Later in this lesson, we'll learn some extra tips to help you out if you need to. For now - give it a go. And good luck!

Easy Riff #5 - Pretty Woman by Roy Orbison

This last song is a little trickier than the others, but it'll help prepare you for our next Transcribing lesson. This classic riff is faster than the previous ones, so you can use software to slow it down and help you transcribe.

💡 I use Transcribe!, but there are loads of different apps available. There's a free one called Audacity that many people like, and a much more modern one called Capo. Choose the one that works best for you!

Make sure you don't slow the song down too much, or it might get harder to transcribe. If you slow it down too much, you can't really hear the pitch of the notes. Start around 70% of the real speed and see how that goes!

You CAN Learn to Transcribe!

Before we go ahead and check out the extra tips on sorting out these riffs, let me assure you: you can learn to transcribe. You'll develop your ears, and transcribing will get easier, even if it's frustrating when you first start. In the beginning, a lot of it will be trial and error, and that's ok! Just have a positive mindset and understand it takes a little bit of grit. You have to sit down and persist! You'll get there.

💡 Transcribing might be difficult even for more experienced guitarists! Sometimes, it'll be frustrating, and sometimes very easy. It's the same for me. Some days, my ear is on fire, and I can work out any song straight away, but there are days when I have to think twice about a chord. The secret is to not give up!

Keep practicing, and develop a great relationship between what you hear and your hand. This is great for songwriting or improvising because you can hear the sounds in your musical imagination, and your fingers can make it happen. Yes, it's magical.

🚨 So, now you should try to sort out those songs without using any extra tips on hints. But if you're feeling stuck, come back here and check out the following information.

Hints to Transcribe These 5 Easy Riffs

If you're reading this, I hope you gave a go at trying to sort out those five easy riffs. But if you're feeling stuck, click on the hints below, which should help. Don't give up; you've got this!

Hint: Satisfaction

This riff is so simple that I don't feel like giving you any hints but ok. To play this Rolling Stones classic, start on note B with your first finger on the second fret of the fifth string. That's the starting note to play Satisfaction!

Hint: Redemption Song

Start with your third finger on the third fret of the thickest string, the note G. You only need your second and third fingers!

Hint: Another One Bites The Dust

This one starts with low E - play it and sort out the rest! You don't need more hints than this. ;)

Hint: Black Night

Start with your third finger on the seventh fret of the fifth string. This one is the only riff you'll play further up the neck. For all of it, you only need your first and third fingers.

Hint: Pretty Woman

Start with the low E, and use only your first and third fingers. Your first finger will be on the second fret and your third finger on the fourth. That's more than enough!

Just Do This! 💪

I KNOW you can transcribe these songs! In 30 years of teaching, I've only met one student who couldn't hear the pitches and couldn't transcribe. So, transcribing is a skill you'll acquire. Just work for it!

All you need to sit down and listen to the songs you're working our until they're solid in your musical imagination. You should start learning to write simple tabs, but just making little notes about what the fingering was or the order might keep you from getting lost. Now, go for it - and happy trails.

You did it! This lesson wraps up Module 17. Next, it's a suggested practice routine for you. See you there!

lessons.text:
Congratulations! You completed Module 17. :)

Now it's time to go through the Module 17 Practice Routine!

But don't forget: at this stage of your beginner journey, you should tweak this suggested practice routine to best fit your needs. My suggestion has a one-hour rounded schedule, but you might choose to leave some of these things out and focus on something else.

💡 Need to review the lessons? Check out Module 17 here!

You may want to practice more, or maybe you want to practice less! You can also choose to split your practice routine over two days. Decide what will work for you because we all start having different needs and different problems at this point.

Module 17: Suggested Practice Routine

My suggestion is a well-rounded, holistic practice routine, but feel free to manipulate it to your needs. You can, and should, swap sections for things that are more important for you right now. So here is a summary of your suggested practice routine for Module 17:

5' Technique - Finger Gym 5' Technique - Picking Individual Strings While Strumming 5' Knowledge - C-Shape Explorer 5' Knowledge - Using Easy Triads 5' Repertoire - Triads In Songs 5' Repertoire - Song Revision 5' Time - Thumb and Finger Strumming 5' Time - Play along with great songs 10' Transcribing - Transcribing Riffs 10' Improvising - Major Scale Improvisation

Let's have a chat about it! It'll help you decide how to adapt your practice routine to best fit your needs. Feel free to keep it as it is as well!

Section #1 - Technique - 2 x 5-minutes

Finger Gym + Picking Individual Strings While Strumming

Your first practice section is all about technique, and you've got two slots of 5 minutes each. The first slot should be Finger Gym unless something else is more important to your technical development.

Then it's time to work on picking individual strings while strumming. Take your time on this - it's a super useful technique to develop.

Section #2 - Knowledge - 2 x 5-minutes

C-Shape explorer + Using Triads

In the first section of your knowledge practice, I suggest you explore your C Shape chords. Experiment and see what cool sounds you can find, and remove the fear of trying new things!

In the second slot, I would suggest starting with triads. Memorize them, and make sure you're confident playing triads before you launch into using them in songs. Once you're hip with them, maybe move on to theory and Understanding Music :)

Section #3 - Repertoire - 2 x 5-minutes

Triads + Revision

Time to ensure that triads are not one of those things you learn but never put to use! As you grow as a guitarist, you'll find triads are very useful in many ways. Get stuck in and put them into practice!

Then, I suggest a good dose of song revision, developing your repertoire, and working on your growers and dreamers. :)

Section #4 - Time - 2 x 5-minutes

Thumb & Finger Strumming + Songs You Love

I'd suggest starting with some work on the thumb and finger strumming, even if you're mostly a pick player. It's a great skill to get into your hands!

The second slot would be playing along with songs you love - a really big deal. You can even try and pretend that you're in the band! :) This is an exercise I'd suggest you keep in your schedule for a long time. I still do it often.

Section #5 - 10-minute slots

Transcribing Riffs

Time to get transcribing some riffs! If you get through the ones I suggested, have a go at any riff you like. The more you do, the better you get. Weird, right? ;)

Section #6 - Improvisation - 10-minutes

Major Scale Improv

This one is optional. If you're working on improvising and looked at Blues the last few weeks, maybe switch to work on some major scale improvisation. What do you enjoy? I've got some jam tracks you can try on!

When to Move On?

Before moving on to Module 18, you should practice this routine for at least two weeks, maybe three or four. Don't be in a hurry to move forward - being able to play a few things well is much more useful than playing many things badly! ;)

Under the video, click on the 'Practice' Tab and save the pre-made practice routine for Module 17. Go to your dashboard to access and edit the items. Ready for Module 18?

modules.intro:
Welcome to Module 18!

We've got plenty of new things to learn. :)

Don't be in a hurry to go through the lessons in this Module. As you wrap up your beginner journey, consolidating your knowledge is a must. It helps you become a stronger Intermediate guitarist.

💬 Reach out to my Community for extra help and feedback! Ask questions and chat with guitarists facing the same challenges as you. :)

Now let's look at what's on the menu for Module 18.

What You'll Learn

Perfectly Starts Slowly - Our first lesson explains why slowing down your guitar journey is important.

Open Tunings - Many beginner guitar players are scared of open tunings, but there's no reason to be! We'll open up a whole new palette of sounds on the guitar!

Minor Pentatonic Legato - We'll play the Minor Pentatonic Scale to practice our hammer-ons and flick-offs. You're already a little bit familiar with that because of our Finger Gym Exercise.

Solo Blues - Time to mix rhythm guitar and some riffs! Eventually, you'll be able to learn to incorporate your licks into it. :)

Triad Chips - Let's explore a new way of learning triads! We'll use them as chips, which are short rhythmic stabs, great as the second guitar part.

Neuroplasticity to Learn Guitar Faster - The latest science to learn guitar - or anything else - is faster, especially if you're 25 years old or older!

Delays - We'll explore Delay effects and learn the difference between digital and analog delays, how they work, and much more!

Transcribing Open Chord - We'll keep working on our ears! Now it's time to transcribe songs using open chords you're familiar with.

By this Module's end, you'll get a practice routine, extra tips, song suggestions, and much more.

👉 Ready? Get started here!

lessons.text:
The Power of Slow Learning

In this food for thought lesson, we'll talk about why it's important to slow down your guitar journey and why that will make you a much better guitar player.

In this information-rich world that we live in, many of us feel like we can and should learn a lot the whole time. Everything goes by so fast; there is so much to learn! But we forget most of what we learn. Some studies suggest that we lose as much as 90% of it!

How to fix that? By slowing down!

Practice Makes Permanent

I'm hoping you heard me say Practice Makes Permanent before. It sure doesn't make Perfect like the old saying our parents told us! There's even a famous quote often attributed to Einstein that defines it beautifully, ​​"Insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting different results."

So if you want to make what you practice go into your memory and muscles permanently… you need to get it right! And you'll do that by slowing down!

The mantra I would encourage you to remember is:

Practice Makes Permanent So Practice Perfectly And Perfectly Starts Slowly

Code It Carefully Once

If you've ever written any code, you know it's far easier to take your time and get the code right the first time than to spend hours debugging it and looking for some dumb syntax mistake!

When you're learning a new thing on the guitar, you are writing very complex code - imagine how many lines of code would be required to get a robotic arm to play and change between chords! Take a minute and think about it.

Once you write the code correctly, it's relatively easy to speed up the reading of the code. For things like learning scales and licks, it's the same! You should always learn things very slowly.

Once you can slowly play them 20 times from memory without a mistake, you'll usually find that mistakes are very uncommon as you speed up. And if you do make one, it would usually be caused by a technical deficiency!

Overwriting A Mistake

Unfortunately, all humans make mistakes, and when we do, it's important to know how to get over them.

It's obviously far better not to make them in the first place, but if you make a mistake when learning something, it's better to stop than keep going. Tell yourself it was a mistake, then start again and get it right. I'm not sure anyone knows why that is so much more effective for learning yet, but it certainly is from my own experience and that of many students over the years.

💡 My guestimation is that it takes 20 correct play-throughs to overwrite a mistake. So try not to make any!

I had a teacher in high school who wrote a scale diagram out wrongly. Even if I knew it didn't sound quite right, I practiced it. And I STILL make that mistake sometimes. After more than 30 years of playing it right, if I ever make a mistake in Pattern 5 of the Major Scale, it's the B string - my 3rd finger goes down instead of the 2nd. Dammit! ;)

Retain More.

But this is not just about getting it right! It's also about how much you retain. Most of us feel the 'hurry' in life to learn things, but if you're not going to retain and be able to use the information - what is the point? Why would you waste hours of your life learning something you will have forgotten in a few weeks or months?

When we learn slower, the retention rate goes up massively. Over the long term, slow learners retain much more information than fast learners.

In his excellent book Thinking Fast and Slow, Daniel Kahneman (pron. Car-nay-man) says, "Intelligence is not only the ability to reason; it is also the ability to find relevant material in memory and to deploy attention when needed."

Let's put that into a musical context of musical intelligence. Licks, scales, chords, and anything else are no use to anyone unless they're in your head and ready to use, right I don't remember seeing Clapton on stage with a lick book. :) You gotta get that stuff in your memory, and slow learning will help!

It's also incredibly frustrating to spend hours doing something and then forget it! It makes us feel like we're wasting our time and that maybe guitar 'isn't for us' when it's much more likely we are learning it wrong!

Chunk It!

Also important is trying not to learn too much too soon. It's much better to learn a small new idea and be able to use it to make music than some super long complex thing that you'll likely never use!

If you want to learn some long and complex piece, such as Coltrane's Giant Steps solo, break it down into manageable chunks and work on each bit individually. For example:

Figure out how to play each 4 or 8 note lick;

Figure out a solid fingering;

Understand how it works harmonically.

When learning a more complex song, take the time to understand what it's played over, how you might use it in your improvisation, and anything else relevant. If you got all the chunks good, putting them together won't be too difficult, and you will have learned a load of useful and interesting things, not just one big long show-off solo!

Timers, Revisiting and Explaining

Three points related to this slow learning and retention are using timers to practice, revisiting material over longer periods, and explaining what you learn. Let's talk about each one of them!

#1 - Using Timers

Using timers to practice is very helpful for focus. Keeping focussed will help stop you from making mistakes, but it can make us feel rushed, so try to stay cool, relaxed, and unhurried when you're learning. And make sure you take a short break after a practice burst to clear your mind and help retain what you just learned.

#2 - Revisit Old Materials!

Revisiting material over weeks and months will also help you remember it and shift it from your brain's RAM (short-term memory) to its hard drive (long-term memory). That is The Spacing Effect, and we'll talk more about that another time!

But don't learn something once! Schedule a reminder and learn it again in a couple of weeks and you'll be amazed and how much you then retain. It's quite incredible! Remember that an hour a day for 10 days is almost always more effective than one 10-hour cramming session.

#3 - Explain The Things You Learn

Explaining what you learn is also incredibly valuable. Teaching someone else what you learn is a great way of doing it and finding gaps in your own knowledge that you might need to fill. But I also write myself essays on new things I learn (which I'm unlikely ever to publish) just to make sure that I understand it properly.

Writing it down is like slow thinking too, making sure I write things clearly and concisely really helps get things clear in my mind. I'm doing it here. I do it with many Stoic Philosophy ideas that resonate with me and with new techniques I learn in BJJ. If I can explain it clearly, I can be confident I know it well.

Summary

To conclude and make sure you understand what you can practically do to learn faster and retain more:

When learning something new, learn it so slowly that you make NO mistakes!

Only when you can play something 10 times without a mistake should you start to speed it up.

Learn one thing well and use it musically before moving on. Don't be in a hurry to move on to something new.

Use a timer when practicing (max 30-minute bursts).

Revisit things you want to remember (everything!?) a week later, a month later, and then 6 months later!

Write a lesson (or essay) on everything you learn, even if you won't share or teach it!

Hope this helps you make the most of your precious time, and also that you stick around with this course. Next, we'll get started with Altered Tunings!
