lessons.text:
Don't Be Afraid of Retuning Your Guitar!

Alterate Tunings on the guitar are very inspiring. And it's easy enough for advancing beginners. :)

This lesson will give you a comprehensive introduction to alternate tunings on the guitar. We'll learn how to get to and use the 4 most common altered tunings you'll encounter in your guitar journey. They are:

Drop D Tuning

Double Drop D Tuning

Open G Tuning

Open D Tuning

When I started playing the guitar, I was scared to explore open tunings. I thought it was something really difficult, and I had heard rumors that my guitar neck would move if I changed the tuning of my instrument. They'd say I'd break strings, that exploring new tunings was hard, but most of that is just… unfounded.

💡 If you re-tune your guitar, the neck might move slightly. But that doesn't matter!

Occasionally, you might break a string if tuning it up a lot, but the open tunings we'll learn today only require that you tune strings down. So, breaking strings is unlikely to be a problem when you try the tunings you're about to learn.

Getting Creative With Open Tunings

First, I'd encourage you to try some of these alternate tunings by playing songs you like! By the end of this lesson, you'll get a list of five songs that use each of these alternate tunings. I've got song lessons for most of them! :) I hope this lesson removes any fear of retuning your guitar you might have, so let's get stuck in.

Drop D Tuning

To get to Drop D Tuning, all you have to do is drop the low E down to a D. Here's a diagram to help you get to Drop D Tuning:

We've got an open D string on the fourth string, so just play the fourth string and tune the thicker string until they sound the same. If you find that difficult, you can also use a harmonic at the 12th fret for the exact pitch. Check out the video tutorial for more details!

Now, go ahead and strum your guitar. How big does that sound, eh? Drop D Tuning is amazing. Don't worry too much about having to play a particular chord or a particular shape. Explore it, and you'll discover super cool sounds.

💡 Drop D tuning is also great for Rock because we can play Power Chords with one finger. :) But before we get there, let me explain what we just did!

When you retune your guitar to Drop D, you only touch the thickest string, so you can play all of the chords that don't use the thickest string the same way as you would play in regular tuning. Some examples are the regular C chord, the D chord, the Mini F, the A Minor chord, and any A Shape Barre Chord that doesn't use the thickest string.

💡 In this lesson, I'm possibly using some unusual fingerings because I've got a fractured little finger. :( I've only just taken the splint off because I wanted to get my little finger working again, but I shouldn't use it too much!

In Drop D, we detuned the thickest string by one tone, which means two frets on the guitar. So, we have to move any chords that use the thickest string up two frets. For example, if we have a G Power Chord, you've got to remember that we're down a tone on that thicker string, so your G5 would be an F Power Chord, and your F Power Chord would be a D Power Chord.

Many Neil Young songs use Drop D Tuning, and he always plays the open G chord - a very common trick in Rock! You should get familiar with those, including how you play the F chord in Drop D. Check out the video lesson for more information about fingerings.

5 Songs in Drop D Tuning

Here are some great songs in Drop D tuning that I'd recommend you check out:

Killing in the Name by Rage Against the Machine

Harvest Moon by Neil Young

Everlong by Foo Fighters

The Chain by Fleetwood Mac

Hold On by Tom Waits

Double Drop D Tuning

To get to Double Drop D tuning, we tune the thinnest and the thickest strings down a tone. In Double Drop D, the thinnest and thickest strings become a D! We've got the fourth string as a reference. ;) Here's your Double Drop D Tuning diagram:

Double Drop D introduces a whole heap of cool things! In regular Drop D, all you get is that lower sound, but when you're in Double Drop D, part of the beauty is this extra note, which you can use to embellish regular open chords.

💡 Experiment with standard chords and see what changes. C, A, and Am are great chords to explore. Try it!

To play a D chord in Double Drop D, you'll generally want to lift off your second finger. If you leave your second finger down, you'd be playing the same as a Dsus2 chord.

💡 When tuning your guitar, don't be afraid to double-check the notes. Keep your ears on it! You can even use a tuner to perfect it.

Double Drop D tuning got loads of interesting things you can use as a creative tool. It's a super-effective tuning for the G chords, but the F chord becomes trickier. Check out the video lesson for more information about chords you can try and details about fingerings.

5 Songs in Double Drop D Tuning

You'll find great songs in Double Drop D - my favorite one is Cortez The Killer by Neil Young! Check out my top 5 recommendations for you:

Cortez The Killer by Neil Young

Going to California by Led Zeppelin

Devils & Dust by Bruce Springsteen (lesson coming soon!)

Your Body Is A Wonderland by John Mayer

Song For George by Eric Johnson

These are mostly acoustic songs, but they work great on electric guitar. I'm using an acoustic guitar today because it's a little simpler to tune them - we don't have to worry about the bridge of the electric guitars. We'll talk more about that later on!

💡 Explore my Song lessons! You can filter songs by tuning, artists, genre, chords, etc. Super handy - and it's free! If you'd like to get the most out of my tutorials, consider JustinGuitarTABS; it'll save you loads of time learning new songs.

When you're in Double Drop D, you're just one string away from getting to the most classic open tunings ever, a proper open chord tuning, Open G. Let's take a look at it!

Open G Tuning

If you're in Double Drop D and want to get to the Open G tuning, all you have to do is tune your A string down one tone. Use the third string as a reference! So, in Open G, we have the following strings: D G D G B D. Check out this diagram to help you tune your guitar to Open G:

You'll notice that all we have in Open G tuning are G, B, and D notes. In Open G, the root note is on the fifth string, not on the thickest string. That's why Keith Richards played a five-string guitar - that lower string, the D string, just gets in the way, and it's not used that much in Open G tuning.

Open G is great if you're playing standard Blues and other things that don't require the thicker string. So, if you have a barre chord in open tuning, you want the tip of your finger to mute the thickest string. In Open G, you're just playing the thinnest strings! The root note here is one tone above.

💡 The trick with open tunings is realizing that if you put your first finger down in the first fret of the second string and your second finger down in the second fret of the fourth string, you end up with this nice movement, great for Blues. It's common in The Rolling Stones' songs and other tunes that Open G. Experiment!

Open G tuning is also great if you dig slide guitar! One of the beautiful things with slides is having these open tunings where you can play a whole chord just in the one fret! Check out the video lesson for more information and see me playing a bit with slide guitar. :)

5 Songs in Open G Tuning

Time to explore Open G tuning in real songs! Here's my top 5 list:

Brown Sugar by The Rolling Stones

Bohemian Like You by The Dandy Warhols

Honky Tonk Woman by The Rolling Stones

Romeo and Juliet by Dire Straits

Uprising by Muse

Some of these songs use trickier chords and are more advanced, but you can still explore them. Use my song tutorials for extra help, and remember: you should always have some Dreamers in your Songlist! :) If you want to get into slide guitar, A Little Red Rooster by The Rolling Stones is a great one to try out; classic Blues things going on there!

Open A Tuning

Have you heard of Open A tuning as well? So here's some extra information for you! Open A is not the focus of this lesson because it involves tuning strings up, making them more likely to break! But if you're in Open G and want to get to Open A, just get strings 2, 3, and 4 up a tone.

Open G and Open A tunings have the same intervallic relationship! That means you can get to Open A by doing Open G and putting a capo on the second fret. Easier than breaking strings! :)

Open D Tuning

Open D tuning has the notes D, A, D, F#, A, and D. Check the diagram:

Open D is a common tuning for slide guitar, particularly older school slide guitar. Join my video tutorial to explore some chords and fingerings with me. :)

Open E Tuning

Open D and Open E tuning are the same, just like Open A and Open G. I always prefer getting to Open D than Open E because we're tuning strings down instead of up. To get to Open E, tune to Open D and put your capo on the second fret. :) In case you'd like to try Open E Tuning, get this diagram:

5 Songs in Open D Tuning

There are some killer songs to try out in Open D! Here are my favorite ones:

She Talks to Angels by The Black Crows

Even Flow by Pearl Jam

Give Me Shelter by The Rolling Stones

Love The One You're With by Stephen Stills

The Tallest Man On Earth by The Gardener

You'll encounter many The Rolling Stone songs that use Open E! Street Fighting Man and Wild Horses are great examples. Explore them to grow your Blues chord vocabulary and get creative with altered tunings!

What Next?

It's time to muck around and explore the joy of altered tunings! These tunings we just learned are the ones I'd recommend you get started with. Still, the D-A-D-G-A-D is also interesting and very common for acoustic guitar! This tuning is not one that I explored a lot other than for specific songs, but it's super creative, so I'd recommend you do! :)

You can also use these foundation tunings and tweak them to see what happens! Loads of great songs do that - Daugther by Pearl Jam is a great example. Its base is Open G tuning, but we've got the lowest string (the thickest one) up to a G. Great trick.

Again - Don't Be Afraid of Alternative Tunings!

Please, don't make the same mistake I made when I started my guitar journey, which was being afraid to move my guitar neck or break some strings. Retuning a floating bridge guitar might be trickier, but it's not a big problem if you've set your guitar properly.

But if you've got a Floyd Rose style tremolo, you don't want to try mucking around with open tunings because that can be very complicated! So, you might want to save your open tunings to fixed bridges guitar. :)

Open tunings are amazing to experiment with. I hope my advancing beginner students get into them as soon as possible.

This lesson is part of my Beginner Grade 3 course. Check out and full program (it's free!) to unleash your guitar skills. Happy trails!

lessons.text:
Learn Legato Playing the A Minor Pentatonic Scale!

Legato means smoothly, and in practice, it means you'll use hammer-ons and flick-offs instead of picking every note. This guitar lesson will teach you how to do that by playing the A Minor Pentatonic Scale. With this scale, we'll be picking when we move to a new string and then hammering on one note or flicking off. But before we get started, let's review a few things you should know!

Flick-Off or Pull-Off?

Most guitar players and teachers call a flick-off a pull-off. Pull-off is a much more common term, but I don't agree with it! You're not pulling it anywhere; the term flick-off better describes the action that you're using. But how you call it doesn't matter! Pull-offs and flick-offs are exactly the same things.

Hammer-Ons & The Finger Gym

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you met hammer-ons when we learned the Finger Gym Exercise. Missed that out? Please, go back and review that lesson. The Finger Gym is the best exercise for developing your hammer-on skill and general finger strength!

Legato Pentatonics

In this lesson, we'll use hammer-ons and flick-offs very practically, combining them with the A Minor Pentatonic Scale, which you should have learned in our Grade 2. If you're not familiar with Pattern 1 of that scale, you'll need to go back and check it out, as we'll be using that scale to practice our legato techniques. Follow these steps:

Play the first note of the A Minor Pentatonic Scale and hammer the little finger down. If you've learned the Finger Gym, you already know this movement!

Do the same thing on the fifth string, but with your third finger because this is how you play the A Minor Pentatonic scale. So, your first finger, little finger, first finger.

Then, your third finger gets that second note with the same volume as the first. It's the same thing on the fourth and third strings.

Use your little finger on the second string, which goes down on the eighth fret.

Do the same on the thinnest string, all of the way up.

Before we go any further, you must be able to play the A Minor Pentatonic Scale with a consistent speed. Don't worry about trying to do it fast yet. It's much better to play it slowly and get it right!

Do it with a metronome if you can, and don't be in a hurry to speed it up. You must feel confident with it way before speeding it up. My advice is to be able to play at least 10 times perfectly from memory before you even think about speeding it up. Don't forget: perfectly starts slowly.

💡Check out the video tutorial to see what happens when we go down the scale - physically up. It's a great exercise to see if your flick is working correctly, and you'll review the strings you should be muting. A common mistake when playing scale is not muting the notes right!

Now, let me answer a question I always get…

Should You Pick Up or Down?

At this stage of your guitar journey, it doesn't really matter if you choose to pick up or down. I'm playing mostly down picks in this tutorial, but it's not really a big deal if you want to use up picks. Later on, when you're able to play a little bit faster, you might want to start thinking about the picking direction! Still, that depends a lot on the context of what you're playing.

Get Your Metronome!

Once you're confident playing the A Minor Pentatonic scale using hammer-ons and flick-offs, it's time to pop it to the metronome! My recommendation is that you use the speed at which you can play the scale consistently. And don't forget about our little rule of playing 10 times perfectly from memory to only then speed it up!

Transform This Exercise Into a Lick!

A cool little trick is to take this exercise from an exercise and make it into a kind of lick that you might use in a solo. :) It's basically playing a group of six notes that you start off of each string. Simple and effective - check out the tutorial to do it with me.

Work Out Your Pinky First!

You might encounter guitarists using the third finger on the thinnest two strings of the Minor Pentatonic instead of the pinky. Still, I don't recommend you do that for now. I'd encourage you to start this kind of exercise using your pinky because your little fingers are weak, so this little workout will do you some good!

This isn't a string bending lesson. Still, if you're into Blues, you might want to start understanding the difference between the angle of your fingers when playing. You'll never bend strings with a squared angle, and sometimes you'll need to transition between angles so you can bend strings! Check out the video for a practical example, and keep in mind this is something you might want to work on.

Ready for more? This lesson is part of my Beginner Grade 3 - your shift to the Intermediate stages!

Mix Licks Into Your Blues Guitar Rhythm

This Lick-in' Riff will get some groove into your sound!

In this lesson, we'll explore how to mix licks into your rhythm playing! Using Blues as a framework, we'll learn some helpful tricks to start improvising in this style. :)

You'll learn all about mixing your shuffle riffs with some lead lines. The key to improvising and sounding cool is starting simple. The idea is not playing random stuff but being aware of the groove and its beat.

This tutorial is part of my Beginner Grade 3 course! If you're new to JustinGuitar, ensure you've done my 12 Bar Blues Progression lesson before you get into this one.

🚨 Download the TAB and Guitar Pro file in the Resource section. Play with it, but I encourage you to work on your own Blues Study. :) Have fun!

The Key Element Of The Blues Riff

When you start mixing lead lines into a rhythm, the most important thing is that you stay aware of the beat. And you need to know where the groove is. It's what Blues guitar is all about!

You shouldn't be playing licks and doing random rhythms here and there. You should follow a certain structure - or else it can lead to confusion! If you're lost in your sequence, it won't feel right when you come back in your lead lines.

💡 The key thing is keeping time through the lead part. Start with is keeping the rhythm of the licks simple. And - stay hyper-aware of the beat!

5 Ways To Make Your Blues Riff Sound Good

#1 Keep it Simple

When you start, you need to keep it simple! As it gets more complicated - it gets a lot harder when you're trying to feel your way through. Keep it simple. This way, you'll know where you are in the progression. You always know where to get back in when you start simple.

#2 Start & Finish on Beat 1

Make sure that you finish whatever section they're on a beat one. Then move into the change, whether it's the lead or the rhythm. I wouldn't recommend starting the rhythm on beat two for some time. Concentrate on finishing the rhythm on beat one for now. Do some lead line, and come back on beat 1 for the rhythm to keep you on track.

#3 Take your time!

Don't be in a hurry! When I was writing this little arrangement, I spent a while trying to find different licks. There were so many options and different ways of playing the blues! Make sure you explore all that stuff on your own!

#4 Explore with other licks

Explore and improvise using licks that you've learned in other songs. See where they fit in all this! There is a lot of fun to be had here.

#5 Make your tab!

Make your tab use your variations, use your licks but write it as a set piece using this format! It's an excellent bridging step between learning my set one and making up your own. There are no rules here. Explore whatever way you like to play the Blues!

I want to watch you playing this riff. Upload your video in the Discussion area, and feel free to ask any questions! :)

lessons.summary: Triad Chips are incredibly useful for Blues, Pop, and Soul. They're like little slices of the chords, and sound great!
lessons.videoChapters:

lessons.text:
Learn how to play Triad Chips on the guitar!

Triad Chips are incredibly useful for Blues, Pop Music, and Soul. They're just a really common kind of second guitar part! We call them Triad Chips because they're like little slices of the chords. :)

💡Arriving now at JustinGuitar Grade 3 Course? Before starting this lesson, you should complete my tutorial on Arpeggiated Triads! We learned the triad shapes on the thinnest three strings and worked out how to find their root note! We'll review it a bit during this video, but I'd strongly recommend you've checked that out before starting this one.

Let's look at Triad Chops and how to get these chords playing nice and tight short, not sustaining!

Playing Triad Chips

Start with an A Major Triad: we're on the fifth fret because there's the root note A! Your first finger covers the thinnest two strings, and your second finger is down one fret higher than the first finger on the third string. The trick here is to play them very shortly:

Play the chord, then relax your fingers immediately afterward, but don't let them off! You'll get some open strings ringing out if you completely lift your fingers from the fretboard, which we don't want.

When recording this lesson, I noticed that my third and fourth fingers touched the thickest strings. That's something I probably do all the time! My fingers lift a little bit when I press the chord down and immediately go down, so as my first and second fingers relax, the third and fourth fingers go down to mute all the strings. That motion should help you, and notice that we use the outer part of your strumming hand, muting all of the strings.

Now, take your time to practice this new technique. Start with the A Major Triad doing some up strums! Practicing that motion and ensuring you get it right is your first step before thinking about a specific rhythm pattern.

Rhythm Pattern

Once you're comfortable with the mechanics to play nice, tight, and staccato triads, you should work on some rhythm patterns. The one I used in the intro of this tutorial isn't great for Blues, but it's a very common one in lots of other styles. We play on beats two and four using down picks to do it!

💡 A great chord progression to practice this is G, C, G, and D - the same one we used to learn our arpeggiated triads. You should also be familiar with Minor Triads by now, and they also work here! Explore it and see how it goes.

Notice that my strumming hand moves slightly like I'm strumming because that's important for giving it the right feel. Keeping the strumming hand moving all the time helps you lock into the groove.

One of my favorite patterns for Blues doesn't emulate the backbeat, but it sounds great! Experiment, but remember that if you're doing a two-bar sequence, you'll need to change chords sometimes mid-way through that sequence at the end of the 12 Bar Blues cycle. It depends on whether you're playing a Quick Change Blues or a Slow Change Blues. Check out the video tutorial to count it along with me. You can even bring your guitar. :)

What Now?

It's time to experiment with Triad Chips and get creative! I'd encourage you to keep your ear out, listening for examples in the real world that you can copy. Experimenting and playing some real-life songs that use Triad Chips is a powerful exercise.

💡Play along with JustinGuitar Lessons & Songs App! You'll find thousands of guitar karaoke for you with the chords coming up on the screen. A great idea is to choose some beginner songs where the chords are real simple, like only A, D, and E, and jam along with them!

Jamming in real life is even better, so if you have a jam friend, don't hesitate to try some guitar duets. It takes your musicianship to the next level!

Real-Life Examples

🎧 You Better Move On - The Rolling Stones (They come in at 0:46)

🎧 Crazy - Patsy Cline

🎧 Ain't No Mountain High Enough - Marvin Gaye

🎧 Respect - Aretha Franklin

🎧 The Wanderer - Dion

🎧 Wait On Time - The Fabulous Thunderbirds

👉 Up for more? JustinGuitar Grade 3 Course elevates your guitar skills! Don't miss out on the other lessons. :)

lessons.title: Neuroplasticity to Learn Guitar Faster
lessons.summary: If you're over 25 years old, you're an older learner. But here's the latest science to help you learn faster!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Welcome! Basic Concepts

01:39 What is Neuroplasticity

05:34 Failure Triggers

13:43 Exercises & Extra Tips
lessons.text:
Neuroplasticity & Guitar Learning

Are you an older learner? Here's the latest science to help you learn guitar faster!

Most of this information comes from two amazing podcasts by Huberman Lab called “How to learn faster by using failures, movement and balance” and another called “How to learn skills faster.”

Andrew D. Huberman is an American neuroscientist and associate professor in the Department of Neurobiology at the Stanford University School of Medicine Department of Neurobiology. He knows his stuff and references numerous studies during the episodes. His work is fascinating on many levels, and an amazing fun twist in the tail makes for a very interesting and mega-effective practice system!

In this lesson, I hope to summarize the key points related to practicing music with as little as possible use of the technical terms. Most of you have heard the term “neuroplasticity” before, but let's start with a basic definition.

What's Neuroplasticity?

Neuroplasticity is the ability of neurons in the brain to grow, adapt and reorganize to function in a different way than they had previously, usually as a response to some direct experience. Neuroplasticity will help you learn guitar faster and better!

Children learn things quickly because their brains are filled with chemicals that allow neural pathways to change and grow quickly and easily. These chemicals decrease steeply around the age of 25 and get less and less as we get older. :(

If you’re under 25 and reading this - please make the most of your youth and try to get a broad education that includes music, languages, meditation, math, science, and physical dexterity. You don’t ever get to learn things as easily - so make the most of it!

How to Trigger Plasticity

Triggering plasticity as you get older takes effort or necessity! I found it fascinating that I have been teaching beginners using many of his suggested approaches; I just didn’t fully understand why they were so effective. Super cool to get some scientific validation.

If you really need to learn something to survive (hunting for food?), you’ll learn that skill amazingly quickly. I’m not sure it’s quite important enough, but I noticed that I learned skills ‘on the band stand’ much quicker than I would at home. I used to play at a late-night jazz piano bar with a great piano player. He’d call a tune I didn’t know, but somehow I could find my way along and learn the melody and chord changes very quickly compared with my regular home practice.

For sure, I made many blunders, but I suspect the need to not shame myself helped me ingest the music faster. I’m not certain I’d triggered plasticity, but it seems likely.

Failure Triggers

The key finding from Huberman is that failure triggers plasticity and that you should aim to do as many repetitions as possible of any given exercise and not worry about making mistakes. Noticing the errors will help create a neuroplastic state, and when you get the exercise right, you will get a Dopamine surge which your brain will understand as a sign that the correct action was made.

It’s very important to rest after doing the exercise (30 seconds to a minute or more) to allow your brain to ‘digest’ the information, and it will miraculously manage to focus on the correct version and remove the versions with errors. It’s important to sit quietly with your eyes closed, not scrolling social rubbish on your phone! The rest time appears much more important than I’d previously thought and works as a consolidation of the practice and will be further solidified when you sleep! Quality sleep is very important in the learning process.

There are different layers to this as you progress. When you start, it’s important to focus on any errors you make. As you get more experienced and better at the skill, you should focus on one (and only one) aspect of the skill for each practice session.

In my experience, this holds true for physical skills more than mental and technical knowledge. So for chord changes, strumming, string bending - that kind of skill - the many repetitions with lots of mistakes is likely to be the most effective way to learn, especially for older learners.

But I don't think making mistakes is a good idea for theory or knowledge-based activities, like learning scales. Experience has shown me that learning something correctly the first time and not making mistakes, and then using The Spacing Effect (more on that another time!) is the best way to learn things like scales - but the triggering plasticity before you start that kind of practice makes it even more effective - and the way to do it is hilarious and crazy good!

Failure to frustration is a great way to trigger the release of the brain chemicals that allow neuroplasticity. Continually getting something wrong (making errors) helps start the plasticity chemicals pumping; feeling frustrated apparently helps too! But the OMG moment was when he explained that when you fail at something repeatedly and get frustrated by it - the ‘plasticity chemicals’ that are released stay in the system for an hour or more! And importantly:

💡 The thing you failed at does not need to be what you want to work on!

For reasons I didn’t fully understand, a movement that requires balance is particularly good for triggering the plasticity chemicals. So if you want to trigger these brain chemicals that promote neuroplasticity, you need to find a balance-based movement that you are not good at. One that you are likely to get frustrated by after 7-10 minutes. Might be standing on one leg. Might be standing on one leg but up on your toes. Might be doing a handstand. Handstand on a wobble board… You won't get the benefit if you can do it confidently already! So you need to find something challenging. And change it when it stops being difficult.

I know. This sounds crazy!

So, this sounds crazy, right? And I wouldn’t have believed it unless it had come from such an eminent scholar in the field… but attempting to do a handstand for 7 minutes and getting frustrated trying to do it will help you learn guitar a lot faster for the following hour.

So, I suggest learning complex technical stuff like scale patterns for post-handstand practice and going super hard on repetitions. Don’t worry about mistakes in all physical skill exercises.

💡 If you want more detail on the exact chemicals released and how it all works, then you should check out Huberman's podcasts. He’s got tons of fascinating stuff on other things too!

I hope you found this interesting and that it might help you on your guitar journey!

Don't miss my other Effective Practice lessons presented in each Grade 3 module!

lessons.title: Transcribing Open Chords
lessons.summary: Time to sort out songs that use open chords only! Here's a list of 10 incredible tunes you can transcribe. :)
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Open Chords Only!

02:56 10 Open Chords Songs to Transcribe

lessons.text:
Hey, how you doing? :)

If you've been following my free Beginner Guitar Course - Grade 3, you're having loads of fun transcribing Power Chords and easy riffs too! We’ll be revisiting those again soon, but now it's time to transcribe some very easy songs that use open chords! We'll use the same 4-step transcribing system we've learned, and if you get really stuck, you can get a hint on where to get going.

Limitations

We'll only draw on songs that use the basic open chords for these exercises. We'll perhaps encounter small embellishments, but importantly no barre chords. As your ear develops, you can tackle those things without fear. For now, we’ll keep it simple and give your ear time to get stronger!

💡My Interval Ear Training app is an extra resource for developing your ears. All musicians should work on ear training. :)

What to Write

To begin with, just see if you can write down the chords for the suggested songs. Writing out rhythms has further complications and isn’t needed to start transcribing. That said - if you know how to count beats and bars, feel free to add that information when or if you write it down!

Seek The Simple

At this point, you must ignore chord embellishments and other layers of guitar. What you are after here is just listening to the chords and seeing if you can figure them out! Don't forget - we're still in a beginner course! You shouldn't be overwhelmed by small details, so start simple.

💡 I still start simple! I work out the basic chords and then worry about embellishments or linking bass notes or fill. :)

For now, just ignore the extras.

10 Open Chords Songs You Can Transcribe Today

Here are 10 easy songs you can transcribe that use open chords only!

Song #1 - Me & Charlie by Lee Hazlewood

This song is not super popular, so it might be a good one to explore! It only contains 3 easy open chords.

Song #2 - Knocking On Heavens Door by Bob Dylan

You might already know how to play this song, but if you don't: give it a try! It has 4 open chords, and you're definitely familiar with them.

Song #3 - Lucky Man by The Verve

This song also has only 3 chords, but here's a hint: one of them isn't Major or Minor chords. :)

Song #4 - Working Class Hero by John Lennon

This John Lesson classic song is a fun one to transcribe! It only has 3 chords, but the bass note changes sometimes. Keep your ears aware of that!

Song #5 - For What It’s Worth by Buffalo Springfield

Another super easy song to transcribe, with 3 open chords you know pretty well. Some chord changes happen faster, but that shouldn't be a problem!

Song #6 - Brown Eyed Girl by Van Morrison

This song contains 4 open chords, but there are a lot of other instrument layers going on at the same time. It might be a bit trickier, but it's an awesome exercise. Go for it!

Song #7 - Glory Day by Bruce Springsteen

Another fun song to transcribe, using only 3 open chords. This one wasn't in my Beginner Course, so if you're not familiar with it, give it a good listen!

Song #8 - Breakfast At Tiffany's by Deep Blue Something

This classic soundtrack only contains 3 open chords, and it's loads of fun to transcribe. Give it a try!

Song #9 - Save Tonight by Eagle Eye Cherry

You'll only need 4 open chords here, but don’t fuss about the rhythm, or you might get in trouble.

Song #10 - Every Rose Has Its Thorn by Poison

This song is in Eb tuning, which should be a problem. :) Also, it only uses Stuck 3&4 Chords.

💬 Have more suggestions? Drop them in the Discussion section!

What Next?

Don't forget your goal here: transcribe only the open chords! Don't worry about getting into rhythm and embellishments; concentrate on your chords only. You can revisit these songs once you're more confident.

You shouldn't try to transcribe songs that use chords you're unfamiliar with, or you might end up in a very frustrating situation. If you have questions or suggestions, reach out to the Community. We're here for you!

Ready for More? Explore my Grade 3 Course. It's free and your ultimate pathway to the Intermediate stages!

lessons.text:
It's time for your practice schedule!

But don't be in a hurry to jump past Module 18. :)

You should ensure you have a good time exploring your open tunings and practicing your Solo Blues. There's not much point in following these lessons if you don't learn them properly!

💡Don't forget to follow a holistic practice routine. You should follow a balanced practice schedule to improve your guitar skills.

Module 18: Suggested Practice Routine

The following suggestions work great for practicing Module 18 but don't forget to adapt it to fit your goals. You'll need to decide a few things to personalize this to your needs. Here's your recommended practice schedule:

5' Technique - Minor Pentatonic Legato 5' Technique - Picking Individual Strings While Strumming 5' Knowledge - Open Tuning 5' Knowledge - Music Theory 5' Repertoire - Using Triad Chips 5' Repertoire - Song Revision 5' Time - Mixing Licks With Rhythm 5' Time - Play along with awesome songs 10' Ear Training - Transcribing Open Chords 10' Improvising - Jam Sessions

Section #1 - Technique - 2 x 5 minutes

Legato Pentatonics + Picking Individual Strings While Strumming

In the first technique slot work on the Legato Pentatonics. Remember to do it with a metronome. Don't be in a hurry to speed it up - aim to play at least 10 times perfectly from memory before you even think about speeding it up.

Decide yourself how to fill the second slot. Perhaps you need more time on Picking Individual Strings While Strumming and you could mix this up with more Finger Gym work if you feel the need.

Section #2 - Knowledge - 2 x 5 minutes

Open Tunings + Music Theory

Explore the new open tunings we learned in this Module! At this stage of your guitar journey, exploring open tunings will help you discover incredible new sounds and stay inspired.

By this stage of your journey, you should understand basic Music Theory. If you haven't started my Theory course, do it now; the first grades are free. You can adapt your studies and practice to fit your guitar goals, but just a bit of Theory can take you there faster - so don't neglect it.

Section #3 - Repertoire - 2 x 5 minutes

Triad Chips + Open Tuning

To consolidate what we learned in this Module, you should practice some songs that use triads and spend some more time exploring open tunings. But don't forget to observe the repertoire you want to play when adapting this routine to your needs!

Section #4 - Time - 2 x 5 minutes

Mixing Rhythm & Licks + Triads

Dedicate time to play along with any songs that you already know. I used to do that when I was a beginner! It's a great exercise to help you consolidate your rhythm and get a solid time feel.

For Module 18, practicing some songs with Triad Chips is a great idea!

Section #5 - Ear Training - 10 minutes

Transcribing

Keep training your ears! Don't miss out on these easy open chords songs you should be able to play by ear. Transcribing is a great practice when transitioning from the beginner stages to the Intermediate level.

Section #6 - Improvising - 10 minutes

Jamming

If you know another musician, don't hesitate to schedule some jam sessions. Dueting benefits your musicianship on many levels, and you'll grow a lot as a guitar player by doing so. Don't have a jam buddy but would love to improvise and have a jam session experience? JustinGuitarJams is the way to go!

🚨 Save the pre-made practice routine for Module 18 to your Dashboard! Under the video, click on the 'Practice' Tab and save the pre-made practice routine for Module 17. Go to your dashboard to access and edit the items. Don't have a JustinGuitar account yet? Register for free!

Ready for More? Let's Go to Module 19! :)

lessons.title: 3 Types of Songs You Should Practice
lessons.summary: Learn to make the best out of your song practice so you keep your motivation high and your repertoire growing!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 WARNING - Just talking today! :)

00:10 Which songs should you practice on guitar?

01:28 Campfire Songs - Why & How

04:45 Campfire Plus Songs - Why & How

05:45 Developers - Why & How

07:54 Dreamers - Why & How

12:12 How to stay motivated when learning guitar

14:00 Effective Practice for Beginners: Extra Tips
lessons.text:
Learning guitar is all about playing songs!

Here's how you make the best out of your practice.

The purpose of a balanced practice routine should be to help you achieve the skills you need to play the songs you want. But what songs should you be working on?

Many guitar students will fall into traps when it comes to choosing their repertoire. Many will fall into traps of playing too easy tunes and then getting bored, or too hard songs and then getting discouraged!

So how does one find the balance? Well, I'm glad you asked. :)

Which Songs Should You Practice On Guitar?

I recommend that all guitar players work on three types of songs at any one time. Here are they:

🏕 Campfire 🎯 Developers 🙌 Dreamers

You might think this makes no difference, but I promise - it's a big deal! And that simple trick can really help you stay motivated, something many guitar players struggle with. It will also help you refine your practice routines and help you explore new techniques and concepts!

Now, let's explore the different types of songs and how and why they are so beneficial. Then I've got a bunch more tips on using your song repertoire to develop any new skill or technique you learn!

🏕 Campfire Songs - How & Why?

If you play guitar, you'll probably want to play songs in front of people at some point! So I still get surprised when encountering people who have played for a long time and never developed a good repertoire! Please, don't be that person - and here are my tricks to help you out.

Well, Campfire Songs is what I call the songs you should be able to play with ease. The ones you can REMEMBER and play confidently. As an advancing beginner guitar player, you should have at least ten songs you can play at a party!

I'd recommend thinking about your social circle when deciding what will be on your list. Think about where and with whom you might play those songs, and then choose appropriately.

For example, in my circle, super popular guitar songs that people will sing along with me are:

Wish You Were Here by Pink Floyd

Hallelujah by Leonard Cohen

Heart Of Gold by Neil Young

Free Fallin' by Tom Petty

But if your social circle's taste is more country or alternative rock, choose your songs accordingly! ;) Pick songs you like that are easy to remember even after a few beers! Campfire songs should NOT be complex songs or push you at all. I also suggest revising them every few months to keep your repertoire in mind. Even do some extra revision if you know you have something coming up where you might be playing!

👉 Need some inspiration? I've got over 600 Song Lessons for you! Step-by-step tutorials with chords, lyrics, and TABS to follow along. :) You can filter by difficulty level, chords, and much more!

🔥 Campfire Plus

There's a subcategory in the Campfire Songs section! :) I call it Campfire Plus, and they are songs that are not easy but that you have put effort into and can now play comfortably!

The point here is to collect tunes that you can play with confidence in any situation. Some suggestions:

Sweet Home Alabama (with riffs!) by Lynyrd Skynyrd

Hole Hearted by Extreme

Blackbird by The Beatles

Under The Bridge by Red Hot Chilli Peppers

Let's go further from our comfort zone and talk about Developers.

🎯 Developers - How & Why?

Developers are songs that you can mostly play but have some things that are still a struggle. You should focus your practice routine on developing skills and techniques to play these songs! They could be any style, but do pick things that you're likely to be able to play after some consistent practice.

Be as realistic as you can about your choices here, but don't stress if you underestimate how hard a song is to play. It happens to me all the time.

Eventually, you should play the Developers so well that they will become Campfire Plus! :) As you get more confident on guitar, the songs in that Campfire collection will likely get more challenging. You can always revisit them and include chord melody arrangements, fancy intros, and more.

Some examples:

Angeles by Elliott Smith

Stairway to Heaven by Led Zeppelin

Norwegian Wood by The Beatles

The Needle And The Damage Done by Neil Young

Can't Stop by Red Hot Chilli Peppers

You could also be working on some Rock riffs or Jazz tunes… whatever it is that flips your switch! In this section, you should still be realistic and focus on the songs you'll be able to play well.

🙌 Dreamers

Now it's time to dream a little bit! In this last category, Dreamers, we have the songs you hope to play one day. If you go at these with the right intention, they can be fun and rewarding. I've met many students who started trying to play Dreamers and got frustrated and upset. The result? They lost interest!

So, you should approach songs like this with curiosity! How hard will you have to work to be able to play it? Test out where you are with it. See what things you might need to get onto your practice routine to play it one day.

Sometimes, you will find that song is easier than you thought. Sometimes, you'll find it harder. But giving it a go is the only thing that will let you know! I don't recommend just keeping on a challenging song without the right attitude. It's just depressing. :(

💭 When teaching this 3 Song Type Concept, I made a list of Dreamers and just had a go. It was wonderfully fun and liberating! The secret is to approaching complex songs with curiosity instead of fear. That changed everything. I’d given up on ever trying any songs by Tommy Emmanuel, assuming they would be just impossible for a mere mortal. Still, when I actually took it slow and gave it a try, I found that I could get my fingers around them easier than I thought. Not saying it was easy by any stretch, but I was thrilled to finally muddle my way through a couple of my faves. Once I realized that some were possible, I popped a few into my Developers list. But in contrast, I’ve always wanted to get Cliffs Of Dover under my fingers, but that Eric Johnson thing just doesn’t work for me. I have a go every now and again… add some picking practice to my routine for a bit, but it seems futile! I don’t think I’ll be doing an Eric Johnson cover band anytime soon, but I really enjoy trying.

Keep It Fun!

As your skill set grows, the distance between the three types of song narrows in some ways and expands in others! :) You'll find that there are far more possible songs than you thought! But if you want to branch out more, you might try things you haven't tried before, like Classical, Jazz, and Flamenco… Use your Dreamer Time to explore and have fun!

Taking the pressure off and remembering to have fun with your guitar is super valuable. That's important for guitar players no matter where they are in their journey!

These days, I've been learning all kinds of songs for work, but what I'm talking about here are songs for yourself (in case you're a working musician too!) Sometimes, I deliberately mix things up and teach songs that I really love, even if many students won't be into learning them! Song For George by Eric Johnson and Angeles by Elliott Smith are recent examples because we all have to balance our work and fun time.

Beginners, try some Growers!

If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, you're familiar with the Growers category! :) That's an extra one, and it's what I call songs that you can easily play but that you could develop when your technique grows.

You'll start with easy chords, maybe in a slower tempo, and as you get comfortable with the basics, you can add some embellishments! Wish You Were Here is a nice one to start with, easy chords, not fast - but you can then add ​​intro, maybe the first solo, some slash chords...

House of The Rising Sun by The Animals is another great example! You can play it with strumming and then learn it on fingerstyle or arpeggios with a pick like the original recording!

Many songs fit in this box - many of which you'll encounter in my Beginner Guitar Lessons.

Not Convinced? Read This!

If you're still unsure about how awesome this "guitar trick" is, here's another point! :) Categorizing the songs you learn will help you apply new songs and techniques!

I suggest that when you learn something new, you first experiment with it on a song you're confident with - like a Campfire song! For example, if you want to try fingerpicking, you should do it with a song you know the chords for. You should be comfortable with its chord changes to give your full attention to the fingerstyle - or whatever the new technique might be!

Effective Guitar Practice

As I mentioned earlier, I think the point is playing the songs you love - or writing them. So, your practice schedule should reflect the things you like.

Use the songs you are learning or want to play to help you decide which skills and exercises you will work on in your practice schedule.

💡 Do remember that I suggest your practice routine is half fun and half work. Songs can be either set practice or the fun bit - totally up to you how you schedule things like that!

If you're uncertain about what or how to practice, check out my Effective Practice Course and make the most of your time. :)

Wishing you many years of guitar fun, y'all take care of yourselves, and see you soon.

Now, let's play? Browse from my Free Song Tutorials & create your Songbook!

lessons.text:
Time to explore the G Shape and refresh your basic open G chord!

The open G Chord can be so tasty. :) In this lesson, we'll learn how to quickly pull out many G chord variations anytime you encounter a regular G chord.

💡 This lesson is part of my Chord Shapes Explorer series - included in my Beginner Course - Grade 3. If you've missed the previous lessons, check them out now.

D Chord Shape Explorer

C Chord Shape Explorer

Moving Up Open Chords

And much more to come!

Note: Explorer lessons for all five CAGED shapes can also be found, grouped together, under All Courses here.

G Chord Best Fingerings

If you're following my free beginner guitar lessons, you already know a few different common approaches to playing the G chord as a beginner. You can choose from lots of different fingering options! But it's time to take that even further. :) We'll now explore why there's a preferred option fingering if you want to get into many embellishments.

Many of you started learning the G chord using three fingers unless you learned to play it with me! In which case, you would have learned to play a 2-finger G Chord - the grip I recommend for beginners - or the 2-finger G Chord that I recommend for the acoustic guitar.

Regarding variations, the 3-finger grip is just not great. You're better off using your fingers 3 & 4 only and easily accessing the full scale. Check out the video tutorial to watch what I mean and explore some incredible G chord variations you can try from there! It's easy and effective. :)

G Chord Variations

Explore the G chord from the fingering that has your fingers 3 & 4 down. Follow this step-by-step:

Place your third finger on the third fret of the thickest string.

Use your third finger to mute the fifth string as well.

Your little finger is on the third fret of the thinnest string.

You've just got loads of G chord embellishments and variations to explore from that starting point! Let's look deeper into some of them.

The Gsus Chord

Add your first finger to the first fret of the second string, and you'll get a Gsus chord. Praise that chord! :) In all seriousness, the Gsus chord is a lovely variation to explore on the guitar. Just popping that extra finger there sounds very interesting. Give it a go and see it for yourself.

The Lydian Mode

Put your second finger down on the second string of the second fret, and you'll encounter a very specific sounding G chord. It's not one you'll use a lot, but it's worth trying. Check out my Theory course to learn more about the Lydian Mode!

Meet the Gaadd9 Chord

More useful than exploring that Lydian Mode would be putting your second finger down on the third string of the second fret. How lovely is this chord? We call it the Gadd9 chord. Easily replace the regular G chord for this variation to spice up your playing!

💡Put the first and the second fingers down at the same time, placed as we learned in the previous two chords! It sounds great, and you can create incredible sounds just by exploring these chord fingerings. This little bonus is one of my favorite G chord variations ever. :)

Rock & More

Now your second finger goes down on the second fret of the fourth string, which gives you a Rock and Roll sound. Very tasteful! Again for bonus points, add your second finger down on the second fret of the fourth string. Your first finger goes down on the first fret of the second string, so it's almost like you're adding a C chord. It sounds lovely!

💡 Sometimes, you'll find that putting your first thing down sounds a little bit hazardous. Explore and see what works and what doesn't. :)

Don't forget to explore hammering on the second finger. It might sound good! Don't worry too much about the technicalities of each chord. Just focus on listening to the chords you're playing and letting your ear decide if it sounds good!

The G7 & Gmaj7 Chords

Lifting off your little finger and putting your first finger down on the first fret gives you a G7 chord. Now put your second finger down, and you have a Gmaj7 chord. You can hear the difference between Major 7 and Dominant 7 sounds. The easiest approach to choosing when to use each one is by listening to them!

Open More Doors!

Be aware that this G chord fingering gives you easy access to a scale, and you'll open a few extra doors! If you're a songwriter, this is the kind of toolkit that can help you find pretty interesting ideas!

Try chord variations on any of the songs you're familiar with, and if things start to go wonky, that's okay too! It doesn't have to sound good immediately. Focus on experimenting with the different fingerings and trying to train your ear to decide what sounds good. Your goal is to link your musical imagination with your hands. :)

Ready to go further and become an Intermediate guitar player? Check out these free lessons!

lessons.text:
Learning to Sing (or how to suck less at singing)

I don't feel I'm a singer, but I enjoy singing, and I think I've improved my singing decently in the last few years. If you've been following my YouTube channel for some time, you'll know I'm responsible for a few atrocious vocal performances! Looking back at it now, I was making some very obvious mistakes that you're probably making too. :) So, today's lesson is all about helping you get over common singing mistakes.

But before we get started…

🚨I'm not a singing teacher.

I have had some singing lessons with super duper singing teachers and vocal coaches. Still, many singing teachers are teaching you to sing high level. They approach things like being aware of your breathing, making sure you're aware of the breaks in your voice, singing exercises, vocal warm-ups, etc.

But, honestly, that's not the singing I wanted to do. My goal was always to be able to sing well enough to sing a song that I've written and sing it in tune. I wanted to be able to sing a song in a YouTube video and not suck.

Back in the day, some of my vocals were pretty appalling, and people piled onto me. When you get loads of negative feedback on stuff, it ruins your confidence and makes you less able to sing!

So, today, I'll share my best tips and tricks that you wouldn't get from a vocal teacher. By the end of this lesson, you'll… be able to suck less at singing! :)

A Practical Approach With 10 Basic Points

We'll start from the very beginning, and you'll learn to identify if you're singing in tune and discover how to use your voice in a way that feels good. You'll learn my favorite tips to help you sing the songs you love in a comfortable way that works with your guitar playing.

In this lesson, we'll learn the first steps of singing and how to make the best out of your voice and sing songs you love in front of people. Without sucking or being out of tune. :)

We won't be approaching the best posture and technical things like that. If you'd like to learn to sing like that, looking for a vocal coach is your way. Starting with the basics is always a great idea.

Now let's explore 10 points to help you sing without annoying your audience. :)

Point #1 - Singing in Tune

Are you singing in tune or not? This is a very common question and the first thing you must learn when getting into singing. But how does that work?

A really good starting point is to play a note on the guitar and then try and sing that pitch. You probably don't want to start too high, which would be difficult even for a great singer.

💡C is an excellent starting point note for most boys and girls. It's the third fret of the fifth string!

A beginner exercise is playing a note on the guitar and then trying to find the pitch with your voice. Start with C and explore it from there, but don't forget: when you're learning a new skill, it's normal to suck at it when you first start.

The more you practice, the quicker you find the right pitch. Consider using a tuner if you're worried about finding the right pitch. It doesn't matter what tuner you've got. Just pick a note, play it, and try to reproduce it with your voice using your tuner to check you out.

🚨The down point about using a tuner is that you won't be developing your confidence in your ability to find a pitch.

You need to be able to find a pitch in a song. Watch the video for an extra tip and some practical examples.

Point #2 - Singing Dynamics

This was probably the biggest mistake I made back in the day. When I watch myself singing back then and sounding bad, it's usually because I was trying too hard and straining.

I've always been a heavy guitar player and attempted to hit the strings pretty hard, so I had to sing loudly and project my voice when singing and playing. It was when I noticed that I needed to work on my singing.

When watching singers like James Taylor, Chris Cornell, Sting, or whatever, they never looked like they were straining - maybe occasionally when they're really going for a note! But most of the time, they looked relaxed, especially James Taylor; it's like he doesn't even seem to open his mouth!

I started experimenting with quieter singing, which made much more sense. Suddenly, my voice sounded better, and I could sing in tune. I wasn't running out of breath, and my voice dramatically improved. I even started playing more fingerstyle, so my guitar would sound quieter, and I wouldn't need to strain my voice!

Point #3 - Learning to Talk-Sing

Mark Knopfler is a great example of this! Talk singing is a great way to get into a song and be able to sing it with confidence. That's because you can always rely on it. Think about your repertoire and what songs you could talk-singing. You can interpret a song in many ways; just be yourself and see what works for you.

💡Learn to play guitar and sing at the same time! If you can't strum and sing a song is because you haven't automated one of the parts. That lesson will teach you just that. :)

Once you can sing an individual pitch note and have worked on your dynamic, the next step is singing scales along with playing! Let's look at it.

Point #4 - Singing Scales

Singing and playing a Major Scale is an excellent starting exercise. Once you're confident, the next stage is trying to sing intervals. Playing and singing a scale up and down will help you discover your range. More about that later in this lesson!

Point #5 - Melodies on Guitar

Working out the melody of songs you want to play on the guitar is also very useful; just doing that will make singing easier.

💡Hallelujah by Jeff Buckley is a relatively easy song to try! It only uses simple chords, and it has a remarkable melody.

If you're one of those people who aren't sure if you are singing in tune, you think you might be, but you're not really sure, finding the melody for the song on the instrument is the way to go. Playing along with it and checking your pitching is one of the best exercises beginners can do. It'll benefit your total musicianship!

🚨One of the biggest beginner mistakes I see is not knowing the starting note. Make sure you always know what's your starting point.

Point #6 - Breathing Exercises?

Breathing is important. Your posture and how you breathe really can change your singing! Personally, I didn't find that breathing exercises helped me sing better. But an improvement in my overall fitness seems to have helped. So, I encourage you to exercise regularly; it helps to make your entire life healthier and improves the quality of your voice. :) A win-win!

Point #7 - Imagine the Sound

You must also imagine how you want your voice to sound. A good tip is listening to singers you love and observing how they phrase things. Does it sound relaxed or strained? How are they ending the notes? Are they holding notes for very long, or do they drop off quickly?

Imagining and researching how you want your voice to sound is a fundamental part of your musical journal.

Point #8 - The Hows & Keys

Experimenting with your voice to see what works and what your voice is capable of can be very empowering. And don't forget: you want to look for a way of sounding natural while staying comfortable.

Point #9 - Absorb Their Style

Copying the singers you like and trying to absorb their styles works great! It's like improvising the Blues, which might open many doors for you! You can find your own style by analyzing and experimenting with references that keep you inspired. Don't forget to notice what you don't like too. It's as important as noticing what you like. :)

💡 Open Mics are a great opportunity to observe how other artists sing. Be an observer and try to figure out what you link and what you don't like when you watch someone singing.

Have you found references and traces that inspire you? Try to emulate them! This process really helps you develop your own style.

Point #10 - Record Yourself

Recording yourself tells you what needs to be done to improve your singing - and playing. It'll help you realize what you do and work, and most importantly, what you need to improve. Recording yourself and listening back helps you identify problems and correct them!

💡Share audio or video of you playing in the JustinGuitar Community. Ask for feedback, listen to peers, and discuss your struggles and successes!

Record yourself and improve your confidence by noticing your improvements and how far you have come!

And… you can do it!

If you're not tone deaf, you can learn how to sing. I'm not saying everyone can sing and sound great - but everyone can learn how to sing! Pay attention to the song's dynamics, your voice volume, and how it all fits together.

Take it slowly, be gentle to yourself, but don't miss out on recording your progress and analyzing the things you can improve on. Ear training and some basic Theory will help you achieve your goals faster. ;)

Let's Play? Choose from one of my 650+ song tutorials!

5 Fingerstyle Patterns in 4:4 Time for (Advancing) Beginners

This lesson will teach you five particular fingerstyle patterns and a very interesting way of practicing them.

🚨 Learning to play guitar? Before you start, ensure you're hip with the fingerstyle basics, such as anchor fingers and finger positions, that we learned in our Grade 2. At this stage, you should be comfortable playing the fingerstyle patterns in 6:8 that we learned back then.

If you haven't checked out that lesson, please do it before embarking on this one.

A Back Story

Let me get into a little bit of the back story. When I was studying classical guitar, everyone used the Giuliani Studies, a set of different fingerpicking patterns based on these two particular chord shapes. Now, when we're playing Modern Pop or Folk fingerstyle, the three fingers cover the thinnest three strings, and the thumb has to cover the three thickest strings, the E, A, and D strings.

In this lesson, we'll use one set chord progression and apply the fingerpicking pattern each time. That chord progression is A minor to C to D Minor to E. A very common chord progression, but we're choosing it mainly because it gives us all the different root notes.

The Chord Progression

We'll use the chord progression Am - C - Dm - E to learn the following patterns. It works great because of the different root notes:

The A minor and the C chords have a fifth string root. Our thumb will be playing the fifth string.

The D minor chord has the root note on the fourth string. Our thumb will be playing the fourth string.

The E chord has the root note on the thickest string. Our thumb will be playing the thickest string!

In all the different patterns, fingers 1, 2, and 3 will stay the same. The thumb will move around from the fifth string twice, then to the fourth string, and then to the thickest string. We repeat that cycle.

One Pattern at a Time!

We'll learn one fingerstyle pattern at a time, and I suggest you get really comfortable with each pattern before moving on to the next one. If you're a JustinGuitar student, you're familiar with this principle: it's better to do a few things well than lots of things badly.

We aim to play each pattern consistently four times and then move on to the next. Make sure you can play the fingerstyle pattern correctly with a good technique. Never practice with a bad technique! You want to do things slow enough to get the technique right and ensure none of your fingers are grabbing.

The Metronome

Get each note ringing out comfortably. Once you can do it perfectly in time, you want to practice it with a metronome. Keep it slow and only speed it up when confident. Practice each pattern until you can play it at least four times perfectly in a row!

4:4 Fingerstyle Pattern #1

The first pattern uses your thumb and fingers 1, 2, and 3. The thumb plays the fifth string, the root note of Am, our first chord, and the fingers 1, 2, and 3 play the thinnest three strings.

We'll always play the third string with the first finger, the second finger plays the second string, and the third finger with the thinnest string. So, this is the pattern 'thumb, one, two, three." The 1, 2, and 3 refer to the finger numbers, not the strings. Don't confuse that.

🚨 You Must Sound Clear! If a note isn't ringing out, it's the fault of your fretting hand. At this point, you should have your chord sounding nice and clear, so make sure you get it right. Fingerstyle is very revealing because you're checking each of the notes in the chord individually! Fingers not pressing hard enough or are too far away from the fret are common problems to watch out for. If it doesn't sound right, fix it!

Before going any further, practice this pattern until you can automate it. You should be concentrating on the technique! Once everything's feeling comfortable technically, you can work on changing chords. Follow this chord progression:

Start with an Am chord, and play the pattern twice. The thumb plays the fifth string.

Change to a C chord and play that pattern again. The root note is still on the fifth string, so the thumb stays where it was.

Then we play the Dm chord, and the thumb moves to the fourth string. The rest of the pattern stays the same!

To wrap up, you have the E chord. The thumb is playing the thicker string

Back to the A minor.

We don't get any gaps between the chords. Don't allow any stops there for the chord change!

🚨D minor might be the challenge here. Go back to One Minute Changes between C and D minor if you need some extra practice. ;)

You'll probably find that you can zone out playing a pattern like this for quite some time, and that's really good practice. Focus on your playing now, but longer-term, fingerpicking patterns have to become automated! And don't forget: practice makes permanent, so practice perfectly. ;)

4:4 Fingerstyle Pattern #2

This pattern is very similar to the previous one, but we're reversing the order of the fingers. Start with the thumb, then the third finger, the second finger, and the first finger. Practice this pattern until you feel relaxed and can zone out!

4:4 Fingerstyle Pattern #3

Now we'll play the bass note on beat one of each bar. All of the rest is going to be with the fingers. The pattern is T, 1, 2, 3, 2, 1, 2, 3.

4:4 Fingerstyle Pattern #4

Pattern 4 is super common, so you're about to learn not only an exercise! :) This pattern is T, 1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2.

💡 You can use your little finger down as an anchor! It might help your technique. Try it out. :)

4:4 Fingerstyle Pattern #5

We're just changing the order of one of the strings here! This pattern has your thumb, then fingers T, 1, 2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1.

What Next?

What I'd recommend that you do now is work on each of the patterns individually. Ensure that you're playing all patterns confidently and in time, and then go through and play each one back to back without stopping; aim for 4 times on each pattern!

Check This Out!

Why would this lesson teach you exactly these five patterns played four times? So you can download the free Guitar Pro file in the Resources tab and have loads of fun practicing!

Please don't rush this lesson out; make sure you practice the patterns and play along with the GP file, speeding it up as you become more confident. Happy trails. :)

Justin here, but without a guitar!

In this lesson, we'll explore Guitar Pro and how that software can help you develop your musicianship and explore and create music on many different levels! It's been 10 years now that I've been using Guitar Pro all the time, and you probably encountered Guitar Pro files in my free lessons before.

Guitar Pro is a fantastic tool for guitar players, and you have endless ways of using it. I'm also a big fan of the company developing that software; they're constantly striving to improve it! Guitar Pro has grown incredibly and recently introduced very helpful new features!

🚨 This lesson is not an ad. Guitar Pro didn't pay me to do this video! I genuinely believe this is a great moment in your guitar journey to start exploring that software if you haven't already. 💸 However, if you buy Guitar Pro through any link on this website, you get a discount on their current price, and I also get a kickback. Use code JUSTINGUITAR on the checkout, and off you go. :)

Now let's explore how you can benefit from a Guitar Pro license!

4 Ways to Use Guitar Pro

I use Guitar Pro in mainly four different ways:

Transcribing

Practicing

Creating

Teaching

#1: Guitar Pro to Transcribe & Explore Rhythm

In the video, we'll discuss some basic things you might want to know when using Guitar Pro. You'll notice how adding rhythm notation to your transcriptions is easy when using Guitar Pro. You'll surely need to understand how rhythm works; however, Guitar Pro makes it easier to experiment with the rhythms in real time.

🚨If you get the wrong number of beats in a bar, Guitar Pro makes that bar turn red so that you know something is going wrong! You still have to do detective work, but use your ears. You'll learn a lot from this exercise.

There are better ways to learn how to read and write rhythms than experimentation. To go that far, take advantage of my Rhythm Maestro Course - Grade 4! When you have an understanding of rhythm, then inputting the notes into Guitar Pro is easy! You don't need to write the dots; Guitar Pro does that. :)

Adding Audio to Your Transcriptions

This new Guitar Pro feature is incredible! It allows you to add audio to your transcription. The general idea of having the bar line scrolling along with the audio is good for many reasons; check the video lesson to learn more, with a practical example!

👉 I'm using a song by Ariel Posen in this video lesson! He kindly said I could use his tune to walk you through Guitar Pro. :) Posen is an incredible artist and guitarist. If you don't know his work already, check him out.

You'll notice that being able to get the audio into where you're adding the transcription is very cool and helpful! You can also add drums and bass, which is great for getting used to the sound and feel of different instruments. Exploring things like this is beneficial for your musicianship!

#2: Guitar Pro to Practice

Guitar Pro can help you practice! You will frequently find that you must slow down a song when first learning it. Whether you use a real backing track or a midi, Guitar Pro allows you to slow the track down easily! You can also loop certain song sections, which is useful for practicing and transcribing.

You can benefit from Guitar Pro even to nail things like scale practice! You can program the scales you want to learn and then play along with them. It's easy to ensure you stay on time and have all the notes.

👌 Be patient! Learning Guitar Pro might take time and effort, but it's intuitive software! Check out my friend Levi Clay for an awesome series of excellent tutorials on how to work effectively in Guitar Pro. Clay is a professional transcriber and uses Guitar Pro all the time.

Notice that on Guitar Pro, it's really easy to hear back to something you're doing or when you need help nailing something a bit more complex! Commonly, I use Guitar Pro to figure out what a trickier finger-style pattern is. Slowing the original down and looping it is my way to go!

#3: Guitar Pro to Create

Guitar Pro is also a fantastic creative tool. You can just start experimenting with many things, including different instruments, and create your music! If you've always wondered how drums work, you could start with a basic drum and experiment; visualizing the rhythms will be an incredible add-on and help you develop your overall musicianship.

#4: Guitar Pro to Teach

Here's an extra tip. :) Teaching with Guitar Pro is a fantastic thing! You can give things to your students to work on and creative interactive sheet music rather than just having to write things on a piece of paper! Teaching is an awesome way to learn and consolidate your skills, even if you don't want to teach for a living. ;)

lessons.text:
You're Ready to Become a Detective!

Unleash your ears as you approach the Intermediate stages. :)

In this lesson, we'll look into some song suggestions that you should transcribe at this stage of your guitar journey!

💡 This lesson is part two of my Transcribing Power Chords little series. Before you start it, ensure you've completed the Transcribing Power Chords - Part 1. In that lesson, we started with easier songs and learned 4 very easy steps to transcribing.

5 Power Chord Songs to Transcribe

Now, we'll explore 5 songs you should try to work out. These songs are based on Power Chords, and each has something particular. It's normal to feel a bit overwhelmed when you start transcribing songs, so I've been scouring Spotify to find songs the ones that work great for you at this stage!

You'll find some extra tips at the bottom of this text, but don't read them unless you're totally stuck. Now let's look at 5 Power Chords songs you can transcribe today. If you're new to JustinGuitar and aren't following my Beginner Guitar Course - Grade 3, you might want to consider checking that out for some extra skillset. ;)

Song #1 - When I Come Around by Green Day

This Pop Punk classic is relatively easy to transcribe on the guitar. It's only got five chords and a very obvious rhythm. The interesting thing about it and that you need to observe is the tuning!

💡 It's time to become a detective and look further under the surface to determine how the songs were played. :)

When I Come Around was originally played on Eb Tuning, meaning each string would have been tuned down one semitone.

But that doesn't matter for now. Try to work it out in regular tuning first and see what happens. You already know you're looking for Power Chords, and the original guitar was tuned down a semitone.

If you can't sort it out, come back for extra tips. But before that, try listening to the original recording a lot, even before you try to pick it up on the guitar. And remember that if you're playing on standard tuning, you'll sound slightly different from the record.

Song #2 - Hate to Say I Told You So by The Hives

This killer tune brings back many fun memories and is relatively easy to transcribe! All the chords are played with a fifth string root, so Power Chords. Listen to the original record and try to understand how the chord on the thickest string sounds different.

💡 This little detail you want to get used to is the sound of a chord played on the fifth string root and the sound of a chord with a sixth string root. You can play the same chord in different places. Which one sounds better, and what's different about it?

Song #3 - Smokin' in The Boys Room by Motley Crue

This classic 50s Rock is an obscure song but a really cool one. :) It's Power Chords all the way through, using side-stepping, which means that the chords go from a semitone below to the main chord. It's a very common trick; you should get used to it. :)

You'll find a Rock and Roll Shuffle Pattern in this song, but you don't have to play it for now - that's pretty difficult! Pay attention to it, and focus on playing the regular Power Chords.

Song # 4 - Fell in Love With a Girl by The White Stripes

Activate your detective ears because this song requires you to hear whether the chords are a 5-string or 6-string root Power Chord. It should be very obvious because there's no bass in this song. It's guitar, drums, and voice.

💡Sometimes, we rely on that bass sound to tell us where the chord's root note is, which can be quite helpful. Taking it away makes transcribing more difficult but a great exercise.

Many of The White Stripe songs are great to transcribe! They use a lot of Power Chords, but you'll also encounter barre chords.

Remember that you can play any Barre Chord as a Power Chord. So, if you're working on a song full of Barre Chords, you can play it using Power Chords - it'll sound okay, and it's great for the acoustic guitar!

🎶 Polly by Nirvana is an obvious example. Try to transcribe it as well!

Song # 5 - Self Esteem by The Offspring

The Offspring has incredible songs you can transcribe, but it can be pretty tricky. Some songs use a lot of chords and movement, like riffs using Power Chords.

🚨You've got to work out whether it's a 6-string root or a 5-string root Power Chords. Again, that can make a difference!

Transcribing bands like The Offspring can be challenging for the rhythm because they don't simply use straight 8th notes. You can write it down using your current knowledge, but we'll get deeper into writing rhythm in Grade 4.

Train Your Ears!

Train your ears to be a detective when you're working out songs! The more you practice, the more accurate the songs will be and the faster you'll transcribe.

Don't forget that transcribing is a skill you can learn, but it takes time and might be frustrating sometimes. Just stick with it, and you'll soon get all the benefits from transcribing.

Hints

Please, only use the following tips if you can't work a song on your own, ok? Don't cheat yourself!

Song #1 - When I Come Around

Hint 1

Start on Gb!

Hint 2

The chords in the wrong order are Cb, Db, Eb, Gb, and Ab.

Song #2 - Hate To Say I Told You So

Hint 1

Start on a D.

Hint 2

The chords in the wrong order are Bb, C, G, D, and F.

Song #3 - Smokin' In The Boss Room

Hint 1

Chords in the wrong order (not including the sidesteps!) are D, Bb, G, and A, with a brief appearance from E.

Hint 2

Around 2:46, there's a cool 'chromatic climb' where the chords step up one fret at a time!

Song #4 - Fell In Love With a Girl

Hint 1

The chords in the wrong order are A, B, D, E, and F#.

Song #5 - Self Esteem

Hint 1

The chords in the wrong order are A, C, D, F, G, and Bb.

Hint 2

There are 3 progressions, and 2 of them use the same chords.

👉 So, how did you go? Leave your comment and any feedback on this Community topic!
