lessons.text:
Welcome to Module 19 Practice Routine!

Everything is building towards you becoming a rounded player. :)

💡Remember the importance of a focussed practice routine. Spend some time practicing the new and consolidating the previously learned skills.

Module 19: Suggested Practice Routine

These are suggestions for practicing Module 19. I encourage you to be prepared to take an increasing role shaping it to your needs.

5' Technique - Singing 5' Technique - What You Need 5' Knowledge - G-Shape Explorer 5' Knowledge - What You Need 5' Repertoire - 4:4 Fingerstyle Songs 5' Repertoire - Campfire / Developers / Dreamer Songs 5' Time - Play Along With Great Songs 5' Time - What You Need 10' Ear Training - Transcribing Power Chord Songs 10' Improvising - Jam Session

Section #1 - Technique - 2 x 5 minutes

Singing + What You Need

As you should already know, we start with two 5-minute slots dedicated to Technique. In one of those slots, I suggest you work on singing! Playing a note on the guitar and trying to get your pitch in tune is an effective exercise, and working a little bit on the tone of your voice will improve your confidence.

💡Learning to Sing is a really great tool to have in your bag if you're a guitar player.

The other five minutes of your Technique slot could be working on any of the things that we've looked at in the previous Grade 3 modules. It could be:

minor pentatonic legato technique

consolidating picking individual strings while strumming

some more finger gym

Make those decisions based on your own assessment of your progress, your guitar goals and your dream repertoire.

Section #2 - Knowledge - 2 x 5 minutes

G-Shape Explorer + Music Theory or What You Need

For Knowledge, you also get two 5-minute slots. You should spend one exploring the G-Shape. The other slot could be revision of:

open tunings

music theory

Again, decide this based on your goals! If you want to unleash your fretboard, theory might really be the missing piece.

Section #3 - Repertoire - 2 x 5 minutes

Revision + 4:4 Fingerstyle

Repertoire comes with a slot of revision. Make sure you're practicing songs you love and that keep you inspired. Take these from your list of Campfire / Developer / Dreamer Songs. The other slot could be working on a song in 4:4 time that you could play using a 4:4 fingerstyle pattern. ;) You can play any song you've learned in 4:4 that you think might sound cool with fingerstyle.

💡No rules here! If it sounds good, it is good. :)

Section #4 - Time - 2 x 5 minutes

What You Need

Working on your time feel is super important so ensure your timing is consistent! You have many options here. Make a choice based on your needs tied to your goals from:

thumb and finger strumming

mixing blues rhythm and licks

flexing time - the falling leaf

playing along with great songs

Section #5 - Ear Training - 10 minutes

Transcribing

We then have Transcribing, which is a longer slot. For Module 19, we're back at Power Chords, but with slightly harder songs. Transcribing is a fundamental piece to explore if you want to progress to the Intermediate stages and become an independent guitar player.

Section #6 - Improvising - 10 minutes

Jamming

And it's time for some Improvising! Using the Major Scale or the Minor Pentatonic, depending on what sort of improvising you enjoyed the most. Try to duet with other guitar players or any musician really. You'll benefit a lot from it!

Don't rush, and practice consistently. When you're ready, move on to Module 20!

Welcome to Module 20!

We have lots of interesting things to learn. :)

Let's check out what's on the menu:

The Spacing Effect - A cool psychological trick that you can use to help you remember your songs, chords, and scales.

The Lifted Barre Chord - A great chord trick, a mix between Power Chords and Barre Chords. ;)

Playing & Singing at the Same Time - How do you play guitar while singing? Well, I've got a 10-step method to help you learn that valuable skill!

Chords & Keys - learn what chords in keys mean and how to (easily) apply that knowledge on the guitar!

How to Co-Write Songs - learning about songwriting will help your general guitar playing even if you're not into writing your music!

And loads more! We'll keep learning about transcribing and other fun stuff to consolidate your skills and prepare you for the Intermediate stage.

lessons.title: The Spacing Effect
lessons.summary: Easily memorize new songs and licks on the guitar! But really - the Spacing Effect is a technique that helps you memorize almost anything. ;)

lessons.text:
The Spacing Effect is a technique you can use to memorize almost anything.

In this lesson, we'll explore how to use this technique to learn songs and licks on the guitar. Memorizing a few things is important to all guitar players! You don't want to always rely on a songbook, licks page, scale diagrams, or whatever. The Spacing Effect technique will help you memorize many things you can access when needed.

This technique involves learning and revising things over a gradually increasing time frame, which is much more effective than trying to learn things in one time block.

The Science Behind It

The Spacing effect has been recognized since the late 19th century, when Hermann Ebbinghaus first wrote about it. It has become one of the most consistently repeatable concepts born out of experimental psychology. Solid science.

The point of this lesson is to teach you how to use this science to help you remember songs and licks. I guarantee this works!

💬 Storytime! I first learned about this idea in 1995 while studying at the Tasmanian Conservatorium of Music. I learned 20 or 30 pieces for my final recital, and I can still remember them today because I applied these principles!

Now let's get started and check out how to use the Spacing Effect technique to boost your guitar playing!

How To Easily Memorize Almost Everything

You always want to ensure that you practice in short, concise blocks, usually around five minutes long. There are a few reasons for this, but it's mostly because people can't fully focus for longer than five minutes. Secondly, if you're trying to learn a whole bunch of things, you don't want to work on them for too long! Thirdly, it'll help you space them out - and here's the trick.

🚨 If you're doing short blocks, leave a little gap between your practice blocks when designing your practice schedule. So, if you're going to practice for five minutes, leave a one-minute gap before you start your next five-minute block. It'll really help consolidate the information!

It's important to give your brain a chance to digest what you're learning. You don't want to go straight from one thing right into another, then right into another. So, practice in five-minute blocks and leave a little one-minute gap in between each of your practice blocks.

☕️ Have a cup of tea or coffee, or look out the window! Stand-up exercise is always a good thing to do - it's a little reset before you hit your next practice block.

From my experience teaching for over 30 years now, it is much much more effective to do 6 five-minute practice blocks during a week than it would be to do a one-hour practice block.

Isn't this a little counterintuitive?

You might think this doesn't sound like a good idea. After the five minutes, you might want to keep going because you haven't finished or are excited. Still, I'd encourage you to try just doing little five-minute blocks, even if you feel you're not done or could go further. Just stop!

How often should you practice guitar a week?

My generation recommendation is to practice 6 days a week for a shorter period. An interesting analogy to help you understand the Spacing Effect is the idea of RAM and hard drive space!

💡RAM stands for Random Access Memory.

When you first learn something, it goes into your short-term memory - your RAM. After some time, it'll disappear off into the long-term storage - your hard drive. When you revisit it again, your brain brings that piece of information back into the RAM. After a few revisits, your new learning will live permanently in a part of your drive that's more easily accessible than the long-term storage!

Key Points to an Effective Learning Process

Some studies show that leaving things for longer than 4 days is like learning them again for the first time. So, particularly in the initial stages, you don't want to wait longer than 3 days before you revive something.

Ideally, you learn it the first day and revise it the next day. Then, maybe leave a gap day and revise it again. That's where you're starting the process of elongating the recalls, which will put things into this permanent memory so you'll never be able to forget stuff, even if you wanted to!

🔑 To get that song, lick, or scale into your permanent memory, you need to gradually increase the time between revisiting the information. That's the key thing!

But don't forget to ensure that you got it right first! Start slowly, and practice carefully.

Memorizing New Songs

I recommend getting your songs up to a performance level. Once you've got it, you want to leave it for a whole week without looking at it. Then, revise it for:

- Two weeks;

- A month;

- Three months;

- Six months;

- A year!

Again, this might sound a little bit crazy, but it works! I still remember songs I learned over 15 years ago!

Studying Music Theory & Learning Scales

Spend one hour learning a scale up and down, and you'll probably find that you can play it pretty confidently. If you went for the five minutes a day, every day for a week, you'd actually have done less practice. Still, your brain would have digested the scale so that you could play up and down inside and out or even jumble up the notes better!

When learning Music Theory in short blocks, you help your brain digest everything and make further connections you wouldn't have had a chance to make if you were learning it all in one large block.

Sleep!

Good sleep is crucial to the way we remember things. So, ensure you get a good night's sleep after a heavy practice session! That really is going to help your attention and your ability to absorb the information.

There's always a lot going on in our subconscious after we've learned new things. We don't even realize that our brains are doing anything, but it's sorting out all the new information! It's cataloging and making connections between different things.

If you're always tired, your brain will not learn new stuff very well. Ensure you find a nice way to get a good night's sleep!

Memorizing Blues Licks

Blues licks are an important part of the Blues language. The Spacing Effect technique is very useful when learning a new language!

When you're learning a new language, you're looking for retention. You don't want to look at a book or a page of licks while doing a solo. You need to access your licks instantly without having to think about them.

So, even though the initial learning phase might take a little longer when using the Spacing Effect technique, your retention will be stronger!

Scheduled Revision

You must use a scheduled revision calendar! You can use a task manager app and set reminders to pop up when it's time to revisit something. You could also do it in a paper book, which I used to do back when I was studying Classical guitar.

Semantic Priming

A beautiful little thing you might like to try is Semantic Priming. The idea here is that when you're learning new information if it's related to something you've learned before, it's easier to remember. So, anytime you're trying to learn a new thing, see if you can find something related to that, so you've already got somewhere to store that information - like a folder on your hard drive!

For example, if learning a new song, you might play a similar song by the same artist or uses a similar technique. Like that, you tell your brain where the new information belongs. It's jaw-dropping, eh?

Learn More! Explore my Advancing Beginner lessons and unleash your guitar fretboard.

lessons.summary: Use this easy trick to transform barre chords like F into lush open chords you can play all over the fretboard!

lessons.text:
Sound Lush on The Guitar!

Use a Barre Chord Shape with some open strings and add extra textures to your guitar playing!

This Barre chord trick will make simple chord progressions sound much more interesting! You can use this simple trick in many different ways, and this lesson will give you loads of insights to try out.

If you can handle an F Barre Chord, remember the hardest part is the actual barre. It's not putting the rest of the fingers down! So, the cool thing about the trick we're about to explore is that it starts with a barre shape but lifts the first finger off all of the notes except the root note.

Before you get started, make sure you know the root notes of the thickest two strings. You'll need that to find chords in your fretboard; just like we did when learning our Power Chords!

The F Chord/E Shape Barre Chord

This lesson will start off using an F chord, which is an E Shape Barre Chord. We call it an E Shape because if we took the barre away and slid it down, it looks like a regular E chord. Check out my Ultimate Guide to Easy Barre Chords to improve your barre chords skills and learn how to slide your E Shape Barre all over your fretboard.

Now, we'll play with our first finger only the thickest string, not the full barre. Watch the video tutorial to learn more about fingering.

When to Lift Your Barre

This trick makes your chord progression sound much richer and more interesting. You shouldn't do it all the time because too much of it would end up sounding boring, but explore some of the chord shapes you already know using this trick and see what you get!

The Lifted Barre Chord is a creative tool, and now it's the perfect time for you to start exploring things like this. Technically, you'll find new chords that sound very lush. If you want to understand the Theory behind them and unleash your musicianship even further, check my Music Theory course!

The Minor Chords

You might encounter a few problems when applying this trick to Minor Chords. You might find that some grips are just too awkward and hard to jump into, especially in live situations. Sometimes, you might even have to remove the root note, and that's completely fine.

💡 Explore some minor grips and you might encounter a chord used in Wild Horses by The Rolling Stones. Watch the video to learn which one!

As a general rule, the chords D, C, B, A, G, F, and F# will give you lush open chords with this trick!

Experiment!

The big takeaway of this lesson is to invite you to experiment! Take a chord progression that you know already and try this trick out. It works great with chord progressions like A, G, C, and A, or G, C, D, and A.

💡 The Blower's Daughter by Damian Rice uses loads of these grips! If you know more songs that use the Lifted Barre Chords trick, let me know in the Discussion section. :)

lessons.text:
Singing and playing the guitar at the same time doesn't have to be a mystery.

I have been playing and singing for a long time, and though I don't consider myself much of a vocalist, I do sing and play at the same time quite a lot - watch my song tutorials to see it. ;)

In this lesson, we'll learn all the steps when I learn a song. That will help you learn how to practice strumming and singing and learn to cover your favorite songs on your own. I broke my technique into a 10-step program to help you get started.

💡 How not to suck at singing! If you're not confident about your singing skills, please watch my lesson on Learning to Sing!

Now let's get started and get you closer to your dream of singing and playing songs on the guitar. Yes, you can do it. 💪

Before We Begin

Before we learn my 10-step method for singing and playing, keep in mind these 5 things:

1 - You can only think about one thing at a time. Don't multitask - it doesn't work.

2 - It's all about automation. Remember how hard it was changing gears when you learned to drive?

3 - You are probably not ready if you are still looking at your chord changes or strumming your hand. Why is strumming so hard? Well, it's not! Here are my best tips for learning how to strum!

4 - Learning one thing at a time before trying to put them together. Don't forget about this! Ever. I've been playing and singing for a few decades and still learn songs like that.

5 - The more you do it, the faster it gets. It might seem a slow process, but do it a few times, and it'll only get faster and easier.

Easy Songs for Singing & Playing

It's also essential that you pick easy songs to start with! Trying to do a hard song when you start will only leave you feeling frustrated and deflated. Start easy and build it up.

Some examples include:

Knockin' On Heaven's Door by Bob Dylan

Three Little Birds by Bob Marley

Feelin' Alright by Traffic

Blowin' In The Wind by Bob Dylan

Brown Eyed Girl by Van Morrison

These super famous songs use the simple chords we learn in my Beginner Guitar Course - Grade 1. They also have simple melodies and are very memorable. You'll need to easily find the song in your musical imagination when trying to sing and play guitar.

Ready?

10-Step Method for singing and playing guitar

Step # 1 - Listen to the song a lot.

And when I say a lot, I mean a lot, at least 10 times in a row, and focus! Try and get inside the track, not just scratch the surface. Try to absorb it. For some reason, headphones seem to work best for me for doing mindful listening.

Step # 2 - Learn the guitar part.

Learning a song on the guitar should require listening, practicing, and possibly playing along with the original recording or with my guitar app. If you struggle with any particular bits, then work on that bit until you get it right.

Step #3 - Have a conversation.

The point here is to distract yourself but keep playing (and sounding good!) Call your imaginary friend because by having a conversation with them, you'll easily be able to tell if you have a guitar part automated enough! It's the best test I know of, and I use it myself. If I can play it and think about something completely different, I know I'm there and ready to think about singing!

♟ I used to play chess games while learning fingerstyle patterns! I'd also review tough matches because I knew that if I could think about that stuff while keeping a solid fingerstyle pattern, I had nailed it.

Step #4. Listen to the song a lot more.

Once you can play the song and keep the rhythm automated, get back to the original recording and listen a lot more. This time, you will listen to the vocals, the melody, how the singer was singing it, and how the lyrics feel on the beat.

Step #5. Study the lyrics.

It's time to write out the lyrics and study them. The better you know the words of a song and have preferably memorized them, the easier it will be to sing and play guitar.

You don't have to memorize the songs completely, but be at least very familiar with them! You can have the lyrics when singing it, but you shouldn't be discovering the words when attempting to sing.

Step #6. Sing along with the original recording.

No playing yet, ok? We will be playing and singing soon, but for now, you should just work on your vocals. Ensure you are comfortable with your pitching and phrasing.

Step #7. Know the syllables when the chords change.

You should know which syllable the chords change within a word, not only what word.

💡 People often write this above the lyrics with an > sign. In my songbooks, you will have the chords written above the syllable of the chord change where possible, which should help you.

This is one of the most important singing tricks I've learned. I still remember when I did - from my friend and incredible singer Salena.

Step #8. Sing along, but with muted strums on each beat.

It's time to put it all together, but don't play chords yet! Just keep the fretting hand loosely on the strings, so you just get a muted click sound. This will help you feel the rhythm of the melody you will be singing.

💡 Learning from my free song tutorials? Don't forget you can get verified chords, tabs, and lyrics with JustinGuitarTabs, so you save time and avoid learning the wrong stuff you find out there. ;)

If you have listened to the song enough, the melody should be in your ear, but internalizing the melody's rhythm takes a little more work for most people! If you struggle with the lyrics at this point, you can try humming along with the melody, but really you want to get those lyrics into your memory bank.

Step #9. Add in the chords, but keep the rhythm simple.

Keeping the rhythm simple will usually mean 4 strums per bar. It will be 3 in 3:4 time! For now, use only down strums and tap your foot with the beat if you can. You should get that foot-tapping automatically, anyway!

Step #10. Play it, fo' real!

It's finally time to add in a strumming pattern! There you go - you are playing the song! If you struggle a bit, don't be afraid to slow it down. It's nearly always easier if you play and sing slower.

More Helper Hints

If you are struggling with any of the steps above, you might find some of these extra hints helpful! But also, be aware that… singing and playing might be tricky, so it takes effort and practice. ;)

The 5-Minute Habit: playing the same thing repeatedly for 5 minutes!

Doing the same thing over and over for 5 minutes every day for a week is a really, really good way to create a habit! So if you struggle with a part of a song, do just that bit! 5 minutes is a long time and will sort out most problems quickly!

Learn to Keep Playing When You Make a Mistake!

Rhythm has been with our species since we made tools out of stones... it's built-in. So it's most likely that nobody will notice if you mix up words or play the wrong chords unless you make a right pig's ear of it!

But almost everyone will notice if you stop or let the rhythm fall apart. So work on keeping playing even if you make a fluff or two. We all do.

Understanding Rhythms Can Help.

Many students told me that understanding and playing rhythms have helped every aspect of their playing, including singing and playing at the same time. So, if you are serious about this stuff, check out my Rhythm Reading book! And go further.

You must automate your fingerstyle (or strumming) patterns by 100%.

If you are still making mistakes in a fingerstyle or strumming pattern, you are most likely to struggle when singing it too. So nail the guitar parts first before you even try!

Switching your focus between the vocal and the guitar.

Some songs have tricky bits and fill between the vocal lines. You will need to learn to switch your focus from the vocal to the guitar and back when playing those. Not that tricky, but like everything else, take some practice!

Harder stuff, like playing over riffs, requires more practice and a solid foundation.

If you want to get into singing over more complex riffs, you will have to work extra hard on them to get them automated. Just going to take a lot more hours of practice and intense concentration.

Will you try this out? Join the Discussion, and let me see how that goes!

lessons.title: Chords In Keys (super easy!)
lessons.summary: This lesson will explain how notes, scales, and chords work and how it all comes together in keys.
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Lesson Welcome

00:59 What is a key?

03:59 Understanding Keys

06:27 Chords in Keys & Guitar

10:21 How does it work?!

13:56 Chords not in key

15:12 What next?
lessons.text:
I wish someone had taught me this trick when I started learning to play guitar.

You're watching a jam session, and the guitar player starts to improvise beautifully. How do they do that? What an insane talent, isn't it? Well, it's not only about talent - that's a magic trick going on there, and today's lesson is all about that! :)

This super easy, simplified tutorial will explain how chords in keys work, which will help you unveil the mystery of improvising.

💡 If you'd like to understand further how the guitar works, check out my Theory Course. In that program, we talk about the Note Circle, intervals, Major Scale construction, and how to use that stuff to play all over your guitar neck and make music freely!

Today's lesson will keep it all simple, as this is part of my Beginner Course - Grade 3. We won't need any Music Theory, but before we get started, there are a few things you should know. Let's take a look at it.

Before Getting Started!

You must know the notes on the thickest 2 strings of the guitar! It would also be helpful if you could play barre chords, but you can still use this lesson if you don't! You can play the chords as open chords when possible, but don't be afraid to experiment.

What is a Key?

A key is a group of notes (usually a scale) that form the foundation for a composition or a section. Oversimplifying, we can say that a key is a group of notes that sound good together.

Why is a key useful?

Understanding keys is one of the most fundamental things to unlock your guitar fretboard. It's essential for understanding harmony! Learn how chords in keys work, and you will:

Be able to find the notes for creating solos, lead lines, and layers

Improvise freely all over the guitar fretboard

Figure out new songs faster

Understand the songs you learn, both chord progressions and solos

Easily write chord progressions for your songs.

But again - this easy lesson is just a shortcut. If you want to go further and unveil your guitar, don't miss out on my Music Theory Course.

The trick you're about to learn is so easy! I wish someone had shown it to me back when I was learning - it would have saved me so much stress. :) We'll learn this Theory-free shortcut in two parts. Ready? Let's go!

How to find the chords in a key?

The first thing you need to do is to memorize the following pattern:

Major - Minor - Minor - Major - Major - Minor

We'll be playing this pattern starting on a G note: play the third fret of the thickest string on the third fret, then we'll miss one note, play one note, miss one note, and play one note. Then, we'll repeat the same pattern on the fifth string, the third fret, the fifth fret, and the seventh fret. Check out the video lesson to learn more and play along with me!

This combination tells you the chords in the key of the first finger placement. How cool is this? However, you must know the notes on the thickest two strings - so don't skip that practice! If you're following my Beginner Guitar Course, we learned essential notes on the thickest two strings when learning our Power Chords. :)

The Missing Note

You might know that the Major Scale has seven notes, but we're leaving off that last note because the chord built from it is very uncommon, at least in Pop and Rock music. That note can overcomplicate things, so we're just going to leave it out and pretend it doesn't exist!

As per curiosity, we call this other chord in a key VII, and it's a semitone lower than the root note, and it's a diminished triad or a minor7b5 chord. You are unlikely ever see it.

That's all awesome. But how does it work?

We'll jump over to the piano to learn this trick, but don't worry - you don't need to have a keyboard at home, and you can easily apply this trick to your guitar! :) We'll start with the Key of C, which uses notes from the C Major Scale - no sharps of flats - just the "white notes" - so it's super easy to see on the piano!

💡Commonly, chords start as triads, a 3-note chord. To play a triad, we play one note, skip one note, play one note, skip one note, and then play one note.

My Theory Course explains how this works, and we can learn it all in-depth. But don't forget to use your ears - or you'll just have to trust me!

Improvise!

When applying this trick to the guitar, you get the idea that the chords and the scale work well together. Watch the video tutorial to see this "pattern" applied on the guitar - but note that I was using this trick very linearly!

But the idea here is ultimately to improvise, so you're normally looking for a bit more motif development. For today's lesson, you just need to clearly understand that the scale and the chords in a key fit together.

🚀 Major Scale Maestro Course! This free Intermediate Grade 4 course has the best tricks to help you get creative and improvise with the Major Scale. :)

For this video lesson, we were in the key of G - but this trick works in any key!

Open Chords Only?

If you're not comfortable with barre chords, you can still use this pattern to figure out the chords and then use them in an open position. It's not just a thing for barre chords - and you don't even need to know the names of the chords! ;)

As long as you stick to the shape and know what key you're in, this cheat will be loads of fun, even if you're only comfortable playing open chords.

Major, Minor, Pentatonic, & Chords not in key

You can use this pattern with the Major Scale, with the Major Pentatonic Scale, and sometimes, it's possible to weave in the Minor Pentatonic. It's theoretically wrong, but there are occasions when you can make it work!

💡The A, D, and E chord progression is a great example. Technically, it should be the Major Scale that works, but sometimes you can wedge in that Minor Pentatonic too.

The Guns and Roses version of Knocking on Heaven's Door is also an excellent exception. Slash plays mostly the Major Scale but then rips into a bit of Minor Pentatonic in there!

So, what about the chords that aren't in a key?

Well, if it sounds good, it is good! There are theory techniques like ‘secondary dominants,' 'borrowed chords,' and 'modal interchange', but basically - it's down to what sounds good!

Improvising over chords that are not in the keys is much more complicated. It's fun, but it's complicated. :) You will find different approaches to doing so! Sometimes, the chords will be mostly in a key, and then they'll just be one or two chords that aren't, in which case you need to treat them separately.

A simple way is to look at the chord shape and pick some notes out of the chords. You will look at a chord and then see the notes you will use! There are more complex versions of doing that, where you can look at modes or a particular scale over a particular chord, but that's not what I'd recommend for your guitar journey.

What Next?

If you want to get good at freely playing your guitar, the answer is pretty simple: you have to practice it. Like with most things! The best way to practice this lesson is by finding a jam buddy! You will agree on a key one, and one person will play the scale while the other plays the chords in any order.

If you don't have a friend to play guitar with, experiment with JustinGuitarJams - or even try to find a local friend in the JustinGuitar Community. :) Good luck!

So, let's keep going with our Beginner Course. This lesson is part of our Grade 3 - don't miss it! ;)

lessons.title: How to co-write a song
lessons.summary: Here is my best advice for beginner songwriters looking to co-write songs!
lessons.text:
I have been songwriting most of my life and have written over a few hundred songs. I've co-written the ones I enjoy the most!

In this video, I hope to inspire you to co-write a song - even if you're still an advanced beginner guitar player. There are no rules for songwriting, and this easy lesson will help you get started and share some of my best practices and tips. But remember: everyone is different - and that's awesome!

The best thing about co-writing for me is your immediate sounding board in the other person. I often find the line between awesome and utter crap is pretty thin, so having someone to bounce ideas around with means that we can greatly accelerate the writing process.

No Rules!

There are no rules for writing songs, either when you're writing on your own or doing a co-write. Everybody has different strengths and weaknesses, and that's cool.

🔑 Great songwriting celebrates individuality.

Don't feel that you should restrict your songwriting partnership in any way! I find that the major benefit of doing a co-write is being able to decide if something is good or not. It's great to get instant feedback! So, it's quite a faster process for me when co-writing.

Sometimes, people are a little afraid of getting into songwriting and bearing their soul to somebody else - but it's worth remembering that many of the greatest songs of all time have come out of songwriting partnerships!

Great Co-Writing Partnerships

Before getting into some more details, let me mention a few famous co-writing partnerships! Lennon/McCartney is an obvious, and Jagger/Richards from the Rolling Stones too. You've also got Benny/Bjorn from ABBA and Page/Plant from Led Zeppelin. There are loads of great examples out there!

In my band, We Came as Strangers, my job mostly comes up with chords, and the singer's job is to find the melody and the lyrics. When dividing your skill set between your different strengths, everything flows better. ;)

How to Find Co-Writers to Work With

You can find somebody to write with in many different ways. I've always preferred being in a room with somebody - so I'd advise you to look for somebody you can meet with locally. I have written several songs online, but capturing the vibe is much more difficult there! It's much easier when you're in the same room.

💬 Join the Discussion in the JustinGuitar Community! You might find somebody to work with locally or virtually. The JustinGuitar Community has thousands of incredible guitar players and musicians from all over the world!

Before you start songwriting with someone, meet them for a coffee or a beer, chat about your favorite songs and references, and get to know each other's vibe. That will make a huge difference!

Be Positive! :)

Find somebody supportive and kind, and don't forget to be that way. :) Don't be too negative! If you're not nice or too picky, with a negative vibe, this won't make for a very cool song.

💡Learning together is way more fun and productive. You can share expertise!

Be flexible, understanding, and supportive. Nobody wants to work with an asshole - especially in something where you will be sharing deep thoughts and feelings. :)

Agreements

It's important to define some basics before getting started! In the beginning, I'd recommend you do an equal split between the people in the room. Some days, you might feel like you've done most of the work, and others, coffee making. On other days, you'll be the one doing less part of the writing, and that's part of the process. Ensure to even things out between you and the co-writers.

Start Simple

You don't need anything more than a guitar and a bit of paper to write a song. If you want to write modern music, meaning heavily produced music, you'll need to get hip with the tech. Still, for starting, try to write something that works well with just guitar and voice!

First Steps into Cowriting a Song

Here is a step-by-step to help you start writing your first song:

1 - You need a few 'seeds' - they are your starting points.

I have a collection of recordings I make on my phone, and then if I have a writing thing coming up, I listen back to a few so that I have some seeds to share! When I meet with a writer, we usually start with a vibe, maybe a style and what we like… then share some seeds - grab one and start to grow it!

2 - Always record your sessions and new ideas.

I also record everything. Usually with two devices - one master and one that we use for rewinding and checking things and recording chunks of material as we get it. Many times someone sings a bit of melody or a new chord, and it's awesome - but they won't remember it later.

3 - Work out your chord progressions and the basics.

Keep your chord progressions simple when you're starting. Use the diatonic chords of a key as a start - but there are no rules except it has to sound good! :) Start with a verse, then decide on a progression and a melody.

Experiment with some words, write another verse… make sure the melody is the same as the first verse. Think simple! Then, experiment with a chorus. It might help to think of verses where you tell your story, and the chorus is where you invite the listener to connect with their own story!

4 - Defining Your Song Form.

Once you have a verse and chorus, it's time to write another verse. Work with the following structure as a starting point:

Verse - Verse - Chorus - Verse - Chorus - Bridge - Chorus - Chorus.

Once you have the lyrics and form, you've written a song. Congratulations! But your song might not be ready, and you're allowed to tweak and change it. Revising and experimenting is common and often a good idea - though learning when to call it DONE is also a good idea!

Don't Expect Too Much

When you're a beginner songwriter, you'll write some crappy songs, and that's ok. You were crap at guitar when you started - so why would this be any different? ;) Study songs you love is, I think, the best way to learn - but that is another lesson for another time. :)

For now - I hope you keep enjoying this Beginner Guitar Course - Grade 3. Happy Trails!

lessons.title: Record Yourself & Production Basics
lessons.summary: Learn how to record yourself playing the guitar and why that's a powerful tool to improve your skills!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Why You Should Record Yourself

03:13 Basic Equipment

06:21 Audio Interface & Software

08:32 Headphones

09:53 Software & Studio Monitors

13:19 Start Recording!
lessons.text:
Recording yourself playing the guitar is so valuable for your journey as a musician!

Recording yourself will boost your confidence when you listen back and realize that you're doing great and improving as a guitarist. It can motivate you to keep going and improve your guitar skills. One of the most significant benefits of recording yourself is getting something tangible at the end of your practice session! When you record yourself, you have something you can show your friends and be proud of at the end! It gives you a sense of accomplishment.

💡 Recording yourself also opens up many other options for collaborating with other musicians. You can give the track to someone else to sing on if you don't like singing. :)

Learning to record yourself is also essential if you're into songwriting. You need to be able to listen to your songs, and recording them will help you present your demo to other writers and singers.

Recording Yourself: Basic Equipment

Recording can be fun, but you need the equipment to start. Let's look at some basic gear you might need!

Microphones

You need to be aware of two main types of microphones: dynamic and condenser. Dynamic microphones are cheaper, and a Shure SM58 is a great starting point for singing, while a Shure SM57 is ideal for recording guitar. If you want higher-quality sound, you can invest in a condenser microphone from Rode. Just make sure that your interface has phantom power to power the microphone.

Today, there are much easier ways to get your electric guitar into your computer. A lot of modern amplifiers have direct outs that include some speaker emulation. I know Boss Katana has one, and most of the more fancy modeling things like the Kemper, the Quad Cortex, and the Helix all have outputs that allow you to record without using any microphone.

You can also use a plug-in, like a little software that works inside the studio recording software and emulates different amplifiers and effects. They sound incredible these days. When they first started, they were a bit ropey, but these days the emulations are so good that it can be pretty hard to tell the difference.

Audio Interface

To get sound into your computer, you need an audio interface. There are hundreds of these available, and you can choose one that suits your budget. A popular choice is the Focusrite Scarlett 2i2, a little red box with two inputs and two outputs. This unit is more than good enough to get started with recording.

Headphones

A decent set of headphones is also helpful if you're recording anything with a microphone, an acoustic guitar, or your voice. You can get away with using your laptop speakers occasionally, but good headphones will likely be a good investment. Here are a couple of things to watch out for:

First of all, don't use Bluetooth. Get wired headphones. If you're going to use Bluetooth, you'll have a latency going on, so you'll hear the sound slightly late, and everything you play won't sync up properly. So no wireless things; ensure you can plug it in!

Second, try to get a closed-back headphone, not an open-back one. Having an open back (the outside of the headphone is open) might make things sound more natural, but a closed-back headphone keeps the sound with your ears and will work best for recording, especially the acoustic guitar.

Recording Software

Once you've set up your equipment, you need software to record it. Many options are available, and a good starting point is GarageBand if you're a Mac user. GarageBand is free and makes recording easy. If you're on PC, check out different free options and see which one feels good.

Studio Monitors

You should invest in a pair of studio monitors at some point. They differ from regular speakers because speakers are designed to provide a pleasant listening experience, whereas studio monitors prioritize an honest representation of sound. This may seem strange, but a flat response is preferable to make it sound nice. If necessary, you could use your laptop or any other speaker you have on hand. However, for a better audio experience, I recommend investing in studio monitors.

Start Recording!

When you have all the equipment, it's time to connect everything correctly and optimize your input gain to start recording, meaning how loud your recording goes into the computer. You don't want it to be too quiet or too loud, so spend some time getting your input gain correct. You shouldn't see any red on the interface or in the software where you're recording!

If you're using a microphone, you need to check the microphone placement, particularly with an acoustic guitar. Experiment with different placements and listen back to see what sounds best.

Check for latency! You must minimize the gap between playing something and hearing it back in your headphones. It's normal to have a bit of latency, but it shouldn't be noticeable. If you notice significant latency, you need to research and figure out how to fix it. You can start by doing a Google search to find out how to reduce latency in your setup.

Learning to play with a click track is also essential. It will help with your timekeeping, and you can listen back and ensure you're playing on time. You can also add drums to your recordings, and there are many built-in drum loops that you can use.

Give It a Try!

Recording can be a lot of fun, and it's a great way to improve your guitar skills, but it's also a new tool to explore. There are many things to learn, from microphone techniques to different effects. It's like a whole new thing to explore, and it's just loads and loads of fun!

Recording yourself is a valuable tool for any musician, and it can motivate you to keep going and improve your skills. It can also help you collaborate with other musicians and present your demos to other writers and singers. So, get started with recording and explore all the different things you can do with it.

💿 Share your recording in the JustinGuitar Community - it's a safe space! Post in the AVOYP.

Transcribing Riffs 2

This lesson is Part 2 of my Transcribing Riffs mini-series. Before getting started, ensure you've worked out the songs of my Transcribing Riffs 1 lesson on your own, hopefully without using the tips! :)

💡The learning curve in Transcribing is very steep, which is why you have this series in Grade 3. It allows you to work on songs that gradually increase your transcribing ability.

Now, let's check out the list of (not that easy) guitar riffs you should transcribe in this Module. The hints are at the end of the list, but don't use them unless you're stuck and can't make progress.

Song #1 - One by Metallica

The section you should try to transcribe is right at the beginning - a great riff to work out, as it sounds relatively clear.

💙 I still remember working out One by Metallica on my own; I was about 13 years old!

You can also try the solo! It's nice as well, but a little harder than the riff. If you're a big Metallica fan, have a go at it. ;)

Song #2 - Money by Pink Floyd

Money has got something weird about it: it's a 7:4 song. Some of you might not have encountered this before! The rhythm might feel weird, but Money has a cool, clear riff you can try and transcribe.

Again, it's relatively simple under the fingers, and you shouldn't have too many problems with it. Just watch out for the timing, and off you go.

Song #3 - Otherside by Red Hot Chilli Peppers

This riff happens further up the neck, so you might find yourself creeping forward a little bit from the open position. ;) The tricky thing here is separating the bass and the guitar lines because the bass line plays a different note from the guitar. You'll have to tune your ear to be capable of separating the parts, but you're just playing a single line!

Song #4 - Break In The Law by Judas Priest

Break In The Law is one of those all-time Metal classics everyone should learn on the guitar! No more comments on this; just give it a go.

Song #5 - Why Do You Only Call Me When You're High by Arctic Monkeys

This Artic Monkeys song is one of my favorite records of all time! It's full of killer wrists and a song that I'm sure you'll love to transcribe. :)

Transcribing Software

Using the correct software is super helpful! The further you get into transcribing, the more useful having proper transcribing software will be.

I did most of my transcribing in my life with a portable compact disc player, which had only a backward and forward button. It was a real pain in the butt, so do yourself a favor and get the software to help you. :)

💡 I use Transcribe! Here's a 30-day free trial for you.

No matter which program you choose, a player that always starts from the same place (and not where it just stopped) is very helpful.

Hints

Coming soon.

So, how did you go? Let me know in the Discussion tab!

lessons.text:
Here is your Module 20 Practice Routine!

5' Technique - Singing & Playing At The Same Time 5' Technique - What You Need 5' Knowledge - Lifted Barre Trick 5' Knowledge - Songwriting 5' Repertoire - Revisit Songs With A Lifted Barre 5' Repertoire - Song Revision 5' Time - Chords In Keys - Rhythm 5' Time - Rhythm & Groove 10' Ear Training - Transcribing (Not So Easy) Riffs 10' Improvising - Chords In Keys - Rhythm & Lead Jamming

Section #1 - Technique - 2 x 5 minutes

Playing & Singing At The Same Time + What You Need

You should start by practicing Singing & Playing at the same time. This skill set is truly valuable for guitarists! Follow everything you learned with my 10-Step Method to Singing and Playing Guitar, and remember to start with a simple song, playing muted strumming, and learning each part individually. You're looking for automation!

ℹ️ Patience! Don't expect too much too soon. Learning to sing and play guitar simultaneously is a process. ;)

I suggest you find something you still need to practice from the previous Grade 3 modules for the second Technique Slot. It could be anything - you know better than me what you need to work on. ;) Choose any one from:

minor pentatonic legato technique

picking individual strings while strumming

linking chords using scales

rolling chords

more finger gym.

🤔 Think! The further down your guitar journey you get, the more things you need to work on.

You may have to start choosing different things each week or every few weeks, and changing your practice routine might be good.

Section #2 - Knowledge - 2 x 5 minutes

Lifted Barre Chord + Songwriting

Start by experimenting with Lifted Barre Chords and how you can include those in a song! First, practice the technique and ensure you memorize the different chord types. Then, have a go using them in some songs!

You can also explore songwriting and its dynamic. You can practice many different songwriting things, but it depends on where you want to get with it, so think about it!

Section #3 - Repertoire- 2 x 5 minutes

Revision + Your Own Songs?

It would be very interesting if you wanted to explore your own songs! You can also revisit songs you already play using Lifted Barre Chords. It's always important to keep reviewing and improving songs you learned as a beginner, applying new things you're learning! Remember - learning guitar involves repetition. ;)

Section #4 - Time - 2 x 5 minutes

Chords In Keys + Groove

Practice your time and rhythm feel based on developing ideas using Chords in Keys. Choose any chords and get creative, making up a rhythm part. Use a metronome or drum track to keep your timing good. If you have a looper pedal you could use this time to practice your looper skills too!

You should work on your groove for the second part of your Time practice! I always talk about it - groove is important; making your playing feel good will help you sound like a pro. :) Focus on making your time feel nice by playing along with the metronome is a good idea, and if you can play with a great groove along with the metronome, that's a good sign that your groove is working well.

😕 A lot of guitar players struggle to feel relaxed when playing with a metronome. They feel very stiff and regimented!

A good test is checking for relaxation while playing with the metronome.

Section #5 - Ear Training - 10 minutes

Transcribing

We had more (not so easy) riffs to work out in this module! Don't skip them if you want to develop your guitar player ears!

Section #6 - Improvising - 10 minutes

Jamming

Jam using the chords in keys idea! You can and should practice by just looking at the chords in a particular key and playing around them. If you don't have a jam buddy see what you come up with on your own. That will be helpful long-term because if you jam with someone, chords in keys will not be completely new to you.

💬 Find a jam buddy in the JustinGuitar Community! Join the Discussion below the video lesson and meet other students at the same guitar level as you. :)

👉 Good to go? Let's head to Module 21! See you soon. :)

lessons.title: The Objective Observer
lessons.summary: Learn this "trick" and banish anxiety for guitar practice wins!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 The Inner Game of Music

01:01 The Objective Observer

04:49 Paradoxical Intention

07:59 Stoic Philosophy & Performance
lessons.text:
This lesson is more Psychology than practical guitar playing, but it's super effective.

I learned about this more than 30 years ago while reading "The Inner Game of Music" by Barry Green and W. Timothy Galway. A lot of this book requires reading music, so some of you might find it challenging to fully use it, but the idea from it is the most powerful little trick in it. It's something that really changed the way I practice.

📕 In the video lesson, I'm holding the copy I bought back in the day! It's got my old phone number in it and stuff. It's a really great book that you should check out.

Now, the big deal for this little trick that I call the "Objective Observer" is that we're trying to remove the emotional relationship between us and what we play. Very often, anxiety and tension cause us to make mistakes. So, the idea behind this lesson is to learn how to banish anxiety for guitar practice wins!

The Objective Observer

To use this tool effectively, you'll try to make a mistake. Two possible things can happen:

The mistake goes away! This happens more often than not; the mistake just disappears. If there's any tension or anxiety around the thing you're trying to work on, and you try to make a mistake, the mistake usually goes away or improves significantly.

The second thing that happens is you watch the mistake as an objective observer, so you're no longer involved with it. You're not criticizing yourself for getting it wrong or anything like that. You're just watching yourself and going, "Well, what's the mistake happening here? Why is this not working properly?" And you really try to watch and listen and figure it out. If you do that, you're most of the way there to fix the problem because you now know the issue.

So, next time you're playing a song and find a consistent stumbling block, and you're trying to figure out what's going on, see if you can be that objective observer. Release any frustration or upset you're feeling because something's not quite going your way, take a mental step back, and just be like somebody, like a teacher, watching you play. See if you can spot the mistake.

Slow Down!

When I cannot see a mistake, it's often because I'm playing too fast. So, if you're trying to go for a really fast passage that you can't quite get right or see what's going on, the first step would be to slow it down.

When you're trying to learn things fast, you must be able to do them well and slowly first! If you find that you slow it down a lot and you can do it, then gradually speed it up until you find that stumble, and then you'll be able to watch it and figure out what the stumbling block is. Figure out what's technically going wrong, and you'll be able to fix it.

I've seen this work thousands of times, both with myself and when I was doing a lot of in-person lessons. I'd use this psychology on the students to go, "Okay, make me the mistake," and they'd try and do it, and very often, the mistake goes away. It's a really incredibly powerful tool.

💡Remember, if you don't know what the mistake is, you're never going to fix it. :) Identifying the issue is your first step!

You may find another way around it, but nearly always, the mistake will go away, or you'll have a clearer understanding of the thing that's going wrong, and you've got a better chance of fixing it.

Paradoxical Intention

"Paradoxical intention" is the psychotherapy name for the technique we're about to explore. It was coined by Victor Frankel, an incredible psychologist who wrote the fantastic book "Man's Search for Meaning" about his time in a Nazi death camp.

📖 "Man's Search for Meaning" by Victor Frankel is in my top 10 books. If you haven't read it, go and check it out. It's an incredible read.

I think it's worth touching on this stuff here is that it's very often anxiety that hinders our performance, particularly when it comes to performing on stage. We get this stage fright, we get a fear of a mistake, and we fear fearing the mistake because fear makes us nervous and tense, and that causes mistakes. It turns into a vicious cycle!

The key element is that if we observe a fear, other than being overwhelmed by it, it gives us a chance to develop a proper perspective on what's going on. The fear of fear is often a problem for guitar players or musicians, generally when you're performing. If you're trying to do a concert, and you've got stage fright, you're feeling really nervous and tense, and you won't play as well as you would if you're just allowing yourself to get into the zone.

We talk about this all the time when it comes to performance anxiety. Being able to stay in the moment, and allowing yourself to be in the music rather than on edge, is key to controlling stage anxiety. If you're really nervous, you're always fighting with it! It becomes uncomfortable to watch it. You can feel it in the audience if somebody's really nervous when they're playing. It's weird. So, you've got to find a way to relax when you play.

Because of that, if you've experienced stage fright, which I have loads of times, once you've experienced it, you know that you don't want that. You don't want that fear. So, it's possible to get into this horrible feedback loop where you fear the fear and get anxious about anxiety. And then, of course, by having a fear of the fear, you're creating the thing that you didn't want anyway. It's a horrible little vicious cycle, but there are two things you can try to break it.

The first thing is the Paradoxical Intention, being able to deliberately try and make the mistake. That can break that cycle! The second thing is the Objective Observer - distancing yourself from the problem to get a better perspective.

📖 Some of you may know that I'm big on Stoic Philosophy, and one of the key teachings from the great philosopher Seneca was that we suffer more in our imagination than we do in reality. And this reads back to this idea of the fear of the fear. The fear is in our imagination! We're worried about what may be, not what actually is. We're worried about a situation that may never happen. Why would you put yourself in this mode? :) Don't put yourself in this vicious cycle before you even get there and be afraid of the fear occurring. It's absolutely crazy.

Treat it as an external thing. That's one of the reasons why mindfulness is so effective! You're much better off worrying about it the moment something happens rather than trying to be anticipating it. :)

Guitar Practice

In this lesson, I presented a whole heap of ideas that I've bundled all together, maybe slightly sloppily, but I'm hoping you find this video useful. If you'd like to learn more, explore many more guitar lessons on practicing effectively in our Beginner Grade 3 Course. Some of them are also psychology-based because I find that personally interesting. I hope it's beneficial for you!

💬 Did you dig this lesson? :) Join the Discussion and let me know your thoughts!

lessons.text:
It's time for more chord explorations!

In this tutorial, we'll check out the A Shape, and how to turn the A chord grips you already know into many others. You'll grow your chord repertoire and allow your musical imagination to express ideas more freely without memorizing new chords from diagrams or even naming them.

💡 This lesson is part of my Chord Shapes Explorer series - included in my Beginner Course - Grade 3. If you've missed the previous lessons, check them out now.

D Chord Shape Explorer

C Chord Shape Explorer

G Chord Shape Explorer

Moving Up Open Chords

And much more to come!

Note: Explorer lessons for all five CAGED shapes can also be found, grouped together, under All Courses here.

Exploring your A Chord

All beginners should be familiar with the A chord, one of the 8 essential open chords we learn in Grade 1. If you've followed my Beginner Course, you might know that I don't play or teach my students the regular A open chord grip. Instead, I prefer the following fingering:

The 1st finger is in the 2nd fret on the 3rd string.

The 2nd finger is in the 2nd fret on the 4th string.

The 3rd finger is in the 2nd fret on the 2nd string.

This fingering sounds better to me and brings many other benefits! Assume that you're happy with that fingering; we can try many variations. The first chord you'll find is an Asus2 - get it by lifting off your third finger. I love this chord!

💡 You don't have to worry about the chord names for this lesson. Join my Music Theory Course to further understand your guitar fretboard and how to name and find any guitar chord!

The second variation is also easy! Lift your first finger off to get an A7 chord. Many people have trouble with this chord because the second finger lays over a little bit. And you don't hear any difference if the underneath of that second finger mutes your third string! So, ensure you're using the tips of your fingers and getting that G chord ringing.

While we're on that, you can easily get to an Amaj7 Chord. If you're playing a song with an A chord, you'll either find that Amaj7 or A7 will work. Rarely they'll both work well in the same context unless it's a specific movement where you'd have an Amaj7 and A7 going to the D chord. Check out the video lesson to explore it further.

🎵 You'll find many songs that you can use these chord variations. Explore lifting some fingers off, or adding your little finger! You'll find loads of interesting things to explore. :)

From the A7 chord, your little finger can go down on the third fret of the thinnest string. It's a great variation for when you're playing the Blues!

When exploring chords like in this lesson, you'll use your ears to decide on the variations and substitutions you might be doing. Sometimes, it'll all be about some hammer-ons and flick-offs.

You can easily get an A6 chord movement from the A7 by putting the little finger underneath, so all the fingers are in the same fret! And there's an easier way of playing that chord - which we'll check out in this tutorial, so don't miss out on the full video lesson!

You can do a lot by exploring the A Shape, including Dominant 7th and 6th, especially if you want to play the Blues. You can explore many of these chord shapes with a 12 Bar Blues Progression, so revisit that Grade 2 lesson too.

Develop Your Musical Imagination!

Try to use different chord shapes when playing the songs you already know. You can also explore songwriting and make songs on your own! See how your creativity can influence the songs you play, and explore as many chord variations as possible!

Remember that you've got to deliberately practice this exercise to make it instinctual. If I'm playing an A chord in any song, anytime, all of those variations are just hanging around and waiting for my musical imagination to get triggered and try something new. That's where you want to be as an Intermediate guitar player.

And it's not difficult; it just requires a little effort to train your musical imagination and your hand to work together and recognize sounds you'd like to play.

Learn More! My Beginner Grade 3 Course will take you right to the Intermediate stages. And it's free. :)

lessons.text:
The Things All Advancing Beginners Should Know About Vibrato

This lesson is a huge moment in your guitar journey; adding Vibrato to chords and lead guitar will make your playing sound super pro! We'll explore 6 types of Vibrato and when to use them, along with the key technical points to help you nail these techniques.

Vibrato confuses many advancing beginner guitarists who have learned some scales and are starting to improvise with them. Beginners will either apply vibrato techniques in the wrong context or attempt to create Vibrato in their way – by shaking the neck, for example.

💡 This lesson is an introduction to vibrato! We'll explore these vibrato techniques much more deeply in the Intermediate Grades.

But before we start experimenting with Vibrato, let's be clear on what we mean by that name. :)

What Is Vibrato?

You can think of Vibrato as pitch oscillation around a fundamental note. It sounds fancy, but it is quite simple. Let me explain!

When we play a note, we create a sound with a particular pitch called the fundamental note. With Vibrato, we move the string such that the pitch moves above and below the fundamental note.

🚨 Always Come Back! Whatever vibrato type we choose, it's crucial we come back to the fundamental note each time. Otherwise, the note tends to sound a little out of tune.

There are many ways of creating Vibrato on the guitar, and most only create sounds higher than the fundamental note.

However, there are loads of possibilities: you can go above only, below only, or above and below! The possibilities depend on the vibrato technique we go for.

The Two Key Vibrato Variables: Rate and Depth

The two variables of vibrato sound are rate and depth. You have to understand them!

Rate is how fast we move to and from the fundamental note. If we move our fingers slowly, the rate will be low. With fast finger movement, we get a lot of Vibrato.

Depth is how far away from the fundamental pitch we go. The further we move the string, the wider the Vibrato.

Now we have the basic concepts, let's look at our first vibrato technique.

Vibrato #1 - Classical Vibrato

Classical Vibrato is the one that guitarists use the most. However, it's mostly inappropriate on electric and acoustic guitars, being more effective on classical guitars.

💡 I call this Classical Vibrato; other teachers call it Wobbling-Finger Vibrato!

Put your third finger in 2:10 (string 2, fret 10), and pick the string. You create this Vibrato by moving your finger left and right along the string within fret 10. Keep your other fingers and thumb off the guitar.

How does this work? When we move our finger towards the nut, we pull the string in that direction and raise the pitch. We do the opposite when we move our finger towards the bridge – we flatten the note below the fundamental. It's a lovely vibrato, but it's very subtle.

🎧 Classical Vibrato In Pop! To hear this Vibrato in a pop context, check out Sting's guitarist, Dominic Miller. He's an incredible musician and guitarist! You'll hear several types of Vibrato in his playing.

I see lots of guitarists using Wobbling-Finger Vibrato out of context. It sounds great on classical guitar because of the nylon strings, meaning you get a deep vibrato. It's almost the only kind of Vibrato that classical guitarists use, but not the best for Pop, Rock, and Blues guitar.

So if classical Vibrato isn't the best choice for contemporary music, what is? I'm glad you asked. :)

Vibrato #2 - Standard Vibrato

Let's check out what I call Standard Vibrato, one you'll often hear on acoustic and electric guitars in contemporary music.

Place finger 3 on 2:10 again. Pick the note, then move finger 3 up and down while keeping the pressure on the string. That's standard Vibrato. You can move the string up, down, or both. :)

Avoid using your fingers to move the string. The best technique is to use the edge of your hand (at the main knuckle of finger 1) as a pivot point.

Keep your fingers locked together and rock your hand to create the Vibrato. It's the same pivot technique that we use for string bending.

🤔 Which Finger? Standard Vibrato works well with all four fingers on every string, but I tend not to use finger 4 for Vibrato or String Bending because mine is really small! It's your decision whether you practice this technique with finger 4 or not.

It's crucial to note that the pitch only goes up. We can't flatten the pitch using this technique. Even if we pull the string downwards, the pitch rises.

I encourage you to explore this kind of Vibrato and make it your default style. There are others, but this is the most widespread and the easiest to play well.

Remember the two variables: depth and rate. Try out your different fingers and the various directions. These factors make a huge difference.

🎸 Standard Vibrato & Famous Guitarists: My favorite example of a guitarist who often uses Standard Vibrato is Mark Knopfler. His Vibrato is just incredible! BB King also has his own signature vibrato with finger 1, called Butterfly Vibrato. It's a kind of quick (high rate) but shallow (low depth) Vibrato.

Standard Vibrato doesn't need to be wide and fast to be effective. That kind of Vibrato tends to sound quite aggressive, so you'll find it in Rock. Listen to Joe Satriani, Steve Vai, and Gary Moore. Most of the Rock gods have amazing Vibrato!

Another kind of Vibrato often appears in Rock and Blues guitar. Let's have a look.

Vibrato #3 - Blues Vibrato

I discovered Blues Vibrato while transcribing Eric Clapton's music. My Vibrato never seemed on point, so I watched him play and saw he was using his own technique. Sometimes, his whole hand comes off the guitar!

Put your finger 3 on 2:10, making sure no other part of your hand is touching the guitar. Pick the note, keep your finger pressing, and start moving it up and down. It's almost a bouncing motion with the forearm. You need a lot of pressure from the hand.

😅 It took me a lot of practice to get this one down. It just didn't come naturally to me! It's not my go-to Vibrato, but it has its own flavor and is handy occasionally.

Vibrato #4 - Neck Vibrato

I love this technique! Unlike most other techniques, neck Vibrato enables you to move the pitch up and down.

🚨 Warning! This is not the same as wobbling the neck around!

To create this sound, you need to clamp the guitar's body tightly with your strumming hand and push the neck forward or back with your fretting hand.

If you push it forward, the pitch decreases. Pull it back, and the pitch increases. Don't apply too much pressure, or you might snap your guitar neck! You need to be careful with this kind of Vibrato on acoustic guitars.

I love using it with chords – it just breathes life into them! I don't tend to use it for single lines, but don't let me stop you. Get creative. :) You might discover you love adding Neck Vibrato over melody.

Vibrato #5 - Bending Vibrato

We haven't looked at string bending yet, so you might find it tricky to play this Vibrato, but I want you to know that it exists. We can use this type to lower the pitch from the fundamental.

We use the pivot point to play string bends, just like we do with the Standard Vibrato, but instead of rocking the hand back and forth, we push the string up. That raises the pitch. Our goal in string-bending is to bend it to the note one semitone or one tone above the note we fret.

💡 String Bend or Fretted Note? Knowing about this technique helps you decide whether a note is played with a bent string or fretted. If there is "up" Vibrato, it's likely to be fretted. If there's "down" Vibrato, chances are there is string bending involved. :)

For example, place finger 3 on 2:10. Pick the note, then rock the fretting hand such that it pushes the string upwards. Stop when it sounds like the note B at 2:12. You can play 2:12 before bending the string so that you know what to aim for. :)

Now that you've bent the string a tone, release it a little bit, then push it back up to B. This is Vibrato!

👉 I recommend you learn string bending and Vibrato independently before trying to combine them. But do be aware that it exists. :)

Vibrato #6 - Whammy-Bar Vibrato

The whammy bar is a little lever found on some electric guitars. You can play "up" Vibrato or "down" Vibrato with the whammy bar, but we use it mostly to create "down-up" Vibrato. It sounds wicked with chords, but plenty of guitarists add Whammy Vibrato to lead guitar.

🎧 Rock and Metal guitar players make some great sounds with it. Steve Vai is the greatest ever whammy-bar player in my opinion. Jeff Beck is also incredible with it! It’s not really my bag, but for many guitarists, it’s an intrinsic part of their sound.

Which Vibrato to Use?

So that's a whole heap of options for Vibrato! How do you know which one to go for? How do you learn them?

As I said, we're going to go really deep with all these types of Vibrato in the Intermediate course. The main point of this lesson is to make it plain that shaking the guitar neck doesn't produce Vibrato!

🚨 You must be aware of the fundamental note! You need to come back to the original pitch after every oscillation. Otherwise, we hear the note as being out of tune. Does your vibrato sound in tune?

Since there are so many types of Vibrato, and Vibrato becomes part of someone's unique voice, I suggest you listen to your favorite guitarists and focus on their Vibrato. Then you can mimic their sound on your guitar.

Once you've repeatedly heard a vibrato and it has become part of your musical imagination, you must teach your body to repeat that sound through the guitar. That's the aim! By doing this, you'll learn new types of Vibrato and be able to re-create those sounds in the right context.

💡 Be Patient: If you're a beginner and have just started learning the Major Scale, experiment with the different kinds of Vibrato. Play around and have fun! Don't expect to master vibrato right away – it takes time to develop your skills. :)

Vibrato is tricky. There are many subtleties involved, particularly when you're copying a singer. For instance, the rate and the depth often gradually increase as the note is sustained.

We'll come back to these techniques in the Intermediate grades. For now, explore all these techniques, listen to your favorite guitarists, and see what gets your juices flowing! Laters. :)

👉 Next, let's learn about Framing: The Double Strumming Technique!

lessons.summary: Learn the strumming technique behind songs like That's Entertainment by The Jam and Sultans of Swing by Dire Straits!

lessons.text:
Use this Strumming Technique for a faster pattern!

In this lesson, we'll learn a strumming technique I call framing. It's also called double strumming and double-quick strumming. If you want to add quick strums to your rhythm guitar, you need this technique.

💡 Real-World Examples! You will find this strumming technique in songs like That's Entertainment by The Jam and Sultans of Swing by Dire Straits!

The idea is that we strum twice as fast for a small part of the bar. It isn't tricky, but you need to get the technique right. Otherwise, it'll always feel tough.

The Mechanics of Framing

I always reiterate the importance of moving your hand consistently when you strum. For instance, if we play 1+2+3+4+, we use down strums on beats and up strums on offbeats (the "and" s), keeping our strumming hand moving throughout. Even if you don't strum on every beat, your hand should continue moving up and down.

💡 Master Strumming Mechanics – if you find consistent strumming tricky, make sure to master these 11 Strumming Tips before attempting double-quick strumming.

When strumming twice as fast, we break this pattern and have to pull our hand up quickly to play the second down strum. Try this:

1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + D U D U D U D D

Notice that instead of playing an up strum on the "and" of 4, we play a down strum. Mute your strings and try playing this rhythm. Now:

1 + 2 + 3 + 4 +a D U D U D U D DU

Practice this a lot before going further! You can do the "+a" on any beat, but it's most common on beat 4.

As you do this faster and faster, it starts to feel awkward. You have to interrupt your consistent strumming, pulling your strumming hand up after beat 4. It just doesn't feel right! How can we get around this?

How to Play Fast Framing

The key to mastering this is to move your wrist instead of your forearm. You rotate the wrist and keep the elbow stable. Use regular strumming for all beats except the frame, then move to "wristy" strumming for the quick strums:

1 + 2 + 3 + 4 +a D U D U D U D D U Elbow Wrist

Your rhythm has to feel good! Master the mechanics first, then focus on making your framing feel relaxed, almost lazy.

Again, try this with muted strings and slowly increase your speed. Don't try to do it fast if you can't do it slowly. I also suggest you use a thin pick. It's way easier! Once you master this, it's time to look at other patterns.

Other Cool Patterns For Framing

Once you can easily play the pattern above, try moving the "+a" to beat 1:

1 +a 2 + 3 + 4 + D DU D U D U D U

Don't worry about strumming all the strings here. Your wrist motion won't be as large as your forearm, so naturally, you strum fewer strings. The effect is more percussive than harmonic.

🚀 Go further! While strumming should feel natural and easy, understanding it deeper is helpful even for confident strummers. Learn more here.

This double-strumming technique will add a lot of spice to your rhythm playing. Remember, this is part of Grade 3, a unit designed for beginners who know their basic chords and rhythm guitar. In this grade, we focus on perfecting chords and rhythm before diving into intermediate content like barre chords and position playing.

🎶 Have lots of fun with framing using it in your favorite songs! :)
