lessons.text:
Stuck in a rut with your guitar practice?

Are you lacking the motivation to practice the guitar? Do you feel that nothing is going right or that you're not progressing? Or are you doubting whether the guitar is worth it at all?

Well, you're not alone – we all get stuck in ruts with the guitar. I've been playing for 30 years, and it happens to me too! They show up whenever we dedicate long periods to something, like work, hobbies, or relationships. With my top 10 Rut Busters, we'll address how to get out of guitar ruts and rekindle your motivation to practice. :)

But before we do that, let's clear up the difference between ruts and plateaus. I don't want you to get confused!

Lacking the Motivation to Practice Guitar: Is It A Rut Or A Plateau?

No matter what we learn, our progression is unlikely linear. In other words, you won't see a constant, steady improvement over time. It just doesn't work that way!

Instead, we tend to progress quickly the first time we learn something. We get all excited, and our skills improve quickly. But at some point, our progress starts to level off. This is a plateau.

💡 Plateaus are really normal! Don’t expect to be constantly improving on the guitar journey – it simply doesn’t happen. :) Your body and brain need time to assimilate new skills and put them into practice.

You might also find your overall progress hits a plateau because you're catching up with other elements that underpin later skills. Hand strength is a good example. Beginners often progress rapidly with chords, chord changes, and strumming, but then they hit a wall with barre chords. That might be due to hand strength. With enough practice, barre chords feel easy. :)

That's a plateau. Meanwhile, ruts are times when you feel uninspired and emotionally disconnected from the guitar. Think about your journey. Do you still feel inspired even though you don't see much improvement? Then it's probably just a plateau. In that case, the key is to keep practicing, though Rut Busters can do the trick. :)

If you've decided you are in a rut and need to regain the motivation to learn guitar, these 10 Rut Busters are perfect for you.

Rut Buster 1: Buy a New Guitar

This is my most popular Rut Buster! If you're in a rut, get a new guitar. I'm not even kidding. :)

Not everyone can afford to spend money on a new guitar flippantly, so I apologize for putting this first in the queue. There are plenty more Rut Busters that are free!

But seriously, new guitars are inspiring. You find a new instrument you've always wanted, get it, and discover a whole new world! If you find yourself in a deep funk and are about to give up the guitar, a new guitar can lift you out of it and give you new inspiration and motivation! It's a great Rut Buster.

🎸 Confession Time: I have never, ever bought a new guitar as a Rut Buster. I only buy them for work. Promise. ;)

Rut Buster 2: Get a New Sound

If the new guitar doesn't work, get a new amplifier or FX pedal! Okay, I'm only kidding. But getting a new sound can be super inspiring. :) I love getting new pedals! I spend hours and hours experimenting with my sound and exploring the new sonic landscape I've discovered.

If this resonates with you, watch the videos on Anderton's, Andy Martin, That Pedal Show, Pete Thorn, or any other gear review channels you love. See what you can find!

You don't have to spend a lot. Sure, the latest trendy FX pedals seem to cost the same as guitars and amplifiers. But you don't have to spend all that money. There are plenty of second-hand pedals out there. :) You can also try new presets. If you have a digital modeler, buy a new preset and explore it.

🚨 Watch For Gear Obsession: On a serious note, it’s important you don’t rely solely on new gear to inspire you. I know lots of guys – yes, they’re usually guys, not girls! – that spend much more time researching gear and watching reviews than practicing! That’s a bad idea for guitar longevity.

So if you find yourself in a funk, by all means, research new gear and explore a new pedal, but don't let it take over your life. As a guitar player, you shouldn't spend so much time researching gear and sounds that you never get your hands on the instrument.

Rut Buster 3: Rethink Your Motivation and Goals

This one is particularly useful for people who don't think about their ultimate destination. But remember: if you don't know where you're going, you'll probably never get there. Here are some questions to help you. :)

What is it that first made you pick up the guitar? What is your current goal? If you don't have a goal, set one! Think about what you'd like to achieve with guitar – what would you like to be able to do? What songs and styles would you like to be able to play? What would excite you to get your bum on the seat and play music again?

💣 Set Your Guitar Goals: I’ve got a whole lesson on setting goals and how to plot a pathway to them. Check it out if you need to clarity your guitar vision. :)

If you've got a goal and are still uninspired, maybe it's not the right goal. You could change it or put it on hold. If you've been working towards one goal for a long time, you might need to take a holiday. Go and visit a different goal for a while! :)

Justin's Journey – there have been times when I've sat down to play guitar and have felt disinterested. On those days, I push through. I've always wanted to make a living from it, and this big-picture goal took me through the struggle. I had a goal, so I had to put the hours in!

Guitar playing shouldn't be a slog. When music and guitar become hard work, keeping it going for long is difficult. Having a clear sense of purpose is great for your practice and motivation levels, especially when you have to slog.

Now it's time for my favorite Rut Buster. :)

Rut Buster 4: Rekindle Your Motivation To Practice With A New Style

Simple, but effective! If you're in a rut, pick a style of music that you've never played, and explore it.

If you're a blues guitarist lacking enthusiasm, check out some country, classical guitar, slide guitar, metal guitar, or any style. The genre doesn't matter! Just make sure it's something you've never explored before and were always curious about.

It's amazing how the freshness of music can inspire you. Funnily, the new genre will likely show you a new perspective on the guitar and give you excitement for your actual practice.

Just be curious about how a certain music style works, and explore it. Again, it doesn't matter what it is, so long as it's completely new. :)

Rut Buster 5: Try An Alternate Tuning

Alternate tunings probably won't get you out of a major funk. Those call for a new guitar! But it's a fun Rut Buster and works well when you're feeling flat one day. :) If you've always played in standard tuning, even drop D (DADGBE) will reveal some awesome new sounds.

🎵 Songwriting: As a songwriter, I love putting the guitar in strange tunings and trying to find some nice sounds. I often find chords I’d never be able to play in standard tuning. Check out my Songwriting course to get going. :)

DADGAD tuning is also a wonderful tuning for fiddling around. Just retune to DADGAD and try things. Many things sound amazing, like strumming all the strings and playing a little melody on the thinnest string. You've created a new sound palette to explore, which will excite and motivate you.

You can also try Open G (DGDGBD), Open E (EBEG#BE), or even make up your own! Just retune your strings to any random notes and see what happens. Sometimes it will not sound very good, but all you need to do is retune and try again. :)

Rut Buster 6: Take a Deep Dive

Let's say you're into the blues, the genre you play most, but lately, you feel uninspired. This is when you can do a deep dive: think about which part of the blues you like.

Let's say it's lead guitar. Then narrow it down further – what do you love most in blues lead guitar and improvising? Then you realize you like Eric Clapton's music.

Now, you can decide to do a deep dive into Eric Clapton's lead guitar playing in the Beano era. See how specific that is?

But it doesn't have to be Eric Clapton. Find an area of music you love and practice regularly, then focus on a specific part. We're often so busy learning new techniques and songs that we don't have the opportunity for deep dives.

💡 My Journey: Your deep dive can go beyond the instrument! I’ve read books on the history of blues guitar and found it very exciting to learn how the different blues players related to one another, how the licks travelled from place to place.

You can do this on a practical level by looking at skills and techniques, or you can study the history of the guitar, the backstory of your favorite musicians, and more. In any case, your goal is to focus on a narrow part of the styles you love.

Rut Buster 7: Lacking the Motivation to Play Guitar? Try New Music

Many guitarists suffer from not listening to music enough. We spend more time playing it than listening to it! And not only that – we don't explore new music.

I fall into this trap too. I like older music and shun modern stuff unless it's Harry Styles! To overcome this, I ask my friends what new music they're listening to. Spotify also suggests new stuff. Occasionally it throws up a real gem that I wasn't familiar with!

Try another era if you only listen to music from the 60s and 70s. Though I tend to avoid the latest music, it has more to offer than it gets credit for.

Many talented guitarists are making great music, like Ariel Posen, Josh Smith, Mateus Asato, and many more. Listening to them might motivate you to explore other genres and get some new sounds in your head. All this will rekindle your love for guitar. :)

Rut Buster 8: Try Another Instrument

Playing another instrument gives you new sonic palettes to explore, can change your relationship with music for the better, and, ultimately, get you excited to play guitar. :)

I'm not suggesting you go and buy a piano, but mucking around on a cheap keyboard can be super inspiring. If you want to stick with stringed instruments, ukuleles are fascinating and easy to pick up – the tuning is the same as a guitar with a capo on fret 5 and the two thickest strings missing. :)

Ukulele chord shapes are also pretty familiar. They're the same as guitar chords but without the lowest notes – it's like your fingers fall off the top of the fretboard.

🎸 My Ukulele Love: I really dig the ukulele! It's pretty innocent. When you grab one and start playing it, people don’t expect anything fancy. You can relax, have fun, start a sing-along and there’s no pressure. Check out my Ukulele course to give it a try. :)

Piano and keyboard are also amazing options. If you have some knowledge of music theory, like chord degrees and the construction of scales, then it's pretty easy to have a go at the piano. Learning new chord inversions on the piano is super inspiring – you can take your new sounds to the guitar.

On top of that, the piano is linear, meaning the theory is very clear. Seeing the notes and chords in this linear form can be valuable for guitarists. You could also try slide guitar, pedal-steel guitar, violin, cello, recorder – whatever!

Rut Buster 9: Explore Songwriting and Composition

Songwriting can be inspiring if you've never done it before. I find that it's very tangible. Though I feel satisfied after spending a few hours practicing licks, scales, and transcribing, I've got nothing tangible to show for my efforts.

Songwriting is different. You create something that lasts. You can say: "Hey, I did this! I wrote this song!" That's great for your inspiration and gives your music time a clear purpose. Then you can enhance your track with your guitar skills. :)

You don't have to go down the singer-songwriter route. You can stick with instruments or write lyrics for someone else to sing. It doesn't matter – the most important is that you're excited to create. Having something tangible at the end is great for your inspiration.

Rut Buster 10: Zero Motivation To Practice Guitar? Take A Complete Break

When you feel like: "Jeez, I'm just not enjoying the guitar at the moment," it's good to take a couple of weeks off. Don't think about the guitar, don't worry about lack of practice, and don't let it stress you out. This Rut Buster has worked for me a few times, and I know many professional guitarists who often use it.

If you start thinking: "Oh jeez, I'm not practicing! All my skills will disappear!" relax. It doesn't matter. That doesn't happen! After a month-long break, your fingers will surely feel sluggish, and your calluses will have worn away, but your skills will come back quickly. It's like riding a bike – once you've developed the skills, they're always there.

I know a couple of famous guitarists who take months and months off between tours. They don't touch the instrument. Then they return, and all their skills return after a few days of rustiness.

💡 I know a famous guitarist who once took three months off. He went straight into a live performance after his break! He didn’t even do a sound check. :) I could tell it wasn’t his best playing, but it was still way better than what I could ever do!

The lesson? It all comes back quite quickly. So if you're just not feeling the guitar now, try leaving it for a set period and see how you feel afterward. If you're a hobbyist, start with two weeks – a month is quite a long time. And if the break doesn't work, try another Rut Buster. :)

I've certainly had periods when it's been an effort and a struggle. It's my living, so I can't just let it fold. I get on with it if I'm not in the mood. But I love playing guitar, and I'm so thankful that it's what I do for a living. If I ever feel bored, I remind myself how lucky I am. That usually does the trick!

🔥 Secret Rut Buster! Time for an unofficial Rut Buster number 11. :) Try reminding yourself of how lucky you are to have this skill and hobby that you really love! This gets me out of my ruts.

Finally, remember you're not the only one stuck in guitar ruts. I don't know any guitar players who are constantly inspired to play, create, practice, and be fully immersed in music! I hope these Rut Busters inspire you to get your bum back on the seat in times of low motivation. Laters. :)

lessons.title: Transcribing: What about the guitar capo?
lessons.summary: We've been training your ears to transcribe songs, but how do you know if and where a guitarist was using a capo?
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Lesson Welcome

00:21 Are they using a capo?

06:05 10 songs with a capo to transcribe

11:01 Extra Tips
lessons.text:
It's time to level up your Transcribing skills and approach a common real-world challenge!

It's a topic that I found ultra frustrating when I started transcribing: how do we know whether the guitarist is using a capo or not?

And what's even more frustrating is that it's quite tricky to give step-by-step advice. There's no simple answer! You gain this skill through tons of trial and error, and it'll get easier with experience and the following tips! They'll steer you in the right direction. :)

💡 Before getting started, ensure you've completed the previous Transcribing lessons from my Beginner Guitar Course - Grade 3. Learning a new skill will be easier if you take it easy first, and then build up your competence!

Now let's get stuck and learn my tricks to figure out the right capo position when transcribing a song to the guitar.

The Secret To Figuring Out The Capo Position

Once we take a trip into capo land, things get confusing. Play the same chord in five or six ways on the neck? Ahh! Yes, it's overwhelming at the start.

The key to nailing this is to train yourself to hear the difference between shapes in different positions. Let's see how.

Top Tips For Figuring Out Chords And Capo Position

My top tips are to listen for the bass note and the highest note in the chord. Know either, and it'll help you figure out the chord and its position on the neck. Know both, and you're almost guaranteed success!

Also, listen out for the number of strings! Does the chord sound full (lots of strings) or thin (fewer strings)?

Embellishments are super common in acoustic playing. You'll hear certain ones used a lot, and they all have distinctive sounds. It can give away both the chords and the capo position!

And finally, look out for two high strings that ring throughout the sequence. A typical example is the G, Cadd9, Dsus4, and Em7 sequence, where the notes on fret 3 of strings 1 and 2 ring out. Wonderwall is an excellent example of a song with this kind of sequence.

💡Learn All About Suspended Chords! Sus chords are easy embellishments and will open up a world of possibilites for you. :)

Use The Shape To Figure Out The Capo Position

If you identify the shape the guitarist is using, say a C shape, try to find the bass note. Then you can locate the correct fret for the capo!

For instance, if you know the chord is a C shape, and find that the bass note is at fret 8 on string 2, then the capo has to be at fret 5.

Playing Chords Around The Neck With A Capo

Let's look at playing an F chord in various positions on the neck and explore the tips we covered above. Can you work out all the ways to play F Major as an open chord using a capo?

The first option is to put the capo on fret 1 and play an open E chord (022100). It is a full sound. Notice that the bottom and top notes are the same, and listen out for this in songs.

Let's move the capo up two frets (to fret 3) and play an open D (XX0232). It's still an F chord, but it sounds very different. The first sounds big and bold; the second sounds smaller and higher. There's less distance between the bass note and the top note.

If you can hear sus2 and sus4 chords, it's likely a D shape chord. Play the Dsus2 (XX0230) and Dsus4 (XX0233) a few times. They have a unique sound – you'll hear them ALL the time!

Then move the capo to fret 5 and play an open C. This chord is also an F – can you see why? The C shape is ultra common, and it has its sound. It's easy to play embellishments – try the sus2 (X30010) and sus 4 (X33010) – and bass riffs. Play around and see what you can find!

In the CAGED System, there are two more positions (can you figure them out?), but It's unlikely you'd hear them in a song, so we won't cover them in depth.

Can You Figure Out The Chords And Capo Position For These 10 Hits?

Homework time! Here are 10 popular hits that use easy open chords and a capo.

🚨 Don’t click the Tip button unless you really can’t work them out yourself. Spend as much time as you can on your own – that’s how you’ll benefit most! :)

See if you can figure out where the capo goes and what chords they use.

🎧 Blowin' In The Wind by Bob Dylan

Song #1 Tip

Dylan uses simple open chords, but the capo is further up than you think.

🎧 Teardrops On My Guitar by Taylor Swift

Song #2 Tip

Many pop and country music uses the same chord shapes (C, Am, F, G) with different capo positions. Listen out for that progression in this one!

🎧 Give Me Love by Ed Sheeran

Song #3 Tip

This one's a little more tricky! Most of the chords are simple, but some are less common. There are a few sections in this tune, and he uses some complex techniques.

🎧 Moonlight Shadow by Mike Oldfield

Song #4 Tip

The acoustic guitar is super obvious, especially at the start. There are some good clues in there – listen up! ;)

🎧 Photograph by Ed Sheeran

Song #5 Tip

This tune has a cool motif, and it might just help you figure out where the capo is. Once you know the capo position and the chords, see if you can work it out! Hint: it fits into the chords. ;)

🎧 Let Her Go by Passenger

Song #6 Tip

This one has lots of embellishments. It's quite a complex fingerstyle song, but the embellishments give you many clues. Use them to work out the chords. Can you do this just by listening?

🎧 Counting Stars by One Republic

Song #7 Tip

There's nice, obvious acoustic guitar in the intro. There are many layers, but you should still be able to figure out the chords!

🎧 That's Entertainment by The Jam

Song #8 Tip

Listen to the clues. In the first couple of chords, you might hear some notes that stay the same! Where are they? And where should the capo go? :)

🎧 Pink Bullets by The Shins

Song #9 Tip

There's something strange with one chord, which you might find a little tricky. Two of these chords are obvious, and one of them is not.

🎧 Free Fallin' by Tom Petty

Song #10 Tip

One of the most iconic guitar parts of all time! This song uses sus chords, but there's a strange part there, too. One finger stays down in one of the chords when you might not expect it. I say no more!

Go Further!

These ten songs all use a capo and quite easy chords, so start exploring the idea of working out chord shapes and embellishments. If you have song suggestions, let me know in the Discussion section.

We're looking at crucial ideas here! Transcribing is one of the most powerful tools for unlocking your musical potential! Good luck with these songs, and take care. :)

Up for more? Explore my free guitar lessons!

Time for your Module 21 Practice Routine!

5' Technique - Vibrato 5' Technique - What You Need 5' Knowledge - A-Shape Explorer 5' Knowledge - What You Need 5' Repertoire - Framing - The Double-Strum 5' Repertoire - Campfire / Developer / Dreamer Songs 5' Time - Framing - The Double-Strum 5' Time - What You Need 10' Ear Training - Transcribing (Open Chord Capo Songs) 10' Improvising - What You Need

Section #1 - Technique - 2 x 5 minutes

Vibrato + What You Need

Start your Technique practice with vibrato and explore all of those different techniques. You'll find some easier than others, and that's okay! But give them all good practice without skipping the harder ones. :)

I assume you know yourself better than I do for the second Technique slot, so think about what things you need to work on. What are you struggling with? That's what you need to practice every time that you sit down to practice! Previous lessons include:

singing & playing at the same time

minor pentatonic legato technique

picking individual strings while strumming

linking chords using scales

rolling chords

finger gym

Section #2 - Knowledge - 2 x 5 minutes

A-Shape Explorer + What You Need

Explore your A-Shape, playing their different chord variations; lift your fingers, move them around, and get used to the sounds of that shape. The A-Shape has so much value, so practice it properly. The second part of your Knowledge practice could be some work on things you've learned before such as:

any of the chord-shape explorers

open tunings

using triads

the lifted barre trick

moving easy chord shapes

or even music theory

Section #3 - Repertoire - 2 x 5-minutes

Framing + Campfire / Developer/ Dreamer Songs

Find a couple of songs that use framing! A clasic example of this is the song That's Entertainment by The Jam, but there are other options you can explore. :) Then, review the songs you already play, considering those 3 types of songs you should practice to become a better guitar player.

Section #4 - Time - 2 x 5 minutes

Framing (again) + What You Need

I recommend working on the double strumming (framing) again. Make it feel good; that's essential! Exploring your looper is also a great idea, so take advantage of that!

Section #5 - Ear Training - 10 minutes

Transcribing

Module 21 has more suggestions on what to transcribe, focusing on open-chord songs. Feel free to add much more transcribing if you're getting really into it; feel free to continue at the end of your dedicated time slot for this section (10 minutes.) Transcribing is the most valuable thing that you can practice on guitar.

Section #5 - Improvising - 10 minutes

Jamming!

Ten minutes of improvising is a great way to explore new things you're learning and boost your musicianship. I strongly recommend you do so, and if you don't have a jam buddy, consider exploring JustinGuitarJams!

👉 Ok. Time to check out our last module of the Beginner Course Module 22. Good luck. :)

Welcome to Module 22!

This module is a big deal: it wraps up our Grade 3!

Congratulations, you made it to the end of your Beginner Guitar Course. But we still have a lot to learn before moving on, and please, take your time. Here's the menu:

Beginner to Intermediate - we'll learn how to develop a practice routine perfect for advancing beginners!

E Shape Explorer - it's time to explore the E Shape; after that, you will have explored all CAGED Shapes.

Easy Barre Chords - barre chords are a thing to develop in the Intermediate grades, but we'll have a go at some easy barres to allow you to play even more songs and not be scared of barre chords!

We'll keep transcribing songs, consolidating your skills, and looking at how to duet with other players.

lessons.text:
Beginner to Intermediate Guitar Player: Bridge The Gap!

How should you be practicing on guitar as an - almost - Intermediate guitarist? This lesson will answer that question and explain how I think Advancing Beginner guitarists should practice and why it's so important to get it right!

🥉 If you've been following my Beginner Guitar Course, you're probably nearing the end of Grade 3; that means you're now an Advancing Beginner! You’re ready to consolidate all the great stuff you’ve learned as a Beginner guitarist before moving on to the Intermediate grades.

But before we discuss your practice routines, let's explore the difference between Beginner and Intermediate guitar players.

What's Beginner Guitar Practice Like?

Beginner guitarists need a lot of guidance. They need to be shown what to practice and for how long, when to move on to new material, which songs are appropriate for them, and so on. But the further along the journey you travel, the more independent you want to be. You'll realize the style of music you enjoy the best, the things you're good at, and the skills you want to develop.

Part of the transition from Beginner to Intermediate grades is developing this independence. The transition starts in the Advancing Beginner grades, which is Grade 3 in the JustinGuitar System.

Beginner Grade 3 Guitar Practice

Grade 3 is the bridge between Beginner and Intermediate stages. In this grade, I want you to consolidate your current skills and develop autonomy. You can do this by assessing yourself and asking yourself, "What do I like? What am I good at? Am I ready to move on?"

This is a tricky transition. You must start making decisions, which can be daunting! So let's look at some simple guidelines to help you structure effective practice routines and stay inspired for the long haul.

💡 Complete Practice: If you'd like more information about structuring your guitar practice, check out my Holistic Practice Routine lesson. We cover how to practice all the different areas of guitar in a way that’s nicely structured, but hopefully not too structured. :)

Practice The Music You Love

It's okay for beginners to dabble around in Country, Folk, Rock, and Pop to develop their skill sets and improve as guitar players. But the better you get, the more you need to focus on the music that gets you going! What will inspire you to keep playing guitar? I often find that people try to learn songs they think they should know rather than the songs they really love. That isn't great for your inspiration!

Ask yourself: "When listening to music, what do I really love? What's going to excite me to play guitar?" Every technique or knowledge you later acquire should focus on helping you play that music.

🙃 One of the biggest mistakes in my early guitar journey was learning things that I thought guitarists should know. The Harmonic Minor Scale is the perfect example! I spent far too long learning it, far too early - I didn't know when to use it, yet I spent ages running those scales up and down. And it was all pretty pointless. Okay, I do use it from time to time. But unless you want to play Jazz or Neo-Classical Rock, there's simply no point learning it.

You need to get clear on the music you love and your end destination, then work backward and decide what you need to learn. Having a refined taste in music makes this process easier. If you've got a really broad taste, you have more options, and you might find it trickier to choose! Trying to focus on too many areas means your progress will be less visible, and your learning will be thinly spread.

I suggest you narrow your focus a little for this part of the journey: focus on one style, genre, and skillset for now. You can broaden it or switch styles later on. :) This focus will help you set a goal and determine a path.

🔥 Want to master your guitar routine? Check out Effective Practice, my free 14-lesson series on how to make the most of your practice sessions.

You Can't Practice Everything

There's a great saying: "as our circle of knowledge expands, so does the circumference of darkness surrounding it." In other words - the more you know, the more you know that you don't know.

At the beginning of the guitar journey, it all seems pretty easy. You go through the steps and learn what you're told to learn. But at some point, you lift your head up and see that there is so much more to explore in all directions! It can be pretty overwhelming when you realize how much there is out there. But take comfort in the fact that you won't try to learn it all. Nobody does, except for a few outstanding guitarists in history who are amazing at a number of styles. So you have to start making choices! If you could be great at one style, which would it be?

😉 I know I'll never be a great Flamenco guitar player. I'd love to be, but it'd take a whole lifetime, and I'd have no time for anything else. So while I love the style and play it in the garden in the summer as a little hobby, I'm pretty hopeless at it. I just don’t have enough time to get good! The same thing goes for Jazz guitar. I'd love to be an amazing Jazz player, but I just don't have the hours.

This depends on your motivation for playing too. If you want to be a professional guitarist like a studio player, a theatre play, or an artist or songwriter, each of these has a different skill set. If playing guitar is a source of comfort for you after a hard day's work and you want to play a little of everything, that's totally fine too.

I find that most people enjoy the journey more if they notice they're progressing. And for that, having a goal, even a short-term one, is really useful. Choose one thing to focus on for now. You can even change it halfway.

💡 The guitar journey is like planning a holiday! You might decide to go hiking in Switzerland then change your mind and go wine tasting in France. Your destination changed, but the important thing is that you still had a destination. You didn't just aimlessly drive around the countryside. Same goes for learning guitar - always have a destination to reach.

Having a focus means you can direct your energy toward it. You can always change your mind later if you get fed up! Without a direction, you wander around and return to your starting point. You look back years later and wonder how you haven't progressed.

While pursuing your goals, you might find a style you love and want to learn for the rest of your life. :)

Identify Your Strengths & Weaknesses On Guitar

We've all got different strengths. Some of us are naturally better at rhythm guitar but struggle with improvising. Others have a great sense of time but have trouble finding melodies. Everyone has their own skillset. So here's the key question: are you going to perfect your strengths or polish your weaknesses?

Playing to your strengths is usually better if you want to be an artist and define your musical vision. Figure out your strengths and put all your energy into developing them so you become great at that one thing. On the other hand, if you want to be a general guitarist, like a player in a cover band or pit band, or a session player, you'll need a broader skillset. You'll learn to play more things but at a lower level.

If there's something you love, focus your energy on it, and you'll find you get much better at that one thing.

🌟 I know lots of incredible guitarists that excel in their field! They're amazing at it, and that's why you've heard of them. But they struggle in other areas! They might be incredible at fingerstyle but can't really play a Blues. They might be an incredible Jazz guitarist but can't play Metal for toffee! There are lots of famous guitarists who compose great solos but can't improvise, and it doesn't matter! That's not a criticism - it's what you expect.

You've got to decide if you want to go broad or narrow. Will you focus on a few things and do them really well, or will you do lots of things to a decent level?

I'm the latter. I can do many things reasonably well, but I don't excel in one area. This stops me from being a famous guitarist like Tommy Emmanuel, Brian May, or Mike Dawes. These guitarists have excelled in one area, so they're the ones you've heard of!

Customize Your Guitar Practice

A common example of this strengths and weaknesses thing is our playing speed. Many older guitar players don't feel they can play fast enough. This is to do with age - when you're young, you have faster twitch fibers in your muscles and can quickly learn to play fast.

You'll need to spend more effort and time on it if you're in your forties or fifties, but it's still possible! You need to decide whether you even need to play quickly or not. If the music you love doesn't involve fast guitar playing, there's no need for it.

🤔 How Fast? I think it's good if you can play faster than necessary so that you can play with ease and comfort. Let your tastes guide you - if you want to play Pink Floyd, then you don't need to play fast lines.

Another point is whether you want to use a pick or play fingerstyle. Some people find fingerstyle much more comfortable than playing with a pick; others find it awkward. If you find using the fingers way more natural, then focusing on finger style is totally okay.

If you want to play Metal guitar really fast, you'd be best learning with a pick. But that didn't stop Jeff Beck! I'd never have taught him to play Rock with his fingers, but he's the greatest of all time. How wrong would I have been? Mark Knopfler seems to do pretty well too!

Like Chris Buck and Ariel Posen, the new blood seems to go for a hybrid approach - pick and fingers. That's fine too. You don't have to stick with one or the other forever, but it's good to have an idea to guide your journey in the short term.

Enjoy Your Guitar Practice!

The most important thing about making a practice routine is that you enjoy it. If you don't, you'll find it much more difficult to get your bum on the seat and practice. If you struggle with motivation, you need to think about your practice routine and change it so that it's inspiring to you.

I've been playing guitar for over 40 years and still only practice things that inspire me to play in the studio. I think about what I still really want to do on guitar and what inspires me to learn. Jeff Beck passed away recently, so I might spend a couple of hours fumbling my way through Nadia and doing a bad job, but I still really enjoy it! I'm doing something I've always wanted to do on the guitar.

💡 If I'm upstairs on the sofa or playing with my daughter and some time opens up, I need to feel motivated to dedicate that time to guitar practice. If I picture myself running scales up and down, playing arpeggios in thirds, practicing Jazz harmony, and learning altered scale positions, there's absolutely no way I'll get my bum on the chair. No chance!

It's mostly about songs because that's what inspires me. I dip into many different genres to keep my bum on the seat and fuel my motivation.

People give up practicing guitar because they forget why they love it. They see an article online like Here are The 20 Things Every Guitarist Should Practice and they start practicing the Harmonic Minor Scale in 20 different positions, playing arpeggios, changing between them... it's no wonder they get fed up!

If you like Bebop, you'll need to know all that stuff, and learning it will inspire you. If not, there's absolutely no point in learning it.

So make sure that your practice is inspiring and that you enjoy it every time you do it. And if that means not having a routine and learning random songs, then that's your practice routine. Along the way, you might find technical areas or knowledge that need work, so those songs will guide the other areas of your routine. :) I hope you follow these tips. If you do, you'll play guitar for a long time and still love it - like me! I really hope this helps you create an inspiring practice routine.

💬 How is your Grade 3 journey going so far? Join the discussion and let me know!

lessons.summary: Learn how to make your simple E Chord sound wicked on the guitar.
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Playthrough

00:15 Lesson Welcome

00:37 Exploring the E Chord

07:35 What Now?
lessons.text:
E Chord Variations All Beginners Should Know

It's time to look at the E Shape and how to make cool sounds using variations of the regular open E chord. Adding fingers, taking them away, all that good stuff. :)

💡 This lesson is part of my Chord Shapes Explorer series - included in my Beginner Course - Grade 3. If you've missed the previous lessons, check them out now.

D Chord Shape Explorer

C Chord Shape Explorer

G Chord Shape Explorer

A Chord Shape Explorer

Moving Up Open Chords

And much more to come!

Note: Explorer lessons for all five CAGED shapes can also be found, grouped together, under All Courses here.

Create Variations by Lifting Fingers Off

First, we'll explore how to create variations by lifting fingers off. Let's start with a regular E Major chord using fingers 1, 2, and 3 (022100). If we lift off finger 1, we get an Em chord (022000).

We can't usually substitute an E Major for an E minor chord – it sounds weird and is harmonically incorrect. What we can do is hammer on with finger 1. That can sound bluesy, especially when combined with Esus4 (see the section on Adding Little Finger).

💡 Chord Naming – Learn how to name chords and much, much more with my course Practical Music Theory.

If we lift off finger 3, we reveal the open D string and get an E7 chord (020100). Since the b7 note (the open D string) is low, it doesn't sound as good as the other open E7 chord (022130). So we should probably avoid it as a chord, but we can use it to embellish.

And if we lift off finger 2, we leave the open A string, which is also great for adding extra notes and embellishing. Try hammering on fret 2 from the open string while playing the chord. It has a country sound but sounds wicked in other styles too.

Variations Using Little Finger

Some of these are tricky for beginner guitarists, but I encourage you to try them! Let's start by adding the little finger to fret 3 of string 1; it gives us 022103, and a strange chord called an Eaddm3! That shouldn't work, but in Blues, it sounds awesome.

We can also add our little finger to fret 2 of string 1, giving us an Eadd9 (022102). It nearly always works, as does adding it to fret 2 of string 2 (022120), which is an E6 chord.

If we add our little finger to fret 2 of string 3 (022200), we get Esus4. This one is super common. You can also play this chord by barring with fingers 2 and 3. If we add our little finger to fret 3 of string 2 (022130), we get an E7, as mentioned earlier.

💡Break The Rules! The point of chord explorer is to break the rules, so try out these chords in songs. If it sounds good, it is good. :)

Time for another strange one! If we add it to fret 3 of string 3, we get an Esus#11 chord! It won't sound good in pop or folk but can work in metal or other alternative genres.

And finally, it's possible to add it to fret 3 of string 6. You can "curl" the note by bending the string down. It sounds wicked.

Practice, Practice, Practice

There are fewer variations in the E shape, so you must get comfortable with them. When you practice, spend some time just working on these variations and getting used to the new sounds. Then try them out when you're practicing songs. 12 Bar Blues in the key of E are a great place to start because E takes up most of the bars.

It's best to use one or two variations well than knowing lots but being unable to use them. Keep your ears open and listen. Practice them until they become instinctual.

If you have any questions or suggestions, leave a comment below. Have fun exploring the E-shape, and again, make sure you use all this in your songs! Cheers. :)

🚨 Don't forget to log in to save your favorite lessons and track your progress. Don't have an account yet? Sign up for free!

lessons.title: Transcribing Difficult Riffs
lessons.summary: Do you dare transcribe these very difficult riffs?
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Lesson Welcome

01:10 5 Riffs to Transcribe

04:55 What now? More tips!
lessons.text:
Are you ready to transcribe these faster, trickier riffs on the guitar?

But hey - this lesson is already the third one about transcribing riffs in our Grade 3! Before you get started with these riffs, make sure you've tried lessons 1 and 2! If not, these songs will be tricky for you. The riffs here will be faster and more complex, and you'll need to move around the neck.

💡 Slowing down the music can help, and it's not cheating. Learn my 4 easy steps to transcribe songs by ear!

Slowing down helps you get an accurate transcription and hear the nuances. I've met some fantastic guitarists who do this when they transcribe; I'm not fantastic, but I definitely do that too. :)

Ready? Now let's get started.

5 Famous Riffs to Transcribe

Your homework for this lesson is to figure out how to play these amazing riffs! Grab your guitar and get started. :)

Riff 1: Beat It by Michael Jackson

One of the greatest guitar riffs in history!

Riff 2: Crazy Train by Ossy Osbourne

Another classic tune. This riff is relatively easy and is very clear in the recording. A lot of fun to work out.

Riff 3: Day Tripper by The Beatles

Yet another riff that everyone should know how to play! You can expand on this one and use it for improvising. :)

💡My Journey – I learned to play guitar mostly by transcribing the music I loved! Read more.

Riff 4: Do I Wanna Know by The Arctic Monkeys

This entire album has great riffs, and the one at the beginning of Do I Wanna Know is a lot of fun to transcribe.

Riff 5: Heartbreaker by Led Zeppelin

Another awesome riff to work out!

Writing Out In Tab

You should write out your transcriptions in TAB! It helps you keep track of the music. Writing down the notes and seeing them on paper make them easier to remember.

When I used to use TAB or any sheet music, it took me ages to learn riffs compared to when I transcribed them. When you work out songs, you have to listen several times and find the notes yourself, meaning you learn the riff too!

Why Work Out Riffs?

Three-quarters of guitarists don't transcribe. Why should we bother to figure out riffs when we can look them up online? You feel ultra satisfied when you work out your favorite riffs alone. It gives you confidence in your playing and inspires you.

You grow your ear and improve the relationship between your hand and musical imagination. And you leave way more than just the songs! If you learned by transcribing alone, having no idea what chords, scales, or notes you were using, you'd become an excellent musician.

💡 Transcription Tales: When teaching at The Guitar Institute, I could immediately tell whether a student had transcribed music or not. It was super obvious!

Transcribing is a habit. The more songs you work out, the more you enjoy them. The sky is the limit! Even the most difficult songs are usually fairly easy to transcribe. They might be hard to play, but you can easily find the chords and notes. Okay, there are exceptions, but this is often true.

Where To Take This?

Now it's time for the songs that you want to learn! Choose songs from your favorite band and try to work out the chords and riffs. You can even try the bassline!

Let me repeat – you'll learn so much from transcribing that you can't learn in books. The players we all love are the ones that have played by ear!

Even when you get it wrong, you're learning. And when you get it right, you get a feeling of satisfaction that songbooks and tabs can't give you. :) Go and have lots of fun playing your favorite songs by ear and see the power of transcribing for yourself.

🎸 Transcribe the Blues! Learn with my Transcribing Blues Solos Course.

lessons.title: Easy Barre Chords For Beginners
lessons.summary: Barre chords don't need to be scary! Start here, build strong barre chord basics as a beginner, and prepare for the intermediate stages!
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 Lesson Intro

00:50 Why Should I Try Them?

02:08 Before You Explore Barre Chords

02:52 E-Shape Major Barre Chords

05:04 A-Shape Minor Barre Chords

08:04 A-Shape Major Barre Chords

09:22 E-Shape Minor Barre Chords

12:02 Next Steps
lessons.text:
Barre chords don't have to be scary! Here's an introduction for beginners. :)

If you're following my Beginner's Course, you'll have already come across the F barre chord. In this lesson, we'll move that shape around your guitar neck to play other barre chords.

If you have the F chord mastered, it's time to expand your chord repertoire. We'll look at Major and Minor barre chords, and it's way easier than you might imagine. :)

But why are we looking at barre chords at this stage?

Why Learn Barre Chords In the Beginner Stage?

At Grade 3, which is Advancing Beginner territory, it's time to consolidate all the material from the Beginner's Course. This includes chords, embellishments, strumming patterns, scales, and more. I recommend 3-6 months for consolidation time. :)

In this revision phase, you're bound to find songs that use barre chords. And we don't want to let one barre chord stop us from learning a great song!

So we'll look at how to play the most common barre grips, taking advantage of the shapes we already know. This lesson is a little taste. We dive deep into barre chords in the Intermediate grades. :)

Taking The Sting Out Of Barre Chords

Most beginners are scared by barre chords! But you should try them even if you don't feel 100% ready. The only potential issue is overexpectation: expecting to nail them and getting disheartened when you realize they're too tricky.

Regardless, I encourage you to have a go. It's useful to get a feel for them ahead of time, and they might be easier than you thought.

If you have big, strong fingers, you might find barre chords easier than some open chords. :)

🎸 Making The Jump: If you find these chords tricky, ask yourself what you need to work on. This could be the names on strings 6 and 5, shifting power chords around the neck, thumb position, or hand strength.

Let's discuss what skills you need before you can tackle these chords.

Beginner Checklist

You need to have these skills under your fingers before looking at barre chords:

The F barre chord: if you struggle with it, spend some time on it then continue with the rest of this lesson.

The notes on the two thickest strings. You don't need to recognize them instantly – it's enough if you can work them out quickly.

How to play power chords and move them around the neck. Knowing the notes on strings 6 and 5 helps.

I strongly suggest you work on these areas before starting this lesson. :) If that's all cool, let's get to those barre chords!

Exploring E-Shape Major Barre Chords

Let's start with our F Major barre chord and discover what new Major chords we can play by moving this shape up and down the neck.

Play the F chord using the E shape: 133211. Finger 1 barres fret 1, finger 3 frets 5:3 (string 5, fret 3), finger 4 plays 4:3 (string 4, fret 3), and finger 2 frets 3:2. This is an E-shape chord because fingers 2, 3, and 4 form the shape of the open E chord. :)

💡 This is a Moveable Shape: You can move this shape up and down the neck to get new Major chords. F Major is the hardest of these – and you can already play it. So the rest should be pretty straightforward. :)

For example, if you slide the whole shape up four frets so that finger 1 barres fret 5, you have an A Major chord (577655). This is because the note under finger 1 on string 6, the root note, is A.

Notice that the positions of the fingers relative to one another don't change. :) If we move this whole shape down one fret, we get a G# Major chord (466544). Now the root note is at 6:4: G#.

🤔 G# or Ab?: G# Major (466544) is harmonically the same as Ab Major (466544). The name we give this chord depends on the context, so these chords are called enharmonic equivalents. If you're doing my Theory Course, you'll know this stuff already. :)

Use F Chord to Play Any Major Chord

Now, move back to the F chord, and see if you can move the shape up one fret at a time, playing a different Major chord in each position. We have F (133211), F# (244322), G (355433), G# (466544), A (577655), A# (688766), B (799877), and so on. So this one shape is the basis for many major chords. :)

This trick is handy for songs with weird chords in them. Bands like The Beatles throw in unusual chords all the time! For example, there's no way to play a G# chord with open chords. This is the beauty of barre chords – you can play ANY chord with them. Chords like G# then become as easy as an F chord!

💡 This is a taster designed to help you play a few songs and explore barre chords. We go into much more depth with barre chords in the Intermediate Grades.

We've looked at a Major barre chord shape – now let's go minor. :)

Exploring A-Shape Minor Barre Chords

We can even play minor chords with the F shape! How is that possible?

Let's look at how to play a Bm chord. Grab an F Barre Chord (133211). To get to Bm, we move this entire shape down one string and up one fret. You should now be holding X24432, with finger 1 at fret 2. You're playing the root note at 5:2, which is B, and holding a minor shape. So this chord is called Bm.

🚨 Bm is a super-common chord often found in songs in the key of G and D. It’s likely you’ll come across it, and now you know how to play it! It’s pretty easy if you know F already.

Notice that string 6 is muted – let the tip of finger 1 lightly touch it so it doesn't ring out. Finger 1 shouldn't be hanging off the end of the fretboard. :)

The barre is now only fretting 5:2 and 1:2, so the finger can be rounder than it was for the E-Shape Major Chord. And even if the barre goes a little wrong and you don't fret 1:2 properly (X2443X), the chord still sounds good.

Now, notice there are no open strings. That means this chord is moveable. :) If we move it up one fret, we get Cm (X35543). This is because the root note is at 5:3, which is the note C, and we're holding a minor shape.

🧐 Cm is super common in Beatles songs in the key of G. The chords often change from C to Cm (chord IV to chord IVm). This is one of the Beatles tricks that bands like Oasis draw on a lot.

We also have Dm (X57765), Em (X79987), Ebm (X68876), and C#m (X46654), a chord often found in songs in A. :) Again, this shape enables us to play any minor chord we like.

Let's sneak peek at the barre chord that people most struggle with: the A Shape Major Barre Chord!

Exploring A-Shape Major Barre Chords

Let's check out this shape with an example. Here's a D Major chord using the A shape: X5777X. Finger 1 frets 5:5 and mutes strings 6 and 1, while finger 3 barres strings 4 to 2 at fret 7. It's harder than it looks!

🤔 Why Is This An A-shape Chord? This D Major chord is an A-shape chord because the notes under finger 3 form a shape that looks like an open A chord. We play the mini-barre because it’s really awkward to use fingers 2, 3, and 4 for the notes on fret 7.

Now you have two options for the awkward major chords! Can you think of two ways to play a C# Major chord? Hint: Consider the two Major barre chord shapes and where you can find C# on each string.

Okay, 6:9 and 4:4 are both the note C#. So you can play C# as an E shape with finger 1 on fret 9 (9 11 11 10 9 9), and as an A shape with finger 1 at fret 4 (X4666X).

As I said, this is tricky. Don't worry if it seems impossible right now! I suggest you hold back from this shape until you're in the Intermediate grades. :) Speaking of tricky barre chords...

Exploring E-Shape Minor Barre Chords

As with the A Major barre chord shape, but don't worry if these are too tricky.

Let's look at a super-common E-Shape Minor Barre Chord: F#m (244222). To play it, grab an F# Major Chord (244322) and lift off finger 2. Now you have F#m. :) This is like lifting off finger 1 from E (022100) to get Em (022000).

🚨 Sorting Out String 3: The main issue with this barre chord is string 3. You might find it doesn’t ring out properly. If that’s the case, you have to work on your barre strength. Finger 1 frets four notes at the same time – it needs to be strong!

If you have big, strong hands, the F#m should be okay. But if you have small or weak hands, it'll take some practice. In any case, it's good to try it. And the more you play it, the stronger your hand will get. :)

Next Steps for Advancing Beginners

I suggest you find some songs that mostly use open chords but have one barre chord - often you find one in the bridge. Give them a try. :)

This lesson gives you a taste of learning barre chords for real. And it'll expand your repertoire. :) If these grips are tricky for you, figure out what skills you're missing.

💡 Consolidate, consolidate, consolidate! Don't be in a rush to learn all these new chords. You’re much better to practice your open chords and make sure you can make good music with them. Build a solid foundation, then look for new techniques.

If you're an advancing beginner guitarist, meaning you know open chords, perhaps one or two barre chords, and some power chords, go and check out the Grade 3 lessons on the website. I've added a heap of fun things you might want to try.

We look at how to move basic chord shapes, interesting strumming patterns, picking out individual notes while strumming, barre chords with open strings, and more! It's not too difficult, but it can add tons of interest to your playing.

Have loads of fun exploring these barre chord shapes! Laters. :)

👉 Ready for more? Keep working on your Beginner Consolidation!

lessons.title: Module 22 Practice Routine
lessons.summary: Your LAST beginner practice suggestion is here. Are you ready? :)
lessons.videoChapters:
00:00 How It Works

00:21 Knowledge & Technique

01:44 Repertoire

02:54 Time

03:21 Transcribing & Improvising
lessons.text:
You made it! You reached the end of the Beginner Guitar Course. Congratulations.

Module 22 was about consolidating everything we've learned in Grade 3, and it's time for your Practice Routine. But as encouraged throughout this Module, you're now more responsible for making your practice routine and how to fill it out to be most appropriate for you. You know better than anyone else what things you should be working on! That said, here's a starting point.

Your Suggested Practice Routine for Module 22!

5' Technique - Easy Barre Chords 5' Technique - What You Need 5' Knowledge - E-Shape Explorer 5' Knowledge - Write Your Own Routine! 5' Repertoire - Devise A 10-Song Setlist 5' Repertoire - What You Need 5' Time - Groove (Looper Or Jam Buddy) 5' Time - What You Need 10' Ear Training - Transcribing (Difficult Riffs) 10' Improvising - What You Need

Section #1 - Technique - 2 x 5 minutes

Easy Barre Chords + What You Need

Use the first Teachnique slot to work on easy barre chords. For the second slot ask yourself what techniques you need to work on the most? You should be able to identify those things and adjust your practice schedule accordingly.

singing & playing at the same time

minor pentatonic legato technique

picking individual strings while strumming

linking chords using scales

rolling chords

finger gym

Section #2 - Knowledge - 2 x 5 minutes

E-Shape Explorer + What You Need

For the first slot you have the E-Shape Explorer. However, you could start exploring all of the chords at this point! If you practice five times weekly, you work on C, A, G, E, and D, playing with each. A good idea would be to focus on just the E-Shape for a week or two, then explore a different chord shape per day.

☝️Don't skip this! The more you practice and explore your chord shapes, the more cool things you will find. The more unusual chords you discover, the more you'll be less afraid of a chord that looks different from the standard shapes you've been used to playing.

Your second Knowledge practice slot could be writing a practice routine for yourself. Please give it some thought, and focus on identifying your weaknesses and strengths. Choose from:

C A G E D chord-shape explorers

open tunings

using triads

the lifted barre trick

moving easy chord shapes

music theory

Section #3 - Repertoire - 2 x 5 minutes

10-Song Set List + What You Need

Ideally, you want to prepare a set list for a duet, so find a jam buddy you can play with and perform for family and friends! If you don't have a jam buddy, design a set with around 10 songs you're comfortable playing alone. Aim to play the guitar and sing, but you could try to find a singer if you can't sing!

The point is to have a set list of 10 songs that you can play all the way through! Remember to leave your comfort zone and try some easy barre chords, like B Minor or F# Minor.

For the second slot, think about your own repertoire needs. You may want to merge all of this time together or think of other aspects to include in your routine according to your needs.

Section #4 - Time - 2 x 5 minutes

Groove + What You Need

For Time, use your looper or play with somebody else to work on your groove for Time! Your focus is to work on the synchronicity between two musicians, an extremely valuable skill to develop. You can also include some practice in playing your barre chords! Fill the second slot with any practice that feeds into your ability to play with good time and rhythm feel.

Section #5 - Ear Training - 10 minutes

Transcribing

Our last Transcribing lesson was about riffs, so spend time working them out. Riffs are such a valuable thing to practice! Byt his stage, you may have figured out that transcribing can be more efficient when the time slots are chunked together. Do not feel constrained to 10 minutes per session, perhaps look at a weekly session of one hour instead.

<🎧 Please transcribe for longer than only 10 minutes. Find songs and bands you love and that inspire you. Transcribing is such a valuable thing!

Section #5 - Improvising - 10 minutes

What You Need (& Enjoy)

Also, remember the 10-minute slot for improvising. You can explore Blues lead and licks, Major Scales Improvisation, and everything we learned in previous lessons. Improvising will help you become a better guitar player and consolidate what you have learned as a beginner.

👀 Grade 3 Feedback: How did it go?

Take a minute to share your thoughts in this quick Grade 3 survey! Let us know what clicked, what was tricky, and how confident you feel—your feedback helps us improve the course!

What's Next?

Take your time to ensure you have a strong foundation. "Don't be in a hurry!" is my strongest advice for advancing beginners.

👉 When you're ready… we'll see each other in Grade 4. Wow! You're an Intermediate guitarist. :)

modules.title: Master Your Major Scales
modules.intro:
Want to know your Major Scales and be able to play nice melodic solos over major chord sequences? Then this one is for you!

In this video, all 5 Major scales will be taught using my unique and practical method - study one pattern at a time and learn not just the shape but how to use it! This is aimed at Intermediate level guitarists!

You'll learn Pattern Studies, Single Finger Solos and Exploring Positions, and once you are able to use a position, you learn the next... then you join them together to eventually be able to play all over the neck. This method works :)

This series is one I am very proud of, having seen many students work through this and come out being able to make music with the major scale confidently all over the neck. We focus on the G Major Scale throughout, exploring one scale pattern at a time and doing multiple exercises to help you USE the major scales. There is little to be learned from playing scales up and down, but a lot to be learned by using them, which is the big goal of this series.

Many people learn scales, but most don't learn HOW TO USE SCALES TO MAKE MUSIC. This 120-minute series will show you how to combine your knowledge and your ear to make cool melodic improvisations!

lessons.title: Master Your Major Scales: Intro
lessons.summary: Welcome to the JustinGuitar course on mastering your major scales! We’ll be learning five major scale positions that will help you expand as a guitarist!
lessons.text:
**Don't forget to download your booklet from the downloads tab above!**

Hello! Welcome to this JustinGuitar course on mastering your major scales! This is great fun stuff, and if you work on it a bit, it will really open up your guitar playing, allowing you to use scales to compose and improvise music.

To do this, we’re going to learn five major scale positions that relate to the CAGED System on the guitar. This teaches you how to use the scales and put them all together to create a tune. We’re going to be learning everything in the key of G, and it really helps to practice these scales with a backing track in the proper key.

Practice Tips

Firstly, always practice SLOWLY! Try to play it as perfectly as possible before speeding anything up, even before practising with a metronome.

Secondly, get into a practice routine of some sort. Personally, I like using a practice chart to track my progress as it really does help to keep things moving along nicely.

Third, understand the difference between playing and practising. Practising involves paying close attention to everything you’re doing and being quite deliberate and slow. Playing is more easy-going and flexible. Overthinking while playing is not a great thing!

Finally, be patient with yourself! These are things you’ll be working on for quite some time, so don’t push yourself too hard. These are pretty fundamental skills, too, so you want to make sure you spend a good amount of time on them to drive them into your head - and into your fingers!

Music Theory

Just a little bit of music theory can go a long way when talking about scales and chords, so bear with me briefly!

As I said, we’ll be learning everything in the key of G major, so we’ll be working with the group of chords that come from the key. There are seven notes in each key, so seven chords as well. Any group of the chords in a key will take on the notes of the corresponding scale. For instance, if you’ve got a song containing chords in the key of G, such as G, Am, C, and Em, you can use your G major scale to build melody lines over those chords.

If you want to get into understanding this on a deep level then check out my Practical Music Theory Course!

lessons.title: MMS Lesson 1
lessons.summary: When practising scales, it really helps to work with a metronome, but only after you’re comfortable playing the scale on its own!
lessons.text:
👉 NOTE: Please download the MMS eBook from the Intro lesson. The Resource links in MMS lessons 1-10 are no longer active.

When learning scales, it helps to practice with a metronome - but not until AFTER you’ve learned and memorized the correct notes in the scale. Work it out on your own, take your time, and once you’re comfortable playing all the way up and down the scale accurately several times in a row, then you can break out the metronome.

To practice, start with a tempo you’re comfortable with, let’s say 80 bpm. Using alternating picks, play one note per click. A good rule of thumb is to be able to play the scale perfectly, up and down, four times consecutively before speeding it up. Try to get all the way up to 160 bpm.

Once you’ve done that, drop it back down to 80 bpm, this time hitting two notes per click. Repeat the process.

Finally, drop back down to 80 bpm again, but try to squeeze in four notes per click.

Remember - you want to be able to play these scales from memory, confidently, evenly, and with minimal movement from your picking hand!

lessons.title: MMS Lesson 2
lessons.summary: Let’s get into Position 1! There are a few different ways you should be practicing this, but it will all help you get super comfortable with the scale.
lessons.text:
👉 NOTE: Please download the MMS eBook from the Intro lesson. The Resource links in MMS lessons 1-10 are no longer active.

Alright, let’s crack into it! Once you’ve got the Position 1 major scale firmly in your memory, you’re ready to start exploring it a bit. This is a good way to practice each of the positions we’ll be learning. Later, we’ll work on combining them all so you sort of make one huge scale that spans the majority of your fretboard.

To start, play the scale comfortably up and down from memory a few times in a row, starting and finishing on the root note.

Then, you’re going to play the scale, but changing directions at random. For example, start going up the scale, but halfway through, start to come back down just a little, and then go back up again.

After that, try jumping strings, making sure to keep to the notes within the scale.

Finally, be aware of where the chord tones are relative to the major scale shape.

This will highlight the importance of LISTENING! Go figure - that’s still a major part of making music! I like to use a little twist on the George Orwell quote, “All notes are equal, but some notes are more equal than others.” All that means is that while some notes technically fit within the pattern, you’ll find that some individual notes simply sound better over certain chords. Just keep an ear open for anything that sounds a little off.

Also, we’re going to start getting into pattern studies. To start off with, we’re going to be playing the scale, but in thirds. This helps to make the scale more musical, but all of these exercises help you get super familiar with the scale, inside and out. It will pay off, I promise!

lessons.title: MMS Lesson 3
lessons.summary: In this lesson, we’re going to be playing the scale in thirds, as well as diving into Position 2.
lessons.text:
👉 NOTE: Please download the MMS eBook from the Intro lesson. The Resource links in MMS lessons 1-10 are no longer active.

In this lesson, we’re going to be exploring those thirds, but we’re also going to explore using just one finger to play a scale. This will help to further familiarize you with the notes in the scale, but it’ll come in especially handy later when we start combining the scales.

When using the same finger to play different frets on the same string, you have the option of either sliding from one fret to the next or shifting to it. When sliding, you’re picking the string once and then maintaining your finger pressure from one fret to the next. When shifting, you’re picking up your finger between each note and picking each note individually.

Practice

Play up and down the scale using a metronome.

Play the scale in thirds using alternate picking.

Start exploring one-minute improvising and start thinking about phrasing.

Position 2

After that, you’re ready for Position 2! This one starts with the lowest root note. You’re going to play the scale up from the root note, come all the way back down, and then go up again to the root note. Remember - you’re always starting and finishing on the root note.

You’ll start to notice some weird fingering things here, too. Depending on your hand position, you’ll find that sometimes you play a note with a different finger on the way down than you did on the way up. Just take notice of it and see what’s comfortable for you.

lessons.title: MMS Lesson 4
lessons.summary: We’re exploring Position 2 in this lesson, as well as learning a new exercise pattern.
lessons.text:
👉 NOTE: Please download the MMS eBook from the Intro lesson. The Resource links in MMS lessons 1-10 are no longer active.

We’re going to be exploring Pattern 2 here, similarly to how we did back in Lesson 2 with Pattern 1.

3 In A Line Melodic Sequence

For this Melodic Sequence, you’re going to be playing three notes in a line - 1 2 3; 2 3 4; 3 4 5; etc. When doing this, try using different fingerings and play around with the pattern. It’s part of the learning process!

Then, apply the thirds pattern to Pattern 2, as well.

Remember - you’ll likely have to spend weeks on this stuff before moving on to the next lesson! Take your time with it, as you need to form a strong foundation here before moving on.

lessons.title: MMS Lesson 5
lessons.summary: For this lesson, we’ll be looking at 134 and 124 shifts, as well as combining Positions 1 and 2.
lessons.text:
👉 NOTE: Please download the MMS eBook from the Intro lesson. The Resource links in MMS lessons 1-10 are no longer active.

Now, the fun stuff! Assuming you’ve mastered Patterns 1 and 2 (if you haven’t - go back now!), we’re going to work on combining the two of them. This can be a lot of fun, as you can really start to build some fun melodies around the two positions. Of course, if you don’t know them super well, you’re going to struggle with this!!

Also, we’ll be looking at the 134 and 124 shifts.

lessons.title: MMS Lesson 6
lessons.summary: Moving on to Position 3, this is an easy one!
lessons.text:
👉 NOTE: Please download the MMS eBook from the Intro lesson. The Resource links in MMS lessons 1-10 are no longer active.

Position 3 is a relatively easy one as each note has its own designated fret. This means you don’t have to shift your fingers around or move up or down the neck.

Continue to explore this position as you did the others!

lessons.title: MMS Lesson 7
lessons.summary: In this lesson, we’ll be combining Positions 1, 2, and 3, as well as learning Position 4.
lessons.text:
👉 NOTE: Please download the MMS eBook from the Intro lesson. The Resource links in MMS lessons 1-10 are no longer active.

Next, we’ll be combining Patterns 1, 2, and 3. It’s sort of like we’re stretching 1 and 2 just a bit more, developing one big scale pattern. Keep working on each position individually as you progress, as you’ll continue to improve on each one, and keep working with a metronome!

After that, you’re ready for Pattern 4, which fits around the A barre chord shape.

lessons.title: MMS Lesson 8
lessons.summary: For this lesson, we’re learning a new pattern - fourths. This will help you get used to some awkward fingerings, which will come in handy once you start soloing!
lessons.text:
👉 NOTE: Please download the MMS eBook from the Intro lesson. The Resource links in MMS lessons 1-10 are no longer active.

I’ve got a new pattern for you now - fourths. This one goes against the grain a bit, and it could force you to make some rather awkward fingering decisions, but that’s not necessarily a bad thing! You don’t have to play any particular note with any particular finger, and once you start soloing, you’ll have to get comfortable making these fingering decisions on the fly.

Keep working on combining Positions 1, 2, and 3, but don’t worry too much about incorporating 4 just yet.

lessons.title: MMS Lesson 9
lessons.summary: Finally, we’re going to combine Patterns 1, 2, 3, and 4, and get into Pattern 5.
lessons.text:
👉 NOTE: Please download the MMS eBook from the Intro lesson. The Resource links in MMS lessons 1-10 are no longer active.

Ok, now we can start adding Pattern 4 into our combination, which spans quite a large portion of your fretboard.

To practice, work with a backing track. Try playing in one position for a bit before moving to the next. Get comfortable with your shifting, especially into Pattern 4.

Also, keep working on your single-finger solos, but this time, focus on Pattern 3. You might even want to try using your 3rd finger rather than your 1st. It’s a little strange to use that finger for this kind of stuff, but it’ll help to open you up to different patterns and possibilities.

Finally, you can move on to Pattern 5! This scale fits around a G shape barre chord.

Then, you’re done! To continue your practice, apply all four of the patterns we learned to each position individually, and work on combining all five of the scales into one huge scale. You’ll be shredding in no time!

lessons.title: MMS Lesson 10
lessons.summary: Here’s a backing track in the key of G major.
lessons.text:
👉 NOTE: Please download the MMS eBook from the Intro lesson. The Resource links in MMS lessons 1-10 are no longer active.

Here’s a backing track in the key of G major for you to jam with! Have fun!

modules.label: BLUES LEAD 1
modules.title: Essential Blues Lead Guitar
modules.intro: Starting your journey into Blues guitar is great fun! Blues is a language and learning to communicate and it's very easy to learn the basics and get 'talking' right away. This first module in Blues Lead Guitar called Essential Blues Lead Guitar will take you through the techniques, vocabulary, scales and concepts you'll need to start improvising and jamming the blues!

lessons.title: The Blues Language
lessons.summary: Few people have said that this is one of the most useful and important lessons on my whole website and they might be right!
lessons.text:
If you want to learn the blues, it really helps to think of it like it is a language. Learn the alphabet (scales) then words (licks) then put them into sentences (phrases) and eventually into poems (solos). The lesson explains this in more detail and it's a pretty big deal if you want to get into playing Blues Lead Guitar. We don't play much this lesson but it will really help you to understand where we're going in this course and help you make the most of it!

Ok, lets flesh out this 'blues as a language' idea a bit.

The Alphabet

Blues is a language and the easiest way to understand it is to compare it to the way we learn a language (especially the way we would learn a second language as an adult). Most children will learn words directly from their environment (much as you might find yourself playing blues licks if you listen to it a lot!) but when at school and learning how to communicate, students are taught the alphabet first. If you want to try and learn a new language the first step will be to learn the alphabet of that language so you can pronounce the words! In the Blues Language, the most basic alphabet is the Minor Pentatonic Scale. It's very important that you learn it correctly and well, so you don't have to think about it, your fingers know where to go instinctively, much the same way as we learn the alphabet by rote.

The Words

Once you know your alphabet you will have trouble communicating anything unless you learn some words. Using English as an example, if you say "gohtsdref" it doesn't make sense to an English speaker. It's only when you start to combine the letters into recognizable words that you'll start communicating an idea.

Often guitar students will start improvising with the minor pentatonic scale and feel it's 'not sounding right' and listeners will think it sounds strange. But when the student starts playing some licks, even just a few, they can start communicating and it 'sounds right', 'feels right' and listeners will recognize the words - 'that person is speaking Blues' and they'll dig it!

Also interesting to observe is that you can use the same letters (with pronunciation changes) to speak other languages, say using our 'English' letters to speak French, merci mon amie! Same in music, we can use the Minor pentatonic scales in other styles of music, but we'd probably be using different licks and changing the way we play it (the accent) to make it sound right in the new language.

The Great Lick Myth

It's often been said that learning licks and set phrases can make your playing soulless and that you will not be expressing yourself. I don't expect or want you to believe me, but simple observation should show you that licks are an essential part of the blues language! If you listen to Eric Clapton you will hear licks that are exactly the same licks Albert King played, and while you can say for sure that Eric was influenced by Albert there is nothing bad about it! You will also hear Stevie Ray Vaughan playing Freddie King licks, Keith Richards playing Chuck Berry licks and the list goes on. Every great blues guitar player uses blues licks and as you develop your own playing you will notice that you can express yourself using licks you stole from someone else, you will put your own emotion into them and the collection of licks you learn will mix into your own style.

The Grammar

Not only do we have words but we also need to learn a little grammar too! We make sure our licks can be understood using space (full stops), repetition (developing an idea) and not over complicating things... You also need to be using the right licks in the right places or things won't be sounding right.

The Story

Once you know some licks and basic grammar you're ready to start telling stories. The more you practice the better you will learn to structure your solos (stories) to have dynamic interest and a build that keeps the listener engaged. There are specific tools you can learn to do this effectively and well which we cover later in the course, but most of this is best learned by experience.

The Old School Approach

I've studied a lot of Blues artists and the history of the blues and I can say for certain that many of the blues masters don't know much about the technical or theoretical elements of the music (language). They learned the same way as people learn a language by experience. Learning a foreign language at school will not be as effective as listening to native speakers, especially if you are completely immersed in it. There are many stories about the British Blues guitarists of the 60's hanging out together listening to blues records by the Three Kings (BB, Freddie and Albert) and stealing licks from them! Learning licks by ear will teach you a lot more than learning by 'book'. You will pick up the 'accent' a lot better and your playing will sound more authentic.

But. It's a lot harder to learn the Old School way and using the approach I give you here will make the journey a lot faster, and in some ways better. Once I show you the alphabet and some words, you'll recognize the words in solos you like and you will find it a lot easier to learn the solos by ear.

YOU MUST LISTEN TO THE BLUES IF YOU WANT TO PLAY IT.

Without a lot of listening you will never pick up the correct accents and pronunciation, it just won't happen. During the course, I will be recommending albums that I think are amazing and I'm sure you will learn better and faster if you can get 30 minutes a day at least to listen to some blues. Pick the artists you like and that stir emotion in you because they are the ones that will resonate best with, and you should learn the words that affect you the most.

I hope all that makes sense and that you are ready to start your journey learning The Blues. Hope you enjoy it.

Homework and Practice

There's no set physical practice this week - but try to find 10 minutes a day to do some concentrated listening of great blues recordings.
