They've got a different timbre to its sound! So, sometimes, you might choose your grip to fit the feeling you want to give to the tune.

My questions for you:

Are you confident with your F Chord?

Do you remember your root notes from your Power Chords?

Then try playing some songs using the E Shape in different parts of your guitar neck! :)

If you're still struggling with getting clear barre chords or knowing which grip to use and when, stick around, and this lesson will help you out.

What's The Difference Between Power Chords and Barre Chords?

Well, one uses just 2 or 3 notes, and the other uses 6! ;) But the real difference is that Power Chords are neither Major nor Minor Chords. That’s why we commonly call them “5th” chords - they contain just the root and the 5th.

As soon as you want that extra harmonic content in your chords, then you'll need to play full Barre Chords. We often associate Power Chords with rock and metal music because that ‘extra harmonic content’ usually doesn’t sound good with distortion! :)

Want to learn more about it? Try out my Music Theory course! It's the perfect shortcut you need to make music faster and better - and, of course, understand what you're playing.

Ok, But How To Find The Root Notes?

If you've come from my Beginner Course, you know the answer! You learned Power Chords - and the 6th Root Power Chords have the same root notes as the E Shape Major Barre Chord - yep, easy as that! The notes on string 6 are below. Take a look:

I hope you know the notes on the thickest string! Again - if you don’t know them by now, you need to get your finger out and do it. You shouldn't rely on the diagram but your memory. ;)

For this Grade 4, I expect you to know the notes on the thickest two strings - the E and the A strings. Your Ultimate Power Chord Guide is here, so go back and review that lesson if you need to.

Ready? Now try moving that E Shape Barre chord around the neck. Check out the following tips to learn how to play comfortably and get a nice sound!

How to Shift Between Barre Chords

There's an easy way of shifting between chords with the same shape! Aim to keep your fingers in contact with the strings but releasing all the pressure.

You can relax your thumb on the back of the guitar, but make sure your fingers are still touching the strings when you slide the shape to its new position. That's important, and it'll make your life easier! Don't allow your fingers to lose contact with the strings.

Play - Relax - Shift - Press - Play!

Let's practice:

Play a G Barre Chord.

Release the pressure but stay in contact with the strings.

Slide the hand to the 7th fret. Aim to keep the shape set!

Reapply the pressure

And play!

Doing the simple exercise of moving between the G and F chords is excellent, and it'll help your muscles develop. Practice enough to get comfortable with this new movement.

🚨 Avoid lifting the chord off completely. It’s a lot slower to have to reposition your fingers every time. It’s one of the most common beginner mistakes - but now you know how not to make it!

Let's take a look at common barre chord questions, mistakes that many players make, and what the mechanics to perfect barre chords really are!

I'm confident that this guide will help you finally nail your barre chords. Let's go!

Are Barre Chords Easier on Electric Guitar?

Yep - barre chords are usually easier to learn on electric guitar. That's because the strings are generally thinner and closer to the fretboard. So, if you have an electric guitar, I’d recommend getting started on it!

If you only have an acoustic or classical guitar, keep in mind that there are a few tricks you can try to make your life easier and your playing less painful. :) I'll get into more details shortly!

Short Fingers, Long Fingers, Weak Fingers?

Oh, the number of times I've heard 'the finger excuses!' Barre chords are indeed easier for those with big and strong hands. But, if it's not your case, you just need to make sure that your fingers are perfectly placed - and then give it some time for the muscles to develop - they will!

I’ve taught barre chords to people with fingers like sausages and children with skinny bean fingers. They've all got there in the end! You can do it too, but it takes practice.

Remember that people with big fingers can play barre chords easily but probably struggled to cram their fingers in for the Open A Chord. We’re all different and will face different challenges on our journey. But differences are to be celebrated.

What you should do is explore all the mechanics related to playing barre chords - and I broke them all down for you! Let's take a look at them. :)

Barre Chord Mechanics - The Secret To Easy Barre Chords :)

Ok, now let's talk about how to get clean notes when playing barre chords - just in case you're still struggling with it! Barre chord mechanics are the secret to play barre chords easily, and I'll give you as many tips and tricks as I can.

There are a few factors that come into play to help you get clean notes under your barre. I've got 7 tips for you - check out the first one next. :)

Barre Chords Tip 1 - All About Your Index Finger!

The first barre chord mechanic you should explore has to do with your barre placement. The best trick here is to remind yourself that your finger should be slight to its side.

Make sure to turn your first finger (the barre) about 45 degrees to its side. You don't want to use the back/flat part of your finger, where the flesh very soft. That'd make everything harder! ;)

You should press the strings with the part of your finger that is not as soft, and it's closer to the bone. Start with the finger right on the fret and just roll it back behind it. Here's an image that shows you the best placement for your index finger when playing barre chords:

And, before you worry about it: it's completely normal to have some lines running down the side of your finger after you practiced. As you can see, I still get many. :) You’ll develop an attractive callus soon enough!

Ok - What about the barre angle? 🧐

Let's take a look at that.

Extra Tip: Get That Angle Right!

Many people worry about getting the barre finger very straight but remember that you are not playing all the notes (yet!) Be aware that, when playing E Shape Major Barre Chords, your first finger is only pressing strings 6, 2, and 1 - keep that in mind at all times!

So, don’t worry too much if your barre is a little rounded for now. We play the other strings with the other fingers, so no need to waste pressure trying to hold them all down.

Ensure that the notes under your first finger sound good. Your barre is the first thing you should get right when trying to get nice-sounding chords.

Another common-ish worry is about your thumb position, but there's not a unique answer here - let's explore some best practices.

Barre Chords Tip 2 - Where Does the Thumb Go?

The ideal would be using the soft ‘pad’ of the thumb, but I use the side of the pad myself. :) Because we all have different anatomy, we are likely to find it comfortable to position our thumbs a little differently, too, and that’s fine.

I don’t think the thumb position matters a great deal if you can make a good sound, but do make adjustments if your thumb hurts.

Keeping your thumb more or less directly behind the barre is the easiest. That will help you a big deal! Take a look at the image below:

That is not a natural position for our fingers, and that's why we'll now approach the position of your wrist. That will help you too!

Barre Chords Tip 3 - Wrist Position

Once you can get your fingers into the right place, it’s time to look at your wrist angle. The wrist position is crucial when playing barre chords! The best wrist position combines the proper mechanics of your index finger and your thumb!

If you've followed my tips 1 and 2, you should already have your wrist position almost right, but here are a few extra observations that will make barre chords more comfortable to play! Here's the main idea:

A very slight rotation of the wrist will help ‘jam’ the barre against the frets. It’s a kind of extension of the barre finger rolling onto its side.

It’s hard, and many people try this and are like, yeah - NO WAY. But guess what? With time and practice, you’ll get your wrist a lot flatter than you ever thought possible!

Your wrist should not be at 90 degrees. The aim is to keep the forearm to the wrist as flat as possible. It won’t be completely flat - but that should be the goal. Depending on which chord you're playing, you might find your wrist angles more than other times.

The 3 previous tips are already making everything easier, aren't they? :) But I still got more for you!

Barre Chords Tip 4 - Let Your Forearm Help!

This tip will help to ease your barre chord pain. In a nutshell, I suggest you slightly pull the strings with your elbow. :) Think about the forearm pulling back slightly, as well as the pinch between the thumb and first finger.

Before we get deeper into that, I want to make sure your wrist position is close to being perfect. :) Tips 3 and 4 work together. First of all, take a look at what you're not supposed to do with your wrist:

I think it's essential to understand why we should keep our wrist flat when playing barre chords! Who's up for some anatomy class?! :)

Our fingers are controlled by tendons, which go down the fingers through a little hole in the middle of the wrist called carpal tunnel - that goes down to your forearm. Take a look:

If you're getting wrist pain when playing your barre chords, it's probably because of your wrist position and the mechanics showed above. You should focus on that so you don't end up with carpal tunnel syndrome. :)

Of course - the wrist position will change according to the chord you're playing. But, your wrist should be as flat as possible, and that, with your forearm help, is where the barre chords should come from.

Now, let's look at something real essential but often overlooked by beginner guitar players: how you should hold your instrument!

Barre Chords Tip 5 - The Right Guitar Position

You shouldn't angle your guitar to look at your fingers. That gives you the worst wrist angle possible! As a guitar player, you should be able to play your grips without starring at your hands.

When you hold your guitar in the proper position, you only see the top of its neck. If you hold the guitar like I'm doing in the image below, you'll get yourself either back pain or a wrist sore!

There's a right way of holding your instrument. We're all different, and we'll need to tweak and try a few things and see what works best for you, but avoid these common beginner mistakes when holding the guitar.

Make sure you get all these tips on barre chord mechanics down. You must understand that barre chords aren't only about your finger strength. Many other fingers are involved here - and it's the combination of them that will allow you to get easy, good-sounding barre chords.

We're almost getting it all covered, I promise! Now let’s discuss the guitar neck angle. Yep - that can make a difference too. :)

Barre Chords Tip 6 - Guitar Neck Angle

I tend to play with a flat guitar neck, but you might find that lifting the headstock a little bit can help. Like that, the neck is pointing toward the air rather than perfectly horizontal. Take a look:

When you point your guitar toward the air, you have better access to the fretboard. That's probably the reason some people place the guitar in the other leg. It doesn't work for me, but many classical guitar players play like that.

There's no need to go crazy with it - but just 10-15˚angle can make a big difference. Try and see what works for you!

Ok - you've got all my barre chords secrets revealed now! And if you're still struggling with your barre chords, it might not be your fault anymore...

Take a look at my last, but not least, tip on how to get perfect barre chords.

Barre Chords Tip 7 - Still Too Hard? Maybe It's Not Your Fault!

If you find that the barre chords are very hard, it might be because your guitar’s action is too high. The strings being far from the frets mean that you have to press an unreasonable amount.

Especially if you only have an acoustic or classical guitar, make sure you check your guitar action. If a guitar's action is too high, it will be tough to play it, especially when you're learning barre chords. For a beginner, a good set-up can make the real difference! Learn more about what's the best guitar for beginners here. ;)

You can also learn how to make basic adjustments to the guitar by yourself, but I still take mine to a professional. Getting a setup from a decent luthier will make a poor guitar playable and an ok guitar even better. I would highly recommend getting it done by a professional! That's what they do, and once you find someone you trust, you'll know what I mean! :)

Now it's time for your hard work! Let's dive into the best practice routine for you the get used to playing barre chords, switching them around the neck, and having loads of fun with it.

While explaining your practice routine, we'll explore some common mistakes beginner guitar players make when learning barre chords. Watch out for them - I'll show you exactly how to correct that stuff!

Ready?

How to Practice Barre Chords & Correct Bad Notes

You'll pick out each note one at a time, making sure that each string rings out clearly. Move your fingers a little bit to fix the notes that are buzzing, muted, or dead.

It sounds familiar, right? The way to get a perfect barre chord is more or less the same as we did for open chords as beginners. :) The key thing here is to observe what your fingers are doing - and what needs a fix!

Let's look at the common mistakes new guitar players make when learning how to play barre chords.

Barre Chords - Common Beginner Mistake 1

Make sure that your 1st and 2nd strings are ringing out clear. Often, people angle the barre too much, and the index finger ends up too far from the fret. Like that, the notes on the thinnest two strings won't ring clean. To fix it, check if your barre is straight next to the fret where those two strings are.

Barre Chords - Common Beginner Mistake 2

Don't mute the String 2! Make sure to check that the underside of Finger 2 is not muting the second string at all. If it's muting, move your finger up a little.

Barre Chords - Common Beginner Mistake 3

If the 3rd string is not ringing out, it's probably because the 4th finger is touching it. Curl the fingers a bit more by moving your palm towards the sky. Get the palm of your hand where your little finger meets your palm up close to the neck - but not touching it.

If it's another note, make sure that the fingers are as close as possible to the frets and that no other fingers are touching that string.

Ensure that your thumb is at the back of the guitar neck. Don't let it over the top. You should be pressing hard, but not crazy hard. Some of the work comes from the arm, but the muscle between your thumb and first finger should still get quite a workout!

Who's up for an extra tip?

Barre Chords - Common Beginner Mistake 4

Watch out for overreaching with Finger 1 too. It should be only just over the top of the strings. The reason is that when you move to barre chords with the root note on string 5, the barring finger will have too far to move to mute string 6. It’s a bad habit. Avoid it from the start. ;) Take a look at how not to do with your index finger:

Building Strength - It Takes Time!

If you've followed along with my Beginner Course, you will know that I emphasize that keeping the thumb behind the neck will help strengthen the muscle between the thumb and the index finger.

But when you start playing songs using barre chords, you'll find that it still is a proper workout. That’s ok! Every time you play, your muscles will get a little stronger.

Don’t practice until the point where you won't be able to play anything else. Work your muscles until you know it’s near failure. Then, stop, massage it a bit and have a rest before finishing your practice - no point in hurting yourself!

And, before you ask, those tools people sell to make your fingers stronger are not a substitute for time spent playing guitar! I guess if you have limited time, you could do some kind of finger workout between your practice session. It might help a little - but the best is more guitar time. :)

Barre Chords - There's No Magic!

Getting the shape right is the key to nailing barre chords, which only happens with regular practice sessions. I also recommend that you spend some time trying to play songs - it builds up stamina and strength!

As usual, don’t rush it. Stick with this for a week or two at least. Ensure that you're comfortable with this shape and play songs with it before moving onto the next lesson.

Almost everyone hates barre chords when they first try them! Nailing barres is a massive step, and in a few months from now, you will look back and remember how hard they were. It’ll give you a mega buzz!

Now that you know my best tricks on playing barre chords and understanding how they work, it's time for your hard work! Check out the practice schedule I suggest below. :)

Practice Routine

Item 1 - 5 Minutes - Chord Practice

I want you to spend 5 minutes just playing the chord. Get the notes right, and don't forget to check your wrist position. It's essential to develop strength! The most comfortable place to start is around the 5th fret for most people, but the fret is not a big deal now. Long term, you'll play any shape, anywhere!

Let's do it together:

Put the chord down roughly in place but without pressing it down.

Check the wrist angle and positions of fingers. Then, press down, rotate the barre onto the side and pull a little with the forearm.

Strum, then pick out the notes one at a time and make any corrections you need to.

Strum again and tell your fingers that this is how you would like them to go next time.

Release the chord and have a few seconds rest.

Repeat.

Item 2 - 5 Minutes - Song Work

Let's have some fun! I want you to choose a song you've learned as a beginner that uses G, C, and D throughout the tune. Now we'll play it with barre chords! :) Here's what you've got to do:

Pick one song that you feel comfortable with the rhythm.

Then, try playing along with the backing track or original recording using barre chords.

See how it goes! Playing barre chords for 5 minutes is tough - don't worry if you can't do it for now. Try it for a minute or two, then take a 30-second break and hit it again!

If you find that playing the D chord way up at the 10th fret is very difficult - you’re not alone - I do too! The good news is that it’s rare to play the D chord way up there. There’s another way to play it, and if you stick with this course, you'll learn it very soon!

For now, you have two options. You can learn a song that uses F, Bb, and C, or take your song that uses G, C, and D and move all the chords down one tone. You won’t be able to play along with the original recording if you do that, but it'll be easier and so maybe more fun!

The more you practice barre chords, the stronger your hand will get and the longer you will be able to play them! Believe it - barre chords will get easier before you can imagine. ;)

Check out some awesome guitar song lessons here and choose your favorite ones to practice with!

lessons.title: E Shape Barre Chords: Minor
lessons.summary: Minor E Shape Barres are harder than Major E Shape Barres - but here's how you'll nail them!
lessons.text:
The difference between Minor E Shape Barre Chords and Major E Shape Barre Chords is only one note. In fact, you lift a finger off to play a Minor, which means that minor barre chords are a bit harder to play.

Huh? Yep, you read right - minor barre chords are harder to play.

Minor E Shape Barres are harder than Major E Shape Barres because now the note on the 3rd string is played by the barre.

For many people, that is where the barre is a little flabby. The best guitar trick here is to adjust your barre position just a little - find that goldilocks position!

Let's take a look.

Have You Mastered The E Shape Major?

Before you start this lesson, make sure you're comfortable with the E Shape Major. To play Minor E Shape barres, you'll need more strength in your hands. So, make sure you've put in some work in your Major grips.

A great workout is to play Dreams by Fleetwood Mac using barre chords only! If you haven't tried that out yet, I suggest you give it a go. :)

You should also be familiar with my 3 tricks to nail barre chords - finger roll, wrist turn, arm pull. Minor E Shapes are harder to play, so use the proper barre chord mechanics and learn faster. ;)

Are you ready? So let's lift that finger off!

E Shape Minor In 3 Easy Steps

The E Minor Shape is the same as the E Major Shape but with your 2nd finger lifted off. Take a look at the diagram below:

Lifting off that finger can be trickier than it seems, so let's check out 3 easy steps to get good-sounding minor barre chords on the guitar. :)

Step 1 - The Minor Barre Placement

First, check out your index finger placement. Start by checking the notes under your barre, and then adjust its placement as you need. If you have trouble getting the 3rd string to ring out clearly, lift the barre up toward the sky about 3-5mm.

This works for most people - it's about finding the right way of placing your barre. We are all a bit different and have different-shaped hands of different strengths. You have to find your way!

Focus your energy on the middle of the bar. You’ll be surprised how sometimes changing the way you think about something changes it in real life. ;)

Getting the 3rd string to sound clear is essential because it is that note that makes the chord minor! Without it, you're playing a kinda extended Power Chord.

Step 2 - Get Some Help!

Once your 2nd finger is off, you can use it to support your 1st Finger. Just place your 2nd finger slightly on top of your 1st finger and press down on top of it. Take a look at the image below:

Some people will see this as a bad habit... and it can be! But it can also be very helpful if you are really struggling with your barre chord. What works for you? Give yourself some time to let the muscles develop - this is hard stuff, and practice will make it permanent!

Step 3 - Find the Root Note

Remember that sharps and flats are going to determine the fret you're on, and Major and Minor will decide if you keep your second finger down or not!

If you can't find the F Sharp Minor Chord - you need to give yourself a bit of practice on that. :)

The root notes and general techniques to play Minor E Shape grips are the same here as for the Major Shape. By this stage, you have no excuse for not knowing the notes on the thickest string very well!

Practice Schedule

Your practice sessions for this lesson only take 10 minutes. :)

Item 1 - 5 mins - Barre Chord Practice

Same drill as the last lesson on E Shape Major chords, but you should work on minors and majors barre chords this time! You can focus on the minors for the first few practice sessions but then alternate between them. Either alternate days or within the same practice session.

Item 2 - 5 Minutes - Song Work

Now you’re looking for any songs that you already learned that use basic Major and Minor chords. You’re going to work on playing them with barre chords! Follow these 3 guidelines:

Start Simple. Choose songs without too many chords, but include at least one minor chord.

Steady Rhythm. Choose songs you are confident with the rhythm so that it doesn't hold you back. The focus here is the barre chords!

Practice Makes Permanent! Choose songs you like, because you'll practice them for a bit! Try playing at least a few songs with only barre chords before moving on. :)

If you get the opportunity to play with someone, try one person playing barre chords and the other open chords. It sounds awesome!

Check out these song tutorials with full chords, lyrics, and tabs for you to follow along with. :)

lessons.title: E Shape Chords: Dominant 7th
lessons.summary: Dominant 7th Grips are a bit everywhere! Learn how to play them and an alternative fingering to sound cooler.
lessons.text:
Dominant 7th Chord has a very useful tension (dissonance), and you'll find it in most music styles. For example, the Beatles used many 7th Chords, and you'll often hear Dominant 7th Chords in classical music, in what we call cadence. They're everywhere!

If you're following my Intermediate Guitar Courses, we've just learned how to play E Shape Barre Chords - major and minor grips. Like the E Shape Minor, they need one finger removal, but that might cause you a different set of problems.

In this lesson, we'll learn the best way to play the E Shape Dominant 7th Chords, explore the common problems you might encounter and how to handle them. The common barre chord 7th grip that we check out first is handy, but sometimes a smaller grip with fewer notes will sound better and really bring out the chord's qualities.

But first things first!

How Do Dominant 7th Chords Sound?

Dominant 7th chords sound full of tension! They sound like they're going somewhere, and the cool thing about that is that they've got some movement. You can easily get what I mean when listening to some examples, especially how it sounds in classical music. :)

How to Play E Shape Dominant 7th Chord

Here's a very easy trick you can try to play E Shape Dominant 7th Chords easily. Start with the regular Major Shape, and then lift off your 4th finger! You'll notice that it can be pretty tricky, so check out these three tricks you can try. Take a look at the chord diagram:

Playing 7th Chord Grips - Tip 1

First, get that index finger in the right position! Don't forget to check if you've rolled your first finger (the barre) slightly over onto its side - about 30 degrees. That's where the flesh is not as soft, and it's closer to the bone. Take a look:

With minor barre chords, the problem was to get the 3rd string ringing out, remember? Now your challenge is to get the 4th string sounding clear and clean. Let's see how to correct that. :)

Playing 7th Chord Grips - Tip 2

Getting the 4th string sounding clean and clear when playing Dom 7th Chord grips can be a struggle.

Sometimes, your best option will be to move the barre a little up or down to get the note sounding good. But first, check that it is not your 3rd finger touching the 4th string - that's such a common problem! :(

Last but not least, check out your thumb position when playing those barre chords - see the next tip.

Playing 7th Chord Grips - Tip 3

Remember to keep your thumb around the back. Roughly, it should be on the other side of the neck to the 2nd finger. But everyone is slightly different, so don't stress if yours is not. ;)

Practice picking out all the notes one at a time and make sure they are all clear. Remember that consistent practice is key here! If you're struggling to follow an effective practice routine, use My Practice Assistant - it might be the key to your success!

Alternative Fingering for Dom 7th Grips

The pinky variation is pretty used! Like that, you'll put your pinky down on the second string, three frets higher than the barre. That is one octave higher than the note on String 4, but it often sounds fantastic!

If you add that note, it doesn’t matter so much if you mute String 4! As long as you get that 7th in there, you will have the right sound. Which one you use is more a case of preference - what do you think sounds good in the situation.

Shhh… The Cool Little Cheat is Here! :)

With all this said - I find these big 7th chords a bit cumbersome. I actually feel they can be pretty heavy and complex to use, so I end up rarely using the full grips when I'm playing songs!

I use a lot more a smaller 3-note 7th Grip, which has quite a few fingering options. Most commonly, I use fingers 1, 2, and 4. Take a look:

Try it out as an alternative to a full 7th chord! Sometimes, it’ll work a lot better - sometimes, it won’t. But generally, I find that this 3-note grip works well because it’s not crowded. The essential notes are there to shine, and getting rid of the trash helps it sing. :)

Root Notes

There are no changes for the 7th Chords - the root notes for all E Shape Barre Chords will be in the same place. :) I’m hoping you know them by now. If you want to dig deeper, check out the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course!

Practice Routine

Your practice session for this lesson only requires 10 minutes! I recommend your start with your barre chord practice and then play songs you really dig.

Item 1 - 5 mins - Barre Chord Practice

Same drill as last as the last couple of lessons, but you should work on 7th Chords and Minor Chords and Major Chords this time!

You can heavily lean on the 7th chords for the first few practice sessions but then alternate between all of them. You can either alternate days or within the same practice session - whatever works best for you!

Item 2 - 5 Minutes - Song Work

I'd suggest that you still spend some time working on the regular Major and Minor Barre Chord grips that we have covered so far, but for Dominant 7th Chord practice - you can’t beat a Blues. ;)

Check out my song tutorials if you need extra help with your repertoire. See you soon.

lessons.title: Introduction to Note Function
lessons.summary: Understanding the function of each note in a chord will help you unleash the fretboard and your guitar playing!
lessons.text:
You don't have to know loads of maths or music theory to become a better guitar player. Still, there are a few things worth knowing, especially when you want to become a more advanced guitar player.

In fact, the further you get along your guitar journey, the more critical it is to understand the function of things, and that's what we are doing today regarding chord tones.

Actually, when I was studying guitar and understood note function, the light bulb went on. I hope this lesson has the same effect on you! Here are some benefits you can expect from understanding notes' function:

A better understanding of how chords are constructed;

It'll be easier to memorize chord grips;

You'll be able to morph one chord into another;

And change Major grips into Minor grips!

We’ll keep it pretty simple in this lesson and look at notes' function in our E Shape Barre Chords. If you're following the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course, you'll already be familiar with most of this. But stick around, so you refresh your memory!

What's Note Function?

By function, I mean the relevance of the chord tone to the root note, usually the tonal center. Of course, long-term, you should aim to know the role of every note in every chord that you play. But that takes time and some study over a few years!

Now let's look at our E Shape Barre Chords. First, we’ll start with an overview of the essential knowledge in the Basic Major Chord structure.

Where Does a Major Chord Come From?

All the notes in a Major Chord come from the same Major Scale.

A triad contains the 1st, 3rd, and 5th notes of the Major Scale. So, for example, if we want to find the notes in a G Major Triad, we need the 1st, 3rd, and 5th notes of the G Major Scale, G, B, and D.

Let's take a look at the C Major Chord.

The C Major Chord has no sharps and flats. The notes in the Key of C Major are C, D, E, F, G, A, B, and C. If we take the first, the third, and the fifth one, we'll get the C, E, and G notes. So when you play an open C Chord, those are the notes you're actually playing! Check it out:

E Shape Barre Note Functions

If you play a C Shape Barre Chord (using the E Shape), you will be playing those exact notes. So you’ll play the root note three times, the 5th twice, and the 3rd just once! Take a look:

If you know the function of each one of those notes, you can easily manipulate that chord and turn it in another one!

How To Change Major Chords Into Minor Chords

You only need to lower the 3rd note by one semitone to change a Major Chord into a Minor Chord. Thus, this flattened 3rd is named a “Minor 3rd” - or commonly a B3, pronounced flat 3.

Because the 3rd only happens once in the E Shape, it's very easy to change this chord grip into its Minor version. That only takes one finger!

Let's think about some open chords that you should be familiar with. Of course, if you've been doing the JustinGuitar Practical Music Theory Course, you'll already be familiar with this exercise. :)

A Chord and A Minor Chords

Notice they’re only one note different - any guesses what that note would be? The function of it? The same thing happens with D Major and D Minor, right?

If you've learned the names of the notes on the fretboard in the open position, you should be able to work it out. But, first, write down the names of the notes in the Major Chord and then the Minor.

What has changed? Did you get it right?

Here's some other food for thought:

Have you ever wondered why there was no Open G Minor or C Minor? The notes in G and G, B, D, and the notes in C are C, E, and G.

DO IT. See if you can work out how to play an Open G Minor and an Open C Minor.

HINT. There are not good practical big open grips - but you will learn a lot in the process of exploring it and seeing what works and what doesn't.

What About Dominant 7th Chords?

Depending on where you are in your guitar journey, you'll be able to manipulate different grips! For example, the 7th chord adds a flat 7 Scale degree to a Major triad, so the root, 3rd, 5th, and FLAT 7th scale degrees.

The flat 7 is one tone LOWER than the root note - so two frets below the root. We’re just getting a taster of this here - and I mainly want you to learn the difference between Major and Minor (for the next lesson) but be aware of the 7th.

Note that the 7th is a Major Triad plus a b7, so you can always play a regular Major Chord if you don’t know a particular 7th chord. It won’t sound quite as spicy, but it'll always sound fine.

Want to Learn More?

My Music Theory course goes deep into this stuff in Grade 4. :) It also covers chords in the keys, common progressions, chord manipulation, and a whole lot more! :) You might find music theory is boring - but that's not the case over here! Give it a try.

Practice Routine

I'd like you to spend some time thinking about everything we've learned in this lesson. There is a lot of food for thought here - explore it and learn! :) Here's my suggestion:

Item 1 - 5 mins - Barre Chord Song Practice

You should continue working on songs that are using all the barre chords you have learned so far. We’re developing the muscles and memory here - make sure you are solid on your root notes. Have a go at playing some new songs and finding the chords instantly if you can!

Item 2 - 5 Minutes - Theory Work

I’d like you to spend some time thinking about the note function and exploring that.

See you next to understand all about Triads!

lessons.title: Introduction to Triads
lessons.summary: Learn how to easily incorporate some triad chords in your guitar playing.
lessons.text:
When I learned how to play triads, it felt like magic.

You might think that triads are some boring music theory, but I promise you: they are not. Instead, triads are a useful little trick, fantastic as a second guitar part, and for creating riffs.

In this lesson, we'll explore how you can easily incorporate triad chords in your guitar playing. That's a nice little jamming trick, and I hope you dig it as much as I do!

Now let's get started.

Before We Start

You must never forget we're studying music, and music is a listening and feeling thing, more than a thinking thing. :) As you learn this bit of theory about triads, make sure you use them to make music.

Before we go any further, take some time to listen to great real-world uses of triads. Brown Eyed Girl by Van Morrison uses triads as a second guitar part. You can hear them picked out and moved around. That's the song that helped me understand triad chords - and that might turn the light bulb on for you too!

If you're a Dire Straits fan, So Far Away uses a whole heap of triad shapes for the main riff. And last but not least, the main riff in Substitute by The Who uses the grips we'll learn in this lesson, and a few more.

What Are Triad Chords?

Triads are 3-note chords. There are some repeated notes in the E Shape Major Barre Chord, but we're just playing three notes when playing Triad Grips, and we don't double any of them! We can name these triad shapes as the full name like G Major or G Minor or just the note name if it's a Major (i.e., G). To be super specific, we might use the term triad (i.e., G Maj Triad), but that wouldn't be common.

There are 3 different shapes for triad chords, and in this lesson, we'll be learning Shape 1. Let's take a look at it!

Triad Chord - Root 1

Shape 1 uses the top 3 strings of the E Shape Barre chord, so it should be pretty easy for you at this point - both Major and Minor. The Major uses just fingers 1 and 2, and the Minor is simply a barre for Finger 1 on the thinnest three strings.

Memorize the shapes and remember the root is on String 1! Take a look at the following diagrams:

How to Use Triads on Guitar

One of the best things about triads is using them to jam! If you're playing with someone else, they can play the strumming pattern, and you can play some triads using the same key! It sounds great, and it's loads of fun. Let me show you how to jam with triads. :)

As I don't have a jam buddy around, I'll just use my looper pedal for this lesson. I'll play one of the most common chord sequences of all time: C, G, Am, and F. Over that, I'll use some triads and jump the shape around my fretboard.

🚨 Notice that, when playing triads, we don't tend to strum the strings as we do when playing other grips. With triads, we usually pick out individual notes - and that's what I recommend you do at this point.

Another cool trick you can try is playing triad chords short and cut. You can play like short riffs, some reggae... Give it a try! See what you can do from it. ;)

Now it's your turn - just set a rhythm and play! I promise it's easy and sounds fantastic.

How To Mute Strings

When you're playing triads on the thinnest three strings, you must keep the thickest rings muted. You'd typically do this with the inside palm of your strumming hand. Sometimes, you might mute the fourth string with the tip of whichever finger is fretting a note on the third string, but this would be supplemental. You should be aiming to mute the thickest three strings with your strumming hand palm.

Triads & Inversions

I often hear of people explaining triads as inversions, which technically they are, I guess. But usually, inversions imply a different bases note to the chord. For example, the G Chord should have a G-bass note. If the G Chord has a B-bass note, it's referred to as a first inversion chord. If the G chord has a D bass note, we will refer to it as a second inversion chord.

Usually, when you play triads, the bass player plays a consistent bass note, so it doesn't matter what the lowest note is of your triad shape. It’s not the bass note. So, I don't recommend that you think of these triad shapes as being inversions. Technically they are, but it's too complicated, and you're better off thinking of them as just different ways of playing the chord.

How to Practice Triad Chords

It's time for some practice! Here's my suggestion to help you make the most out of your time.

Practice Item - 10 minutes

Let’s get these into use! The best way to practice triad is by actually playing them! The grips shouldn't be much of a struggle if you're comfortable playing and moving around the E Shape Barre Chord, eh? ;)

Now, find an easy song that uses Triads, and you're comfortable playing it. Then, see if you can jam along with it using the Root 1 grips. Pick the notes out in a pattern or randomly. Experiment. Can you strum them? Or play them all together but very short?

You can always use the same string root for them all too - or mix it all up. Get playful with it. Curiosity is the father of invention! :)

Before You Move On

This is the last lesson of our E Shape Barre Chord studies for Grade 4! Before you move on to the next grade, make sure you're comfortable and can play everything we've learned so far. Here's a recap:

E Shape Major Barre Chords

Learn the E Shape Major and all my secrets to easily play barre chords. Don't forget: get down the basics before moving further will help you move faster. ;)

E Shape Minor Barre Chords

Minor E Shape Barres are harder to play than Major E Shape Barres. Make sure you nail them!

E Shape 7th Dominant Chords

Dominant 7th Grips are a bit everywhere! Learn how to play them and an alternative fingering to sound cooler.

Note Function 1

Understanding the function of each note in a chord will help you unleash the fretboard and your guitar playing!

First Triads

Please - try to go jamming! That's an awesome thing all rhythm guitar players should explore, and triads are the little secret! ;)

In Grade 5, we'll learn the A Shape Barre Chord - and new challenges will appear! There's a reason why I recommend you to nail the E Shape before moving further - trust me here, that will be a big help later on in your guitar journey. Take the time to explore this muscle - you're developing not only your musicianship but your hand muscles. Hand strength is essential to help you play clean, good-sounding chords on the guitar, making sure you don't skip any essential practice.

Good Luck! See You In Grade 5!

modules.title: Major Scale Maestro 1
modules.intro:
Introduction

The Major Scale Maestro Course will get you making music before you know it. It is one of the most fun, musical, and comprehensive courses on Major Scales ever made!

The lessons are spread over three grades. You'll learn all the essential techniques to play scales well - but not only that! You'll also complete practical exercises and have access to backing tracks and printouts.

By the end of this course, you'll have everything you need to make music using the Major Scale.

I recommend you master this module before starting the Major Scale Modes module. They use the same scale patterns but in a different harmonic context. It'll be a lot easier to learn them if you are already very familiar with the scale patterns.

So, let's get started!

Pricing

This course is big and deep and worth a lot of money, but I want to keep my lessons free for those who can’t afford a quality music education. If you like this program, please donate. The suggested amount is $50, half of what I could sell it for. Your donation helps many people out there! If you're still unsure about it, read why I run JustinGuitar this way.

Grade 4

Our Scales journey begins with the basics, but making music from the very beginning! Scales are not boring - unless you forget to use them to make music. :) You'll start by learning the 5 Pattern System. They link perfectly with the CAGED System of Chord Shapes! Together, they form a complete guitar framework.

We'll always learn new things in the Key of G, but you will get familiar with other keys as we go through the course. There are plenty of backing tracks to help you with that too!

Here's what we'll learn in Grade 4:

How to make music with the Major Scale

Re-Active Listening

Patterns 1, 2, and 3 of the Major Scale

Solos with 1 Finger

Transitioning between patterns

Playing Scales “In 3rds.”

Framework Development!

Grade 5

In Grade 5, we'll develop your skillset. You'll learn to play with scales all over the neck and in all keys! Fun enough? :)

Here's what we'll learn in Grade 5:

Using legato in scales

Patterns 4 and 5 of The Major Scale

Exploring Melodic Patterns

How to play all over the guitar neck

Getting comfortable with all keys

Introduction to key changes!

Grade 6

Have you heard about the 3 Note Per String System (3NPS)? It's another very popular system for scale patterns. As the name suggests, it has three notes on every string - which has some advantages and disadvantages. Overall, it's a very useful system, especially when you combine it with the 5 Pattern System.

Here's what we'll learn in Grade 6:

What is the 3NPS, and why is it cool?

Learn all the seven patterns of the system

Learn to link the 3NPS with the 5 Pattern System

Explore techniques that use the 3NPS

Learn how to play long flowing and fast scale passages!

lessons.title: Major Scale Pattern 1
lessons.summary: Let's explore Pattern 1 of the Major Scale and start jamming with it!
lessons.text:
In this first lesson of our Major Scale Maestro course, we'll learn how to explore Pattern 1 of the G Major Scale. It's reasonably easy to play! It's not a big stretch, and it fits perfectly around the E Shape Barre Chord, which you know well.

What You'll Learn

The best way to learn and explore scales

Memorize Pattern 1 of the Major Scale

Play the Pattern 1 in the keys of G and C

Improvising over a backing track with the major scale.

Before You Start

Here is some general advice for you:

Learn scales slowly. Do not make mistakes! Start with all-down picks, and focus on getting the notes clean and clear, and memorized.

At first, start by playing the scale ascending only. Repeat the scale until you memorize it. Do not make any mistakes! Yep - that again. ;)

When you're confident that the scale is solid in your memory, you can start playing it descending too. Do it slowly - and don't make any mistakes!

When you can play the scale up and down, experiment moving to alternate picking (down, up.)

Only when you can play the scale at an even tempo on your own, it's time to try playing it with a metronome.

Do not make mistakes!

Major Scale Pattern 1 Diagram

Take a good look at the Major Scale Pattern 1 Diagram. Here's how it looks like:

Let’s do it together!

Let’s learn this with the G Major Scale together. I will take you through it very slowly. Painfully slowly. But this is how you should learn scales - without mistakes and memorizing each section as you go. Making mistakes will slow down the memorization process a lot, so let’s not do that!

Let’s start with Finger 2 on the 3rd fret of the thickest string - this is the root note.

The next note that you will play is with your Finger 4, which will go down in the 5th fret. Memorize this! Then, we go onto the next string, and we will play fingers 1, 2, and 4. They will go in frets 2, 3, and 5.

Before moving any further, concentrate on these two strings. Engrave the visual pattern of the notes into your memory!

We add strings 4 and 3 with fingers 1, 3, and 4 on each string. Do it very slowly, and don’t let a wrong finger go down. Concentrate. Think. Be certain. Then, act!

Practice and memorize getting up to this point.

Ready to finish it off? Let's go to String 2. Start with Finger 2 and then 4 - the same as we had on the thickest string! The thinnest string takes the same finger pattern that String 5 did - 1, 2, and 4.

Now take some time working on this whole pattern over and over. Be sure that you have it firmly in your memory!

Only when you are doing it with confidence should you start doing it descending as well. Aim to make no mistakes. If you are uncertain, do not play. Check the diagram as you go along if you need to!

When you get back to your starting point, you will go down one note to Fret 2 with Finger 1. Then, go back to the root note and finish there.

Take a 30-second break and then do it again. Make sure the pattern is perfect every time.

Start and end on the lowest root note!

When you're playing scales, you must hear them correctly. So, we will always start and end on the lowest root note. Diagrams usually show the root note with an ® - sometimes, it'll have a different color.

You need to know where the root notes are for each scale - especially as we change keys and learn more patterns!

The E Shape

It’s useful to see how the scale relates to the Major Barre chord in the same area - in this case, the E Shape. See the image below with the E Shape chord tones in blue.

Try to picture this chord shape in the scale, and be aware of the relationship at all times! It’s a lot easier to visualize chords that you often play than a complex scale shape. It makes moving and recalling the scale shape a lot easier!

16 Note Scale Patterns

All 5 Patterns in this system have 16 notes in total. When working with a metronome, you will play the scale ascending and descending over 2 bars. Then, come back to the root note where you started on beat 1. It's a great way of making sure you’re getting things right!

Get with the Metronome!

Playing scales with a metronome helps develop speed and hand synchronization. I have a whole lesson on it. Check it out at some point soon - maybe even right now!

As I already said, only work with a metronome when you can play the scale from memory. And with a slow and even tempo - no pauses! And if you need a metronome - don't forget about my Time Trainer Metronome! It's much more than just an excellent metronome, and it costs almost nothing. :)

Moving Root Notes

We learned this scale in G Major. G was the root note under our second finger, where we started. If you move that second finger up to the 8th fret, it will be on the note C, and you will be playing the C Major Scale. I want you to practice both G and C Major before you start the next lesson.

Improvising

As well as playing the scales, I want you to have a go at using them to improvise. We'll still explore many tools for making music with scales. Don’t get stressed if things feel awkward at this point!

Have a go at it and see what you discover! Many things are better when you learn them on your own. I hope to give you enough tools and direction to help you find them! ;)

Food for thought while you are at it…

Make sure you take ‘breaths’ when you play.

Repetition is GREAT - use it.

Less is often more.

Backing Tracks - Free Download!

I have a project with my friend Dave Marks called JustinGuitar Jams. We make awesome backing tracks! I get together with some session player friends and make the jam tracks in real-time - so it really is just like jamming with a band. These cats are great players, and I'm sure you'll feel us having fun while we make them too!

We have a collection called Jam Major. It's the perfect fit for this series. There are 12 tracks in a range of different keys and styles for you to explore. :) Our Jam Modes collection would be interesting, too, for sure. While modes are a bit more of an advanced concept, most of the tracks in that set use the G Major Scale as the parent scale. You can use them for working on your G Major Scale. It'll sound pretty hip! :)

I've included one of the tracks from the Jam Major for free! It's the one we call Wishful - it's in G Major, and you'll have a lot of fun jamming along with it, I'm sure. If you dig it - check out our other jam tracks!

GuitarPro File

There's also a GuitarPro file included in this course! So you can practice your G Major Scale along and make sure you are getting it right. I don't recommend it for long-term practice, but a great way to start and make sure you are playing the right notes and to work on your timing!

Practice Schedule

We'll dig into your practice schedule after the next lesson about Chords In Keys. In this Major Scale Maestro series, there are two lessons to check out for each unit, and the second will contain the practice info!

lessons.title: Chords In Keys - For Jamming
lessons.summary: Learn how to find chords in any key and get started with jamming in G and C Major. The Unit 1 Practice Schedule is here!
lessons.text:
In this lesson, we'll learn about Scale Chord Theory. You must understand that a group of chords come from the same major scale. It is why you can use one scale over many different chords!

We won't go too deep into music theory in this module. I cover much more in my Practical Music Theory course. I’m sure you'll enjoy checking that out too! Now, let's get started.

A Review on Basic Chords

Basic chords consist of 3rds, which means a scale tone separates the notes. For example, the C Major Chord notes are C, E and G and the first, third, and fifth notes of the C Major Scale. C (D) E (F) G.

When we apply this pattern starting from each scale degree, we get a sequence of chords. We call it the Diatonic Chord Sequence. It's this collection of chords that we will use for this entire course!

We name the scale degrees in roman numerals when we build chords from them. We won’t be dealing with Chord VII much. We don't really use it other than in jazz, and to get into it, you'll need a higher understanding of music theory.

The C Major Scale

I C E G = C Major (MAJOR)

II D F A = D Minor (MINOR)

III E G B = E Minor (MINOR)

IV F A C = F Major (MAJOR)

V G B D = G Major (MAJOR)

VI A C E = A Minor (MINOR)

VII B D F = B Dim (let’s not worry about this one!)

The Chord Order

The order of the chord types will always be the same. It applies to every Major Scale and Major Key.

Chords I, IV, and V will be Major.

Chords II, III, and VI will be Minor.

Learn more about the notes in the Major Scale in my Practical Music Theory course.

The G Major Scale

If you look at the G Major Scale, you'll see its notes are G A B C D E F#.

The I, IV, and V will be G, C, and D.

The II, III, and VI will be Am, Bm, and Em.

So, the chords in the key of G are G, C, D, Am, Bm, and Em. It makes sense, right? :) And yes, I could have written them as G, Am, Bm, C, D, and Em. I just think it’s helpful to see the major and minor separated too.

How do you jam over scales?

Now you understand how to find the chords in a key. But how can you jam with your buddy in the key of G, for example? That's easy!

He plays the G Major Scale, and you play any of the chords in the key of G in any order. You don’t have to use them all. In fact, you might try just using one at a time for a while. We call this vamping - more on that later!

Do you want to try jamming in C, too? Play The C Major Scale, and your buddy will use the chords in the key of C. They are C, F, G, Dm, Em, and Am. Remember: you can play any of them, in any order you want!

Always ensure that you stick with the right chords and the right scale notes, or it might all go wrong.

HAVE FUN! :)

Unit 1 Practice Schedule

Homework

Your homework this week needs 10 minutes a day of practice. Here's what you'll have to do:

5 minutes - Scale Practice

Play the scale up and down, slowly and carefully. Get every note correct, and make sure you memorize the pattern. Hopefully, after a few days, you will be able to do it slowly with a metronome.

Watch my lesson on practicing with a metronome! Start playing one note per click at 60 BPM. If that’s too fast, then don’t work with a metronome yet.

Gradually, work it up to 120 BPM. Then, cut back to 60 BPM but playing two notes per click (8th notes). Target between 80 and 120 BPM if you can. But speed is not your goal!

5 minutes - Improvisation

Use the available backing tracks to explore playing over the tracks. Start working with just the G Major one for at least five practice sessions.

Then, have a go at the one in C Major. Alternate between them so you don’t get stuck in G.

If you have a jam buddy, they can use the chords shown in the Major Scale Chord Theory lesson (coming next) in any order. It’s great fun to jam with friends and learn together. It was how I learned all this stuff!

Start using only the thinnest two strings! Add in one or two more strings over the first few practice sessions as you feel you are getting the hang of it.

Using fewer notes will help you learn some of the essential lessons we're exploring, but you are likely to struggle and get bored doing it. Try to push through that! Important things are coming on the other side. ;)

Feedback & Support

I would love to see a video of your early attempts at playing with the backing track! It's also a valuable thing for yourself to look back on too! Please, film yourself, pop it up on YouTube and post a link in the website comments.

I will check out as many as I can and give you some feedback. I’m sure you will also enjoy sharing constructive feedback with your fellow students! We can all learn from each other.

Student Resources (Downloads)

PDF - Major Scale 5 Pattern System Diagrams

MP3 - Backing Track in G Major "Wishful"

GuitarPro - G Major Scale in 8th notes and 16th notes for practice (if needed)

lessons.title: One Finger Solos
lessons.summary: Don't skip this lesson. It's one of the most powerful scale exercises EVER!
lessons.text:
Playing solos with just one finger is a powerful exercise to develop your skills! In this lesson, we'll have fun using Pattern 1 of the Major Scale - but playing it with only the first finger. Before we start, make sure you're comfortable jamming with the G and C Major Scale over the backing tracks.

If you're following my Major Scale Maestro Course, remember not to rush it! Music is not a race; it’s an art. And art needs time to develop and bloom! :)

Now, let's get started!

But first... Why One Finger Solos?

I’d be disappointed if you didn’t ask why just one finger! It's an excellent question, and I've got a perfect answer for you. :) Playing solos with only one finger is a powerful exercise, and there are good reasons to work on it:

Playing with one finger stops your fingers from relying on ‘muscle memory.’ You've been practicing your scales up and down, so now we now need to break that. Why? Because scales are not music. They are a tool we can use to help make music - but playing scales up and down is not music! Breaking out of the patterns that your fingers are used to. It will help your ear become the master, and that is what we want.

Practicing with one finger will force you to memorize the shape of the pattern. I'm talking about your musical imagination! It's a big deal and helps you explore the scale in many new and exciting ways.

When you improvise with one finger, you will probably play less because playing fast is very hard. It'll make you play more melodically and with more taste and style!

Crossing strings vertically is sometimes easier than going up or down one string. You might explore sounds and melodies that you would not have done before!

When we learn the next pattern, you will find that transitioning to it will be pretty easy. You won't be afraid to move out of the box. :)

Playing solos with just one finger works - I promise. I've helped hundreds of students develop their musicality with this exercise, especially when combined with my Re-Active Listening Method!

lessons.title: Re-Active Listening ™
lessons.summary: Learn to develop your ears and your ability to identify chord tones and how to land on good notes when soloing!
lessons.text:
During all my teaching years, I've seen an incredibly high number of students who knew all the scales. They could play them up and down real fast - but couldn’t play a decent melodic solo if their life depended on it!

Why? Mostly because they never listened. :(

When you play a note, the audience hears that note and the backing track or whatever you are playing over it. It’s easy to get lost in your own world when improvising, but it doesn't help you make great music. You need to listen and be in the music, not on it.

In this lesson, we'll explore what I call the Re-Active Listening Method. In a nutshell, you'll learn how to actively listen to what you’re playing and then react to it. You'll become a better musician and will be able to really make music!

Good Note or Bad?

It might take you some time to hear if a note you're playing is a good one or not. The good news is that good and bad are subjective anyway! Sometimes, a ‘bad’ note will be the perfect one in a specific situation.

When improvising, you need to listen if the note you stop on is sitting happily with the backing track. Usually, that means that you'll play a chord tone. Any scale notes when you play in a run will sound fine. It’s just the note you stop on that needs to sit well.

At this point, many guitar players start learning all notes in every chord and knowing the target notes on the neck. Both are great things to do, but it takes a lot of time and effort! It's not the best approach for learning how to improvise.

The Secret of Making Music

If you stop on a note and it sounds great, you don't need to do anything. But if it does not sound right, all you need to do is move a scale step up or down. Then, you’ll probably be on a great note!

To listen and react to what you're listening to is music easier and more musical than a whole lot of thinking. The more you think, the more you stink! Remember that the ‘good notes’ will change every time the chord changes. Thinking about the notes in each chord and the scale tones can get really complicated! ;)

Statistical Reasoning

I should point out how logical this approach is! I'm sure many of you have a 'statistic mind.' :)

Let’s say you are playing over a C Major chord. The chord tones are C, E, and G. The total available notes are seven:

C D E F G A B

If you land on a C, E, or G, you are quids in. You don't need anything else - it'll sound great!

If you land on an D or F, you can move in either direction to land on a chord tone.

Land on A, and you’ll need to move one step down or two steps up.

Land on B, and you’ll need to move one step up or two steps down.

Your chances of hitting a good note or quickly stepping to a great one are very high! If you sidestep a ‘bad note’ (not a chord tone), you'll land on a chord tone 7 out of 9 times - if my statistical skills are right!

The fantastic news is that after some practice, you will just know which way to go. Our ears and musical imagination are incredible, and they will help you find the best notes. You'll create beautiful melodies without much effort, but it does take practice. And time!

How to Develop Re-Active Listening

Just playing over chords one at a time and listening to what you are playing is already great! You can even use a looper. Make sure you work on recognizing if you're on a chord tone or not. It's an excellent practice!

I often do this with students in workshops. It’s amazing how quickly some people pick it up - but others can find it hard going. I've never met anyone who didn’t get re-active listening after a few weeks of consistent practice. So, don’t be discouraged if you don’t get it right away. You'll get there!

Working on this with a Jam Buddy is super cool and fun, and you can help each other. You can also use the practice session at the end of the video lesson a few times. If it’s not working, it might be a good idea to seek out an in-person class with someone who gets it!

Re-active listening is a big deal! If you get this down, it'll help you in every aspect of your playing and musicianship. Listen to what you're playing - and then react to it! That's the way to go. ;)

Unit 2 Practice Schedule

Homework

Homework for this lesson is only 10 minutes. We're still using only the Major Scale Pattern 1. If you know others, do not use them. Build the foundation strong, and we will get high!

Part 1: 5 Minutes - Scale Practice

Continue working on playing Pattern 1 of the Major Scale up and down with the metronome.

Try to add changes in a random direction. Not always playing the whole scale but still playing even notes without stopping. Do it for the full 5 minutes if you can!

A more advanced option is to play random notes within the scale but making sure you never hit a wrong note. It's the test to see if the pattern is in your memory!

Part 2: 5 Minutes - Re-Active Listening

The aim here is to play the scale across all the strings and find the good notes over the chords as they move

If you have a jam buddy, great, take turns. One plays the chords, one tries to find the good notes. If not, then make a chord progression for yourself on a looper pedal. Or, download and use the backing track.

This exercise is all about listening and feeling what sounds good, what sounds right.

Part 3: 5 Minutes - One Finger Improvisation

Start with the G Major Backing track and jam over it using only your first finger. Remember our improvisation tips:

Breath.

Leave space.

Use repetition.

Most importantly - use Re-Active Listening! Try to hear if what you are playing fits with the backing. If it doesn’t, move to the note one scale step in either direction. You're very likely to be on a great note!

Don't forget that the ‘good’ notes change with the chord changes. So, a ‘bad note’ might change to a good one when the chords change! Experiment and explore. :)

Feedback & Support

I want to see a video of your early attempts at playing with the backing track! Recording yourself is a fantastic way of keeping track of your progress. Please, film yourself, pop it up on YouTube, and post a link in the website comments.

I will check out as many as I can and give you some feedback. I’m sure you will also get some awesome tips from fellow students!

lessons.title: Major Scale Pattern 2
lessons.summary: Learn Pattern 2 and a very effective approach to switching between individual notes on the fretboard.
lessons.text:
In this lesson, we'll learn Pattern 2 of the Major Scale. As I always say - learning more patterns is not the answer to make music well! So, if you still can't make music out of Pattern 1, you shouldn't try making music with Pattern 2 - it won't make you a better musician.

Your goal is to improve your Re-Active Listening - and the outcome is to help you enjoy making music! Before you start, you should be confident with Pattern 1 of the Major Scale and the tools we already learned.

Pattern 1 vs. Pattern 2

I want you to realize that Pattern 1 and Pattern 2 have the same notes - and that's why it is so important that you've learned Pattern 1 well. They're the same scale, and we'll start - as usual - with G Major. Pattern 2 has two higher notes, taking away two of the lowest notes, including the low root note!

The Root Note in Pattern 2

In Pattern 2, the lowest root is on string 4. As I said before, we'll always start and end playing on the lowest root note. So, in Pattern 2, we'll start and end on string 4.

Many of you might not be so confident with the notes on string 4. Luckily, you can just look back two frets and go down two strings (an octave). You'll see the root note on string 6, which you need to know for your E Shape Barre Chords. I’m assuming you are confident with them - you should be!

Let’s Play!

When learning how to play a scale, use all down picks until you memorize it. It avoids the risk of developing any bad picking habits.

So, we'll start with Finger 2 up on String 4, Fret 5. That's the note G, and we’ll play the G Major Scale.

Notice that Pattern 2 starts the same as Patterns 1, with the fingers 2 and 4 and then 1, 2, and 4 on the next string (string 3). Practice only this section until you memorize it.

Then, we go onto finger numbers 1, 3, and 4 for both the thinnest two strings. It's the same as the middle strings in Pattern 1! Noticing the similarities can help you memorize the patterns. Again, work on only this section until you learn it.

Then, try to descend back to the root note. Slowly. Carefully. Check where needed. The goal is to get it right!

Notice that you now have Finger 1 behind the root note, so the middle strings descending are 421 and 421.

When descending, use Finger 4 on String 5, Fret 7. You’ll then play Fret 5 with Finger 1. Same string, of course. Then, you will have fingers 4, 3, and 1 on the thickest string. Practice this full descending section and memorize it.

Then, try it all again. Start from the lowest root (String 4), go all the way up. Then, turn around and go all the way down. Go back up to the thickest string. Your Finger 1 will be back in String 5, Fret 5.

Meet the Finger Swap!

When we descended, we used Finger 4 on String 5, Fret 7. Now we will use Finger 3 on our way up!

I get that this might seem over-complicated, but it’s for a good reason. For nearly all students I've met, the finger swap is a great tool. It allows the hand to not over-stretch and to stay relaxed.

But the proof is in the pudding - try it and see! :) Play it by using either finger for both directions and observe how it feels. Maybe, one way will feel better than the other for you. And that is ok! As usual, the most important thing here is to get it right.

Practicing Scales: Metronome, Moving Roots…

The same rules I gave you when learning how to practice Pattern 1 apply here. The rules are consistent! :)

Do not attempt to play Pattern 2 with a metronome until you have it consistent and with the correct fingering on your own.

Then, start with one note per click at 70 BPM. Build it up to 120 BPM, then drop back to 60 BPM at two notes per click. See where you can take it!

The shape moves around, but you’ll need to know your notes on String 4 to use it effectively. It sounds like something you should explore, eh? :) Learn all the notes here.

lessons.title: Moving Between Scale Patterns
lessons.summary: Learn how to choose which Major Scale pattern to play and the best way of switching between patterns.
lessons.text:
Once you have learned more than one Major Scale pattern, a new problem arises: which one to use when! :)

The big picture here is that you want to combine the patterns to not think of one or the other at all. They are just one big pattern, and developing that is easier than you might think.

Before you start this lesson, make sure you've memorized how to play Pattern 1 and Pattern 2 of the Major Scale.

Now, let's get started!

You Already Shifted Position!

When you were exploring to be more melodic with One Finger Solos, you were already moving out of ‘position’ - which is excellent! :) It wasn’t so scary, was it? It’s actually fun! The difference now is that you might use that kind of technique to shift into a new Pattern. And stay there for a while. :)

Experiment Moving Between Patterns

It’s ok just to mess about and try moving between patterns as you feel it, but I want to give you some tools to make sure you don’t fall into bad habits. We want to avoid having just one or two ‘links’ that you use all the time to join patterns!

We all find some little tricks to move between patterns that feel and sound cool to us. Having some ‘pet licks’ is not a problem, but it's better to move freely between patterns and not be restricted by them.

3 Steps To Practice Moving Between Patterns

1 - Restrict To Be Free

By far, the most effective tool you can use to work on linking patterns is to restrict what you use to join. There are quite a few techniques and concepts you can use, but to start with, you should focus on using slides and shifts on one or two strings at a time.

You can choose to use just one finger to navigate both patterns, too. It will help you develop that mental image of the scale patterns and keep open to further position movements!

2 - Explore The Middle Strings

Playing only on String 4 is a great starting point. You can use the root note on String 4 as a foundation and keep returning to it.

3 - Change It Up

Try using a different set of strings for each practice session.

How To Move Between Patterns

There are many ways to move between patterns, but sliding is a super fun one. It's very musical and helpful!

You can slide with any finger, but I recommend sliding one scale tone with Finger 1 to start. It will move you to the new pattern in one go, and it is usually easier.

Once you feel confident with it, try using other fingers. But you should start with Finger 1!

How Much Pressure to Apply When Sliding

When sliding with a finger, you will need to keep the pressure down if you want the sound to remain as you slide it. It might feel a bit odd at first, but as with most things - it’s just practice!

Slide Right!

Make sure you always know exactly where you are sliding to. Don’t fudge it - know it! It helps if you look at the place you want to slide to. That is more important when you make bigger jumps, but it's an excellent habit to have.

Only One Rule!

It's worth mentioning that, at this point, there is only one rule:

If it sounds good, it is good.

There will be times that something I say you shouldn’t do sounds great. In that case, you should keep doing it! The exceptions to the rules are often the most amazing things.

Don’t be afraid to explore what you're playing. Knowing and understanding how it all works will give you the confidence you need to try new things. You'll end up with a solid understanding of music to fall back on!

Unit 3 Practice Schedule

The homework for this lesson is 10 minutes divided into two 5-minute blocks.

Part 1: 5 Minutes - Scale Practice

Start by working on playing Pattern 2 of the Major Scale up and down with the metronome.

Start slowly and get it right.

Explore the fingering for the 5th string - see what feels comfortable for you!

When you feel confident and are getting the notes right all the time, you might like to move on to some of the things you were exploring in Pattern 1: Play along with a metronome. Start slow and only move up after playing it four times consecutively without any mistakes. Play along with a metronome but adding in random direction changes. Play the scale using random notes.

Part 2: 5 Minutes - Improvisation

Use your backing tracks to explore Pattern 2. Ask yourself these questions: How does it feel? What feels easier? What’s different? How does it feel that the ‘home notes’ are in different places?

After a week of only Pattern 2, you could start mixing Patterns 1 & 2. Then, try to let them merge.

Worth spending some practice session just focussing on putting 3rds into practice - probably not in the first week - let the musical memory build a little first. Often you have to force new ideas in for a while before our musical imagination gets a hold of them and starts putting them in subconsciously!

Feedback & Support

I want to see a video of your jams with the backing track! Please, film yourself, pop it up on YouTube, and post a link in the website comments.

I will check out as many as I can and give you some feedback. I’m sure you will also get some excellent tips from fellow students!

lessons.title: Major Scale In 3rds
lessons.summary: This lesson will help you create more melodic solos on guitar - playing scales in 3rds!
lessons.text:
The interval of a 3rd is two steps along a scale. If you play a note, miss a note, and then play the next one, you'll have played the interval of “a third.”

Thirds are essential because basic major and minor chords are built using two 3rds. Look back at the lesson on Major Scale Chord Theory, and you'll see that all the chords follow the pattern of note, miss a note, note, miss a note, note.

When you are on a good note, the other chord tones (the ‘good notes’) are often a 3rd away. That's why it makes sense to practice scales like that - and that's what we’ll learn in this lesson!

Number Sequence

Think about this as a basic number sequence that we apply to a scale. Let's check it out!

Number the G Major Scale Pattern 1 from the low root being 1. You can imagine it or use paper if you prefer. To play the scale in 3rds, you'll simply follow the following math sequence:

1 3 - 2 4 - 3 5 - 4 6 - 5 7 - 6 8 - 7 9 - etc.

When I first learned it, I thought of it as being “miss one note then back to the one you missed. Repeat.”

Practicing Major Scales in 3rds

Now it's time for some practice! Below is the TAB for this exercise. As always, follow along and do it slowly - the focus is on getting it right!

Remember that you don’t want to read the TAB for too long - aim to play it by memory. You should use the TAB just to get you started! Once you get it, you will be able to apply the sequence to any and every scale you learn.

You can also download a GuitarPro file for this exercise and play along with it. Slow it down in the early stages of your practice.

Technical Challenges

While most Pattern 1 in 3rds is not too tricky, the move between String 3 and 4 can feel pretty awkward since you're jumping across strings with the pinky. Yuk. You will need to use the Finger Rolling technique to get through it.

When faced with an obstacle, you have three options - go around it, over it or turn and go back!

In this case, you can:

Practice it until you get used to jumping with the pinky.

Find an alternative fingering.

Not do that interval in that pattern at all.

All three options are valid - what kind of approach do you prefer? I recommend at least having a go and see how it feels for you. I chose to practice it, but I find it rarely comes out when I’m improvising!

Pattern 2 of the Major Scale poses many more challenges for playing in 3rds. You will need to be doing quite a lot of finger rolling and some position jumps too. It's not easy, but it's good for you. ;)

The Stats

When we explored Re-Active Listening I took you through the stats of using your ears to help guide you to good notes.

Being that chords tones are built in 3rds, if you are on a chord tone and move up or down in a 3rd, you are likely to land on another good note :) maybe not a chord tone, but if you start on a chord tone then the melodic step will probably feel strong enough to make a ‘bad’ note sound good!

It’s dodgy math for sure - but starting on a chord tone and moving a 3rd usually feels like a strong meloid movement.

You Are What You Eat

Nobody wants to go and listen to scale players - they want to listen to music. So, a big part of your journey now is to make music with scales.

Once you've learned this scale pattern, stop practicing scale patterns straight up and down unless it's for technical development, picking speed, or hand synchronization. Work on using melodic sequences like this one in 3rds. There are many more to explore as we progress through the lessons!

Practicing scales in 3rds is a lot more musical than playing them up and down. And you are training both your muscle memory and ears to hear the interval of a 3rd! With practice, you're likely to find that it just comes out on its own.

lessons.title: Motif Development
lessons.summary: Here's how you make your guitar solos flow better.
lessons.text:
Wondering How To Make Your Guitar Solos Flow better?

Meet Motif Development, your new best friend!

I’ve mentioned a few times already that repetition is a great thing. Musically, it's a powerful tool to help your improvising make more sense to the listener. Exact repetition can be a lot more exciting than just playing the same thing over and over.

In a nutshell, the idea is to make a short statement and then explore it. You need to keep at least one element the same and explore things around it. There are loads of ways of doing this!

In this lesson, let's explore motif development and improve your guitar solo skills!

Repeat 3 Times - Then Go Crazy

Repeat the same element three times, and then go crazy! This trick is very well-used in most styles, super common in Blues. It's a fun way of developing a solo!

This method is awesome when improvising! The idea is to repeat a motif three times using any of the options shown below. Then, play something completely different.

The repetition makes the listener get in tune with what you're saying. Then, the contrast of something different makes it sounds even cooler than it might have on its own.

Straight Repetition
